title: ssh-manager: listRemoteServers inlines the port-range check instead of using validPort
body:
# ssh-manager: listRemoteServers inlines the port-range check instead of using validPort

## Evidence (verified on main 6f39d55ed, 2026-10-24)

`packages/electron/ssh-manager.mjs:467` defines the canonical helper, with a comment explaining why the range matters (a finite number alone lets 99999, -1 or 8080.9 through the sanitizers):

```js
const validPort = (value) => (Number.isInteger(value) && value >= 1 && value <= 65535 ? value : null);
```

The sanitizers use it (lines 885, 887, 930, 939), but `listRemoteServers` re-implements the identical predicate inline at line 1380:

```js
.filter((entry) => entry.runtime === 'cli' && Number.isInteger(entry.port) && entry.port >= 1 && entry.port <= 65535)
```

`parseServedPortLine` at line 437 also repeats the range half (`value >= 1 && value <= 65535`) after `parseInt` — there the integer half is guaranteed by construction, so that one is defensible, but it should be a deliberate choice, not drift.

## Why it matters

The comment on `validPort` says "The same range check guards discovered servers in listRemoteServers" — the intent is one shared check. With the predicate copied inline, a future change to the valid-port rule (or a typo in one copy) silently diverges between stored-port sanitizing and discovered-server filtering: the exact class of inconsistency the #313/#316 fixes (closed) were filed for. Origin: pr-diff-review REVIEW-FINDING carried in the openchamber backlog, re-verified on current main this run (an earlier grep scoped to `packages/web/server/` wrongly reported it stale; the code is in `packages/electron/`).

## Acceptance criteria

- `listRemoteServers`' filter uses `validPort(entry.port) !== null` (keeping the `entry.runtime === 'cli'` condition).
- The inline range check in `parseServedPortLine` is either routed through `validPort` or left with a one-line comment saying why it stays inline.
- Existing `packages/electron/ssh-manager.test.mjs` tests pass, including the `listRemoteServers` cases (out-of-range ports 0 / -1 / 99999 are filtered out).
- No behaviour change: same servers returned for the same registry payloads.

title: Local model download streams unbounded: oversize body is fully written to disk before the size check runs
body:
## Problem

`downloadModel` in `packages/web/server/lib/routing/route-local-model.js` streams the whole response body to the `.part` file before it ever checks the size. The pinned model is 1,117,320,736 bytes (`LOCAL_MODEL.bytes`, route-local-model.js:22) with a pinned SHA-256, so the correct size is known before the fetch starts — but the loop (route-local-model.js:83-89) writes every chunk unconditionally, and the `received !== model.bytes` check only runs after the stream ends (lines 97-100).

A broken, redirected, or hostile endpoint can therefore write arbitrarily many bytes into the user's cache directory (`~/.cache/openchamber/models/`) before the download is discarded — a slow disk-fill with no bound but the disk itself. The over-long case is also misreported: it throws "The model download was incomplete; try again", the opposite of what happened.

## Evidence (verified 2026-10-24 on main ef743458e)

Driving the real `downloadModel` with a stub model (pinned `bytes: 100`, digest of 100 bytes) and a `fetchImpl` whose body yields 50 chunks of 100 bytes:

```
threw: The model download was incomplete; try again
bytes pulled from body: 5000 (pinned bytes: 100)
```

All 5,000 bytes were pulled and written to the `.part` file before the post-stream check discarded it. The digest check has the same shape (necessarily — a digest can only be judged whole), but the size is known up front, so the size guard does not need to wait.

## Suggested fix

In the streaming loop, stop as soon as `received > model.bytes`: abort/destroy the stream, remove the partial file (the existing catch path already does this), and throw a distinct error that says the download was larger than the pinned size. Add a regression test beside the existing `downloadModel` tests in `route-local-model.test.js` whose body yields more than the pinned size and asserts the download aborts early (the body is not consumed to the end), no model or partial file remains, and the error names the real cause.

## Acceptance criteria

- A response body longer than `model.bytes` is aborted promptly — the downloader does not consume or write the whole body.
- The error for the over-long case says the download exceeded the expected size (not "incomplete").
- No `.part` or model file is left behind, matching the existing digest-mismatch cleanup.
- Existing behaviour is unchanged for exact-size, short, and digest-mismatching downloads; the `route-local-model` suite passes.

title: Model pool validator accepts a pattern target fully shadowed by an earlier pattern target — the entry never applies (pattern-vs-pattern case deferred by PR #398)
body:
## Finding (from PR diff review)

Merged PR #398 (fixes #383) made the model pool validator refuse a **concrete** target fully shadowed by an earlier pattern target, and explicitly left the pattern-vs-pattern case out: "Pattern-vs-pattern full coverage is not folded in; this change judges only the concrete case the issue specifies precisely." That deferred case is still a live silent-no-op on current main.

## Evidence

Verified on current main (`a887e1a7d`) by importing `validateModelRoute` from `packages/web/server/lib/routing/model-routes.js` directly (express import stubbed for the probe):

```js
validateModelRoute('r1', { targets: ['openai/*', 'openai/gpt-*'] })                 // -> null (accepted)
validateModelRoute('r1', { targets: ['openai/*#high', 'openai/gpt-*#high'] })       // -> null (accepted)
validateModelRoute('r1', { targets: ['openai/gpt-*', 'openai/gpt-5*'] })            // -> null (accepted)
```

In each case the later pattern's model set is a strict subset of the earlier pattern's, with the same `#variant`. OpenCode's expansion (`developing-today/opencode`, `packages/core/src/config/plugin/model-routes.ts:266-273`) iterates each pattern's `matchingModels(...)` and skips any model whose `provider/id#variant` key is already in `seen` — so every model the later pattern would attach is already attached by the earlier one, under the earlier target's settings. The later entry, including any `defaultVariant` / `variants` / `until` it carries, contributes zero leaves and never applies — the same dead-entry shape #383/#398 refuse for a concrete target.

Controls that must stay accepted (also probed / reasoned from the same semantics):

- Partial overlap is live: `['openai/gpt-*', 'openai/*']` — the later pattern covers models the earlier does not.
- A different `#variant` is a distinct attach key: `['openai/*', 'openai/gpt-*#high']`.
- An earlier pattern carrying a future `until` shadows only until it expires (the carve-out PR #398 already applies to the concrete case).

The current check in `model-routes.js` (the `earlierTargets` loop added by #398) only fires when the later target's reference contains no `*`, so pattern targets are never judged against earlier patterns.

## Why it matters

A user who narrows a pool — e.g. adds `openai/gpt-*` with a variant remap below an existing `openai/*` — gets no error and no effect: the entry saves, looks meaningful in the editor, and silently does nothing. That is exactly the failure class this validator exists to name, and PR #398's body records the pattern case as deliberately deferred rather than decided against.

## Acceptance criteria

- `validateModelRoute` refuses a later pattern target whose model set is fully covered by an earlier pattern target in the same route with the same `#variant` suffix, with a message in the style of the #398 refusal naming both targets.
- The judgement is a real pattern-subset judgement (provider equal, later pattern's matches all matched by the earlier pattern), not string equality — identical duplicate patterns are already refused by the duplicate-target check.
- Stays accepted: partial overlaps in either order, a different `#variant`, an earlier pattern with a future `until`, disjoint providers, and pattern-after-concrete orderings.
- Regression tests in `packages/web/server/lib/routing/model-routes.test.js` cover the refused shapes and the accepted controls above.
- `packages/web/server/lib/routing/DOCUMENTATION.md` refused-shapes list gains the new shape.

title: Model pool validator accepts defaultVariant/variants on a route-reference target — saved but never read by OpenCode
body:
## Problem

The model pool validator refuses an `until` on a route-reference target because OpenCode never reads it there, but it accepts `defaultVariant` and `variants` on a route-reference target — and OpenCode never reads those there either. The pool saves cleanly, and the variant settings silently do nothing: every model the referenced route expands to runs at its own default / its own route's remaps, not the ones the referencing target declares.

## Evidence

OpenChamber validator (`packages/web/server/lib/routing/model-routes.js`):

- Line 297-298: `until` on a route reference is refused — "OpenCode includes the referenced route unconditionally and never reads until on a reference, so the until would never apply".
- Lines 301-309: `defaultVariant` and `variants` are validated only for shape (non-empty string / string map). There is no route-reference check, so both are accepted on a reference target.

Reproduced this run against current main (`9c3ff7c18`) by importing the validator directly:

```js
validateModelRoutes({
  main:  { targets: [{ model: 'opencode-route/other', defaultVariant: 'high', variants: { low: 'high' } }] },
  other: { targets: ['openai/gpt-6-luna'] },
})
// -> null (accepted)

validateModelRoutes({
  main:  { targets: [{ model: 'opencode-route/other', until: 1893575040000 }] },
  other: { targets: ['openai/gpt-6-luna'] },
})
// -> 'route "main" has a bad target: its until is on a route reference: ...'
```

OpenCode expansion (`developing-today/opencode`, `packages/core/src/config/plugin/model-routes.ts`):

- Lines 256-259: for a route-reference target, expansion only forwards `ref.variant ?? inheritedVariant` into `visit(...)` and then `continue`s. The referencing target's `defaultVariant` and `variants` are never consulted on this path.
- Lines 274-285: `defaultVariant` and the variant remap map are computed only for concrete leaf targets, from that leaf target's own spec inside its own route.

So a saved pool can carry `defaultVariant`/`variants` on a reference that no code path ever reads — the exact silent-no-op shape the `until` check (and the duplicate/shadowed-target checks) exist to prevent.

## Why it matters

A user who nests one pool inside another and sets a default variant or a variant remap on the nested reference gets no error and no effect: sessions run at the wrong variant with no signal anywhere. The validator is the only place this can be named, because OpenCode drops the fields silently during expansion.

## Acceptance criteria

- `validateTarget` (or the set-level validation) refuses an object target whose `model` is an `opencode-route/<id>` reference when it carries `defaultVariant` or `variants`, with a message in the existing style explaining that OpenCode expands the referenced route from its own targets and never reads variant settings on the reference — mirroring the existing `until`-on-a-reference refusal.
- A `#variant` suffix on the reference itself (`opencode-route/other#high`, string or object form) stays accepted: that variant IS read (it becomes the inherited variant during expansion).
- Regression tests in `packages/web/server/lib/routing/model-routes.test.js` cover: `defaultVariant` on a reference refused, `variants` on a reference refused, and a reference with a `#variant` suffix (and a plain reference) still accepted.
- `DOCUMENTATION.md` for the routing module updated if it enumerates the validator's refusals (the `until` refusal is documented there).

title: Model pool validator accepts a concrete target fully shadowed by an earlier pattern target — the entry and its variant settings never apply
body:
## Problem

The model pool validator accepts a route where a concrete target is fully shadowed by an earlier `*` pattern target in the same `targets` list. OpenCode's route expansion attaches each concrete model once, keyed by model plus `#variant`, and silently skips any later entry whose key is already seen — so the shadowed entry is saved, looks meaningful in the editor, and never applies, including any `defaultVariant`, `variants` remap or `until` it carries.

This is the pattern-overlap question #377 explicitly left open ("a pattern (`openai/*`) plus a concrete model it covers is order-dependent in the same expansion, but that overlap is a separate question"). It can now be judged precisely for the fully-shadowed case:

- Validator on current main (`039bb005f`), direct probe — all return `null` (accepted):
  - `{targets: ["openai/*", {model: "openai/gpt-5", defaultVariant: "high"}]}` → the object entry never attaches; its `defaultVariant` is never read.
  - `{targets: ["openai/gpt-*", {model: "openai/gpt-5", until: 1999999999999}]}` → the `until` entry never attaches.
  - `{targets: ["openai/*#high", {model: "openai/gpt-5#high", defaultVariant: "low"}]}` → same-variant shadowing, also accepted.

- Controls that are correctly accepted and must stay accepted (distinct attach keys or real coverage):
  - `["openai/*#high", "openai/gpt-5"]` and `["openai/*", "openai/gpt-5#high"]` — the `#variant` is part of the attach key, so these are two distinct leaves.
  - `["openai/gpt-*", "anthropic/claude-1"]` — disjoint.
  - `["openai/gpt-5", "openai/*"]` — concrete first: it attaches, and the pattern still serves its other models (the pattern's own per-target settings not applying to the already-seen model is a subtler partial shadow; see below).

## Evidence

Validator, `packages/web/server/lib/routing/model-routes.js` on main `039bb005f`:

- `validateModelRoute`'s target loop (lines 375–386) tracks only exact attach keys in `seenTargets` (the #377 fix): a pattern and a different concrete string are different keys, so the shadow is never named. The module already has the precise matcher for this judgment: `keyNamesTarget(concreteReference, patternTarget)` (line 325) returns true exactly when the pattern covers the concrete reference.

OpenCode expansion, `packages/core/src/config/plugin/model-routes.ts` (developing-today/opencode):

- Line 221: one `seen` set for the whole expansion.
- Lines 260–272: targets are visited in list order; a pattern target expands via `matchingModels` to every model of the provider it matches, and each leaf's attach key is `` `${providerID}/${id}${variant ? `#${variant}` : ""}` `` with `if (seen.has(key)) continue` dropping any later entry with the same key — before that entry's `defaultVariant`/`variants` are ever read (lines 275–283 run only for attached leaves).
- A concrete model id is covered by a pattern exactly when the pattern's glob matches the id, which is what `keyNamesTarget` already encodes — so whenever the later concrete target would attach anything at all, the earlier pattern has already attached it under the pattern's own settings.

## Fix direction

In `validateModelRoute`'s target loop, when a later target's reference carries no `*`, refuse it if an earlier target in the same route is a pattern that covers it (`keyNamesTarget` on the variant-stripped references) **and** the two carry the same `#variant` suffix (both absent, or equal) — naming the shadowed target, the pattern, and the route, in the validator's existing voice, e.g. `route "r1" target "openai/gpt-5" is already covered by the earlier pattern target "openai/*": OpenCode attaches each model once, so this entry and its variant settings would never apply`.

Judgment calls to settle in the fix, not silently:

- An earlier pattern carrying a future `until` shadows only until it expires (the expansion is rebuilt on reload); refusing the pair would also block that staging shape. Either carve it out or refuse with a message that names the trade-off.
- The reverse order (concrete first, pattern later) leaves the pattern serving its other models, so it is not a dead entry — do not refuse it under this issue; the pattern's settings not applying to the one already-seen model can be noted as a follow-on if it matters.
- Pattern-vs-pattern partial overlap is the schedules question already handled by `patternsOverlap` reasoning (#353/#364); a later pattern *fully* covered by an earlier one is the same dead-entry shape and may be folded in only if it can be judged as precisely (subset, not mere overlap).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `validateModelRoutes` refuses `["openai/*", {model: "openai/gpt-5", defaultVariant: "high"}]`, `["openai/gpt-*", {model: "openai/gpt-5", until: <future>}]`, and `["openai/*#high", {model: "openai/gpt-5#high", ...}]`, naming the shadowed target and the covering pattern.
- [ ] Controls stay accepted: different-`#variant` pairs, disjoint concrete targets, concrete-before-pattern, and a pattern whose only covered concrete target is itself the route's sole other entry in either order where the later entry still attaches something.
- [ ] Regression tests in `model-routes.test.js` cover the refused shapes and the controls; ablation: the new tests fail with only the new check removed.
- [ ] The `until`-bearing earlier pattern is either carved out with a test, or refused with the trade-off stated in the error message and in this issue.

title: Model pool validator accepts a route-reference target that is trail-dead — referenced route reaches models only back through the referencing route
body:
## Finding

The model pool validator accepts a route-reference target that can never contribute a model to the referencing route's pool: the referenced route's only path to a concrete target runs back through the referencing route itself, which is already on OpenCode's expansion trail, so the reference is silently dropped for that route. Every route in the set still "expands" by the validator's global check, the referenced route exists, and it is not a self-reference — so none of the existing guards (#356, #379) catch it.

## Evidence

Verified on current openchamber main `039bb005f` by driving the real `validateModelRoutes` (`packages/web/server/lib/routing/model-routes.js`), both returning `null` (accepted):

- `{ a: { targets: ['openai/gpt-x', 'opencode-route/b'] }, b: { targets: ['opencode-route/a'] } }` — in route `a`'s pool, `opencode-route/b` contributes nothing: expanding `b` from `a` reaches only `opencode-route/a`, which is on the trail.
- `{ a: { targets: ['opencode-route/b'] }, b: { targets: ['opencode-route/a', 'openai/gpt-y'] } }` — route `b`'s `opencode-route/a` entry is dead from every entry point: `a` is only reachable through `b`, and whenever `a` is visited, its only target (`b`) is already on the trail, so the group is always empty.

Why the current guards miss it (`model-routes.js`):

- The reference loop (lines ~449–460) refuses only a direct self-reference (`referenced === id`, #379) and references to routes not in the set (#356).
- The expansion check (lines ~466–484) is a global fixpoint: a route counts as "expanding" if any reference chain reaches a concrete target, ignoring the trail. In both probes every route is marked expanding, even though the specific reference entry is dead in the referencing route.
- The trail-aware helper already in the file, `expandedTargetsOf` (line 348), walks with a visited set seeded at the route itself — expanding `a` in probe 1 yields only `openai/gpt-x` (the `b` reference contributes zero leaves) — but nothing checks that each reference target contributes at least one leaf.

OpenCode side (developing-today/opencode, `packages/core/src/config/plugin/model-routes.ts`, `expand`/`visit`, line 230): `if (trail.has(routeID)) return` — a route already on the trail is not attached, and a referenced group whose expansion comes back empty is never attached to the parent node (`child !== undefined` check), with no warning. The dead target sits in the saved config and in route `a`'s target list, looking like a live fallback that never serves.

## Why it matters

Same silent-dead-config class as #347/#349/#356/#379: the user configures a fallback/group target that can never serve a model in that route, and nothing tells them. Failover they believe exists does not.

## Acceptance criteria

- `validateModelRoutes` refuses a reference target when expanding the referenced route with the referencing route already on the trail reaches no concrete model target, with a message naming the route, the target, and why (e.g. `route "a" target "opencode-route/b" can never serve a model in this route: route "b" reaches models only through route "a" itself, which OpenCode will not revisit during expansion`).
- Both probe shapes above are refused; legitimate indirect references still pass (e.g. `a → b`, `b → [a-ref is dead but b also has concrete]` only refuses the dead entry in `b`; a diamond `a → b, a → c, b → d, c → d` with `d` concrete is accepted; a longer cycle `a → b → c → a` where `c` also has a concrete target is judged per entry: `a`'s reference to `b` is live, `c`'s reference to `a` is dead only if it reaches nothing without revisiting).
- New tests in `packages/web/server/lib/routing/model-routes.test.js` cover the refused shapes and the accepted controls; the refused-shapes enumeration in `packages/web/server/lib/routing/DOCUMENTATION.md` gains the new shape.
- Single-repo: the validator lives only in openchamber; no mirror copy exists in code/opencode/nix (the OpenCode `expand` cited is the behavior being judged, not code to change).

title: Model pool validator accepts a target that references its own route — saved but always dropped by OpenCode
body:
## Finding

The model pool validator accepts a target that references its own route (`opencode-route/<its own id>`) when the route also has a real target. That entry can never apply: OpenCode's expansion always drops it, silently, so the pool saves a failover/nesting entry that does nothing.

This is the residual shape of #356. That issue's fix refuses a reference cycle that leaves a route expanding to no models (a self-reference as the *only* target, or a mutual cycle with no concrete target anywhere). A self-reference *beside* a concrete target passes that check because the route still expands — but the self-reference entry itself is dead in every expansion.

## Evidence

- OpenChamber validator, `packages/web/server/lib/routing/model-routes.js` (current main `1b8da0843`): the dead-reference check in `validateModelRoutes` (~line 425) refuses only references to routes not in the set, and the expanding-set check (~lines 435–456) refuses only routes that reach no concrete target. Nothing refuses a target whose `routeReferenceOf(target)` equals the id of the route that contains it.
- Verified by driving the real `validateModelRoutes` on current main (probe removed after the run):
  - `{ a: { targets: ['openai/gpt-x', 'opencode-route/a'] } }` → `null` (accepted)
  - `{ a: { targets: ['openai/gpt-x', { model: 'opencode-route/a' }] } }` → `null` (accepted, object form)
  - Controls behave correctly: `{ a: { targets: ['opencode-route/a'] } }` (self-reference only) → refused ("would expand to no models"); a mutual cycle with no concrete target → refused; valid nesting (`b` referencing `a`, both with concrete targets) → accepted.
- OpenCode side (developing-today/opencode, `packages/core/src/config/plugin/model-routes.ts`, `expand()`): `visit(routeID, …, trail)` returns `undefined` when `trail.has(routeID)`. A route is always in its own trail when its targets are visited, so a target referencing the route itself always resolves to `visit(own id)` with the id already on the trail — the child is never attached, with no error or warning. Unlike a mutual reference (live when expansion enters from the other route), a self-reference is dead from every entry point.

## Why it matters

The user believes the pool contains an extra layer — typically a mistaken paste or an imported/hand-written config — and the pool behaves as if it were not there. The validator exists to name exactly this class of saved-but-dead configuration at save time (#347, #349, #354, #356, …); this entry shape is the one reference case it still lets through.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Saving a route set where a target references its own route id (`opencode-route/<same id>`, string or `{ model }` form) is refused, with a message naming the route and the target and saying a route cannot reference itself.
- [ ] Valid nesting keeps validating exactly as today: references to other routes, including cycle members that reach concrete targets (the #356 acceptance cases), and the existing `model-routes.test.js` cases.
- [ ] New cases are pinned in `packages/web/server/lib/routing/model-routes.test.js` (self-reference beside a concrete target refused in both forms; cross-route reference still accepted), and the existing model-routes tests still pass.

title: Model pool validator accepts duplicate targets in one route — OpenCode attaches each model once and silently drops the later entry
body:
## Problem

The model pool validator accepts a route whose `targets` list names the same target twice. OpenCode's route expansion attaches each concrete model only once — a second entry with the same attach key is silently skipped — so the duplicate is saved, looks meaningful in the editor, and does nothing. This is the same saved-but-silently-ignored class the validator already refuses elsewhere (pattern weights keys, budgets on fixed routes, empty variant settings).

Three shapes, all verified accepted by the real validator on current main (`1b8da0843`):

1. **Exact duplicate strings:** `targets: ["openai/gpt-x", "openai/gpt-x"]` → `validateModelRoutes` returns `null`.
2. **Object duplicates with different settings:** `targets: [{model: "openai/gpt-x", defaultVariant: "low"}, {model: "openai/gpt-x", defaultVariant: "high"}]` → `null`. The second entry's `defaultVariant`/`variants`/`until` are the ones that get dropped, so the editor shows a per-target setting OpenCode never reads.
3. **Duplicate route references:** route `a` with `targets: ["opencode-route/b", "opencode-route/b"]` → `null`. The reference branch has no dedupe guard; the second visit's leaves all hit the expansion's seen set, so the duplicate group attaches with no models of its own.

Controls that must stay accepted (also probed, all `null` today and correct): `["openai/gpt-x#low", "openai/gpt-x#high"]` (the `#variant` is part of the attach key, so these are two distinct leaves) and `["openai/gpt-x", "openai/gpt-y"]`.

## Evidence

Validator, `packages/web/server/lib/routing/model-routes.js` on main `1b8da0843`:

- `validateModelRoute` (line 362) loops `route.targets` and runs `validateTarget` on each entry in isolation; nothing tracks which attach keys have already been seen, so a repeat is never named.

OpenCode expansion, `packages/core/src/config/plugin/model-routes.ts` (developing-today/opencode):

- Line 221: one `seen` set for the whole expansion.
- Lines 271–273: the attach key is `` `${providerID}/${id}${variant ? `#${variant}` : ""}` `` — model plus `#variant`, with `defaultVariant` not part of the key — and `if (seen.has(key)) continue` drops any later entry with the same key before it can attach (line 284).
- Lines 256–258: the route-reference branch attaches without consulting `seen`; a repeated reference re-visits the route, whose leaves are then all dropped by the same guard.

Direct probe against the real validator on current main:

```js
validateModelRoutes({ a: { targets: ["openai/gpt-x", "openai/gpt-x"] } }); // → null
validateModelRoutes({ a: { targets: [{ model: "openai/gpt-x", defaultVariant: "low" }, { model: "openai/gpt-x", defaultVariant: "high" }] } }); // → null
validateModelRoutes({ a: { targets: ["opencode-route/b", "opencode-route/b"] }, b: { targets: ["openai/gpt-x"] } }); // → null
validateModelRoutes({ a: { targets: ["openai/gpt-x#low", "openai/gpt-x#high"] } }); // → null (correct: distinct leaves)
```

## Fix direction

In `validateModelRoute`'s target loop, track the attach key of each entry — the full model reference (`target.model ?? target`, including any `#variant` suffix, regardless of string or object form) — and refuse a repeat, naming the duplicated target and the route, in the validator's existing voice (e.g. `route "a" lists target "openai/gpt-x" twice: OpenCode attaches each model once and silently drops the later entry, including its variant settings`).

Keep accepting distinct `#variant` spellings of one model and pattern targets: a pattern (`openai/*`) plus a concrete model it covers is order-dependent in the same expansion, but that overlap is a separate question — note it, do not fold it into this refusal unless it can be judged as precisely.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A route listing the same full target reference twice (string form, object form, or mixed) is refused with a message naming the route and the duplicated target.
- [ ] A route listing the same `opencode-route/<id>` reference twice is refused the same way.
- [ ] `["openai/gpt-x#low", "openai/gpt-x#high"]` and distinct-model lists still validate.
- [ ] Regression tests in `model-routes.test.js` cover the three refused shapes and the two controls.

title: Model pool validator misjudges schedule targets through route references — concrete leaf entry refused but would apply, route-reference entry saved but never matches

Model pool validator accepts weights and budgets on a fixed route — OpenCode silently ignores both below the rules autonomy level
body:
## Problem

The model pool validator (`packages/web/server/lib/routing/model-routes.js`) refuses a non-`ordered` `selection` on a route with `autonomy: "fixed"`, because OpenCode ignores selection modes below the `rules` autonomy level. But it accepts `weights` and `budgets` on a `fixed` route — and OpenCode silently ignores both there too, so the pool saves cleanly and the user's weights/budgets never apply.

## Evidence

Validator probe on current main (`fc7acbbb4`), driving `validateModelRoute` directly:

- `validateModelRoute("r", { targets: [...], autonomy: "fixed", weights: { "openai/gpt-6-luna": 3 } })` → `null` (accepted)
- `validateModelRoute("r", { targets: [...], autonomy: "fixed", budgets: { "openai/gpt-6-luna": { requestsPerDay: 10 } } })` → `null` (accepted)
- Same route with `selection: "weighted"` → refused: `route "r" is fixed, so it keeps its configured order; selection "weighted" needs autonomy rules or higher` (the existing check this issue extends)

OpenCode side (developing-today/opencode, `packages/core/src/config/plugin/model-routes.ts`):

- Weights: line 251 — `node.weights.push(ModelRouteAutonomy.usesRules(current.autonomy) ? (current.weights?.[key] ?? 1) : 1)` — on a `fixed` route every configured weight is replaced by 1.
- Budgets: lines 289–290 — budgets are only collected from routes where `ModelRouteAutonomy.usesRules(routes.get(id)?.autonomy)` holds, so a `fixed` route's budgets are dropped entirely.
- `usesRules` is `reaches(level, "rules")`, and `reaches` treats an **unset** autonomy as reaching every level — so only an explicit `autonomy: "fixed"` is affected. Routes with no `autonomy` key, or `rules` and above, must stay accepted (verified: unset + weights and `rules` + weights both validate today and do apply in OpenCode).

The schema description agrees (`packages/schema/src/config/model-routes.ts:204`): "rules: adds selection modes, weights, budgets and provider rate-limit holds."

## Why it matters

This is the exact failure shape this validator exists to prevent (see its comments: keys OpenCode does not read "would be saved and silently ignored"). A user who sets a pool to `fixed` for predictable failover order, while keeping weights or budgets from an earlier configuration, gets a successful save and silently loses the budget caps — the one of the two with a cost/quota consequence.

## Acceptance criteria

- `validateModelRoute` refuses a route with `autonomy: "fixed"` that carries `weights`, with a message naming the problem the way the existing selection message does (fixed keeps its configured order / needs autonomy rules or higher).
- Same refusal for `budgets` on a `fixed` route.
- Routes with unset autonomy, or `rules`/`adaptive`/`predictive`/`agent`, carrying weights or budgets still validate.
- Regression tests beside the existing fixed/selection test in `packages/web/server/lib/routing/model-routes.test.js` (around line 482).
- Out of scope: `schedules` (OpenCode's `routeWeightRules` is not autonomy-gated in `expand()`) and `health` (cooldowns apply on fixed routes).

Found by the new-issue-creator sweep, 2026-10-23.

title: Model pool validator misjudges schedule targets with a #variant or different case — variant entries saved but never apply, case-differing entries refused but would apply
body:
## Finding

The model pool validator judges schedule `targets` entries differently from the way OpenCode applies them, in both directions:

1. **Accepted but dead:** a schedule entry carrying a `#variant` suffix (`openai/gpt-6-luna#high`, `openai/*#high`) is accepted and saved, but OpenCode never matches it — its scheduled weight change silently never applies.
2. **Refused but live:** a schedule entry that differs from a route target only by letter case (`OpenAI/gpt-6-luna`, `OPENAI/*`) is refused as "matches no target in the route", but OpenCode's schedule matcher is case-insensitive, so the entry would have applied.

This is the same judge-it-the-way-OpenCode-judges-it class as #347/#349/#353/#354, applied to the schedule-target matcher itself.

## Evidence

- OpenChamber validator, `packages/web/server/lib/routing/model-routes.js` (current main `fc7acbbb4`): in `validateSchedules` (lines 234–242) an entry is matched via `keyNamesTarget(entry, target) || keyNamesTarget(targetReference, entry)`, and `referenceOf` (line 284) strips everything from `#` on. The reverse call therefore compares the target's variant-less reference against the entry *as a target*, whose own variant is stripped before comparison — so `openai/gpt-6-luna#high` "matches" target `openai/gpt-6-luna` even though the saved entry keeps its `#high`. All comparisons are case-sensitive.
- Verified by driving the real `validateModelRoute` on current main (probe removed after the run), route `{ targets: ["openai/gpt-6-luna", "anthropic/claude-1"] }`, schedule `when: { start: "09:00", end: "17:00" }, factor: 0.5`:
  - entry `openai/gpt-6-luna#high` → `null` (accepted)
  - entry `openai/*#high` → `null` (accepted)
  - entry `anthropic/claude-1#x` → `null` (accepted)
  - entry `OpenAI/gpt-6-luna` → refused: `schedule 1 target "OpenAI/gpt-6-luna" matches no target in the route`
  - entry `OPENAI/*` → refused, same message
- OpenCode side (developing-today/opencode, current main): `routeWeightRules` in `packages/core/src/config/plugin/model-routes.ts` copies `schedule.targets` verbatim (trim only) into the rule's `match.targets`. At apply time `ruleMatches` in `packages/core/src/model-route.ts` builds the reference as `` `${target.providerID}/${target.id}` `` — **no variant** — and tests each entry with `ModelRouteOverrides.matchesPattern(pattern, ref)`, whose glob is built with the `i` flag (`packages/core/src/model-route-overrides.ts`: `` new RegExp(`^...$`, "i") ``) — **case-insensitive**. A pattern containing `#` can never match a reference that contains no `#`, and a differently-cased pattern matches fine.

## Why it matters

The validator is the only backstop for hand-written or imported pool config. A variant-suffixed schedule entry is exactly the spelling a user copies from a target (`provider/model#variant` is the target spelling everywhere else in this config), so this is a likely typo class: the pool saves, the schedule shows in the editor, and the peak-hours weight change simply never happens. The case direction is the mirror harm of #353: a working schedule cannot be saved at all.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Saving a schedule whose `targets` entry carries a `#variant` suffix is refused, with a message naming the route, the schedule, and the entry, and saying OpenCode matches schedule targets without a variant (or the entry is otherwise judged exactly as OpenCode judges it — state the choice in the PR).
- [ ] A schedule entry that differs from a route target (or from a model a pattern target covers) only by letter case validates the same way OpenCode would apply it — accepted — or the refusal message states the case rule explicitly; either way the behaviour is pinned by a test.
- [ ] New cases are pinned in `packages/web/server/lib/routing/model-routes.test.js`: variant-suffixed concrete entry refused, variant-suffixed pattern entry refused, case-differing entry judged per the chosen rule, and the existing exact/pattern/overlap cases from #349/#353 still pass.
- [ ] The existing model-routes tests still pass.

title: Model pool validator accepts targets referencing nonexistent or cyclic routes — saved and silently dropped by OpenCode, route can expand to zero models
body:
## Finding

The model pool validator never checks `opencode-route/<id>` targets. A target that references a route which does not exist in the saved set, the route itself, or a cycle of routes is accepted and saved — and OpenCode silently drops it during expansion, so the target (or the whole route, when it is the only target) never serves any model.

This is the same silent-dead-config class as #347 (a budgets key naming no target) and #349 (schedule targets naming no route target), applied to route-reference targets, which the validator does not inspect at all.

## Evidence

- OpenChamber validator, `packages/web/server/lib/routing/model-routes.js` (current main `90cb8d8b5`): `validateTarget` (line 224) only tests the string against `TARGET_PATTERN` (`provider/model`), which `opencode-route/<anything>` passes. Nothing in the file resolves the reference — `grep "opencode-route"` in the validator finds only the header comment. `validateModelRoutes` (line 307) validates each route in isolation and never cross-checks references against the set being saved, even though the PUT handler (line 368) replaces `experimental.model_routes` with exactly that set.
- Verified by driving the real `validateModelRoute` / `validateModelRoutes` on current main (probe removed after the run), all returning `null` (accepted):
  - `{ targets: ['opencode-route/mine'] }` for route `mine` (self-reference, its only target)
  - `{ targets: ['opencode-route/nope'] }` (nonexistent route, its only target)
  - `{ targets: ['openai/gpt-x', 'opencode-route/nope'] }` (nonexistent reference beside a real target)
  - The set `{ a: { targets: ['opencode-route/b'] }, b: { targets: ['opencode-route/a'] } }` (a two-route cycle with no concrete target anywhere)
- OpenCode side (developing-today/opencode, `packages/core/src/config/plugin/model-routes.ts`, `expand()` lines 216–262): for a route-reference target it calls `visit(ref.id, …)`; `visit` returns `undefined` when the referenced route is not in the map (`if (!current) return`) and when the route is already in the trail (`if (trail.has(routeID)) return` — the cycle guard). An undefined child is simply not attached, with no error or warning. A route whose targets all resolve this way expands to a group node with zero leaves.
- The schema explicitly permits route references (`packages/schema/src/config/model-routes.ts`: "A route may reference another route"), and OpenChamber's own UI builds them from existing routes (`packages/ui/src/lib/routing/poolAdvanced.ts:79`, `routeReferenceID` / `routeReference`), so the editor path is safe — but a hand-written or imported config goes through the server validator as the only backstop, and it lets a dead reference through.

## Why it matters

A pool that expands to zero models fails only when a session tries to use it, and a dead reference beside real targets quietly removes the failover target the user thought they had. Both fail silently at save time, which is exactly what this validator exists to prevent for every other key/target class.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Saving a route set where a target references an `opencode-route/<id>` that is not a route in the set is refused, with a message naming the route, the target, and the missing reference.
- [ ] A reference cycle that leaves a route with no concrete model target reachable (self-reference as the only target; mutual references with no concrete target in the cycle) is refused, with a message that says the route would expand to no models.
- [ ] Valid nesting keeps validating exactly as today: a reference to an existing route, including a cycle member that also reaches concrete targets through another path (OpenCode's trail guard handles that case), and the existing `model-routes.test.js` cases.
- [ ] New cases are pinned in `packages/web/server/lib/routing/model-routes.test.js` (unknown reference refused, self-reference-only refused, mutual-cycle-with-no-concrete-target refused, known reference accepted), and the existing model-routes tests still pass.

title: Model pool validator accepts a pattern budgets key — saved and silently never applies, OpenCode reads budgets by concrete model
body:
## Finding

The model pool validator accepts a `budgets` key that contains a `*` pattern — either exactly the pattern target (`openai/*` for target `openai/*`) or a sub-pattern it covers (`openai/gpt-*` for target `openai/*`). The pool saves, but OpenCode never reads that budget: budgets are looked up by the concrete model each pattern expands to, so the allowance silently never applies.

This is the false-negative mirror of #347 (a budgets key that names no target), which added the `keyNamesTarget` match check in `validateBudgets`. That check judges a key by pattern coverage, but OpenCode's budget lookup is not pattern-based at all.

## Evidence

- OpenChamber validator, `packages/web/server/lib/routing/model-routes.js:96-99` (current main `90cb8d8b5`): `validateBudgets` accepts a key when `targets.some((candidate) => keyNamesTarget(target, candidate))`. `keyNamesTarget` (line 249) returns true when the key equals the target reference, and when the target reference is a `*` pattern whose matcher covers the key — so a pattern key passes in both cases above.
- Verified by driving the real `validateModelRoute` on current main (probe removed after the run):
  - `{ targets: ['openai/*'], budgets: { 'openai/*': { requestsPerDay: 100 } } }` → `null` (accepted)
  - `{ targets: ['openai/*'], budgets: { 'openai/gpt-*': { requestsPerDay: 100 } } }` → `null` (accepted)
  - Controls behave correctly: concrete key for a pattern target (`openai/gpt-x` for `openai/*`) accepted; pattern key for a concrete-only route (`openai/*` for `openai/gpt-x`) refused as "matches no target"; the #347 no-target key refused.
- OpenCode side (developing-today/opencode, `packages/core/src/config/plugin/model-routes.ts:283-290`): a pattern target is expanded to concrete leaves, `leafKey = ${providerID}/${id}` is the concrete model, and the budget is read as `routes.get(id)?.budgets?.[leafKey]` — an exact concrete-key lookup. A `budgets` entry keyed `openai/*` or `openai/gpt-*` matches no leaf, so every expanded model gets no budget.
- OpenChamber's own UI already encodes this rule: `packages/ui/src/lib/routing/poolAdvanced.ts:9` — "A pattern such as `openai/*` names several models, so it cannot carry its own budget or weight" — and the advanced fields only offer budget fields for concrete targets. A hand-written or imported config bypasses that UI restriction, and the server validator is the backstop that currently lets it through.
- The existing test suite pins the concrete-key-for-pattern-target case (`model-routes.test.js:442`: target `openai/gpt-*`, budget key `openai/gpt-6-luna` accepted) but has no case for a pattern budget key.

Scope note: pattern-keyed `weights` have the same OpenCode lookup shape, but that case is already tracked in #307 (its third acceptance criterion covers a pattern-keyed weight being flagged on save). This issue is budgets only, so the two do not duplicate.

## Why it matters

A budget is a cost/quota guardrail. A user who writes `budgets: { "openai/*": { tokensPerDay: … } }` — the natural way to cap a whole provider — gets a save that succeeds and a cap that never applies, for exactly the pattern targets that fan out to the most models. The failure is silent and only surfaces as an unexpected bill or quota exhaustion.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `validateModelRoute` refuses a `budgets` key containing `*`, with a message that says OpenCode reads budgets by concrete model reference, so a pattern key would never apply (e.g. `route "x" budget for "openai/*" …`).
- [ ] Concrete budget keys keep validating exactly as today, including a concrete key for a pattern target (the `model-routes.test.js:442` case) and a `#variant`-stripped key (line 441 case).
- [ ] New cases are pinned in `packages/web/server/lib/routing/model-routes.test.js` (exact pattern key and sub-pattern key refused), and the existing model-routes tests still pass.

title: Model pool validator refuses a schedule whose target pattern partially overlaps a route target pattern — the schedule can apply, but the pool cannot be saved
body:
## Finding

PR #350 (fix for #349) made the model-pool validator refuse a schedule `targets` entry that matches no route target. The check in `validateSchedules` (`packages/web/server/lib/routing/model-routes.js`, current main 90cb8d8b5875) accepts an entry only when one pattern covers the other:

```js
if (!targets.some((target) => keyNamesTarget(entry, target) || keyNamesTarget(referenceOf(target), entry)))
  return `route "${id}" ${label} target "${entry}" matches no target in the route`;
```

Two `*` patterns that *partially* overlap satisfy neither direction, so the schedule is refused even though concrete models exist that match both patterns — and OpenCode's match filter would apply the schedule to exactly those models.

## Evidence

Verified against current main by driving the real `validateModelRoute` (probe removed after the run):

- Route targets `['openai/*-luna']`, schedule `{ when: {}, factor: 2, targets: ['openai/gpt-*'] }` → refused: `schedule 1 target "openai/gpt-*" matches no target in the route`. But `openai/gpt-6-luna` matches both patterns, so the schedule can apply.
- Controls all behave correctly: exact entry accepted; pattern entry covering a concrete target (`deepseek/*` vs `deepseek/v4`) accepted; entry covered by a pattern route target (`openai/gpt-6-luna` vs `openai/gpt-*`) accepted; variant-suffixed entry (`a/b#high` vs target `a/b`) accepted; object-form targets accepted/refused correctly; the #349 typo entry and the empty `targets` list are still refused.

Cross-checked: the validator's own focused suite passes on main (51 pass), and PR #350's CI was green (build/lint/type-check/tests on head 9c0c67d11) — this is a logic gap in the new check, not a test failure.

## Why it matters

A pool that pairs a pattern route target with a pattern schedule target — a plausible hand-written config, e.g. boosting `openai/gpt-*` inside a broader `openai/*-luna` route — saved fine before #350 and applied as written. It now cannot be re-saved from Settings at all; the refusal message also misleads, saying the target "matches no target in the route" when the patterns do intersect. This is the false-positive mirror of #349's false negative.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A schedule entry whose `*` pattern has a non-empty intersection with a route target's `*` pattern validates (e.g. entry `openai/gpt-*` with route target `openai/*-luna`).
- [ ] Disjoint patterns are still refused (e.g. entry `openai/gpt-*` with route target `anthropic/*`), as are the #349 typo entry and the empty `targets` list.
- [ ] New cases are pinned in `packages/web/server/lib/routing/model-routes.test.js`, and the existing schedule/budget/weight tests still pass.

Found by the pr-diff-review sweep reviewing PR #350.

title: Model pool validator accepts schedule targets that name no route target — saved and silently never applies; an empty targets list applies to every target
body:
## Problem

`validateModelRoute` checks a schedule's `targets` list only for being a list of non-empty strings (`packages/web/server/lib/routing/model-routes.js`, `validateSchedules`). It never checks the entries against the route's own targets, and it accepts an empty list. Both spellings save cleanly and then do something other than what the author wrote:

1. **A target that names no target in the route is silently never applied.** OpenCode's config plugin turns `schedule.targets` into a `match.targets` filter (`packages/core/src/config/plugin/model-routes.ts`, `routeWeightRules`: the trimmed list becomes `match: { targets }`), and the runtime only applies the rule when some pattern matches the target being judged (`model-route.ts`, `ruleMatches`). A typo'd or renamed model therefore matches nothing, forever, with no error anywhere.
2. **An empty `targets` list widens to every target.** The same plugin code only sets `match.targets` when the list is non-empty (`...(targets.length > 0 ? { match: { targets } } : {})`), and a rule with no match applies to every target in reach. So `targets: []` — the natural spelling of "no targets" — means "all targets", the opposite of what was written.

The same validator already refuses both shapes elsewhere, which is the precedent this arm is missing:

- A `weights` key that matches no target is refused: `route "x" weight for "<key>" matches no target in the route` (via `keyNamesTarget`, which also covers `*` pattern targets). Budgets keys get the same check under #347.
- Empty `daysOfWeek` / `daysOfMonth` window lists are refused with an explanation of the surprising empty semantics, rather than saved.

## Evidence (verified on openchamber main `32658f266`, driving the real validator)

```js
import { validateModelRoute } from './packages/web/server/lib/routing/model-routes.js';
const base = { targets: ['deepseek/v4', 'openai/x'] };

validateModelRoute('x', { ...base, schedules: [{ when: {}, factor: 2, targets: ['anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6'] }] })
// => null  (accepted; the schedule can never match any target in the route)

validateModelRoute('x', { ...base, schedules: [{ when: {}, factor: 2, targets: [] }] })
// => null  (accepted; OpenCode applies a target-less rule to every target)

validateModelRoute('x', { ...base, schedules: [{ when: {}, factor: 2, targets: ['deepseek/v4'] }] })
// => null  (control: exact target, correctly accepted)
validateModelRoute('x', { ...base, schedules: [{ when: {}, factor: 2, targets: ['deepseek/*'] }] })
// => null  (control: pattern target, correctly accepted)

validateModelRoute('x', { ...base, weights: { 'anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6': 2 } })
// => 'route "x" weight for "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6" matches no target in the route'  (the weights arm refuses the same typo)
```

## Why it matters

Schedules are the pool mechanism for time-bound weight changes (peak-hour demotions and the like). A schedule that names a mistyped or since-renamed model fails completely silently: the pool keeps the un-scheduled weights at exactly the hours the operator meant to change them. An empty list is worse — it applies the factor/weight to targets the author never named. Both are saved through `PUT /api/model-routes` into the user's `opencode.json(c)`, so the bad definition persists across restarts.

## Acceptance criteria

- `validateModelRoute` refuses a schedule whose `targets` list is empty, with a message that says an empty list would apply to every target, so the key should be left out for that.
- `validateModelRoute` refuses a schedule target entry that matches no target in the route (exact reference or `*` pattern, judged the way OpenCode's `matchesPattern` / this file's `keyNamesTarget` judge a reference), naming the entry and the schedule.
- Exact and `*`-pattern entries that do match a route target stay accepted, including the existing full-schedule test fixture (`targets: ['deepseek/*']` beside `deepseek/v4`).
- A schedule with no `targets` key at all stays accepted (that is OpenCode's deliberate "everything in reach" spelling).
- New tests in `model-routes.test.js` cover the typo, the empty list, and both controls; the routing suite stays green.
- `DOCUMENTATION.md` for the routing module notes the new refusals, matching how the other validator refusals are documented there.

## Notes

- Single-repo: the validator exists only in OpenChamber (no `validateModelRoute` copy in developing-today/code, developing-today/opencode, or dezren39/nix).
- Sibling gap, same shape: budgets keys naming no target are tracked in #347; weights keys are already refused in the same function. This issue is the schedules arm only — `validateSchedules` currently receives no route targets at all, so the fix passes them in, like the budgets fix does.

title: Model pool validator accepts a budgets key that names no target — the budget is saved and silently never applies
body:
## Problem

The model-pool validator refuses a `weights` key that names no target in the route, but accepts a `budgets` key that names no target — so a budget keyed to a mistyped or renamed model is saved to `opencode.json` and silently never applies. OpenCode's `Budget` is "request and token allowances for one target" (`packages/schema/src/config/model-routes.ts` in developing-today/opencode), keyed by the same target reference as weights; a key that matches nothing is dead configuration, exactly the class of saved-and-silently-ignored value this validator exists to refuse (see the `ROUTE_KEYS` comment in the validator: "any other key would be saved and silently ignored").

The validator's own comment above `referenceOf` even says "A weight **or budget** key names a target by its reference" — but `validateBudgets` never uses `keyNamesTarget`; only the weights arm checks.

## Evidence (verified on openchamber main `32658f266`)

`packages/web/server/lib/routing/model-routes.js`:

- `validateBudgets(id, budgets)` (line ~104) validates each budget object but is never given the route's targets and never checks the key.
- The weights arm in `validateModelRoute` (lines ~272-281) does check: `if (!route.targets.some((target) => keyNamesTarget(key, target))) return ... weight for "<key>" matches no target in the route`.
- `validateModelRoute` calls `validateBudgets(id, route.budgets)` without targets.

Direct probe against the real validator:

```js
import { validateModelRoute } from './packages/web/server/lib/routing/model-routes.js';
validateModelRoute('pool1', {
  targets: ['anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5'],
  budgets: { 'anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6': { requestsPerDay: 100 } },
});
// → null (accepted — the budget names no target and can never apply)

validateModelRoute('pool1', {
  targets: ['anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5'],
  weights: { 'anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6': 2 },
});
// → 'route "pool1" weight for "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6" matches no target in the route'
```

## Why it matters

Budgets are the pool's spend guardrails (requests/tokens per minute/day plus `softLimit`). A typo'd or stale key leaves the operator believing a target is capped when nothing enforces it — a silent no-op on a safety control, and inconsistent with the weights arm one screen away in the same validator.

## Acceptance criteria

- `validateModelRoute` refuses a `budgets` key that names no target in the route, with a message mirroring the weights arm (e.g. `route "<id>" budget for "<key>" matches no target in the route`).
- Matching uses the existing `keyNamesTarget` semantics: exact reference (any `#variant` stripped) and `*` pattern targets cover the concrete models they match, same as weights.
- A budget keyed to a real target (including via a `*` pattern target) still validates.
- Tests in `packages/web/server/lib/routing/model-routes.test.js` cover: typo'd key refused, pattern-covered key accepted, exact key accepted; existing routing tests still pass.
- `DOCUMENTATION.md` for the routing lib updated if it describes the budgets validation contract.

Single-repo: the validator exists only in developing-today/openchamber (no copy in code/opencode/nix).

title: Model pool validator accepts Infinity for weights and minOutputTokensPerSecond — OpenCode requires finite, and saving writes null
body:
## Problem

The model pool validator (`validateModelRoute` in `packages/web/server/lib/routing/model-routes.js`) accepts `Infinity` for two numeric fields where OpenCode requires a **finite** positive number:

- route `weights` values — the check is `typeof weight !== "number" || !(weight > 0)`, and `Infinity > 0` is true;
- `health.minOutputTokensPerSecond` — the check is `typeof value === "number" && value > 0`, same gap.

OpenCode's schema requires finite on both: `weights` is `Schema.Finite.check(Schema.isGreaterThan(0))` and `Health.minOutputTokensPerSecond` is `PositiveFinite` (`packages/schema/src/config/model-routes.ts` in developing-today/opencode).

The same file already does this correctly elsewhere: `isPositiveNumber` (`Number.isFinite(value) && value > 0`) is used for schedule `factor`/`weight`, and a schedule factor of `Infinity` is refused with "must be a positive number". The two spots above just don't use it.

## Why it is reachable and why it matters

This is not a theoretical JS-only value. The save endpoint parses the request with `express.json`, and JSON numbers that overflow parse to `Infinity`:

```js
JSON.parse('1e999') === Infinity
```

So a `PUT /api/model-routes` body such as `{"routes":{"x":{"targets":["openai/gpt-5"],"weights":{"openai/gpt-5":1e999}}}}` passes validation today. What then gets saved to the user's `opencode.json` is worse than a rejected value: `JSON.stringify` turns `Infinity` into `null`, so the file ends up with `"weights": {"openai/gpt-5": null}` — a saved config OpenCode's schema cannot read as that pool's weight.

## Evidence (verified on main 74bc62741)

Direct probes of `validateModelRoute('x', …)` with base `{targets: ['openai/gpt-5']}`:

- `weights: {'openai/gpt-5': Infinity}` → `null` (accepted)
- `weights: {'openai/gpt-5': JSON.parse('1e999')}` → `null` (accepted)
- `health: {minOutputTokensPerSecond: Infinity}` → `null` (accepted)
- control — `schedules: [{when: {start: '09:00'}, factor: Infinity}]` → refused: `route "x" schedule 1 factor must be a positive number`
- control — `weights: {'openai/gpt-5': 2}` → `null` (accepted, correctly)
- `JSON.stringify({weights: {'openai/gpt-5': Infinity}})` → `{"weights":{"openai/gpt-5":null}}`

## Acceptance criteria

- `validateModelRoute` refuses a non-finite (`Infinity` / `-Infinity`) weight with the existing "must be a positive number" wording, and likewise for `health.minOutputTokensPerSecond`.
- Ordinary finite positive values still pass for both fields.
- Regression tests cover both fields (the `1e999`-style overflow spelling is the realistic input).
- `packages/web/server/lib/routing/DOCUMENTATION.md` notes the finite requirement if it documents these checks.

Suggested fix: use the file's existing `isPositiveNumber` helper in both spots.

title: Model pool validator accepts a schedule window with equal start and end, which OpenCode treats as an empty window that never applies
body:
## Finding

The model pool validator added in PR #340 accepts a schedule whose `when` window has the same `start` and `end` (for example `"09:00"` to `"09:00"`, or `"00:00"` to `"00:00"` written as an all-day window). OpenCode treats an equal start and end as an **empty window that is never active**, so the schedule saves successfully in Settings and then silently never applies — the exact class of silently-dead hand-written schedule this validator was built to refuse.

## Evidence

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/openchamber/pull/340 (commit `6d605ed79a6f4f87b38931788cf618588165304b`, merged as `02d5b94a433cdee68931df80043249222c40e450`, fixes #298).
- `packages/web/server/lib/routing/model-routes.js` on current main (`02d5b94a`): `validateScheduleWindow` (lines 158–160) checks `start` and `end` only individually through `isWindowTime` (lines 119–123); nothing compares them. The same function does refuse the analogous never-applies case at lines 166–167: `window.from must be before window.until: OpenCode drops a window that can never apply`.
- OpenCode's semantics, in developing-today/opencode: `packages/core/src/model-route-schedule.ts`, `minuteMatches` — `if (start === end) return false`; pinned by its own test `packages/core/test/model-route-schedule.test.ts:96`: "an equal start and end is an empty window, not a full day" (`parse({ start: "09:00", end: "09:00" })` is kept, and `active(...)` is false).
- Verified by running `validateModelRoute` from current main: `{ when: { start: "09:00", end: "09:00" }, factor: 0.5 }` returns `null` (accepted), `{ when: { start: "00:00", end: "00:00" }, weight: 2 }` returns `null`, while `{ when: { from: 2000, until: 1000 }, factor: 0.5 }` is refused. An overnight window (`22:00` → `06:00`) is accepted, correctly — OpenCode runs those past midnight.

## Why it matters

PR #340's stated policy is that values OpenCode would drop or silently ignore are refused at save time with the reason, so the user edits the entry instead of losing the schedule silently. An equal start/end is the one remaining window shape that can never apply yet passes: a user who writes `00:00`–`00:00` (or repeats a time by typo) gets a successful save and a peak/weight schedule that never fires, with no signal anywhere.

## Acceptance criteria

- `validateModelRoute` refuses a schedule whose window sets both `start` and `end` to the same time, with an error that names the problem (in the style of the existing `from`/`until` refusal).
- Windows with only `start`, only `end`, or `start` later than `end` (overnight) still validate as before.
- Regression tests in `packages/web/server/lib/routing/model-routes.test.js` cover the equal-times refusal (including `00:00`/`00:00`) and keep the overnight acceptance pinned.
- The `schedules` bullet in `packages/web/server/lib/routing/DOCUMENTATION.md` mentions the refusal alongside the other never-applies cases.

Cross-repo note: the validator exists only in this repo (no twin in developing-today/code, developing-today/opencode or dezren39/nix); OpenCode owns the window semantics referenced above.

title: test(settings): no test pins a refused closing send overlapping an in-flight send — delivered-on-success rule unpinned for the closing path
body:
## Summary

`createDeviceSettingsReporter` (`packages/ui/src/lib/settings/deviceSettingsReport.ts`) has two delivery rules that are each pinned by a test on their own, but their combination — the closing path — is not:

1. A report the server refused counts as not delivered, so the next flush sends it again (`sendLatest`, lines 106–117; the `delivered`/`deliveredRevision` record updates only inside the `await send(...) && sentFor === generation && sentRevision > deliveredRevision` branch at line 113).
2. A closing send does not wait for an in-flight send; it goes out at once, alongside it (`flush`, lines 119–127), and the revisions keep the overlap from leaving either side on the older report.

Existing coverage in `packages/ui/src/lib/settings/deviceSettingsReport.test.ts`:

- "sends again after the server refused a report" (lines 52–61) — a single, sequential refused send.
- "a closing report that lands first stays delivered when the older in-flight send lands after it" (lines 94–124) — overlapping sends, but both resolve `true`.

No test exercises overlapping sends where the newer (closing) send is **refused** and the older in-flight send then succeeds. That is exactly the `pagehide`/hidden-flush order: the closing send is the last one the page will ever make, so if it is wrongly recorded as delivered, the newer settings are silently lost with no later retry.

## Evidence (verified on main `e6dccd7dc`)

A probe test driving the real reporter with deferred send resolvers — in-flight send (older snapshot), then `flush(true)` (newer snapshot), resolve the closing send `false`, then resolve the older send `true` — passes on current main: the delivered record is the older snapshot and a further flush re-sends the newer one (3 sends total, then no more once it succeeds).

Mutation check: changing only the closing path so a closing send records delivery even when refused (`(await send(...) || closing)` in the line-113 guard) leaves **all 11 existing tests green** and fails only the probe. A refactor that "optimistically" marks a closing report delivered — plausible precisely because the page is going away — would merge undetected.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `deviceSettingsReport.test.ts` gains a test in the closing/switching group covering: older send in flight → closing send with a newer snapshot → closing send resolves `false` → older send resolves `true` → delivered record is the older snapshot, i.e. a further flush re-sends the newer snapshot, and once that succeeds a further flush sends nothing.
- [ ] The new test fails under the closing-path mutation above and passes on unmodified code.
- [ ] No production-code change is needed (current behavior is correct); if the test exposes a real defect, fix `sendLatest` minimally instead.
- [ ] `bun test src/lib/settings/deviceSettingsReport.test.ts` (from `packages/ui`) passes and `bun run check:changed` is green for the change.

Found by new-issue-creator; the gap was first noted as a pr-diff-review finding on PR #318 and is filed standalone here with the mutation evidence.

title: Queued-goal forced-queue fix in PR #270 has no test: applyGoalChoice ordering in ChatInput is unprotected
body:
## Finding

PR #270 fixed queued goals losing their flags (`settled`, `briefAgent`, `ignoreLimit`) on the forced-queue paths, but that fix — unlike the edit/retry fix in the same PR — has no test at all, so a future refactor of `ChatInput`'s submit handler can silently reintroduce the flag loss.

## Evidence

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/openchamber/pull/270 (MERGED, merge commit `d9cf53025`; current main `d2820cb36`)
- The PR body states it directly, in its Validation table: "The forced-queue ordering (finding 2) has no test: it sits inside `ChatInput`'s submit handler."
- On current main, `packages/ui/src/components/chat/ChatInput.tsx`:
  - `applyGoalChoice` (line ~1350) maps a `GoalSubmitChoice` onto the session-goal arm (`none` → disarm; `unchanged` → armed with `{ settled: true }`; otherwise armed with the spec plus `briefAgent`/`ignoreLimit` from the choice).
  - It is applied at the two forced-queue exits — the auto-review queue (lines ~1906-1907) and the pending-permission/form queue (lines ~1928-1929), each immediately before `handleQueueMessage(options?.presetText)` — and last on the normal send path (line ~2389). `handleQueueMessage` consumes the arm when it builds the queued goal, so if a future edit drops or reorders either forced-queue application, the queued goal takes whatever stale arm the composer happened to hold.
  - The sibling fix in the same PR *was* made testable: `rearmQueuedGoal` was extracted into `packages/ui/src/stores/useSessionGoalArmStore.ts` and has unit tests in `useSessionGoalArmStore.test.ts` covering the flags round-trip. `applyGoalChoice` remains inline in the component with no equivalent coverage.

## Why it matters

This is the same bug class PR #270 was filed to fix — a queued goal silently dropping `settled` (a settled spec gets rewritten by the goal writer), `briefAgent` (the agent is not briefed with the approved spec), or `ignoreLimit` (the objective gets truncated) — except the regression would now arrive through the two queueing exits that only fire under a pending permission/form or a running auto-review, exactly the conditions nobody exercises by hand. The untested ordering is the only thing protecting those flags on those paths.

## Acceptance criteria

- The choice → arm mapping is testable without rendering `ChatInput` (e.g. extracted alongside `rearmQueuedGoal` in `useSessionGoalArmStore.ts`), or an equivalent component-level test exists.
- Tests cover, for each of the two forced-queue exits and the normal send: a `none` choice disarms, an `unchanged` choice arms settled with no objective, and a spec choice arms with the spec and its `briefAgent`/`ignoreLimit` flags — and the queued message built afterwards carries those flags.
- Removing `applyGoalChoice` from either forced-queue exit makes at least one test fail (ablation-checked, as this repo's PRs usually do).

body:
`packages/web/server/lib/routing/model-pools-folder-config.test.js` "reads parent folders, .opencode folders, sibling json and jsonc and OPENCODE_CONFIG, the last file winning" fails on any machine whose real `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json` defines model pools: the result gains the real pools (here `fast-pool`, `medium-pool`, `strong-pool`).

Fix: resolve the directory per call (a function instead of a module constant), or have the test set the environment before importing `shared.js` (`vi.resetModules()` plus a dynamic import). ## Acceptance criteria

- Either the config directory is resolved per call in `shared.js`, or the test isolates the module (e.g. `vi.resetModules()` with env set before import) — the chosen approach is recorded on this issue.

title: fix(quota): shared toTimestamp/normalizeTimestamp leak Infinity and NaN instead of null

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

The shared quota timestamp helpers in `packages/web/server/lib/quota/utils/transformers.js` leak non-finite values instead of returning `null`, unlike every other conversion path in the same file.

- `toTimestamp` (transformers.js:16-26): the string path returns `null` for unparseable input (`Number.isNaN(parsed) ? null : parsed`), and `toNumber` (transformers.js:5-14) returns `null` for non-finite numbers — but the numeric path only checks `value < 1_000_000_000_000`, so `toTimestamp(Infinity)` returns `Infinity` and `toTimestamp(-Infinity)` returns `-Infinity`.
- `normalizeTimestamp` (transformers.js:28-31): only checks `typeof value !== 'number'`, so `normalizeTimestamp(NaN)` returns `NaN`, and `normalizeTimestamp(Infinity)` / `normalizeTimestamp(-Infinity)` return those values unchanged.

## Evidence (verified this run on main 8711e6d56)

Node probe importing the module directly:

```
toTimestamp(Infinity)        => Infinity
toTimestamp(-Infinity)       => -Infinity
toTimestamp('garbage')       => null        (string path correctly rejects)
toTimestamp(NaN)             => null        (only because NaN is falsy at the `if (!value)` guard)
normalizeTimestamp(NaN)      => NaN
normalizeTimestamp(Infinity) => Infinity
normalizeTimestamp(-1000)    => -1000000    (negative values are also scaled, not rejected)
```

## Why it matters

`normalizeTimestamp` is used for reset times in `providers/zai.js:194,211` and `providers/zhipuai-coding-plan.js:158,173` (guarded only by a truthiness check on `nextResetTime`, which `Infinity` passes) and for credential expiries in `providers/claude/auth.js:52,89`. `toTimestamp` is used by ~20 quota providers for `resetAt`. A non-finite `resetAt` then flows into `toUsageWindow` in `utils/formatters.js`: the derived fields happen to be guarded there, but the raw `resetAt: Infinity` / `resetAt: NaN` is stored in the window object itself, so consumers that read `resetAt` directly (rather than the formatted derivatives) get a value that is neither a valid epoch-ms timestamp nor `null` — the contract every other path in this file maintains. This is the same defect class as #489 / #492, in the shared helpers those fixes rely on.

## Acceptance criteria

- `toTimestamp` returns `null` for `NaN`, `Infinity`, and `-Infinity` numeric inputs.
- `normalizeTimestamp` returns `null` for `NaN`, `Infinity`, and `-Infinity`.
- Existing behaviour is unchanged for finite numbers (seconds are scaled to ms below 1e12, ms values pass through), strings, `null`/`undefined`.
- New unit tests for both helpers cover the non-finite cases above (there is currently no test file for `transformers.js`; `utils/formatters.test.js` is the precedent in the same directory).
- Related: decide in the same change whether negative numeric timestamps should also be rejected or left as-is, and note the decision in the PR.

## Suggested fix

Guard both helpers with `Number.isFinite(value)` on the numeric path, mirroring `toNumber` in the same file.

title: fix(quota): VS Code quota port converts unparseable resetTime to NaN in google and antigravity paths — the #489 defect in quotaProviders.ts

body:
## Finding

The VS Code quota port (`packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.ts`) carries the same NaN-reset bug as the web Google transform in #489 — in **two** places #489 does not cover (its scope is the web `google` provider only):

```ts
// quotaProviders.ts:1318-1320 (google, models payload path)
const resetAt = quotaInfo?.resetTime
  ? new Date(quotaInfo.resetTime).getTime()
  : null;

// quotaProviders.ts:1543 (antigravity, fallback quotaInfo path)
const resetAt = quotaInfo?.resetTime ? new Date(quotaInfo.resetTime).getTime() : null;
```

For any unparseable `resetTime` string both yield `NaN`, which flows into the usage window's `resetAt`. The same file already has the shared helper — `toTimestamp` at `quotaProviders.ts:418-428`, which returns `null` for unparseable strings and handles epoch seconds/milliseconds — and the sibling bucket paths in the same file already use it (`:1289` google buckets, `:1466` antigravity buckets). So within one file, the bucket paths degrade to `null` on bad input while the models/fallback paths emit `NaN`, exactly the split #489 documents for the web tree.

## Evidence (verified on main 8711e6d56, 2026-10-26)

- `grep -n "new Date(" packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.ts` → the only unguarded `.getTime()` conversions are :1319 and :1543 (the :465 and :2545 sites construct from already-numeric values).
- `node -e "console.log(new Date('not-a-date').getTime())"` → `NaN`.
- A `NaN` reset timestamp is worse than `null` for in-process consumers: comparisons/arithmetic silently produce `NaN`/`false` instead of taking the "no reset time" path, and it only becomes `null` by accident across a JSON boundary.
- Dedup: `gh issue list --state all` searches for "quotaProviders NaN resetAt" and "vscode quota resetTime" returned nothing; #489's acceptance criteria cover only `packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/google/transforms.js`.

## Why it matters

The VS Code extension is the second shipping surface for the same quota data. Anyone on the extension whose Google or Antigravity models payload carries a malformed/unexpected `resetTime` gets a poisoned window (`resetAt: NaN`) instead of the "no reset time known" degradation every sibling path implements. Fixing only the web copy (#489) leaves the identical defect live in the port — the two implementations will keep drifting unless both raw conversions are retired.

## Acceptance criteria

- Both raw `new Date(quotaInfo.resetTime).getTime()` conversions in `packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.ts` (google models path and antigravity fallback path) use the file's `toTimestamp` helper, so an unparseable `resetTime` yields `resetAt: null`.
- No code path in the VS Code google/antigravity quota code can emit a non-finite `resetAt`.
- A targeted test (following the existing `packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.test.ts` / `antigravityQuota.test.ts` patterns) pins: unparseable `resetTime` → `null`, valid ISO `resetTime` → correct epoch ms.
- Existing VS Code quota tests still pass.

Related: #489 (the web-tree instance of the same defect).

title: test(quota): minimax-shared (249 lines) and wafer (130 lines) are the only quota providers with no tests — pin the token-plan usage inversion, model-pick precedence, weekly suppression and wafer overage clamping
