labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

body:
## Problem

Two quota providers with nontrivial parsing logic ship with no tests at all, in a directory where 21 sibling provider files all have test files (`packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/`):

### 1. `minimax-shared.js` (249 lines) — backs both `minimax-coding-plan` and `minimax-cn-coding-plan`

The 15-line wrapper files delegate everything to this shared factory, and none of it is pinned:

- `pickChatModel` precedence (lines 18-35): a `minimax-m*` model with `current_interval_total_count > 0` wins, then `general`/`chat`/`text` names, then any model with a numeric remaining percent, then the first entry.
- Token-plan usage inversion in `calculateUsage`: when the payload came from the token-plan endpoint, used count is computed as `total - usage_count`; from the coding-plan endpoint it is `usage_count` directly. A flip here silently inverts every MiniMax user's reported usage.
- Endpoint fallback: token-plan URL first, coding-plan URL only when the first returns an unusable payload (`base_resp.status_code !== 0` or empty `model_remains` counts as unusable).
- Weekly window suppression: status `3` (`WINDOW_STATUS_INACTIVE`) or missing weekly data omits the `weekly` window entirely.
- `calculateWindowSeconds`: prefers `end - start`, falls back to `remains_time` (documented in-code as milliseconds, from live API testing).

### 2. `wafer.js` (130 lines)

- Overage clamp asymmetry (lines 84-87): with overage, `usedPercent` is clamped only at 0 (can exceed 100); without overage it is clamped to 0-100.
- "No quota data" decision: only when `remaining`, `limit`, `overage` and `usedPercent` are *all* null.
- Window seconds derived from `window_end - window_start`, falling back to a fixed 5h, with the label from `resolveWindowLabel`.
- Error discrimination in the catch: timeout (`AbortError` on its own 15s signal) vs JSON parse error (`SyntaxError`) vs generic failure produce three different messages.

Verified on main `46f89f696` this run: `ls` of the providers directory shows no `minimax-shared.test.js`, no `minimax-coding-plan.test.js`, no `minimax-cn-coding-plan.test.js`, and no `wafer.test.js`, while e.g. `zai.test.js`, `zenmux.test.js`, `neuralwatt.test.js` and `ollama-cloud.test.js` show the established sibling test pattern (mocked credential read + mocked `fetch`). Dedup: no open or closed issue mentions wafer or minimax test coverage.

## Why it matters

These parsers translate third-party payloads whose field semantics were reverse-engineered (the `remains_time`-is-ms and token-plan-inversion facts exist only as code comments). Without tests, any refactor of the shared quota utils — a frequent area of change, cf. PR #474 — can silently flip a usage percentage or resurrect a weekly window for legacy plans, and nothing in CI would notice.

## Acceptance criteria

- `minimax-shared.test.js` (or tests through the two wrapper providers) pins: model-pick precedence, token-plan vs coding-plan usage inversion, endpoint fallback on unusable payload, status-3 weekly suppression, and the `remains_time` window-seconds fallback.
- `wafer.test.js` pins: the all-null "No quota data" case, overage vs non-overage clamping, the `remaining / limit left` value label with plan tier and overage suffix, window seconds from start/end vs the 5h fallback, and the timeout vs parse-error messages.
- Tests follow the sibling pattern (mocked auth read and `fetch`, no network) and pass under the package's existing test command; ablation spot-check: reverting the token-plan inversion makes the new minimax tests fail.

## Finding

PR #475 (merged, commit `e2998eb59a`) added the Open Design (AMR) quota provider on the server and CLI, but the provider is unreachable from the web UI, and its own error messages direct users to a Settings import flow that does not exist for it.

## Evidence (verified on current main `46f89f696`)

Server/CLI side is complete:

- `packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/opendesign.js:18-19` — `IMPORT_REQUIRED_ERROR = 'Import the Open Design session cookie in Settings to read Open Design quota'` and `SESSION_EXPIRED_ERROR = 'Open Design session expired; import a fresh session cookie in Settings'`.
- `packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/index.js:156-161` — registry entry; `isConfigured` (opendesign.js:184) is `Boolean(readManagedCredential(providerId))`, so the provider only appears in the configured listing after a credential exists.
- `packages/web/server/lib/quota/credentials/store.js:6` — `opendesign` is a managed credential provider; `packages/web/server/lib/quota/routes.js:18` wires its validator, so `PUT /api/quota/credentials/opendesign` works via raw API calls.

Web UI side has no trace of it:

- `packages/ui/src/lib/quota/providers/index.ts` — `QUOTA_PROVIDERS` (the Usage page provider list) has no `opendesign` entry, so it cannot be selected at all.
- `packages/ui/src/types/quota.ts` — the `QuotaProviderId` union has no `'opendesign'`.
- `packages/ui/src/components/sections/usage/UsagePage.tsx:93-97` — `credentialProviderId` is only `'exe-dev' | 'cursor' | 'zenmux'`.
- `packages/ui/src/components/sections/usage/QuotaCredentials.tsx:8` — `QuotaCredentialProviderId = 'exe-dev' | 'cursor' | 'zenmux'`, and the form has no `cookie` / `workspaceId` fields (the two fields the server normalizer in `credentials/providers.js` requires).

Net effect: the only ways to store the credential are hand-writing `~/.config/openchamber/quota/opendesign.json` or a raw `PUT` to the credentials API. A user who hits the import/expired errors and follows them to Settings finds nothing to fill in.

## Why it matters

The feature PR #475 exists to serve (plan windows for the AMR account) cannot be turned on by the audience its error text addresses. The provider silently does not exist in the product surface, and the re-import path on session expiry — the normal lifecycle for a cookie credential — is also missing.

## Acceptance criteria

- `opendesign` appears in the Usage page provider list (`QUOTA_PROVIDERS` + `QuotaProviderId`) and can be selected while unconfigured.
- Selecting it shows a credentials form (cookie + workspace id) wired to the existing `/api/quota/credentials/opendesign` routes, following the existing `QuotaCredentials` pattern for exe-dev/cursor/zenmux, so both first import and re-import after expiry work from Settings.
- The stored credential is never returned through the API (existing managed-credential behavior preserved).
- A UI test covers the unconfigured → form-shown path for opendesign, matching the coverage the other managed providers have.

title: opencode-update workflow: failure excerpt is empty when the error is one long line (tail -n +2 drops the only line)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

body:
## Summary

The `opencode-update` workflow's failure excerpt can come out **completely empty** exactly when the failing step's log ends in one very long line — the shape nix/JSON errors most often take. The excerpt is the only error detail posted to the automated-update tracking issue (#449), so those failures land on the issue with no diagnostic content at all.

## Evidence (main `fbcaa56cdad5`)

`.github/workflows/opencode-update.yml:188-192`:

```bash
grep -v "copying path" "${ERROR_LOG}" | tail -n 80 | sed 's/~~~/---/g' > "$RUNNER_TEMP/excerpt-full.txt" || true
if [ "$(wc -c < "$RUNNER_TEMP/excerpt-full.txt")" -gt 5000 ]; then
  tail -c 5000 "$RUNNER_TEMP/excerpt-full.txt" | tail -n +2 > "$RUNNER_TEMP/excerpt.txt"
else
  cp "$RUNNER_TEMP/excerpt-full.txt" "$RUNNER_TEMP/excerpt.txt"
fi
```

`tail -n +2` unconditionally drops the first line of the 5,000-byte chunk. That is meant to remove a partial line when the byte cut lands mid-line, but:

1. **Single long line → empty excerpt.** If the chunk contains no newline (one line longer than 5,000 bytes), `tail -n +2` outputs nothing. Reproduced locally this run: a file whose last line is 6,000 bytes → `tail -c 5000 | tail -n +2 | wc -c` = **0**. The same happens when the single line ends with the chunk's only newline.
2. **Boundary-aligned cut → one complete line dropped needlessly.** When the cut lands exactly on a line boundary, the first line of the chunk is whole and is still discarded.

This is a residual edge in the fix for #450 (PR #451), which replaced the old head-truncation with this tail-based excerpt. The developing-today/code copy of this workflow uses a different excerpt mechanism and its head-truncation flaw is tracked separately (developing-today/code#917) — this issue is openchamber-only.

## Why it matters

The tracking issue exists so a failed automated opencode update can be diagnosed without opening the Actions run. A failure whose final error is a single long line (a nix evaluation error with a long store path, a minified JSON blob, a long compiler line) produces an excerpt section that is present but empty — worse than an obviously missing one, because it looks like the step produced no output.

## Suggested fix

Only drop the first line of the chunk when a second line exists (e.g. count lines with `awk 'END{print NR}'` on the chunk: drop via `tail -n +2` when the count is ≥ 2, otherwise copy the chunk whole). A truncated single line is far more useful than an empty excerpt.

## Acceptance criteria

- Excerpt logic exercised against fixtures (shell-level): (a) >5,000-byte excerpt-full ending in a single >5,000-byte line → excerpt is non-empty and contains the tail of that line; (b) multi-line excerpt-full with the cut landing mid-line → partial first line dropped, remaining lines intact; (c) excerpt-full ≤ 5,000 bytes → unchanged (existing copy path); (d) excerpt is never empty when excerpt-full is non-empty.
- No other workflow behavior changes (attempt counting, history, close-on-success paths untouched).

body:
## Finding

PR #468 added the `subagentPolicy` passthrough with two different local validation rules: the update path judges the value, the create paths forward anything.

Verified on current main (`fbcaa56cdad5d3b7fb2eb3bd4c46c9b49bdba1c0`):

- Update judges it — `packages/web/server/lib/openchamber-control/session-actions.js:165-166` (`setSubagentPolicy`):
  ```js
  if (!isRecord(input.subagentPolicy)) {
    throw new OpenChamberControlError('subagentPolicy must be an object with models, excludedModels, or agentOverrides', 400);
  }
  ```
  Its tests cover a string / missing policy → 400.
- Create does not — `packages/web/server/lib/openchamber-control/service.js:875-876`:
  ```js
  if (action === 'session.create' && input.subagentPolicy !== undefined) {
    payload.subagentPolicy = input.subagentPolicy;
  }
  ```
  and `packages/web/server/lib/openchamber-sessions/routes.js:272` forwards it into the create input the same way, unchecked. The create tests use only a well-formed policy object; there is no malformed-create test.

## Why it matters

1. **No clean local 400 on create.** A string, array, or number `subagentPolicy` sent to `POST /api/openchamber/sessions` or control `session.create` is forwarded to OpenCode's session create instead of being refused at this layer with the message the update path already uses. Callers get whatever the backend produces for a malformed policy rather than the documented local error.
2. **The routes response asserts the caller's value as fact.** `routes.js:1133` sets `result.subagentPolicy = payload.subagentPolicy` — the response echoes what the caller sent, regardless of what the backend stored, normalised, or dropped. Combined with (1), a malformed or partially-recognised policy can be reported back as if it were the session's policy.
3. **The asymmetry is invisible to maintainers.** The PR's stated design is "OpenCode owns the shape and its checks, so this layer never narrows or rewrites it" — but the update path does judge the shape locally. Either rule is defensible; having both is not: the two entry points for the same field behave differently, and the tests mirror the asymmetry (malformed-input coverage exists only for update).

Source PR: #468 (merged 2026-10-26, merge commit `9ce6327bbfbefedca9443465b06cda2cfa834442`), commits `0cbb5ff922` (web passthrough) and `f47a905dbc` (CLI).

Dedupe: no open or closed issue covers subagentPolicy create validation (searches for "subagentPolicy create validation" and related terms return nothing). Single-repo: the forwarding code lives only in this repo; the policy shape owned by OpenCode is unchanged either way.

## Acceptance criteria

- One rule for the field on every entry point: either create (control `session.create` and `POST /api/openchamber/sessions`) refuses a non-object `subagentPolicy` with the same 400 and message as `session.subagentPolicy`, or the update path's local check is removed deliberately and the design doc updated to say so — the inconsistency, not a specific choice, is the bug.
- If create keeps forwarding: the sessions route response reports the policy the backend actually stored (from the created session record), not the caller's payload.
- Tests mirror whichever rule is chosen on both paths: malformed create inputs (string, array, number) covered the same way malformed update inputs already are, and the existing well-formed create/update forwarding tests still pass.

Found by the pr-diff-review job reviewing PR #468's diff against current main.

title: opencode-update workflow: failure-issue lookup caps at 100 open issues, so the tracking issue can be missed, duplicated, and never closed

labels.name: kind/ci
labels.description: CI/CD pipelines, workflows, and build automation

labels.description: Filed by the pr-diff-review job

labels.name: priority/normal

labels.name: effort/m
labels.description: Medium: expected under 1 day of work

labels.name: meta/enriched

body:
## Finding

The `opencode-update` workflow's "one tracking issue" guarantee rests on a capped, client-side-filtered lookup. If the existing failure issue is not among the issues that lookup returns, the workflow behaves as if none exists — and every path that depends on finding it breaks at once.

Source: PR #448 (merged, commit `530e24af04`), still present verbatim on current main (`fbcaa56cdad5`) at `.github/workflows/opencode-update.yml:62-64`:

```yaml
- name: Find an open failure issue
  id: failure-issue
  run: |
    gh issue list --state open --limit 100 --json number,title > "$RUNNER_TEMP/issues.json"
    number=$(jq -r --arg title "$FAILURE_ISSUE_TITLE" \
      '.[] | select(.title == $title) | .number' "$RUNNER_TEMP/issues.json" | head -n 1)
```

The lookup fetches at most 100 open issues (no server-side title search, no pagination, no label or marker search — even though the workflow stamps its issue body with an `<!-- automated-failure-issue: opencode-update -->` marker it never searches by) and filters by exact title in `jq`. This repo already has ~50 open issues, so the cap is within reach of ordinary backlog growth.

## What breaks when the lookup misses

All of these consume `steps.failure-issue.outputs.number` on current main:

1. **Duplicate tracking issues.** The failure-recording step treats an empty number as "no existing issue" and runs `gh issue create` with the same title — a second (third, …) `chore(deps): automated opencode update failing` issue, contradicting the workflow's stated one-issue design (file header, PR #448).
2. **Attempt history resets.** The duplicate starts at `Attempts: 1` with an empty failure history; the real history stays stranded on the issue that was missed.
3. **Verify-on-recovery never engages.** The plan step only forces build+test while a failure issue is open (`opencode-update.yml:100`). A missed issue means a manual fix landed elsewhere is never verified against the unchanged pin.
4. **Success never closes it.** Both closing paths — the merged-update path and the "pin already current" path (`opencode-update.yml:304`) — are gated on a non-empty failure-issue number, so the real tracking issue stays open forever even after updates resume succeeding. The `Fixes #<n>` line in the update PR is likewise only added when the number was found.

## Cross-repo: the same lookup exists in developing-today/code

Filed in the repo whose PR was reviewed, per the one-issue-per-finding rule. Note (added on a later correction pass, same run): the code copy of this exact finding was already tracked by developing-today/code#913, filed earlier that night by the code review run — so for code this section is a cross-reference to #913, not a second tracker; this issue's own scope is the openchamber copy below and in the Finding section. The same relationship holds for the sibling findings from the same workflow family: code's history-growth and duplicate-PR flaws are tracked by code#947 and code#946 respectively.

`developing-today/code` carries a sibling workflow built from the same template — `.github/workflows/flake-inputs-update.yml` on current code main (`a2eef6f7920a4dbc98a1f1059924e9adeb967f5d`, verified via `gh api` contents):

- Line 45: `FAILURE_ISSUE_TITLE: "chore(deps): automated openchamber+opencode input update failing"` — the same one-tracking-issue design (file header, line 18).
- Lines 63–67: the identical lookup — `gh issue list --state open --limit 100 --json number,title` filtered client-side by exact title in `jq`.
- The same consumers of the (possibly empty) number: verify-while-open at line 103, failure recording with the same `gh issue create` fallback at lines 147/204, publish at line 216, and the already-current close path gated at line 285.

In code the cap is not hypothetical headroom: the repo already has 159 open issues (GitHub search API, 2026-10-26), i.e. the lookup's 100-issue window is already smaller than the backlog it searches. No live tracking issue with that title exists in code yet, so the first failure there will create one — and later failures will only find it while it stays inside the first 100 returned.

The pattern exists in no other repo of the set: `developing-today/opencode` and `dezren39/nix` have neither workflow file in their `.github/workflows/` listings (verified via `gh api`, 2026-10-26).

## Evidence

- PR #448: https://github.com/developing-today/openchamber/pull/448 (merged 2026-10-25, merge commit `be39dda819`)
- Current main `.github/workflows/opencode-update.yml:64`: the `--limit 100` list call above, verified 2026-10-26 against `gh api repos/developing-today/openchamber/contents/.github/workflows/opencode-update.yml?ref=main` (main HEAD `fbcaa56cdad5`).
- The live tracking issue is #449, currently open with `Attempts: 2` — it is findable today (~50 open issues), so this is a latent break, not a live one.
- Dedupe: no open or closed issue covers this lookup in either repo (searches for the failure-issue titles / duplicate-failure-issue return only #449 itself in this repo and nothing in code; the related workflow findings #450 and #457 are closed and cover different steps).
- Correction (2026-10-26, same run): the original filing stated this workflow exists in no other repo, based on a filename check for `opencode-update.yml` only. A full-text grep then surfaced code's differently-named sibling workflow above, and the cross-repo section was added the same run. The finding, the fix, and the acceptance criteria below apply to both copies.

## Acceptance criteria

- In BOTH copies of the workflow (this repo's `opencode-update.yml` and code's `flake-inputs-update.yml`), the failure-issue lookup finds the existing tracking issue regardless of how many open issues the repo has — e.g. a server-side search (`gh issue list --search` on the exact title or the body's `automated-failure-issue` marker), a dedicated label applied at creation and searched by, or full pagination of the list.
- With the tracking issue open and more than 100 other issues open, a failed run still edits that same issue in place (attempt count and history continue; no duplicate is created).
- A subsequent successful run still closes the tracking issue via both success paths, and still forces verification while the issue is open.
- No other workflow behavior changes: failure recording, excerpt handling, and the merge/handoff paths keep working as they do today.

body:
## Problem

`GET /api/git/commit-diff` judges its `context` query parameter a third way — different from both sibling styles in the same file — and a fractional value makes the endpoint fail with a 500:

- `packages/web/server/lib/git/routes.js:1907`: `const context = Number(req.query.context ?? 3);` with `contextLines: Number.isFinite(context) ? context : 3`.
- `Number('2.9')` is finite, so `context=2.9` passes through to `packages/web/server/lib/git/service.js:6710` (`getCommitDiff`), which builds `-U${Math.max(0, contextLines)}` → `-U2.9`.
- Git rejects that outright. Probe on main `2264681f2`: `git diff -U2.9 HEAD~1 -- ROADMAP.md` → `error: --unified expects a numerical value`. Through the route this surfaces as a 500 (`Failed to get commit diff` path) for a merely malformed query parameter.

The three styles now present in `git/routes.js` for the same conceptual parameter:

| `context` | `GET /api/git/diff`, `/range-diff` (parseInt) | `POST /api/git/diffs` (strict) | `GET /api/git/commit-diff` (Number + isFinite) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `10junk` | 10 | default 3 | default 3 (NaN) |
| `2.9` | 2 | default 3 | **500 — git rejects `-U2.9`** |
| `-5` | −5 → 0 lines in service | default 3 | −5 → 0 lines in service |
| `5` / `0` | 5 / 0 | 5 / 0 | 5 / 0 |

## Evidence (verified on main `2264681f2`)

- routes.js:1907 and service.js:6705-6712 as quoted above.
- `git diff -U2.9` probe output: `error: --unified expects a numerical value` (exit non-zero).
- Sibling strict pattern at routes.js ~line 932 (`POST /api/git/diffs`): `Number.isInteger(context) && context >= 0 ? context : 3`.

## Why it matters

A client bug or a hand-edited URL turns a read-only diff request into a server error, and the four diff endpoints in one file now disagree on the same parameter in three different ways — an invitation for more drift. #464 covers the GET diff/range-diff half; this issue covers commit-diff, whose failure mode (500) is distinct and worse.

## Acceptance criteria

- `GET /api/git/commit-diff` judges `context` with the same strict rule as `POST /api/git/diffs` (whole-value integer, `>= 0`, otherwise default 3) — ideally via one shared helper used by all the diff endpoints in `git/routes.js` (see #464).
- `context=2.9` returns a normal 3-context diff (HTTP 200), never a 500; `context=-5` no longer silently becomes a 0-context diff; `context=10junk` stays defaulted.
- Valid values (`0`, `3`, `10`) behave exactly as today.
- Tests cover the fractional/negative/malformed cases for commit-diff, following the existing `packages/web/server/lib/git/routes.test.js` patterns.

body:
## Problem

The two GET diff endpoints judge their `context` query parameter with a bare `parseInt`, while their sibling `POST /api/git/diffs` in the same file judges the same parameter strictly. The same malformed value therefore produces different diffs depending on which endpoint the client calls:

| `context` value | `GET /api/git/diff` and `GET /api/git/range-diff` | `POST /api/git/diffs` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `10junk` | 10 lines | default 3 |
| `2.9` | 2 lines | default 3 |
| `-5` | −5, silently clamped to **0** lines in the service | default 3 |
| `abc` | default 3 | default 3 |
| `5` / `0` | 5 / 0 | 5 / 0 |

## Evidence (verified on main `2264681f2`)

- `packages/web/server/lib/git/routes.js:897` (`GET /api/git/diff`) and `routes.js:994` (`GET /api/git/range-diff`): `const context = req.query.context ? parseInt(String(req.query.context), 10) : undefined;` then `contextLines: Number.isFinite(context) ? context : 3`.
- `routes.js` ~line 932 (`POST /api/git/diffs`): `const context = Number(req.body?.context);` with `contextLines: Number.isInteger(context) && context >= 0 ? context : 3` — the strict pattern already established in this file.
- The negative value is hidden downstream: `packages/web/server/lib/git/service.js:3402-3404` (`readDiff`) and `service.js:3327-3328` (`getNoIndexDiff`) push `-U${Math.max(0, contextLines)}`, so `-5` becomes a zero-context diff with no signal to the caller.
- Probe of the exact expressions (node): `10junk → GET 10 / POST 3`, `2.9 → GET 2 / POST 3`, `-5 → GET -5 (→0 in service) / POST 3`, `abc → 3 / 3`, `5 → 5 / 5`, `0 → 0 / 0`.

## Why it matters

Diff context changes what a reviewer (or an agent reading the diff) actually sees. Silently accepting `10junk` as 10 on one endpoint and defaulting it on another, and silently turning a negative into zero-context — the least informative diff — is the same silent-reinterpretation class fixed for the Web CLI in #433/#446, and it makes the three diff endpoints disagree with each other.

## Acceptance criteria

- `GET /api/git/diff` and `GET /api/git/range-diff` judge `context` exactly as `POST /api/git/diffs` does (one shared helper is ideal): whole-value integer, `>= 0`, otherwise the default of 3.
- `context=10junk`, `context=2.9`, and `context=-5` produce the default 3-line context (or a 400 — pick the POST endpoint's defaulting behavior for consistency) on all three endpoints.
- Valid values (`0`, `3`, `10`) behave exactly as today on all three endpoints.
- Tests cover the malformed/fractional/negative cases for the GET endpoints, following the existing `packages/web/server/lib/git/routes.test.js` patterns.

Related but distinct: #463 covers the same bare-`parseInt` pattern on `GET /api/git/log`'s `maxCount`, where a negative value is worse (unbounded history) — the two fixes touch different parameters and can land independently, though a shared strict-parsing helper would serve both.

body:
## Problem

`GET /api/git/log` judges its `maxCount` query parameter with a bare `parseInt`, and the service turns any falsy result into the default of 50. Malformed and out-of-range values are silently reinterpreted instead of rejected or defaulted consistently:

- `maxCount=10junk` → parsed as `10`
- `maxCount=1e3` → parsed as `1`
- `maxCount=abc` → `NaN` → silently becomes `50` in the service
- `maxCount=0` → falsy → silently becomes `50` (the caller asked for none and gets 50 commits)
- `maxCount=-5` → passes through to git as `--max-count=-5`, which git treats as **unlimited**: the endpoint returns the repository's entire history

## Evidence (verified on main `2264681f2`)

- `packages/web/server/lib/git/routes.js:1869` — `maxCount: maxCount ? parseInt(maxCount) : undefined`
- `packages/web/server/lib/git/service.js:6362` — `const maxCount = options.maxCount || 50;`, then interpolated as `--max-count=${maxCount}` (lines 6367/6448/6455)
- Probe in this repo: `git log --max-count=-5 --oneline | wc -l` → `5804`, identical to the full `git log --oneline | wc -l` (`5804`); `git log --max-count=5` → `5`. So a negative `maxCount` really is an unbounded history dump.
- `node -e` probe of the exact expressions: `parseInt('10junk')=10`, `parseInt('1e3')=1`, `parseInt('-5')=-5`, `parseInt('abc')||50 → 50`, `parseInt('0')||50 → 50`.
- Contrast in the same routes file: `POST /api/git/diffs` judges its numeric `context` strictly — `Number(req.body?.context)` with `Number.isInteger(context) && context >= 0 ? context : 3` (routes.js ~line 932). The log endpoint has no equivalent guard.
- UI callers pass sane values (`maxCount` 1–50 in `packages/ui`), so strict validation breaks no first-party caller.

## Why it matters

A single hand-crafted or buggy request can make the server serialize a repository's entire commit history (unbounded response size, memory, and time), and ordinary typos (`0`, `abc`) silently return a different result set than requested — the same silent-reinterpretation class fixed for the Web CLI in #433/#446.

## Acceptance criteria

- `GET /api/git/log` rejects (400) or consistently defaults `maxCount` values that are not positive integers: `abc`, `10junk`, `1e3`, `2.5`, `0`, and negatives must never reach git as `--max-count`.
- A negative `maxCount` can no longer produce an unbounded history response.
- Valid values (e.g. `1`, `50`) behave exactly as today; omitting `maxCount` still defaults to 50.
- The service layer does not silently convert an explicit `0`/invalid value into 50 (guard at the route, the service, or both — matching the strict pattern already used for `POST /api/git/diffs` context).
- Tests cover the malformed/zero/negative cases (route-level or service-level, following the existing `packages/web/server/lib/git/routes.test.js` / `service.test.js` patterns).

title: opencode-update workflow: a failed bun install step is never recorded on the failure tracking issue
body:
## Finding

The `opencode-update` workflow added in PR #448 (`.github/workflows/opencode-update.yml`, still present unchanged in this respect on current main `c313b5bf42811ec7d545456ffceaca5d23c29ada`) promises in its header that failures are tracked in ONE issue: the first failure opens it, later failures edit it in place, and the next success closes it. That tracking silently does not happen when the **Install dependencies** step fails.

Evidence on current main:

- The Install step has no `id`, no `continue-on-error`, and does not tee a log:
  ```yaml
  - name: Install dependencies
    if: steps.plan.outputs.verify == 'true'
    run: bun install --frozen-lockfile
  ```
- The "Decide the outcome" step (`if: always()`) enumerates only three failure sources — `nix flake update opencode` (`steps.update.outcome`), `nix build .#openchamber` (`steps.build.outcome`), and `bun run test` (`steps.tests.outcome`). It has no branch for an install failure, and cannot reference one because the install step has no id.
- The "Record the failure on the tracking issue" step is gated on `steps.outcome.outputs.result == 'failure'`.

So when `bun install --frozen-lockfile` fails (exactly the failure mode this repo has already seen in CI — see #405, where every CI job failed at frozen-lockfile install because the lockfile was out of sync), the job fails at install, build/tests are skipped, "Decide the outcome" finds none of its three steps marked failure and outputs `result=success`, and the tracking issue is never opened or updated. A broken automated update can therefore fail every daily run with no entry on the tracking issue the workflow exists to maintain.

PR #452 (merged 2026-10-25T22:42:53Z) reworked this workflow's excerpt and merge-handoff logic but did not touch the install step or the outcome enumeration; the gap is still live on current main.

## Why it matters

The tracking issue (#449 is the current instance) is the workflow's only persistent failure signal. An install-stage failure — a plausible failure precisely when a dependency change lands — bypasses it entirely, so the daily update can be dead while the tracking issue says the last failure was something else, or is closed by an unrelated success path.

## Acceptance criteria

- The Install dependencies step has an `id`, `continue-on-error: true`, and captures its output to a log file (e.g. `$RUNNER_TEMP/install.log`) like the update/build/test steps.
- "Decide the outcome" maps an install failure to `result=failure` with `failed_step` naming the install step and `error_log` pointing at its log, so "Record the failure" opens/updates the tracking issue with an excerpt.
- A simulated or real run with a failing `bun install --frozen-lockfile` records the failure on the tracking issue (attempt count increments, excerpt present) instead of ending with `result=success` from the outcome step.
- Existing behavior for update/build/test failures and for the success/publish paths is unchanged.

Source: PR #448 (commit `530e24af0`), re-verified against current main `c313b5bf4`; filed by the pr-diff-review job.

title: opencode-update workflow: failure excerpt truncates the tail from the head, so the actual error never reaches the tracking issue
body:
## Problem

The `opencode-update` workflow's failure excerpt drops the actual error. When a run fails, the "Record the failure on the tracking issue" step builds the excerpt with (`.github/workflows/opencode-update.yml`, "Record the failure" step):

```bash
tail -n 80 "${ERROR_LOG}" | sed 's/~~~/---/g' | head -c 5000 > "$RUNNER_TEMP/excerpt.txt"
```

`head -c 5000` truncates from the **head** of the last-80-lines: it keeps the oldest lines of the tail and cuts off the final lines — exactly where `nix build` / `bun run test` print the error — mid-line if necessary.

## Evidence (live, from the workflow's own tracking issue)

Issue #449, attempt 1 (run 40220273922, failed step `nix build .#openchamber`, 2026-10-25):

- The excerpt is ~5,000 chars of `copying path '/nix/store/...' from 'https://cache.nixos.org'...` progress lines.
- It ends mid-line: `copying path '/n` — the 5,000-char cut.
- The word "error" appears once in the whole issue body, in the "Error excerpt" header itself. The build error that failed the run appears nowhere in the issue, so the tracking issue cannot be triaged without opening the run log (which expires).

Verified on main `be39dda81` (workflow added by PR #448).

## Why it matters

The workflow was designed so one durable issue carries the failure diagnosis ("the failing step's error excerpt"). As written, any failing step whose last 80 log lines exceed 5,000 chars — the normal case for `nix build`, which emits long store-path lines — produces an excerpt with no error in it, defeating the issue's purpose.

## Acceptance criteria

- The excerpt in the failure issue ends with the **final** lines of the failing step's log: when the tail exceeds the cap, truncation discards from the start of the excerpt, not the end (e.g. build the excerpt then `tail -c 5000`, or take more tail lines and keep the last N chars).
- The excerpt does not end mid-line where avoidable (trim to the last complete line within the cap).
- A synthetic check demonstrates it: a log whose last 80 lines exceed 5,000 chars with a distinctive final error line produces an excerpt containing that error line.
- The `~~~` fence-neutralizing `sed` and the rest of the failure-recording behavior (attempt count, history, first/last failure) are unchanged.

title: Web CLI --timeout silently reinterprets non-numeric values as the 600s default; fractional/out-of-range values fail only at the server
body:
## Problem

The Web CLI's `--timeout <seconds>` option (session `send` / `fork` / `create` / `messages`, used with `--wait`) is never validated at parse time, unlike every sibling numeric option. Malformed values are silently reinterpreted or surface as a confusing downstream server error instead of a CLI usage error.

## Evidence (verified on main 5f3cf10e2)

- `packages/web/bin/lib/cli-args.js` (`case 'timeout'`): stores the raw string with no check. Contrast the same file's `--port` (whole-string `/^-?\d+$/` + range 1-65535), `--lines` / `--limit` (whole-string `/^\d+$/` + >= 1, added for #433), and `packages/web/bin/lib/cli-goal.js` `parseGoalTokenBudget` (`/^\d+$/` + range 1000-100000000).
- `packages/web/bin/lib/commands-session.js:245,274,317`: the value is forwarded as `timeout: Number(options.timeout)`.
- Direct probe of `parseArgs` + `resolveControlTimeoutMs` (`packages/web/bin/lib/cli-control.js:29`) on main:
  - `--timeout abc` and `--timeout 10junk` -> `Number(...)` is `NaN`; `requestControlAction` JSON-serializes `NaN` as `null`, and the server's `normalizeWaitTimeoutMs` (`packages/web/server/lib/openchamber-control/service.js:40-44`) treats `null` as unset, so the wait **silently uses the 600-second default** the user never asked for.
  - `--timeout 0` and `--timeout -5` -> `-5` is not even consumed as the value (no negative-value handling like `--port` has), so the flag is silently ignored; `0` reaches the server and fails there.
  - `--timeout 1.5`, `--timeout 999999`, `--timeout 86401` -> pass the CLI untouched and fail only at the server with `timeout must be from 1 to 86400 seconds` (a 400 control error), even though the CLI's own help (`commands-session.js`, ACTION OPTIONS) already documents `(default: 600, max: 86400)`.

So the documented contract (integer seconds, 1..86400) is enforced only by the server, late, and not at all for the non-numeric case, which is silently reinterpreted as the default.

## Why it matters

A user who typos `--timeout 60s` or `--timeout abc` gets a 10-minute wait instead of an error, with no indication their value was discarded — the same silent-reinterpretation class #433 fixed for `--lines`/`--limit`. Fractional and out-of-range values produce a server-flavoured error for what is a local usage mistake.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `--timeout` is judged at parse time in `cli-args.js`, like `--lines`/`--limit`: a non-integer, zero, negative, or > 86400 value throws a `TunnelCliError` usage error naming the option (e.g. `Invalid timeout value. Provide an integer number of seconds from 1 to 86400.`).
- [ ] Valid values (`1`, `60`, `600`, `86400`) keep working and are forwarded unchanged.
- [ ] Tests in `packages/web/bin/lib/cli-args.test.js` cover the malformed set (`abc`, `10junk`, `1e3`, `10.9`, `0`, `-5`, `86401`) and the valid boundary values, in the style of the existing `--lines`/`--limit` test.
- [ ] No change to the server-side `normalizeWaitTimeoutMs` contract (defense in depth stays).

title: Model pool validator accepts padded variant settings (defaultVariant / variants) that never apply
body:
## Problem

The model-route validator refuses empty variant settings on a target (#369) but accepts whitespace-padded ones: a padded `defaultVariant`, a padded key in the `variants` remap, or a padded remap value. Variant names contain no spaces and OpenCode does not trim them, so the setting is saved and silently never applies — the target runs at its own default variant, or the remap never fires.

## Evidence (verified 2026-10-25 on main cd9219324)

`validateTarget` in `packages/web/server/lib/routing/model-routes.js` (defaultVariant check ~line 371, variants loop ~lines 374-380) tests only emptiness: `target.defaultVariant === ""`, `from === ""`, `to === ""`. Direct run of `validateModelRoutes`:

- `{ model: "openai/gpt-5", defaultVariant: " high" }` → ACCEPTED
- `{ model: "openai/gpt-5", variants: { " high": "low" } }` → ACCEPTED
- `{ model: "openai/gpt-5", variants: { high: " low" } }` → ACCEPTED
- the unpadded equivalents → ACCEPTED (correctly)

This is the padded-spelling sibling of #439 (padded/empty-segment target references), in the variant-settings checks rather than the target reference pattern; the two fixes touch different checks and messages, so they are tracked separately.

## Why it matters

Same failure shape this validator exists to prevent: configuration that saves cleanly, looks live in Settings, and is silently ignored by OpenCode. A variant name pasted with a stray space is an easy typo, and nothing anywhere reports it.

## Acceptance criteria

- `validateTarget` refuses a `defaultVariant`, a `variants` key, or a `variants` value that differs from its trimmed spelling, with a message naming the padded setting.
- Unpadded variant settings still validate, including on pattern targets.
- New cases in `packages/web/server/lib/routing/model-routes.test.js` cover padded defaultVariant, padded remap key, and padded remap value.

title: Model pool validator accepts padded and empty-segment target references that can never match a model
body:
## Problem

The model-route validator accepts target references whose provider, model, or variant segment is padded with whitespace, and references with an empty segment — spellings that can never match a real provider/model in OpenCode, so the target is saved, looks live in Settings, and silently never serves.

## Evidence (verified 2026-10-25 on main cd9219324)

`TARGET_PATTERN` at `packages/web/server/lib/routing/model-routes.js:19` is `/^[^/#]+\/[^#]+(?:#[^#]+)?$/` — every segment class accepts spaces, and the model class accepts `/`, so all of these pass `validateTarget` (`model-routes.js:355,359`). Direct run of `validateModelRoutes({ r1: { targets: [v] } })`:

- `" openai/gpt-5"` → ACCEPTED (padded provider)
- `"openai/ gpt-5"` → ACCEPTED (padded model)
- `"openai/gpt-5 "` → ACCEPTED (trailing padding)
- `"openai//gpt-5"` → ACCEPTED (empty segment: model ID becomes `/gpt-5`)
- `"openai/gpt-5# high"` → ACCEPTED (padded variant)

Provider IDs, model IDs, and variant names contain no spaces, and OpenCode does not trim target references (trimming is specific to schedule entries — see the #432/#437 fix in `validateSchedules`, which trims because OpenCode's schedule matcher does). A padded or empty-segment target therefore attaches under a key no real model ever has.

Weights and budget keys do not have this hole: they are anchored by matching against the route's targets (`keyNamesTarget`), so a padded key is refused as matching no target. Only the target spelling itself is unanchored.

Related but separate code: the same class of gap in OpenCode core's own alias parsing is tracked as developing-today/opencode#436 and #437; this issue is OpenChamber's validator only.

## Why it matters

This validator's whole job (see the long series of "saved but never applies" refusals in this file) is to refuse configuration OpenCode would silently ignore. A typo'd space pasted from a spreadsheet or a hand-edited `opencode.json` currently saves cleanly and the pool just never routes to that target, with no signal anywhere.

## Acceptance criteria

- `validateTarget` refuses a target whose provider, model, or `#variant` segment differs from its trimmed spelling, with a message naming the padding.
- `validateTarget` refuses a target with an empty segment (`provider//model`, and a model segment that is only `/`-joined empties as applicable), with a message saying the segment is empty.
- Legitimate model IDs containing `/` (e.g. `openrouter/anthropic/claude-sonnet-4`) still validate.
- New cases in `packages/web/server/lib/routing/model-routes.test.js` cover padded provider/model/variant and the empty-segment spelling, for both the string and `{ model }` target forms.

title: Web CLI --lines and --limit silently reinterpret malformed values (10junk→10, 1e3→1) instead of rejecting them
body:
## Summary

The web CLI's `--lines` (logs) and `--limit` options are parsed with bare `parseInt`, so malformed values are silently reinterpreted instead of rejected — unlike `--port` in the same file, which was made strict in #228/#233.

## Evidence (verified on main `54175bf55`)

`packages/web/bin/lib/cli-args.js`:

- `lines` case (~line 474): `const parsed = parseInt(value ?? '', 10); if (Number.isFinite(parsed) && parsed > 0) { options.lines = parsed; }` — an invalid value silently keeps the default, and a partly-numeric value is truncated to its numeric prefix.
- `limit` case (~line 483): same `parseInt`, throwing `Invalid limit value` only when the result is NaN or < 1 — so a partly-numeric value never reaches its own error.

Probe against `parseArgs` on current main:

```
parseArgs(['logs',   '--lines', '10junk']) → lines: 10     (expected: usage error)
parseArgs(['logs',   '--lines', '1e3'])    → lines: 1      (expected: usage error)
parseArgs(['logs',   '--lines', '10.9'])   → lines: 10     (expected: usage error)
parseArgs(['logs',   '--lines', 'abc'])    → lines: 200    (default kept, no error at all)
parseArgs(['status', '--limit', '10junk']) → limit: 10     (expected: its 'Invalid limit value' error)
parseArgs(['status', '--limit', '1e3'])    → limit: 1
parseArgs(['status', '--limit', '10.9'])   → limit: 10
```

For contrast, the `port` case in the same file validates with `/^-?\d+$/` plus a 1–65535 range check and throws `Invalid port value: 8080junk` for `tunnel --port 8080junk` (verified in the same probe) — the strict contract the other numeric options in this parser were given in #228/#233/#235.

## Why it matters

- A typo like `--lines 200x` or `--limit 1e3` does not fail; it quietly tails 200→(parsed prefix) lines or pages results at a limit the user never asked for, making scripts and one-off debugging commands silently wrong.
- The two options are also inconsistent with each other: `--limit abc` errors, `--lines abc` silently uses the default 200.

## Acceptance criteria

- `--lines` and `--limit` accept only a canonical positive-integer spelling (the same whole-string judgement `--port` uses, e.g. `/^\d+$/` after the existing handling), and reject `10junk`, `1e3`, `10.9`, `abc`, `-5`, and `0` with a usage error naming the option — no silent truncation and no silent default.
- Valid values (`--lines 50`, `--limit 25`, including a leading-zero spelling if `--port`'s contract accepts the equivalent there — judge both options the same way) keep working unchanged.
- Tests in `packages/web/bin/lib/cli-args.test.js` cover the malformed spellings for both options.

title: Model pool validator refuses padded schedule targets that OpenCode trims and applies
body:
## Summary

The model-pool validator judges a schedule's `targets` entries exactly as spelled, but OpenCode trims each entry before matching — so a padded entry that OpenCode would apply is refused here as matching no target in the route.

## Evidence (verified on openchamber main `54175bf55`)

`packages/web/server/lib/routing/model-routes.js`, `validateSchedules`: each schedule entry is checked with `entry.includes("#")`, `routeReferenceOf(entry)`, and `keyNamesTarget(entryReference, …)` against the route targets, with no trimming. A whitespace-only entry is rejected as not a "non-empty target reference", but a padded real reference falls through to the matching check and fails it.

Probe against the validator on current main:

```
validateModelRoute('x', { targets: ['openai/gpt-5'],
  schedules: [{ when: {}, factor: 2, targets: [' openai/gpt-5 '] }] })
→ 'route "x" schedule 1 target " openai/gpt-5 " matches no target in the route'

validateModelRoute('x', { targets: ['openai/gpt-5'],
  schedules: [{ when: {}, factor: 2, targets: ['openai/gpt-5'] }] })
→ null
```

OpenCode's runtime does the opposite: `routeWeightRules` in `packages/core/src/config/plugin/model-routes.ts` (developing-today/opencode) builds the schedule's match list with `(schedule.targets ?? []).map((target) => target.trim()).filter(Boolean)`, so `' openai/gpt-5 '` becomes `openai/gpt-5` and the schedule applies to that target. The OpenCode config schema (`packages/schema/src/config/model-routes.ts`, `Schedule.targets`) accepts any string, padded included.

So the validator's central contract — judge a route the way OpenCode applies it (see the case-insensitivity fix in #358/#362 and the route-reference judging in #363/#364) — is violated for padded entries: a hand-edited or API-submitted config that OpenCode would honour cannot be saved through OpenChamber, and the error message states the opposite of what OpenCode would do.

The same untrimmed judging also mislabels the padded variants of the two earlier checks: `' opencode-route/b '` is reported as "matches no target" rather than as a route reference, and `' openai/gpt-5#high '` likewise, even though after OpenCode's trim the `#variant` / route-reference rules are the ones that decide them.

## Why it matters

- Users who hand-edit `opencode.json` (the config this UI round-trips) or submit routes through the API hit a refusal for a schedule OpenCode itself accepts and applies.
- The refusal text misdirects debugging: it claims the target is not in the route when the only problem is surrounding whitespace.

## Acceptance criteria

- A schedule entry that differs from a route target only by surrounding whitespace is judged as OpenCode judges it: either accepted (trim before every check — emptiness, `#variant`, route-reference, and matching) or refused with a message that names the padding as the problem — not "matches no target in the route".
- Padded `#variant` and padded route-reference entries get the same specific verdicts as their unpadded spellings, if they are refused.
- Tests in `packages/web/server/lib/routing/model-routes.test.js` cover padded plain, padded pattern, padded `#variant`, and padded route-reference schedule entries.
- Existing model-routes tests still pass.

title: test(dictation): PR #424's cached-archive pin re-verification (archiveMatchesPins) has no test coverage and is not unit-testable as written
body:
## Finding

PR #424 added cached-archive re-verification to the dictation model downloader — a previously downloaded archive in `.downloads/` is now re-checked against the catalog's pinned size and SHA-256 (`archiveMatchesPins`) and discarded + re-downloaded when it does not match, instead of being trusted for being non-empty. That branch has **no test coverage**, and as written it cannot be exercised by a unit test without refactoring: the helper is module-private and its only caller hard-wires the real catalog spec and the global `fetch`.

## Evidence

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/openchamber/pull/424 (commit `1173534f5b965888ff703cf4de15dfdbc4366547`, merge commit `626dcfa9e1716ca9e50fd62428596e97dc84d966`, fixes #417). Its body lists the 6 new tests: oversize stream aborted early, digest mismatch refused, short download refused, no-pins refused before fetch, correct download accepted, every catalog entry pinned. None of them touches the cached-archive path.
- Current `main` (`9bdd6f9cfbfad8c1bfa56ecb51755d0f8755731d`), `packages/web/server/lib/dictation/local/model-downloader.js`:
  - `:108` — `async function archiveMatchesPins(archivePath, expected)` is declared but **not exported**.
  - `:202-205` — the only call site, in `ensureLocalSttModel`: on mismatch it deletes the cached archive and calls `downloadToFile(spec.archiveUrl, archivePath, onProgress, spec)`, where `spec` comes straight from the static catalog lookup and `downloadToFile` defaults to the global `fetch`.
- `packages/web/server/lib/dictation/local/model-downloader.test.js` on current main imports only `describeTarFailure` and `downloadToFile`; grepping it for `ensureLocal`, `archiveMatches`, `cached` or `cache` returns nothing.
- Because the catalog pins are hashes of the real multi-hundred-MB release archives, a test cannot fabricate a small archive that matches a real catalog pin — so the reuse-without-fetch path (matching cache) is unreachable in a test today, and the mismatch path can only be reached by letting a real download proceed to extraction.

## Why it matters

The re-verification is the part of #424 that protects users who already have bytes on disk from before the pins existed (#417's threat model: a corrupted or substituted archive "was accepted, extracted, and loaded"). The fresh-download path is well tested, but a regression in `archiveMatchesPins` — e.g. accepting on size alone, or swallowing a read error as a match — would silently restore the exact pre-#424 behavior for cached archives while every existing test stayed green.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `archiveMatchesPins` (or an equivalent verification helper) is exported or otherwise made unit-testable, and tests cover: exact size+digest match returns true; size mismatch returns false; same size but different digest returns false; missing/unreadable file returns false.
- [ ] A test at the `ensureLocalSttModel` level (with fetch/catalog injectable, or via the exported helper plus a stubbed download) proves a pin-mismatched cached archive is discarded and re-downloaded, and a pin-matching cached archive is reused without a fetch.
- [ ] The new tests fail if `archiveMatchesPins` is replaced with the old non-empty-file check, and the existing dictation suites still pass.

```
         specified: sha256-l/YLyGlVTz60KAD9ylwVqKaN+DMxP+gAE2ba0ROvaIc=
            got:    sha256-UTeYcuNWiTMZiOHzLoGNmRj8L0Kf3CJcmr/nytukvtM=
```

title: Dictation model download is unbounded and unverified: catalog pins no size or digest, downloader enforces neither
body:
## Problem

The dictation model downloader has the same unbounded-download shape that #412 fixed for the local-interpreter model route, plus no integrity check:

- `packages/web/server/lib/dictation/local/model-catalog.js` pins no byte size and no sha256 for any STT/TTS archive it lists.
- `packages/web/server/lib/dictation/local/model-downloader.js` `downloadToFile` (~lines 34–63) streams the response body to disk via `pipeline`; the `content-length` header is used only for progress reporting, never enforced, and there is no digest check after the download completes. A server (or a compromised/misbehaving mirror) that streams forever fills the disk; a corrupted or substituted archive is accepted, then extracted and loaded.

PR #413 deliberately left this downloader alone because it "has no pinned size to judge against" — the catalog needs pins before the downloader can enforce anything. This issue is that follow-up, flagged by pr-diff-review on 2026-10-24 and left unfiled until now.

## Evidence

- Verified on current main (b12d18307): `grep -n "bytes\|sha256\|size" packages/web/server/lib/dictation/local/model-catalog.js` returns nothing; `downloadToFile` in model-downloader.js reads `content-length` into `totalBytes` solely for the `onProgress` callback.
- Dedup: open-issue searches for dictation download / model-downloader / unbounded return only #412 (closed, the local-interpreter route, a different downloader).

## Acceptance criteria

- Add a pinned byte size and sha256 for every archive in `model-catalog.js`.
- Enforce during streaming in `downloadToFile`, mirroring the #413 fix: abort as soon as the received bytes pass the pinned size instead of writing the whole body first, and refuse the file when the completed download's digest differs from the pin.
- Tests cover: oversize stream aborted early, digest mismatch refused, and a correct download still accepted (existing `model-downloader.test.js` patterns).

body:
## Finding

The mobile tooling names Gradle product flavors that no build in this repo defines. There is no `productFlavors` block in any Gradle file under `packages/mobile/android/` (verified by grep on current main and on PR #386's base and head), so every build produces the flavorless output layout — and two callers point at flavored paths/tasks that can never exist.

### Leg 1 — live on current main (`5de4f1021`): the debug install path never exists

- `packages/mobile/package.json:12` — `build:android:debug` runs `./android/gradlew -p android assembleDebug`. With no flavors, that task produces `packages/mobile/android/app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk`.
- `packages/mobile/scripts/android-device.mjs:13` — `APK_PATH` is `.../apk/standard/debug/app-standard-debug.apk`, i.e. it expects a `standard` product flavor.
- Result: after a successful debug build, `bun run mobile:build:android:debug` followed by `android:install` / `android:run` always fails in `requireApk()` with "Debug APK not found at .../app-standard-debug.apk". Introduced on main by commit `91fcc4330` ("fix(mobile): explain failed adb installs", 2026-10-19), whose install-failure hints are unreachable for the normal build-then-install flow because the APK lookup fails first.

### Leg 2 — in open PR #386: the release workflow calls tasks that do not exist

PR #386 (commit `54fa6f5e5dcda109393ba8bb8f9211a1a10bcb83`, draft, stacked on PR #385) repeats the same pattern for a `fork` flavor:

- Its `mobile-release.yml` changes the release build to `./gradlew ... bundleForkRelease assembleForkRelease` and the artifact paths to `bundle/forkRelease/*.aab` and `apk/fork/release/*.apk`. Those tasks and output directories exist only if a `fork` product flavor is defined.
- Its `build.gradle` defines no flavor: it sets the release application id via `androidComponents { onVariants(selector().withBuildType('release')) ... }`, so the release tasks remain `bundleRelease`/`assembleRelease` with outputs under `bundle/release` and `apk/release`.
- Its `android-device.mjs` hunk makes the same `standard` change as leg 1.
- Merging #386 as written would break the mobile release workflow (Gradle "task 'bundleForkRelease' not found" / upload-artifact `if-no-files-found: error`), the mirror image of leg 1.

Related: #389 tracks adapting PR #386 to current main in general terms; this issue names the specific defect so the adaptation does not carry the `fork`/`standard` names forward. Note also that #386's other mobile substance (PushKeyPlugin `pushAvailable`, `useNativePushRegistration` guard, MobileApp store pages, release app id `today.developing.openchamber`) is already on main in evolved form (commits `cf00d746c`, `1c1050d81`, `ae6cf0641`, `a33620b12`, unified for all build types by `eb3d5b8b1`), so the flavored workflow is the part of #386 that must not be revived as-is.

Cross-repo: `git grep android-device|bundleForkRelease` on the mains of developing-today/code, developing-today/opencode and dezren39/nix returns nothing — the mobile tooling lives only in this repo, so this is a single-repo issue.

## Why it matters

`android:install`/`android:run` are the documented device loop for the mobile app; they are broken on main today for anyone who builds the debug APK the documented way. And the same naming trap is sitting in an open PR whose stated next step (#389) is a rebase-and-merge — without this note, the rebase keeps workflow task names that Gradle cannot resolve.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] On current main, `bun run mobile:build:android:debug` followed by the `android-device.mjs` install/run flow finds the APK that `assembleDebug` actually produced (either `APK_PATH` matches the flavorless output `apk/debug/app-debug.apk`, or a real `standard` product flavor is defined in Gradle and the build script builds it — one consistent choice, not both names).
- [ ] PR #386's adaptation (per #389) does not keep `bundleForkRelease`/`assembleForkRelease` or `forkRelease`/`fork/release` artifact paths unless a matching `fork` product flavor is actually defined in `build.gradle`; otherwise the workflow keeps the `bundleRelease`/`assembleRelease` + `release` paths that current main uses.
- [ ] A grep for `app-standard-debug`, `bundleForkRelease` and `forkRelease` in the repo returns only names that a defined Gradle variant can actually produce.

title: Tool, MCP and skill toggles break the prompt cache: measure, warn, and consider a stable search-only tool surface
body:
## Question

Does turning tools, MCP servers or skills on and off break the prompt cache, and should all tools go through mcpx so the agent sees only a search tool plus a few loaded by context or settings?

My words: "does changing tools bust cache? or do those go at the end or a separate part of the arg? should i leave them enabled to preserve cache? are tools essentially the same problem as skills and mcp and we should eventually look into moving so any tool can run through mcpx and handle it all there and the agent sees nothing but search and whatever autoloaded based on context or settings?"

## What I found

- **Tools go first, not last.** OpenCode builds each turn as tool definitions, then the system prompt, then the messages. The default system prompt also lists the tool names (`SessionSystemPrompt.make(tool names)`, `packages/core/src/session/model-request.ts:110-118`, OpenCode at `1668a0350b`).
- **The cache matches from the start.** Anthropic caches tools, then system, then messages, as one cumulative prefix ([prompt caching](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching)). OpenAI's cache is an exact prefix that includes tools ([prompt caching](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/prompt-caching)). OpenCode marks a cache breakpoint on the last tool definition (`packages/ai/src/cache-policy.ts:17-21`).
- **So yes:** adding, removing or changing one tool mid-session changes the first block. The whole cached prefix is lost on the next turn: tools, system prompt and every earlier message.
- **Keep the set stable within a session.** Switching tools between sessions costs nothing extra; switching inside a running session costs a full uncached turn. Leaving tools on to keep the cache is right only if they stay on for the whole session.
- **Unverified:** whether skills and MCP servers change the tool block, the system prompt, or both, in OpenCode 2. A skill list in the system prompt has the same effect as a tool change.

## Proposal

1. Measure first: run one session, toggle a tool mid-session, and read the cache-read tokens of the next turn from the assistant record's `tokens.cache.read`.
2. If confirmed, show it where the toggle is: "Changing tools in a running session makes its next turn uncached."
3. Evaluate a stable tool surface: the agent always sees the same small set (a search tool and a call tool, as in mcpx Code Mode), and everything else is found and called through it. The tool block then never changes, and adding tools costs nothing in the prefix.

Not a dependency of the goal editor work; filed from the same conversation.

title: Route pools: short and long descriptions given to the classifier

Route pools (`opencode-route/*`) should carry a short and a long description of what each pool is for. Jev and the small model read those descriptions when they classify a request and pick a pool, the way skills and agents carry descriptions today.

My words: "maybe route pools need short/long description that is provided to jev/the model for classification kind of like how there are descriptions for skills/agents?"

The classifier sees a pool's name and members. A name such as `strong-pool` says little about when to use it. A description such as "long refactors across many files; slow; costs the most" tells the classifier what the pool is for.

- Pass them to the classification prompt and to Jev's pool choice.
- The `plan_info` pool `purpose` field already holds similar text; decide whether it becomes the description or stays separate.

Related: #147 (notes from manual model choices).

title: fix(web): delta-coalesce window env value is judged by bare Number() — 1e3 silently becomes the 1000 ms maximum and 0x64 becomes 100 ms instead of the 50 ms default (event-stream #697 remainder)

body:
## Summary

`resolveDeltaCoalesceWindowMs` documents its own contract — "Anything that is not a whole number of milliseconds up to one second keeps the default rather than silently running with a guessed value" (`delta-coalescer.js:36-41`) — but the judgement is `Number(raw)` plus `Number.isInteger`, so non-decimal spellings that happen to land on an in-bounds integer are silently honoured with **no warning**: `1e3` becomes a 1000 ms coalesce window (the maximum, 20× the 50 ms default), `0x64` becomes 100 ms, `0b101` becomes 5 ms, and `50.0` / `+50` are accepted as 50 ms. Only spellings that miss the integer/bounds check (`50junk`, `5.9`, `-1`, `1001`) warn and fall back.

This is the event-stream sibling the #697 fix did not cover: #697/#700 made the three timeout readers in the same directory (`event-stream/timeouts.js`) judge by whole-text plain decimal (`/^\d+$/` after trim), but the coalesce-window reader in `delta-coalescer.js` — wired into the same hub construction (`packages/web/server/index.js:1128`) — still uses bare `Number()`.

## Evidence (verified on main `9e8aef49a`)

- `packages/web/server/lib/event-stream/delta-coalescer.js:42-51` — `resolveDeltaCoalesceWindowMs` trims, then `const value = Number(raw)` (line 45) and accepts any `Number.isInteger(value)` within 0–1000. It judges `OPENCHAMBER_EVENT_DELTA_COALESCE_MS` (default 50, `0` disables coalescing).
- Laptop probe of the **real exported function** (imported from the laptop clone at the same file hash `b5c73c108d3b6b2373503615f6f5664a` as sandbox main; probe `~/git/fleet/probe-delta-coalesce-env/probe.mjs`):

  | spelling | result | warning |
  |---|---|---|
  | `''` / `' '` | 50 (default) | — (correct: unset) |
  | `0` | 0 | — |
  | `25` | 25 | — |
  | `1e2` | **100** | **none** |
  | `1e3` | **1000** | **none** |
  | `0x64` | **100** | **none** |
  | `0b101` | **5** | **none** |
  | `50.0` | **50** | **none** |
  | `+50` | **50** | **none** |
  | `50junk` | 50 (default) | warned |
  | `5.9` | 50 (default) | warned |
  | `-1` / `1001` / `1e9` | 50 (default) | warned |

- `packages/web/server/lib/event-stream/delta-coalescer.test.js:288-302` pins unset/`0`/`25` and the warning cases `-1`, `1001`, `12.5`, `fast`, `NaN`, `1e9` — note `1e9` only warns because it is out of bounds, not because of its spelling; no in-bounds exponent/radix/signed/`.0` spelling (`1e2`, `1e3`, `0x64`, `0b101`, `50.0`, `+50`) is pinned.
- The sibling precedent in the same directory: `event-stream/timeouts.js` `resolveTimeoutSetting` (fixed for #697 in PR #700) requires `/^\d+$/` on the whole trimmed text before converting, so none of these spellings pass there.

Dedup: searches for `DELTA_COALESCE`, `resolveDeltaCoalesceWindowMs`, and "coalesce env" across open and closed issues return nothing; #697 covers only the three `timeouts.js` readers, #689/#696 cover other modules.

## Why it matters

This reader exists specifically to avoid "running with a guessed value" for a stream-timing window, and its warning is the only signal an operator gets that a value was rejected. The silent-acceptance gap defeats both halves for the spellings most likely to appear in real config (scientific notation from generated config, hex from a copied constant, a trailing `.0` from a templating engine), and one of them (`1e3`) silently sets the maximum 1000 ms window — twenty times the default — adding up to a second of latency to every coalesced delta flush. Consistency with the whole-text decimal judgement the same directory's timeout readers already use (#697) closes the class.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `resolveDeltaCoalesceWindowMs` in `event-stream/delta-coalescer.js` accepts only a whole-text plain decimal spelling (after the existing trim) within the existing 0–1000 bounds — the same `/^\d+$/` judgement as `timeouts.js` in the same directory; exponent, radix-prefixed, signed, and fraction spellings (`1e2`, `1e3`, `0x64`, `0b101`, `50.0`, `+50`) warn and keep the 50 ms default, matching the function's documented contract.
- [ ] Plain in-bounds values (`0`, `25`, `50`, `1000`) and the empty/unset case behave exactly as today (`0` still disables coalescing).
- [ ] Unit tests in `delta-coalescer.test.js` pin the spellings: `1e2`, `1e3`, `0x64`, `0b101`, `50.0`, `+50` warn + fall back; the existing pins stay green.
- [ ] No change to the coalescer's merge behaviour, bounds, or defaults.

title: fix(web): ensureOpenCodeProjectId writes the project ID to <worktree>/.git/opencode — creates a stray .git dir inside bare repos and never caches for separate git dirs

labels.name: source/new-issue-creator

body:
## Summary

`ensureOpenCodeProjectId` in the web git service always places the OpenCode project-ID file at `<primaryWorktree>/.git/opencode`. That is only correct for a plain primary checkout. For the two layouts its own caller explicitly supports — a **bare repository** and a **separate git dir** — the path is wrong, in different ways:

- **Bare repo:** it creates a stray `.git/` directory *inside* the user's bare repository and writes the ID there, a location that is not the repository's git dir at all.
- **Separate git dir** (where `<worktree>/.git` is a pointer file, not a directory): the write fails, the failure is swallowed, and the project ID is re-derived from a full `rev-list` on every worktree-context resolution.

## Evidence (verified on main `71c21cd97fec32b4ac8378ce6ff9da56a492887b`)

- `packages/web/server/lib/git/service.js:1923-1949` — `ensureOpenCodeProjectId(primaryWorktree)`:
  - `:1924` `const gitDir = path.join(primaryWorktree, '.git');`
  - `:1925` `const idFile = path.join(gitDir, 'opencode');`
  - `:1948-1949` `fsp.mkdir(gitDir, { recursive: true }).catch(() => undefined)` and `fsp.writeFile(idFile, projectId, 'utf8').catch(() => undefined)` — both failures silently swallowed.
- Its only caller, `resolveWorktreeProjectContext` (`service.js:1954ff`, ID call at `:1979`), deliberately supports these layouts:
  - `:1962` comment: "A bare repository has no work tree, so `--show-toplevel` fails there; the bare directory itself still answers the object-level commands worktree creation runs against it."
  - `:1975-1978` comment: "`<root>/.git` resolves to the primary checkout; any other layout (a bare repository, a separate git dir) has no primary worktree, and the sandbox directory is the closest thing to one." — so for a bare repo, `primaryWorktree` **is the bare directory itself**, and `:1924` resolves to `<bare>/.git`.
- Git behaviour verified with the git CLI this run: in a bare clone, `git rev-parse --git-common-dir` prints `.` (the bare directory itself) and `--absolute-git-dir` prints the bare directory; there is no `.git` entry inside it.
- The same file already resolves the real git dir elsewhere (`service.js:1401`, `:1444`, `:1473` use `rev-parse --absolute-git-dir` / `--git-common-dir`), and `repository-root.js`'s `primaryWorktreeRootFromGitDir` documents that non-`<root>/.git` layouts return null — `ensureOpenCodeProjectId` is the one place that still assumes the plain layout.
- Callers of `resolveWorktreeProjectContext` on the worktree create/list/remove paths: `service.js:5044`, `:5246`, `:5690`, `:6172`, `:6648` — so the separate-git-dir case pays a `rev-list --max-parents=0 --all` re-derivation (`:1932-1936`) on every call, and the bare case mutates the user's repository with a directory git never asked for.
- The derived ID keys the legacy worktree root (`service.js:1983`, `path.join(getOpenCodeDataPath(), 'worktree', projectID)`), so an ID cached in the wrong place also risks OpenChamber and any reader of the real `<git-common-dir>/opencode` disagreeing about the project's identity.

## Why it matters

Worktree flows from bare clones are a supported, commented code path (hub-style bare repos are a common way to drive multiple worktrees). Today that path silently (a) writes a stray `.git/` directory and ID file into the user's bare repository where nothing will ever read them back as a git dir, and (b) for separate-git-dir layouts, silently never caches the ID at all. Both failures are invisible because the write errors are swallowed — the worst kind of wrong: it looks like it worked.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `ensureOpenCodeProjectId` resolves the repository's real git common dir (e.g. via the existing `--git-common-dir` / `--absolute-git-dir` helpers in the same file) and reads/writes the `opencode` ID file there, for plain, bare, linked-worktree, and separate-git-dir layouts alike.
- [ ] No `.git` directory is created inside a bare repository, and no write is attempted through a `.git` pointer file.
- [ ] A failed ID-file write is no longer silently swallowed without trace (at minimum a `console.warn` naming the path), or the caching is dropped deliberately with a comment saying so.
- [ ] Tests in `packages/web/server/lib/git/service.test.js` (or a sibling) cover: bare repository (ID file lands at `<bare>/opencode`, no `<bare>/.git` created) and separate-git-dir / linked-worktree layout (ID persisted and re-read, not re-derived).
- [ ] Existing plain-checkout behaviour is unchanged: ID still read from / written to `<root>/.git/opencode`.

title: fix(web): skill install copies through a symlinked skill directory — copyDirectoryNoSymlinks never checks the root and its traversal guard anchors outside the clone

labels.name: kind/security

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Finding

Skill install (`POST /api/config/skills/install`) copies a selected skill directory out of a freshly cloned repository with `copyDirectoryNoSymlinks`, whose contract is "symlinks are not supported in skills" and whose traversal guard is supposed to keep the copy inside the selected directory. Both protections fail when the selected directory itself is a symlink:

- `installSkillsFromRepository` (`packages/web/server/lib/skills-catalog/install.js:259`) builds the source path with `toFsPath` (`:36-42`), which splits the caller-supplied `skillDir` on `/` and joins it under the clone dir without rejecting `..` segments or symlinks, and only checks that `SKILL.md` exists through that path (`:260-264`).
- `copyDirectoryNoSymlinks` (`:48-91`) never `lstat`s the root `srcDir` itself. It sets `srcReal = realpath(srcDir)` (`:49`) — for a symlinked root that resolves to the target outside the clone — and the per-entry traversal guard (`:63-67`) then compares each entry's real parent against that already-escaped `srcReal`, so it passes vacuously for every file in the target directory. Only entries *below* the root are checked for being symlinks.
- The route (`packages/web/server/lib/opencode/skill-routes.js:565-607`) passes the request body's `selections` straight into the installer; nothing validates that a selection is a real directory inside the clone (the scan flow only ever lists real tree paths, but the install endpoint does not require selections to come from a scan).

So a repository that contains a symlink in place of a skill directory — e.g. `linkdir -> /some/host/dir` where the target contains a `SKILL.md` — plus an install request naming that selection copies the host directory's files into the user's (or project's) skills folder, where they are then loaded as an installed skill. The target must contain a top-level `SKILL.md`, which other skill directories (the obvious target class) do by definition.

## Evidence

Verified on main `180e76a61734bff6c7c884b8e6f082981191fd49`:

- Code reading above: `install.js:36-42` (`toFsPath`, no `..`/symlink handling), `:48-67` (root never `lstat`ed; guard anchored at `realpath(srcDir)`), `:259-264` (existence check follows the symlink), `:289` (copy call); `skill-routes.js:592-607` (body `selections` passed through unvalidated).
- Laptop git probe (the installer's exact clone/checkout sequence: `clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --no-checkout`, `sparse-checkout init --cone`, `sparse-checkout set linkdir`, `checkout --force HEAD`) on a repo whose `linkdir` is a committed symlink (mode 120000) to an outside directory containing `SKILL.md`: `sparse-checkout set linkdir` exits 0, checkout materialises `linkdir -> /tmp/evil-skill2`, `test -f linkdir/SKILL.md` succeeds, and `realpath(linkdir)` resolves outside the clone — i.e. every gate before the copy step passes, and the copy walk's guard then anchors at the outside directory.
- Control in the same probe series: `..` selections (`../../evil-skill`, `myskill/../../evil-skill`, `../evil-skill`) are rejected today — but only incidentally, by git's sparse-checkout path normalisation (exit 128, "could not normalize path"), not by any check in the installer itself. The symlink path needs no `..` and is not normalised away.
- Secondary weakness in the same guard: `:65` uses `nextRealParent.startsWith(srcReal)` with no path-separator boundary, so a sibling directory whose name merely shares the prefix (`skill-evil` next to `skill`) also satisfies the check.
- Dedup: searches for "skills-catalog symlink", "installSkillsFromRepository", "skill install symlink", "copyDirectoryNoSymlinks", "sparse-checkout skill" across open and closed issues returned nothing.

## Why it matters

The skills catalog installs third-party repository content into a directory OpenCode then loads and runs as skills. The copy step is the boundary that is supposed to keep that content confined to the cloned repository; its own comments promise symlink rejection and traversal protection, but the root-directory case defeats both. A crafted repo (or a crafted install request against any repo containing a directory symlink) can pull host files that live in a `SKILL.md`-bearing directory into an installed skill, where their contents become agent-visible context.

## Acceptance criteria

- Installing a selection whose directory (or any path component of it) is a symlink is refused/skipped with a clear reason, matching the existing "Symlinks are not supported in skills" behaviour for entries below the root.
- The copy's containment check is anchored at the clone directory (the real path of `tempBase`), not at `realpath(srcDir)`: a source directory resolving outside the clone is never copied, and the prefix comparison uses a separator-boundary-aware check.
- `skillDir` values containing `..` segments are rejected by the installer itself, without relying on git sparse-checkout normalisation to fail first.
- A regression test covers the symlinked-root case: a clone fixture whose selected skill directory is a symlink to a directory outside the clone (containing a `SKILL.md`) installs nothing from the target and reports the skill as skipped/refused; existing install tests (real directories, in-repo symlinks below the root) still pass.
