## Summary

The self-handoff timeout is still judged by a bare `Number(...)`: `OPENCHAMBER_HANDOFF_TIMEOUT_MS=1e3` becomes a **1000 ms** timeout and `0x10` becomes **16 ms**, instead of the 30 s default. The event-stream timeout readers were made strict in #697 (merged today) and pin exactly these spellings as invalid; this timeout reader was missed.

## Evidence (verified on main `91e2be837`)

- `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/self-handoff.js:31-34` — `resolveHandoffTimeoutMs` is `Number(env.OPENCHAMBER_HANDOFF_TIMEOUT_MS)` with an `Number.isInteger(value) && value > 0` check. The integer check rejects fractional spellings, but exponent/hex/signed/decimal-point spellings that happen to be integral pass: `1e3`, `0x4E20`, `+20000`, `20000.0`.
- Consumers: `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/self-handoff.js:96` (the successor-ready wait — on timeout the predecessor **kills the successor** and keeps serving) and `packages/web/bin/lib/commands-lifecycle.js:406` (CLI deadline = timeout + 10 s).
- The strict precedent, merged today: `packages/web/server/lib/event-stream/timeouts.js` (#697) requires `/^\d+$/` before `Number(...)`, and its test pins `1e3`, `0x4E20`, `20000.0`, `+20000`, `20000junk`, `5.9` as invalid spellings that keep the default.
- Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-strict-env-remain/probe.mjs`) against the **real exported** `resolveHandoffTimeoutMs` (file hash identical to current main): `5000`→5000, `1e3`→**1000**, `0x10`→**16**, `+5000`→5000, `5000.0`→5000; `5.9`/`''`/`5000junk` correctly fall back to 30 000.
- Existing test `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/self-handoff.test.js:85-90` pins only unset / `250` / `0` / `soon` — no exponent, hex, signed, or decimal-point spelling.

Dedup: searches for `HANDOFF_TIMEOUT_MS`, `resolveHandoffTimeoutMs`, and `plain decimal` returned no covering issue. #697 covered the event-stream timeout vars only.

## Why it matters

The handoff timeout decides how long a predecessor waits for its successor to report ready before killing it and keeping the old process. A generated or typo'd value like `1e3` (an operator writing "1e3 ms" thinking of the default's scale, or a templating artifact) silently shrinks a 30 s grace period to 1 s — successors get killed before they can serve, and the handoff quietly never happens. Strict-with-fallback is the established house behaviour for env numbers (#624, #688–#701).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `resolveHandoffTimeoutMs` accepts only a whole-text plain decimal spelling (the `/^\d+$/` pattern used by the event-stream and fs readers) and otherwise returns the 30 000 ms default.
- [ ] Tests pin the spellings: `1e3`, `0x10`/`0x4E20`, `+5000`, `5000.0` fall back to 30 000; a plain value (`250`) is honoured; `0` still falls back.

## Summary

The VS Code bridge copies of the git read-cache TTL and git check-ignore timeout readers still judge their env values with a bare `Number(...)`. The web copies of the **same readers, for the same env vars**, were made strict in #696 (merged today) — the VS Code port was not carried over. A bare `Number(...)` silently honours `''` and `' '` as 0, `1e3` as 1000, `0x10` as 16, and `5.9` as a fractional 5.9.

## Evidence (verified on main `91e2be837`)

- `packages/vscode/src/bridge-fs-runtime.ts:48-58` — `createGitReadCacheTtlMs` (`Number(process.env.OPENCHAMBER_GIT_READ_CACHE_TTL_MS)`, finite `>= 0` accepted, default 30 000) and `createGitCheckIgnoreTimeoutMs` (`OPENCHAMBER_GIT_CHECK_IGNORE_TIMEOUT_MS`, default 2500). Both are evaluated once at module load (`:68-69`) and govern the bridge's git read cache and the check-ignore kill timeout.
- `packages/vscode/src/bridge-fs-helpers-runtime.ts:9-15` — a second copy of `createGitCheckIgnoreTimeoutMs` with the identical bare-`Number` judgement.
- The web precedents fixed in #696, same names/env vars:
  - `packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.js:149-153` `createGitReadCacheTtlMs` now uses `parsePlainDecimalInt` (`/^\d+$/` + safe integer).
  - `packages/web/server/lib/fs/search.js:99-110` `createGitCheckIgnoreTimeoutMs` now requires a plain decimal spelling, with the comment: a bare `Number(...)` would "silently honour `''` and `' '` as 0 (disarming the check-ignore kill timeout), `1e3` as 1000, `0x10` as 16, and `5.9` as a fractional timeout".
- Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-strict-env-remain/probe.mjs`, Node, file hashes verified identical to current main): evaluating the verbatim VS Code expressions — `''`→**0**, `' '`→**0**, `1e3`→1000, `0x10`→16, `5.9`→**5.9**, `+5000`→5000, `5000.0`→5000; only trailing-junk spellings (`5000junk`) fall back, because they parse as `NaN`.
- No VS Code test pins either reader (no test references `createGitReadCacheTtlMs` / `createGitCheckIgnoreTimeoutMs` in `packages/vscode`).

Dedup: searches for `GIT_READ_CACHE_TTL_MS vscode`, `bridge-fs`, `HANDOFF_TIMEOUT_MS`, `guestUploadMaxBytes`, and `plain decimal` returned no covering issue. #696 covered only the web copies in `fs/routes.js` + `fs/search.js`.

## Why it matters

- An empty or whitespace-only env value (a common accident when a variable is exported from a templated config) **disables the git read cache** (TTL 0 — where only an explicit `0` is documented to do that) and **disarms the check-ignore kill timeout** (0), in the VS Code bridge only, while the web surface falls back to its defaults for the identical configuration.
- Exponent/hex/fractional spellings silently become values nobody wrote (`1e3`→1000 ms, `0x10`→16 ms, `5.9` ms), diverging between the two runtimes that share these env vars.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Both VS Code readers (all three sites, both files) accept only a whole-text plain decimal spelling (the #696 `parsePlainDecimalInt` pattern) and otherwise fall back to their defaults (TTL 30 000, check-ignore 2500).
- [ ] An explicit `0` keeps working where it is documented (TTL 0 disables caching; check-ignore 0 disables the timeout); `''`/`' '` no longer produce 0.
- [ ] Tests pin the spellings: `''`, `' '`, `1e3`, `0x10`, `5.9`, `+5000`, `5000.0` fall back; plain values (`5000`, `0`) are honoured.

body:
## Summary

`resolveEventStreamTimeouts` documents its own contract — "Each value is a whole number of milliseconds within the bounds. Anything else keeps that window's default, with a warning, rather than running with a guessed value" (`timeouts.js:26-27`) — but the judgement is `Number(raw)` plus `Number.isInteger`, so non-decimal spellings that happen to land on an in-bounds integer are silently honoured with **no warning**: `1e3` becomes a 1000 ms stall window, `0x4E20` becomes 20000, `20000.0` becomes 20000, and `+20000` is accepted. Only spellings that miss the integer/bounds check (`20000junk`, `5.9`) warn and fall back.

The `1e3` case is the sharp one: 1000 ms is the reader's minimum bound, and the same file's header comment (`timeouts.js:8-12`) explains that a stall window at or below OpenCode's 15 s heartbeat "tears down and reopens every idle stream" — the failure mode that once produced ~80% of OpenChamber's log lines. An operator writing `1e3` (or pasting a scientific-notation value) gets exactly that behaviour, silently, where the documented contract promises the default plus a warning.

## Evidence (verified on main `6a3096cf8`)

- `packages/web/server/lib/event-stream/timeouts.js:28-38` — `resolveTimeoutSetting` trims, then `const value = Number(raw)` and accepts any `Number.isInteger(value)` within 1000–600000. It judges `OPENCHAMBER_UPSTREAM_STALL_TIMEOUT_MS` (default 20000), `OPENCHAMBER_UPSTREAM_STALL_TIMEOUT_CONCURRENT_MS` (default 40000), and `OPENCHAMBER_RESUME_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS` (default 10000).
- Probe of the **real exported function** (`resolveEventStreamTimeouts(env, warn)`, imported from the module on the laptop; probe `~/git/fleet/probe-fs-env/probe2.mjs`), stall window:

  | spelling | result | warning |
  |---|---|---|
  | `20000` | 20000 | — |
  | `1e3` | **1000** | **none** |
  | `20000.0` | **20000** | **none** |
  | `0x4E20` | **20000** | **none** |
  | `+20000` | **20000** | **none** |
  | `20000junk` | 20000 (default) | warned |
  | `5.9` | 20000 (default) | warned |
  | `''` | 20000 (default) | — (correct: treated as unset) |

- `packages/web/server/lib/event-stream/timeouts.test.js` pins none of the exponent/radix/fraction spellings (no `1e3`/`0x`/`.0` cases).
- The house pattern this reader is cited as following — `ui-auth.js` `readRateLimitMaxAttempts` (#624) — requires `/^\d+$/` on the whole text before converting, so none of these spellings pass there.

Dedup: #689 cites this reader as a strict precedent for the `parseInt` remainder and does not cover these spellings; searches for `UPSTREAM_STALL` / `resolveEventStreamTimeouts` across open and closed issues return only #689. #696 covers the fs `Number(...)` readers, a different module.

## Why it matters

This reader exists specifically to avoid "running with a guessed value" for the event stream's timing windows, and its warning is the only signal an operator gets that a value was rejected. The silent-acceptance gap defeats both halves for the spellings most likely to appear in real config (scientific notation from generated config, hex from a copied constant, a trailing `.0` from a templating engine), and one of them (`1e3`) lands on the exact stall-window hazard the file's own header documents. Consistency with the whole-text decimal judgement used by the other strict env readers (#624, and #689/#696 for the remaining ones) closes the class.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `resolveTimeoutSetting` in `event-stream/timeouts.js` accepts only a whole-text plain decimal spelling (after the existing trim) within the existing bounds; exponent, radix-prefixed, signed, and fraction spellings (`1e3`, `0x4E20`, `20000.0`, `+20000`) warn and keep the default, matching the file's documented contract.
- [ ] Plain in-bounds values (`20000`, `1000`, `600000`) and the empty/unset case behave exactly as today.
- [ ] Unit tests in `timeouts.test.js` pin the spellings: `1e3`, `0x4E20`, `20000.0`, `+20000` warn + fall back for at least the stall window; `20000junk`/`5.9` coverage already implied by the contract is pinned if missing.

body:
## Summary

Four fs timing/size settings are judged by bare `Number(...)` plus a range check. Trailing junk falls back (it becomes `NaN`), but three other spelling classes are silently reinterpreted instead of falling back to the documented default:

- **Empty-but-present** (`VAR=` — the classic compose/systemd/shell-export accident): `Number('')` is `0`, and the two readers whose range check is `>= 0` accept it. An empty `OPENCHAMBER_GIT_READ_CACHE_TTL_MS` silently disables the git-read cache, and an empty `OPENCHAMBER_GIT_CHECK_IGNORE_TIMEOUT_MS` silently disarms the `git check-ignore` kill timeout — while the same variables *unset* give the defaults (30000 / 2500). Whitespace-only (`' '`) does the same.
- **Exponent / radix spellings**: `1e3` is honoured as 1000 and `0x10` as 16 by all four readers.
- **Fractions**: `5.9` is honoured as a 5.9 ms command timeout / check-ignore timeout / cache TTL, and as a 5-byte upload cap after `Math.floor`.

The strict precedent is established in this codebase (`ui-auth.js` `readRateLimitMaxAttempts`, #624, requires `/^\d+$/` first, with a comment naming exactly this failure mode); #689 covers the `parseInt` readers in lifecycle/relay. These four `Number(...)` readers are the remainder — #689's body mentions them only to note that junk becomes `NaN` there; the empty-string and exponent/radix acceptance was not covered.

## Evidence (verified on main `6a3096cf8`)

- `packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.js:126-130` — `createCommandTimeoutMs`: `Number(process.env.OPENCHAMBER_FS_EXEC_TIMEOUT_MS)`, accepts any finite `> 0` (default 5 min).
- `packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.js:136-140` — `createGitReadCacheTtlMs`: accepts any finite `>= 0` (default 30 s). The comment above it documents `0` as the intentional disable spelling; at `routes.js:679` `gitReadCacheTtlMs <= 0` bypasses the cache entirely.
- `packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.js:142-146` — `createUploadMaxBytes`: accepts any finite `> 0`, floored (default 100 MiB).
- `packages/web/server/lib/fs/search.js:99-103` — `createGitCheckIgnoreTimeoutMs`: accepts any finite `>= 0` (default 2500). At `search.js:160` the SIGKILL timeout for the spawned `git check-ignore` is only armed when the value is `> 0`, so `0` means a hung child is never killed and the search waits on its `close` event.
- Semantics probe (the exact reader expressions, copied verbatim, evaluated on Node on the laptop; probe `~/git/fleet/probe-fs-env`):

  | spelling | EXEC_TIMEOUT (def 300000) | CACHE_TTL (def 30000) | UPLOAD_MAX (def 104857600) | CHECK_IGNORE (def 2500) |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | unset | 300000 | 30000 | 104857600 | 2500 |
  | `''` | 300000 | **0** | 104857600 | **0** |
  | `' '` | 300000 | **0** | 104857600 | **0** |
  | `1e3` | 1000 | 1000 | 1000 | 1000 |
  | `0x10` | 16 | 16 | 16 | 16 |
  | `5.9` | 5.9 | 5.9 | 5 | 5.9 |
  | `5000junk` | 300000 | 30000 | 104857600 | 2500 |
  | `0` | 300000 | 0 | 104857600 | 0 |

- Existing tests pin only plain spellings (`'50'` in `fs/search.test.js:75`, `'5'` in `fs/routes.test.js:785`); no test pins empty, exponent, radix, or fraction spellings for any of the four.

Dedup: searches for `GIT_READ_CACHE_TTL`, `FS_UPLOAD_MAX`, `GIT_CHECK_IGNORE`, `FS_EXEC_TIMEOUT` across open and closed issues return nothing; #689 (the `parseInt` remainder) and #624 (login rate-limit vars) do not cover these readers.

## Why it matters

The empty-string case is the sharp edge: deployment files routinely carry a variable with an empty value, and here that silently (a) turns off the git-read cache the comment at `routes.js:131-135` added to absorb reload bursts, and (b) removes the only bound on a spawned `git check-ignore` child, so one hung git process hangs filesystem search with no timeout and no log line. Neither produces an error or a warning — the operator sees a slow UI, not a misread setting. The exponent/radix/fraction acceptance is the same inconsistency #624/#689 are eliminating everywhere else: a unit-suffixed or scientific value should fall back to the default, not become a 16 ms timeout or a 5-byte upload cap.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] All four readers (`createCommandTimeoutMs`, `createGitReadCacheTtlMs`, `createUploadMaxBytes` in `fs/routes.js`; `createGitCheckIgnoreTimeoutMs` in `fs/search.js`) accept only a whole-text plain decimal spelling (the `readRateLimitMaxAttempts` pattern) and otherwise return their default.
- [ ] An empty or whitespace-only value behaves exactly like unset (the default) for all four — in particular it must not disable the git-read cache or disarm the check-ignore timeout. An explicit `0` keeps working for the two readers that document it (cache TTL, check-ignore timeout).
- [ ] Unit tests pin the spellings for each reader: `''`, `' '`, `1e3`, `0x10`, `5.9`, `5000junk` fall back; plain values (`5000`, `50`, `5`, explicit `0` where documented) are honoured.

## Summary

Five environment timing settings are still judged by bare `parseInt`, which truncates and reinterprets malformed values instead of falling back to the default: `5000junk` is honoured as 5000, `5.9` becomes 5, and `1e3` becomes **1** — a 1 ms OpenCode health-check timeout, or a 1 ms relay batch window. The codebase's newer env readers all judge strictly and fall back with the default (one of them carries a comment explaining exactly this failure mode); these two readers are the remainder.

## Evidence (verified on main `83e200f62`)

- `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/lifecycle.js:48-59` — `parsePositiveInt` is `Number.parseInt(String(value ?? ''), 10)` with a `> 0` check. It judges four settings: `OPENCHAMBER_OPENCODE_HEALTH_TIMEOUT_MS` (default 5000, used as the health-probe `AbortSignal.timeout` at `:471`/`:861` and the manual abort timer at `:1395`), `OPENCHAMBER_OPENCODE_HEALTH_CONSECUTIVE_FAILURES` (default 20, the restart threshold at `:1874-1876`), `OPENCHAMBER_OPENCODE_HEALTH_INTERVAL_MS` (default 0, `:1911`), and `OPENCHAMBER_OPENCODE_HEALTH_CACHE_MS` (default 750, `:1798`).
- `packages/web/server/lib/relay/host-client.js:70-76` — `resolveBatchWindowMs` reads `OPENCHAMBER_RELAY_BATCH_WINDOW_MS` with `Number.parseInt(..., 10)` and accepts any finite result `>= 0`. Used for the frame-batching flush window at `:98`.
- Semantics check (the readers are module-private / evaluated at import, so the exact expressions were evaluated on Node 24 on the laptop; the parse expressions are copied verbatim):
  - lifecycle `parsePositiveInt(v, 5000)`: `5000`→5000, `5000junk`→**5000**, `5.9`→**5**, `1e3`→**1**, `0x10`→5000 (parseInt stops at `x`, yields 0, fallback), `-5`→5000, empty→5000.
  - relay window reader (default 150): `150`→150, `150junk`→**150**, `2.9`→**2**, `1e3`→**1**, `0x10`→**0** (a zero batch window — batching effectively disabled — from a hex spelling), `-5`→150, empty→150.
- The strict precedents in the same codebase:
  - `packages/web/server/lib/ui-auth/ui-auth.js:36-45` `readRateLimitMaxAttempts` (#624) requires `/^\d+$/` first, with the comment: "a bare Number(...) would silently honour '-5' …, '2.9', and '1e3'".
  - `packages/web/server/lib/event-stream/timeouts.js:28-38` — env timeout readers trim, then require an integer within bounds, warn, and keep the default.
  - `packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.js:126-147` and `fs/search.js:99-103` — `Number(...)` plus `Number.isFinite` and range checks (a trailing-junk value is `NaN` there and falls back; `parseInt` is the only common reader that *honours* the junk prefix).
- No test pins the parsing of either reader (searches for `HEALTH_TIMEOUT` / `BATCH_WINDOW` in test files return nothing).

Dedup: #624 covered only the two login rate-limit vars; #235 covered port env vars (`OPENCODE_PORT` etc.); #446 the CLI `--timeout`. No open or closed issue mentions `parsePositiveInt`, the `OPENCHAMBER_OPENCODE_HEALTH_*` vars, or `OPENCHAMBER_RELAY_BATCH_WINDOW_MS`.

## Why it matters

These are operator-facing knobs for exactly the moments an operator is debugging: health-check behaviour of the managed OpenCode (timeout, failure threshold before restart, probe interval/cache) and relay batching. A typo'd or unit-suffixed value (`5000ms`, `1e3`) does not produce an error or the default — it silently produces a nearly-zero timeout that makes the managed server look permanently unhealthy (restart loops against the consecutive-failures threshold) or a 1 ms batch window. Strict-with-fallback is the established house behaviour for env numbers; these readers are how the remaining inconsistency bites.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `parsePositiveInt` in `lifecycle.js` (or its replacement) accepts only a whole-text plain decimal spelling (the `readRateLimitMaxAttempts` pattern) and otherwise returns the fallback for all four `OPENCHAMBER_OPENCODE_HEALTH_*` settings.
- [ ] `resolveBatchWindowMs` in `relay/host-client.js` applies the same strict judgement to `OPENCHAMBER_RELAY_BATCH_WINDOW_MS` (an explicit in-range `0` may keep working if it is intentional; a hex/exponent spelling may not become 0/1).
- [ ] Unit tests pin the spellings: `5000junk`, `5.9`, `1e3`, `0x10` fall back for both readers; plain values (`5000`, `150`) are honoured.

## Summary

Two read routes still judge their `limit` query parameter with `z.coerce.number()` — the loose numeric judging the fleet has been removing route by route (#554, #592, #604, #632). `z.coerce` is `Number(...)` underneath, so spellings that are not plain decimal integers are silently reinterpreted instead of falling back to the route's default: `1e3` becomes 1000, `0x10` becomes 16, `2.0` becomes 2, an empty `?limit=` becomes 0, and `-5` passes through as -5. Only outright junk (`10junk`) reaches the `.catch(...)` fallback.

## Evidence (verified on main `83e200f62`)

- `packages/web/server/lib/model-choices/routes.js:37` — `z.coerce.number().int().catch(undefined).parse(req.query.limit)` feeds `modelChoiceService.summary({ limit })`. The service (`packages/web/server/lib/model-choices/service.js:37-40`) defaults an absent limit to 50 and clamps to 0..500, so a reinterpreted value changes the answer's meaning: `?limit=` (empty) yields **0 events** instead of the default 50, `-5` also yields 0 events, and `1e3` yields the 500 maximum instead of 50.
- `packages/web/server/lib/message-search/routes.js:37` — `limit: z.coerce.number().int().catch(20)` in the query schema, documented in the same file's header (`:14`) as "limit — page size, 1..200". The runtime (`packages/web/server/lib/message-search/runtime.js:187`) clamps to 1..200, so `?limit=` yields a page size of **1** instead of the default 20, `-5` also yields 1, and `1e3` yields 200.
- The house pattern these two routes missed: strict whole-text decimal helpers with a named fallback — e.g. `packages/web/server/lib/git/routes.js` `parseLogMaxCount`/`parseDiffContextLines` (header comment at `:25-31` explains exactly this defect class), `packages/web/server/lib/github/routes.js:88-99` and `packages/web/server/lib/gitlab/routes.js:139-152` canonical-number readers, and `packages/web/server/lib/routing` after #604/#632.
- Tests: `model-choices.test.js` exercises only `limit=2` and the service-level `limit: 0/1/undefined`; no route test pins a malformed limit spelling for either route.

### Laptop probe (against the real route registrations, stub service/runtime capturing the parsed limit)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-coerce-limits/probe.test.js` on the laptop (module files identical to main `83e200f62`), 2/2 pass, observed:

| `?limit=` | model-choices → service | message-search → runtime |
|---|---|---|
| `2` / `20` | 2 | 20 |
| `1e3` | **1000** | **1000** |
| `0x10` | **16** | **16** |
| `2.0` | **2** | **2** |
| *(empty)* | **0** | **0** |
| `-5` | **-5** | **-5** |
| `10junk` | undefined (default) | 20 (default) |
| absent | undefined (default) | 20 (default) |

Dedup: #554 covered GitLab MR number, GitHub page/number, find-in-files and plan-notes limits; #592 bindingRevision; #604/#632 routing hours/activeMinutes. No open or closed issue mentions the model-choices or message-search limit parsing.

## Why it matters

These are the last two `z.coerce.number()` query readers in the web server (repo-wide search). A client that serialises a limit oddly — or a hand-written request with a trailing/empty value — gets a silently different page size or, for model-choices, an empty event list that reads as "no history", instead of the documented default every sibling route now falls back to. Consistency is the point of the earlier fixes: a caller should be able to predict that a malformed number means "default" everywhere.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Both routes judge `limit` by a strict whole-text decimal rule (the existing canonical-number helper pattern): `1e3`, `0x10`, `2.0`, empty, and negative spellings fall back to the route default (model-choices: service default; message-search: 20); plain values like `0` (model-choices' deliberate no-events case, pinned by its service test) and `2` keep working.
- [ ] Route tests pin the fallbacks: at least `1e3`, empty, and `-5` for each route return the default-sized answer.
- [ ] No change to the services' own clamping (model-choices 0..500, message-search runtime 1..200) — the fix is at the parsing boundary only.

## Summary

In the VS Code runtime, a skill that lives at a repository root (`.agents/skills/…`, `.opencode/skills/…`, `.claude/skills/…`) is classified as `scope: 'user'` instead of `scope: 'project'` whenever the session's working directory is a **subdirectory** of a normal repository (where `.git` is a directory). The same layout in a linked worktree (where `.git` is a file), or a session opened at the repository root itself, classifies correctly as `project`. The web runtime classifies all of these correctly.

## Evidence (verified on main `83e200f62`)

- `packages/vscode/src/bridge-settings-runtime.ts:38-55` — `findWorktreeRootForSkills` stats each ancestor's `.git` and only stops when `stat.isFile()` is true (`:45`). In a normal repository `.git` is a directory, so the walk climbs past the repository root to the filesystem root and returns `null`.
- `packages/vscode/src/bridge-settings-runtime.ts:57-70` — `getProjectAncestors` then falls back to `stop = … || current`, so the ancestor list is just the working directory itself; the repository root is never in it.
- `packages/vscode/src/bridge-settings-runtime.ts:72-99` — `inferSkillScopeAndSourceFromLocation` checks whether the skill path is inside `<ancestor>/.opencode`, `<ancestor>/.claude/skills`, or `<ancestor>/.agents/skills` for one of those ancestors; with the root missing, a root-level project skill falls through to the user-roots check and returns `{ scope: 'user' }`. The result is consumed by `fetchOpenCodeSkillsFromApi` at `:168`.
- The web counterpart does it correctly: `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/skill-routes.js:119-132` — its `findWorktreeRootForSkills` stops on `fs.existsSync(path.join(current, '.git'))`, which matches both the directory (normal repo) and the file (linked worktree). The VS Code file's own sibling helper agrees: `packages/vscode/src/opencodeConfig.ts:815-822` `findWorktreeRoot` also uses `existsSync`.
- Existing tests do not cover the subdirectory case: `packages/vscode/src/bridge-settings-runtime.test.js` only exercises a working directory equal to the project root (which works by the `|| current` fallback, with no `.git` present at all).

### Laptop probe (against the real `fetchOpenCodeSkillsFromApi`, vscode/fetch stubbed as in the existing test)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-vscode-skill-scope/probe.test.ts` on the laptop (fork files identical to main `83e200f62` for this module — no commits touched it in between), 4/4 pass, observed scopes:

- normal repo (`.git` directory), working dir = repo root → `project` (correct)
- normal repo (`.git` directory), working dir = `packages/foo` under the root, skill at `<root>/.agents/skills/demo` → **`user`** (wrong)
- linked worktree (`.git` file), working dir = a subdirectory, skill at worktree root → `project` (correct)
- normal repo, working dir = `apps/bar`, skill at `<root>/.opencode/skills/demo` → **`user`** (wrong)

## Why it matters

Scope drives how the Settings/skills panel groups and treats a skill (project vs user). Any VS Code session opened on a folder inside a repository — monorepo package folders are the common case — silently demotes every repository-level skill to "user" scope, disagreeing with the web surface for the same project and the same OpenCode skill list. The asymmetry (works at the root and in linked worktrees, fails in subdirectories of a normal repo) makes it look like a data problem with the user's skills rather than a classification bug.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `findWorktreeRootForSkills` in `bridge-settings-runtime.ts` recognises a `.git` directory as well as a `.git` file (parity with the web `skill-routes.js` helper and with `opencodeConfig.ts`'s `findWorktreeRoot`), so ancestors include the repository root for a subdirectory working directory.
- [ ] Regression tests in `bridge-settings-runtime.test.js`: subdirectory of a normal repo classifies root-level `.agents`/`.opencode` skills as `project`; the linked-worktree and repo-root cases keep passing.
- [ ] No behaviour change for directories outside any repository (ancestors remain just the working directory) or for genuinely user-level skills under the home config roots.

## Summary

The probe-and-release port race that failed CI once in #666 (fixed for `gatekeeper-program.test.js`, follow-up filed as #676 for `self-handoff-process.test.js`) survives in two more test files that neither issue covers. Both pick a port by binding port 0, closing the probe, and handing the bare number to a spawned server — the same TOCTOU window: any other process on the machine can take the released port before the child binds, and the child then dies at startup or the suite's readiness loop talks to a stranger's listener.

Both suites are env-gated off by default, which is why CI has not hit this yet — but that is also when the race bites: a developer who enables the gate locally is usually running other suites and servers on the same machine, exactly the contention that makes probe-and-release lose.

## Evidence (verified on main `416570742` by code reading)

- `packages/web/server/opencode-sse-resume.test.js:341-350` — `freePort()` binds port 0 on 127.0.0.1, closes the probe, resolves the number.
- `packages/web/server/opencode-sse-resume.test.js:422` — `upstreamPort = await freePort()`, then `startUpstream()` (`:364-376`) spawns the real OpenCode driver with `OC_PORT=String(upstreamPort)`. A lost race surfaces as `OpenCode exited before it listened` or a 120 s `OpenCode did not start in time` readiness timeout. The suite is `describe.skipIf(!upstreamDriver)` (`:352`, gate `OPENCODE_RESUME_DRIVER`) — no CI workflow sets it, so this only ever runs on a developer machine. (The suite's own proxy server already does it the safe way: it binds port 0 itself and reads `proxyServer.address().port` at `:434`.)
- `packages/web/server/lib/spaces/places/dispatcher.docker.live.test.js:204-211` — identical `freePort()` probe-and-release helper.
- `packages/web/server/lib/spaces/places/dispatcher.docker.live.test.js:268` — `startServer({ ..., port: await freePort() })` spawns the real server with `--port <n>` (`:213-218`); a lost race surfaces as `the server left early` / `the server did not become healthy` after a 60 s deadline. Gated by `describe.skipIf(!LIVE_DOCKER_ENABLED)` (`:252`, imported from `docker-live-support.js:20`).
- Dedup: #666 covers `gatekeeper-program.test.js` and names only `self-handoff-process.test.js` as the sibling; #676 covers `self-handoff-process.test.js` only. A repo-wide search for `freePort` definitions on main returns exactly four test files — the two above are the uncovered remainder. No open or closed issue mentions `sse-resume` port selection or the dispatcher live test's port selection.

## Why it matters

title: fix(vscode): conflict-details reports success with an empty merge conflict when git cannot read the directory — bridge handler never checks the status/diff exit codes

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/vscode
labels.description: Package: vscode (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

In the VS Code runtime, `api:git/conflict-details` reports **success with an empty merge conflict** when git cannot read the directory at all — a non-repository, or any failure of the underlying `git status` / `git diff` commands. The web runtime rejects the same call, so the shared ConflictDialog's error path (`loadError` → "failed to load") never fires on VS Code; instead the dialog presents an empty conflict for a `merge` operation that may not exist, and the AI conflict-resolution context is built from that empty data.

This is the AGENTS.md invariant violation: *never let fetch failure masquerade as authoritative empty success.*

## Evidence (verified on main `4c11d1806`)

`packages/vscode/src/bridge-git-special-runtime.ts`, case `api:git/conflict-details` (:476):

- :483 `git status --porcelain` — `statusResult.exitCode` never checked; stdout read unconditionally.
- :486 `git diff --name-only --diff-filter=U` — exit code never checked.
- :492 `git diff` — exit code never checked.
- :498/:522 the `rev-parse --verify --quiet MERGE_HEAD` / `REBASE_HEAD` probes legitimately use the exit code (absence is their contract), and `operation` defaults to `'merge'` when neither exists.
- :535 the handler returns `success: true` with whatever the (possibly failed) reads produced. The surrounding `try/catch` cannot fire for git failures: `execGit` in `packages/vscode/src/bridge-git-process-runtime.ts:116-118` *returns* `{ exitCode: 1, stderr }` on failure — it never throws.

Web contrast — `packages/web/server/lib/git/service.js:7060` `getConflictDetails` first calls `createRepositoryGitContext(directory)` (:7061, defined :614), which throws for a non-repository before any read; its individual `.catch(() => '')` reads happen only after the repository is validated.

Consumer — `packages/ui/src/components/views/git/ConflictDialog.tsx:58-70`: a rejected read sets `loadError`; a successful empty read sets `conflictDetails` and `buildConflictContext` (:79+) then builds the AI resolve prompt from `operation: 'merge'`, empty `unmergedFiles`, empty `diff`, empty `headInfo`.

Existing tests — `packages/vscode/src/bridge-git-special-runtime.test.js` covers conflict-details for a main worktree, a linked worktree, and a genuinely absent MERGE_MSG (#656), but has no failure / non-repository case.

### Laptop probe (this run)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-vscode-conflict-failopen/probe.test.ts` on the laptop, importing the real `handleSpecialGitBridgeMessage` with a real `execGit` (temp dirs, bun test, 2 pass):

- Non-repository temp dir → `{"success":true,"data":{"statusPorcelain":"","unmergedFiles":[],"diff":"","headInfo":"","operation":"merge"}}`
- Control: a real conflicted merge in a temp repo → `success:true` with `statusPorcelain "UU file.txt"`, `unmergedFiles ["file.txt"]`, the conflict diff, and `headInfo` containing the merge message. The success path is healthy; only the failure path is indistinguishable from it in shape.

## Why it matters

The conflict dialog is opened precisely when the repository is in an unusual state. If git cannot read that state (wrong directory after a worktree move, corrupt/locked repository, git error), VS Code tells the user there is a merge with no conflicted files and no diff — and offers an AI resolution flow whose context payload is empty. The web surface reports the failure honestly for the identical UI.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `api:git/conflict-details` returns `success: false` with the git error surfaced when the directory is not a git repository, or when the `git status` read fails (the authoritative read); a failed `diff`/`diff --diff-filter=U` read is likewise not silently read as "no conflicts / no diff" — either the call fails or the failure is explicit in the response.
- [ ] The `MERGE_HEAD` / `REBASE_HEAD` quiet probes keep their absence-is-normal semantics (a repository with no operation in progress still answers successfully, as today).
- [ ] Successful-path behaviour is unchanged: the existing main-worktree, linked-worktree, and absent-MERGE_MSG tests pass unmodified in shape (same data fields and values).
- [ ] New regression tests in `packages/vscode/src/bridge-git-special-runtime.test.js`: (1) non-repository directory → `success: false`; (2) a stubbed `execGit` whose `status` call exits non-zero → `success: false` (or the explicit-failure shape chosen above).
- [ ] The fix lives in the bridge handler / its owning module, not in the shared UI: `ConflictDialog` already handles rejection correctly via its `loadError` path.

Dedup: searches for `conflict-details`, `getConflictDetails`, and "conflict details empty" returned only #656 (MERGE_MSG in linked worktrees, now closed via PR #658) — that issue was scoped to the merge-message read inside a working conflict read; this one is the unchecked status/diff reads and the missing repository validation. Sibling of the #650/#661/#662 fail-open family, in the bridge module rather than `gitService.ts`.

title: fix(vscode): selected-files commit can commit the wrong files — createGitCommit ignores every staging step's exit code

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/vscode
labels.description: Package: vscode (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

In the VS Code runtime, a commit of *selected* files can silently commit the wrong set of files. The selective-commit path in `createGitCommit` performs its index surgery (unstage everything not selected, stage the selection, commit, restore) while ignoring the exit code of every staging step. If the unstage or the stage step fails, the commit still runs — over whatever the index actually contains — and reports success.

## Evidence (verified on main `4c11d1806` by code reading)

`packages/vscode/src/gitService.ts`, `createGitCommit` selective path (`options.files` + `options.stageFiles`), `:2976-3020`:

- `:2983` — `stagedResult = await execGit(['diff', '--cached', '--name-only'], directory)` — exit code never checked; on failure its empty stdout is read as "nothing is staged", so no non-selected files are unstaged.
- `:2991` — `await execGit(['restore', '--staged', '--', ...temporarilyUnstagedFiles], directory)` — exit code never checked. If this unstage fails (index lock, corrupt index, pathspec error), the non-selected staged files **stay staged**.
- `:2994` — `await execGit(['add', '--', ...options.stageFiles], directory)` — exit code never checked. If staging a selected file fails, the commit proceeds anyway.
- `:2997-3006` — the subsequent `git commit` exit code *is* checked, and on success the function returns `success: true` with the new hash. So the failure sequence "unstage failed → commit runs over the un-unstaged index" produces a successful commit containing files the user explicitly did not select. Symmetrically, "add failed → nothing selected is staged, but other files were already staged" commits those other files as if they were the selection.
- `:3017` — the `finally` restore (`git add` of the temporarily unstaged files) is likewise unchecked and unlogged, so a failed restore silently leaves the user's index in the altered state.
- The bridge passes the result straight through: `packages/vscode/src/bridge-git-runtime.ts:350-364` (`api:git/commit`) returns `success: true` with `createGitCommit`'s result as data.

## Contrast (the web runtime does this correctly)

`packages/web/server/lib/git/service.js` `commit` (`:4327` onward) implements the same selective-commit dance defensively:

- It resolves and validates the selection against live `git status()` and **throws** "No selected files are available to commit" when the selection matches nothing (`:4384-4386`).
- Every staging step goes through simple-git (`git.raw(['restore', '--staged', ...])` at `:4398`, `git.raw(['add', ...])` at `:4424`), which **rejects on a non-zero exit**, aborting the commit.
- Commit errors are rethrown (`:4457-4464`), and restore failures after the commit are at least logged (`:4439-4441`, `:4452-4454`).

The VS Code port checks none of this. This violates the repo's correctness invariants (`AGENTS.md`): "Make partial results, rollback, cleanup, and stale-data behavior explicit" and "Never let fetch failure masquerade as authoritative empty success."

## Verification note

Verified by code reading on current main; the unchecked calls are literal in source and the web counterpart's checks are explicit. No laptop probe this run: laptop SSH is unreachable fleet-wide today ("Connection closed by UNKNOWN port 65535", rechecked this run; tracked in dezren39/nix#1020 / developing-today/code#1667).

Dedup: searches for `createGitCommit`, "temporarily unstaged", and "selected files commit vscode" returned no covering issue.

## Why it matters

Committing files the user did not select is one of the worst silent failures a source-control UI can produce: work-in-progress, secrets-adjacent scratch files, or another change's half-finished edits can be published inside a commit whose message describes a different change — and the UI reports it as the intended, successful commit.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The selective path checks every staging step: a failed `diff --cached`, `restore --staged`, or `add` aborts the commit with the git error surfaced (throw or `success: false` carrying the error) — no commit is attempted over an index whose state is not the intended one.
- [ ] A failed restore of temporarily unstaged files (in the `finally`) is surfaced or at minimum logged, matching the web implementation — never silently swallowed.
- [ ] Regression tests (following the existing `gitService.*.test.*` patterns) cover: normal selective commit commits exactly the selection (unchanged behaviour); unstage failure → no commit created and failure reported; stage failure for a selected file → no commit of other staged files.
- [ ] The non-selective paths (Git API repository path, raw add-all/files fallback) are unchanged except where the same unchecked-step defect applies to them.
- [ ] Successful-path behaviour is unchanged: same commit contents, hash/branch reporting, and index restoration as today.

title: fix(vscode): git identity write reports success when every git config write fails — setGitIdentity raw fallback ignores all exit codes

body:
## Problem

In the VS Code runtime, writing a git identity reports success even when every underlying `git config` write failed. A user (or the identity picker) can pick an identity, be told it was applied, and then commit under the old/wrong author — or no author — with no error anywhere.

## Evidence (verified on main `4c11d1806` by code reading)

- `packages/vscode/src/gitService.ts:3825` — `setGitIdentity(directory, userName, userEmail, sshKey, signCommits, signingKey)`.
- `packages/vscode/src/gitService.ts:3858-3866` — the raw fallback path runs `git config user.name`, `user.email`, and (when requested) `core.sshCommand`, `gpg.format`, `user.signingkey`, `commit.gpgsign` via `execGit(...)` and **discards every result** — no `exitCode` is ever checked.
- `packages/vscode/src/gitService.ts:3869` — the function then returns `{ success: true }` unconditionally.
- The fallback is reached whenever the VS Code Git API repository lookup returns null (`getRepository`, `gitService.ts:246-262`: API unavailable, repository not yet discovered/openable). In a directory that is not a git repository, every one of those `git config` invocations exits non-zero (fatal: not in a git directory) and writes nothing — yet the caller still receives success. The same masking applies to a locked/unwritable `.git/config` or a failed signing-key write in a real repository: a partial identity (name set, signing config missing) is reported as fully applied.
- The bridge compounds it: `packages/vscode/src/bridge-git-runtime.ts:613-647` (`api:git/identity`, POST) validates only that `userName`/`userEmail` are non-empty and returns `success: true` with the result as data.
- The primary (Git API) path at `gitService.ts:3843-3855` at least logs a `setConfig` failure before falling through — but the fallthrough then masks it via the unchecked raw path above.

## Contrast (the web runtime does this correctly)

- `packages/web/server/lib/git/service.js` `setLocalIdentity` (~:2671-2691): the same writes go through simple-git and a failure is rethrown (`console.error(...); throw error;`).
- `clearLocalIdentity` in the same file (~:2656-2669) documents the discipline explicitly: `git config --unset` exit 5 (key not set) is the ordinary case; "Anything else (a locked `.git/config`, a repository that is not one) means the author stayed" — and it throws.

This also violates the repo invariant in `AGENTS.md`: "Never let fetch failure masquerade as authoritative empty success" — here a *write* failure masquerades as a successful write.

## Verification note

Verified by code reading on current main; the defect is a literal unconditional `return { success: true }` after unchecked calls, and the web contrast is explicit in source. No laptop probe this run: laptop SSH is unreachable fleet-wide today ("Connection closed by UNKNOWN port 65535", rechecked this run; tracked in dezren39/nix#1020 / developing-today/code#1667). No existing VS Code test references `setGitIdentity` or the `api:git/identity` failure path.

Dedup: searches for `setGitIdentity`, "git identity success", and "identity config" returned no covering issue (closest are the sibling VS Code fail-open filings #661/#662/#663/#664/#665, which cover branch/remote/reset/list reads — not identity writes).

## Why it matters

Identity is authorship. A silently unapplied identity means commits attributed to the wrong person, unsigned commits where signing was requested and reported on, and a settings UI that cannot be trusted — discovered, if at all, only after the commits are pushed.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `setGitIdentity`'s raw fallback checks every `execGit` result: a non-zero exit surfaces as a failure (throw, or `{ success: false }` with the git error) instead of unconditional `{ success: true }`.
- [ ] Calling it for a non-repository directory reports failure and writes nothing.
- [ ] A partial failure (e.g. `user.name` written, signing config failed) is reported as a failure, not as a fully applied identity.
- [ ] The bridge `api:git/identity` POST no longer wraps a failed write in an unqualified `success: true` envelope.
- [ ] Regression tests cover: successful write (unchanged behaviour), non-repository directory, and a failing config write (e.g. locked config) — following the existing `gitService.*.test.*` patterns.
- [ ] Successful-path behaviour is unchanged: same keys written, same order, SSH/signing configuration identical.

## Finding

`packages/web/server/lib/source-control/audit-storage.test.js` — "preserves sibling lifecycle writes from independent processes and allows one terminal transition" — failed once in CI today, and the failure as recorded cannot be diagnosed: the assertion at `audit-storage.test.js:45` is

```js
expect(results.every((result) => result.ok)).toBe(true);
```

which throws away *which* child call failed and *what error it returned*. The CI log shows only `AssertionError: expected false to be true`. The next occurrence will be just as opaque unless the test surfaces the failing results.

## Evidence

- CI run 40666724995 (oc-review, push to main, 2026-10-28T09:45Z): the tests job failed on exactly this one test; type-check, lint and build passed, and later oc-review runs on main the same day passed — intermittent, not a steady regression.
- The test spawns two independent child processes (`storage-process.test-support.js`) that plan/start/finish sibling records against one audit file. Writes go through `withSourceControlFileLock` (`audit-storage.js:194,205`) with a default `lockWaitMs` of **2000 ms**: if a sibling holds the lock longer than that under load, the waiting call fails with `SOURCE_CONTROL_LOCK_BUSY`. The full CI suite runs ~500 s of tests across parallel workers, so a >2 s lock wait under load is plausible — but with the error discarded, this is a guess, and a genuine lost-update or stale-lock bug in the store cannot be ruled out either.
- Dedup: no open or closed issue covers this test or failure (`audit-storage` search returns only unrelated closed issues #117 and #531).

- [ ] The audit-storage suite passes repeatedly under parallel load (full `packages/web` suite, not only the file solo).

body:
# fix(web): walkthrough silently drops every untracked file when `git ls-files` fails — listUntrackedPaths returns [] on any failure

## Evidence (verified on main `4c11d1806`, code reading)

- `packages/web/server/lib/git/service.js:3467-3475` — `listUntrackedPaths`:

  ```js
  const { repoRoot } = await createRepositoryGitContext(directory);
  const result = await runGitCommand(repoRoot, ['ls-files', '--others', '--exclude-standard']);
  if (!result.success) return [];
  ```

  `createRepositoryGitContext` (`service.js:614-625`) already throws for a
  non-repository (via `resolveGitRepositoryRoot`), so by the time `ls-files`
  runs the directory **is** a repository — the `return []` can only fire on a
  real git failure (corrupt index, dubious-ownership refusal, unreadable path),
  and it discards git's stderr and reports "there are no untracked files".
- Sole production caller: `packages/web/server/lib/walkthrough/sources.js:96-102`
  — `untrackedSections` treats `[]` as authoritative: a walkthrough of local
  work then contains only tracked diffs, with no signal that the untracked set
  could not be read. The header at `sources.js:93-95` explains untracked files
  are included precisely because "a brand-new file would be invisible in a
  walkthrough of local work" — a failed read makes *every* new file invisible,
  silently, which is the failure mode that inclusion exists to prevent.
- The function's own doc (`service.js:3455-3466`) is careful about a different
  silent-loss mode (why `--directory` is not used) but says nothing about
  failure — unlike its neighbours, which document and implement the
  distinction: `getWorktrees` (`service.js:4871`, `[]` only for
  `isNotGitRepositoryError`, throw otherwise, with a comment explaining why)
  and `getRemotes` (`service.js:6839-6841`, same shape). `runGitCommand`
  (`service.js:1173-1208`) already returns `message`/`stderr` for the throw.
- No test pins the failure branch: `listUntrackedPaths` appears in tests only
  as a mock (`walkthrough/jobs.test.js:16`, `walkthrough/language.test.js:14`).

## Why it matters

A walkthrough is a review surface: a reader trusts that the sections shown are
the whole change. A transient or repository-state git failure currently
produces a walkthrough that looks complete but omits every untracked file —
new files are usually the most important part of local work. This violates the
repo invariant in `AGENTS.md`: "Never let fetch failure masquerade as
authoritative empty success."

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `listUntrackedPaths` throws (surfacing git's error text) when the
      `ls-files` read fails; it returns `[]` only when the read succeeds and
      there genuinely are no untracked files. (Non-repositories already throw
      earlier via `createRepositoryGitContext` — that behaviour is unchanged.)
- [ ] A walkthrough of local work on a repository whose `ls-files` fails now
      surfaces the failure instead of presenting a tracked-only walkthrough as
      complete.
- [ ] Successful behaviour is byte-identical: same paths, same order, ignore
      rules still honoured (`--exclude-standard`), no `--directory`.
- [ ] Regression tests cover: repository with untracked files (unchanged

# fix(web): repository remote list reports any `git remote` failure as 'no remotes' — getRepositoryRemoteUrls returns [] on failure, unlike its own per-remote fallback

## Evidence (verified on main `4c11d1806`, code reading)

- `packages/web/server/lib/git/service.js:1526-1531` — `getRepositoryRemoteUrls`
  runs `git remote` and `git remote -v` in parallel, then:

  ```js
  if (!namesResult.success) return [];
  ```

  Any failure of the names read — corrupt `.git/config`, dubious-ownership
  refusal, a git binary error — is returned as an authoritative empty remote
  list, with stderr discarded. There is no not-a-repository distinction.
- The function's own header (`service.js:1519-1525`) states the design intent
  for the sibling read: "When the listing itself fails, each remote is asked on
  its own, **so a failure never reads as URL-less remotes**." The names read
  violates the same principle one step earlier: a failure reads as *no remotes
  at all*, which is strictly worse.
- Callers have already established that the directory is a repository before
  this is called on the identity path:
  `packages/web/server/lib/source-control/repository-identity.js:15-17`
  (`resolveRepositoryGitPaths` first; unsupported repositories return early),
  so on that path `[]` cannot be a legitimate not-a-repository answer — yet the
  resolver at `:22-27` folds the empty list into `remotes: []` and into the
  `configRevision` hash at `:33-42`. A transient git failure therefore produces
  a different, wrong-but-authoritative repository identity (and a flapping
  config revision when git recovers).
- Second caller: `packages/web/server/lib/git/worktree-creation.js:124-125` and
  `:139-140` — change-request worktree creation looks up the primary remote in
  the result; an empty list silently drops `requestedRemoteName`/`remoteUrl`
  resolution instead of surfacing the failure.
- In-repo precedents for the correct shape: web `getRemotes`
  (`service.js:6839-6841`) returns `[]` only for `isNotGitRepositoryError` and
  throws otherwise; web `getWorktrees` (`service.js:4871`) does the same with an
  explicit comment that any other failure is a failure. `runGitCommand`
  (`service.js:1173-1208`) already returns `message`/`stderr` for the throw.
- Existing tests (`service.test.js:5447-5491`) cover only the success paths of
  `getRepositoryRemoteUrls`; no test pins the failure branch.

## Why it matters

Repository identity feeds source-control binding and credential decisions, and
its `configRevision` is meant to change only when the repository's remotes
actually change. Today a single failed `git remote` makes the server believe —
and record — that the repository has no remotes, contradicting the repo
invariant in `AGENTS.md`: "Never let fetch failure masquerade as authoritative
empty success."

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `getRepositoryRemoteUrls` throws (surfacing git's error text) when the
      `git remote` names read fails for a reason other than not-a-repository;
      it returns `[]` only for the not-a-repository case (matching `getRemotes`
      / `getWorktrees`).
- [ ] The existing `-v` listing failure path is unchanged: per-remote
      `get-url` fallback still runs, and successful reads return exactly what
      they return today (including the partial-clone annotation handling).
- [ ] `resolveRepositoryIdentity` on a real repository whose `git remote`
      fails now surfaces the failure instead of minting an identity with
      `remotes: []` / an empty-remotes `configRevision`.
- [ ] Regression tests cover: repository with remotes (unchanged output),
      repository with genuinely no remotes (`[]`), non-repository (`[]`), and
      a names-read failure (e.g. corrupt `.git/config`) rejecting.
- [ ] No change to `parseRemoteListing` or the `{name, fetchUrl, pushUrl}`
      shape.

Verification note: laptop SSH was unreachable this run (fleet-wide outage
since ~06:17 CDT), so no laptop probe was run; the defect is a literal
unconditional `return []` on `!namesResult.success`, contrasted with the
function's own documented intent and two sibling functions in the same file.
Dedup: searches for `getRepositoryRemoteUrls`, `remote urls identity`, and
`untracked paths` returned no covering issue; #662 covers the VS Code
`getRemotes`, not this web function.

# fix(vscode): hard-reset safety check fails open — resetToCommit treats a failed `git status` as a clean tree

## Evidence (verified on main `4c11d1806`, code reading against the web counterpart)

- `packages/vscode/src/gitService.ts:4136-4142` — `resetToCommit`'s uncommitted-changes guard for `mode === 'hard' && !force`:

  ```ts
  const statusResult = await execGit(['status', '--porcelain'], directory);
  const isDirty = statusResult.stdout.trim().length > 0;
  ```

  `statusResult.exitCode` is never checked. On any `git status` failure, stdout is
  empty, so `isDirty` is `false` and the guard passes — the code then runs
  `git reset --hard <hash>` at `:4145-4148`. A failed status read is
  indistinguishable from a clean tree in this code.
- The web counterpart fails closed: `packages/web/server/lib/git/service.js:4799-4813`
  — `resetToCommit` awaits `git.status()` (simple-git), which **rejects** on a git
  failure, so the reset never runs when the status read fails. Its dirty case is
  pinned by `service.test.js:5219` (hard reset on a dirty tree rejects).
- The bridge exposes this directly: `packages/vscode/src/bridge-git-runtime.ts:568`
  calls `gitService.resetToCommit(directory, hash, mode, force)` for
  `api:git/reset` after validating hash and mode only.
- No VS Code `gitService` test covers `resetToCommit` (only the bridge mock in
  `bridge-git-runtime.test.js`); the guard's failure branch is untested.
- This violates the repo invariant in `AGENTS.md`: "Never let fetch failure
  masquerade as authoritative empty success" — here, as an authoritative *clean*
  success in front of a destructive operation.

## Why it matters

The guard is the only thing standing between the UI and `git reset --hard`
discarding uncommitted work when the caller did not pass `force`. A status
failure (corrupt index, dubious-ownership refusal, an unreadable path that makes
porcelain exit non-zero, a broken submodule) silently disarms it exactly in the
repositories that are already in a strange state — the ones where an accidental
hard reset hurts most. The web runtime proves the intended semantics: unknown
status means no reset.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `resetToCommit` throws (surfacing git's stderr) when the pre-reset
      `git status --porcelain` exits non-zero, for `mode === 'hard' && !force`;
      the reset command is not executed in that case.
- [ ] Clean tree + hard reset without force still succeeds; dirty tree + hard
      reset without force still throws the existing "Cannot hard reset" error;
      `force: true` still skips the check; soft/mixed modes are unchanged.
- [ ] Regression tests in the existing VS Code gitService test style cover: a
      status failure (e.g. corrupt `.git/config` or a non-repository directory)
      rejects and does not move HEAD, plus the clean/dirty cases above.
- [ ] No change to the web service, the bridge contract, or the
      `isValidCommitHash` validation.

Verification note: laptop SSH was unreachable this run (fleet-wide outage since
~06:17 CDT), so no laptop probe was run; the defect is a literal unchecked
`exitCode` on the guard's only read, contrasted with the web implementation in
the same repo. Dedup: searches for `resetToCommit`, `hard reset`, and
`uncommitted changes` returned no covering issue (#653 covers option-like ref
arguments to reset-adjacent commands, not this guard).

## Problem

In the VS Code runtime, `getRemotes` returns an empty list on **any** `git remote -v` failure. A corrupt repository, a dubious-ownership (`safe.directory`) refusal, or any other git error is indistinguishable from a repository that genuinely has no remotes — under a `success: true` bridge response. The web runtime makes exactly the distinction the VS Code port drops: it returns `[]` only for the not-a-repository case and throws for every other failure.

## Evidence (verified on main `3eed3e1bb`)

- `packages/vscode/src/gitService.ts:3877-3882` `getRemotes`: `if (result.exitCode !== 0) { return []; }` — no stderr inspection, no distinction between "not a repository" and any other failure, and unlike sibling functions in the same file there is no VS Code Git API path: this raw call is the only path.
- The bridge turns that into success: `packages/vscode/src/bridge-git-runtime.ts:451` `api:git/remotes` (GET) returns `{ success: true, data: result }` for whatever `getRemotes` returns.
- The web service draws the line explicitly: `packages/web/server/lib/git/service.js` `getRemotes` (`:6827-6845`) returns `[]` **only** when `isNotGitRepositoryError(error)` (`:6839-6841`) and otherwise logs and throws (`console.error('Failed to get remotes:', error); throw error;`). The repo's own `AGENTS.md:58` invariant: "Never let fetch failure masquerade as authoritative empty success."
- The fixed sibling in the same file sets the precedent: `getGitStatusRaw` (`gitService.ts:614-622`, fixed for #650) throws with git's stderr instead of fabricating an empty success.
- Consumers treat the empty list as authoritative: `packages/ui/src/components/views/GitView.tsx:989-994` and `packages/ui/src/apps/MobileChangesSurface.tsx:637` read the remote list to drive push/pull/remote UI — a failed read silently presents "this repository has no remotes", hiding the controls and the actual error (e.g. git's dubious-ownership message, which is actionable).
- No test pins any of this: no file under `packages/vscode/src/*.test.*` references `getRemotes`.
- Verification this run is by code reading against the web counterpart (the laptop is unreachable — SSH outage since ~06:17 CDT 2026-10-28 — so the usual laptop probe could not run; the defect is a literal unconditional `return []` on `exitCode !== 0`, and the web contrast is explicit in source).

## Why it matters

Remotes are the user's path to push/pull. When the read fails for a real, fixable reason — most concretely git's `detected dubious ownership` refusal, whose stderr tells the user exactly how to fix it — the VS Code surface silently claims there are no remotes at all. The user loses the remote UI and never sees the actionable error, and the surface disagrees with the web runtime for the same directory. Same silent-empty family as #644/#645/#650, in the remotes path.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `getRemotes` returns `[]` only for the not-a-repository case (matching the web `isNotGitRepositoryError` distinction, e.g. by matching git's stderr or probing with `rev-parse` as `checkIsGitRepository` at `gitService.ts:356` does) and throws — surfacing stderr — for any other `git remote -v` failure.
- [ ] `api:git/remotes` consequently answers `success: false` for a corrupt/dubious-ownership directory instead of `success: true` with an empty list, while a non-repository directory keeps answering an empty list as the web does.
- [ ] A real repository's remotes (name, fetchUrl, pushUrl via `parseGitRemoteListing`) are returned exactly as today, and a repository with genuinely no remotes still returns `[]`.
- [ ] Regression tests in the existing VS Code gitService bun-test style (mocked `vscode`, temp dirs) prove: real repo with a remote returns it; repo with no remotes returns `[]`; non-repo returns `[]`; a failure that is not "not a repository" (e.g. a corrupt `.git/config`) rejects.
- [ ] No change to the web service (already distinguishes the cases) and no change to the `GitRemote` shape.

## Problem

In the VS Code runtime, when the raw git fallback cannot list branches at all, `getGitBranches` returns a fabricated success: no branches, no current branch, an empty branch map. A directory that is not a git repository, a corrupt repository, a dubious-ownership (`safe.directory`) refusal, or any other `git branch` failure is indistinguishable from a repository that genuinely has no branches — under a `success: true` bridge response. The web runtime throws for the same inputs, and the sibling status fallback in the same file was already fixed to throw (#650).

## Evidence (verified on main `3eed3e1bb`)

- `packages/vscode/src/gitService.ts:766-771` `getGitBranchesRaw` (the fallback `getGitBranches` uses at `:713` when `getRepository` returns null — VS Code Git API unavailable or the repository not opened): on **any** non-zero `git branch` exit it returns `{ all: [], current: '', branches: {} }`. The stderr is discarded, so no caller can tell failure from an empty branch list.
- The bridge turns that into success: `packages/vscode/src/bridge-git-runtime.ts:115-116` `api:git/branches` (GET) returns `{ success: true, data: branches }` for whatever `getGitBranches` returns.
- The web service is explicit about the opposite contract: `packages/web/server/lib/git/service.js` `getBranches` (`:4467`) builds its context via `createRepositoryGitContext` (which throws for a non-repository) and re-throws branch failures after logging (`:4492-4495`, `console.error('Failed to get branches:', error); throw error;`). The repo's own `AGENTS.md:58` invariant states it directly: "Never let fetch failure masquerade as authoritative empty success."
- The fixed sibling in the same file sets the precedent: `getGitStatusRaw` (`gitService.ts:614-622`, fixed for #650) throws with git's stderr, with a comment stating "A failed status read is not a clean repository: surface git's error instead of fabricating an empty success."
- Secondary consumer inside the same module: `getGitUnpushedBranchCounts` (`gitService.ts:692`) builds its local-branch set from `getGitBranchesRaw`, so a failed branch read silently reports `{ counts: {} }` (no unpushed commits anywhere) for a repository whose branches could not be read at all.
- UI consumers trust the list as authoritative: the branch picker and `packages/ui/src/lib/worktrees/worktreeCreate.ts:55` / `autoDraftWorktree.ts:236` read branch state through `getGitBranches` to decide checkout/worktree behaviour; an authoritative-empty answer on a real repository reads as "no branches exist".
- No test pins any of this: no file under `packages/vscode/src/*.test.*` references `getGitBranches` or `getGitBranchesRaw`.
- Verification this run is by code reading against the web counterpart (the laptop is unreachable — SSH outage since ~06:17 CDT 2026-10-28 — so the usual laptop probe could not run; the defect is a literal unconditional return on `exitCode !== 0` with stderr discarded, and the web contrast is explicit in source).

## Why it matters

A branch read that fails — the directory was moved, the repo is corrupt, git refused on dubious ownership — currently renders in VS Code as a repository with no branches and no current branch. That hides exactly the situations a user most needs surfaced, can steer worktree creation and branch switching against a phantom empty state, and breaks parity with the web runtime, which errors. This is the same silent-empty family as #644/#645/#650, in the branch-list path instead of the diff/commit/status paths.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `getGitBranchesRaw` throws on a non-zero `git branch` exit (surfacing stderr), mirroring the web `getBranches` contract — including a recognisable `fatal: not a git repository…` error for a non-repository directory.
- [ ] `api:git/branches` consequently answers `success: false` for a non-repository/corrupt directory instead of `success: true` with an empty branch list.
- [ ] A real repository's branch list (local + remote, current branch, tracking info) is returned exactly as today, on both the raw fallback and the VS Code Git API path; a genuinely branch-less repository state keeps working.
- [ ] `getGitUnpushedBranchCounts` no longer silently reports `{ counts: {} }` when the underlying branch read failed.
- [ ] Regression tests in the existing VS Code gitService bun-test style (mocked `vscode`, temp dirs) prove: non-repo directory rejects; a real repo returns its branches and current branch.
- [ ] No change to the web service (already throws) and no change to the `GitBranchResult` shape.

title: fix(quota): Meta provider read fails after the 5h window rolls — /api/quota/meta returns 'No quota data in response'

body:
## Bug

The Meta (Muse High Usage) quota provider in OpenChamber's quota API has returned no data since its 5-hour window rolled at 00:01 CDT on 2026-10-28. Every read of `/api/quota/meta` since then returns `ok:false` with the error **"No quota data in response"**.

The provider itself is live — it shipped with the #523 work and was deployed on 2026-10-27 (~14:32 CDT). It is the post-roll state that breaks it.

## Evidence (fleet-observed, laptop OpenChamber instance)

- **2026-10-27, all evening:** reads healthy — snapshots from the babysitter/steward rounds show Meta at 5h 0% / weekly 10%.
- **2026-10-28 00:01 CDT:** the Meta 5h window rolled, expiring **unspent** (the second consecutive window to expire unspent).
- **2026-10-28 ~00:19 CDT onward:** every `/api/quota/meta` read fails with `ok:false`, "No quota data in response". Confirmed independently by the babysitter, dispatcher, and pool-quota-steward rounds at ~00:19, ~02:17, ~04:24, and ~05:58 CDT — the failure is continuous, not intermittent.
- Reads of the other providers on the same instance were unaffected in the same rounds (opencode-go, cline-pass, command-code all returned data), so this is specific to the Meta provider's handling of its upstream response, not a general quota-API outage.
- Note: reads after ~06:17 CDT on 2026-10-28 are additionally blocked by a laptop SSH outage (unrelated, tracked separately); the last verified state before that outage was still failing.

## Why it matters

- The dispatcher's binding measurement gate treats an unreadable pool as **closed**: no fleet session may draw on the Meta plan until a fresh read succeeds. The pool's quota is currently unusable *and* unverifiable — there is no way to tell how much of the window remains.
- A window roll happens every 5 hours, so if the trigger is the roll (especially an unspent expiry), this recurs constantly and the Meta pool is effectively permanently dark to the fleet.
- Process note: the failure was logged by three oversight jobs for ~5 hours before this issue was filed. Filed by the operator per the file-the-issue rule once that gap was spotted.

## Suspected shape (for triage to confirm)

The provider's parse/read path likely mishandles the upstream response shape in the post-roll state — e.g. a fresh window with no usage records yet, or an empty/absent current-window entry after an unspent expiry — and reports the generic "No quota data in response" instead of a zero/empty reading. Triage should reproduce against the live endpoint's upstream response in the post-roll state and pin the exact branch.

## Acceptance criteria

- `/api/quota/meta` returns `ok:true` with current 5h/weekly figures immediately after a window roll, including when the prior window expired unspent.
- Regression coverage for the post-roll / empty-window upstream response shape that reproduces this failure.
- If the upstream genuinely carries no usage data in that state, the endpoint distinguishes "window open, no usage yet" (a zero reading) from a read failure, so the measurement gate can tell an empty pool from a broken one.

title: fix(ui): a disabled-provider read started before a Settings toggle can overwrite the post-toggle snapshot (PR #588 race)

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

body:
## Finding

PR #588's disabled-provider snapshot can be overwritten by a read that started before a Settings toggle. `loadDisabledProviders` guards the snapshot only against other *reads* (the `latestRead` counter), but `setProviderDisabled` records the post-toggle list through `rememberDisabledProviders`, which does not advance that counter. A slow read started before the toggle that resolves after it therefore still passes the `read === latestRead` check and writes its pre-toggle list back into the snapshot. Because `ensureDisabledProviders` serves the snapshot without refetching once one exists, the stale list then keeps filtering every location's catalog: a provider just turned off can reappear in pickers (the exact failure #323 / PR #588 set out to fix), and a provider just turned back on can stay hidden, until something calls `loadDisabledProviders` again (e.g. opening Settings > Providers).

The same supersession gap applies to the value a caller awaits: `loadDisabledProviders` returns its own fetched list even when a newer read/write has superseded it, and `useConfigStore` filters the catalog it is applying with that returned value.

## Evidence

- Source PR: #588 (`fix(providers): filter turned-off providers from every location picker`, commit `7c0eeb14`, merge `5ed28ea5`) introduced the snapshot, `latestRead`, `loadDisabledProviders`, `ensureDisabledProviders`, and the `rememberDisabledProviders` call in `setProviderDisabled`.
- Current main `packages/ui/src/lib/disabledProviders.ts:31` — `let latestRead = 0;` is only incremented inside `loadDisabledProviders` (line 50).
- Current main `packages/ui/src/lib/disabledProviders.ts:38-40` — `rememberDisabledProviders` sets `snapshot` without touching `latestRead`, so it does not invalidate a read already in flight.
- Current main `packages/ui/src/lib/disabledProviders.ts:48-56` — `loadDisabledProviders` writes `snapshot = { runtimeKey, providers }` whenever `read === latestRead`, including a read whose fetch began (and whose server response was produced) before a toggle landed via `setProviderDisabled` (line 102, `rememberDisabledProviders(providers)`).
- Current main `packages/ui/src/lib/disabledProviders.ts:64-67` — `ensureDisabledProviders` returns the existing snapshot without refetching, so a stale snapshot persists for later catalog loads.
- The PR's own comment states the intent the write path misses: "A read started earlier never replaces one started later, so a slow first read cannot bring back the state from before a Settings change" — a Settings *change* is exactly the `setProviderDisabled` write, not another read.
- No test in PR #588 covers a read/write interleaving; its new store test covers only the plain second-location filtering case.

## Why it matters

This is a narrow race (a catalog/prefetch read must be in flight while the user toggles a provider), but its effect is sticky rather than transient: the stale snapshot is cached for the runtime and reused by every later catalog load and cache hydration, so the wrong provider set can be offered for the rest of the session with no error anywhere.

## Acceptance criteria

- A read that started before a `setProviderDisabled` write can no longer overwrite the post-write snapshot (e.g. the write path advances/invalidates the same generation counter the read path checks, or reads re-check a write generation before committing).
- A superseded read's returned value is not used to filter a catalog being applied; callers filter with the latest snapshot (or the read is retried/replaced) instead.
- A regression test with a deferred fetch pins the interleaving: start a load, complete a toggle via `setProviderDisabled`, then resolve the load with the pre-toggle list and assert `peekDisabledProviders` / a subsequent catalog filter still reflect the toggled list (and the mirror case for turning a provider back on).
- Existing disabled-provider behavior is unchanged otherwise: a failed read still answers no list and filters nothing, a `null` list (no OpenChamber server) still filters nothing, and snapshots stay keyed per runtime.

body:
## Problem

In the VS Code runtime, `api:git/conflict-details` loses the merge message during a conflicted merge in a **linked git worktree** — which is exactly what OpenChamber spaces are. The operation, unmerged files and diff are all correct, but `headInfo` comes back as just `MERGE_HEAD: <sha>` with no `Merge branch '…'` line, because the handler reads `MERGE_MSG` from `<directory>/.git/MERGE_MSG` and `.git` is a **file**, not a directory, in a linked worktree. The web runtime returns the message for the same state.

This is the #648 defect class in a third location: #648's fix (PR #651) added `resolveGitDir` to `packages/vscode/src/gitService.ts` and applied it in `checkInProgressOperations`; this handler lives in a different module (`bridge-git-special-runtime.ts`) and does not use it. #655 tracks the same class in `canonicalizeWorktreeState`.

## Evidence (verified on main `3304bfbe7`)

- `packages/vscode/src/bridge-git-special-runtime.ts:506`: `const mergeMsgPath = path.join(directory, '.git', 'MERGE_MSG')`, read at `:507` inside a `catch` that swallows the failure ("MERGE_MSG may not exist"). The merge itself is detected portably at `:501` via `rev-parse --verify --quiet MERGE_HEAD`, so only the message is lost. In a linked worktree the read always fails with ENOTDIR, because `.git` is a file (`gitdir: <main>/.git/worktrees/<name>`).
- The web service does it the portable way: `packages/web/server/lib/git/service.js:7085` (`getConflictDetails`) resolves `MERGE_MSG` through `resolveGitInternalPath` (`:635`), which follows the worktree gitdir.
- Consumers: `packages/ui/src/components/views/git/ConflictDialog.tsx:220-224` renders `headInfo` as the conflict dialog's HEAD information, and `:79-99` passes `headInfo` as `head_info` into the AI conflict-resolution prompt — so the resolver also loses which branch is being merged.
- Laptop probe (real handler + real `execGit` deps, `gitService`/`@opencode/client` mocked per the existing bridge-git-special-runtime test pattern, temp repos) — `~/git/fleet/probe-vscode-conflict-msg/probe.test.ts`:
  - Main worktree with a conflicted merge (control): `headInfo = "MERGE_HEAD: 8610ad9…\nMerge branch 'feature'\n\n# Conflicts:\n#\tfile.txt"` — message present.
  - Linked worktree (`git worktree add`) with the same conflicted merge: `MERGE_MSG` verified present at the real gitdir with first line `Merge branch 'feature' into wtbranch`, `operation = "merge"`, `unmergedFiles = ["file.txt"]`, but `headInfo = "MERGE_HEAD: 8610ad9…"` — message absent.

## Why it matters

The conflict dialog is how a user in a space understands and resolves a stopped merge. Losing the merge message removes the one human-readable line that says what is being merged into what, and silently degrades the context handed to the AI conflict resolver — on exactly the surface (linked worktrees / spaces, VS Code) where the state is most common. The repo's correctness invariants require runtime-specific differences to be intentional and visible; this one is neither.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] In a linked worktree, `api:git/conflict-details` returns `headInfo` containing the `MERGE_HEAD` line plus the merge message (first line `Merge branch '…' into '…'`), matching the web `getConflictDetails` result for the same state.
- [ ] The `MERGE_MSG` path is resolved through git itself (e.g. `git rev-parse --git-path MERGE_MSG`, or the `resolveGitDir` helper added to `gitService.ts` by PR #651) rather than assuming `<directory>/.git` is a directory; main-worktree behaviour is unchanged, and a genuinely absent `MERGE_MSG` still degrades to the bare `MERGE_HEAD` line.
- [ ] Regression tests in the existing VS Code bridge-git-special-runtime bun-test style cover: linked-worktree conflicted merge (message present), main-worktree conflicted merge (control), and a merge with no `MERGE_MSG` (graceful degradation preserved).
- [ ] No change to the web service (already correct) and no change to the returned conflict-details shape.
