## Summary

Same class as #332 (auto-model-routing) and #339 (install / notes-todos-plans / desktop-browser): translated docs mirrors are missing whole sections that the English pages have. A heading-count sweep across all docs pages this run (2026-10-27) found three more pages with deficits that neither #332 nor #339 covers.

Verified on main `67d7e88ed` by comparing the `## ` headings of each English page against its 11 translated mirrors in `packages/docs/content/docs/{de,es,fr,ja,ko,nl,pl,pt-br,tr,uk,zh-cn}/`.

## Evidence

**1. `projects.mdx` — "Group sessions in folders" missing in all 11 mirrors.**
English has 6 sections (Add a project :10, Switch projects :20, Make a project recognizable :24, Group sessions in folders :30, Project environment :42, Related :55; 60 lines). Every mirror has 5 and jumps from "Make a project recognizable" straight to "Project environment" (e.g. de/projects.mdx:24 → :30, 48 lines). The missing section is the only documentation of grouping sessions in folders on the projects page.

**2. `scheduled-tasks.mdx` — "Loops: scheduled tasks as markdown files" missing in 9 mirrors.**
English has 5 sections (Create a task :10, Loops: scheduled tasks as markdown files :26, What success looks like :68, Keep in mind :72, Related :76; 78 lines). de, es, fr, ja, ko, pl, pt-br, uk and zh-cn have 4 and jump from "Create a task" to "What success looks like" (de/scheduled-tasks.mdx is 35 lines vs 78 English — the missing section is 42 lines, more than half the English page). nl and tr have all 5 (nl/scheduled-tasks.mdx:26 carries the Loops section), so the section was translated for some locales and never carried to the rest. This is the only explanation of the markdown-file loop format on this page.

**3. `walkthrough.mdx` — "How a stop is marked" missing in 8 mirrors.**
English has 8 sections, starting with How a stop is marked at :14, then What it can review :28. es, fr, ja, ko, pl, pt-br, uk and zh-cn have 7 and start at "What it can review" (es/walkthrough.mdx is 71 lines vs 85 English). de, nl and tr have all 8. The missing section is the first one on the page, so readers of those mirrors start mid-explanation.

## Why it matters

Readers of the translated docs never learn these features exist — most sharply the scheduled-tasks Loops section, which is more than half the English page and the sole description of scheduled tasks as markdown files, and the projects folder-grouping section, missing in every single mirror. The mirrors otherwise track the English pages section-by-section, so these read as sections added to English and never carried over (the same failure #332 and #339 record for other pages).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `projects.mdx`: all 11 translated mirrors gain a translation of "Group sessions in folders", placed where the English page has it (between "Make a project recognizable" and "Project environment"), so every mirror has 6 `## ` sections.
- [ ] `scheduled-tasks.mdx`: the 9 mirrors missing it (de, es, fr, ja, ko, pl, pt-br, uk, zh-cn) gain a translation of "Loops: scheduled tasks as markdown files", placed after "Create a task" — every mirror reaches 5 `## ` sections. nl/tr are not touched.
- [ ] `walkthrough.mdx`: the 8 mirrors missing it (es, fr, ja, ko, pl, pt-br, uk, zh-cn) gain a translation of "How a stop is marked" as the first section — every mirror reaches 8 `## ` sections. de/nl/tr are not touched.
- [ ] Translations follow the terminology each mirror already uses on the same page, and no other sections or pages change.
- [ ] After the change, a heading-count sweep over these three pages shows no deficit in any locale.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for `projects.mdx`, `scheduled-tasks`, `walkthrough` and "translated mirrors": the hits are #332 (auto-model-routing only) and #339 (install, notes-todos-plans, desktop-browser only) — neither lists projects, scheduled-tasks or walkthrough. The heading sweep this run re-checked every docs page: apart from the pages #332/#339 already cover, these three are the only pages with a section deficit (the `sdk/` and `troubleshooting/` subdirectories under the docs tree are not locales).

body:
## Summary

The opt-in local-dev origin helpers in `request-security.js` recognize only two of the three loopback spellings the rest of the request-security code treats as aliases: `isLocalDevClientOrigin` accepts `localhost` and `127.0.0.1` origins but not `[::1]`, and `buildFrameAncestorsPolicy`'s dev sources add `http://127.0.0.1:*` and `http://localhost:*` but no `[::1]` source. A development UI served from an IPv6 loopback address (e.g. Vite/Electron HMR bound to `::1`) is therefore not believed as a dev client and cannot frame the app, while the identical setup on `127.0.0.1` works. This is the dev-mode sibling of the alias asymmetry #589 tracks for the main origin candidates (its PR #591 fixes `getRequestOriginCandidates` only; these two helpers are untouched by it).

Verified on main `5ed28ea5a` (2026-10-27).

## Evidence

- `packages/web/server/lib/security/request-security.js:24`:
  ```js
  export const isLocalDevClientOrigin = (origin) => /^https?:\/\/(localhost|127\.0\.0\.1):\d+$/.test(origin);
  ```
  Used wherever a dev origin is believed: the request-security runtime (`request-security.js:188`) and the CORS middleware in `packages/web/server/index.js:2391`.
- `packages/web/server/lib/security/request-security.js:37`:
  ```js
  if (allowLocalDevOrigins) sources.push('http://127.0.0.1:*', 'http://localhost:*');
  ```
  No `http://[::1]:*` source. The existing test (`request-security.test.js:182`) pins only the `127.0.0.1` containment.
- The same file's main path treats all three spellings as one loopback family (`getRequestOriginCandidates`, `request-security.js:157-165` on main; completed by PR #591 for #589), and `packages/web/server/lib/ui-auth/ui-passkeys.js:67` likewise counts `::1` as local (`rpID === 'localhost' || '127.0.0.1' || '::1'`). The dev helpers are the only loopback lists in the security surface still missing the IPv6 spelling.
- These helpers are strictly opt-in: `allowsLocalDevOrigins` (`request-security.js:23`) requires `OPENCHAMBER_ELECTRON_DEV=1` or `OPENCHAMBER_ALLOW_DEV_ORIGINS=1`; a released server never believes dev origins (the file's own comment at :13-19 explains why).

### Probe (laptop, `~/git/fleet/probe-devloopback/probe.mjs`, this run — the exact regex and push from main)

```text
http://localhost:5173     -> true
http://127.0.0.1:5173     -> true
http://[::1]:5173         -> false
https://[::1]:5173        -> false
https://evil.example.com:5173 -> false
frame-ancestors dev sources: 'self' http://127.0.0.1:* http://localhost:* | has [::1]: false
```

## Why it matters

- Dev servers increasingly bind IPv6 loopback (Node/Vite resolve `localhost` to `::1` first on many systems), so the dev UI's origin can be `http://[::1]:<port>` even when the developer typed `localhost`. With dev origins enabled, that UI gets no CORS allowance and its socket/API origins are not believed — the same confusing "works on 127.0.0.1, broken on the other loopback spelling" failure class #500/#589 removed from the main path, surviving in the dev path.
- The inconsistency is a trap for the next edit: three loopback lists in one security file (origin candidates, dev-origin regex, frame-ancestors sources) should name the same set; today one of them silently differs.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `isLocalDevClientOrigin` accepts `http://[::1]:<port>` and `https://[::1]:<port>` origins, and continues to reject non-loopback origins and port-less loopback origins (dev servers always carry a port — that requirement is deliberate and stays).
- [ ] `buildFrameAncestorsPolicy({ allowLocalDevOrigins: true })` includes an `[::1]` dev source alongside `http://127.0.0.1:*` and `http://localhost:*`; with dev origins off, the policy is byte-identical to today.
- [ ] Regression tests in `request-security.test.js` pin both: the `[::1]` dev origin (accepted) and a non-loopback lookalike (rejected), plus the `[::1]` frame-ancestors source.
- [ ] No change to the main origin-candidate alias logic (#589 / PR #591), the packaged-client origin set, or the opt-in gating (`allowsLocalDevOrigins`).

title: fix(routes): bindingRevision query param is judged loosely — 1e3, 0x10, 2.0 and empty all reinterpret to a valid revision in GitHub and GitLab read routes (#554 remainder)

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

The GitHub and GitLab source-control read routes convert the `bindingRevision` query parameter with bare `Number(...)`, so malformed spellings are silently reinterpreted before the value reaches the binding-authority check: `1e3` becomes 1000, `0x10` becomes 16, `2.0` / ` 2 ` / `+2` become 2, and an empty value becomes 0. Any of those passes the downstream integer gate and can equal the current binding revision, so a request whose revision text was never a plain decimal integer is accepted as if the client had sent the exact current revision. This is the strict-parsing defect class fixed repeatedly in this repo (#433, #446, #463–#465, #554) — #554 fixed `page`/`number`/`limit` in these same files but missed `bindingRevision`, which both files convert identically.

Verified on main `5ed28ea5a` (2026-10-27).

## Evidence

### The loose conversions (one per provider, identical shape)

- `packages/web/server/lib/github/routes.js:436` — `bindingRevision: Number(req.query?.bindingRevision)` inside `validateReadContext`.
- `packages/web/server/lib/gitlab/routes.js:377` — `bindingRevision: Number(req.query?.bindingRevision)` inside `validateReadContext`.

### The downstream check the reinterpretation defeats

`packages/web/server/lib/source-control/binding-service.js:434-441` (`validateAuthority`):

```js
const bindingRevision = input.bindingRevision;
if (!Number.isInteger(bindingRevision) || bindingRevision < 0) throw makeContextError('bindingRevision is required');
...
if (current.revision !== bindingRevision || (current.binding && current.binding.revision !== bindingRevision)) {
  throw staleBindingError('Source control repository binding changed', current);
}
```

The gate judges the already-converted number, not the text the client sent — so any spelling `Number()` maps onto the current revision is indistinguishable from the exact decimal spelling.

### The strict standard already in the same files

- GitHub: `readPositiveIntegerQuery` (`github/routes.js:86-91`) — `/^[1-9]\d*$/` + `Number.isSafeInteger`.
- GitLab: `requestIssueNumber` (`gitlab/routes.js:139-143`) — same pattern.

Both helpers are positive-only, and a binding revision can legitimately be `0`, so the fix needs a non-negative variant (e.g. `/^(0|[1-9]\d*)$/` + safe-integer check), not a direct reuse.

### Probe (laptop, `~/git/fleet/probe-bindingrev/probe.mjs`, this run)

The exact route expression fed through the downstream gate:

```text
raw="2"      -> Number=2     integerGate=true  matchesRev2=true
raw="2.0"    -> Number=2     integerGate=true  matchesRev2=true
raw=" 2 "    -> Number=2     integerGate=true  matchesRev2=true
raw="+2"     -> Number=2     integerGate=true  matchesRev2=true
raw="1e3"    -> Number=1000  integerGate=true  matchesRev1000=true
raw="0x10"   -> Number=16    integerGate=true  matchesRev16=true
raw=""       -> Number=0     integerGate=true  matchesRev0=true
raw="2.9"    -> Number=2.9   integerGate=false
raw="10junk" -> Number=NaN   integerGate=false
raw=undefined -> Number=NaN  integerGate=false
```

(Fractions and trailing junk are caught downstream only because they fail `Number.isInteger` / become NaN — the spellings above sail through.)

## Why it matters

- `bindingRevision` is a staleness/authority token: it exists so a read is served only against the exact source-control binding the client saw. Accepting `1e3`, `0x10`, `2.0`, or an empty string as that token weakens the exact-match contract the binding service enforces everywhere else (network-operation plans and storage judge the same field with `Number.isSafeInteger` + exact equality, e.g. `git/network-operation-plan.js:368`).
- The empty-string case is the sharpest: `?bindingRevision=` on a repository whose current revision is 0 validates as revision 0, while omitting the parameter entirely (NaN) is refused — presence with empty text is treated as more authoritative than absence.
- It is the last loose numeric query conversion in these two route files (grep for `Number(req.query` / `Number(.*query` across `packages/web/server` returns only these two sites outside tests), so fixing it closes the #554 remainder instead of leaving one trap for the next copy-paste.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Both `validateReadContext` implementations (github/routes.js, gitlab/routes.js) parse `bindingRevision` strictly: only a plain non-negative decimal integer (`0`, or digits with no leading zero, sign, whitespace, fraction, exponent, or radix prefix) within safe-integer range is accepted; anything else is refused the same way a missing/non-integer revision is refused today.
- [ ] Legitimate values keep working unchanged: `0` and ordinary decimal revisions validate exactly as before, and the across-repositories path (JSON body contexts, already numeric) is untouched.
- [ ] Regression tests cover both providers: `1e3`, `0x10`, `2.0`, ` 2 `, `+2`, and the empty string are refused even when the reinterpreted value equals the current revision; `0` and a plain decimal revision are accepted.
- [ ] No other route's parsing changes; the strict helper added follows the existing `readPositiveIntegerQuery` / `requestIssueNumber` shape in each file.

title: fix(security): loopback origin aliases are incomplete — 127.0.0.1 and [::1] hosts don't alias each other (#500 remainder)

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: kind/security
labels.description: Security issue or security hardening

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal

labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Finding

#500 (fixed by PR #544) made the `[::1]` loopback origin alias fire at all: the bracket-aware Host parser in `getRequestOriginCandidates` now reaches the alias branch. But the alias set each loopback Host spelling grants is still asymmetric — only a `localhost` Host grants the full set of loopback aliases. The two IP spellings grant each other nothing:

- Host `localhost:3000` → origins add `127.0.0.1:3000` **and** `[::1]:3000` (both aliases).
- Host `127.0.0.1:3000` → origins add only `localhost:3000`. An `Origin: http://[::1]:3000` request is **rejected**.
- Host `[::1]:3000` → origins add only `localhost:3000`. An `Origin: http://127.0.0.1:3000` request is **rejected**.

## Evidence

- `packages/web/server/lib/security/request-security.js` on current main (`0f6a93a52`), in `getRequestOriginCandidates`:
  - `localhost` branch: `origins.add(...127.0.0.1${portSuffix})` and `origins.add(...[::1]${portSuffix})`.
  - `127.0.0.1` / `[::1]` branch: `origins.add(...localhost${portSuffix})` only — the other IP spelling is never added.
- Verified this run with a probe on the laptop against the current-main module (`createRequestSecurityRuntime` with an empty settings store), all with port 3000:
  - `Origin http://127.0.0.1:3000`, Host `[::1]:3000` → **false**
  - `Origin http://[::1]:3000`, Host `127.0.0.1:3000` → **false**
  - `Origin http://[::1]:3000`, Host `localhost:3000` → true
  - `Origin http://127.0.0.1:3000`, Host `localhost:3000` → true
  - `Origin http://localhost:3000`, Host `[::1]:3000` → true
  - `Origin http://localhost:3000`, Host `127.0.0.1:3000` → true
- The existing tests in `packages/web/server/lib/security/request-security.test.js` pin the localhost↔IP directions ("allows the [::1] alias when the server is reached via localhost", "allows loopback aliases when the server is reached via [::1]" — the latter checks only the `[::1]` and `localhost` origins), so the IP↔IP directions are untested and currently fail.
- Dedup: searches for "loopback alias", "origin alias", "request-security origin", and "[::1]" return only #500 (the dead-branch defect, fixed) and its PR #544. No open or closed issue covers the cross-IP alias gap.

## Why it matters

The three loopback spellings name the same machine; the origin check already treats them as aliases in five of the six directions. A user (or a dev tool / WebView) that reaches the server via one IP spelling while its page origin uses the other gets its API requests origin-rejected — the same class of confusing loopback failure #500 set out to remove, left behind in the two directions its fix didn't add. The failure is fail-closed ( legitimate local requests rejected, no security weakening), so this is a correctness/completeness bug, not a vulnerability.

## Acceptance criteria

- With Host `127.0.0.1:<port>`, an `Origin: http://[::1]:<port>` request is allowed; with Host `[::1]:<port>`, an `Origin: http://127.0.0.1:<port>` request is allowed — i.e. every loopback Host spelling grants the same full alias set (`localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `[::1]`, same port, same protocol), with and without a port.
- Non-loopback origins (e.g. `https://evil.example.com`) stay rejected for every loopback Host spelling, and non-loopback Host handling is unchanged.
- New tests in `request-security.test.js` cover both IP↔IP directions alongside the existing alias tests.
- No change to the bracket-aware Host parsing from PR #544 or to the `publicOrigin` settings path.

title: fix(routing-ui): schedule editor rejects single-digit seconds (09:30:5) that OpenCode and the server now accept — PR #561 UI remainder

body:
## Finding

PR #561 (fix for #559) made the server schedule validator read window seconds the way OpenCode does: single-digit seconds are accepted (`09:30:5` is valid and rounds down to the same minute as `09:30`). The UI half of that round-trip was not updated: the schedule editor's stored-time normalizer still requires exactly two second digits, so the same stored value is judged invalid in the editor.

## Evidence

- PR #561, commit `68e0cb45f`: `packages/web/server/lib/routing/model-routes.js` `windowTimeMinutes` now captures seconds as `(\d{1,2})` and only refuses seconds > 59. Regression tests pin the acceptance: `packages/web/server/lib/routing/model-routes.test.js:733,744,1340` use `09:30:5` as a valid window time.
- Current main: `packages/ui/src/lib/routing/routeSchedules.ts:31` — `STORED_TIME = /^(\d{1,2}):(\d{1,2})(?::(\d{2}))?$/` still requires two second digits, and the comment above it (line 30) still claims OpenCode reads only `9:30`, `09:30` and `09:30:15`.
- Verified this run by executing the current `timeInputValue` logic: `9:5 -> 09:05` (single-digit minutes are accepted and zero-padded), `09:30:05 -> 09:30:05`, `09:30:99 -> null` (correct), but `09:30:5 -> null`.
- Effect in the editor: `packages/ui/src/components/sections/routing/RouteScheduleFields.tsx:106-117` — `TimeField` renders a stored value with `display === null` as a text field, and `CheckedInput` (`:51-95`) marks it `aria-invalid` with a destructive border and the error text, and refuses to commit it. So a hand-written window that OpenCode applies and the server now accepts shows as an error in the editor and cannot be committed from that field until the user rewrites it as `09:30:05`.

Note: #559 explicitly checked this UI normalizer and scoped it out on the grounds that `<input type="time">` values are always zero-padded. That holds for typed input, but `timeInputValue`'s input is the *stored config value* — and the same function already accepts and pads single-digit hours/minutes for exactly that reason (`9:5 -> 09:05`, pinned in `routeSchedules.test.ts:69`). Single-digit seconds are the one remaining asymmetry.

## Why it matters

The point of #559/#561 was that a hand-written config value should round-trip through OpenChamber the way OpenCode reads it. The server half now does; the editor still flags a valid stored window as invalid, which trains users to distrust the editor's errors and forces a needless rewrite of a working config value.

## Acceptance criteria

- `timeInputValue('09:30:5')` returns `09:30:05` (single-digit seconds accepted and zero-padded, mirroring how single-digit minutes are handled today).
- Out-of-range seconds stay rejected: `timeInputValue('09:30:99')` and `timeInputValue('09:30:60')` return null.
- The stale comment at `routeSchedules.ts:30` is updated to name the single-digit-seconds form OpenCode accepts.
- A regression test in `packages/ui/src/lib/routing/routeSchedules.test.ts` covers single-digit seconds alongside the existing `9:5` and `12:00:61` cases.
- No change to server validation (`model-routes.js`) or to which stored values are preserved verbatim on save.

title: fix(quota): VS Code Meta port drops the provider message on the exhausted path — require_payment hardcodes message: null, detail fallback missing

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/vscode
labels.description: Package: vscode (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

The VS Code Meta quota port drops the provider's own message on the exhausted (plan-wall) path, where the web provider it mirrors keeps it — and the two implementations are explicitly supposed to stay in sync (`meta.js` header: "Keep this in sync with `packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.ts` (`fetchMetaQuota`)"; the port header: "Mirrors `packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/meta.js`").

Divergences, all in the exhausted-result construction:

1. **`require_payment` message discarded.** Web (`packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/meta.js:181-183`): the exhausted outcome carries `message: errorMessage(body)`. VS Code (`packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.ts:3962-3964`): the same branch hardcodes `message: null`, so the VS Code usage surface always shows the generic `Subscription quota exhausted` even when the body explained the wall.
2. **`detail` field never read.** Web `errorMessage` (`meta.js:111-114`) falls back through `error.message` → `body.message` → `body.detail`. The VS Code 402/429 path (`quotaProviders.ts:3953`) reads only the first two, and its `MetaKeyResponse` type (`quotaProviders.ts:3863-3876`) has no `detail` field at all.
3. **Related shape gaps to disposition at triage:** the web exhausted result also carries `quotaLimitKind` (`meta.js:258`, pinned by `meta.test.js:203`) and the web usage result carries `accountLabel` from `body.user_email` (`meta.js:241`); the VS Code `ProviderResult` type (`quotaProviders.ts:255-268`) has neither field for any provider, and its `MetaKeyResponse` has no `user_email`. These may be intentional VS Code surface differences — triage should either extend the port's result shape or record the omission as deliberate in the port header, so the "mirrors" claim is accurate.

## Why it matters

The Meta provider's failure classes are deliberately distinct (its header: a 402-class wall "the babysitter must not confuse with a read failure"), and the provider's own message is part of that signal. On the VS Code surface the wall currently reads as a bare generic error in exactly the `require_payment` case, and a maintainer reading the two files side by side cannot tell which of the other gaps are deliberate.

## Evidence

- `packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/meta.js:111-114` — `errorMessage` reads `error.message` ?? `message` ?? `detail`.
- `packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/meta.js:164` and `:182` — both the 402/429 path and the `require_payment` path pass `message: errorMessage(body)`.
- `packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.ts:3953` — 402/429 message is `error.message` ?? `message` only (no `detail`).
- `packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.ts:3962-3964` — `require_payment` branch returns `message: null` unconditionally.
- `packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.ts:3863-3876` — `MetaKeyResponse` type declares no `detail` or `user_email` field.
- `packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/meta.test.js:220-231` — the web `require_payment` test pins only `quotaExhausted`/`ok`, not the message; the VS Code suite likewise has no `require_payment` message assertion (its Meta block covers the 402 wall at `quotaProviders.test.ts` ~:3157).
- Dedup: searches for Meta VS Code / Meta port / require_payment / quotaLimitKind returned only closed #572 (the usedPercent clamp, a different field) plus unrelated #331/#139. No issue covers the exhausted-message divergence.

## Acceptance criteria

- The VS Code Meta `require_payment` path surfaces the body's message the same way the web provider does (via its `error.message` / `message` / `detail` chain), so the exhausted error text matches across surfaces for the same payload.
- The VS Code 402/429 message extraction matches the web chain, including the `detail` fallback (and `MetaKeyResponse` declares the field).
- Triage disposition for `quotaLimitKind` and `accountLabel`: either the VS Code port carries them like the web provider, or the port header comment records the omission as a deliberate surface difference.
- Tests in `packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.test.ts` pin the `require_payment` message and the `detail` fallback for the Meta port; web behavior unchanged.

title: fix(context): server context-obligatory reader accepts createdAt values that crash toISOString — one bad pin disables re-injection for the session

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

The server-side context-obligatory runtime accepts a pinned message whose `createdAt` is any number, then throws on it — so one out-of-range pin silently disables compaction context re-injection for the whole session, forever.

`packages/web/server/lib/context-obligatory/runtime.js:10-16` (`readContextState`) filters stored pins with only:

```js
typeof item.createdAt === 'number'
```

`buildContextPrompt` then formats the pin at `runtime.js:22`:

```js
const timestamp = new Date(pinned.createdAt).toISOString();
```

`new Date(value).toISOString()` throws `RangeError: Invalid time value` for `NaN`, `±Infinity`, and any finite number outside the Date range (verified on the laptop this run: `new Date(1e21).toISOString()` throws; `Number.isFinite(1e21)` is `true`). The sort at `runtime.js:117` also subtracts the raw values.

The UI reader for the exact same stored field is stricter — `packages/ui/src/lib/contextObligatoryMessages.ts:26-27` requires `typeof value.createdAt === 'number' && Number.isFinite(value.createdAt)` — so the two readers of `context_obligatory_messages` disagree about what a valid pin is: the UI can show a pin (any finite value, including `1e21`) that the server runtime then crashes on.

## Why it matters

`tick()` runs `buildContextPrompt` before `persistContextCursor` (`runtime.js:134-135`). When it throws, `processPayload` catches the error, logs one `injection failed` warning, and the compaction cursor is never recorded — so every later `session.compacted` event for that session retries the same failing pin set and fails the same way. The user's explicitly pinned "must keep" messages are never re-injected after compaction, with no user-visible signal. Session metadata is client-supplied at create time (v2 accepts metadata only at create), and the server's own pin writer in `session-actions.js` preserves existing stored entries verbatim when appending a new pin, so the runtime cannot assume stored entries were validated by its own writer.

## Evidence

- `packages/web/server/lib/context-obligatory/runtime.js:14` — filter is `typeof item.createdAt === 'number'` only (no finite/range check).
- `packages/web/server/lib/context-obligatory/runtime.js:22` — `new Date(pinned.createdAt).toISOString()` throws `RangeError` on invalid values.
- Laptop probe (2026-10-27): `new Date(1e21).toISOString()` → `RangeError: Invalid time value`; `new Date(NaN).toISOString()` → `RangeError`; `Number.isFinite(1e21)` → `true`.
- `packages/ui/src/lib/contextObligatoryMessages.ts:26-27` — the UI reader for the same field already requires `Number.isFinite`, proving the intended validity rule.
- `packages/web/server/lib/context-obligatory/runtime.js:117` — sort subtracts raw `createdAt` values.
- `packages/web/server/lib/context-obligatory/runtime.js:134-135` — the cursor is persisted only after the prompt is built and sent, so a throw leaves the session permanently unhandled for that pin set.
- `packages/web/server/lib/context-obligatory/runtime.test.js` — no test covers a non-finite or out-of-Date-range `createdAt`.
- Dedup: searches for context-obligatory / pinned messages / createdAt / toISOString across open and closed issues returned only #152 (an unrelated 2026-10-20 tracking thread), closed #484 and closed #534. No issue covers this.

## Acceptance criteria

- `readContextState` in `runtime.js` drops pins whose `createdAt` is not a finite number that a `Date` can represent (mirroring — or sharing — the UI reader's rule in `contextObligatoryMessages.ts`), instead of passing them through to `buildContextPrompt`.
- A session whose stored pins include such an entry still gets its valid pins re-injected after a compaction, and the compaction cursor is persisted.
- `buildContextPrompt` can no longer be reached with a `createdAt` that makes `toISOString()` throw.
- New tests in `packages/web/server/lib/context-obligatory/runtime.test.js` cover at least: a `NaN`/`Infinity` `createdAt` pin and an out-of-Date-range finite `createdAt` (e.g. `1e21`) alongside a valid pin — the valid pin is re-injected and the cursor is recorded.
- Existing context-obligatory runtime tests keep passing; valid-pin behavior is unchanged.

body:
## Problem

PR #469 (for #464/#465) made every git **route** judge the diff `context` parameter strictly (`parseDiffContextLines`, `packages/web/server/lib/git/routes.js:31-34`), but the **service** functions underneath still build the git `-U` argument from whatever number they are handed. A fractional or non-finite `contextLines` passed programmatically reaches git verbatim and git rejects it:

- `packages/web/server/lib/git/service.js:3327-3328` — `getNoIndexDiff`: guard is only `Number.isFinite(contextLines)`, then `` `-U${Math.max(0, contextLines)}` `` → `2.9` becomes `-U2.9`.
- `packages/web/server/lib/git/service.js:3402-3403` — `readDiff` (behind `getDiff`/`getPathDiff`/`getPathDiffs`): same pattern (`typeof === 'number' && !Number.isNaN`).
- `packages/web/server/lib/git/service.js:3589-3590` — `getRangeDiff`: same pattern.
- `packages/web/server/lib/git/service.js:6713` — `getCommitDiff`: **no guard at all** — `` `-U${Math.max(0, contextLines)}` `` turns `2.9` into `-U2.9` and `NaN` into `-UNaN`.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `d7f4a4064`)

- The four sites above, read on current main.
- Probe with plain git in a scratch repo: `git diff -U2.9 -- f.txt` → `error: --unified expects a numerical value`, exit **129**; `git diff -U2` exits 0.
- In-service precedent: `getLog` normalizes its own numeric option in the service — `service.js:6365`: `Number.isInteger(options.maxCount) && options.maxCount > 0 ? options.maxCount : 50` — so a caller can never hand git a bad `--max-count`. `contextLines` has no equivalent normalization.
- Recorded earlier as an unfiled REVIEW-FINDING from the PR #469 review (2026-10-26): "routes now judge diff context strictly, and getLog guards its own maxCount, but the git service diff functions still pass a fractional contextLines through to git as -U2.9 (exit 129)."

## Why it matters

No HTTP caller reaches this today — the routes guard it — so this is defense-in-depth, not a live 500. But the service is the layer every future caller (routes, control actions, scripts) will trust, and its four diff entry points currently disagree with both the routes above them and the `getLog` precedent in the same file. The next caller that forwards a computed (non-integer) context value reintroduces the #465 failure mode — a git exit-129 error surfacing as a failed diff — with no malformed input anywhere near the HTTP layer.

## Acceptance criteria

- One shared normalization for `contextLines` in `packages/web/server/lib/git/service.js` (integer, `>= 0`, otherwise the default 3 — the same rule `parseDiffContextLines` applies at the routes), used by `getNoIndexDiff`, `readDiff`, `getRangeDiff`, and `getCommitDiff`.
- A fractional (`2.9`), negative, or `NaN` `contextLines` passed directly to any of those service functions produces a normal diff with the default context instead of a git error.
- Valid values (`0`, `3`, `10`) behave exactly as today, and route behavior is unchanged.
- Tests in `packages/web/server/lib/git/service.test.js` (or the existing git test files, following their patterns) pin the fractional/NaN cases at the service layer.

body:
## Finding

The Cursor enterprise `windowSeconds` fix landed twice — PR #537 for the web provider (MERGED, merge `c5acfec57d75a7d713c28862842c8169779f9059`, commit `93f7a18e66`, fixing #495) and PR #538 for the VS Code port (MERGED, merge `0a3f98313a2e8ad1ae34df2c07ecab5594622a10`, commit `37114068b8`, fixing #506) — but the two implementations read the billing-cycle **start** from different payload sources, so the same enterprise payload yields a duration on one surface and `null` on the other.

- Web (`packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/cursor.js`, current main `:302-307`, `buildEnterpriseWindows`): the cycle **end** prefers the plan payload (`plan?.planInfo?.billingCycleEnd ?? usage?.billingCycleEnd`, the same source order as `resetAt`), but the cycle **start** is read only from the usage payload: `cycleWindowSeconds(usage?.billingCycleStart, …)`.
- VS Code (`packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.ts`, current main `:2511-2514`, `cursorEnterpriseWindows`): both endpoints prefer planInfo: `cursorCycleWindowSeconds(planInfo?.billingCycleStart ?? usage?.billingCycleStart, planInfo?.billingCycleEnd ?? usage?.billingCycleEnd)`. PR #538's body states this was deliberate: the start is read "from the same payload sources as `resetAt`".

So when an enterprise payload carries `billingCycleStart` only in `planInfo` (usage payload omits it), VS Code reports the true cycle duration while web reports `windowSeconds: null` — the headline-window ranking the #495 fix exists to correct then treats the web window as durationless. The web provider's non-enterprise path has the same asymmetry in reverse order (start from usage only, end `usage ?? plan`), but there both endpoints at least come from one primary source; the enterprise path mixes sources for end while ignoring the preferred source for start.

## Evidence

- PRs: https://github.com/developing-today/openchamber/pull/537 and https://github.com/developing-today/openchamber/pull/538
- Web current main `cursor.js:304-306` (verified 2026-10-27): `cycleWindowSeconds(usage?.billingCycleStart, plan?.planInfo?.billingCycleEnd ?? usage?.billingCycleEnd)`; `resetAt` at `:303` uses the plan-first end source.
- VS Code current main `quotaProviders.ts:2514`: plan-first for both start and end.
- The web test fixture (`cursor.test.js` `enterpriseRoutes`) carries `billingCycleStart` only in the usage payload and no `planInfo.billingCycleStart`, so the divergence is invisible to the web suite; the VS Code test added by #538 likewise never sets a planInfo-only start.
- Dedupe: searches for `billingCycleStart` return only the closed originals #495/#506 — no issue covers the start-source divergence.

## Why it matters

`windowSeconds` feeds the usage headline's shortest-window ranking; a spurious `null` on web (but not VS Code) makes the two surfaces rank and label the same Cursor enterprise account differently, and quietly reintroduces part of the #495 defect for plan-sourced cycle starts.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The web enterprise path reads the cycle start from the same source order as the cycle end / `resetAt` (`planInfo.billingCycleStart ?? usage.billingCycleStart`), matching the VS Code port — or, if usage-only start is shown to be the correct reading of the real Cursor payload, the VS Code port is aligned to it instead and the choice is documented in both files.
- [ ] A web regression test covers an enterprise payload whose `billingCycleStart` appears only in `planInfo` and expects the cycle duration (288471-style fixture arithmetic), plus the existing missing-start → `null` cases keep passing.
- [ ] Web and VS Code enterprise `windowSeconds` agree for all combinations of start/end presence across the usage and plan payloads.

body:
## Finding

PR #548 (MERGED, merge commit `ac6b0ef2a17d1f3a4faefcc31229e4b3f07c370e`, commit `dff5dffdd2`) ported the z.ai/zhipu usedPercent clamp (#509) to the VS Code provider, but its `clampPercent` has **no non-finite guard**, and three read sites feed it raw API values behind only a `typeof === 'number'` check. A non-finite percentage (`Infinity`, e.g. a JSON body carrying `1e999`, which `JSON.parse` yields as `Infinity`) therefore does not become `null` as the web providers require — and `NaN` (reachable from JS-side payload construction/mocks) passes straight through as a `NaN` usedPercent and remainingPercent.

The web fix in PR #547 states the contract explicitly in both `zai.js` and `zhipuai-coding-plan.js`: "Non-finite or non-number input stays null", with a regression test ("reports a non-finite percentage as null instead of leaking it into the window"). The VS Code port dropped that half of the contract and has no non-finite test.

## Evidence

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/openchamber/pull/548 (the #510 port); web counterpart PR #547.
- Current main `packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.ts:171`: `const clampPercent = (value: number) => Math.min(100, Math.max(0, value));` — `clampPercent(Infinity)` is 100 (not null), `clampPercent(NaN)` is `NaN`.
- Unguarded read sites on current main (all `typeof … === 'number' ? clampPercent(…) : null`, and `typeof NaN === 'number'`):
  - `:2902` — z.ai TOKENS_LIMIT windows
  - `:2915` — z.ai MCP Tools window
  - `:3068` — zhipuai MCP Tools window
- Downstream, the port's `toUsageWindow` (`quotaProviders.ts:499-512`) passes `usedPercent` through verbatim and derives `remainingPercent` as `Math.max(0, 100 - usedPercent)`, so a `NaN` input yields `NaN` for both fields.
- The one safe path proves the guard exists elsewhere in the same file: `resolveZhipuaiUsedPercent` (`:171` area, used for zhipuai credit windows) routes through `toNumber` (`:409-417`), which rejects non-finite values — the three sites above bypass it.
- PR #548's tests cover 150 / -20 clamping only; no non-finite case. Verified on current main on 2026-10-27; dedupe search (`non-finite`) returned #494/#560 (timestamp guards) and #546/#567 (ClinePass clamp) — nothing covers non-finite percentages in the VS Code z.ai/zhipu paths.

## Why it matters

The two ports of the same providers now disagree on the same payload: web reports `usedPercent: null` (window renders as unknown), VS Code reports `100` for `Infinity` or `NaN`/`NaN` for `NaN`. This is the same port-parity defect class as #492/#560, filed and fixed before.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Non-finite percentages (`Infinity`, `-Infinity`, `NaN`) at the z.ai and zhipuai read sites in `packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.ts` produce `usedPercent: null` (and `remainingPercent: null`), matching the web providers' contract from PR #547.
- [ ] Finite out-of-range values still clamp to [0, 100] exactly as PR #548 established.
- [ ] Regression tests in `packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.test.ts` mirror the web suite's non-finite case for at least the z.ai token window and one MCP Tools window.

## Finding

PR #540 (OPEN, head `afcd89cceb1fd1c6c320dbba2226d6d344ec97a1`) adds the new Meta (Muse Code High Usage) quota provider, but passes the plan API's `used_percent` values into its usage windows **unclamped** — the exact defect this repo has been fixing provider by provider in the #507–#521 clamp family (google/antigravity #507, zai/zhipu #509, ClinePass #512, Claude #515, Codex #516, Cursor #517, and their VS Code ports). Meta is the one provider added after that campaign began that does not clamp.

## Evidence

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/openchamber/pull/540 (closes #523), commits `2b0257d4af`, `42ed6c5457`, `f79eb89e3c`, `afcd89cceb`.
- Web provider, `packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/meta.js:196` and `:205` (PR head): `usedPercent: toNumber(rolling.used_percent)` and `usedPercent: toNumber(weekly.used_percent)` in `buildWindows` — no clamp at either read site.
- VS Code mirror, `packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.ts:3954` and `:3963` (PR head): the same two unclamped `toNumber(…used_percent)` reads in `fetchMetaQuota`.
- The shared `toUsageWindow` helper deliberately does **not** clamp (wafer's overage branch exceeds 100 on purpose — see the comment added by PR #547 in `zai.js`); its `remainingPercent` is only floored via `Math.max(0, 100 - usedPercent)`. So a Meta payload reporting `used_percent: 150` would surface `usedPercent: 150` with `remainingPercent: 0`, and `-20` would surface `usedPercent: -20`.
- The PR's own tests (`meta.test.js`, `quotaProviders.test.ts` Meta blocks) only exercise in-range values (6 and 10), so nothing pins the out-of-range behavior.
- Verification: read at PR head `afcd89cc` on 2026-10-27; dedupe searches for a Meta clamp issue (`meta`, `clamp`) returned only #523 (the missing-provider issue #540 closes) — no open or closed issue covers clamping for this provider.

## Why it matters

Every sibling provider was clamped because real quota APIs do report percentages outside [0, 100], and the UI renders impossible values ("150% used") when they leak. The new provider reintroduces the defect class on both surfaces (web + VS Code) the day the rest of the fleet finished removing it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Meta rolling and weekly windows clamp `used_percent` to [0, 100] at the read site in `packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/meta.js` (non-finite / unparseable values stay `null`, matching the sibling providers' convention).
- [ ] The same clamp is applied in the VS Code mirror `fetchMetaQuota` (`packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.ts`), keeping the two implementations in sync as the file header of `meta.js` requires.
- [ ] Regression tests in both test suites cover `used_percent` of 150 → 100 and -20 → 0 for at least the rolling window (ideally both windows).
- [ ] Fix lands either as an added commit on PR #540 before merge or as a follow-up PR referencing this issue; `toUsageWindow` itself stays unclamped (wafer overage).

body:
## Problem

The VS Code Google and Antigravity quota paths (`packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.ts`) derive `usedPercent` from `remainingFraction` with only a lower clamp — `Math.max(0, 100 - remainingPercent)` — so a negative `remainingFraction` produces a `usedPercent` above 100 that flows straight into the usage window. This is the #507 defect in the port that was not covered by it: the web transforms were fixed in PR #541, the VS Code port still has the one-sided expression at four sites.

## Evidence (verified on main `3428a415d`, 2026-10-27)

All four sites use the identical one-sided derivation `remainingPercent !== null ? Math.max(0, 100 - remainingPercent) : null`:

- `packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.ts:1298` — Google quota buckets (`remainingFraction` from the buckets payload)
- `packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.ts:1327` — Google models payload (`quotaInfo.remainingFraction`)
- `packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.ts:1473` — Antigravity quota-summary groups
- `packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.ts:1550` — Antigravity models payload (`quotaInfo.remainingFraction`)

- The VS Code `toUsageWindow` (`quotaProviders.ts:498-512`) does not rescue the value: it stores `usedPercent` as given.
- The web transforms now clamp both bounds for the same derivation: `packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/google/transforms.js:47,73` and `antigravity/transforms.js:24,138` use `Math.min(100, Math.max(0, 100 - remainingPercent))` since #507 / PR #541. (Notably, the VS Code Ollama path in the same file already clamps both bounds at :2374.)
- Laptop probe this run (`~/git/fleet/probe-quota-clamp-20261027/probe.mjs`, laptop fork at the same commit) evaluating the port's exact derivation: `remainingFraction=-0.2 -> usedPercent=120`; `0.4 -> 60`; `1.2 -> 0`.
- Dedup: searches for "clamp google antigravity VS Code" and "usedPercent clamp" across open+closed issues return no VS Code Google/Antigravity item; `git show --stat fc8ecedf2` confirms #541 touched only the web `google/transforms.js` and `antigravity/transforms.js` + their tests.

## Why it matters

Google and Antigravity are headline quota providers on the VS Code surface. A `remainingFraction` slightly below zero — the API reporting a bucket marginally over its limit — renders as 100+% usage in VS Code while the web UI reports the same account clamped to 100, and the derived `remainingPercent` disagrees with the bar.

## Acceptance criteria

- All four derivation sites in `packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.ts` (Google buckets, Google models, Antigravity groups, Antigravity models) clamp the derived `usedPercent` to [0, 100], e.g. via the file's existing `clampPercent` helper at :171; `null` (missing fraction) behavior unchanged.
- New tests in `packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.test.ts` pin at least one Google and one Antigravity path: `remainingFraction: -0.2 -> usedPercent 100`, `remainingFraction: 0.4 -> usedPercent 60` unchanged, `remainingFraction: 1.2 -> usedPercent 0`.
- Existing VS Code quota tests still pass.

## Problem

The VS Code Cursor provider's non-enterprise path (`packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.ts`, `fetchCursorQuota`) passes the API's explicit `planUsage.totalPercentUsed` straight into `toUsageWindow` with no clamp — the same defect fixed in the web provider as #517 (PR #555, "clamp Cursor usedPercent to [0,100] on the explicit-percent paths"), in the port that was not covered by it.

An out-of-range `totalPercentUsed` therefore leaks into the VS Code usage UI: `totalPercentUsed: 150` renders as `usedPercent: 150`, and a negative value renders as a negative `usedPercent` with `remainingPercent` above 100. The enterprise paths in the same file were already clamped; this individual-plan path is the one that was missed.

## Evidence (verified on main `3428a415d`, 2026-10-27)

- `packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.ts:2559-2560` — `const usedPercent = toNumber(planUsage.totalPercentUsed); return buildResult({ ... usage: { windows: { billing_cycle: toUsageWindow({ usedPercent, ... }) } } })` — no clamp.
- The VS Code `toUsageWindow` (`quotaProviders.ts:498-512`) stores `usedPercent` as given and derives `remainingPercent: Math.max(0, 100 - usedPercent)` — one-sided only, so -5 becomes remainingPercent 105.
- Contrast inside the same provider: the enterprise windows clamp their computed percents (`quotaProviders.ts:2517,2522` use `Math.min(100, Math.max(0, ...))`), and the web provider's `percentFromSpend` clamps the explicit value first (`packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/cursor.js`: `if (explicit !== null) return clampPercent(explicit);`, since #517/#555).
- Existing VS Code Cursor test (`packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.test.ts:2045`) exercises `totalPercentUsed: 42` only — no out-of-range case. The web fix added exactly such cases to `cursor.test.js` ("clamps billing_cycle totalPercentUsed %s to %s").
- Dedup: searches for "clamp Cursor VS Code" and "usedPercent clamp" across open+closed issues return no VS Code Cursor item; `git show --stat 372388d31` confirms #555 touched only `packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/cursor.js` + its test.

## Why it matters

Cursor is a headline quota provider and VS Code is a primary surface. The individual-plan path is the common case, and it is precisely the path the web fix named ("explicit-percent paths") — the port still renders >100% or negative usage for the same account the web UI now reports correctly.

## Acceptance criteria

- The non-enterprise Cursor path in `packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.ts` clamps `totalPercentUsed` to [0, 100] (the file's existing `clampPercent` helper at :171) before building the billing_cycle window; a missing value stays `null`.
- New tests in `packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.test.ts` pin: `totalPercentUsed: 150 -> usedPercent 100`, `totalPercentUsed: -5 -> usedPercent 0` (and `remainingPercent` 100), in-range 42 unchanged.
- Existing VS Code quota tests still pass.

## Problem

The web OpenAI quota provider (`packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/openai.js`) passes the ChatGPT wham/usage endpoint's `used_percent` values straight into the usage window with no clamping and no numeric coercion, so an out-of-range payload leaks into the usage UI: `usedPercent: 150` with `remainingPercent: 0`, or `usedPercent: -5` with `remainingPercent: 105`.

This is the one wham/usage reader that was missed by the recent clamp series: the sibling Codex provider (`packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/codex.js`, same endpoint, same fields) clamps via `clampPercent(toNumber(...))` since #551 / PR #145d8f4, and the VS Code Codex port clamps since #519.

## Evidence (verified on main `3428a415d`, 2026-10-27)

- `packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/openai.js:56` — `usedPercent: primary.used_percent ?? null` (5h window)
- `packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/openai.js:63` — `usedPercent: secondary.used_percent ?? null` (weekly window)
- No `toNumber`, no clamp: a non-numeric or out-of-range `used_percent` flows verbatim. Contrast `codex.js:94,102,134`: `usedPercent: clampPercent(toNumber(primary.used_percent))` etc.
- The shared window builder does not rescue it: `packages/web/server/lib/quota/utils/formatters.js:40-46` (`toUsageWindow`) stores `usedPercent` as given and derives `remainingPercent: Math.max(0, 100 - usedPercent)` — one-sided only.
- Laptop probe this run (`~/git/fleet/probe-quota-clamp-20261027/probe.mjs` on the laptop fork at the same commit, importing the repo's real `toUsageWindow`): `used_percent=150 -> shipped usedPercent=150 remainingPercent=0`; `used_percent=-5 -> shipped usedPercent=-5 remainingPercent=105`; in-range `42 -> 42/58` unchanged.
- There is no `openai.test.js` in `packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/` — the provider has no targeted test file at all (the registry tests in `index.test.js` exercise the Codex per-credential path, not this provider's windows).
- Dedup: searches for "openai used_percent clamp", "usedPercent clamp", "clamp Cursor VS Code" etc. across open+closed issues return no issue covering this provider; #516/#551 covered `codex.js` only.

## Why it matters

The Usage page renders whatever `usedPercent` the provider returns (progress bars, tone thresholds, remaining/used toggle). An over-100 or negative reading from this provider misreports the account's real usage and disagrees with the Codex provider's reading of the same account and endpoint.

## Acceptance criteria

- `openai.js` coerces `used_percent` with `toNumber` and clamps the result to [0, 100] for both the primary (5h) and secondary (weekly) windows, matching `codex.js`; missing/non-numeric values stay `null`.
- A new targeted test file (or registry-level test) pins: `used_percent: 150 -> usedPercent 100`, `used_percent: -5 -> usedPercent 0` (and `remainingPercent` 100), an in-range value unchanged, and a missing window field staying `null`.
- Existing quota tests still pass.

body:
## Summary

The VS Code quota port's timestamp helpers in `packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.ts` never got the non-finite guard that fixed the web helpers in #494 (PR #501). Both port helpers pass `Infinity` / `-Infinity` (and, for `normalizeTimestamp`, `NaN`) straight through as `resetAt` instead of returning `null`.

This is the #494 defect in the VS Code port, filed separately per the established port precedent (#489 → #492, #509 → #510, #515 → #518).

## Evidence (verified on main `3428a415d`, 2026-10-27)

`packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.ts:420-431` — the port's `toTimestamp` number branch has no finite check:

```ts
const toTimestamp = (value: unknown): number | null => {
  if (!value) return null;
  if (typeof value === 'number') {
    return value < 1_000_000_000_000 ? value * 1000 : value;   // Infinity → Infinity, -Infinity → -Infinity
  }
  ...
```

`packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.ts:2763-2766` — the port's `normalizeTimestamp` has no guard at all:

```ts
const normalizeTimestamp = (value: unknown) => {
  if (typeof value !== 'number') return null;
  return value < 1_000_000_000_000 ? value * 1000 : value;     // NaN → NaN, ±Infinity → ±Infinity
};
```

Verbatim-expression probe of both helpers (Node, this run):

```
toTimestamp(Infinity)        = Infinity
toTimestamp(-Infinity)       = -Infinity
toTimestamp(JSON.parse('1e999')) = Infinity     // JSON can actually deliver this
normalizeTimestamp(Infinity)  = Infinity
normalizeTimestamp(-Infinity) = -Infinity
normalizeTimestamp(NaN)       = NaN
```

The web counterparts (`packages/web/server/lib/quota/utils/transformers.js`, fixed by #494) return `null` for every non-finite input.

### Where the leaked values land

- `toTimestamp` feeds `resetAt` for Codex (`:1044`, `:1052`), google/antigravity (`:1299`, `:1328`, `:1474`, `:1551`), Claude (`:1639` and following), and the OAuth credential expiry at `:1134` — `expires: toTimestamp(oauthObject.expires) ?? undefined`, so an infinite expiry is treated as a credential that never expires.
- `normalizeTimestamp` feeds z.ai / zhipu `resetAt` from API-supplied `limit.nextResetTime` (`:2899`, `:2915`, `:3050`, `:3065`) and the Cursor cycle fallback (`:2502`).
- Downstream, the port's `calculateResetAfterSeconds` (`:492-496`) turns `resetAt = Infinity` into `resetAfterSeconds = Infinity` in the emitted usage window, and `formatResetTime(Infinity)` formats an Invalid Date.

## Why it matters

Every other timestamp path in both codebases now treats a non-finite timestamp as "unknown" (`null`). The port silently emits infinite/NaN reset times and a never-expiring credential expiry, so the VS Code quota surface can show nonsense reset information (or trust a credential forever) on a drifting or malformed upstream payload — exactly the failure #494 closed on the web side.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Port `toTimestamp` returns `null` for `Infinity`, `-Infinity`, and `NaN` numeric inputs (finite numbers, strings, and the seconds→ms scaling behave exactly as today).
- [ ] Port `normalizeTimestamp` returns `null` for `Infinity`, `-Infinity`, and `NaN` (finite behavior unchanged).
- [ ] Regression tests in `packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.test.ts` (or a sibling test file) cover the non-finite inputs for both helpers' reachable paths.
- [ ] Existing VS Code quota tests pass.

Scope note: fix the two helpers only — do not change `calculateResetAfterSeconds` or `toUsageWindow`; with the helpers guarded they never see a non-finite `resetAt` from these paths.

body:
## Problem

OpenChamber's server-side schedule-window validator judges window times differently from OpenCode in both directions. This is the openchamber remainder of the cross-repo set tracked by developing-today/opencode#517 (fixed there by PRs #518 and #573, both merged); the opencode part is done — only this port remains.

`windowTimeMinutes` in `packages/web/server/lib/routing/model-routes.js:182-187` (main `a8861ed03`):

```js
const match = /^(\d{1,2}):(\d{1,2})(?::\d{2})?$/.exec(value.trim());
if (match === null || Number(match[1]) > 23 || Number(match[2]) > 59) return undefined;
```

The seconds group is never captured and never range-checked, and it requires exactly two digits. OpenCode's current `minutesOf` (`packages/core/src/model-route-schedule.ts:80-88` in developing-today/opencode) captures seconds as `(\d{1,2})` and rejects `seconds > 59`.

Verified this run by probing the exported `validateModelRouteSchedules` on current main:

```
"09:30:99" -> null (accepted)     OpenCode: rejected (seconds > 59)
"09:30:60" -> null (accepted)     OpenCode: rejected (seconds > 59)
"09:30:59" -> null (accepted)     OpenCode: accepted (correct)
"09:30:5"  -> refused ("must be a local time")   OpenCode: accepted since #573 (single-digit seconds)
"09:30"    -> null (accepted)     OpenCode: accepted (correct)
"24:00"    -> refused             OpenCode: rejected (correct)
"09:60"    -> refused             OpenCode: rejected (correct)
```

## Why it matters

The validator's stated contract (`model-routes.js:201-202`) is that a window is "judged the way OpenCode judges it", because OpenCode's parser "drops a window it cannot read and takes the whole schedule with it":

- **False accept (the serious direction):** a schedule saved through OpenChamber with `start: "09:30:99"` passes validation, is written to config, and is then silently dropped in full by OpenCode — the weight change never applies and the operator gets no signal. This is exactly the typo class opencode#517 was filed to catch.
- **False refuse:** `start: "09:30:5"` is a form OpenCode accepts and applies (opencode#528/#573), but OpenChamber refuses it at save time, so a hand-written config value cannot be round-tripped through the OpenChamber UI/API.

`windowTimeMinutes` backs both schedule surfaces: per-route schedules via `validateModelRoute` and global schedules via `validateModelRouteSchedules` (both go through `validateScheduleWindow`, `model-routes.js:203ff`, call sites at `:225` and `:230`). One fix covers both.

Checked and NOT part of this defect: the UI's stored-time normalizer `packages/ui/src/lib/routing/routeSchedules.ts:31-45` captures seconds and range-checks `> 59`; it normalizes `<input type="time">` values (always zero-padded), so its two-digit requirement is not the save-path validator's contract.

## Acceptance criteria

- `validateModelRouteSchedules` and `validateModelRoute` refuse a window whose start or end carries seconds outside 0-59 (`09:30:60`, `09:30:99` return the "must be a local time" problem, matching OpenCode's rejection).
- Single-digit seconds are accepted the way OpenCode accepts them: `09:30:5` validates and is judged equal to `09:30` for the start==end check (seconds round down, per OpenCode's `minutesOf`).
- Existing valid forms are unchanged: `09:30`, `09:30:00`, `09:30:59`, `9:30` behave exactly as before; hour/minute range checks untouched.
- A regression test in `packages/web/server/lib/routing/model-routes.test.js` covers out-of-range seconds (60 and 99) and single-digit seconds alongside the existing time cases.
- `bun run check:changed` passes for the changed files.

## Cross-repo set

- Origin: developing-today/opencode#517 — CLOSED. Fix: PR #518 (reject out-of-range seconds) + PR #573 (allow single-digit seconds, #528), both merged; current opencode `minutesOf` shown above.
- This repo: the port described here. No other repo carries this validator (checked: the time regex exists only at `model-routes.js:184` in this repo's server code).
- This filing discharges the SET-REMAINDER pointer recorded in `backlog-devtoday-openchamber.md` on 2026-10-26 ("when opencode #517 lands its seconds range check, port the same refusal here"); #517 landed 2026-10-26, and the single-digit-seconds divergence from #573 is new since the pointer was written.

body:
## Summary

Several server routes still judge numeric query parameters with bare `parseInt` / `Number(...)` + a finiteness check, so malformed values are silently reinterpreted instead of falling back or being refused: `10junk` becomes 10, `2.9` becomes 2 (or stays 2.9 and is sent upstream), and `1e3` becomes 1. The repo has already fixed this exact defect class repeatedly (#433, #446, #463, #464, #465) and codified the standard in `packages/web/server/lib/git/routes.js:25-29`: "Every git endpoint judges its numeric parameters the same strict way … the value's whole text must be digits … Bare parseInt reinterpreted '10junk' as 10". The sites below never got that treatment — and two of the affected files already contain a strict helper that the loose sites bypass.

Verified on main `2dd83a589` (2026-10-27).

## Evidence

### 1. GitLab source-control routes — `requestNumber` is loose, its sibling in the same file is strict

`packages/web/server/lib/gitlab/routes.js:139-142`:

```js
function requestNumber(value) {
  const number = Number.parseInt(String(value ?? ''), 10);
  return Number.isInteger(number) && number > 0 ? number : null;
}
```

Directly below it, `requestIssueNumber` (:144-149) judges the same kind of parameter strictly (`/^[1-9]\d*$/` + `Number.isSafeInteger`) and is used by `issues/get` (:1218) and `issues/comments` (:1238). The loose helper is used for:

- `GET /api/source-control/gitlab/pulls/context` — `number` (:1172): `?number=10junk` silently loads merge request **10**; `?number=2.9` loads MR **2**. The endpoint 400s only when the helper returns null (:1177 area, `if (!number)`), so it clearly intends to validate — the loose helper defeats that intent for trailing junk and fractions.
- `GET /api/source-control/gitlab/pulls/list` — `page` (:1157) and `GET /api/source-control/gitlab/issues/list` — `page` (:1204): `?page=2.9` becomes page 2, `?page=10junk` becomes page 10, instead of the `?? 1` default a malformed page gets when it parses to NaN.

### 2. GitHub source-control routes — fractional page/number pass the finiteness guard

`packages/web/server/lib/github/routes.js` has the strict helper `readPositiveIntegerQuery` (:86-91, `/^[1-9]\d*$/` + safe integer), used e.g. at :2285 — but:

- `GET …/issues/list` (:2473): `const page = requestedPage ? Number(requestedPage) : 1;` with `effectivePage = Number.isFinite(page) && page > 0 ? page : 1` (:2507). `?page=2.9` is finite and > 0, so **2.9 is sent to the GitHub API as the page**.
- `GET …/pulls/list` (:2825): same pattern, `Number(req.query.page)` → same effectivePage guard → 2.9 passes.
- `GET …/pulls/context` (:3033): `const number = typeof req.query?.number === 'string' ? Number(req.query.number) : null;` — the `!number` check at :3048 catches NaN/0, but `?number=2.9` passes and is used as the pull request number downstream.

(Trailing junk is safe here — `Number('10junk')` is NaN — so for the GitHub sites the defect is fractions only, the #465 sub-class.)

### 3. Find-in-files route — `limit` judged by bare parseInt

`packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.js:1036-1039`:

```js
const requestedLimit = isString(req.query.limit) ? Number.parseInt(String(req.query.limit), 10) : Number.NaN;
const limit = Number.isInteger(requestedLimit)
  ? Math.min(Math.max(1, requestedLimit), CONTENT_SEARCH_MAX_LIMIT)
  : CONTENT_SEARCH_DEFAULT_LIMIT;
```

`?limit=10junk` → 10 results, `?limit=2.9` → 2, `?limit=1e3` → 1, instead of the default (200, `CONTENT_SEARCH_DEFAULT_LIMIT`, max 500 in `fs/content-search.js:15-16`). The route 400s a malformed `query` (:1033) but silently reinterprets a malformed `limit`.

### 4. Routing plan-notes route — `clampLimit` judged by bare parseInt

`packages/web/server/lib/routing/plan-routes.js:26-29`:

```js
const clampLimit = (value) => {
  const number = Number.parseInt(typeof value === 'string' ? value : '', 10);
  return Number.isFinite(number) ? Math.min(Math.max(number, 1), 500) : 50;
};
```

feeds `GET /api/routing/plans/notes` (:95): `?limit=10junk` → 10, `?limit=2.9` → 2, `?limit=1e3` → 1, instead of the 50 default.

### Probe (the four helpers' exact expressions, run this run)

```text
10junk  requestNumber= 10  planClampLimit= 10  fsLimit= 10
2.9     requestNumber=  2  planClampLimit=  2  fsLimit=  2
1e3     requestNumber=  1  planClampLimit=  1  fsLimit=  1
10      requestNumber= 10  planClampLimit= 10  fsLimit= 10
0       requestNumber= null planClampLimit= 1  fsLimit=  1
-5      requestNumber= null planClampLimit= 1  fsLimit=  1
abc     requestNumber= null planClampLimit= 50 fsLimit= 200 (defaults)
```

(fsLimit uses the real constants: default 200, max 500.)

## Why it matters

- The GitLab pulls/context case is the sharp one: a mistyped or hand-edited MR number does not error — it silently shows a *different merge request's* context, the same "wrong data presented as authoritative" failure the strict-parsing series exists to prevent.
- Fractions reaching the GitHub API as `page: 2.9` / a pull number of 2.9 produce upstream errors or empty results that look like "no such PR", masking the real cause.
- The inconsistency itself is a trap: two helpers in one file (gitlab `requestNumber` vs `requestIssueNumber`; github loose sites vs `readPositiveIntegerQuery`) judge the same parameter kind differently, so the next endpoint copy-picks whichever it finds first.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every site above judges its numeric query parameter by whole text (digits only, positive, safe integer where an identifier), reusing the strict helpers that already exist in the same file where there is one (`requestIssueNumber` pattern in gitlab/routes.js, `readPositiveIntegerQuery` in github/routes.js).
- [ ] Malformed values behave exactly as the strict siblings do today: `page`/`limit` fall back to their existing defaults (1 / 200 / 50), and `number` parameters are refused (400 / null path) — no silent reinterpretation of `10junk`, `2.9`, or `1e3` anywhere.
- [ ] Well-formed values (`10`, `2`, `500`) behave exactly as before, including existing clamping (fs limit max 500, plan-notes limit 1–500).
- [ ] Regression tests cover at least: gitlab pulls/context `number=10junk` and `number=2.9` refused; gitlab page and github page `2.9` → default page 1 (not 2.9 upstream); find-in-files and plan-notes `limit=10junk`/`2.9`/`1e3` → defaults.
- [ ] No other route's parameter handling changes; the git routes' strict parsers are untouched.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for `parseInt`, `10junk`, `requestNumber`, `find-in-files`: the hits are the closed strict-parsing family for *other* sites (#433 CLI --lines/--limit, #446 CLI --timeout, #463/#464/#465 git endpoints, #264/#274 ports, #209 weekdays) — none covers the gitlab/github source-control routes, the find-in-files limit, or the plan-notes limit.

# fix(quota): VS Code port leaks out-of-range usedPercent in ClinePass path — the #512 defect in quotaProviders.ts

## Problem

The web ClinePass provider's unclamped-`percentUsed` defect (#512) also exists in the VS Code port's own copy of the provider. #512 scopes only the web provider (`packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/cline-pass.js`); the port in `packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.ts` is a separate implementation and is not covered, following the #509 → #510 / #515 → #518 / #516 → #519 / #517 → #521 port precedent.

## Evidence (verified this run on main 0a3f98313)

`packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.ts:3544-3548` (`fetchClinePassQuota`):

```ts
const usedPercent = toNumber(asNonEmptyString(limit.percentUsed)
  ?? (Number.isFinite(limit.percentUsed) ? limit.percentUsed : null));
if (usedPercent === null) continue;
windows[kind.key] = toUsageWindow({ usedPercent, ... });
```

The port's `toUsageWindow` (:496-501) only lower-clamps the derived `remainingPercent` (`Math.max(0, 100 - usedPercent)`), so an out-of-range `usedPercent` reaches the window unchanged.

Runtime probe this run (temporary bun test calling the exported `fetchClinePassQuota` with injected `readAuth`/`fetchImpl`, probe removed after the run):

- `percentUsed: 150` → window `{usedPercent: 150, remainingPercent: 0}`
- `percentUsed: '-20'` → window `{usedPercent: -20, remainingPercent: 120}`
- `percentUsed: -20` → window `{usedPercent: -20, remainingPercent: 120}`

The port's own ClinePass tests (`quotaProviders.test.ts`, "ClinePass quota provider (VS Code parity)") pin acceptance of finite percentages (`[0, '0', '51']`) but never an out-of-range one — the same gap as the web provider. The same file clamps both bounds in its NanoGPT port path (:3181: `Math.max(0, Math.min(100, percentUsed * 100))`).

Dedup: searched open + closed issues for "vscode cline", "cline-pass quotaProviders", and related terms on 2026-10-27 — no VS Code ClinePass issue exists. #512 is web-only. (The sibling Google/Antigravity port defect is already tracked separately as #545 — do not fold this into it; different provider and read site.)

## Why it matters

If the ClinePass API reports over-consumption or a drifting/negative percentage, VS Code users see "150% used" / "120% remaining" on the quota surface, and threshold coloring and gift-reset math (`100 - usedPercent`) consume the corrupt value — exactly the failure #512 fixes for web users.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `fetchClinePassQuota` in `packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.ts` clamps `percentUsed` to [0, 100] for both the numeric and string forms; non-finite/unparseable values stay skipped as today
- [ ] Regression tests in `packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.test.ts` (ClinePass parity block): 150 → 100, -20 / '-20' → 0, in-range values (43, '51') unchanged
- [ ] Existing ClinePass VS Code tests still pass
- [ ] No clamp added inside the shared `toUsageWindow` as the only fix (the wafer overage branch deliberately allows >100 — same constraint as #512)

body:
## Finding

PR #541 fixes #507 — Google and Antigravity quota transforms computing `usedPercent` with only a lower clamp, so a negative `remainingFraction` (e.g. -0.5) displays 150% usage — but its Affected-surfaces table says "VS Code: Not applicable — the VS Code port does not carry these transforms." That is incorrect: the VS Code port carries its own copies of the same Google and Antigravity transforms in `packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.ts`, and all four sites still use the unclamped expression.

## Evidence

Verified verbatim on current main `0a3f98313a2e8ad1ae34df2c07ecab5594622a10` (`packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.ts`):

- Line 1288 — Google quota-bucket path (`fetchGoogleQuota`, gemini buckets): `Math.max(0, 100 - remainingPercent)`
- Line 1317 — Google model-data path: same expression
- Line 1463 — Antigravity summary-bucket path: same expression
- Line 1540 — Antigravity model-data path: same expression

The same file already clamps both bounds elsewhere (line 2361: `Math.min(100, Math.max(0, 100 - remainingPercent))`), and PR #541 (commit `d6ba2ac6`) applies exactly that two-bound clamp to the four web-server sites in `packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/{google,antigravity}/transforms.js`. With `remainingFraction: -0.5`, `remainingPercent` rounds to -50 and each VS Code site above yields `usedPercent: 150`.

This is the same counterpart pattern as #510/#518/#519/#521 (VS Code port copies of web-provider clamp defects); no VS Code google/antigravity counterpart to #507 exists yet (searched 2026-10-27).

## Why it matters

VS Code users on Google/Antigravity quotas see the same impossible >100% usage the web fix removes, and the incorrect "not applicable" note in PR #541 makes the gap invisible to anyone tracing #507's coverage.

## Acceptance criteria

- All four sites in `packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.ts` (Google bucket, Google model-data, Antigravity bucket, Antigravity model-data) clamp `usedPercent` to [0, 100], matching PR #541's web fix.
- Tests in `packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.test.ts` pin a negative `remainingFraction` (e.g. -0.5 → `usedPercent` 100) for both providers.
- No behavior change for in-range fractions.

body:
## Problem

Settings search reveals a result by finding `[data-settings-item="<id>"]` on the page. If an entry's id has no matching anchor, clicking the search result highlights nothing — that was bug #325, fixed for the routing page with an anchor-existence test.

That test only covers the routing page. The other ~250 search entries have no anchor coverage at all, and 7 of them resolve only through dynamic construction that a literal source scan cannot see — so they are one refactor away from silently breaking the same way #325 did, with no test to catch it.

## Evidence (verified 2026-10-27, main `efdd08b70`)

- `packages/ui/src/lib/settings/search.test.ts:195-224` — the `settings search anchors` test extracts only ids matching `id: '...', page: 'routing'` from `search.ts` (9 ids) and asserts each exists as a literal `settingsItem=` / `data-settings-item=` anchor in component sources.
- `packages/ui/src/lib/settings/search.ts` contains 259 `id:`/`page:` entries across 26 pages (chat 50, general 40, sessions 23, appearance 19, messaging 16, integrations 15, …) — 250 of them are not anchor-checked.
- Replicating the test's literal scan over ALL ids (same regex, run this run) flags exactly 7 ids with no literal anchor:
  - `magic-prompts.visible-prompt`, `magic-prompts.instructions` — anchor comes from a ternary `settingsItem` prop;
  - `shortcuts.keyboard-shortcuts` — ternary `settingsItem` prop;
  - `integrations.third-party.opencode-claude` — dynamic `settingsItem` from the plugin id (`ThirdPartyIntegrationsSection.tsx`, plugin id in `thirdPartyPlugins.ts`);
  - `integrations.extensions.excalidraw`, `integrations.extensions.resource-monitor` — dynamic `settingsItem` from catalog guest ids (`CatalogExtensionsSection.tsx`, `catalogExtensions.ts`);
  - `extensions.gitIdentity` — special case in `SettingsView.tsx`.
  A prior triage (backlog, 2026-10-26) confirmed all 7 resolve today through those dynamic paths — they are NOT currently broken; they are currently untestable by the existing scan.
- History: #325 (closed) — "Settings search: three routing results point at anchors that don't exist, so nothing is highlighted" — the same failure class, on the one page that now has coverage.

## Why it matters

Settings search is the discovery path for ~259 settings. An anchor renamed in a component, a plugin/catalog id changed, or the `SettingsView` special case dropped would silently break reveal for that entry — no error, no failing test — exactly the #325 failure mode, on pages nobody re-checks by hand.

## Acceptance criteria

- The anchor test (or a companion test) covers every entry id in `search.ts`, not only `page: 'routing'`.
- The 7 dynamic cases above are covered in a way that fails if their dynamic construction breaks (e.g. the test derives the expected anchors from the same plugin/catalog sources the components use, or asserts the special-case/ternary sources still produce those ids) — simply allow-listing the 7 ids as exempt does NOT satisfy this.
- The test still fails when a literal anchor is removed (existing routing behavior preserved).
- `bun test packages/ui/src/lib/settings/search.test.ts` passes; no production behavior change is needed unless coverage reveals a genuinely missing anchor, in which case file it separately.
