body:
## Problem

Both npm-registry metadata caches grow forever: entries are never evicted, the 1-hour TTL is only checked lazily when the *same* package name is looked up again, and there is no size/entry cap and no sweep.

- Web: `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/npm-registry.js` — module-level `_cache` Map (line 33). `cacheResult` (lines 70-74) sets an entry for every distinct name that returns ok/404; `getNpmInfo` (lines ~128-133) checks `Date.now() - cached.fetchedAt < NPM_CACHE_TTL_MS` only for the name being requested. Nothing ever deletes an entry. The module does export `clearCache()` (line 153), but its only production import — `clearNpmCache` in `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/feature-routes-runtime.js:53` — is never called anywhere in that file (grep: the import line is the sole occurrence); only tests call it.
- VS Code twin: `packages/vscode/src/opencodeConfig.ts` — `npmInfoCache` Map (line 1477), `getNpmInfo`/`lookupNpmPackage` (lines 1484-1524) with the same lazy TTL check and no eviction, no clear function, and no cap at all.

Each retained payload holds the package's **full version list** (`versions: Object.keys(data.versions)` — npm-registry.js `parseVersions`; opencodeConfig.ts line ~1493): hundreds to thousands of strings for mature packages, plus dist-tags.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `cf5011987`)

Laptop probe against the real module (`~/git/fleet/probe-oc-npm-cache-20261030/probe.mjs`; `npm-registry.js` md5 `63f066019a4b9232f4e14b0a58005f6f`, byte-identical to main; fetch stubbed, no network):

- Populated 3,000 distinct names × 400 versions each: heap 4.3 MB → **16.2 MB retained**.
- Re-query of a live entry within TTL: no refetch (cache works as intended).
- After simulating +2h (past TTL): re-querying one name refetches only that name; heap stays **16.2 MB** — the other 2,999 stale entries are never swept.
- `clearCache()` + GC drops heap to 6.5 MB, proving it is the only release path — and production never calls it.

Callers are the plugin routes (`plugin-routes.js:145`, `feature-routes-runtime.js:442`), so every distinct plugin/package name a long-lived server or extension host ever looks up is retained for the life of the process. Same grow-forever class as fixed #903 (template caches) and #875 (notification maps), in a surface those sweeps missed.

Dedup: `gh` search for npm/registry cache and eviction terms across open+closed issues returns no filing for these caches.

## Why it matters

OpenChamber servers and VS Code extension hosts run for days to weeks. A slow, unbounded memory creep keyed on user/plugin-controlled package names is exactly the leak class this repo has been fixing cache by cache; these two duplicated caches were left behind, and the dead `clearNpmCache` import makes the web one look handled when it is not.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Both caches bound retention: expired entries are actually removed (sweep on access/insert, or a periodic prune), and/or a max-entries bound with oldest/TTL eviction is enforced.
- [ ] The web module's dead `clearNpmCache` import in `feature-routes-runtime.js` is either wired to a real lifecycle point or removed.
- [ ] Tests pin the bound in both surfaces: after the TTL passes or the cap is exceeded, entries for names that are never re-queried are gone (extending `npm-registry.test.js` / `opencodeConfig-npm-registry.test.ts` cache cases).
- [ ] Normal behavior unchanged: cache hit within TTL does not refetch, 404s remain cached, network failures remain uncached.

title: fix(web): agent-tool action resolver resolves Object.prototype tool names — 'constructor'/'toString'/'__proto__' throw a TypeError instead of the unsupported-action usage error

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Summary

The agent-tool action resolver looks the calling tool's name up in a plain object literal, so a tool name that matches an `Object.prototype` member (`constructor`, `toString`, `hasOwnProperty`, `valueOf`, `__proto__`) resolves to an inherited value instead of "unknown tool". `resolveAgentToolAction` then throws `TypeError: known.includes is not a function` instead of returning its documented `{ error: "Unsupported OpenChamber action: … Use one of: …" }` result. The agent-tool route converts that throw into a `kind: "runtime"` failure with the raw TypeError message, so the calling model gets a misleading internal error and none of the action list the resolver exists to provide — exactly the "one wrong name becomes three" failure the resolver's own comment warns about.

The same unguarded pattern sits in two sibling dispatch tables in the same module family (currently masked by the service-level allowlist, so latent rather than reachable today).

## Evidence (main `70ea4558b`, verified this run)

- `packages/web/server/lib/openchamber-control/actions.js:181-190` — `ACTIONS_BY_TOOL` is a plain object literal (frozen, but freezing does not stop prototype lookup); `:209` does `const scoped = ACTIONS_BY_TOOL[toolName] ?? null;` with no own-property check, and `:212`/`:228` call `known.includes(value)` / `known.join(', ')` on the result.
- `packages/web/server/lib/agent-tool/runtime.js:764` — `execute()` calls `resolveAgentToolAction(requested, asNonEmptyString(payload.tool))` **outside** its `try` (the `try` at ~:800 covers only `executeAction`); the route at `runtime.js:845-867` catches the throw and returns `createResult({ ok: false, error: { message: <TypeError text>, kind: 'runtime' } })` instead of the resolver's `kind: 'usage'` answer with the valid-action list.
- Reproduced this run on the laptop (probe `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-proto-tool/probe.mjs`, importing the real `actions.js` from a tree whose md5s match sandbox main for all four files involved):

| Tool name | Actual | Expected (cf. `openchamber_future` / unknown tool) |
|---|---|---|
| `constructor`, `toString`, `hasOwnProperty`, `valueOf`, `__proto__` | throws `TypeError: known.includes is not a function` | `{ error: "Unsupported OpenChamber action: read. Use one of: <full action list>" }` (unknown tools fall back to the full list) |
| `openchamber_memory`, `openchamber_future`, `null` | resolves normally (`memory.read` for bare `read`) | — (unchanged) |

- Same-pattern latent sites (guarded today only by `service.js`'s `CONTROL_ACTIONS` Set check and each module's `actions.includes(action)` gate in `service.js:1086-1094`, so not independently reachable — but one refactor away from the quota-layer bug in #939):
  - `packages/web/server/lib/openchamber-control/provider-actions.js:667` — `const handler = handlers[action];`
  - `packages/web/server/lib/openchamber-control/integration-service-actions.js:435` — `const handler = handlers[action];`
  - For both, `handlers['constructor']` / `handlers['toString']` are truthy functions and `handlers['__proto__']` is a truthy non-function, so the `if (!handler) throw badRequest(…)` guard would not fire.
  - The sibling that got it right: `packages/web/server/lib/openchamber-control/session-actions.js:435` already uses `Object.hasOwn(handlers, action) ? handlers[action] : null`.

Distinct from #939 (quota provider registries) and #944 (getProviderAuth): this is the openchamber-control / agent-tool dispatch layer, a different surface with different callers.

## Why it matters

The agent-tool callback is how managed OpenCode sessions drive OpenChamber. Its resolver was built specifically so a wrong or unidentifiable tool/action name gets a self-correcting usage error listing the valid actions. A prototype-named tool instead crashes resolution and reports an internal TypeError as a runtime failure — the model cannot recover from it, and operators reading the result see a server bug instead of a bad tool name. The `tool` field comes from the caller's payload, so any plugin/tool that names itself (or is misconfigured as) a prototype member hits this deterministically.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `resolveAgentToolAction` treats prototype-member tool names (`constructor`, `toString`, `hasOwnProperty`, `valueOf`, `__proto__`) exactly like any other unknown tool: no throw, fallback to the full action list, and the standard "Unsupported… Use one of:" error for unresolvable actions.
- [ ] `provider-actions.js` and `integration-service-actions.js` dispatch with own-property semantics (e.g. `Object.hasOwn`, matching `session-actions.js:435`), so a prototype-named action gets the modules' own `Unsupported … action` 400.
- [ ] Real tool names (`openchamber`, `openchamber_memory`, `openchamber_schedule`, `openchamber_web`, `openchamber_knowledge`, `openchamber_notify`, `openchamber_render`) and all real actions behave exactly as before.
- [ ] Tests pin the prototype-name cases in `action-resolution.test.js` (resolver level) and, for the two dispatchers, alongside their existing unsupported-action cases in `provider-actions.test.js` / `integration-service-actions.test.js`.

title: fix(web): realtime proxy WebSocket queue is unbounded and the upstream handshake has no timeout — a stalled remote buffers every client byte forever

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

The WebSocket half of the realtime proxy (`packages/web/server/lib/realtime-proxy.js`) queues and forwards with no bounds of any kind:

1. **No upstream handshake timeout.** The upstream socket is created at `realtime-proxy.js:205-210` as `new WebSocket(target, { headers, origin })` — no `handshakeTimeout`, and nothing else in the handler times the connection out. An upstream that accepts the TCP connection but never completes the WebSocket upgrade (wedged server, middlebox, half-open NAT) leaves the pair hanging forever.
2. **Unbounded pre-open queue.** While the upstream is `CONNECTING`, every client message is pushed onto `pending` (`realtime-proxy.js:210, 219-227`) with no byte or count cap — contrast the dev-tunnel in the same codebase, which caps its identical pre-open buffer at `MAX_PENDING_BYTES` (256 KiB) and drops the connection past it (`dev-tunnel/client.js:24, 155-176`; `dev-tunnel/runtime.js` likewise).
3. **No post-open backpressure.** Once open, `upstream.send(data)` and `client.send(data)` (`realtime-proxy.js:219-221, 229-233`) ignore `bufferedAmount` in both directions — contrast the event-stream protocol, which closes a client past a 16 MiB buffered cap (`event-stream/protocol.js:8, 88-106`, close code 1013 "client is too slow"), and the relay tunnel-host's v1 backpressure rule (pause at 4 MiB).

## Verification (this run, laptop probe against the real module)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-realtime-proxy-20261030/probe.mjs` on the laptop, importing the real `attachRealtimeProxy` from main `25daf4929` (file md5 `a5b3358c…` identical on laptop fork and sandbox clone). The upstream is a raw TCP server that accepts the connection and stays silent (never answers the upgrade). A client connects through the proxy and sends 512 × 64 KiB = 32 MiB.

```json
{"phase":"stalled-12s","sentMB":32,"clientReadyState":1,"upstreamHandshakeDone":false,"rssDeltaMB":90.1}
{"phase":"after-handshake-3s","bytesFlushedToUpstreamMB":32}
```

After 12 s the handshake was still incomplete, the proxy had not closed or timed out anything, the client was still open, and the process had grown +90 MB RSS. When the upstream finally completed the handshake, the full 32 MiB flushed out of the proxy — every byte had been sitting in the proxy's `pending` queue (plus copies) the whole time.

## Why it matters

- The proxy fronts exactly the connections most likely to stall: remote/relayed OpenChamber instances (event, terminal, and global-event sockets, `realtime-proxy.js:16-24`). A remote that wedges mid-handshake turns each connected client into an unbounded memory sink and a permanently dead session the UI never sees fail.
- Every sibling piping surface in this codebase bounds this exact shape (dev-tunnel pending caps, event-stream slow-client close, relay backpressure) — the realtime proxy is the remaining outlier.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The upstream WebSocket gets a bounded handshake timeout (named constant, house range ~10-15 s); on expiry the upstream attempt is terminated and the client socket is closed with an error code, not left hanging.
- [ ] The pre-open `pending` queue is byte/count bounded (dev-tunnel `MAX_PENDING_BYTES` precedent); overflow closes the pair instead of buffering further.
- [ ] Post-open forwarding respects `bufferedAmount` in both directions (pause the producer or close a peer past the event-stream's 16 MiB slow-peer cap).
- [ ] Regression tests: silent-upstream handshake times out and closes the client; a client flooding a stalled handshake is cut at the pending bound and the queued bytes are never flushed; healthy proxying (open upstream, normal frames both ways) is unchanged.

title: fix(web): dev-tunnel piping has no backpressure after connect — a stalled consumer buffers the whole stream in process memory

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/m
labels.description: Medium: expected under 1 day of work

body:
## Problem

The dev-tunnel piping has no backpressure after connect, except in one of its four directions. A fast producer paired with a slow or stalled consumer buffers the entire stream in the OpenChamber/desktop process's memory, without limit.

The one guarded direction proves the hazard is known in this feature: on the server side, `packages/web/server/lib/dev-tunnel/runtime.js:119-136` pauses the dev-server socket while the WebSocket drains —

```js
socket.send(chunk);
// Stop reading from the dev server while the socket drains, otherwise a
// fast response against a slow client buffers the whole body in memory.
if (socket.bufferedAmount > 1_000_000) { upstream.pause(); /* poll + resume */ }
```

The other three piping directions have no equivalent guard:

1. **Client, upstream → local (probe-verified):** `packages/web/server/lib/dev-tunnel/client.js:138-141`
   ```js
   upstream.on('message', (data) => {
     if (socket.destroyed) return;
     socket.write(data);   // return value ignored; ws never paused
   });
   ```
2. **Client, local → upstream:** `client.js:155-162` — after `open`, `upstream.send(chunk)` runs for every TCP chunk with no `upstream.bufferedAmount` check; the local socket is paused only for the pre-open pending buffer (`MAX_PENDING_BYTES`, client.js:23), never after connect.
3. **Runtime, WebSocket → dev server:** `runtime.js:166-170` — `upstream.write(data)` with the return value ignored, so a dev server that reads slowly (or not at all) accumulates the client's whole upload in the server process.

## Verification (this run, laptop probe against the real module)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-devtunnel-bp-20261030/probe.mjs` on the laptop, importing the real `createDevTunnelClient` from main `25daf4929` (file md5 identical on laptop fork and sandbox clone). A WebSocket upstream floods 256 KiB chunks (128 MiB total); the local TCP consumer connects and reads **nothing** for 4 s.

```json
{"phase":"paused-4s","serverSentMB":128,"receivedMB":0,"rssDeltaMB":152.1}
{"phase":"after-resume-4s","serverSentMB":128,"receivedMB":128}
```

The upstream was never slowed: it sent all 128 MiB while the consumer read 0 bytes, the tunnel process grew +152 MB RSS, and on resume the consumer received the full 128 MiB — it had all been buffered inside the tunnel process. With the runtime's own rule (pause at >1 MB buffered) the run-ahead would be a few MiB, not the whole stream.

Real-world shape: a dev server streaming a large response (file download, log tail, media, HMR payload) to a local browser/process that stalls or is suspended wedges the desktop app's memory; symmetrically, a fast local upload to a slow dev server grows the server process.

## Why it matters

- Unbounded memory growth in a long-lived desktop/server process, triggered by ordinary traffic shapes (one stalled tab or suspended local process is enough) — the exact failure the runtime's existing guard was written to prevent, left open on the mirror paths.
- The pre-connect buffers in both files are carefully bounded (`MAX_PENDING_BYTES`), so the post-connect hole reads as an oversight, not a design choice.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Client upstream→local: when the local socket's write buffer exceeds a bounded threshold (the runtime's 1 MB precedent or a named constant), pause the WebSocket reads (or equivalent) and resume on drain; a stalled consumer can no longer make the process buffer more than a bounded amount.
- [ ] Client local→upstream: when `upstream.bufferedAmount` exceeds the threshold, pause the local socket and resume when it drains.
- [ ] Runtime WebSocket→dev-server: respect `upstream.write()`'s return / `drain` (pause WS reads while the dev server's socket is backed up), matching the already-guarded opposite direction.
- [ ] Regression tests in `packages/web/server/lib/dev-tunnel/tunnel.test.js` style: fake producer/consumer pair where the consumer stalls — producer is paused (or the connection is dropped at a bounded limit) instead of the full stream being buffered; normal fast-consumer piping is unchanged.
- [ ] No behavior change for healthy flows: handshake timeout, pre-open pending cap, and teardown semantics stay as they are.

title: fix(web): project start-command read has no deadline — a stalled OpenCode wedges worktree bootstrap before the bounded start command runs

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

body:
## Problem

The project start-command reader in `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/project-start-command.js` asks the running OpenCode for the project's `commands.start` through a bare `@opencode/client` with no deadline:

- `project-start-command.js:37-41` — `OpenCode.make({ baseUrl, headers, … })` with no `fetch` wrapper, then `await Promise.all([client.location.get(), client.project.list()])` with no request options.

In `@opencode/client` 2.0.32 the generated client's `prepare()` sets `signal: requestOptions?.signal` and nothing else — there is no SDK default timeout, so these calls wait forever when OpenCode accepts the connection but never answers. Sibling readers in the same codebase do bound their clients: `opencode/skill-routes.js` wraps fetch with `AbortSignal.timeout(8_000)` (its comment even lists "timeout" as an expected failure mode), and the worktree instance disposer in `git/routes.js` wraps fetch with `WORKTREE_INSTANCE_DISPOSE_TIMEOUT_MS`.

## Why it matters

The read sits on the worktree bootstrap path, ahead of the start-command execution that the #861/#868/#884 work bounded so carefully:

- `git/service.js:2349` — `runWorktreeStartScripts` awaits `readProjectStartCommand(projectDirectory)` inside the queued worktree bootstrap; the bootstrap cannot reach git-ready until it returns.
- `git/service.js:1428` — `inspectContributorCheckoutActions` awaits the same read to build the contributor trust prompt.

`readProjectStartCommand` (`project-start-command.js:48-57`) is written to degrade gracefully: a failed read logs a warning and returns `''`, and the module documentation (`opencode/DOCUMENTATION.md`) states "A failed read runs no command and logs a warning; the worktree is still created." A *stalled* read is not a failed read — it never rejects, so the graceful path never runs: one wedged OpenCode (e.g. a location whose MCP fleet hangs on boot) wedges every worktree creation that needs the project command, indefinitely and silently — the same wedge class as #861, one step earlier in the same flow.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `f0d3428b8`)

Laptop probe against the real module (`~/git/fleet/probe-oc-sdk-deadline-20261030/probe.mjs`; fork at `f0d3428b8`, file md5 matched main):

- Control server (answers promptly): `openCodeProjectStartCommandSource(...).read('/tmp')` settled immediately, returning the served `"npm run start"`.
- Stall server (accepts TCP, never responds): the same `read()` was still **unsettled after 3,000 ms** — no rejection, so `readProjectStartCommand`'s catch-and-return-`''` fallback could never fire.

## Acceptance criteria

- The reader's OpenCode calls (`location.get`, `project.list`) run under a bounded deadline (per-call `{ signal }` with `AbortSignal.timeout(...)`, or a `fetch` wrapper on the client, matching the house patterns in `skill-routes.js` / `git/routes.js`).
- On deadline expiry the read behaves exactly like today's failed read: warning logged, `''` returned, worktree creation proceeds without the project start command.
- A regression test pins the stall case: against a never-answering transport, `read()` settles with `''` within the deadline; the test fails if the deadline is removed.
- `bun run check:changed` passes; no behavior change when OpenCode answers promptly.

body:
## Problem

The small-model catalog reads in `packages/web/server/lib/small-model/client.js` are made through a bare `@opencode/client` with no deadline of any kind:

- `client.js:53` — `OpenCode.make({ baseUrl, headers })`: no `fetch` wrapper (contrast `opencode/skill-routes.js`, which wraps fetch with `AbortSignal.timeout(8_000)`, and `git/routes.js`, whose disposer wraps with a timeout).
- `client.js:81` — `client.model.list()` (in `listModelInfos`)
- `client.js:96` — `client.provider.list()` (in `listProviderInfos`)
- `client.js:107` — `client.model.default()` (in `getDefaultModelInfo`)
- `client.js:123` — `client.agent.get({ agentID: 'title' })` (in `getConfiguredSmallModelRef`)

None passes request options. In `@opencode/client` 2.0.32 the generated client's `prepare()` sets `signal: requestOptions?.signal` and nothing else — there is no SDK default timeout, so a call without options waits forever when OpenCode accepts the connection but never answers (a wedged location boot / hung MCP fleet on the scoped directory is the realistic stall: these reads are directory-scoped, and a location read boots that directory's MCP fleet).

## Why it matters

Every small-model feature resolves its model through these reads *before* the one call that does carry a deadline:

- `small-model/index.js:195-218` — `resolveSmallModel` awaits `getConfiguredSmallModelRef`, `listModelInfos`, and `getDefaultModelInfo`.
- `small-model/index.js:301,318` — `generateSmallModelText` awaits resolution and a second `listModelInfos` before the generation request is built with the composed deadline at `index.js:277-285,342`. A caller-supplied abort signal is likewise only composed into the generation request — it cannot cancel the resolution reads.
- `listModelInfos`' keep-the-previous-answer fallback (`client.js`, catch returns the cached list) never fires on a hang, because the promise never settles; the 30 s cache only means the stall is re-hit on every cache miss/expiry per directory.

So one stalled OpenCode hangs, indefinitely and silently: session-assist recaps/suggestions (`session-assist/runtime.js:225,240`), session-goal generation (`session-goal/create.js:42`, `session-goal/runtime.js:486`, `session-goal/spec-writer.js:132`), the diff walkthrough (`walkthrough/index.js:205,517`), and guest generation (`guests/routes.js:707`). No error, no fallback, no log — the awaiting feature simply never completes until the server restarts.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `f0d3428b8`)

Laptop probe against the real modules (`~/git/fleet/probe-oc-sdk-deadline-20261030/probe.mjs`, `probe2.mjs`; fork at `f0d3428b8`, file md5s matched main):

- Control server (answers promptly): `listModelInfos`, `getConfiguredSmallModelRef`, `getDefaultModelInfo`, `listProviderInfos` all settled immediately with the served values.
- Stall server (accepts TCP, never responds): all four reads were still **unsettled after 3,000 ms** — `listModelInfos` probed with a cache-miss directory so the 30 s cache could not mask it.

## Acceptance criteria

- Each catalog read in `small-model/client.js` (`model.list`, `provider.list`, `model.default`, `agent.get`) runs under a bounded deadline (per-call `{ signal }` with `AbortSignal.timeout(...)`, or a `fetch` wrapper on the client, matching the house patterns in `skill-routes.js` / `git/routes.js`).
- On deadline expiry the reads behave like a failed read today: `listModelInfos` falls back to the previous cached answer for the directory (or `[]`), `listProviderInfos` returns `[]`, `getDefaultModelInfo` / `getConfiguredSmallModelRef` return `null` — resolution proceeds to its existing fallbacks instead of hanging.
- A regression test pins the stall case: against a never-answering transport, each read settles (rejects/is treated as failed) within the deadline; the test fails if the deadline is removed.
- `bun run check:changed` passes; no behavior change when OpenCode answers promptly.

body:
## Finding

The #782 wedge had two halves: provider fetches had no deadline, **and** the dispatcher's `pendingFetches` coalescing only releases an entry when the fetch promise settles — so one stalled provider froze that provider's quota until a server restart. Closed PR #784 pinned the second half with a dispatcher-level test ("releases the coalescing entry once a timed-out provider settles"). Merged PR #785 — the same fix, re-landed — dropped that test file change: its per-provider tests pin the 15s deadline per provider, but nothing pins the dispatcher behaviour that was the actual wedge.

If a future refactor reintroduces a never-settling path (or a provider whose deadline does not settle its promise), no test fails.

## Evidence

- PRs: https://github.com/developing-today/openchamber/pull/784 (closed, commit e48e1d6b — included `providers/index.test.js +25`, the coalescing-release test) and https://github.com/developing-today/openchamber/pull/785 (merged 74473882, commit a59a4e47, for #782; same provider files, **no** `index.test.js` change). File-list diff between the two PRs: only `index.test.js` differs.
- Current main `f0d3428b8c21ea0cb989623bbfe018d8a39f180a`:
  - `packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/index.js:275` `pendingFetches` map; `:527-533` get/finally-delete/set.
  - `packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/index.test.js` — `grep "releases the coalescing"` finds nothing; the registry describe block pins coalescing of concurrent refreshes (`:115`) but not release-after-timeout.
- Dedupe: no issue covers this test gap (open or closed).

## Why it matters

The coalescing release is the load-bearing half of the #782 fix — deadlines only help because the settled promise releases the entry. Leaving it unpinned invites a silent regression back to a restart-only wedge.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A dispatcher test in `providers/index.test.js`: a provider fetch that settles via its deadline (e.g. `AbortSignal.timeout` stubbed to ~1 ms against a never-answering fetch stub) returns the provider's timeout error result, and a subsequent fetch for the same provider fetches fresh and can succeed.
- [ ] The test fails if the `pendingFetches` entry is not released on settle.

body:
## Finding

PR #771 split OpenCode Go quota into per-credential rows via the dispatcher's `fetchPerCredential`, iterating the provider's `credentialAliases` in order — `['opencode-go', 'opencode']`, API key first. Before #771, the combined `fetchQuota` explicitly preferred the Console (`opencode`) sign-in and used the API key only as a fallback.

When both an `opencode-go` API key and an `opencode` Console sign-in are stored, each integration can have its own active credential. Both rows then carry `credentialActive: true`, key row first — and the Usage page selects the **first** active result as the primary row. The primary OpenCode Go quota therefore shows the key's usage (or its authentication error) even when the selected Console workspace has healthy quota — a precedence regression from the pre-#771 behaviour.

## Evidence

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/openchamber/pull/771 (merged 13adb886, commit bb958bed, closes #768/#736)
- Current main `f0d3428b8c21ea0cb989623bbfe018d8a39f180a`:
  - `packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/index.js:240` — `credentialAliases: ['opencode-go', 'opencode']`.
  - `packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/index.js:426` `fetchPerCredential` pushes rows in `integrationIds` order, tagging each `credentialActive: row.active`.
  - `packages/ui/src/components/sections/usage/UsagePage.tsx:84` — `selectedResults.find((entry) => entry.credentialActive) ?? selectedResults[0]`.
- Codex P2 comment 4410551507 on PR #771 (undispositioned; single-commit PR).
- Dedupe: no open/closed issue covers Console-vs-key precedence for the primary row (#736, closed, was the per-workspace feature itself).

## Why it matters

The primary quota row is what the Usage page and pool checks read first. Users with both credential types — the exact population #771 was built for — can see the wrong workspace's meters or a spurious auth error as their headline OpenCode Go state.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] When both credential types are present, the Console sign-in's row is the primary (first active) result, matching the pre-#771 precedence; the API-key row is still returned as its own labeled row.
- [ ] All per-workspace Console rows from #771 keep working (one labeled row per workspace credential).
- [ ] A dispatcher test pins the both-stored ordering: Console row precedes the key row in the results.

body:
## Finding

PR #764 taught the Antigravity quota provider to resolve auth from OpenCode's credential store: it accepts the `google` / `google.oauth` integration entry whenever it carries a refresh token. That entry is also where a plain **Gemini CLI OAuth** sign-in lives — the Google quota provider accepts the same credential shape, including pipe-packed project context. Nothing distinguishes which login issued the token, but `refreshAntigravityToken()` exchanges tokens exclusively with the distinct Antigravity OAuth client.

So a user signed in through Gemini CLI OAuth with no Antigravity account is advertised as Antigravity-configured (`isConfigured` returns true) and then gets a persistent "Failed to refresh Antigravity token" error for a provider they never configured.

## Evidence

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/openchamber/pull/764 (merged a6795179, commits 52c74cc1 + d274ae59)
- Current main `f0d3428b8c21ea0cb989623bbfe018d8a39f180a`, `packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/antigravity/auth.js`:
  - `:56` `resolveAntigravityStoreAuth` accepts `getAuthEntry(authObject, ['google', 'google.oauth'])` with any refresh token from `parseGoogleRefreshToken`.
  - `:82` `isConfigured = (auth) => resolveAntigravityAuth() !== null || resolveAntigravityStoreAuth(auth) !== null`.
- Codex P2 comment 4409997855 on PR #764 (undispositioned). Its sibling P2 on the same PR (credential-store errors swallowed) was fixed separately by PR #860 for #858; this classification finding was not.
- Dedupe: `gh issue list --search "Gemini Antigravity classification"` and related terms return no covering issue (open or closed).

## Why it matters

A wrong-client token can never refresh, so the failure is permanent, not transient: the Usage page shows a broken Antigravity row for every Gemini-CLI-only user, masking the provider's real state and generating spurious failure noise in quota reads.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Where the issuing login can be distinguished (stored entry shape/metadata), a Gemini-issued credential does not make Antigravity report configured.
- [ ] A confirmed wrong-client rejection from the Antigravity token exchange is handled as an unavailable Antigravity source, not a broken-account error state.
- [ ] Genuine Antigravity store sign-ins (the #764 case) still resolve and report quota; the legacy accounts-file path is unchanged.
- [ ] Tests pin: Gemini-shaped store entry → not configured / unavailable; Antigravity-shaped entry → configured.

title: fix(ci): repo-sweeper intake re-check treats a failed comment fetch as 'no marker' and can post a duplicate intake (PR #760)

labels.name: kind/ci

labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: effort/xs

body:
## Finding

PR #760 added a duplicate-post guard to the repo-sweeper's issue-intake leg: before posting, the leg re-checks the issue's live comments for the intake marker and skips if present. The check is a shell pipeline inside an `if` condition:

```bash
if gh api "repos/${GITHUB_REPOSITORY}/issues/${ISSUE_NUMBER}/comments" --paginate --jq '.[].body // ""' | grep -qF '**For the maintainer:**'; then
```

A **failed** fetch is indistinguishable from "marker absent": bash `set -e` does not stop failures inside an `if` condition, so a transient `gh api` error makes the condition false and the leg proceeds to post a duplicate intake comment and re-apply labels. The pipeline can also fail under `pipefail` when `grep -q` finds the marker early and closes the pipe while `gh` is still writing a large paginated response (SIGPIPE) — the same false-negative path.

## Evidence

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/openchamber/pull/760 (merged 12737f56, commit d515a71d, fixes #758)
- Current main `f0d3428b8c21ea0cb989623bbfe018d8a39f180a`, `.github/workflows/repo-sweeper.yml:532` — the pipeline above is unchanged.
- Codex P2 comment 4409579124 on PR #760 (undispositioned; the PR has a single commit, so it was never addressed in-PR).
- Dedupe: `gh issue list --search "repo-sweeper comment fetch"` returns nothing covering this.

## Why it matters

The guard exists to stop duplicate intake comments from displaced pending legs. The failure mode it mishandles — a transient API error at exactly the recheck moment — is the moment the guard is most likely to be exercised, and the result is the duplicate post (plus label churn) the guard was added to prevent.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The re-check fetches all comments to a file/variable first and aborts the step (non-zero exit, no post) when the fetch fails.
- [ ] The marker test runs against the fully fetched content (no early-close pipe into `grep -q` on a live paginated stream).
- [ ] Behaviour when the marker is genuinely present/absent is unchanged: present → skip post + label sync; absent → post once.

title: fix(web): mcpx daemon Unix-socket transport has no absolute deadline — a trickling response defeats the 10s timeout (PR #777)

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.description: Filed by the pr-diff-review job

labels.name: priority/normal

labels.name: app/web

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Finding

PR #777 gave the mcpx daemon client a 10s timeout, but only the HTTP transport got an absolute deadline. The Unix-socket transport still relies on `req.setTimeout(...)`, which is an **inactivity** timer: it resets on every socket chunk. A daemon that keeps sending small chunks without ever completing its response holds a `/api/mcpx/*` request open far beyond the configured timeout — the exact hang #774 was filed to eliminate, still reachable on the socket path.

## Evidence

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/openchamber/pull/777 (merged 655df99c, commit 26810e9d, fixes #774)
- Current main `f0d3428b8c21ea0cb989623bbfe018d8a39f180a`, `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/mcpx-daemon.js`:
  - `:56` HTTP path: `signal: AbortSignal.timeout(timeoutMs)` — absolute deadline.
  - `:122` socket path: `req.setTimeout(timeoutMs, () => { fail(...); req.destroy(); })` — idle-only; no separate deadline timer anywhere in the socket branch.
- Codex P2 comment 4411008915 on PR #777 (undispositioned): reproduced with a daemon sending a chunk every 30 ms — a request configured for 100 ms completed after 477 ms.
- Dedupe: `gh issue list --search "mcpx socket deadline trickle"` (open + closed) returns nothing; #774 is closed by #777 and does not cover the idle-vs-absolute distinction.

## Why it matters

The socket transport is the local-daemon path — the common case. A wedged or trickling mcpx daemon still wedges `/api/mcpx/*` requests indefinitely (subject only to the 5 MiB response cap), so the #774 fix gives false confidence.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The Unix-socket request carries an absolute deadline (a timer armed at request start, cleared on settle) in addition to any idle timeout; a trickling response is destroyed and rejects with the same timeout error shape as the HTTP path.
- [ ] A test pins a trickling socket response (chunks inside the idle window, total duration beyond the deadline) rejecting as a timeout.
- [ ] Existing mcpx-daemon tests still pass; healthy socket behaviour (JSON parse, non-JSON text, HTTP >= 400) unchanged.

title: fix(web): getProviderAuth resolves Object.prototype members — prototype-name provider ids fabricate stored auth and bypass the provider-save credential gate

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

`getProviderAuth()` in `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/auth.js` looks up a caller-supplied provider id in the projected OpenCode credentials object — a plain `{}` literal built by `projectCredentialEntries()` — with no own-property guard. Provider ids that collide with `Object.prototype` members (`constructor`, `toString`, `hasOwnProperty`, `valueOf`, `__proto__`) therefore "find" a credential that does not exist: the inherited function/object is returned as if it were a stored credential. Routes that treat the result's truthiness as "this provider has stored auth" then fabricate that state, including bypassing the provider-save credential gate.

Sibling of #939 (same class, different module): #939 covers the quota registries in `lib/quota/*`; this lookup in `lib/opencode/auth.js` was not part of that filing and is not fixed by fixing the quota maps.

## Evidence (main `f0d3428b8`, verified this run)

- `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/auth.js:261-267` — `projectCredentialEntries` builds `const result = {}` and assigns `result[entry.integrationID] = ...`.
- `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/auth.js:350-353` — `getProviderAuth(providerId)` is `return credentials[providerId] || null;` with no `Object.hasOwn` / prototype guard.
- Consumers that trust truthiness:
  - `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/routes.js:367-370` — provider-sources route: `sources.auth.exists = ... Boolean(await getProviderAuth(providerId))` for a URL-supplied `providerId`.
  - `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/routes.js:450-452` — provider upsert: `hasStoredAuth = req.body?.hasCredential === true || Boolean(await getProviderAuth(providerID))`, and `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/providers.js:172-173` refuses a credential-less provider save only when `env.length === 0 && !hasStoredAuth` — so a prototype-name provider id passes the gate with no env var and no credential.
- Probe (laptop, against the real module at `f0d3428b8` via the `configureOpenCodeCredentials` seam, store containing exactly one credential for `deepseek`; probe dir `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-provider-auth-20261030/`):
  - `getProviderAuth('deepseek')` → `{type:'api', key:…}` (control, truthy) and `getProviderAuth('openai')` → `null` (control).
  - `getProviderAuth('constructor')` → the `Object` constructor **function** (truthy), `'toString'` / `'hasOwnProperty'` / `'valueOf'` → the inherited functions (truthy), `'__proto__'` → `{}` (truthy). Every one reads as "has stored auth" to the routes above.
  - Secondary: `projectCredentialEntries` with an entry whose `integrationID` is `'__proto__'` does not create an own key — the projected object's own keys were only `['deepseek']` and the credential value became the object's *prototype* (`Object.getPrototypeOf(projected).key === 'polluted-key'`). Not a global pollution (plain `{}` assignment semantics), but that credential is stored where enumeration/`Object.keys` consumers cannot see it while keyed reads can.

## Why it matters

The provider settings UI decides whether a provider is connected, and whether a save needs a credential, from these answers. A prototype-name id — reachable wherever a provider id comes from a URL, a request body, or an OpenCode store row — gets a fabricated "authenticated" state and can be saved without any credential, producing a provider entry that can never work and that later debugging will read as configured. #939 established that this fleet treats prototype-name ids as a real bug class, not a curiosity; this is the remaining unguarded lookup on the auth path.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `getProviderAuth('constructor' | 'toString' | 'hasOwnProperty' | 'valueOf' | '__proto__')` returns `null` when no such credential is actually stored (own-property guard, `Object.hasOwn`, a null-prototype projection object, or a `Map` — implementer's choice, consistent with the #939 fix if one exists by then).
- [ ] `projectCredentialEntries` stores a `'__proto__'` integration id as a real, enumerable own entry (or explicitly drops it with a comment) — never as the projection's prototype.
- [ ] Regression tests in `auth.test.js` cover the prototype-name ids for `getProviderAuth` and the `'__proto__'` projection case; existing auth tests keep passing.
- [ ] Provider-sources `auth.exists` and the upsert `hasStoredAuth` gate give the same answers as today for genuinely stored and genuinely absent providers.

title: fix(web): dictation model tar extraction has no timeout — a hung tar wedges the model download state forever

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Summary

The local STT model **extraction** step has no timeout of any kind. `extractTarArchive` in `packages/web/server/lib/dictation/local/model-downloader.js` spawns the system `tar` and waits for its `close` event with no deadline, no stall timer, and no kill path. If `tar` (or the `bzip2` helper GNU tar delegates `.tar.bz2` to) hangs, the promise never settles — and because the dictation service holds the in-flight promise in a map that is only cleared on settle, that model is wedged in the `downloading` state until the server restarts, and every retry returns the same wedged promise.

This is the one unbounded step left in a module that otherwise bounds everything carefully: the download half of the same file has a 60-second **stall** timer that is re-armed on every chunk (`DOWNLOAD_STALL_TIMEOUT_MS`, model-downloader.js:16-19 and the `armStallTimer` machinery in `downloadToFile`).

## Evidence (main `f0d3428b8`, verified this run)

- `packages/web/server/lib/dictation/local/model-downloader.js:181-199` — `extractTarArchive`:
  ```js
  const child = spawn('tar', ['xf', archivePath, '-C', destDir], {
    stdio: ['ignore', 'ignore', 'pipe'],
    windowsHide: true,
  });
  // resolves on 'close' code 0, rejects on 'error' / non-zero close — nothing else can settle it
  ```
  No `timeout` spawn option, no timer, no `child.kill(...)` anywhere in the function.
- `packages/web/server/lib/dictation/service.js:47-84` — `startModelDownload` stores the `ensureLocalSttModel(...)` promise in `downloadPromises` and sets `downloadStates` to `'downloading'`; both are cleared only in `.then`/`.catch`. An extraction that never settles leaves the state at `'downloading'` forever and every later `startModelDownload(modelId)` returns the same pending promise.
- Probe (laptop, against the real module at `f0d3428b8`, probe dir `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-tar-extract-20261030/`): a fake `tar` first in `PATH` that writes a marker and sleeps, a cached archive matching a spec override's pinned size/SHA-256 (so the download half is skipped and the real `extractTarArchive` runs): `ensureLocalSttModel(...)` was still **unsettled after 3,000 ms**, the fake tar had started, and nothing killed it. The probe exited by design at that point; the child would have slept on.
- Dedup: #814/#828 (closed) bounded the **download** fetch/stall side; #417/#412 (closed) covered download size/pins. No open or closed issue covers the extraction spawn — `gh search issues "extractTarArchive"` returns nothing and `"tar extraction"` returns only #814.

Realistic hang sources: a `bzip2` decompressor that stalls on a damaged-but-pin-matching archive (pins verify the compressed bytes, not that decompression terminates), a filesystem/NFS stall under the models directory, or a pathological archive whose expansion runs effectively forever. The archive's *compressed* size is pinned, but nothing bounds extraction time or expanded work.

## Why it matters

Local dictation is a headline feature, and the model download is its first-run path. One hung extraction silently bricks that model for the life of the server process: the UI shows `downloading` forever, retry is a no-op (same promise), and there is no log line pointing at `tar` — the failure mode the download half of this same file was explicitly hardened against in #814 ("wedges the model download state forever").

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `extractTarArchive` cannot wait forever: a hung `tar` is killed (process tree where the platform needs it) and the extraction rejects with a clear error within a bounded time. A stall-style bound (silence/progress-based) or a generous total bound are both acceptable if the choice is justified in a comment, consistent with the download half's reasoning that large archives make total time legitimately variable.
- [ ] After such a rejection, the dictation service state recovers through the existing `.catch` path (`downloadStates` → `'error'`, `downloadPromises` cleared) and a subsequent `startModelDownload` for the same model actually retries.
- [ ] A regression test drives extraction with a never-exiting fake `tar` (or an injected spawn seam) and asserts the rejection + kill happen within the bound; existing model-downloader tests keep passing.
- [ ] Normal extraction (including the `describeTarFailure` bzip2 message, #2887) is unchanged.

body:
# fix(web): TTS speech body read has a deadline but no byte cap — a streaming speech server grows server memory chunk by chunk, and the no-reader fallback has neither cap nor deadline

## Evidence (verified on main `14bc745e9`, 2026-10-30)

- `packages/web/server/lib/tts/service.js:27-68` — `readSpeechBody(response, timeoutMs)` reads the speech response through its reader and accumulates every chunk (`total += value.byteLength`, line 39) with **no maximum**: the only bound is the 60 s deadline (`SPEECH_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS`, line 18). There is no size constant anywhere in `packages/web/server/lib/tts/service.js`.
- The fallback at line 29 is worse: when `response.body` has no `getReader`, it returns `response.arrayBuffer()` directly — no byte cap **and no deadline at all** (`timeoutMs` is ignored on that path).
- Both speech entry points use it: `generateSpeechStream` (line 193, reached from `packages/web/server/lib/tts/routes.js:117`) and `generateSpeechBuffer` (line 236).
- The endpoint is not necessarily OpenAI: `generateSpeechStream` accepts a user-configured custom `baseURL` (an OpenAI-compatible local speech server, normalized by `normalizeCustomOpenAIBaseURL`). A loopback server can deliver far more in 60 s than any network endpoint — hundreds of MB to GBs of "audio" held in the chunk array, then copied into a `Uint8Array`, then `Buffer.from(...)` — three concurrent copies at peak.

## Why it matters

#824 bounded this call in *time*; nothing bounds it in *space*. The house rule since #802/#803 is that outbound bodies are read through bounded primitives (`readBoundedResponseBytes` in `packages/web/server/lib/shared/response-body.js` exists for exactly this), and every comparable buffer-whole finding (#737, #744, #759, #763, #770, #776, #848) was fixed. Speech audio for one request is legitimately a few MB at most (the input text is a single utterance), so a generous cap loses nothing real, while an uncapped read lets a buggy or hostile user-configured speech server OOM the OpenChamber server that every surface depends on. The fix must preserve the reason this reader exists (see the comment at lines 20-26): the deadline cancels the *active* read through the reader, because `body.cancel()` cannot — a cap check inside the read loop keeps that property; swapping in a plain `arrayBuffer()`-based bounded helper would regress PR #839's fix.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `readSpeechBody` rejects (and cancels the reader) as soon as the accumulated body exceeds an explicit byte cap sized generously for one speech response, named as a constant next to `SPEECH_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS`.
- [ ] The no-`getReader` fallback is bounded too, or removed with evidence no supported response shape needs it; it must not remain an uncapped, undeadlined `arrayBuffer()`.
- [ ] Deadline behavior from #824/PR #839 is preserved: a body that stalls mid-stream still fails at `timeoutMs` via reader cancellation, covered by a test.
- [ ] New tests in `packages/web/server/lib/tts/service.test.js`: an over-cap streaming body fails fast without buffering the whole body; a normal small audio response still returns byte-identical output through both `generateSpeechStream` and `generateSpeechBuffer`.

## Dedup

Checked open and closed issues this run: #824 (closed) added the deadline only; #802/#803 created the shared bounded primitives; no issue covers a byte cap for the speech body read or its fallback path.

# fix(ci): pm-dispatch smoke workflow has no concurrency group — overlapping dispatches file duplicate smoke issues/tasks in opencode

## Evidence (verified on main `14bc745e9`, 2026-10-30)

- `.github/workflows/pm-dispatch-smoke.yml` is the **only** workflow in this repo with no `concurrency:` block: 23 of the 24 files under `.github/workflows/*.yml` define one (verified by grep this run); this file has none at any level.
- The workflow is `workflow_dispatch`-only (`.github/workflows/pm-dispatch-smoke.yml:10-11`), so nothing in its trigger serializes runs either.
- Its single job is non-idempotent and cross-repo: the `queue` step (lines 21-31) calls `developing-today/code/.github/actions/pm-dispatch-queue@main` with `repo: developing-today/opencode` and `issue: "true"` — every run queues one task **and files one new issue** in opencode.
- The file's own header (lines 4-7) states the invariant the missing group breaks: "each run queues exactly one task … and files exactly one issue … The task and issue are smoke-test artifacts and are cleaned up after each run."

## Why it matters

Two dispatches seconds apart (a double-click, a re-run while the first is still queued, two maintainers proving the mesh at once) run fully in parallel. That produces duplicate "SMOKE TEST" issues and duplicate queue tasks in `developing-today/opencode`, and the per-run cleanup the header describes can close or cancel the *other* run's artifacts. Every other workflow in this repo — including the other dispatch-only, side-effecting ones (`sdk-preview.yml`, `mobile-release.yml`, `opencode-smoke.yml`) — carries a concurrency group precisely to prevent this class of overlap (see the #84 concurrency audit comments throughout `.github/workflows/`). This workflow was added after that audit and missed the house pattern.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `.github/workflows/pm-dispatch-smoke.yml` declares a `concurrency:` group scoped so two smoke dispatches cannot execute at the same time (a static workflow group is sufficient — the dispatch target is fixed).
- [ ] The cancel/queue semantics are chosen deliberately for a non-idempotent side effect and stated in a comment, following the repo's existing concurrency-audit comment style: cancelling a run that has already passed the `queue` step must not leave its filed issue/task orphaned, so queueing (e.g. `queue: max`) rather than mid-run cancellation is the expected default unless the PR argues otherwise.
- [ ] No other workflow file changes; the smoke job's steps, permissions, and outputs are unchanged.
- [ ] Workflow YAML validates (e.g. `actionlint` or GitHub's workflow parse on the PR).

## Dedup

Checked open and recently closed issues for "concurrency" / "pm-dispatch smoke" this run: #918 covers `release-desktop-smoke.yml`'s group *key* (different workflow, different defect); closed #72/#86/#89 cover other workflows' groups. No issue covers this workflow having no group at all.

Origin: the workflow was added in PR #904 (`be4346948`) without a concurrency block.

## Finding

PR #748 (merged, head `c6819ec5d348322e0fc3c8624766eeaf6ea35242`, merge `de2f9511fdab920f814723cb96fc65790a72c40b`) exposed the OpenCode Go plan as `planLabel` on the **web** quota result (`packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/opencode-go.js`). Its body explicitly left the twin surface behind: "The VS Code quota mirror (`packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.ts`) has its own OpenCode Go fetch and does not get planLabel in this packet-scoped slice; noted here as a follow-up gap." No issue was ever filed for that follow-up.

The gap is still open on current main `14bc745e9c2669dd7f56dc7cb67cebae7ac21262`, and the VS Code side already does the hard part:

- `packages/vscode/src/opencodeGoQuota.ts:96` parses the Console payload's `product`, and `:177` validates it against `CONSOLE_PRODUCTS` (throwing the no-subscription error otherwise) — then `:178-182` returns **only the windows**, discarding the validated product.

The two quota surfaces disagree: the same Console account shows its Go plan (`go` / `go-plus`) on web and no plan in VS Code. #736's point was one consistent plan-status signal; the mirror silently lagging is how the surfaces drift apart unnoticed.

- The VS Code Console path returns `planLabel` (`go` / `go-plus`, from the already-validated `product`) on the `opencode-go` result, mirroring the web provider; the API-key path leaves it unset, as on web.
- Tests in the VS Code quota suite pin Console `go` → `planLabel: 'go'`, `go-plus` → `'go-plus'`, and API-key → unset, mirroring `opencode-go.test.js` on the web side.

# fix(ci): desktop smoke concurrency group ignores platform inputs — a Windows-only dispatch cancels a running macOS-only build for the same ref

## Finding

PR #752 (merged, head `b7e6fd769fb2cc3fc25eefba8eef284f0468d0db`, merge `2b7904504796261bfe2eb2aa58854c1bee651c93`) added the concurrency block to `.github/workflows/release-desktop-smoke.yml`. On current main `14bc745e9c2669dd7f56dc7cb67cebae7ac21262` it is (`release-desktop-smoke.yml:49-51`):

```yaml
concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ inputs.repository }}-${{ inputs.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true
```

The workflow's platform selections are independent inputs — `build_macos`, `build_windows`, `build_linux` (`:15-29`), each gating its own job — but none of them participates in the group. Dispatching a Windows-only smoke for a repository+ref therefore **cancels a running macOS-only smoke** for the same repository+ref, even though the second run does none of the first run's work and produces none of its artifacts; the macOS build (a 90-minute-timeout job) is simply lost. The Codex review on PR #752 raised this (comment 4409021996); it was not dispositioned and the group is unchanged on current main.

## Why it matters

Smoke builds are dispatched by hand to answer "does this ref build on platform X". Silently cancelling an unrelated platform's build wastes the elapsed build time and can leave a maintainer believing a platform was verified when its run was killed by a later dispatch.

## Acceptance criteria

- The concurrency group includes the platform selections (`build_macos`/`build_windows`/`build_linux`), so dispatches with different platform sets for the same repository+ref run independently, while a re-dispatch with the **same** platform set still cancels its stale predecessor (the Phase 1 intent).
- The header comment above the block is updated to describe the platform-aware key.

## Evidence / dedupe

- Source PR: #752, https://github.com/developing-today/openchamber/pull/752. Verified against current main `14bc745e9c2669dd7f56dc7cb67cebae7ac21262` at `release-desktop-smoke.yml:15-29` and `:49-51`.

# fix(ci): pr-review comment runs now run concurrently, but verdict verification picks the latest bot comment — one run can consume another's verdict

## Finding

PR #752 (merged, head `b7e6fd769fb2cc3fc25eefba8eef284f0468d0db`, merge `2b7904504796261bfe2eb2aa58854c1bee651c93`) changed `.github/workflows/pr-review.yml` so comment-triggered reviews are keyed by the individual comment id (current main `14bc745e9c2669dd7f56dc7cb67cebae7ac21262`, `pr-review.yml:28`): two `/oc-review` commands on the same PR now run **simultaneously** instead of serializing.

The verdict step was not made per-run. `Verify and enforce review verdict` selects the bot's review comment by timestamp, not by identity: `pr-review.yml:523` filters comments to `created_at >= $REVIEW_STARTED_AT` with the bot login and the review-meta marker, then takes `last`. If both concurrent reviews post before either verifies, one run consumes the other's verdict: for the same HEAD a blocking review can be silently accepted as the other's pass and the PR marked `review:ready`; across HEADs a passing current review can be marked `review:automation-failed`. The Codex review on PR #752 raised exactly this (comment 4409021992); it was not dispositioned and the selection code is unchanged on current main.

## Why it matters

The verdict gate is what turns a bot review into a merge signal. Cross-consuming verdicts corrupts that signal in both directions — a blocked change can look approved, and a good change can be failed — with no trace in either run's log that the verdict came from a different review.

## Acceptance criteria

- A run verifies **the exact comment it posted**: the posting step captures its comment id and the verify step fetches/selects that id (falling back to a failure, never to another run's comment), **or** manual comment reviews on the same PR are serialized again while PR-event reviews keep the Phase 1 concurrency.
- Two `/oc-review` commands issued back-to-back on one PR each enforce their own verdict — no `review:ready` / `review:automation-failed` label is applied from a verdict produced by the other run.

## Evidence / dedupe

- Source PR: #752, https://github.com/developing-today/openchamber/pull/752. Verified against current main `14bc745e9c2669dd7f56dc7cb67cebae7ac21262` at `pr-review.yml:9-29` (concurrency) and `:484-523` (started-at capture and latest-comment verdict selection).

# fix(ci): main-broken watcher lookup-and-create is not serialized — simultaneous failures with the same Breakage-ID file duplicate critical issues

## Finding

PR #753 (merged, head `f92f6fb568ca51697a53a2bd40776cd5464c433f`, merge `f65af1ed0ec332a3e0b43e24c04e3c44d05a28d8`) added `.github/workflows/main-broken.yml`. Its deduplication is a non-atomic search-then-create:

- The concurrency group is **per watched run**: `main-broken-${{ github.event.workflow_run.id || inputs.run_id || github.run_id }}` (current main `14bc745e9c2669dd7f56dc7cb67cebae7ac21262`, `main-broken.yml:45`), so two watcher runs never serialize against each other.
- The script searches open `main-broken` issues for the Breakage-ID (`main-broken.yml:108-109`) and files a new issue when the search comes back empty.

`pr checks` preserves every push-to-main run (run_id-keyed groups, by design in PR #752), so two main-gate runs with the same failing job set can complete around the same time. Both watchers search before either filing lands, both find nothing, and each files its own `priority/critical` issue with the **same Breakage-ID** — the exact duplicate the Breakage-ID mechanism exists to prevent, with duplicate remediation enqueued for each. The Codex review on PR #753 raised this (comment 4409029439); it was not dispositioned, and the later pm-dispatch restructuring kept both the per-run group and the search-then-file shape.

## Why it matters

Duplicate critical breakage issues split the holder trail, double the remediation spend, and leave one twin to be closed as a duplicate by hand — the watcher's core promise is "exactly one owned breakage issue per distinct failure signature".

## Acceptance criteria

- The lookup-and-create section is serialized across watcher runs (e.g. a single shared concurrency group for the filing step, or an atomic claim keyed by Breakage-ID), while different Breakage-IDs still file independently.
- Two watcher runs for the same Breakage-ID completing back-to-back produce exactly one filed issue; the second appends to it (or exits as a no-op duplicate) — demonstrated by a dry-run/replay sequence or a documented concurrency test of the workflow shape.

## Finding

PR #753 (merged, head `f92f6fb568ca51697a53a2bd40776cd5464c433f`, merge `f65af1ed0ec332a3e0b43e24c04e3c44d05a28d8`) added `.github/workflows/main-broken.yml`, which files a `priority/critical` main-breakage issue when the watched `pr checks` workflow fails "on main". - As merged: the job `if` required `workflow_run.conclusion == 'failure' && workflow_run.head_branch == 'main'`, and the script re-checked `head_branch != "main"` only.
- Still true on current main `14bc745e9c2669dd7f56dc7cb67cebae7ac21262`: job `if` at `main-broken.yml:56-60` and the script check at `:92-95` test `head_branch` alone; nothing reads the watched run's `event`.

`pr checks` (`oc-review.yml`) runs on both `push` and `pull_request`. A failed pull request opened from a **fork's `main` branch** produces a workflow run in this repository with `head_branch == 'main'` and `event == 'pull_request'` — so the watcher files a critical "main is broken" issue for unmerged contributor code while this repo's main is healthy. The Codex review on PR #753 raised exactly this (comment 4409029442); it was not dispositioned, and the later pm-dispatch restructuring of the watcher kept the same guard.

## Why it matters

`main-broken` issues are the fleet's top-priority signal ("anything that breaks main is top priority") and they enqueue remediation work. False positives from fork PRs train everyone to ignore the signal and burn remediation cycles on code that was never on main.

## Acceptance criteria

- The watcher only files when the watched run's `event` is `push` (and `head_branch == 'main'`), checked both in the job `if` (via `workflow_run.event`) and in the script's API-response validation, so the manual `workflow_dispatch` replay path cannot file for a PR run either.

# fix(vscode): PR #735's revert guard rejects tracked symlinks pointing outside the repo — legitimate symlink reverts now throw

## Finding

PR #735 (merged, head `2c84e1f532af4ca32f1cc314526914135ffdd5f5`, merge `a1dbdf9051ecec38c17f7627bc80bdbaf9117fcd`) added the deletion guard to `revertGitFile` in `packages/vscode/src/gitService.ts`. The guard canonicalizes the **final target** before checking containment:

- Current main `14bc745e9c2669dd7f56dc7cb67cebae7ac21262`, `gitService.ts:2821-2829`: `target = await canonicalizePath(path.resolve(directory, filePath))`, then `if (!target.startsWith(repoRoot + path.sep)) throw … Path is outside repository`.
- `canonicalizePath` at `gitService.ts:4279-4286` is `fs.promises.realpath`, which **follows the final symlink**.

So a tracked symlink inside the repository that points outside it (a common pattern: `link -> ../shared/file`) can never be reverted: changing the link target and choosing revert throws "Path is outside repository" before the tracked check at `:2830` is ever reached — even though `git restore -- link` restores the link itself safely and never touches the destination. The Codex review on PR #735 reproduced this (comment 4407791445: committed `link -> ../original` changed to `link -> ../modified`; the guard throws, `git restore` succeeds). The finding was not dispositioned and the code is unchanged on current main.

## Why it matters

#735 fixed a real deletion hazard, but the guard as written regresses a legitimate, safe operation: any repo using outward-pointing tracked symlinks loses the revert action for those files in the VS Code surface, with a misleading "outside repository" error.

## Acceptance criteria

- Containment is validated on the symlink's **parent directory** (canonicalized) plus the final entry name, without following the final symlink itself, so a tracked symlink whose target is outside the repo can be reverted through the normal tracked `restore`/`checkout` path.
- The #735 deletion protections are unchanged for the removal path: an untracked path is still only removed after the affirmative `ls-files --others --error-unmatch` check, and `.`, the repo root, and genuinely outside paths still throw and delete nothing.
- A regression test in `gitService.revert-guard.test.js` pins the outward-symlink case (modified tracked symlink reverts to its committed target) alongside the existing guard cases.

## Evidence / dedupe

- Source PR: #735, https://github.com/developing-today/openchamber/pull/735 (fixes #734). Verified against current main `14bc745e9c2669dd7f56dc7cb67cebae7ac21262` at `gitService.ts:2807-2844` and `:4279-4286`.

# fs/exec output cap and timeout kill only the shell — descendants keep the pipes open and the result never settles

## Finding

PR #739 (merged, head `e553d4d79cbdf536cf78ea1a465ef3710719f416`) capped `/api/fs/exec` output in `packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.js`, and PR #747 (merged, head `9b55f487357152a18e36aa513d75fffb1801356e`) applied the same cap to the VS Code bridge handler in `packages/vscode/src/bridge-fs-runtime.ts` (whose spawn form itself came from PR #733). In both implementations the cap and the timeout kill **only the direct shell child**:

- Web, current main `14bc745e9c2669dd7f56dc7cb67cebae7ac21262`: `killForOutputLimit` at `routes.js:567-574` does `child.kill('SIGKILL')`; the timeout at `:600` does the same; the result promise resolves only in `child.on('close', ...)` at `:633`.
- VS Code, current main: `killForOutputLimit` at `bridge-fs-runtime.ts:443-451` does `child.kill('SIGKILL')`, and the 300 s timeout kills the same single child.

For a pipeline or compound command the child is `/bin/sh -c …`: killing the shell leaves the actual output-producing descendant alive, holding the inherited stdout/stderr pipes open. Node's `close` event waits for those pipes, so the capped/timed-out result **does not settle** until the descendant exits on its own — a continuously running producer keeps the request/job stuck indefinitely and blocks subsequent commands in the same exec job. The Codex reviews on both PRs reproduced exactly this (PR #739 comment 4408026807; PR #747 comment 4408752893, with a 1 KiB cap repro); neither finding was dispositioned, and the code is unchanged on current main.

This is the same defect class already fixed/tracked for other surfaces (#868 worktree start commands, #877 credential helper) — the two fs/exec surfaces were not included in either.

## Why it matters

The caps added by #739/#747 were meant to bound a verbose command; instead an over-cap compound command can hang the exec job forever (worse than returning unbounded output), and the timeout path has the same hole. One stuck producer wedges its job queue slot and keeps consuming CPU.

## Acceptance criteria

- On output overflow **and** on timeout, both fs/exec implementations terminate the whole process tree/group of the spawned shell (POSIX process group or equivalent; Windows behaviour considered), not just the shell.
- The capped result settles promptly with `output-too-large` (overflow) or the timeout error even when a descendant keeps stdout/stderr open; a regression test with a shell compound command whose descendant outlives the shell pins this in both `routes.test.js` and the bridge fs runtime tests.
- Under-cap, in-time results keep their current shape and bytes.

## Evidence / dedupe

- Source PRs: #739 (web), #747 (vscode), #733 (vscode spawn form). Verified against current main `14bc745e9c2669dd7f56dc7cb67cebae7ac21262` at the file:line references above.
- Dedupe: issue search for fs/exec tree/descendant kills returns #868 (worktree start-command surface, closed) and #877 (credential-helper surface, open) — different code paths; no issue covers the fs/exec surfaces.

That follow-up was never filed, and the gap is still present on current main — the VS Code OpenCode Go result never carries a plan label, so the extension cannot show which Go plan a workspace is on while the web UI can.

## Evidence

- PR #748 (commit c6819ec5d3, MERGED): web `fetchConsoleGoUsage` now returns `{ windows, planLabel: payload.product }` (`packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/opencode-go.js:175` on current main) and `fetchQuota` threads it into `buildResult` (line 271), with tests pinning `go`, `go-plus`, and API-key-path-unset.
- Current main (14bc745e9c): `packages/vscode/src/opencodeGoQuota.ts:161-186` — `fetchConsoleUsage` validates `parsed.data.product` against `CONSOLE_PRODUCTS` (line 177, throws the no-subscription error for anything else) but then returns only `windows` (line 182); `fetchOpenCodeGoUsage` returns that windows-only shape for both credential kinds.
- Current main: `packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.ts:4624-4643` — the `opencode-go` case calls `buildResult({ ..., usage: { windows: await fetchOpenCodeGoUsage(...) } })` with no `planLabel` on either the Console or the API-key path, even though `buildResult` in the same file already supports `planLabel` (line 529/540).
- Deduped: issue search for the VS Code planLabel gap returns no open or closed issue covering it; PR #771's per-workspace rows also landed web-only, which makes this mirror divergence the standing pattern to close for the plan label at minimum.

## Why it matters

The plan label is how a user (and the fleet's quota checks) tells a `go` workspace from a `go-plus` one. Web and CLI show it; the VS Code quota view silently lacks it, for the same credential and the same Console payload — the product value is already fetched and validated in the extension, then thrown away.

## Acceptance criteria

- VS Code Console path: `fetchConsoleUsage`/`fetchOpenCodeGoUsage` surface the validated `product` and the `opencode-go` case passes it to `buildResult` as `planLabel`, mirroring web PR #748.
- API-key path leaves `planLabel` unset (no invented plan), matching web.
- Unknown product still produces the existing no-subscription error.
- Tests pin: Console `go` -> `planLabel: 'go'`, `go-plus` -> `planLabel: 'go-plus'`, API-key path -> `planLabel` undefined.
