## Finding

PR #764 fixed the web Antigravity quota provider to resolve auth from OpenCode's credential store as well as the legacy accounts file. The VS Code quota mirror was never given the same source, so the exact bug #764 describes is still live in the extension: a current `opencode-antigravity-auth` sign-in (which writes the `google` integration's OAuth credential to the credential store and never writes `antigravity-accounts.json`) reads as "Not configured" in VS Code.

## Evidence

- PR #764 (commits 52c74cc192, d274ae591f, MERGED): adds `resolveAntigravityStoreAuth` in `packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/antigravity/auth.js` (current main: line 56) and makes web `isConfigured` check both sources (line 82). Its own documentation note states: current plugin versions sign in through the credential store and never write the legacy file, and the file sits in the config directory where a redeploy can remove it — reading only the file reports a working login as "not configured", silently, with no error row.
- Current main (14bc745e9c): `packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.ts:1153` `resolveAntigravityAuth()` iterates only `ANTIGRAVITY_ACCOUNTS_PATHS` (the legacy `antigravity-accounts.json` locations). The configured check at `:885` and `fetchAntigravityQuota` at `:1435-1436` use only that resolver. No credential-store (`google` OAuth) source exists in the VS Code Antigravity path.
- PR #860 later wired credential-store reading into `packages/vscode/src/opencodeAuth.ts` for the web provider's error-state fix, so the store-reading infrastructure exists on the VS Code side — it is just not consulted by the Antigravity quota resolver.

## Why it matters

Same user-visible failure #764 fixed for web, still present in the extension: Antigravity silently drops out of the VS Code quota view for anyone signed in with a current plugin version, and returns after a config redeploy removes the legacy file even when it once existed. The fleet's quota measurement depends on these rows being present wherever quota is read.

## Acceptance criteria

- VS Code `resolveAntigravityAuth` (or a sibling store resolver) also resolves the `google` integration's OAuth credential from the OpenCode credential store, mirroring web `resolveAntigravityStoreAuth`: accounts file first, then the store, an API-key `google` entry resolves to nothing.
- `listConfiguredQuotaProviders`' Antigravity check and `fetchAntigravityQuota` both see the store source.
- Tests pin: store-only sign-in is configured and fetches; file-only still works; API-key `google` entry is not treated as an Antigravity login.
- No credential value is logged, returned, or written anywhere new (same constraint as #764).

title: fix(web): Linear auth reads corrupt files as empty — reconnecting one workspace erases every stored token, and the session-comments toggle can rewrite the whole settings.json as one key

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

The Linear auth module's private JSON reader treats a corrupt file as "no data" for both files it manages — and one of those files is the **main `settings.json`**. `readJsonFile` returns `null` on any parse failure, so:

1. A corrupt `linear-auth.json` reads as zero workspaces: Linear appears disconnected, and the natural recovery — connecting one workspace — rewrites the file with only that workspace, permanently destroying every other workspace's stored token.
2. A corrupt `settings.json` reads as `{}` inside this module, and toggling the single Linear session-comments preference rewrites the **entire** settings file with just that one key — every other user setting is permanently destroyed by an unrelated toggle.

The writes themselves are atomic (temp + chmod 0600 + `renameSyncWithRetry`); the gap is only the corrupt-read path. The module's own siblings in the same directory — `mapping.js` and `status.js` — throw a `MALFORMED` error in exactly this situation; `auth.js` is the outlier.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `39f690bec`)

- `packages/web/server/lib/linear/auth.js:38-57` — `readJsonFile` catches the `JSON.parse` error, logs it, and returns `null`; non-object JSON also returns `null`. Nothing distinguishes "missing" from "malformed".
- `packages/web/server/lib/linear/auth.js:195-215` — `readAuthList()` returns `[]` when `readJsonFile` returns `null`; `writeAuthList` persists whatever list it is given (and deletes the file when the list is empty).
- `packages/web/server/lib/linear/auth.js:274-287` — `setLinearAuth` builds on `readAuthList()`, so a save after a corrupt read starts from an empty list. `activateLinearAuth`/`clearLinearAuth` share the same base.
- `packages/web/server/lib/linear/auth.js:218-224, 458-467` — `readSettings()` is `readJsonFile(settingsFile()) || {}`, where `settingsFile()` is the shared data-dir `settings.json` (line 29-31); `setLinearSessionCommentsEnabled` mutates that object and `writeSettings` rewrites the **whole file** with it. This writer bypasses the settings runtime entirely.
- `packages/web/server/lib/linear/mapping.js:102-127` and `status.js` (`readRecords`) — the sibling contract in the same folder: a malformed file throws (`LinearMappingError`/`LinearSessionStatusError`, code `MALFORMED`), never an empty store.
- `packages/web/server/lib/linear/auth.test.js` — no malformed-file case for either file (grep: no `corrupt`/`malformed` in the test file).
- Laptop probe against the real module (`~/git/fleet/probe-oc-linear-auth/probe.mjs`, openchamber-fork @ `641bde8ab`; `auth.js` byte-identical to main, md5 `50565c0b595432ab97568beaef7cb85e`):
  - Corrupt `linear-auth.json` still visibly holding two workspaces' tokens: `getLinearAuth()` → `null`, `getLinearAuthWorkspaces()` → `[]`. After `setLinearAuth` for one new workspace, the file contained only the new entry — both original tokens gone, no `.corrupt`/backup sibling.
  - Corrupt `settings.json` still visibly holding user settings (`uiTheme`, `sessionGoalObjectiveCharLimit`, …): after `setLinearSessionCommentsEnabled(true)`, `settings.json` contained exactly `{"linearSessionComments": true}` — every original setting gone.

## Why it matters

Both files hold data the user cannot reconstruct from the UI: OAuth tokens for every connected Linear workspace, and the entire OpenChamber settings object. The corruption precondition is a single torn write or hand-edit typo; the destructive trigger is an ordinary, encouraged action (reconnect a workspace, flip a preference). Because the corrupt state masquerades as "disconnected" / "defaults", the user is led to perform exactly the action that destroys the data. #899 hardened the settings runtime's own migration path, but this second, private writer of the same `settings.json` was not covered.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A malformed `linear-auth.json` is never used as an empty base for a write: `setLinearAuth`/`activateLinearAuth`/`clearLinearAuth` refuse with a clear error or preserve the original bytes (`.corrupt-*` sibling, following the #889/#897 pattern) before any rewrite; connecting a new workspace cannot erase existing ones via a corrupt read.
- [ ] `setLinearSessionCommentsEnabled` can never shrink `settings.json`: on a malformed settings file it refuses (or preserves-and-refuses) instead of writing a one-key file; on a healthy file it still changes only its own key.
- [ ] Missing files still read as empty (first connect and first toggle keep working), and read-only status paths (`getLinearAuth`, `getLinearAuthWorkspaces`, `getLinearSessionCommentsEnabled`) keep answering without throwing, while the malformed state is distinguishable from "not connected / not set".
- [ ] New regression tests in `linear/auth.test.js`: corrupt auth file survives a `setLinearAuth` attempt with its bytes preserved; corrupt settings file survives a `setLinearSessionCommentsEnabled` attempt unchanged (or preserved as a sibling).
- [ ] No change to token shapes, vault (`op://`) references, workspace normalization/dedup behavior, or the broker/OAuth flow.

Found by the new-issue-creator fleet job; sibling corrupt-read issues: #905 (voice-keys, filed this run), #887/#889/#897 (fixed) — the Linear auth module and its settings writer were not covered by any of them. #899 covers the settings runtime's migration path, not this writer.

title: fix(web): voice-keys store reads a corrupt file as empty and the next key update overwrites it — every stored voice API key is silently lost

body:
## Problem

The voice-keys store (`voice-keys.json`, mode 0600 — the user's OpenAI, OpenAI-compatible speech, and STT API keys typed in Settings) treats a corrupt or unreadable file as an empty store. The next time the user sets or removes **any one** key, `updateVoiceKeys` spreads that empty result and atomically rewrites the file — permanently destroying every other stored key, with no preserved copy and no error surfaced. The write path itself is already atomic; the gap is only the corrupt-read path, which is exactly the half the sibling stores got fixed for in #887/#889/#897 and this store missed.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `39f690bec`)

- `packages/web/server/lib/tts/voice-keys.js:36-52` — `readStoredKeys()` returns `{}` on **any** failure: a non-ENOENT read error (line 40-45, warn only) and a JSON parse / schema failure (line 47-52, warn only). Nothing distinguishes "no file yet" from "file exists but is malformed".
- `packages/web/server/lib/tts/voice-keys.js:23-27` — `storedKeysSchema` uses per-field `.catch(undefined)`, so even a parseable file silently drops any individually invalid key entry on the next rewrite.
- `packages/web/server/lib/tts/voice-keys.js:67-84` — `updateVoiceKeys` builds `next` from `{ ...readStoredKeys() }` and rewrites the whole file (atomic temp + `renameSyncWithRetry`, mode 0600, lines 79-81). A corrupt file therefore becomes an empty base for every patch.
- `packages/web/server/lib/tts/voice-keys.test.js` — covers the happy path, key removal, and a malformed **patch**; there is no test with a malformed/unreadable **store file**.
- The house pattern elsewhere is the opposite: `model-choices/store.js` throws on a malformed history ("writing over it would erase what it held"), `routing/plans.js` and `routing/pool-plan-links.js` throw 409 on malformed JSON, and `linear/mapping.js` / `linear/status.js` throw a `MALFORMED` error. The fixed sibling stores (#887 magic-prompts, #889 client-auth/push/APNs, #897 ui-passkeys) preserve the corrupt original and refuse to mutate until it is dealt with.
- Laptop probe against the real module (`~/git/fleet/probe-oc-voice-keys/probe.mjs`, openchamber-fork @ `641bde8ab`; `voice-keys.js` byte-identical to main, md5 `67238e3fd8a40742e5919f56b9edcfe3`): seeded `voice-keys.json` with a torn write still visibly containing two keys (`{"openai": "sk-openai-ORIGINAL", "stt": "sk-stt-ORIGINAL",`):
  - `describeVoiceKeys()` → `{openai:false, openaiCompatible:false, stt:false}`; `readVoiceKey('openai')` → `undefined` (only a console warning).
  - `updateVoiceKeys({ openaiCompatible: 'sk-compat-NEW' })` succeeded, and the file afterwards contained **only** the new key — neither original key remained anywhere in the file, and the directory held no `.corrupt`/backup sibling. Both original keys are unrecoverable.

## Why it matters

These are credentials the user typed once and cannot recover from the UI (routes only ever expose whether a key is set). A single torn write, disk error, or hand-edit typo turns the store into a time bomb: everything looks merely "unset" until the user touches any one key in Settings, at which point the remaining keys are silently and permanently erased. The failure also masquerades as "not configured", sending diagnosis in the wrong direction. This is the same failure class as #887/#889/#897, in the one credential store those sweeps did not cover.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A malformed or unreadable `voice-keys.json` is never treated as an empty store for a write: `updateVoiceKeys` refuses (throws a clear error, as the malformed-patch path already does) or preserves the original bytes (e.g. a `.corrupt-*` sibling, following the #889/#897 pattern) before writing — the original file's bytes remain recoverable after any patch attempt.
- [ ] Read paths (`readVoiceKey`, `describeVoiceKeys`) keep working without throwing for routes that only need a key or a set/unset answer, but the malformed state is distinguishable from "no keys stored" in logs/errors, not just a warning identical in effect to empty.
- [ ] Per-field schema failures no longer silently drop a stored key on the next rewrite: either the whole file is treated as malformed (above) or the dropped field is surfaced.
- [ ] Missing file (`ENOENT`) still reads as an empty store and first-time key setting still works; the existing happy-path, removal, and malformed-patch tests keep passing.
- [ ] New regression tests in `voice-keys.test.js`: a corrupt store file survives an `updateVoiceKeys` patch attempt with its bytes preserved (in place or as a preserved sibling), and a non-ENOENT read failure is not silently overwritten.

Found by the new-issue-creator fleet job; sibling corrupt-read issues: #887, #889, #897 (all fixed) — this store was not covered by any of them.

title: fix(web): notification template runtime's session title/info caches grow forever — no cap, no eviction, and the title cache has no TTL

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

The notification template runtime keeps two per-session caches for the life of the process and never bounds either of them. `sessionTitleCache` has no TTL and no size cap at all; `sessionInfoCache` checks a 60-second TTL on read but never deletes expired entries and has no size cap — so both maps grow by one entry for every distinct host session the long-lived server ever sees.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `575b151e2`)

- `packages/web/server/lib/notifications/template-runtime.js:28-29` — `sessionTitleCache` and `sessionInfoCache` are plain `Map`s created once per runtime; the runtime is created once at server startup (`packages/web/server/index.js:107`).
- `:185-193` — `cacheSessionTitle` sets an entry for any non-empty session id/title; `getCachedSessionTitle` returns it with no expiry check. There is no TTL constant for titles (only `SESSION_INFO_CACHE_TTL_MS` for info, `:24`).
- `:196-205` — `maybeCacheSessionInfoFromEvent` caches the title from **every** host `session.created`/`session.updated` event, so cardinality is every session ever created or renamed, not just sessions that notify.
- `:210-231` — `fetchSessionInfo` returns a cached entry only while fresh (`:211`), but an expired entry is never deleted, and every fetched session's **full session data object** is stored (`:231`). Nothing in the file calls `.delete(` or `.clear(` on either map (verified by grep: only `set`/`get` sites exist).
- The sibling runtime in the same directory already knows the bounded pattern: `notifications/runtime.js` caps `assistantStepMeta`/`lastAssistantStepBySession` at `ASSISTANT_STEP_CACHE_LIMIT` with oldest-entry eviction, and #875 bounded that file's permission-request set and cooldown maps. The template runtime's caches were not covered by #875 (different file, different structures).
- Laptop probe against the real module (`~/git/fleet/probe-oc-template-cache/probe.mjs`, openchamber-fork @ `22c9976a8`; `template-runtime.js` byte-identical to main `575b151e2`, md5 `1baf59ef525db123d0e5204e02bffcc3`): feeding distinct host `session.updated` events through the real `maybeCacheSessionInfoFromEvent` in batches of 50,000 with full GC between batches:
  - baseline heapUsed 3,985,256
  - 50k sessions: 10,520,104
  - 100k: 16,763,032
  - 150k: 24,833,280
  - 200k: 29,233,328 — linear, ~126 bytes/session, no plateau
  - Control (identical events with a `spaceId`, which the cache path explicitly skips): flat at ~4.4 MB after warm-up.

## Why it matters

OpenChamber's managed server runs for weeks and fleet use creates thousands of sessions. A title only matters while a notification for that session could plausibly be composed; retaining every title — and the full session-info object for every fetched session — forever buys nothing after a short window, while the cost is a slow, certain memory leak in the long-lived server process. It is the same failure class as #756, #848 and #875, in the one notifications module those sweeps did not cover. The info cache's stale-but-retained entries are also dead weight with a correctness smell: expiry is enforced on read, so the retained data can never be used again — it is pure leak.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `sessionTitleCache` is bounded (entry cap with oldest-first eviction, TTL expiry, or both) and cannot grow past the bound no matter how many distinct sessions are seen.
- [ ] `sessionInfoCache` is likewise bounded, and expired entries are actually removed (on read, on write, or by sweep), not merely ignored.
- [ ] Notification behavior is preserved: a title cached from a recent `session.created`/`session.updated` event is still used when composing a notification, and a fresh session-info fetch still populates the cache (existing `template-runtime.test.js` and `trigger-runtime.test.js` tests keep passing).
- [ ] New regression test: feeding more distinct session ids than the bound leaves retention at the bound while a recent session's title still resolves.
- [ ] No change to notification content, templates, channels, or the space-session exclusion (space sessions must still never be cached).

Found by the new-issue-creator fleet job; sibling unbounded-retention issues: #875 (fixed, `notifications/runtime.js`), #848, #756 — this one is the template runtime's pair of caches, not covered by any of them.

title: fix(web): settings-runtime project migration writes the only merged copy non-atomically, then deletes the source — one torn write destroys both

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: priority/normal

labels.name: app/web

body:
## Problem

In `settings-runtime.js`, the project-storage migration and orphan-recovery writes use a plain non-atomic `writeJsonFile` — in the same module that already has `writeJsonFileAtomic` and a comment explaining exactly why non-atomic writes to these files are dangerous. Each of those writes produces the **only** merged copy of a project's config/context and is immediately followed by deleting the source file, so one torn write destroys both copies.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `22c9976a8`)

- `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/settings-runtime.js:118-121` — `writeJsonFile` is a plain `fsPromises.writeFile(filePath, JSON.stringify(...))` to the final path: no temp file, no rename, no mode.
- Call sites, all write-then-delete-source:
  - `:294` `mergeProjectContextFiles` writes the merged `context.json` (notes/todos/plans), then `:306` `fsPromises.rm(oldContextPath)`.
  - `:321` `migrateProjectScopedStorage` writes the merged per-project config, then `:326` `fsPromises.rm(oldConfigPath)`.
  - `:527` orphan recovery writes the merged config into the canonical project's file, then `:529` `fsPromises.rm(orphan.filePath)`.
- `:696-706` — the same file's `writeJsonFileAtomic` (used for settings/preferences) does temp + `0o600` + atomic replace, with the comment: *"A partial read during a non-atomic writeFile would make their next read-modify-write wipe the file."* The migration writes are the outliers the comment's reasoning already covers.
- Laptop probe against the real module (`~/git/fleet/probe-oc-settings-migration-20261030/probe.mjs`, openchamber-fork @ `22c9976a8`, real `createSettingsRuntime` + real `project-id.js`): seeded `projects/<oldStem>.json` (`OLD-CONFIG-ONLY`) and `projects/<canonicalStem>.json`, settings carrying the legacy id → `readSettingsFromDiskMigrated` merged both into the canonical file (`shared: "new"` won, old-only key preserved) and the old file no longer existed (`RESULT merge-then-delete-source: true`). After that merge the canonical file — written non-atomically — is the sole copy of both sides' data.
- `settings-runtime.test.js` covers the happy-path merges (`:324`, `:368`, `:488`) and atomic replacement for settings.json (`:414`, `:549`), but nothing exercises a torn/corrupt migration write or the write-then-delete sequence.

## Why it matters

These migrations run automatically on settings reads at startup, exactly once per project, over data the user cannot recreate from anywhere else (per-project config, setup-worktree commands, context notes/todos/plans). A crash, power loss, or disk-full during that single write leaves a truncated merged file and no source to re-merge from — silent, permanent loss of the project's stored config, caused by the migration that was supposed to preserve it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The three migration/orphan-recovery writes (`context.json` merge, per-project config migration, orphan recovery) go through the module's atomic write path (`writeJsonFileAtomic` or an equivalent temp + rename with retry), and the source file is deleted only after the merged write has durably replaced the destination.
- [ ] A torn/truncated destination left by an interrupted migration does not cause the source copy to be deleted on a later run (the merge can be retried or the corrupt destination is preserved, per the repo's `.corrupt-<timestamp>` pattern).
- [ ] New tests in `settings-runtime.test.js`: migration merge remains intact when the destination write is interrupted/simulated torn, source not deleted before a successful merged write, existing happy-path migration tests unchanged.
- [ ] No change to file locations/names, on-disk formats, project-id derivation, merge precedence, or exported signatures.

Found by the new-issue-creator fleet job; sibling store-loss issues: #887 (fixed), #889, #891, #892, #897, #898 — this one is the migration-write outlier inside `settings-runtime.js`, not covered by any of them.

## Problem

The managed Cloudflare remote-tunnel config (`cloudflare-managed-remote-tunnels.json` — the file that holds every managed tunnel's **token**) persists with a direct, non-atomic write, and a corrupt read is treated as an empty config. One torn write silently destroys every stored tunnel token on the next routine update.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `22c9976a8`)

- `packages/web/server/lib/tunnels/managed-config.js:52-55` — `writeManagedRemoteTunnelConfigToDisk` is a plain `fsPromises.writeFile` to the final path: no temp file, no rename. (The write does use mode `0o600` — the tokens are credentials — but atomicity is missing.)
- `packages/web/server/lib/tunnels/managed-config.js:77-96` — `readManagedRemoteTunnelConfigFromDisk` catches every non-ENOENT error, logs one `console.warn` (`:93`), and returns `{ version, tunnels: [] }`.
- `packages/web/server/lib/tunnels/managed-config.js:98-112` — `updateManagedRemoteTunnelConfig` is read-modify-write under a lock: it reads the (possibly emptied) config, mutates it, and persists the result. `upsertManagedRemoteTunnelToken` (`:144`) and `syncManagedRemoteTunnelConfigWithPresets` both go through it, so the first routine token upsert or preset sync after a corrupt read overwrites the file with the empty view — the surviving bytes of every other tunnel's token are permanently lost, with no backup anywhere.
- Laptop probe against the real modules (`~/git/fleet/probe-oc-tunnels-20261030/probe.mjs`, openchamber-fork @ `22c9976a8`, real `createManagedTunnelConfigRuntime` + real settings-normalization runtime): upserted `tun-alpha`/`token-alpha` and `tun-beta`/`token-beta` and read both back; truncated the file to half its length (exactly what a crash during the direct `writeFile` leaves) → read returned `{ tunnels: [] }`; one further upsert (`tun-gamma`) → final file contains neither `token-alpha` nor `token-beta`; directory contained no `.corrupt` backup.
- There is no `managed-config.test.js` — the tunnels test files cover routes/index/install-help/types, not this store's persistence or corrupt-read behaviour.
- The fixed sibling pattern already exists in-repo: `lib/magic-prompts/runtime.js` (fixed for #887, PR #888) writes temp + `renameSyncWithRetry` from `lib/shared/atomic-rename.js` and preserves an unparseable file to a `.corrupt-<timestamp>` sibling with a warning naming the path.

## Why it matters

These tokens are the credentials that bring the user's managed remote tunnels up. Losing them is not a cosmetic reset: every managed tunnel silently stops being startable until the user re-creates each tunnel in Cloudflare and re-pastes each token — and the failure surfaces only when a tunnel is next needed, with no trace of what was lost or when.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `writeManagedRemoteTunnelConfigToDisk` writes atomically: temp file in the same directory + rename (with the repo's `renameSyncWithRetry`/equivalent retry semantics), temp cleaned up on failure, mode `0o600` preserved.
- [ ] An existing unparseable config file is preserved before any overwrite (`.corrupt-<timestamp>` sibling + warning naming the path, per the #887 pattern) or the update refuses to overwrite it; stored tunnel tokens are never silently discarded. ENOENT still routes to the legacy-file migration exactly as today.
- [ ] New `managed-config.test.js`: atomic write, corrupt file preserved + tokens not silently lost on the next upsert, missing-file/legacy-migration behaviour unchanged, upsert/resolve round trips.
- [ ] No change to the config file location/name, on-disk format, exported signatures, or the preset-sync semantics.

Found by the new-issue-creator fleet job; sibling store-loss issues: #887 (fixed), #889, #891, #892, #897 — this module is a distinct store not covered by any of them.

## Problem

The UI passkey store (`ui-passkeys.json` — every registered WebAuthn credential for UI login) persists with a direct, non-atomic write, treats a corrupt file as an empty store, and creates the file world-readable. One torn write silently destroys every registered passkey.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `22c9976a8`)

- `packages/web/server/lib/ui-auth/ui-passkeys.js:134-137` — `persistStore` is a plain `fs.writeFileSync(storeFile, JSON.stringify(store, null, 2))` to the final path: no temp file, no rename, and no `mode` (sibling credential stores write `0o600`; this file is created `0644` under a default umask).
- `packages/web/server/lib/ui-auth/ui-passkeys.js:146-163` — `loadStore` catches every read/parse error, logs one `console.warn` (`:161`), and continues with an empty store (`passkeys: []`). Every mutating operation (register / rename `:320` / revoke `:279`) is load-modify-persist, so the next operation after a corrupt read overwrites the file with only what the empty read saw — the original credentials are gone with no backup anywhere.
- Laptop probe against the real module (`~/git/fleet/probe-oc-passkeys-20261030/probe.mjs`, openchamber-fork @ `22c9976a8`): seeded a valid store with `cred-alpha` + `cred-beta` → `listPasskeys` returned both; truncated the file to half its length (exactly what a crash during the direct `writeFileSync` leaves) → `listPasskeys` returned `[]`, `getStatus` reported `passkeyCount: 0, hasPasskeys: false`, directory contained no `.corrupt` backup; a freshly created store file had mode `644`.
- `packages/web/server/lib/ui-auth/ui-passkeys.test.js` covers only `renamePasskey` validation — no corrupt-file, atomicity, or file-mode tests.
- The fixed sibling pattern already exists in-repo: `lib/magic-prompts/runtime.js` (fixed for #887, PR #888) writes temp + `renameSyncWithRetry` from `lib/shared/atomic-rename.js` and preserves an unparseable file to a `.corrupt-<timestamp>` sibling with a warning naming the path; `lib/routing/plans.js` refuses a malformed store instead of overwriting it.

## Why it matters

Passkeys are a login factor for the UI. A crash, power loss, or disk-full during any passkey operation can truncate `ui-passkeys.json`; from then on the server behaves as if no passkey was ever registered, and the next passkey operation makes the loss permanent and unrecoverable — the user finds out only when passkey sign-in stops working. The `0644` creation mode also exposes the credential store (credential IDs, public keys, sign counters, RP IDs) to any local user, unlike every sibling credential store in the data dir.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `persistStore` writes atomically: temp file in the same directory + `renameSyncWithRetry` (`lib/shared/atomic-rename.js`), temp cleaned up on failure, store file mode `0o600`.
- [ ] An existing unparseable store file is preserved before any overwrite (`.corrupt-<timestamp>` sibling + warning naming the path, per the #887 pattern) or the operation refuses to overwrite it; previously registered passkeys are never silently discarded.
- [ ] Missing-file behaviour unchanged: a fresh empty store is created, no warning, no backup file.
- [ ] New tests in `ui-passkeys.test.js` (or a sibling test file): atomic write leaves no partial file, corrupt store is preserved and not silently emptied, fresh store is created with `0o600`, existing rename/list/revoke behaviour unchanged.
- [ ] No change to the store file location/name, on-disk format, `passwordBinding` reset semantics, or exported signatures.

body:
# fix(web): routing override and route-settings stores write non-atomically and corrupt reads silently discard every rule / reset learned settings — the outliers in lib/routing

## Evidence

Two persisted stores in `packages/web/server/lib/routing/` at main `b67030d04` share the direct-write + silent-empty-read shape, while their sibling stores in the **same directory** already do it correctly:

### route-overrides-store.js — all routing rules lost

- `save` (lines 61-66) writes straight to the final path, `route-overrides.json` in OpenCode's data dir:

```js
const save = (overrides) => {
  const live = overrides.filter((item) => item.until > now());
  fs.mkdirSync(dataDir, { recursive: true });
  fs.writeFileSync(overridesFile, JSON.stringify({ version: 1, overrides: live }, null, 2));
  return live;
};
```

  No temp file, no rename — a crash or kill mid-write leaves a truncated file. This file is not private to OpenChamber: the module header (lines 1-5) notes OpenCode itself reads `route-overrides.json` at routing time, so a torn write is also served to OpenCode's parser.

- `readAll` (lines 53-59) catches **every** error, parse failure included, and returns `[]` with no warning. A torn file is indistinguishable from "no rules".
- `add` / `remove` (lines 72-82) are read-modify-write, so after a torn write the next ordinary rule change (the route-rules interpreter commits decisions through `store.add`, `route-rules-routes.js` `commit`) reads the empty fallback and persists it — permanently discarding every user and interpreter-learned override. No backup of the corrupt bytes is kept.

### route-settings.js — learned thresholds and stage toggles silently reset

- `write` (lines 51-56) writes `route-settings.json` (~/.config/openchamber) directly to the final path, same torn-write exposure.
- `read` (lines 44-50) catches every error and returns `normalizeSettings({})` — the defaults — with no warning. After a torn write, the user's settings silently revert: stage toggles flip back on, `learnAfter` / `waitPercentile` / `waitMinSamples` return to defaults, and the interpreter's behaviour changes with no trace of why.

### The sibling stores in the same directory already solved this

- `plans.js` `writePlanStore` (lines 119-127): temp file + `renameSyncWithRetry` from `lib/shared/atomic-rename.js`; its reader throws a 409 `PLAN_STORE_MALFORMED` ("Fix or move it before saving plan information") instead of silently emptying.
- `pool-plan-links.js` `writePoolPlanLinks` (lines 56-64): same temp + `renameSyncWithRetry` pattern, same malformed-store refusal.
- `routing/store.js` (line 31) also imports the shared atomic-rename helpers.

Neither `route-overrides-store.js` nor `route-settings.js` imports them, and neither test file pins corruption behaviour (`grep corrupt|atomic|rename` in `route-overrides-store.test.js` / `route-learning-wait-settings.test.js`: no matches).

### Verified this run (laptop probe vs the real modules)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-routing-stores-20261030/probe.mjs` on the laptop, importing the real `createOverrideStore` / `createSettingsStore` from main `b67030d04` with a temp data dir:

1. Overrides seeded through the real store (`ov-alpha` avoid, `ov-beta` prefer) — `list()` returned both.
2. File truncated to half its length (torn-write state): `list()` returned `[]`, silently.
3. One ordinary `add(ov-gamma)` afterwards left a file containing only `ov-gamma` — `RESULT overrides alpha/beta lost: true`, no `.corrupt-*` backup in the directory.
4. Route-settings seeded with `learnAfter: 7, waitPercentile: 50, waitMinSamples: 9, stages.keywords: false`; after the same truncation, `read()` returned the defaults (`learnAfter: 3, waitPercentile: 25, waitMinSamples: 5, keywords: true`) — a silent behavioural reset.

## Why it matters

Route overrides are the routing layer's learned and user-authored rules — the interpreter accumulates them over time, and OpenCode consumes the same file at routing time. One unclean shutdown during a small write currently converts the whole rule set to empty on the next rule commit, silently, and silently re-enables interpreter stages the user turned off via route-settings. Every comparable store in this directory already uses the shared atomic-rename helper and refuses to overwrite a malformed store; these two were missed.

## Acceptance criteria

- `route-overrides-store.js` `save` and `route-settings.js` `write` write to a temp file in the same directory and rename into place using the shared `renameSyncWithRetry` helper from `lib/shared/atomic-rename.js` (the plans.js / pool-plan-links.js pattern), cleaning up the temp file on failure; a reader never observes a partially written file.
- A file that exists but does not parse is not silently treated as empty/defaults: it is preserved before any overwrite (e.g. `.corrupt-<timestamp>` sibling) with a warning naming the path, or the store refuses to overwrite it (plans.js malformed-store style). A subsequent mutation must not silently destroy the only copy of the previous rules/settings.
- Genuinely missing file behaviour is unchanged: overrides read as `[]`, settings read as defaults, no warning, no backup.
- Tests added to `route-overrides-store.test.js` and the route-settings tests pin: atomic write via temp + rename, corrupt-file preservation (or refusal), missing-file behaviour, and the existing add/remove/list and read/write round trips.
- No change to file locations/names, on-disk formats (`{version: 1, overrides}`; the normalized settings shape), exported signatures, or override expiry semantics (`save` still drops expired entries).

## Dedup

Checked open + recently closed issues 2026-10-30: `gh issue list --search "route-overrides"` returns only #295 (session-move feature) and closed #358 (validator) — neither covers persistence; `--search "route-settings OR routing store atomic"` returns no persistence issue. #887/#889/#891 cover other stores (magic-prompts, client-auth, push/APNs) in other modules; the routing stores are not named in any of them. Closed #99/#117 concern rename-retry on already-atomic stores.

# fix(vscode): magic-prompts store in bridge-settings-runtime writes non-atomically and a corrupt read silently discards every override — the VS Code twin of #887, on the same shared file

## Evidence

`packages/vscode/src/bridge-settings-runtime.ts` at main `b67030d04`:

- The magic-prompts path is the **same shared file** the web server uses (the one #887 covers for the web runtime): line 27, `path.join(os.homedir(), '.config', 'openchamber', 'magic-prompts.json')`.
- `writeMagicPromptFile` (lines 359-362) writes straight to that final path:

```ts
const writeMagicPromptFile = async (state: { version: number; overrides: Record<string, string> }): Promise<void> => {
  await fs.promises.mkdir(path.dirname(OPENCHAMBER_MAGIC_PROMPTS_PATH), { recursive: true });
  await fs.promises.writeFile(OPENCHAMBER_MAGIC_PROMPTS_PATH, JSON.stringify(state, null, 2), 'utf8');
};
```

  No temp file, no rename — a crash, kill, or extension-host shutdown mid-write leaves a truncated file on disk, and it corrupts the store for **both** surfaces (web and VS Code read/write this one file).

- `readMagicPromptFile` (lines 343-357) catches **every** error — parse failure included — and returns `{ version: 1, overrides: {} }` with no warning at all (the web twin at least logs). A torn file is indistinguishable from "no overrides yet".

- Every mutation is read-modify-write (`saveMagicPromptOverride` lines 521-529, `resetMagicPromptOverride` lines 539-549): after a torn write, the next ordinary edit from the VS Code surface reads the empty fallback and persists it — permanently discarding every prompt override, with no backup copy of the corrupt bytes anywhere.

This module already knows the correct pattern — it is the outlier inside its own file:

- `writeJsonAtomic` / `writeJsonAtomicSync` (lines 243-270, same file) write settings/preferences via temp file + `renameWithRetry` from `./bridge-atomic-write`, with temp cleanup on failure. The magic-prompts functions, added beside them, do not use them.
- `readPreferencesFromDisk` (same file) fails closed on an unreadable preferences file (`preferencesUnavailable`, writes drop profile keys rather than replacing a file whose content cannot be seen). The magic-prompts read fails **open** to empty instead.

The module's test file (`bridge-settings-runtime.test.js`, 178 lines) has **no magic-prompt tests at all** — `grep magic` returns nothing.

### Verified this run (laptop probe vs the real module)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-vscode-magic-20261030/probe.test.ts` on the laptop, importing the real `bridge-settings-runtime.ts` from main `b67030d04` (vscode module mocked exactly as the module's own test file does, `HOME` pointed at a temp dir), run with `bun test`:

1. Two overrides seeded through the real runtime (`alpha.visible`, `beta.visible`) — file on disk contained both.
2. The file was truncated to half its length (the torn state a mid-write crash leaves). `readMagicPromptOverrides()` returned `{"version":1,"overrides":{}}` — silently, no warning.
3. One ordinary `saveMagicPromptOverride('gamma.visible', …)` afterwards produced a file containing only `gamma.visible` — both seeded overrides permanently lost (`RESULT alpha/beta lost: true`), and the directory held no `.corrupt-*` backup, just `magic-prompts.json`.

## Why it matters

Magic prompts are user-authored prompt overrides persisted across restarts and shared between the web and VS Code surfaces. #887 fixes the web writer; as long as the VS Code writer keeps writing directly to the same shared file, an unclean extension-host shutdown during one small write can still tear the file, and the next edit from either surface converts the whole store to empty, silently. The fix pattern already exists in the same file (`writeJsonAtomic`), so this is a small, clearly scoped application of it.

## Acceptance criteria

- `writeMagicPromptFile` writes atomically via the file's own `writeJsonAtomic` helper (temp file in the same directory + `renameWithRetry`, temp cleaned up on failure); a reader never observes a partially written `magic-prompts.json`.
- A file that exists but does not parse is preserved before any overwrite (e.g. renamed to a `.corrupt-<timestamp>` sibling, as the web dispatch-results store does) and a warning names the preserved path; a subsequent mutation must not silently destroy the only copy of the previous overrides. (Fail-closed, preferences-style handling is also acceptable if it guarantees no silent loss.)
- Genuinely missing file (ENOENT) behaviour is unchanged: empty state, no warning, no backup.
- New tests in `bridge-settings-runtime.test.js` pin: atomic write via temp + rename, corrupt-file preservation (or fail-closed equivalent), ENOENT empty state, and the existing set/reset/reset-all round trips through the real runtime exports.
- No change to the file location/name, the on-disk format (`{version: 1, overrides}`), the exported function signatures, or the id/text validation rules.

## Dedup

Checked open + recently closed issues 2026-10-30: #887 covers only the web runtime (`packages/web/server/lib/magic-prompts/runtime.js`) — its acceptance criteria name that module and forbid route/format changes; it does not mention the VS Code bridge. `gh issue list --search "magic-prompts vscode"` and `--search "bridge-settings"` return no issue covering `bridge-settings-runtime.ts`'s magic-prompt persistence. Closed #99/#117 concern rename-retry on already-atomic stores, not this direct-write store.

body:
## Problem

The device-auth token stores write their JSON files **directly to the final path** and treat an **unparseable read as an empty store with no warning**, so one truncated write silently destroys every paired device's credential — and the next routine write makes the loss permanent.

This is the same defect class as #887 (magic-prompts), but the data at risk here is authentication state, and these stores do not even log the discard (the notifications stores below at least `console.warn`).

## Evidence (verified on main `168f3d193`)

### Client-auth stores — no warning at all

- `packages/web/server/lib/client-auth/remote-clients.js:109` — `writeStore` does `fsPromises.writeFile(storePath, …)` directly to the final path (no temp file, no rename). This file holds the `tokenHash` of **every paired remote client** (minted at `createClient`, :158+; checked by `authenticateBearerToken`, :245).
- `packages/web/server/lib/client-auth/remote-clients.js:37-43,97-105` — `safeJsonParse` returns `null` on any parse error; `readStore` passes it to `normalizeStore`, which yields `clients: []`. No log, no backup, no error.
- `packages/web/server/lib/client-auth/pairing.js:158` — identical direct `writeFile` in `writeStore`; `:47-53,146-154` — identical silent `safeJsonParse → null → empty sessions` read. Pairing sessions are short-lived (10 min TTL), so impact is lower, but the shape is the same.

### Notifications token stores — warn, but still discard + overwrite

- `packages/web/server/lib/notifications/push-runtime.js:77` — `writePushSubscriptionsToDisk` writes directly to `PUSH_SUBSCRIPTIONS_FILE_PATH`; the read path (:40-73) catches parse errors, warns, returns an empty store, and the next `persistPushSubscriptionUpdate` overwrites the file.
- `packages/web/server/lib/notifications/apns-runtime.js:162` — `writeTokensToDisk` writes directly to `APNS_TOKENS_FILE_PATH`; read path (:132-158) same warn-and-empty shape.

### The house pattern these stores missed

Sibling stores write a temp file in the same directory and rename it over the target with `renameWithRetry` from `packages/web/server/lib/shared/atomic-rename.js` — e.g. `agent-memory/runtime.js:251-252`, `github/auth.js:197-199`, `gitlab/auth-storage.js:183-185`, `guests/auth-store.js:105-106`, `git/ssh-credential-storage.js:80-82`. The client-auth and notification token stores are the remaining direct-to-final-path JSON stores found in a census of `packages/web/server/lib` this run.

### Laptop probe (real modules, fork at `168f3d193`)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-clientauth-atomic-20261030/probe.mjs` on the laptop, importing the real `remote-clients.js`:

- Created two clients (`Phone A`, `Desktop B`); `authenticateBearerToken(tokenA)` → `true`.
- Truncated the store file to 586 of 1173 bytes (what a crash/power loss mid-`writeFile` leaves behind).
- `listClients()` → **0 clients, no error, no warning**; `authenticateBearerToken(tokenA)` → `false`.
- One further routine `createClient` rewrote the file: the original client ids/token hashes are **gone from disk permanently**.

## Why it matters

A crash, power loss, or killed process during any client mint/revoke/last-used write truncates the store in place. On next start every paired phone/desktop silently loses access (token hashes gone), with nothing in the logs to explain why, and the first subsequent write destroys any chance of recovering the file by hand. The pairing store and the push/APNs token stores fail the same way, forcing every device to re-register.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `remote-clients.js` and `pairing.js` writes are atomic: temp file in the same directory + `renameWithRetry` (shared helper), temp cleaned up on failure, existing `0o600` mode/chmod behaviour preserved.
- [ ] `push-runtime.js` and `apns-runtime.js` token/subscription writes get the same atomic treatment.
- [ ] An unparseable store file is **not** silently treated as empty: the corrupt bytes are preserved (e.g. renamed to a `.corrupt-<timestamp>` sibling, as in the #887 fix) and a warning names the store path — for the client-auth stores too, which currently log nothing.
- [ ] A genuinely missing file (`ENOENT`) still yields an empty store with no warning/backup noise.
- [ ] Regression tests (extending `client-auth/remote-clients.test.js` / `pairing.test.js` and the notifications tests): (1) a truncated/corrupt store preserves the original bytes in the backup and does not lose previously stored clients on the next write cycle beyond the documented recovery behaviour; (2) a simulated mid-write failure leaves the previous valid file intact.
- [ ] No change to store formats, token/session semantics, TTLs, or public runtime APIs.

# fix(web): magic-prompts store writes its JSON file non-atomically and a corrupt read silently discards every override

## Evidence

`packages/web/server/lib/magic-prompts/runtime.js` at main `0d0dab311`:

- `writePromptState` (runtime.js:52-55) writes straight to the final path:

```js
const writePromptState = async (state) => {
  await fsPromises.mkdir(path.dirname(filePath), { recursive: true });
  await fsPromises.writeFile(filePath, JSON.stringify(state, null, 2), 'utf8');
};
```

  The file is `magic-prompts.json` in the OpenChamber data dir (routes.js:13). There is no temp file and no rename, so a crash, power loss, or kill mid-write leaves a truncated file on disk.

- `readPromptState` (runtime.js:32-48) treats every non-ENOENT read failure the same way: it logs `Failed to read magic prompts file:` and returns `{ version: 1, overrides: {} }`. A JSON parse failure is indistinguishable from "no overrides yet".

- Every mutation (`persist`, runtime.js:57-66) is read-modify-write: it reads the current state, applies the mutator, and writes the result. So after a torn write, the *next ordinary edit* reads the empty fallback and persists it — permanently discarding every prompt override the user had, with only a console warning as a trace. No backup copy of the corrupt bytes is kept anywhere.

This module is the outlier among the server's JSON stores. Its siblings all write atomically and treat corruption as data worth preserving:

- `model-choices/store.js:96-98` — writes `${filePath}.${pid}.${ts}.tmp`, then `renameWithRetry` from `lib/shared/atomic-rename.js`.
- `session-folders/routes.js:164-171` — same tmp + `renameWithRetry` pattern, with temp-file cleanup on rename failure.
- `dispatch-results/runtime.js` (its `readFile`) — on malformed JSON it renames the file to `${filePath}.corrupt-${now()}` and warns, explicitly so the bytes are kept and a later write does not clobber them.
- Roughly twenty modules under `packages/web/server/lib/` import `renameWithRetry`; `magic-prompts` is a persisted user-data store that does not.

The module also has no tests at all: `packages/web/server/lib/magic-prompts/` contains only `routes.js` and `runtime.js`, while the sibling stores above all carry test files pinning exactly these write/corruption behaviours (e.g. `session-folders/routes.test.js` asserts temp-path writes and temp cleanup on rename failure).

### Verified this run (laptop probe vs the real module)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-magic-prompts-20261030/probe.mjs` on the laptop, importing the real `createMagicPromptRuntime` from main `0d0dab311` with an instrumented `fsPromises` and a temp data dir:

1. Two overrides seeded through the real runtime (`alpha.visible`, `beta.visible`). Filesystem calls recorded during the writes: `writeFile->magic-prompts.json` twice — direct writes to the final path, `rename` never called.
2. The file was then truncated to half its length (the torn state a mid-write crash leaves). `readPromptState()` returned `{"version":1,"overrides":{}}`; the only trace was the `Failed to read magic prompts file: SyntaxError: Unexpected end of JSON input` warning.
3. One ordinary `setOverride('gamma.visible', …)` afterwards produced a file containing only `gamma.visible` — both seeded overrides permanently lost (`RESULT alpha/beta lost: true`), and the directory held no `.corrupt-*` backup, just `magic-prompts.json`.

## Why it matters

Magic prompts are user-authored prompt overrides persisted across restarts — exactly the kind of data a user notices losing and cannot reconstruct from memory. The failure needs no exotic trigger: any unclean shutdown during one small write converts the whole store to empty on the next edit, silently. Every comparable store in this codebase already solved this exact problem with the shared atomic-rename helper and a preserve-the-bytes corruption path; this one was missed.

## Acceptance criteria

- `writePromptState` writes to a temp file in the same directory and renames it into place using the shared `renameWithRetry` helper from `lib/shared/atomic-rename.js` (the model-choices/session-folders pattern), cleaning up the temp file when the rename fails; a reader never observes a partially written `magic-prompts.json`.
- A file that exists but does not parse is preserved before any overwrite (e.g. renamed to a `.corrupt-<timestamp>` sibling, as dispatch-results does) and the warning names the preserved path; a subsequent mutation must not silently destroy the only copy of the previous overrides.
- Genuinely missing file (ENOENT) behaviour is unchanged: empty state, no warning, no backup.
- New tests for the module (it currently has none) pin: atomic write via temp + rename, corrupt-file preservation, ENOENT empty state, and the existing set/reset/reset-all round trips through the real runtime.
- No change to the routes, the file location/name, the on-disk format (`{version: 1, overrides}`), or the id/text validation rules.

## Dedup

Checked open + recently closed issues 2026-10-30: `gh issue list --search "magic prompt"` and `--search "magic-prompts"` return no issue about this store's persistence (only the unrelated closed settings-search test issue #535). The atomic-write/corruption work in sibling stores (model-choices, session-folders, dispatch-results) landed without an issue covering magic-prompts.

body:
# fix(web): ui-auth session TTL env readers are still judged by bare Number() — '1e3' becomes a 1000-hour session and '0x10' a 16-hour one, in the file #624 already cleaned up for the same class

## Evidence

`packages/web/server/lib/ui-auth/ui-auth.js:19-31` at main `389e42c52`:

```js
export const readSessionTtlMs = (raw, unitMs, fallbackMs) => {
  const value = Number(String(raw ?? '').trim());
  return Number.isFinite(value) && value > 0 ? Math.round(value * unitMs) : fallbackMs;
};

const SESSION_TTL_MS = readSessionTtlMs(process.env.OPENCHAMBER_UI_SESSION_TTL_HOURS, HOUR_MS, 12 * HOUR_MS);
const TRUSTED_DEVICE_SESSION_TTL_MS = readSessionTtlMs(
  process.env.OPENCHAMBER_UI_TRUSTED_SESSION_TTL_DAYS,
  24 * HOUR_MS,
  7 * 24 * HOUR_MS,
);
```

This is the one env reader in the file that #624 did not migrate. A few lines below it, the rate-limit reader carries the house comment (`ui-auth.js:36-40`): a bare `Number(...)` "would silently honour '-5' (lockout after one failure), '2.9', and '1e3' (a 1000-attempt budget) for the login brute-force limit" — and was moved to the strict `parsePositiveIntWithDefault` from `lib/shared/parse-int.js` for exactly that reason. The session-lifetime reader directly above it still does what the comment warns against, for the two values that decide how long a UI session (and a trusted-device session) stays valid.

Fractional lifetimes are intentional here and must stay: the existing test (`ui-auth.test.js:427-431`) pins `readSessionTtlMs(' 0.5 ', 1000, 5) === 500`. What is not intentional is the rest of `Number()`'s grammar — exponent and hex spellings, a leading `+`, and trailing `.0` on an integer — plus the total absence of an upper bound.

### Verified this run (laptop probe vs the real module)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-worktree-timeout-20261029/probe-ttl.mjs` on the laptop, importing the real `readSessionTtlMs` from `packages/web/server/lib/ui-auth/ui-auth.js` at `389e42c52`:

| input | as hours (`unitMs = 3_600_000`) | as days (`unitMs = 86_400_000`) |
|---|---|---|
| `'12'` | 43_200_000 ms (12 h, correct) | 1_036_800_000 ms |
| `' 0.5 '` | 1_800_000 ms (intentional, test-pinned) | 43_200_000 ms |
| `'1e3'` | **3_600_000_000 ms (1000 h ≈ 41.7 days)** | **86_400_000_000 ms (≈ 2.7 years)** |
| `'0x10'` | **57_600_000 ms (16 h)** | 1_382_400_000 ms |
| `'+12'` | 43_200_000 ms (honoured) | 1_036_800_000 ms |
| `'1e6'` | **3_600_000_000_000 ms (≈ 114 years)** | **86_400_000_000_000 ms (≈ 2738 years)** |
| `'abc'`, `''`, `'-3'` | fallback (correct) | fallback (correct) |

So an operator who writes `OPENCHAMBER_UI_SESSION_TTL_HOURS=1e3` — or a config generator that emits exponent form — silently gets a 41-day UI session instead of any lifetime they had in mind, and the trusted-device variant can be pushed to millennia. Session lifetime is a security control; its spelling should not be reinterpreted by JavaScript's numeric grammar.

## Why it matters

Every other env reader in this file and its sibling modules was moved to a strict spelling judgement through #624, #689, #696, #697, #703 and the #802/#804 shared-parser migration; the session TTL reader is the leftover. The misread direction is the dangerous one for a lifetime: values only ever get *longer* than the plain-decimal reading (exponent/hex forms), quietly weakening session expiry on a password-gated UI.

## Acceptance criteria

- `readSessionTtlMs` accepts only an explicit plain-decimal spelling: digits with at most one decimal point and at least one digit (e.g. `12`, `0.5`, `12.0` if the fixer chooses to keep it), with surrounding whitespace trimmed. Exponent (`1e3`), hex (`0x10`), leading `+`/`-`, and empty spellings fall back to the default, as `abc` already does.
- Fractional lifetimes keep working: `readSessionTtlMs(' 0.5 ', 1000, 5) === 500` and the existing test at `ui-auth.test.js:427-431` still passes; that test's invalid list is extended with `'1e3'`, `'0x10'`, and `'+12'`.
- The result is bounded to a sane named maximum (fixer's choice, stated in a comment — e.g. 400 days in ms) so no spelling can mint a session that effectively never expires; values above it fall back to the default rather than clamping silently, matching the house fallback pattern.
- No change to the defaults (12 h / 7 days), the env var names, or the rate-limit readers.

## Dedup

Checked open + closed issues 2026-10-30: #624 covered this file's *rate-limit* env vars and is closed; #689/#696/#697/#703 cover health/relay, fs, event-stream and VS Code bridge readers. `gh search issues` for `SESSION_TTL_HOURS` / session TTL returns none of them covering `readSessionTtlMs` — it is the un-migrated remainder in the same file #624 touched.

title: fix(web): notification runtime retains every permission request forever — notifiedPermissionRequests and the per-session cooldown maps are never pruned

body:
## Summary

The notification trigger runtime retains one entry for every permission request it has ever seen, for the life of the process. `notifiedPermissionRequests` (`packages/web/server/lib/notifications/runtime.js:192`) is added to at three sites (lines 865, 878, 935) and checked at line 854, but nothing in the file ever deletes from it or clears it. The runtime is created once at server startup (`packages/web/server/index.js:104`), and OpenChamber's managed server runs for weeks at a time, so the set grows monotonically with the highest-frequency event class in agent work: permission requests (one key `sessionId:requestId` per request, runtime.js:853).

The two per-session cooldown maps in the same runtime have the same shape: `lastReadyNotificationAt` (set at line 584) and `lastErrorNotificationAt` (set at line 659) are keyed by session id and are never deleted from either.

## Evidence

Verified on main `a1ada4c63` (2026-10-29):

- `grep -n "notifiedPermissionRequests.delete|notifiedPermissionRequests.clear"` in `runtime.js`: no matches. The only `.delete(`/`.clear()` calls in the file target other structures (`autoAcceptingSessions`, `sessionParentIdCache`, the debounce timers, `assistantStepMeta`).
- The same file already knows the bounded pattern: `assistantStepMeta` and `lastAssistantStepBySession` are capped at `ASSISTANT_STEP_CACHE_LIMIT = 500` with oldest-entry eviction (runtime.js:255-282), and the comment there says "Bounded: a session emits a handful of steps and the map is per process." The permission-request set — far higher cardinality than steps — got no such bound.
- Laptop probe against the real module (`~/git/fleet/probe-notif-set/probe3.mjs`, fork at 519bfefe6; the file is byte-identical at the cited lines on current main): a runtime whose session is auto-accepting (the path that adds the key at line 865 and returns) fed distinct `permission.asked` events in batches of 50,000, with a 600 ms settle and full GC between batches:
  - baseline heapUsed 7,126,608
  - 50k requests: 13,425,472
  - 100k: 19,527,320
  - 150k: 26,948,096
  - 200k: 31,747,568 — linear, ~123 bytes/request, no plateau
  - Control (identical events, session not auto-accepting, debounce-timer path): flat at ~10.4 MB after warm-up.
- Functional check (`probe2.mjs` Part A): a delivered permission notification is correctly suppressed on identical re-delivery — the set is load-bearing for dedup, so the fix must bound it, not remove it.

## Why it matters

The dedup only needs to remember requests that could plausibly be re-delivered: a request that was answered, expired, or superseded will not be re-announced by OpenCode. Retaining every key forever buys nothing after a short window, while the cost is a slow, certain memory leak in the long-lived server process — the same failure class as #756 (SSE buffers) and #848 (Octokit cache), in a surface those sweeps did not cover. Permission-heavy fleet sessions generate thousands of requests per day, so a server up for weeks accumulates hundreds of thousands of dead keys.

## Acceptance criteria

- `notifiedPermissionRequests` is bounded (entry cap with oldest-first eviction, TTL expiry, or deletion once the request is known resolved/answered) and cannot grow past the bound no matter how many distinct requests arrive.
- `lastReadyNotificationAt` and `lastErrorNotificationAt` are likewise bounded or pruned (a session's cooldown entry is useless once the cooldown window has passed).
- Dedup behavior is preserved: re-delivery of a recent request id still produces no second notification (existing trigger-runtime tests keep passing, plus a regression test that feeds more distinct request ids than the bound and asserts retention stays at the bound while a recent duplicate is still suppressed).
- No change to notification content, channels, or debounce timing.

body:
## Finding

PR #740 (commit `2daeeffcf3`, merged 2026-10-29) made the quota CLI judge `OPENCHAMBER_QUOTA_TIMEOUT_MS` by whole-text plain decimal, but bounded only the value's *spelling*, not its *magnitude* — the exact gap #832 filed for the server/VS Code timer readers and PR #836 then fixed there. This CLI reader was not among #836's covered readers, and it feeds its value straight into a timer, so the hole is still live on current main (`519bfefe6f`).

On current main, `packages/web/bin/lib/commands-quota.js`:

- `resolveQuotaTimeoutMs` (lines 239–242) returns any plain-decimal safe integer greater than 0:
  ```js
  const parsed = parsePlainDecimalInt(env.OPENCHAMBER_QUOTA_TIMEOUT_MS);
  return parsed !== null && parsed > 0 ? parsed : DEFAULT_QUOTA_TIMEOUT_MS;
  ```
  `parsePlainDecimalInt` (lines 13–20 in the PR diff) caps only at `Number.isSafeInteger` — up to 9,007,199,254,740,991.
- That value is the deadline in `fetchProviderWithTimeout` (lines 265–269): `timer = setTimeout(() => resolve(null), timeoutMs)`, reached via line 391 (`const timeoutMs = resolveQuotaTimeoutMs(env)`).

A value above 2,147,483,647 ms does not give a long timeout: Node/Bun timers reject it with `TimeoutOverflowWarning: … does not fit into a 32-bit signed integer. Timeout duration was set to 1.` and fire after ~1 ms. Verified independently this run (twice): `node -e 'setTimeout(..., 3000000000)'` prints the overflow warning, sets the duration to 1, and fires immediately (elapsed 1–7 ms). So an operator who raises `OPENCHAMBER_QUOTA_TIMEOUT_MS` to debug a slow provider gets the opposite: every provider fetch "times out" instantly and the CLI reports `Quota fetch timed out after 3000000000 ms` rows for all providers.

## Contrasts in the same batch / follow-up

- PR #743 in this same batch bounded its new timer reader: `createGitExecTimeoutMs` in `packages/vscode/src/bridge-git-process-runtime.ts` accepts only `raw <= 2_147_483_647`, with a comment naming this exact overflow — the house pattern to follow.
- PR #836 (fixing #832) bounded the handoff, fs-exec, git check-ignore (web + both VS Code copies) and relay batch-window readers, and explicitly left *non-timer* readers (upload caps, cache TTL, drain grace) unbounded because large values are legitimate there. The quota CLI timeout is a timer reader, not a cap/TTL, but it lives in `packages/web/bin/` and was not in #836's list.
- PR #740's own tests pin only spellings (`1e3`, `10000junk`, `10.9`, `250ms`, `0x10` → default); no magnitude case is pinned.

## Why it matters

A plainly written, valid-spelling env value silently inverts the timeout it configures — the same failure class the fleet spent #696–#714 / #832 / #836 eliminating — and it strikes exactly when someone raises the timeout because a provider is already slow.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `resolveQuotaTimeoutMs` falls back to the 10,000 ms default for values above 2,147,483,647 ms, following the `createGitExecTimeoutMs` shape from PR #743.
- [ ] Tests in `commands-quota.test.js` pin: `2147483647` accepted, `3000000000` and an unsafe-integer spelling (e.g. `9007199254740993`) fall back to the default.
- [ ] No change to the spelling rules, the 10,000 ms default, or `OPENCODE_PORT` handling from PR #740.

Found by the pr-diff-review job reviewing PRs #718–#743 (batch watermark 717 → 743); source PR: https://github.com/developing-today/openchamber/pull/740

# Server-persisted Detailed rows dropped by #723 — `sidebarDetailedZoneRows` is not carried into `sidebarSessionRowDisplay`

## Finding

PR #723 (merged, merge commit `4ab427b37f40afc2cb8c8d7203a0abb041d0611c`, https://github.com/developing-today/openchamber/pull/723) replaced the Detailed rows toggle with the new Sidebar rows control. The local (localStorage) store migration was handled: `migrateSessionDisplayState` v11→v12 folds `detailedZoneRows` into `sessionRowDisplay.zoneLines` (`packages/ui/src/stores/useSessionDisplayStore.ts:162-167` on current main `519bfefe6f17b2f3a1e498eb632728c2555092d3`), with tests.

The **server-persisted profile value was not carried over**:

- Before #723, the server settings sanitizer kept the profile field explicitly: `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/settings-helpers.js:401-402` (at the PR's parent) copied `candidate.sidebarDetailedZoneRows` (true/false) into the persisted result, and the UI settings registry exposed it as a profile-scoped, per-surface field (`sidebarDetailedZoneRows: field({ scope: 'profile', perSurface: true, ... })`).
- On current main (`519bfefe6f17b2f3a1e498eb632728c2555092d3`) there is **no occurrence of `sidebarDetailedZoneRows` anywhere in `packages/`**. The server sanitizer only parses the new key: `sessionRowDisplaySchema` at `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/settings-helpers.js:123` and its application at `:414-420`, which copies only `sidebarSessionRowDisplay` into the result.

So a user whose Detailed rows = true lived in their server profile settings (the synced, per-surface copy) silently reverts to one-line Tree zone rows after upgrading — the exact outcome the PR's own Risks section noted ("Server-persisted Detailed rows=true from an older client is not carried into the new key … an upgraded user with Detailed rows on sees one-line Tree zones until they pick two lines again"). That risk was never filed, and it is **not** part of the staged remainder recorded on #22 (List one-line unification, per-kind line counts for Chats/project rows, pin/done-hint toggles, phone element parity — see the 2026-10-28T22:46Z comment on #22).

## Why it matters

A user preference set on one surface and synced through the profile is silently lost on upgrade, with no prompt and no record. The local migration proves the intended mapping (`true → zoneLines: 'two'`); only the server-profile path was missed, so the fix is small and the correct behavior is already defined.

## Acceptance criteria

- The server settings sanitizer (or the profile-settings load path) maps a legacy persisted `sidebarDetailedZoneRows: true` to `sidebarSessionRowDisplay.zoneLines: 'two'` (and `false` to `'one'` only when no new-key value exists — the new key wins when both are present).
- A test in `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/settings-helpers.test.js` pins the legacy-true, legacy-false, and both-keys-present cases.
- After the mapping lands, a persisted profile containing only the old key round-trips without silently dropping the user's two-line Tree rows.

## Evidence / dedupe

- Source PR: #723, merge commit `4ab427b37f40afc2cb8c8d7203a0abb041d0611c`; its Risks section names this gap.
- Verified against current main `519bfefe6f17b2f3a1e498eb632728c2555092d3`: `git grep sidebarDetailedZoneRows origin/main -- packages` returns nothing; local migration at `useSessionDisplayStore.ts:162-167` exists and is tested (`useSessionDisplayStore.test.ts:175-180`).
- Dedupe: issue search for `sidebarDetailedZoneRows` / detailed-rows migration returns only #22 (open); #22's recorded remainder does not include this item. No open issue covers it.

body:
Follow-up to #861 / PR #864 (Codex P2 finding on PR #864, discussion r4419969179):

The #861 fix bounds `runWorktreeStartCommand` with `execFile` `timeout` + `killSignal: 'SIGKILL'` in both twins (`packages/web/server/lib/git/service.js`, `packages/vscode/src/gitService.ts`). That kills only the direct child (bash/cmd). A start command that itself launches subprocesses (e.g. `sleep 30 & …; wait`, or a package-manager script spawning children) can leave descendants running after the timeout, while bootstrap advances to ready/setup-ready. Surviving processes could keep writing files or holding ports, and worktree removal could race them.

Explicitly out of scope for #861 per its triage verdict (task 3743) and fix packet (task 3751): "Process-tree/group kill machinery beyond execFile's direct-child timeout kill."

Acceptance for this follow-up:
- On timeout, the owned process tree/group is terminated and awaited before bootstrap completes, on POSIX and Windows, in both twins.
- Regression test: a start command with descendants outliving a shortened test timeout leaves no surviving descendants and bootstrap still completes.
- No behavior change for commands finishing within the bound.

title: fix(web): repository credential helper's delegate 'git credential fill' has no timeout — a stalled user credential chain hangs git operations indefinitely

body:
## Problem

The repository credential helper (`repository-credential-helper.js`, installed into a repo's `.git/config` by OpenChamber) falls back to the person's own credential chain through `delegate()`, which spawns `git credential fill` with **no timeout and no kill path**. The helper exits only when that child closes. If the person's configured credential helper stalls — a GUI credential manager waiting on something, a network-backed helper whose server hangs — the OpenChamber helper never exits, and because Git waits on its credential helper, the `git push` / `git fetch` that asked for credentials hangs indefinitely and silently.

`GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0` is set, so terminal prompts are off — but that does not bound a *configured helper program*, which is exactly what `git credential fill` invokes.

## Evidence (verified this run at main `519bfefe6`)

- `packages/web/server/lib/git/repository-credential-helper.js:20-35` — `delegate()`: `spawn('git', ['credential', 'fill'], …)` with no timeout option and no timer/kill; the only exits are `child.once('error', …)` and `child.once('close', () => process.exit(0))`.
- Same file, `:57-60` — the invalid-endpoint fallback calls `delegate(query)` and then awaits a promise that never resolves, so process lifetime is entirely the delegate child's.
- Same file, `:91` — `request.on('error', () => delegate(query))`: the server-unreachable path (a normal state — "a closed app never blocks a push" is the design goal stated in the header comment) lands in the same unbounded delegate.
- Contrast inside the same file: the server request carries `timeout: 10_000` with `request.on('timeout', …)` (`:64-68`) and the response read is capped at `MAX_BYTES = 64 KiB`. The delegate spawn is the only unbounded operation in the file.
- Laptop probe running the **real helper script** (probe: laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-upgrade-helper-20261029/`, repo at the same HEAD) with a fake `git` first in PATH that sleeps 30 s: the helper **did not exit within 3 s** (killed by the outer `timeout`, exit 124) on both the bad-endpoint fallback path and the dead-server path. Control fake `git` that answers promptly: helper exited 0 in **72 ms** with the credentials piped through unchanged.

## Why it matters

This helper sits on the critical path of ordinary Git operations in every repository OpenChamber has given an account to, including when the app is closed (by design). A stalled user credential chain currently turns into a permanently hanging `git push` with no output and no deadline — the exact failure the helper's header comment promises to avoid ("a helper that fails only makes Git print a warning"; a helper that *hangs* does much worse).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `delegate()`'s child is bounded by a named deadline in line with the file's existing 10 s server-request timeout class; on expiry the child is killed and the helper exits 0 promptly (preserving the fail-quiet contract: Git prints its own warning, no partial credential output is emitted beyond what was already piped).
- [ ] Behavior when the delegate answers promptly is unchanged (stdout piped through verbatim; exit 0 on error/close as today).
- [ ] Regression test (the runtime test file already exercises the real helper script — `repository-credential-runtime.test.js`): a fake `git credential fill` that never exits makes the helper exit within a bounded time; a promptly-answering fake still yields its credentials.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for `credential`: the credential-adjacent filings are #822 (Cursor sqlite import timeout, closed — different file/mechanism) and #304 (Linear op:// accounts, open feature). The backlog's earlier "credential-helper accumulators capped" check covered `lib/git/credential-helper.js`'s bounded readers, not this helper script's delegate spawn. No filing covers `repository-credential-helper.js`'s unbounded delegate.

body:
## Problem

`runOpenCodeCliUpgrade` runs `opencode upgrade` via `execFile` with **no timeout** — the only bound in the options is `maxBuffer: 1024 * 1024`, which caps output bytes, not elapsed time. A stalled upgrade (package-manager network stall, a registry that accepts the connection and never answers, a child waiting on something other than stdin) never settles the promise.

The caller makes it permanent: `POST /api/opencode/upgrade` stores the attempt in `upgradeInFlight` and clears it only in `.finally()` — i.e. only on settle. One stalled upgrade therefore wedges the route for the life of the server process: every later upgrade attempt, from any tab, awaits the same never-settling promise and hangs its request, and the user can never retry the upgrade short of restarting OpenChamber.

## Evidence (verified this run at main `519bfefe6`)

- `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/cli-upgrade.js:6-13` — `execFile(launch.binary, [...launch.args, 'upgrade'], { cwd, env, windowsHide: true, maxBuffer: 1024 * 1024 }, …)`; no `timeout` option, no manual kill timer. `child.stdin?.end()` (EOF) is handled, so this is specifically the no-elapsed-deadline case.
- `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/routes.js:155,173-176` — `upgradeInFlight = upgradeOpenCodeCli().finally(() => { upgradeInFlight = null; })`; cleared only when the promise settles.
- `packages/web/server/index.js:2709-2712` — production wiring of `upgradeOpenCodeCli` to `runOpenCodeCliUpgrade` with the managed launch spec.
- Laptop probe against the **real** `runOpenCodeCliUpgrade` (probe: laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-upgrade-helper-20261029/probe-upgrade.mjs`, repo at the same HEAD): a child that never exits (`node -e 'setInterval…'`) left the promise **UNSETTLED after 2,500 ms**; a control child exiting 0 settled in **28 ms**.
- Contrast in the same surface: the upgrade *status/version* probes in the same routes file carry `AbortSignal.timeout(openCodeInfoDeadlineMs)`, and `installOpenCodeV2` downloads are deadline-bound — the actual upgrade execution is the unbounded outlier.

## Why it matters

Upgrading OpenCode is a headline action of the managed-server layer. A single network stall during it silently bricks the upgrade path (and leaves an HTTP request hanging per attempt) until the whole server is restarted — with no error, no log line naming a deadline, and no way for the user to distinguish "still working" from "stuck forever".

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The upgrade child runs under a named, generous but finite deadline (installs can be slow; pick and document a bound in the style of the repo's other named timeout constants), after which the child is killed (with SIGKILL escalation if it ignores the first kill) and the promise rejects with the existing generic failure message (installer output still never logged/returned — it can contain registry credentials).
- [ ] `cli-upgrade.d.ts` reflects any option added.
- [ ] Regression test in `cli-upgrade.test.js`: a never-exiting child rejects at the deadline (test uses a short injected/fixture deadline, not the production bound), and the existing success / nonzero-exit / spawn-error / signal-exit tests still pass.
- [ ] After a deadline rejection, a subsequent `POST /api/opencode/upgrade` can start a fresh attempt (the route's `upgradeInFlight` clears on settle — rejection counts).

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for `upgrade` / `cli upgrade` / `execFile`: the upgrade-adjacent filings are the version/info *probe* deadlines (#789, #796, both closed) and the v2-install download caps (#834, closed) — none covers the upgrade *execution* child in `cli-upgrade.js`.

title: fix(web,vscode): gpgconf probes in resolveSshAuthSock have no timeout — a hung gpgconf wedges every git command when SSH_AUTH_SOCK is unset
