body:
## Problem

When `SSH_AUTH_SOCK` is unset, nearly every git command first resolves the ssh-agent socket through `gpgconf` — with **no timeout, no output cap, and no caching** — in both implementations:

- `packages/web/server/lib/git/service.js:361-371` — `runGpgconf` inside `resolveSshAuthSock` (:346) runs `execFileAsync(candidate, args)` with no options at all, looping over 3 candidates (`gpgconf`, `/opt/homebrew/bin/gpgconf`, `/usr/local/bin/gpgconf`), and up to 3 invocations per resolve (`--list-dirs`, `--launch gpg-agent`, `--list-dirs` again).
- `packages/vscode/src/gitService.ts:151-160` — the identical twin (`resolveSshAuthSock` :136, called from `buildGitEnv` :179).

The call is on the hot path: `buildGitEnv` (`service.js:425`) awaits `resolveSshAuthSock()` whenever the env lacks `SSH_AUTH_SOCK`, and `runGitCommand` (`service.js:1177`) awaits `buildGitEnv(cwd)` for essentially every git command. There is no memoization, so the probe cost — and the hang risk — recurs per command, not once per process.

A `gpgconf` that hangs (a locked or wedged gpg-agent, a smartcard/PIN prompt shape, a broken GnuPG install) therefore wedges **every git operation in the server / extension host**, sequentially and silently: each command's own probe timeout (`GIT_PROBE_TIMEOUT_MS` etc.) never gets a chance to apply, because the hang happens before git is even spawned.

## Verification (this run, laptop probe vs the real modules)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-gpgconf-timeout/probe.mjs` (laptop), driving the real exported `isGitRepository` from `packages/web/server/lib/git/service.js` on main `84c0acf4e` (file unchanged through `519bfefe6`), with a hermetic env: `SSH_AUTH_SOCK` unset, `HOME` without a `~/.gnupg/S.gpg-agent.ssh` socket, and a fake `gpgconf` first on `PATH`:

- Control — fake `gpgconf` answers instantly (nonexistent socket path): `isGitRepository` settled `true` in **33 ms**.
- Wedge — fake `gpgconf` = `sleep 120`: one ordinary git probe **never settled** within a 10 s observation window; the probe killed the fake itself — nothing in the product bounds it.

## Why it matters

Git operations are a living surface of OpenChamber (status, branches, worktrees, diff). One wedged helper binary on the user's machine turns into a total, silent git outage inside the app, repeated on every command, with no error pointing at gpgconf.

## Acceptance criteria

- Both `runGpgconf` implementations (web `service.js`, vscode `gitService.ts`) run each candidate with a short timeout (seconds — `gpgconf --list-dirs` is a local probe; the file's git probes use `GIT_PROBE_TIMEOUT_MS`-scale bounds) and a bounded `maxBuffer`; a timed-out candidate is treated like a failed candidate (fall through / return empty), matching the existing `catch { continue }` shape.
- A hung `gpgconf` can no longer wedge a git command: the exported git operations settle (with `SSH_AUTH_SOCK` unresolved) in bounded time.
- Regression test with a fake hanging `gpgconf` on `PATH` (or an injected exec seam) proving a git operation settles within the bound; existing git service tests still pass.
- No behavior change when `SSH_AUTH_SOCK` is already set or a socket file exists (those paths already skip `gpgconf`).

body:
## Problem

The worktree start command — the project's OpenCode `commands.start` (e.g. a dependency install) plus any caller-supplied setup command — runs with **no timeout** in both implementations:

- `packages/web/server/lib/git/service.js:2144-2173` — `runWorktreeStartCommand` calls `execFileAsync('bash', ['-lc', text], { cwd, env, maxBuffer: 20 MiB })` (and the `cmd /c` twin on win32) with no `timeout` option.
- `packages/vscode/src/gitService.ts:1543-1588` — the identical twin, also no `timeout`.

The worktree bootstrap only advances after the start scripts settle:

- web: `service.js` awaits `runWorktreeStartScripts(...)` before `setWorktreeBootstrapState(..., WORKTREE_BOOTSTRAP_READY, WORKTREE_BOOTSTRAP_PHASE_SETUP_READY)` (~:2297-2307).
- vscode: `gitService.ts:1698-1703` awaits `runWorktreeStartScripts(...)` before `setWorktreeBootstrapState(directory, WORKTREE_BOOTSTRAP_READY, WORKTREE_PHASE_SETUP_READY)`.

So a start command that never exits — a dev-server-shaped command (`npm run dev`), an install waiting on a network prompt, a wedged package manager — leaves the worktree in `pending` / `git-ready` **forever**: no error, no failure state, and the child process is never killed. The failure path only fires on rejection, which a hung child never produces.

Contrast in the same web file: `runGitCommand` (`service.js:1173-1182`) supports `timeoutMs` with `killSignal: 'SIGKILL'`, and short probes pass `GIT_PROBE_TIMEOUT_MS`. The start command is the unbounded outlier.

## Verification (this run, laptop probe vs the real modules)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-worktree-start-timeout/probe.mjs` (laptop), driving the real exported `createWorktree` / `getWorktreeBootstrapStatus` from `packages/web/server/lib/git/service.js` on main `84c0acf4e` (both cited files unchanged through `519bfefe6`):

- Control — quick start command (writes a marker, exits): bootstrap reached `status=ready phase=setup-ready`.
- Wedge — start command = node script sleeping 120 s: after a 12 s observation window the bootstrap was still `status=pending phase=git-ready error=null`, the child had started and was **still alive**; the probe had to kill it itself — nothing in the product bounds or kills it.

## Why it matters

Worktree creation is a living surface of OpenChamber (every new session in a fresh worktree passes through this bootstrap). A project-controlled command that hangs wedges that worktree's session bootstrap silently and permanently, with a leaked child process, and the user gets no signal about which step stalled.

## Acceptance criteria

- Both `runWorktreeStartCommand` implementations (web + vscode) run the child with a generous named-constant timeout (start commands legitimately run long — installs — so minutes, not seconds) and kill it on expiry, consistent with `runGitCommand`'s SIGKILL approach.
- On timeout the command is treated as a failed start command under the existing semantics: a warning naming the timeout is logged and the bootstrap proceeds to `ready`/`setup-ready` instead of staying `pending` forever (a failing start command already does not fail worktree creation — preserve that).
- Regression tests in the existing harnesses (`packages/web/server/lib/git/service.test.js`, `packages/vscode/src/gitService.worktree-bootstrap.test.js`) cover a start command that outlives a shortened test timeout: bootstrap completes and the child is gone.
- No behavior change for start commands that finish within the bound.

body:
# fix(quota): /api/quota/antigravity reports "Not configured" while the aggregator hub reads the pool fine — the dispatcher gate treats a primary pool as unavailable

## Symptom (observed 2026-10-29, verified twice from independent readers)

- The aggregator hub reads the Antigravity pool **fine**: `quota-current.json` tick `2026-10-30T00:15:11Z` (laptop pm-aggregator gatherer, heartbeat ok) carries antigravity state `ok` — Gemini-model weekly 4%, Claude-model weekly 57%, all 5h windows 0%.
- The classic live endpoint the fleet's dispatcher and steward probe, `GET /api/quota/antigravity`, answers `{"ok":false,"configured":false,"error":"Not configured"}` (live pull 2026-10-29 19:47 CDT, saved at goal `hidden_files/dispatch-packets/quota-2026-10-29-1945.json.txt`). In that same pull, on the same server, `google` answered `ok:true` with live per-model windows.

## Why it matters

The fleet measurement gate (pool map, Drew 2026-10-27) forbids any placement on a pool without a quota read ≤60 min old. The dispatcher gates on the live endpoint, so Antigravity reads as **unavailable and is never seated** — while the pool map makes it a primary source: the Gemini Flash pool rides Antigravity *only*, and Claude seats draw on its Claude bucket. The steward already consumes the hub figure for this pool (precedent noted in the pool-change ledger, 2026-10-29 08:22Z: "the classic /api/quota/antigravity endpoint still returns 'Not configured', a different source — the hub entry is the consumed figure"), but the dispatcher's gate still trusts the broken endpoint. The unused weekly windows are a standing burn-by-expiry loss — the current weekly window resets **Sat Oct 31, 8:11 AM CDT** at 4–57% used.

## Root-cause evidence (code, main 86604564b)

`GET /api/quota/:providerId` (`packages/web/server/lib/quota/routes.js:107`) reaches `antigravity.fetchQuota()`, which returns `configured:false, error:'Not configured'` in exactly one place: when `resolveAuthCandidates()` finds zero candidates (`packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/antigravity/index.js:44-53`). There are only two candidate sources (`index.js:26-42`, `providers/antigravity/auth.js`):

1. **The legacy accounts file** — `antigravity-accounts.json` under `OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR` / `~/.local/share/opencode` (`lib/quota/utils/auth.js:9-12`). The provider's own comment states current plugin versions sign in through the credential store and **never write this file** (`auth.js:56-63`) — it is a fallback that is empty on current installs.
2. **The credential store's `google` entry** — `resolveAntigravityStoreAuth` (`auth.js:69-94`) returns null unless the entry carries a **refresh token**. The sibling google provider resolves the *same* store entry with an access token alone (`providers/google/auth.js:25-46`: null only when access *and* refresh are both missing). Antigravity is the strictest consumer of this entry.

The two readers feed that store read from **different sources**:

- The web server wires `openCodeCredentialSource` (`packages/web/server/index.js:1647-1652`): credentials come from the **running OpenCode server's `GET /api/credential`** (`lib/opencode/auth.js:91`, `client().credential.list()`), projected by `projectCredentialEntries` / `projectCredentialValue` (`auth.js:203-230`) — only *active* rows, with the value copied from whatever the server API hands back.
- The hub gatherer deliberately replaces that source with a **direct read-only read of `opencode.db`** (developing-today/code `pm-stack/aggregator/scripts/gather-quota.ts:10-19, 116-149`), expressly because the server-API path is known to diverge ("so a stopped server cannot zero the tick", code#1251).

**Hypothesis (discriminated by the same-server google/antigravity split above):** in the server process, the projected `google` entry reaches the provider *without* a usable refresh token — or the store read fails silently — while the gatherer's raw DB read sees the full stored row. Either way antigravity gets zero candidates while google, needing only an access token, succeeds. A compounding defect: `resolveAuthCandidates` swallows credential-store errors (`index.js:36-38`, "Credential store unwired or unreachable: the accounts file alone decides"), so a failed read is indistinguishable from "no login exists" — a fetch failure masquerading as an authoritative not-configured state.

Not this bug: closed #507/#545/#570 were usedPercent clamp defects in the same provider's transforms — different code path, already fixed.

## Acceptance criteria

- `GET /api/quota/antigravity` on the laptop instance returns `ok:true` with live per-model windows that agree with the hub's antigravity entry (same used % / resets, within one tick).
- The reason the server-side read missed the credential is identified and fixed at its source (store projection, resolver requirement, or wiring) — not papered over by pointing consumers at the hub file.
- A credential-store read failure surfaces as an error state distinct from `configured:false` "Not configured".
- Regression coverage: a google store entry in the shape the running server actually projects resolves as configured for antigravity; a store read that throws does not produce `configured:false`.
- With the endpoint fixed, the dispatcher's measurement gate can verify the pool and Antigravity seats become placeable again.

body:
## Summary

The Android app's direct GitHub release check has no deadline — a stalled `api.github.com` answer hangs the update check forever and blocks the server fallback that exists for exactly that case.

In `packages/ui/src/lib/mobileReleaseUpdate.ts`:

- `fetchLatestMobileRelease` (:66-72) calls `fetchImpl(LATEST_RELEASE_URL, { headers: { Accept: 'application/vnd.github+json' } })` — no `signal`, no timeout. The `ReleaseFetch` type (:38) does not even admit a signal: `(url, init: { headers: { Accept: string } }) => Promise<Response>`.
- `checkMobileReleaseUpdate` (:103-115) passes the raw global `fetch` as that impl, so the production path is equally unbounded (browser/Capacitor `fetch` has no default timeout).
- The module's own contract (header comment, :10-13) is "Every failure returns null" so the caller can fall back — a stall is the one failure mode that never returns at all.

The caller makes it worse: `useUpdateStore.ts:302-306` (mobile runtime) does `info = await checkMobileReleaseUpdate(); if (!info) { info = await checkForWebUpdates('mobile', ...) }` — the server check runs only after the direct check settles. While the direct check hangs, the store's `checking` flag never clears, `lastChecked` never updates, and the server fallback — whose stated purpose is answering "when the phone cannot [reach GitHub]" — never gets its say.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `86604564b`)

Laptop probe (`bun test`, temporary probe test importing the real `packages/ui/src/lib/mobileReleaseUpdate.ts` in the laptop checkout at the same commit `86604564b`, removed after the run) with a never-settling `fetchImpl`:

```
PROBE settledAfter1500ms= false initKeys= [ "headers" ] initSignal= null
1 pass
```

`fetchLatestMobileRelease('2.3.3', neverSettles)` stayed pending for the full 1.5 s observation window, and the init the real module produced carries only `headers` — no `signal`.

Existing tests (`packages/ui/src/lib/mobileReleaseUpdate.test.ts`) cover version comparison, malformed payloads, non-OK responses and a throwing fetch — every stub settles immediately; there is no never-settling case and no signal assertion.

## Why it matters

On a phone with a captive portal, a filtered proxy, or a GitHub connection that accepts and then stalls, the update check silently wedges for the session: the UI can sit in "checking" indefinitely and the user is never told about a newer release, even though the connected server could have answered. It is the same no-deadline class as the recently fixed quota/tunnel/download fetches, on the one remaining UI-side outbound call whose type signature forbids a signal outright.

## Acceptance criteria

- `fetchLatestMobileRelease` performs the release fetch under a bounded deadline (e.g. an `AbortSignal.timeout(...)` with a named constant); the `ReleaseFetch` init type is widened to carry the signal, and `checkMobileReleaseUpdate`'s raw-`fetch` impl forwards it.
- A stalled release answer resolves as `null` within the bound (the module's "every failure returns null" contract), so `useUpdateStore` proceeds to the server fallback and `checking` clears.
- Regression tests in `packages/ui/src/lib/mobileReleaseUpdate.test.ts`: a never-settling fetch stub resolves `null` within the deadline (fake timers or a short injected bound are fine), and the fetch init carries a signal.
- Healthy-path behaviour unchanged: existing mobileReleaseUpdate tests keep passing.

body:
## Summary

The UI's URL-auth token mint fetches have no deadline, and the mint is coalesced behind a single shared promise — one stalled `/auth/url-token` answer wedges URL auth for the whole UI session.

In `packages/ui/src/lib/runtime-auth.ts`:

- `postUrlAuthTokenMint` (:242-247) calls raw `fetch(buildAuthUrl(apiBaseUrl, route), { method: 'POST', headers, credentials: 'include' })` — no `signal`, no timeout. The relay variant (`relay.fetch(route, ...)`) has the same absence at the call site.
- `mintLocalRuntimeUrlAuthToken` (:309-312) repeats the pattern for the local origin: `fetch(buildAuthUrl(origin, '/auth/url-token'), { method: 'POST', credentials: 'include' })` — no `signal`.
- `mintRuntimeUrlAuthToken` (:268-298) coalesces: while `runtimeUrlAuthRefreshPromise` is set, every caller gets that same promise, and it is cleared only in `.finally()` — i.e. only when the fetch settles. A never-settling fetch means the shared promise never clears.
- The proactive refresh loop (`scheduleUrlAuthRefresh`, :397-420) reschedules only in the mint's `.finally()`. A stalled mint therefore also stops the refresh loop: the current token expires on its server TTL and is never replaced.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `86604564b`)

Laptop probe (`bun test`, temporary probe test importing the real `packages/ui/src/lib/runtime-auth.ts` in the laptop checkout at the same commit `86604564b`, removed after the run) with `globalThis.fetch` stubbed to a never-settling promise:

```
PROBE settledAfter1500ms= false initSignal= null initKeys= [ "method", "headers", "credentials" ]
1 pass
```

So: `refreshRuntimeUrlAuthToken()` stayed pending for the full 1.5 s observation window, and the fetch init the real module produced carries exactly `method`, `headers`, `credentials` — no `signal` at all. Browser `fetch` has no default timeout: a server (or relay) that accepts the connection and then stalls — e.g. a server whose event loop is wedged, the exact failure mode several recent server-side issues describe — leaves this promise pending indefinitely.

Consumers that depend on the mint: `refreshRuntimeUrlAuthToken` callers in `FilesView.tsx:803`, `inlineMarkdownImages.ts:210`, `markdownVideo.ts:125`, `gitlabUploads.ts:78`, `devTunnel.ts`; the guest-frame mint `mintGuestFrameUrlAuthToken` (:256-262, used by `guests/frame-url.ts:38`); and the proactive loop driven by `acquireRuntimeUrlAuthToken`. All of them inherit the wedge through the one coalesced promise.

Existing tests (`packages/ui/src/lib/runtime-auth.test.ts`, 199 lines) stub `fetch` with immediately resolving/rejecting responses and never exercise a never-settling fetch, and never assert a `signal` on the mint calls.

## Why it matters

URL-auth tokens gate file/raw URLs, markdown images and videos, GitLab uploads, and guest frames. Because the failure is in the shared coalesced mint (not in any one consumer), a single stalled token request silently disables all of those surfaces until the page is reloaded — with no error surfaced, because the promise never rejects either.

## Acceptance criteria

- Both mint fetches (the `postUrlAuthTokenMint` path including its relay call site insofar as the relay API accepts a signal, and the `mintLocalRuntimeUrlAuthToken` path) carry a bounded deadline (e.g. `AbortSignal.timeout(...)` with a named constant in line with the house style), so a stalled `/auth/url-token` answer rejects within the bound instead of hanging.
- On deadline expiry the coalesced refresh promise clears, so the next `refreshRuntimeUrlAuthToken` / proactive-loop tick retries a fresh mint rather than returning the wedged promise forever; the proactive refresh loop keeps rescheduling after a timed-out mint.
- Regression tests in `packages/ui/src/lib/runtime-auth.test.ts`: a never-settling stubbed fetch causes the mint to reject within the deadline (fake timers or a short injected bound are fine), a subsequent mint retries, and the mint fetch init carries a signal.
- Healthy-path behaviour unchanged: existing runtime-auth tests keep passing.

## Problem

`useGitmojiList` fetches the gitmoji catalog with no deadline, and its module-level in-flight dedupe turns one stalled request into a permanent outage of the feature for the rest of the page session.

`packages/ui/src/hooks/useGitmojiList.ts`:

- Line 76: `const response = await fetch(GITMOJI_SOURCE_URL);` — no `signal`, no timeout. A connection that stalls (accepted but never answering, or a body that never finishes — `response.json()` at line 80 is equally unbounded) never settles.
- Lines 70/93/97: `inflightFetch` is cleared only in the inner promise's `finally`, i.e. only on settle. While the fetch hangs, every later `fetchGitmojiList()` call returns the same hung in-flight promise — no retry is ever possible.
- Lines 145-149 / 159-167: the hook's effect sets `isLoading(true)` and clears it in `fetchGitmojiList().finally(...)`, and `ensureLoaded()` returns `fetchGitmojiList()` directly — both hang forever behind the stalled request.

## Verified this run (laptop probe, actual source)

Probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-oc-gitmoji-20261029/`) imports the real `useGitmojiList.ts` source (with `fetchGitmojiList` re-exported for the harness) and stubs `fetch` to a never-settling promise:

```json
{"fetchCalls":1,"firstSettledAfter3s":false,"secondSettledAfter2s":false}
```

One fetch call total; neither the first caller nor a second caller (issued 1s later) ever settles. In the real UI this means: gitmoji suggestions in the Git view (`packages/ui/src/components/views/GitView.tsx:656`) silently never load, the loading state never clears, and nothing recovers until a full page reload — and a reload against the same stalled upstream reproduces it.

## Why it matters

This is the same unbounded-external-fetch shape the web server side has been systematically fixing (e.g. #844 Kimi quota fetch, #819 ngrok poll), here on the UI side with a worse failure mode: the dedupe cache converts a transient stall into a session-permanent one, with no error surfaced (the `catch` that warns and notifies subscribers with `[]` only runs if the fetch eventually rejects).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The gitmoji fetch carries a bounded deadline (e.g. `AbortSignal.timeout(...)` and/or a composed signal), covering both the response and the `response.json()` body read.
- [ ] On deadline expiry the in-flight entry is cleared and subscribers are notified through the existing failure path, so a later `ensureLoaded()` / effect run issues a fresh fetch.
- [ ] A regression test with a never-settling (or deadline-exceeding) stubbed `fetch` shows the call settling (empty list via the failure path) and a subsequent call re-fetching.
- [ ] Warm-cache behavior unchanged: fresh localStorage cache still skips the network entirely.

body:
## Summary

The GitLab client's error path in the web server reads the **whole** error body and embeds it entire in the thrown error — both as the `Error` message and as `cause.description`. The fetches feeding it are deadline-bounded (10 s per attempt) but not size-bounded, and the upstream is a user-configured, possibly self-managed GitLab instance (or whatever answers on its address), whose error answers can be arbitrarily large HTML/proxy pages.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `8c2e6e2af`)

- `packages/web/server/lib/gitlab/client.js:55-68` — `requestError` does `const content = await response.text().catch(() => '')`, then builds `new Error(description …)` where `description` is the whole content (for JSON it extracts `error`/`message`, but for non-JSON the raw body is used whole, unsliced). The same whole string is stored in `cause.description`.
- The requester (`client.js:115-145`) bounds each attempt with a 10 s deadline (`GITLAB_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS`, :16) — a time bound only: a fast upstream can deliver an arbitrarily large body well inside it. This is the module that #781 added deadlines to; no size bound was added on the error read.
- Laptop probe against the real module (file md5-identical to sandbox main; probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-gitlab-error-body-20261029/probe.mjs` on the laptop): the real `createGitLabClient` with a stub fetch returning status 500 with a streamed 32 MiB body (no `content-length`) — **all 33,554,432 bytes were produced**, and the thrown error's `message` **and** `cause.description` were each **33,554,432 characters**. That string propagates to callers, logs, and error surfaces. Control: `readBoundedResponseText` (the shared bounded reader from #803) on the identical stream stopped after 131,072 bytes produced; a small error body (`project not found`, 404) still surfaces verbatim through the real client.

## Why it matters

An error path should be the safest path in the system; here it is an unbounded memory and log amplifier — the same shape as #845 (OpenCode error-detail reads), in a different subsystem with a less-trusted upstream: self-managed GitLab instances and their proxies are exactly the servers that answer errors with huge HTML pages. The fix pattern already exists in-tree: read the error body through a bounded read and keep only a short excerpt at the error surface.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `requestError` reads the error body through a bounded read (e.g. `readBoundedResponseText` with a small named cap, `lib/shared/response-body.js`) and the thrown error's message and `cause.description` carry at most a short excerpt, never the whole body.
- [ ] JSON error extraction (`error` / `message` fields) still works for ordinary small JSON error bodies; non-JSON excerpts keep the existing fallback (`GitLab request failed with status …` when empty).
- [ ] Tests cover an oversize streamed error body: the read stops at the cap (stream not fully consumed) and the error message length stays bounded; existing `client.test.js` error/retry behaviour is unchanged.
- [ ] Success-path body handling (`parseBody`) and the retry/deadline policy are untouched.

## Related

- #845 — the same whole-error-body pattern in the OpenCode prompt/dispatch/message-queue paths; the two fixes can share the bounded-read approach but are separate modules and upstreams.
- #781 — added this client's per-attempt deadlines; this issue is the missing size bound on its error read.

body:
## Summary

The GitHub Octokit conditional-request (ETag) cache in the web server buffers every cacheable GET response whole with `response.arrayBuffer()` and keeps it in memory, with a count cap (300 entries) but **no per-entry size cap and no total byte budget**. One oversized GitHub API answer is retained whole for the life of the process; up to 300 of them can accumulate.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `8c2e6e2af`)

- `packages/web/server/lib/github/octokit.js:70` — on a successful GET with an `etag` header, `const body = await response.arrayBuffer()` buffers the whole body before `rememberEtag` stores it.
- `packages/web/server/lib/github/octokit.js:35-46` — `ETAG_CACHE_MAX_ENTRIES = 300` and `rememberEtag` evicts only by entry count (LRU). There is no byte accounting anywhere in the module: no per-entry cap, no total cache budget, no `content-length` pre-check.
- The per-request fetch is time-bounded (`OCTOKIT_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS = 8000`, `octokit.js:18-26`) but not size-bounded: a fast upstream can deliver an arbitrarily large body well inside 8 s. Large legitimate GitHub answers exist (long PR/check lists, big repo payloads), and a compromised or misbehaving GitHub Enterprise / proxy endpoint answering on the API base can return far more.
- Laptop probe against the real module (file md5-identical to sandbox main; probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-octokit-etag-20261029/probe.mjs` on the laptop): stubbed `fetch` returning a streamed ~32 MiB JSON body (no `content-length`) with an `etag` header, driven through the real `createOctokit(...).rest.users.getAuthenticated()` — **all 33,554,420 payload bytes were produced and consumed**, the parsed result carried the full body, and a second call answered `304` was **served from the cache with the full 33,554,420-byte body replayed** (`fetchCalls: 2`, second login length identical). Control: a small body caches and replays correctly.

## Why it matters

This cache exists to make PR/check polling rate-limit-free, so it sits on a hot, always-on path in the long-lived web server. Its only bound is entry count: worst-case retained memory is 300 × the largest GitHub answer ever seen, and nothing ever shrinks it except LRU churn. That is exactly the unbounded-retention shape the shared bounded reader (`lib/shared/response-body.js`, #803) was built to prevent on the read side — this site retains the body *after* the read, indefinitely. A fair cap is a design call (per-entry cap vs total byte budget vs both; oversized answers should simply skip caching and stream through uncached), which is why this is filed as triage rather than a prescribed small fix.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A triage decision is recorded: the cache bound chosen (per-entry byte cap, total byte budget, or both) and the skip-caching behaviour for oversized answers.
- [ ] Cacheable GET responses above the chosen bound are **not** retained: the caller still receives the full, correct response, but no oversized `ArrayBuffer` is stored in `etagCache`.
- [ ] The cache's worst-case retained bytes are bounded by a named constant, and 304 replay for under-bound responses is unchanged.
- [ ] Tests cover an oversize streamed response with an `etag`: it is returned whole to the caller, is not replayed from cache on a later 304 (or is evicted per the chosen design), and a small response still caches/replays as today.
- [ ] Existing GitHub/octokit tests pass.

## Related

- Same unbounded-body family, different mechanism: #845 (error-detail reads), #842 (login keeper, fixed), #803/#804 (shared bounded reader primitives — note that helper bounds a *read*, this issue is about *retention*, so a cache-side bound is needed rather than a direct reuse).

## Summary

Three OpenCode error-detail reads in the web server buffer the whole error
body before using any of it. The shared helper is the worst instance: it
embeds the **entire** body in the thrown error, unsliced. The other two read
the whole body only to keep the first 200 characters. The shared bounded
reader landed for exactly this pattern (`lib/shared/response-body.js`,
#803) is not used at any of the three sites.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `bdad58d7c`)

- `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/prompt-response.js:4-9` —
  `assertPromptResponse` does `const body = await response.text()` on a
  non-ok response and throws `` `${operation} failed (${status}): ${body}` ``
  with **no truncation at all**. Callers: `message-queue/runtime.js:455`
  (every OpenCode dispatch POST), `session-goal/runtime.js:391`
  (`session.prompt`), `context-obligatory/runtime.js:77`
  (`session.synthetic`).
- `packages/web/server/lib/dispatch-results/runtime.js:298` —
  `const detail = await response.text()` then only `detail.slice(0, 200)`
  is used in the thrown error.
- `packages/web/server/lib/message-queue/runtime.js:451` — same spelling:
  whole `response.text()`, only `detail.slice(0, 200)` used.
- The fetches feeding these reads are time-bounded (`AbortSignal.timeout`
  in both runtimes) but not size-bounded: a fast upstream can deliver an
  arbitrarily large body well inside the deadline. The upstream here is the
  OpenCode server / whatever answers on its port — a misconfigured or
  wedged upstream returning a huge HTML/error page is exactly the case
  `prompt-response.js` exists to diagnose (its sibling export rejects HTML

- Laptop probe against the real module (md5 identical to sandbox main;

  laptop): a `Response` with status 500 and a streamed 32 MiB body (no

  pulled** and the thrown error's message was **33,554,461 characters**.
  That string is then propagated to callers, logs, and queue/dispatch error
  surfaces.

## Why it matters

An error path should be the safest path in the system; here it is an
unbounded memory and log amplifier. One oversized error answer from a
wedged/misconfigured OpenCode holds the whole body in memory and then
duplicates it into an exception message that downstream code logs and
stores. The fix pattern already exists in-tree: `readBoundedResponseText`
in `packages/web/server/lib/shared/response-body.js` enforces its cap
during the read and cancels the stream when crossed (#802 rule 3, #803).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `assertPromptResponse` reads a non-ok body through a bounded read
      (e.g. `readBoundedResponseText` with a small named cap) and the thrown
      error carries at most a short excerpt (comparable to the 200-char

      `slice(0, 200)` excerpt behavior at the error surface is unchanged.
- [ ] Tests cover an oversize streamed error body for at least

## Summary

The web Kimi quota provider's primary fetch has no deadline. It is the one
unbounded fetch left among the web quota providers — the provider the #782
sweep missed, in the same shape as NanoGPT in #827. A stalled
`api.kimi.com` endpoint never settles the fetch, and because the quota
aggregator coalesces per provider through a map that only clears on settle,
`kimi-for-coding` is wedged for the whole server session.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `bdad58d7c`)

- `packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/kimi.js:152-160` — `fetchQuota`
  calls `fetchImpl('https://api.kimi.com/coding/v1/usages', { method,
  headers })` with **no `signal`**.
- Same file, `kimi.js:24-27` — the Moonshot balance fallback in the same
  provider DOES pass `signal: AbortSignal.timeout(15_000)`. The primary call
  is the odd one out in its own file.
- Full scan this run of every `fetch(`/`fetchImpl(` in
  `packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/**`: every other provider call is
  bounded; `kimi.js:152` is the only NO-SIGNAL site.
- `packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/index.js:275,527-534` —
  `pendingFetches` coalescing: `fetchQuotaForProvider` stores the pending
  promise and deletes the entry only in `.finally()`. A never-settling fetch
  therefore wedges the provider permanently; every later request returns the
  same pending promise.
- `packages/web/server/lib/quota/routes.js:99-108` — `GET
  /api/quota/:providerId` awaits `fetchQuotaForProvider(providerId)` with no
  deadline of its own.
- Laptop probe against the real module (laptop clone, `kimi.js` md5
  identical to sandbox main; probe:
  `~/git/fleet/probe-kimi-web-timeout/probe.mjs` on the laptop): injected a
  stalled `fetchImpl` that honours an abort signal like real fetch.
  Result: init keys were only `[method, headers]` (`signal` absent), and
  `fetchQuota` was **UNSETTLED after 3000 ms** with no abort fired.

## Why it matters

One stalled third-party endpoint silently hangs the Kimi quota route and
permanently wedges the `kimi-for-coding` quota surface until the server
restarts — no error, no retry possible, because the coalesced pending entry
never clears. This is exactly the failure #782 fixed for seven providers and
#827 for NanoGPT; Kimi's primary call is the remaining instance on the web
side. (The VS Code twin was covered separately by #812.)

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `kimi.js` `fetchQuota` passes a deadline signal consistent with the
      file's own convention (`AbortSignal.timeout(15_000)`, matching the
      Moonshot fallback at `kimi.js:27`) to the `api.kimi.com/coding/v1/usages`
      fetch.
- [ ] A stalled Kimi endpoint surfaces as a bounded per-provider error via
      the existing `catch -> buildResult({ ok: false, ... })` path in
      `fetchQuota`, and the `pendingFetches` entry in `providers/index.js`
      clears so a later quota request can retry.
- [ ] `packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/kimi.test.js` covers the
      primary fetch's deadline (e.g. asserts the injected `fetchImpl`
      receives a signal, and/or that a fetch that only settles on abort
      resolves to an `ok: false` result instead of hanging).
- [ ] No behavior change for the Moonshot balance fallback or for any other
      provider.

title: fix(web): login keeper's 64 KiB issuer-answer cap is checked only after buffering the whole body — a streamed oversize answer is fully read into memory before rejection

body:
## Problem

The spaces login keeper's token exchange checks its 64 KiB answer cap only **after** buffering the issuer's whole response, so the cap does not bound memory during the read.

`packages/web/server/lib/spaces/login-keeper.js`:

- `:33-34` — `EXCHANGE_TIMEOUT_MS = 30_000` and `MAX_ANSWER_BYTES = 64 * 1024`.
- `:98-99` — the docstring promise: "a body over 64 KiB or one that is not the token answer is an error."
- `:120-121` — the implementation:

```js
const text = await response.text();
if (text.length > MAX_ANSWER_BYTES) throw new Error('The login issuer answered with too large a body');
```

`response.text()` consumes the entire body before the length check runs. A response with no `Content-Length` (chunked/streamed) that sends far more than 64 KiB — a misbehaving or compromised issuer endpoint, a broken proxy, or an endless chunked stream within the 30 s deadline — is fully buffered in the web server's memory first. The deadline bounds time, not bytes: a fast sender can deliver hundreds of MiB inside 30 s. This is exactly the pattern fixed for the Electron favicon in #817 ("buffers the whole body before its 512 KiB cap"), and the shared bounded reader built for it in #803 already exists — this call site just doesn't use it:

- `packages/web/server/lib/shared/response-body.js:13` — `readBoundedResponseText(response, maxBytes)` enforces the cap **while streaming**, rejects a declared oversize `Content-Length` up front, and cancels the stream as soon as the cap is crossed. `login-keeper.js` does not import it.

The existing test only covers the post-buffer case: `login-keeper.test.js:76-81` fakes `fetch` with a plain object whose `text()` returns an already-materialised 64 KiB+1 string, so the streaming behaviour is untested.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `c085ebc8b`)

Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-oc-login-keeper-cap-20261029/probe.mjs`, run against the real `createLoginExchange` imported from the laptop checkout — `login-keeper.js` md5-identical to sandbox main; the module's `fetch` is injectable by design):

- Real module + streaming `Response` (no `Content-Length`) producing 32 MiB in 64 KiB chunks: rejected with "too large a body" only after the stream had produced **33,554,432 bytes** — the full 32 MiB was pulled and buffered despite the 64 KiB cap.
- Control — `readBoundedResponseText` on an identical stream with a 64 KiB cap: `tooLarge: true` after only **131,072 bytes** produced (cap + one chunk), stream cancelled.
- Control — small valid token answer through the real module: still resolves correctly (`access`/`refresh` parsed).

Dedup: searched open + closed issues for "login keeper", "login-keeper", and "too large a body" on 2026-10-29 — no covering issue. #802/#803/#804 built and migrated the shared primitives; this site was not among the migrated readers. #775 (Linear/OAuth broker timeouts) is about deadlines, not this cap-after-buffer read.

## Why it matters

The keeper renews the host's ChatGPT/Codex login for running spaces on a minute cycle (`KEEP_INTERVAL_MS`). Its issuer request is one of the few outbound calls whose peer answer is parsed as credentials; the 64 KiB cap exists precisely because the answer is expected to be tiny. As written, the cap gives false assurance — memory use is bounded only by what the peer can send in 30 s, in the long-lived web server process that also serves every session.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The exchange reads the issuer answer through a bounded read (e.g. `readBoundedResponseText` from `lib/shared/response-body.js`) so the stream is cancelled as soon as the body crosses 64 KiB, and a declared `Content-Length` over the cap is refused without reading.
- [ ] The oversize error stays exactly "The login issuer answered with too large a body", and no token material appears in any error (existing behaviour preserved).
- [ ] Healthy path unchanged: a valid token answer under the cap resolves to the same exchanged login as today; the 30 s deadline (`AbortSignal.timeout(EXCHANGE_TIMEOUT_MS)`) is preserved.
- [ ] A new test drives the exchange with a **streaming** body (real `Response` with a chunked stream, no `Content-Length`) and asserts the exchange rejects as too large without consuming the whole stream; the existing login-keeper tests keep passing (their plain-object `fetch` fakes may need `headers`/`body` added, or be replaced with real `Response`s).

body:
## Problem

The OpenChamber CLI's own synchronous child calls have **no `timeout`** — in the same package tree where the sibling helper already bounds every one of its calls. `spawnSync` waits for the child's entire life, so a hung system tool hangs the CLI command the user is sitting in front of, forever, with no error.

- `packages/web/bin/lib/cli-startup.js:296-306` — `runStartupCommand(command, args, options)` runs `spawnSync(command, args, { encoding: 'utf8', stdio: options.stdio || 'pipe', windowsHide: true })` with no `timeout` and no `maxBuffer`. **Every** startup-management call goes through it (15 call sites, `:348-453`): `loginctl show-user`, `schtasks.exe /Query|/Run|/End|/Delete`, `systemctl --user is-enabled|is-active|daemon-reload|enable --now|disable --now`, and `/bin/launchctl bootout|bootstrap|kickstart`. These back `openchamber startup enable|disable|status` — and `systemctl --user` / `launchctl bootstrap` against a wedged user session manager are textbook indefinite hangs.
- `packages/web/bin/cli.js:144-152` — `isBunInstalled()` runs `spawnSync(BUN_BIN, ['--version'], { stdio: 'ignore', env: process.env, windowsHide: true })` with no timeout. `BUN_BIN` is resolved from the environment (`getBunBinary`, `cli.js:128-134`: `$BUN_INSTALL/bin/bun(.exe)` or plain `bun` from PATH) — a shim, wrapper script, or stuck network-drive binary at that path hangs every CLI invocation that probes the runtime (`getPreferredServerRuntime` calls it on the startup path), before any output at all.

## Census (verified this run, main `774bbaea9`)

`spawnSync`/`execFileSync`/`execSync` in `packages/web/bin` (excluding tests): the only other helper, `cli-process.js`, bounds **all three** of its calls (`ps` at `:110` — `timeout: 3000`; `taskkill` at `:218` — `timeout: 3000`; `taskkill /f` at `:231` — `timeout: 5000`). `cli-startup.js`'s shared wrapper and `cli.js`'s bun probe are the outliers — one wrapper fix covers all 15 startup call sites. Same defect class as the merged web tunnel fix #820 and the Electron sites filed as #833, in the CLI surface.

## Evidence

- Read `runStartupCommand` and all 15 call sites, `isBunInstalled`/`getBunBinary`/`getPreferredServerRuntime`, and the full `packages/web/bin` census above on main `774bbaea9`.
- Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-oc-spawnsync-v2install-20261029/probe-spawnsync.mjs`) replicating the exact option shapes (the wrapper and probe functions are not exported, so the probe pins the call semantics): `spawnSync` of a 3 s child with the production options and no timeout took **3,004 ms** with a 50 ms interval timer firing **0 times** — nothing bounds a child that never exits; the control with `timeout: 500` returned in **502 ms** with `ETIMEDOUT`.
- Dedup: searched open + closed issues for `runStartupCommand`, `systemctl`, startup, and `spawnSync` on 2026-10-29 — no issue covers the CLI bin calls. (#820 covered the web server's tunnel checks; #833 covers the Electron package.)

## Why it matters

The startup commands are how a user installs OpenChamber as a boot service — a first-run surface. A wedged `systemctl --user` (stuck user manager, dead D-Bus session) currently turns `openchamber startup enable` into a silent permanent hang instead of an actionable error, and a bad `bun` shim does the same to ordinary CLI startup. Both calls' results are already treated as fallible by their callers (`allowFailure`, status checks), so a timeout lands naturally in the existing error shapes.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `runStartupCommand` passes a named `timeout` (consistent with the tree's 3–10 s probe bounds; a longer justified bound is acceptable for `enable --now`/`bootstrap`-class operations if stated) — a timed-out child surfaces through the existing shapes: `result.error` throw for required commands, the failure result for `allowFailure` ones.
- [ ] `isBunInstalled()` passes a named `timeout`; a timed-out probe returns `false` (the existing non-zero/error outcome), so runtime selection falls back to Node instead of hanging.
- [ ] Healthy behaviour unchanged: promptly answering system tools and bun probes produce exactly the current results and error messages.
- [ ] Tests pin the timeout outcome where the harness allows (following the existing `cli.test.js` startup-command patterns with injected dependencies); existing CLI tests keep passing.

title: fix(web): OpenCode v2 install downloads have no size cap — the installer script is buffered whole (then executed) and the Windows archive is buffered whole before its integrity check

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

The OpenCode v2 installer (`packages/web/server/lib/opencode/v2-install.js`) bounds every download's **time** (15 s / 5 min `AbortSignal.timeout`) but none of its **sizes** — both payloads are buffered whole in memory with no cap, in a server whose other download paths all carry an explicit byte bound (theme catalog: 1 MB / 512 KB / 20 MB caps at `lib/opencode/theme-catalog.js:83-98`; the bounded-response primitives from #802/#803):

- `v2-install.js:67` (`prepareInstallerScript`) — `await fs.writeFile(script, await response.text(), …)` reads the whole installer body from `https://opencode.ai/v2/install`, then **executes it as bash** (`runInstaller`). A shell installer is a few hundred KB at most, yet any size is accepted, written, and run: nothing rejects a 100 MB (or endless-until-timeout) body.
- `v2-install.js:82` (`prepareWindowsBinary`) — `Buffer.from(await archiveResponse.arrayBuffer())` buffers the whole npm tarball before the sha512 integrity check at `:83` runs. The integrity check is the right control for authenticity, but it only fires **after** the entire body is already in memory, so an oversized or slowly-streaming body from the tarball URL grows server memory without bound for up to the 5-minute fetch timeout. (The metadata/release `.json()` reads at `:78`/`:121` are the same shape at smaller expected sizes.)

## Evidence (verified this run, main `774bbaea9`)

- Read `v2-install.js` in full: three fetch sites, all time-bounded, none size-bounded; no `readBounded*` helper is used anywhere in the file.
- Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-oc-spawnsync-v2install-20261029/probe-v2install.mjs`, laptop fork file-identical at `774bbaea9`) against the **real** `installOpenCodeV2` with its injected `fetchImpl`/`homeDirectory` seams (the same seams `v2-install.test.js` uses):
  - Installer path: a **33,554,540-byte** "installer script" (valid `#!/bin/sh` script padded with a 32 MB comment) was accepted, written, and **executed** — the script copied itself to the probe out-dir at full size (33,554,540 bytes) before the install failed later on the version check (`OpenCode 1.18.30 is installed…`). No size ever rejected it.
  - Windows path (`probe-v2install-b.mjs`): a **67,108,864-byte** tarball body whose hash does not match the published integrity was consumed **in full** (the tarball URL was fetched and read) and rejected only afterwards, with `The downloaded OpenCode v2 package failed its integrity check.` — proving the whole body is buffered before any check can reject it.
- Dedup: searched open + closed issues for `v2-install`, installer script, and install download on 2026-10-29 — no covering issue. (#814/#828 covered the STT/local-model downloaders, which now carry exactly the caps this path lacks.)

## Why it matters

This runs inside the long-lived OpenChamber server (and the VS Code extension imports the same module) when a user accepts the v2 upgrade. The endpoints are first-party, but the failure mode the rest of the fleet has been closing for two days — a compromised, misconfigured, or just pathological endpoint streaming far more than the expected payload — costs unbounded memory here, and in the script case the oversized body is not just stored, it is executed. A cap converts both into a clean, early `Could not download…` failure.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The installer-script read rejects a body over a named cap sized for a shell script (order of 1 MB, justified in code) **before** the file is written or run, surfacing the existing `Could not download the OpenCode installer.`-class error.
- [ ] The Windows archive read rejects a body over a named cap sized with headroom for the real platform package **before** buffering it whole (e.g. a bounded/streaming read that aborts past the cap); the sha512 integrity check still runs on everything that is kept, and a within-cap archive installs exactly as before.
- [ ] The release/metadata JSON reads are either brought under the same treatment or explicitly justified as out of scope in the PR.
- [ ] New tests in `v2-install.test.js` pin the over-cap cases for both paths (oversized script is never executed; oversized archive fails as a download error, not an integrity mismatch after a full read), following the file's existing injected-`fetchImpl` patterns; existing v2-install tests keep passing.

title: fix(electron): four production spawnSync calls have no timeout — a hung helper freezes the Electron main process indefinitely

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/electron
labels.description: Package: electron (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

Four production `spawnSync` calls in the Electron package pass **no `timeout`** — while the census shows every other production synchronous child call in the package (and its siblings in web/VS Code) carries one. `spawnSync` blocks the Electron **main process** event loop for the child's entire life, so a hung helper does not just hang one feature: it freezes every window, IPC call and tray action in the desktop app indefinitely.

- `packages/electron/early-startup.mjs:218` — `macosMajorVersion()` runs `spawnSync('/usr/bin/sw_vers', ['-productVersion'], { encoding: 'utf8' })` with no timeout. It is called on the startup path (`early-startup.mjs:416` builds a launch arg from it; `main.mjs:1828` and `:3251/:3300` also call it / `macTrafficLightPosition()`).
- `packages/electron/main.mjs:4009` — `runWhere(program)` runs `spawnSync('where.exe', [program], { encoding: 'utf8', windowsHide: true })` with no timeout and no `maxBuffer`. It is on the Windows app-discovery path: `findWindowsExecutable`, `findWindowsAppNameExecutable`, and `resolveWindowsLaunchProgram` call it repeatedly (per candidate program, per app) from `desktop_filter_installed_apps` and the open-in-app handlers.
- `packages/electron/main.mjs:4053` — `resolveWindowsTerminalPackagePath()` runs `spawnSync(powershell, ['-NoProfile', '-NonInteractive', '-Command', <Get-AppxPackage …>], { encoding: 'utf8', windowsHide: true })` with no timeout and no `maxBuffer`. PowerShell / AppX queries are a classic multi-second-to-hung Windows operation, and this runs synchronously in main.
- `packages/electron/main.mjs:4359` — `runSpecChain(specs, appName)` (the macOS open-in-app path, handlers at `main.mjs:5018/5035/5053/5070`) runs `spawnSync(spec.program, spec.args, { stdio: 'ignore', windowsHide: true })` with no timeout. Its programs are `open` and the editor CLIs from `CLI_BY_APP_ID` (`main.mjs:3965`: `code`, `cursor`, `codium`, `windsurf`, `zed`). The Windows (`launchWindowsSpec`, detached `spawn`) and Linux (`spawnDetachedLinux` at `main.mjs:3866`, resolves on the `spawn` event) equivalents in the same file are already asynchronous and detached — macOS is the only platform whose open-in-app waits synchronously for the launched program.

## Census (verified this run, main `774bbaea9`)

Production `spawnSync`/`execFileSync`/`execSync` in `packages/electron` excluding `scripts/` and tests: the only other sites already carry a timeout — `linux-app-discovery.mjs:426` (`xdg-mime`, `timeout: 1500`) and `early-startup.mjs:611` (`reg.exe`, `timeout: 10_000`). The four sites above are the outliers. This is the same defect class as the merged web fixes #820 (`spawnSync` tunnel checks) and #822 (`execFileSync` Cursor import), one package over.

## Evidence

- Read all four call sites, their callers, and the full Electron production census above on main `774bbaea9`.
- Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-oc-spawnsync-v2install-20261029/probe-spawnsync.mjs`) replicating the exact option shapes (a `spawnSync` of a 3 s child with `{ encoding: 'utf8', windowsHide: true }` and no timeout — the functions themselves are not exported and are platform-gated, so the probe pins the call semantics): the call took **3,004 ms** and a 50 ms interval timer fired **0 times** during it — the loop is frozen for the child's whole life, and nothing bounds a child that never exits. Control with `timeout: 500` returned in **502 ms** with `ETIMEDOUT`.
- Dedup: searched open + closed issues for `spawnSync`, `where.exe`, `sw_vers`, and open-in-app on 2026-10-29 — #820/#822 cover the web/VS Code sites only; no issue covers the Electron package.

## Why it matters

Electron main is a single-threaded host for the whole desktop app, exactly like the web server in #820/#822. A wedged `where.exe` walking a dead network-drive PATH entry, a stuck PowerShell AppX query, or an editor CLI that waits instead of delegating turns "Open in …" / app filtering / startup into a permanent app freeze with no error to act on — and `macosMajorVersion` can do it before the first window even appears.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every production `spawnSync` in `packages/electron` (the four sites above) passes a named `timeout` consistent with the tree's other probes (1.5–10 s range; the open-in-app chain may instead be converted to the detached async pattern its Windows/Linux siblings already use, which is equally acceptable if behaviour is preserved).
- [ ] A timed-out child surfaces through each caller's existing failure shape: `macosMajorVersion` falls back to `0`, `runWhere` returns `null`, the terminal-package lookup falls through to its filesystem scan / `null` cache, and `runSpecChain` records the spec as failed and tries the next candidate — never a hang.
- [ ] Healthy behaviour unchanged: promptly answering helpers resolve exactly as before (version number, executable path, terminal package path, successful app launch).
- [ ] New tests pin the hang case where the harness allows (e.g. an injected/fake child that never exits settles within the timeout as the existing failure shape), following the existing Electron test patterns; existing Electron tests keep passing.

title: fix(web,vscode): strict env readers from #698/#706/#714 leave timer values unbounded — a value over 2^31-1 ms collapses the timeout to ~1 ms

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/pr-diff-review
labels.description: Filed by the pr-diff-review job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/vscode
labels.description: Package: vscode (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Finding

The strict plain-decimal env-parsing batch (PRs #698, #706, #714) bounded the *spelling* of timer values but not their *magnitude*. Several readers that feed a value straight into `setTimeout` accept any plain-decimal integer up to `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` (or, for the handoff reader, any integer at all). A value above 2,147,483,647 ms does not give a long timeout: Node timers reject it with `TimeoutOverflowWarning: … does not fit into a 32-bit signed integer. Timeout duration was set to 1.` — the timer fires after ~1 ms, inverting the operator's intent.

Verified in this environment: `node -e "setTimeout(..., 3000000000)"` prints the overflow warning, sets the duration to 1, and fires immediately.

Contrast within the same batch: PR #700's event-stream reader does bound its timers (`MIN_TIMEOUT_MS`–`MAX_TIMEOUT_MS`, 600,000 ms) before use. The readers below never got an upper bound.

## Evidence (current main `774bbaea91`)

- PR #706 (commit `699b40f333`) — `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/self-handoff.js:31` `resolveHandoffTimeoutMs`: `/^\d+$/` + `Number.isInteger(value) && value > 0`, no safe-integer or upper bound. The result is the `setTimeout` delay at `self-handoff.js:126` in `awaitSuccessorReady` — so `OPENCHAMBER_HANDOFF_TIMEOUT_MS=3000000000` kills a handoff successor after ~1 ms instead of waiting ~34 days; the predecessor keeps serving and every handoff attempt fails as a timeout.
- PR #698 (commit `242626b66f`) — `packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.js:131-137`: `createCommandTimeoutMs` parses via `parseBoundedIntWithDefault(raw, null, 0, Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER)` and the value is the `setTimeout` SIGKILL delay at `routes.js:594` in `runCommandInDirectory` — an oversized `OPENCHAMBER_FS_EXEC_TIMEOUT_MS` kills every `/api/fs/exec` command after ~1 ms.
- PR #698 — `packages/web/server/lib/fs/search.js:101` `createGitCheckIgnoreTimeoutMs` (safe-integer checked, no timer bound) → `setTimeout` SIGKILL at `search.js:166`.
- PR #714 (commit `029551bd5a`, the merged successor of closed PR #708) — the same check-ignore reader in VS Code: `packages/vscode/src/bridge-fs-runtime.ts:67` → `setTimeout` at `bridge-fs-runtime.ts:165`, and `packages/vscode/src/bridge-fs-helpers-runtime.ts:22` → `execGit(..., { timeoutMs })` at `bridge-fs-helpers-runtime.ts:139`.

Non-timer readers from the same batch (upload caps, cache TTL) are not affected — a large value there is just a large cap/TTL — and are out of scope.

## Why it matters

These are exactly the timeouts the fleet spent two days hardening against silent misreads (#696/#703/#705 chains). The remaining hole turns a plainly-written, valid-spelling value into the opposite behaviour — an effectively-zero timeout — with only a runtime warning in the logs. It is also a trap for anyone raising a timeout to debug a slow handoff or exec.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every env reader whose value feeds `setTimeout` / a timer `timeoutMs` (the four sites above) rejects or clamps values above 2,147,483,647 ms, falling back to its existing default (the house pattern: an out-of-contract value behaves like an invalid spelling).
- [ ] `resolveHandoffTimeoutMs` also gains the safe-integer check its sibling readers already have.
- [ ] Tests pin the overflow case for each reader (e.g. `3000000000` and a >2^53 spelling fall back to the default), alongside the existing spelling cases.
- [ ] A grep for other env-fed `setTimeout` delays in `packages/web` and `packages/vscode` either finds no further unbounded readers or lists them in this issue before closing.

title: test(web): sse-resume restart retry in #686 can move the upstream port the proxy was built with

labels.name: kind/test
labels.description: Test coverage, test infrastructure, or test-only fixes

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/pr-diff-review
labels.description: Filed by the pr-diff-review job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Finding

PR #686 added a bounded retry to `startUpstream` in the env-gated
`opencode-sse-resume` suite, but the retry reassigns the shared
`upstreamPort` on every attempt after the first — including on the
**restart** call, where the port must not change.

The suite's own comment states the invariant: "The first attempt reuses
upstreamPort when one is already chosen, because the restart in the test
below has to come back on the port its proxy was built with." The proxy
captures the port by value when it is built, so a retry that moves the
driver to a fresh port leaves the proxy (and the test's `upstreamBase`
and control stream) pointing at the old port. The restarted driver then
reports ready on the new port, the start returns success, and the test
fails only later — as a 90-second `waitFor` timeout for `server.resync`
against a port nothing (or a stranger) is listening on — instead of the
loud bind/start failure the retry was meant to surface.

## Evidence

- Source PR: #686 (merged, head `e19919054c5f7122dd6fd8c096e5c908341c5a02`,
  merge `b6e099b7464d027584e85f6254ad3e38a9e1a070`), which closed #685.
- Still present on current main `774bbaea9`,
  `packages/web/server/opencode-sse-resume.test.js`:
  - `:366-368` — `startUpstream`: `if (attempt > 1 || upstreamPort === null)
    upstreamPort = await freePort();` reassigns the outer `upstreamPort`
    on any retry, whatever the call site.
  - `:449-454` — `proxyServer = await startProxy({ upstreamPort, ... })`
    captures that port; `startProxy`'s `buildOpenCodeUrl` closes over it
    (`:105-111` in the same file's helper section).
  - `:488-490` — the restart: `await stopUpstream(upstreamChild);
    upstreamChild = await startUpstream();` followed by a 90 s wait for
    the proxy to deliver `server.resync`.
- The readiness loop inside `startUpstream` fetches the *current*
  `upstreamPort`, so a moved restart passes readiness on the new port —
  nothing ever checks that the port the proxy holds is the port the
  restarted driver bound.

Trigger: the restart's first attempt exits before listening (the exact
probe-and-release collision #686 set out to absorb, a slow port release
after `stopUpstream`, or any transient driver startup failure — the loop
retries *any* early exit, not only bind failures).

## Why it matters

This is the suite that guards SSE resume across a real OpenCode restart.
A retry that silently moves the restart target converts a rare, loud
bind failure into a rare, misleading 90-second resync timeout — the
class of flake that gets misdiagnosed as a proxy/resume regression and
burns investigation time on the wrong component.

## Acceptance criteria

- A retry of the restart call cannot change the port the already-built
  proxy targets: either retries stay on the same port (bounded, then
  throw with the child's output), or the start fails loudly instead of
  returning a driver on a different port.
- The initial-start path may still take a fresh port per attempt.
- A test or simulation pins the restart-retry behaviour (e.g. first
  restart attempt exits early; the suite either recovers on the same
  port or fails with the bind/start error, never with a resync timeout
  caused by a moved port).

title: fix(web): routing local-model download has no stall deadline — a silent connection wedges the Settings download state forever and blocks retry

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

The routing interpreter's local-model download has **no deadline of any kind** — neither on the initial fetch nor while streaming the body:

- `packages/web/server/lib/routing/route-local-model.js:64` — `downloadModel` calls `fetchImpl(model.url)` with no options object at all (no `signal`).
- `route-local-model.js:73-97` — the body loop streams chunks to the `.part` file with a size cap (#412) and end-of-download size/SHA-256 verification, but nothing that fires when bytes stop arriving: a connection that sends some chunks and then goes silent loops forever.

The model is a 1.1 GB GGUF from Hugging Face (`LOCAL_MODEL.bytes: 1117320736`, `route-local-model.js:20-26`), so a total-duration deadline would be wrong — but a **stall** deadline is exactly what the sibling downloader got under #814: `packages/web/server/lib/dictation/local/model-downloader.js:17,51-99` arms a timer that aborts the download when no bytes arrive for `DOWNLOAD_STALL_TIMEOUT_MS`, discards the partial, and reports "timed out … try again". This downloader never got the same treatment.

## Why it matters

- The caller tracks the download as shared state: `startDownload` in `packages/web/server/lib/routing/route-rules-routes.js:103-113` sets `download.active = true` and only clears it in `.finally(...)`; it also refuses to start while `download.active` is set (`:104`). A download that never settles therefore wedges the Settings surface permanently: status reports `downloading: true` forever, the error field never fills, and **the user cannot retry** — the only recovery is restarting the OpenChamber server.
- The partial `.part` file (up to the full 1.1 GB, since the size cap only fires on *over*-delivery) sits in the user's cache directory indefinitely with no signal that anything is wrong.
- The failure is silent and plausible in the real world: a wedged CDN edge, a proxy that stops forwarding, or a network drop that leaves the TCP connection half-open all produce exactly this shape — headers (or some bytes) arrive, then nothing, and TCP never errors.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `48682079f`)

- Read `downloadModel` end to end (`route-local-model.js:61-115`), its caller/state handling (`route-rules-routes.js:96-113`), and the #814 sibling pattern (`dictation/local/model-downloader.js:17,51-99`). Grep: no `signal`, `timeout`, `stall`, or `deadline` anywhere in `route-local-model.js`.
- Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-oc-localmodel-stall-20261029/`) against the **real** `downloadModel` (laptop clone at the same main `48682079f`), using the module's injected `fetchImpl` seam and the test file's small stand-in model:
  - Headers stall (fetch never resolves): `downloadModel` **UNSETTLED after 2,502 ms**; the fetch was called with no signal option.
  - Body stall (stream enqueues 4 bytes, then never yields/closes): **UNSETTLED after 2,503 ms**; the `.part` file existed holding exactly those 4 bytes.
  - Control (full body answers): settled with `installed: true` in **2 ms**.
- Dedup: searched open + closed issues for the routing local-model download on 2026-10-29 — #412 (closed) covered the *oversize* body being written before the size check, a different defect in this same function; #814 (closed) fixed the stall deadline for the *dictation/STT* downloader, a different module; #417 (closed) covered the dictation catalog's missing pins. No issue covers a stall deadline for `route-local-model.js`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `downloadModel` bounds a stalled download the way #814's downloader does: a no-bytes-arriving stall timer (not a total-duration cap — the model is 1.1 GB) covers both the wait for the response and the body stream; when it fires, the fetch/stream is aborted, the `.part` file is discarded, and the thrown error says the download timed out and can be retried.
- [ ] After a stall, the route state recovers: `download.active` clears and a subsequent `startDownload` can begin a fresh attempt.
- [ ] Healthy downloads are unchanged: full-body downloads still verify size + SHA-256 and install; the oversize refusal from #412 still fires mid-stream.
- [ ] `route-local-model.test.js` gains stall coverage following its existing injected-`fetchImpl` pattern: a never-resolving fetch and/or a body that stops mid-stream both reject with the timeout error and leave no `.part` file — with the stall duration injectable/short in tests, as in `model-downloader.js` (`stallTimeoutMs`).

body:
## Problem

The web NanoGPT quota provider fetches its usage endpoint with **no deadline at all** — the one web quota provider the #782 sweep missed:

- `packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/nanogpt.js:64` — `fetchQuota` calls `fetchImpl('https://nano-gpt.com/api/subscription/v1/usage', { method: 'GET', headers: { … } })`. The options object contains no `signal` (verified by census and by probe capture below).

Every other web quota provider now bounds its fetch with `AbortSignal.timeout(15_000)` — the seven #782 providers (codex, copilot, cursor, zai, zhipuai, minimax, claude) were fixed, and the rest already had it. A full census this run (every `providers/*.js` and `providers/*/*.js` file containing a `fetch`/`fetchImpl` call, checked for any signal) finds `nanogpt.js` is the **only** remaining unbounded one.

The VS Code twin of this exact fetcher proves the intended pattern: `fetchNanoGptQuota` in `packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.ts` (same endpoint) now passes `signal: AbortSignal.timeout(15_000)` after #812 — the web original was left behind when both sweeps enumerated their provider lists.

## Why it matters

Same failure shape as #782, one provider smaller:

1. A NanoGPT endpoint (or proxy in front of it) that accepts the connection and then stalls makes this fetch never settle — `fetch` has no default timeout.
2. **The stall is permanent for that provider.** `fetchQuotaForProvider` (`quota/providers/index.js:526-536`) coalesces concurrent calls in the `pendingFetches` map and only deletes the entry in `.finally(...)`; a promise that never settles stays in the map, so every later `GET /api/quota/nano-gpt` (route: `quota/routes.js:95-108`, which awaits the result directly) returns the same hung promise until the server restarts. That pool's quota surface silently freezes — in a repo whose routing decisions depend on fresh quota reads.
3. The provider's existing `catch` → `buildResult({ ok: false, … })` path would report the failure cleanly if the fetch ever rejected — a deadline is the only missing piece.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `48682079f`)

- Read the call site (`nanogpt.js:48-72`), the coalescing wrapper (`index.js:526-536`), and the route (`routes.js:95-108`).
- Census: scripted check over all web quota provider files — `nanogpt.js` is the sole file with a fetch call and no `signal`/`AbortSignal.timeout` anywhere in the file.
- Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-oc-nanogpt-timeout-20261029/`) against the **real** `fetchQuota` from `nanogpt.js` (laptop clone at the same main `48682079f`), injecting the module's own `readAuth`/`fetchImpl` seams:
  - Never-resolving `fetchImpl`: `fetchQuota` was **UNSETTLED after 2,502 ms**; the captured options object was exactly `{ method, headers }` — `hasSignal: false`.
  - Control (immediately answering `fetchImpl`): settled `ok: true` in **17 ms**.
- Dedup: searched open + closed issues for `nanogpt`, `nano-gpt`, `NanoGPT` on 2026-10-29 — hits are #782 (web sweep; its provider list does not include NanoGPT), #812 (VS Code sweep; fixed the twin in `quotaProviders.ts`, web file untouched), and older percent-clamp issues (#509-#517 family, different defect). No issue covers the web NanoGPT fetch.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `nanogpt.js`'s usage fetch passes a deadline consistent with the sibling providers and its own VS Code twin: `signal: AbortSignal.timeout(15_000)` (or a named constant equal to it).
- [ ] A stalled NanoGPT endpoint now surfaces as the provider's existing bounded error result (`ok: false`) within the deadline, and the `pendingFetches` entry clears so a later quota request can retry.
- [ ] `nanogpt.test.js` (or a sibling test) pins the deadline: the injected `fetchImpl` receives a signal, and/or a never-resolving fetch settles as an error result once the signal fires — following the existing injected-`fetchImpl` test pattern in that file.
- [ ] No behavior change for a healthy endpoint: existing NanoGPT parsing/window tests keep passing unchanged.

title: fix(web): TTS and STT calls configure no deadline — the OpenAI SDK clients set no timeout, so a stalled local speech/transcription server holds the voice routes indefinitely in practice

body:
## Problem

The web server's two OpenAI-SDK audio calls configure **no deadline at all** — no client `timeout`, no per-request timeout, no `AbortSignal` — in a server where every other outbound call carries an explicit bound (the quota providers in the same tree use `AbortSignal.timeout(15_000)` throughout; the bounded-call primitives from #802/#803 exist for exactly this):

- `packages/web/server/lib/tts/service.js:64` — the shared client: `new OpenAI({ apiKey })` (no `timeout`, no `maxRetries`).
- `packages/web/server/lib/tts/service.js:103` — the per-request client for a custom `baseURL`/`apiKey`: `clientOpts` gains only `apiKey`/`baseURL`.
- `packages/web/server/lib/tts/service.js:133` and `:168` — `client.audio.speech.create(...)` with no request options; the awaited route is `POST /api/tts` (`packages/web/server/lib/tts/routes.js:117`, via `generateSpeechStream`).
- `packages/web/server/lib/tts/stt.js:43` — `new OpenAI(clientOpts)` (no `timeout`), and `:52` — `client.audio.transcriptions.create(...)` with no request options. Callers: `POST /api/stt/transcribe` (`packages/web/server/lib/tts/routes.js:304`) and the dictation session (`packages/web/server/lib/dictation/openai-compatible-session.js:78`).

So the only deadline on a speech or transcription request is whatever the OpenAI SDK defaults to — a default this repo never chose, far longer than its own 15 s standard, and lengthened further by the SDK's default retries. The endpoints these calls usually target are **user-configured local servers** (a custom OpenAI-compatible TTS server; a faster-whisper-style STT server named by the `x-base-url` header): a local model server that has wedged — model loading forever, deadlocked worker, GPU stall — accepts the connection and never answers, and the OpenChamber request (and, for dictation, the session's transcript pipeline) hangs with it, holding the HTTP request open and giving the user no error to act on.

## Why it matters

- Every comparable call in this server is bounded: quota fetches at 15 s (#782), the installer downloads at 15 s / 5 min by phase, guests at their named timeout. The audio services are the remaining calls whose deadline is an SDK default rather than a decision in the code — invisible to anyone reading the route.
- The failure target is the user's own local speech server, the component most likely to stall in normal use (first-run model loads, GPU contention), and both voice surfaces (read-aloud TTS and dictation/STT) share the gap.

## Evidence (verified this run, main 006769951)

- Read all three client constructions and both `create` calls; `grep -n timeout packages/web/server/lib/tts/*.js` (non-test) returns **zero** hits.
- Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-oc-tts-deadline-20261029/probe.mjs`) against the **real** modules (`TTSService.generateSpeechStream`, `transcribeAudio`) pointed at a local HTTP server that accepts and never responds:
  - TTS: **UNSETTLED after 12,005 ms** (probe raced it at 12 s).
  - STT: **UNSETTLED after 12,004 ms**.
  - Controls (same calls, server answers immediately): TTS settled ok in **24 ms**, STT in **18 ms**.
- Dedup: searched open + recently closed issues for TTS / text-to-speech / transcription / OpenAI SDK on 2026-10-29 — no covering issue. (#814 covered the STT *model download*; this is the speech/transcription *inference* calls.)

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Both services configure an explicit, named deadline consistent with the server's bounded-call standard (client `timeout` and/or per-request options on the `create` calls), covering all three constructions: `service.js:64`, `service.js:103`, `stt.js:43`.
- [ ] Retries are considered explicitly: the configured retry behaviour cannot multiply a stall into several consecutive deadline-length waits without that being a stated choice.
- [ ] A stalled endpoint now fails the TTS/STT request with a clear timeout error through the routes' existing error shapes, instead of holding the request open; healthy behaviour (bytes/content-type passthrough, transcript text) is unchanged.
- [ ] New tests pin the stall case against a never-responding local server (the `service.test.js` harness already spins real HTTP servers), for speech and transcription; existing TTS/STT tests keep passing.
