body:
## Problem

Nothing under `packages/web/server/lib/linear/` ever sets a fetch deadline. A grep for `AbortSignal`, `signal`, or `timeout` across the whole `linear/` directory (non-test files) returns **zero hits**, while every fetch site assumes the peer answers:

- `client.js:101-110` — `fetchLinearGraphql` (the single GraphQL entry point used by `issues.js` :419/:451/:462/:533/:544/:566/:597/:621 and `teams.js` :43) calls `fetch(LINEAR_GRAPHQL_URL, {...})` with no `signal`.
- `oauth.js:83` — `postForm` (token exchange/refresh against Linear) has no `signal`.
- `oauth.js:127` (`/start`), `:187` (`/poll`), `:216` (`/complete`), `:331` (revoke) — the authorization-broker fetches have no `signal` either. The broker is a separate deployed service, so this path depends on two network peers, neither bounded.

## Why it matters

A stalled connection — Linear or the broker accepting the socket and answering slowly or never, a dead network path with no RST — hangs the awaiting OpenChamber request/operation indefinitely. There is no server-side recovery: the route handlers that call these (issue lookups, comment creates, the OAuth connect flow) simply never answer, and repeated retries pile up hung promises/sockets. Sibling integrations in this same codebase do bound their fetches: the GitHub Octokit wrapper (`github/octokit.js:21-25`) attaches `AbortSignal.timeout(OCTKIT_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS)` when no caller signal exists, the device-flow does the same, and the OpenCode-facing runtimes use `AbortSignal.timeout(FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS)`. Linear is the outlier. (Note the one related constant that does exist, `CONNECT_ATTEMPT_TIMEOUT_MS` in `network-defaults.js`, only caps TCP happy-eyeballs attempts — it does nothing for a connected-but-silent peer.)

## Evidence (verified this run, main 719cc8f01)

- `grep -n "AbortSignal\|signal\|timeout" packages/web/server/lib/linear/*.js` (excluding tests): no matches.
- Read `fetchLinearGraphql` (client.js:90-132) and `postForm` + broker calls in oauth.js: fetch options carry method/headers/body only.
- Dedup: searched open + closed issues for "Linear timeout", "no timeout fetch", "hangs indefinitely" — no issue covers the Linear client (open #304 is the unrelated Linear op:// account feature).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every fetch in `linear/` carries a deadline: one named timeout constant for the GraphQL client and one for the OAuth/broker calls (they may share a value), applied via `AbortSignal.timeout(...)`.
- [ ] A timeout surfaces as the module's existing error types (`LinearApiError` / `LinearOAuthError`) with a message that says the request timed out — not a raw `TimeoutError` leaking to route handlers, and never a silently swallowed failure.
- [ ] Tests (client/oauth test files already exist) pin: a fetch that never resolves is rejected at the deadline and mapped to the right error type; healthy responses are unaffected.
- [ ] The broker poll flow still works end-to-end under the deadline (a legitimately slow-but-answering broker inside the bound is not broken).

title: fix(web): mcpx daemon client has no timeout and no response cap — a stalled daemon hangs /api/mcpx/* requests forever and an endless body grows memory without bound

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

body:
## Problem

`callDaemon` in `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/mcpx-daemon.js` talks to the mcpx daemon with **no deadline on either transport and no cap on the response size**:

- HTTP path (mcpx-daemon.js:40-46): `fetch(...)` is called with no `signal` / `AbortSignal.timeout(...)`; the error path reads the whole body with `await res.text()` and the success path with `await res.json()`.
- Unix-socket path (mcpx-daemon.js:56-84): `http.request(...)` sets no `timeout`, and the response handler accumulates the whole body with `let data = ''` + `res.on('data', (chunk) => { data += chunk; })` (line 63) — no byte cap, no stall deadline, and no `req.on('timeout')` handling.

Every caller is a live Express route in `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/mcpx-routes.js` that awaits this directly: `/api/mcpx/status` (:37), `/api/mcpx/namespaces` (:47), `/api/mcpx/tools` (:58), `/api/mcpx/types` (:69), `/api/mcpx/log` (:80), plus the secret relay paths in `mcpx-secrets.js` (:27, :55).

## Why it matters

A daemon that accepts the connection and then stalls (wedged daemon, a half-dead socket, a `/v1/log` answer that never ends) hangs the corresponding OpenChamber request forever — the route handler never answers, never 502s, and the socket/connection is held indefinitely. A daemon (or a process that has taken over the endpoint/socket) that streams an endless or huge body grows server memory without bound in the socket path's `data += chunk`. This is the same failure class the repo has been closing one surface at a time (#756 SSE buffers, #759 non-SSE upstream, #763 Jev, #770 guest surface) — the mcpx client is a remaining instance, and it is worse than most: it lacks even a time bound. Sibling clients in this codebase do carry deadlines (e.g. the GitHub Octokit wrapper attaches `AbortSignal.timeout`, dispatch/message-queue use `FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS` with `AbortSignal.timeout`).

There is also no `mcpx-daemon.test.js` — `mcpx-routes.test.js` exists but does not pin the daemon client's timeout/cap behaviour.

## Evidence (verified this run, main 719cc8f01)

- Read `mcpx-daemon.js` in full: no `AbortSignal`, `signal`, `timeout`, or size constant anywhere in the file.
- Grepped callers: only `mcpx-routes.js` and `mcpx-secrets.js`; all await `callDaemon` with no wrapping deadline.
- Dedup: searched open + closed issues for "mcpx daemon timeout", "callDaemon", and "mcpx" — no issue covers this (only #149/#95/#152/#302 mention mcpx in other contexts).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Both transports get a deadline: the HTTP fetch carries an `AbortSignal.timeout(...)` (named constant), and the socket request gets an equivalent timeout that destroys the request and rejects with a clear "mcpx daemon timed out" style error.
- [ ] The response body is bounded **during the read** on both paths (a named byte cap; exceeding it aborts/destroys the read and rejects) — not a length check after the whole body has been buffered. The error-body read on the HTTP path is bounded the same way.
- [ ] Existing behaviour is preserved for healthy daemons: JSON answers parse as before, non-JSON answers still resolve as text on the socket path, HTTP >= 400 still throws with status + (bounded) body.
- [ ] New `mcpx-daemon.test.js` (or equivalent) pins: a never-answering daemon rejects within the deadline on both transports, an over-cap body rejects without buffering it whole, and the healthy-path cases above.
- [ ] `/api/mcpx/*` routes surface a stalled daemon as a prompt 502 instead of a hung request.

title: fix(web): guest surface host buffers extension service responses whole — resize/clipboard text(), frame arrayBuffer(), and discard drains have no cap during the read

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

Every response the guest-surface host reads from an extension's service in `packages/web/server/lib/guests/surface.js` is buffered whole, with no size cap during the read — even though the same package already has the bounded reader (`readBoundedResponseText`, `packages/web/server/lib/guests/response-body.js`) and uses it on the panel path (`service.js:753` `proxyGuestServiceRequest`, `request.js:40`, both capped at `GUEST_REQUEST_RESPONSE_MAX`).

The service is, by the code's own description, "a third-party process running as the user" (`packages/web/server/lib/guests/service.js`, `openGuestServiceRequest`). A buggy or malicious extension service can therefore grow the OpenChamber server's memory without bound from loopback, inside the per-request timeout window (10 s for these calls, `QUICK_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS`, surface.js:61).

## Sites (main `cd31bf177`)

1. **Clipboard read — `surface.js:452`**: `const text = await response.text().catch(() => '');` in `handleClipboardRead`. The legitimate answer is schema-bounded to `text` of at most `SURFACE_TEXT_MAX = 64_000` chars (`packages/sdk/src/service-surface-schemas.ts:77`, `service-surface.ts:63`), but the cap is only applied by `safeParse` **after** the whole body is in memory.
2. **Resize — `surface.js:424`**: same `response.text()` pattern in `handleResize`. The legitimate answer is two dimensions (`surfaceResizeAnswerSchema`, `service-surface-schemas.ts:76`) — a few dozen bytes.
3. **Frame read — `surface.js:262-271`** (`readFrame`): a declared `content-length` over `SURFACE_FRAME_MAX_BYTES` (8 MB) is refused up front, and the buffered bytes are length-checked after the read — but a chunked body (no `content-length`) is pulled whole by `await response.arrayBuffer()` before that check, so memory during the read is unbounded and the check only limits what is *kept*.
4. **Discard drains — `surface.js:186` (control notify), :311/:316 (pump 204 / non-200), :397 (input)**: `await response.arrayBuffer().catch(() => undefined)` drains a body nobody reads, again whole and uncapped; a service that answers a control/input POST with a never-ending or huge body is buffered in full just to be thrown away.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop probe against the real surface runtime (module hash-identical to main; probe: laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-surface-text/`), using the same fake-service harness shape as `surface.test.js`: the clipboard endpoint answers with a chunked stream of 32 MiB of junk (no `content-length`). The handler pulled **all 33,554,432 bytes** before rejecting the answer as `CLIPBOARD_UNAVAILABLE` — 500× the largest legitimate clipboard answer, consumed whole because `response.text()` has no cap and the stream is never cancelled early. A bounded reader would have stopped at the cap and cancelled.

Controls: the panel path for the same services (`proxyGuestServiceRequest`) refuses over-cap answers via `readBoundedResponseText` and reports `RESPONSE_TOO_LARGE` (`service.js:747-770`); `surface.test.js` covers resize/clipboard round-trips but no oversized-answer case.

## Why it matters

- The surface host is the long-lived path: a surface session holds the service running and pumps frames continuously, so the frame and drain sites are exercised constantly, not once.
- `#763` (Jev) and the `#744/#745/#737/#741/#742` family established the house rule: a response from a less-trusted process is read through a bounded reader, with the cap enforced *during* the read and the stream cancelled on overflow. The surface host is the remaining guest path that does not follow it.
- The timeout does not substitute for a cap: loopback throughput fills memory far faster than 10 s, and `response.text()` additionally delays `finished()` (the idle-stop settle) until the whole body arrives.

## Acceptance criteria

- Resize and clipboard answers are read through a bounded reader (e.g. `readBoundedResponseText`) with a documented cap sized to the schemas (clipboard: comfortably above `SURFACE_TEXT_MAX` UTF-8 bytes; resize: a small fixed cap); an over-cap answer behaves exactly like today's unparseable answer (resize: no `resized` message; clipboard: `CLIPBOARD_UNAVAILABLE`) and the stream is cancelled at the cap, not after the body ends.
- `readFrame` enforces `SURFACE_FRAME_MAX_BYTES` during the read (streaming count + cancel), so a chunked frame body cannot exceed the cap in memory; frames at/under the cap, including chunked ones with no `content-length`, still parse exactly as today.
- The discard drains (control, input, pump 204/non-200) no longer buffer the body: they cancel/destroy the response body (or drain through a bounded discard) instead of `arrayBuffer()`.
- Regression tests in `surface.test.js` style: oversized chunked clipboard answer (viewer gets `CLIPBOARD_UNAVAILABLE`, service stream cancelled early), oversized chunked frame (session handling unchanged from today's invalid-frame path, body not fully consumed), and the existing resize/clipboard/frame round-trip tests still pass.
- `bun run check:changed` green.

title: fix(web): drain grace env judged by bare Number() — '1e3' becomes a 1 s grace, '0x10' 16 ms, and a whitespace-only value silently becomes 0 instead of the 30-minute default

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

`resolveOpenCodeDrainGraceMs` (`packages/web/server/lib/opencode/draining-opencode.js:4-9`) judges `OPENCHAMBER_OPENCODE_DRAIN_GRACE_MS` by a bare `Number(...)`:

```js
export const resolveOpenCodeDrainGraceMs = (env) => {
  const raw = env.OPENCHAMBER_OPENCODE_DRAIN_GRACE_MS;
  if (raw === undefined || raw === '') return DEFAULT_OPENCODE_DRAIN_GRACE_MS;
  const value = Number(raw);
  return Number.isFinite(value) && value >= 0 ? value : DEFAULT_OPENCODE_DRAIN_GRACE_MS;
};
```

Non-decimal spellings are silently reinterpreted instead of falling back to the 30-minute default (`DEFAULT_OPENCODE_DRAIN_GRACE_MS = 30 * 60 * 1000`, :1). The registry built with this value (`packages/web/server/lib/opencode/lifecycle.js:527`) force-releases a replaced OpenCode once the grace expires — even while sessions that were busy at replacement time are still busy (`draining-opencode.js`, `check()` / `release(entry, 'grace-expired')`).

## Evidence (verified this run, main `cd31bf177`)

Laptop probe against the real module (file hash-identical between the sandbox clone at `cd31bf177` and the laptop copy: md5 `23277e14e6ed6caf55139b95dc56dfac`; probe: laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-drain-grace/probe.mjs`):

| value | result | expected under the house contract |
|---|---|---|
| `'5000'` | 5000 | 5000 ✓ |
| `'0'` | 0 | 0 ✓ |
| `'soon'`, `'-1'`, `''` | 1800000 (default) | default ✓ |
| `'1e3'` | **1000** | default |
| `'0x10'` | **16** | default |
| `'5.9'` | **5.9** | default |
| `' '` (whitespace only) | **0** | default |
| `'+5000'` | **5000** | default |
| `'5000.0'` | **5000** | default |

The whitespace case is the worst: `''` is special-cased to the default, but `' '` slips past it and `Number(' ')` is `0`, so a stray-space value silently sets a **zero** drain grace — the replaced OpenCode is released at the first 1 s poll tick regardless of busy sessions.

## Why this is a bug, not a style nit

The house contract is explicit and already applied to the sibling readers in the same directory and neighbouring modules:

- `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/self-handoff.js` (`resolveHandoffTimeoutMs`, fixed for #705): "Only a plain decimal spelling counts: a bare Number(...) would silently honour '1e3' (a 1 s grace period), '0x10' (16 ms), '+5000', and '5000.0'."
- `packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.js` (`parsePlainDecimalInt`): "a bare Number(...) would silently honour '' and ' ' as 0, '1e3' as 1000, '0x10' as 16, and '5.9' as a fractional value."
- Same strict helper in `packages/web/server/lib/guests/upload.js` (#696/#704 class).

This reader is the remaining production env reader in that class: an operator who writes `1e3` (or whose config tooling emits `5000.0`, or a value with stray whitespace) gets a drain grace of milliseconds-to-zero instead of either the value a plain-decimal reading would give or the documented 30-minute default — and a drained OpenCode can be closed under still-busy sessions.

Existing tests (`packages/web/server/lib/opencode/draining-opencode.test.js:128-138`) pin the default, `'5000'`, `'0'`, `'soon'` and `'-1'`, but no non-decimal spelling.

## Acceptance criteria

- `resolveOpenCodeDrainGraceMs` accepts only a plain decimal spelling (after the trim the sibling strict helpers use): `^\d+$` with a safe-integer, `>= 0` result; every other spelling — `'1e3'`, `'0x10'`, `'5.9'`, `' '` (whitespace only), `'+5000'`, `'5000.0'` — falls back to `DEFAULT_OPENCODE_DRAIN_GRACE_MS`.
- Explicit `'0'` still means 0 (pinned by the existing test) and `''`/unset still mean the default.
- Regression tests added alongside `draining-opencode.test.js:128-138` covering at least `'1e3'`, `'0x10'`, `'5.9'`, `' '` and `'5000.0'`.
- No behaviour change for plain-decimal values; `bun run check:changed` green.

title: fix(web): Jev classifier client buffers the endpoint response whole — response.text() with no size cap on a configurable endpoint

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

`createJevClient().ask` in `packages/web/server/lib/routing/jev.js` reads the classifier endpoint's response with an unbounded `await response.text()` — no size cap and no early cancellation. The only bound is the 4-second timeout (`JEV_TIMEOUT_MS` in `packages/web/server/lib/routing/defaults.js:72`), which limits duration, not bytes: a fast or local endpoint can deliver hundreds of megabytes inside that window, all of it buffered in memory before `JSON.parse` runs.

The endpoint is not always a fixed trusted service: routing supports a **custom classifier endpoint** chosen in Settings, and an administrator-pinned one via the machine policy file / `OPENCHAMBER_JEV_URL` (`packages/web/server/lib/routing/classifier.js`, `readPinnedCustomEndpoint`). A misconfigured, compromised, or simply broken endpoint therefore gets to allocate unbounded server memory per routing/permission decision — and `ask` is called on the routing hot path (`route-rules-routes.js:75`, `runtime.js:526`, `runtime.js:653`).

## Evidence (verified this run, main `12737f569`)

- `packages/web/server/lib/routing/jev.js:139` — `const text = await response.text();` with no cap; the parsed answer is a small JSON object validated by `responseSchema` (direct/wrapped `{ answers: record }`).
- The repo already has the bounded pattern for exactly this shape of read, twice:
  - `packages/web/server/lib/guests/response-body.js:13` — `readBoundedResponseText(response, maxBytes)`: checks declared `content-length`, streams with a reader, cancels the stream as soon as the cap is crossed.
  - `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/model-discovery.js:175` — `readBoundedJson(response, maxBytes)` with `MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES = 5 MiB` for a comparable provider JSON response.
- Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-jev-unbounded/probe.mjs`, run against the real `createJevClient` from the laptop fork, `jev.js` md5-verified identical to main): a stub `fetchImpl` streaming a 48 MiB body —
  - Jev: `pulled=50331648 of 50331648` bytes before throwing a JSON parse error — the whole body was consumed and buffered; nothing cancelled early.
  - Control, the repo's own `readBoundedResponseText` with a 1 MiB cap on the identical stream: `tooLarge=true pulled=1114112` — stops at the cap.

## Why it matters

- A single routing decision can be turned into a large transient memory allocation by any endpoint the user/admin points Jev at; repeated decisions (permission checks, probe calls) multiply it.
- It contradicts the codebase's own established contract for external JSON reads (model-discovery, guests), so the gap is an inconsistency, not a design choice.
- The failure mode today is also poor: an oversized-but-valid-prefix body surfaces as a generic JSON parse error after full download, instead of a clear "response too large" error.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `createJevClient().ask` reads the response through a bounded reader (declared-length pre-check + streaming cap + stream cancellation on overflow), reusing or mirroring `readBoundedResponseText` / `readBoundedJson`.
- [ ] The cap is sized for the answer shape (a small `{ answers }` JSON object; something in the 256 KiB–1 MiB range is ample) and named as a constant near the client.
- [ ] An over-cap response fails with a distinct, identifiable error (not a JSON parse error), and the underlying stream is cancelled promptly — a test with a streaming body proves the client stops pulling shortly past the cap rather than consuming the whole body.
- [ ] Existing Jev tests (`runtime.test.js`, `route-rules-routes.test.js`) still pass; new tests cover: over-cap declared `content-length`, over-cap streamed (chunked, no length), and a normal small answer.

title: fix(web): event-stream proxy buffers a non-SSE upstream response whole — no cap, no stall deadline, client sees nothing until it ends

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`forwardSseRequest` in `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/proxy.js` handles an upstream that answers the event-stream request with a **non-SSE content type** by buffering the entire body in memory before sending anything:

```js
// proxy.js:670-676 (main 30eac4203)
if (!upstream.body) {
  res.end(await upstream.text().catch(() => ''));
  return;
}
if (!isEventStream) {
  res.end(await upstream.text());
  return;
}
```

There is no size cap and no deadline on this branch:

- The SSE stall watchdog, heartbeat and resume machinery all live in `pumpUpstream`, which this branch never reaches — a slow-trickle non-SSE body is not timed out by anything except the browser going away (`req.on('close')` → abort).
- The response status/headers are set (`res.status(...)`, `applyForwardProxyResponseHeaders`) but nothing is flushed until `res.end(...)`, so the browser sees a pending request while the proxy accumulates.
- `fetchSessionListPayload` (`proxy.js:920`) has the same shape (`await upstream.text()` on the whole body, then `JSON.parse`) for session-list routes, though its bodies are at least expected to be JSON lists.

## Verification (laptop probe vs the real module, main `30eac4203`)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-proxy-nonsse/` on the laptop — a standalone script in the laptop clone (proxy.js md5-verified against sandbox main) wiring `registerOpenCodeProxy` exactly as `packages/web/server/opencode-proxy.test.js` does, against a fake upstream that answers `/api/event` with `Content-Type: text/plain` and writes 64 KiB every 20 ms **without ever ending**:

- After 6 s the upstream had sent **19,202,048 bytes (~18.3 MiB)**; the client had received **0 bytes** and the fetch promise had **not even resolved to response headers** — no error, no disconnect, no stall timeout. Process RSS+external grew **+87 MiB** over the same window (all three roles share the probe process, so treat this as directional; the retained copy is the proxy's — the client provably holds nothing and the upstream's writes are transient).
- Control: the same upstream ending after 512 KiB → the client receives the whole 512 KiB at once, status 200 — the branch works, it just buffers everything first.

## Why it matters

The upstream is not always OpenChamber's own managed process: external/user-configured OpenCode servers and space servers are remote input. One that answers the event route with the wrong content type and a large or never-ending body (a misconfigured reverse proxy serving an HTML page, a hung server trickling a log file) pins a browser request and grows the OpenChamber server's memory without bound, with every health signal silent — the exact failure class #756 fixed for the SSE branches, left open on the non-SSE branch of the same handler. `AGENTS.md`: partial results and stale-data behavior must be explicit; an unbounded silent buffer is the opposite.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The non-SSE branch of `forwardSseRequest` is bounded: either it streams the body through with backpressure (preferred — it is a proxy) or it caps the buffered body at a named constant and ends the response observably (status/log reason) past the cap.
- [ ] A non-SSE body that never ends cannot pin the request forever: a deadline/stall rule applies to this branch too, or the streaming rewrite makes the existing close/stall semantics apply.
- [ ] Normal non-SSE answers behave exactly as today (status, forwarded headers, full body, e.g. JSON error payloads from upstream); existing `opencode-proxy.test.js` tests pass.
- [ ] New regression tests pin both floods: a non-SSE body past the cap, and a non-SSE trickle that never ends.
- [ ] Scope check: `fetchSessionListPayload`'s whole-body read is either covered by the same bound or explicitly assessed in the fix with a stated reason.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for `proxy non-SSE`, `upstream.text`, `event stream content-type`, `proxy buffers response`, `forwardSseRequest` — no covering issue. #756 covers the two SSE partial-block buffers (`upstream-reader`, `sse-cursor`); its scope explicitly excludes this non-SSE branch, which buffers the *whole* body rather than a partial block.

title: fix(ci): repo-sweeper's cancel-in-progress can kill a 25-minute issue intake at the next 15-minute tick — a slow intake can never finish and blocks the oldest-first queue

labels.name: kind/ci
labels.description: CI/CD pipelines, workflows, and build automation

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: area/ci
labels.description: CI, workflows, and build infrastructure

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

The new consolidated sweeper (`.github/workflows/repo-sweeper.yml`, landed 2026-10-29 in PRs #753–#755) can cancel its own issue-intake jobs before they finish — and an intake that needs more than 15 minutes can never finish at all:

- `:30-31` — the workflow runs on a **15-minute schedule** (`cron: '*/15 * * * *'`).
- `:39-41` — a single workflow-level concurrency group `repo-sweeper` with **`cancel-in-progress: true`**: every new tick cancels the previous sweep wherever it is.
- `:347` — the `issue-intake` job allows `timeout-minutes: 35`, and `:478` gives its `opencode run` agent step a **25-minute** timeout (`timeout --signal=TERM --kill-after=30s 25m`). `pr-intake` alone allows 20 minutes (`:46`). The longest legal sweep (collect → intake) is ~45 minutes — three schedule intervals.

The header comment (`:36-38`) justifies cancellation with "its passes are idempotent label/comment syncs". That is true for the label jobs, but not for `issue-intake`: the agent's only output is the comment produced at the **end** of a paid LLM run. Cancelling at the next tick discards the whole run, and `issue-collect` then re-selects the same issue next sweep — it picks the **oldest five un-intaked issues first** (`:343-344`, marker check `:338`), so one slow issue can be cancelled and retried forever while every newer issue starves behind it.

## Contrast in the same landing

- The deleted event-driven `issue-intake.yml` deliberately used `cancel-in-progress: false` + `queue: max`, with a header comment documenting the cancellation hazards (#77, #84): no event cancels an intake.
- `main-broken.yml`, merged in the same CI rework, kept that audit explicitly (`:47-51`: literal `false`, "so queue: max can never pair with a true-evaluating cancel expression here").
- The sweeper consolidation dropped the protection for exactly the job that needs it most.

## Observed

The sweeper's first `workflow_dispatch` run (40826288774, 2026-10-29) took **50m13s wall** (05:56:51Z → 06:47:04Z) — the jobs sat queued for runners for most of it. A scheduled sweep whose jobs wait longer than 15 minutes for a runner, or whose agent runs long, is cancelled by construction, not by bad luck.

## Why it matters

Issue intake is the maintainer-facing triage for every new issue. As written, any issue whose intake takes >15 minutes (a big bug report needing real code tracing is exactly that case) can never receive its intake comment via the scheduled path: it is silently retried every 15 minutes, burning a fresh agent run each time, and it blocks the oldest-first queue for everything filed after it. Nothing in the run output distinguishes "cancelled by the next tick" from a genuine intake failure.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] No scheduled tick can cancel an in-progress `issue-intake` (or other job) from a previous sweep — e.g. `cancel-in-progress: false` with a bounded queue, a separate concurrency group/workflow for intake, or an intake budget provably inside the interval with margin; the chosen mechanism is documented in the workflow header.
- [ ] The header comment's idempotency claim matches reality for every job in the workflow, and the concurrency block is re-audited against the #77/#84 lessons recorded in the deleted `issue-intake.yml` and in `main-broken.yml`.
- [ ] Overlapping-sweep behaviour is bounded: label/comment passes cannot pile up as duplicate pending runs, and a cancelled-or-queued duplicate never posts a second intake comment (the `**For the maintainer:**` marker contract still holds).
- [ ] Demonstrated with an overlapping dispatch (or equivalent evidence): a >15-minute intake completes and posts exactly one comment; the label sweeps still land within one interval under normal runner load.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for `repo-sweeper`, `sweeper cancel`, `cancel-in-progress`, `concurrency sweeper`, `intake cancelled` — no covering issue. #87 is the labeler/infra family, #77/#84 are the historical per-event collapse/cancellation bugs whose fixes this regresses in a new shape.

title: fix(web): SSE partial-block buffers grow without bound — upstream-reader and sse-cursor retain a separator-less stream forever

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

Two SSE partial-block buffers in the web server grow without any bound when the upstream OpenCode stream sends data that never contains the `\n\n` block separator:

1. **`packages/web/server/lib/event-stream/upstream-reader.js:184,195`** — `let buffer = ''`, then `buffer += decoder.decode(value, …)` per chunk; the buffer is only drained inside the `while (separatorIndex !== -1)` loop. There is no size check anywhere in the file. The stall watchdog does not save it: `resetStallTimer()` runs on **every** chunk (line 194, just before the append), so a steady trickle of separator-less data keeps the connection "healthy" forever while memory grows.
2. **`packages/web/server/lib/event-stream/sse-cursor.js` (`createSseCursor.observe`)** — `pending = \`${pending}${text}\``, drained only on `\n\n`. Every upstream chunk of the proxied event stream passes through it (`packages/web/server/lib/opencode/proxy.js:655`, observed per chunk in `pumpUpstream`). The full-string concatenation also makes the cost quadratic in the retained size.

The in-repo precedent is that partial SSE state **is** capped: the proxy's own `createSseBoundaryTracker` (`proxy.js:246`) truncates its tail at 4096 bytes, and `event-stream/protocol.js` caps per-client WS buffering at `MESSAGE_STREAM_WS_MAX_BUFFERED_BYTES` (16 MiB). These two buffers are the outliers.

Consumers of `createUpstreamSseReader` (all fed by an OpenCode upstream — managed, external/user-configured, or a space's server): `event-stream/global-hub.js:386,501`, `event-stream/runtime.js:209`, `event-stream/directory-ws-bridge.js:99`, `opencode/watcher.js:92`, `spaces/space-events.js:137,234`.

## Verification (laptop probe vs the real modules, main `2b7904504`)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-sse-buffer-cap/` on the laptop (files copied verbatim from main, md5-verified), Node v24.21.0, `node --expose-gc probe.mjs`:

- `createSseCursor`: fed 16 MiB of separator-less text in 256 × 64 KiB `observe()` calls → **0 blocks returned, heap 4 → 20 MiB** (everything retained), and the observe loop took **5071 ms** (quadratic copying). Control: a `\n\n`-terminated block returns 1 block with its id, as today.
- `createUpstreamSseReader` with a fake upstream that enqueues a 64 KiB separator-less chunk every 20 ms and `stallTimeoutMs: 5000`: after 6 s (~19 MiB) — **events=0, errors=0, disconnects=0, heap 20 → 38 MiB**, still connected. The stall timer never fires because every chunk resets it.

## Why it matters

The upstream is not always OpenChamber's own managed process: external OpenCode servers and space servers are user-configured remotes. A buggy, compromised, or simply nonconforming upstream that streams without blank-line separators (or one pathological giant event) grows the OpenChamber server's memory without limit while every health signal looks fine — no stall, no error, no reconnect. `AGENTS.md`: partial results and stale-data behavior must be explicit; an unbounded silent buffer is the opposite.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Both buffers are bounded by a named constant (per buffer; a few MiB at most, justified against the existing 4096-byte boundary tail and 16 MiB WS caps).
- [ ] Overflow in `upstream-reader` ends the read observably — drop/reconnect with an `onError`/disconnect reason naming the overflow — instead of retaining or silently discarding data.
- [ ] Overflow in `sse-cursor.observe` cannot retain more than the cap and does not corrupt the cursor for subsequent complete blocks.
- [ ] Normal streams behave exactly as today: blocks split across chunks, CRLF, heartbeat comment lines, resync handling; existing `upstream-reader.test.js`, `sse-cursor.test.js`, `global-hub`/`global-resume` and proxy tests pass.
- [ ] New regression tests pin both floods: a separator-less stream past the cap triggers the bound in each module.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for `upstream-reader`, `SSE buffer`, `event stream buffer`, `separator`, `unbounded` — no covering issue. The recently closed output-cap issues (#737/#741/#742/#744/#745) cover child-process/HTTP capture buffers, not the SSE stream readers.

title: fix(vscode): worktree list reports any git failure as a repository with no worktrees — listGitWorktrees returns [] on any error, unlike the web service which only empties for a non-repository

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/vscode
labels.description: Package: vscode (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

`listGitWorktrees` in the VS Code runtime returns an empty list for **every** git failure, not just for a directory that is not a repository. A repository whose `git worktree list` fails for any other reason (corrupt config, dubious ownership, a broken git dir) silently reads as "this project has no worktrees" — a fetch failure masquerading as authoritative empty success. The web runtime's twin function already implements the correct contract; the VS Code runtime is the remaining outlier in its own family.

## Evidence (verified at main `3b407a216`)

- `packages/vscode/src/gitService.ts:1802-1825` — `listGitWorktrees` wraps `runGitCommandOrThrow(directoryPath, ['worktree', 'list', '--porcelain'], …)` in a catch-all: `console.warn('[GitService] Failed to list worktrees, returning empty list:', …); return [];`. The comment above the early return even states the assumption: "A non-repository fails the git command below and reads as an empty list all the same" — true for a non-repository, false for every other failure class.
- The web twin, `packages/web/server/lib/git/service.js` `getWorktrees` (~lines 4863-4898), documents and implements the intended contract: return `[]` only when `isNotGitRepositoryError(error)`, otherwise `throw error` — "Any other failure is a failure: callers keep their last known topology instead of treating 'git could not answer' as 'there are no worktrees'."
- Sibling VS Code functions were already fixed to this same contract, with the reasoning recorded in their comments: `getRemotes` (`gitService.ts:3951-3965`, only not-a-repository empties, other failures throw with git's stderr), `getGitBranchesRaw` (#661), `getGitStatusRaw` (#650), `getCommitFiles` (#645). `listGitWorktrees` is the one list/read function in the module that still fabricates an empty success.
- Callers: `packages/vscode/src/bridge-git-runtime.ts:184` serves the result straight to the shared UI worktree list; the UI cannot distinguish "no worktrees" from "git could not answer".

## Reproduction (laptop probe against the real module)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-vscode-worktrees-empty/probe.ts` on the laptop, importing the real `gitService.ts` from `~/git/openchamber-fork` (main `3b407a216`) with the same `vscode` module mock the repo's own `gitService.bare-repository.test.js` uses:

1. Healthy repo: `listGitWorktrees` returns its one worktree correctly.
2. Same repo with a corrupted `.git/config` (appended `[broken`): direct `git worktree list --porcelain` exits **128** with `fatal: bad config line 10 in file .git/config` — not a not-a-repository error. `listGitWorktrees` **does not throw and returns `[]`**, logging only a console warning.
3. Control, plain non-repository directory: returns `[]` (correct, and must stay correct — the existing bare-repository test at `packages/vscode/src/gitService.bare-repository.test.js:84` pins this).

## Why it matters

Worktree topology drives which checkouts the UI offers to open, attach sessions to, and clean up. Reading a damaged-but-real repository as worktree-less hides the user's linked worktrees with no error anywhere the user can see, and it breaks the invariant the rest of this module (and the web service) now upholds: only an authoritative not-a-repository answer may read as empty.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `listGitWorktrees` returns `[]` only for the not-a-repository failure (matching the web `getWorktrees` / VS Code `getRemotes` distinction); any other git failure surfaces as a thrown error carrying git's stderr/message.
- [ ] Bare repositories and linked worktrees keep listing exactly as today (`gitService.bare-repository.test.js` stays green, including the non-repository `[]` case).
- [ ] A regression test pins the corrupt-config (or equivalent non-not-a-repo failure) case: the call rejects instead of returning `[]`.
- [ ] The bridge caller (`bridge-git-runtime.ts`) behaviour on a thrown error is checked: the bridge returns a failure response for that request rather than a successful empty list.

body:
## Problem

Every remote command the Electron desktop app runs over SSH goes through one helper that (a) accumulates the command's stdout in memory with no size cap, and (b) has no execution timeout at all — it settles only when the ssh child closes. A chatty remote command grows the desktop app's memory without bound, and a hung remote command hangs the calling flow (connect, install, status, probe) forever. The `timeoutSec` callers pass looks like a timeout but is only ssh's `ConnectTimeout`, which stops applying once the connection is up.

## Evidence (verified on main `ccd30d9c9`)

- `packages/electron/ssh-manager.mjs:553-582` — `runSshOutput`: `stdout += chunk.toString()` at `:563-565` with no length check; no timer is armed anywhere in the function; the promise resolves on the child's `close` and rejects only on `error`.
- The asymmetry is in the same function: stderr is tail-capped — `stderr = (stderr + chunk).slice(-MAX_PROCESS_ERROR_CAPTURE_CHARS)` at `:566-568` (`MAX_PROCESS_ERROR_CAPTURE_CHARS = 4000`, `:49`) — and the diagnostic capture in `trackSshProcess` (`:518-524`) is capped the same way. Stdout was missed.
- `packages/electron/ssh-manager.mjs:583-597` — `runRemoteCommand(parsed, controlPath, script, timeoutSec = DEFAULT_CONNECTION_TIMEOUT_SEC)` passes `timeoutSec` only as `-o ConnectTimeout=${timeoutSec}` in the ssh arguments. `ConnectTimeout` bounds connection establishment; it does not bound how long the remote command may run or stay silent.
- Remote-controlled callers through this path include: remote install (`installOpenChamberManaged` runs `bun add -g` / `npm install -g` via `runRemoteCommand`), `startRemoteServerManaged` (`openchamber serve --quiet`, `:1293`), `listRemoteServers` (`status --json`), the remote probe scripts, and `resolveRemoteTool`. Their stdout is whatever the remote host prints.
- Precedents in the same app/repo: `packages/electron/shell-environment.mjs` caps its shell-probe stdout at 1 MiB and arms a 5 s timeout; the web `run-command` caps captured output at 4 MiB with a timeout (`packages/web/server/lib/spaces/run-command.js`).
- Laptop probe against the real `ElectronSshManager` using the constructor's `spawn` seam — the same seam `packages/electron/ssh-manager.test.mjs` uses (probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-electron-ssh-output/` on the laptop, fork at `ccd30d9c9`): a fake child emitting 8 MiB on each stream and exiting 0 resolved with `stdout.length === 8388608` (whole), while stderr came back capped; a child that printed once and then stayed open left `runSshOutput` still unsettled after 2,500 ms — and the code contains no timer that would ever settle it.

## Why it matters

The remote host is the less-trusted side of this boundary: a compromised or simply verbose/broken remote (an install that spews progress forever, a wedged remote CLI that never exits) currently has no ceiling in the desktop app — memory grows for as long as the command runs, and a hang is indistinguishable from a slow connection, freezing the connect/install flow with no error and no way out short of restarting the app. Every comparable runner in this repo pairs its capture with a documented bound and a deadline.

## Acceptance criteria

- `runSshOutput` enforces a documented stdout bound (consistent with the file's existing diagnostic caps, or a larger documented bound where a caller legitimately needs more); exceeding it terminates the child and settles with a distinguishable failure instead of returning unbounded output.
- Remote command execution has a real deadline: `runRemoteCommand`/`runSshOutput` kills the child and rejects when the deadline passes. The deadline is per-caller aware — short probes keep a short bound; the remote install path, which legitimately runs long, gets an explicitly generous/configured one rather than none.
- Under-cap, in-time behaviour is byte-identical: served-port parsing, `status --json` parsing, tool resolution and the probe scripts all work exactly as today, and stderr handling is unchanged.
- Tests in `packages/electron/ssh-manager.test.mjs` (fake-spawn seam) pin: under-cap output returned whole with its exit code; over-cap stdout terminates the child and is not returned full; a silent child is killed and rejected at the deadline; `ConnectTimeout` is still passed for connection establishment.

body:
## Problem

The guest update check reads a guest repository's `package.json` through a git helper that accumulates the command's whole stdout in memory with no size cap. The file's content is controlled by the guest's remote repository, so a guest repo carrying an oversized `package.json` blob makes every update check load that blob whole into the OpenChamber server's memory — and then throw it away, because a manifest that large cannot parse as a valid guest manifest anyway.

## Evidence (verified on main `ccd30d9c9`)

- `packages/web/server/lib/guests/clone.js:186` — `runGit(args, { …, capture = false, … })`. When `capture` is set, stdout is collected with no bound: `packages/web/server/lib/guests/clone.js:210-212` — `const chunks = []; … child.stdout.on('data', (chunk) => chunks.push(chunk));`, returned whole at `:237` via `Buffer.concat(chunks).toString('utf8')`.
- The same function caps what it actually needs to bound: stderr keeps only a tail (`STDERR_TAIL_BYTES = 4096`, `clone.js:177`, applied at `:214-218`), and a timer (`CLONE_TIMEOUT_MS = 60_000`, `clone.js:7`) bounds time — but nothing bounds captured stdout bytes.
- The only production `capture: true` caller is the guest update check: `packages/web/server/lib/guests/updates.js:106` — `runGit(['show', 'FETCH_HEAD:package.json'], { gitBinary, cwd, timeoutMs, capture: true })`, whose output is fed straight to `parseManifestJson(shown.stdout ?? '')` at `updates.js:110`. The bytes come from `FETCH_HEAD` — i.e. from the guest's remote origin, fetched at `updates.js:99-103` — so the blob size is repo-controlled, not authored by the local user.
- Sibling git runners in the same server all cap captured output: `packages/web/server/lib/skills-catalog/git.js` runs git through `execFile` with `DEFAULT_MAX_BUFFER = 4 * 1024 * 1024`; the web git service caps every command at `maxBuffer: 20 * 1024 * 1024` (`packages/web/server/lib/git/service.js`, `runGitCommand`).
- Laptop probe against the real exported `runGit` (probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-guest-rungit-cap/` on the laptop, fork at `ccd30d9c9`): a real git repo was created with an 8,388,647-byte `package.json`; `runGit(['show', 'HEAD:package.json'], { capture: true })` resolved `ok: true` with `stdout.length === 8388647` — the whole blob. Control: the same call with `capture: false` returned `stdout.length === 0`, as designed.

## Why it matters

Guests are third-party packages. The update check runs automatically against the guest's remote, so the trigger is not a local user action: one installed guest whose repository gains a huge `package.json` (accidentally generated, or maliciously planted) turns a routine background check into an unbounded memory load in the server process, repeated on every check. The repo's own convention elsewhere — the fs exec cap (#737), the VS Code bridge caps (#741, #742), the skills-catalog and git-service `maxBuffer`s — is that captured command output always has a documented bound.

## Acceptance criteria

- `runGit` with `capture: true` enforces a documented stdout bound (a manifest-appropriate bound, at most the 4 MiB skills-catalog class); exceeding it stops the accumulation (and the child, where applicable) and resolves with a failure the caller can distinguish — never the whole oversized output.
- `checkGuestUpdate` treats an over-cap `package.json` the same as an unparseable one (`invalid-manifest`), without buffering the blob whole.
- Under-cap behaviour is unchanged: a normal `package.json` is returned whole and the update check parses/compares versions exactly as today; stderr tail behaviour and the timeout are unchanged.
- Tests pin: a manifest just under the cap parses and reports an available update as today; an over-cap manifest is rejected without the full bytes being returned/parsed (in `packages/web/server/lib/guests/updates.test.js` and/or a `clone` test suite).

body:
## Problem

Every git command the VS Code extension runs goes through one executor, `execGit` in `packages/vscode/src/bridge-git-process-runtime.ts`, and that executor collects stdout/stderr with **no size cap** and applies **no timeout unless the caller passes one** — and effectively no caller does. A huge diff/status/log output grows extension-host memory without bound, and a git process that never exits (blocked on a lock, a slow filesystem, or a network operation) hangs its caller forever. The web git service caps every command it runs; the VS Code executor caps none.

## Evidence (verified on main `5a007a5ab`, 2026-10-28)

- `packages/vscode/src/bridge-git-process-runtime.ts:90-125` `execGit`:
  - `:102` `process.child.stdout.on('data', (data) => { stdout += data.toString(); });`
  - `:103` same for stderr — no length check, truncation, or kill.
  - `:107` a timeout timer is armed only when `options.timeoutMs > 0`.
- Callers: `packages/vscode/src/gitService.ts:316-317` wraps it as its own `execGit` with `{ binary, env }` only — no `timeoutMs` — so **every** gitService operation (status, diff, range diff, log, branch, stash, worktree, commit paths) runs unbounded and timeless. The bridge git runtimes call the same executor the same way. The sole caller passing a timeout is `bridge-fs-helpers-runtime.ts:139` (check-ignore, `GIT_CHECK_IGNORE_TIMEOUT_MS`).
- Laptop probe against the **real** exported `execGit` (probe at laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-vscode-git-exec-cap/probe.test.js`, `bun test` on main `5a007a5ab`, using `/bin/sh` as the binary to isolate the executor from git itself):
  - 8,000,000-char stdout → `exitCode: 0, stdout.length: 8000000` returned whole.
  - 4,000,000-char stderr → returned whole, `exitCode: 0`.
  - Control `printf hello` → `{ stdout: 'hello', stderr: '', exitCode: 0 }`.
- The web counterpart treats both bounds as required: `packages/web/server/lib/git/service.js` `runGitCommand` sets `maxBuffer: 20 * 1024 * 1024` (`:1179`, also `:2155`/`:2168`; 50 MiB for two bulk paths at `:3927`/`:3950`) and the simple-git layer adds a stall timeout (`:486-508`). Sibling output-cap defects: #737 (web `/api/fs/exec`), #741 (VS Code bridge fs exec).

## Why it matters

This executor sits under every VS Code git surface — the status read alone (`git status -uall`, diff and range-diff reads) can legitimately produce very large output in a big or dirty repository, and an accidental pathological output (a diff over a huge generated/lock file, `log -p` over a long history) currently has no ceiling at all: the extension host absorbs all of it, and the caller waits indefinitely for a process that may never finish. The web runtime answers the same commands with a 20 MiB ceiling and a clear failure.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `execGit` enforces a documented output bound for stdout and stderr (combined or per-stream); exceeding it terminates the child and resolves with a distinguishable failure (non-zero exit with an output-too-large message in stderr, or an explicit marker), never unbounded accumulation.
- [ ] The bound is at least in the web service's class (20 MiB default) or a larger per-call bound is available for the call sites that legitimately return bulk output (diff/range-diff), mirroring the web service's 50 MiB bulk paths; normal results are byte-identical to today.
- [ ] A default timeout (or a documented, deliberate decision per call-site class about which commands stay timeless, e.g. interactive network operations) — a short probe must not be able to hang forever, and the chosen behaviour is pinned by tests.
- [ ] Tests in a `bridge-git-process-runtime` suite pin: under-cap output returned whole with its real exit code; over-cap stdout and stderr terminate the child and do not return the full stream; a caller-supplied `timeoutMs` still wins over the default.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues 2026-10-28: `execGit output`, `git executor cap`, `bridge-git-process`, `git command timeout vscode`, `maxBuffer vscode git` — no existing issue covers a size cap or default timeout for the VS Code git executor (hits were the fs-exec siblings #737/#741 and unrelated items).

body:
## Problem

The VS Code extension's `api:fs:exec` bridge handler runs shell commands in a workspace and collects their output with **no size ceiling**. A verbose command can grow the extension host's memory without bound for the full command timeout (300,000 ms), and the accumulated string is then returned whole over the bridge. This is the VS Code twin of the web defect filed as #737 — the web fix does not touch this handler.

## Evidence (verified on main `5a007a5ab`, 2026-10-28)

- `packages/vscode/src/bridge-fs-runtime.ts` `api:fs:exec` handler (`:396`), inner `runCommand`:
  - `:453` `stdout += chunk.toString();`
  - `:456` `stderr += chunk.toString();`
  - Neither handler checks a length, truncates, or kills the child. The only bound is the hardcoded 300,000 ms timeout timer (`:445-452`).
- The git-read cache in the same file is byte-capped (`GIT_READ_CACHE_MAX_BYTES = 1024 * 1024`, `:84`, eviction at `:101-102`) — but it only stores results *after* a cacheable git read has already accumulated in full, and arbitrary (non-git-read) commands never pass through any cap at all.
- Laptop probe against the **real** `handleFsBridgeMessage` (only `vscode` mocked, real `/bin/sh`, pattern of `bridge-fs-runtime.spawn.test.js`; probe at laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-vscode-fs-exec-cap/probe.test.js`, run with `bun test` on main `5a007a5ab`):
  - `head -c 8000000 /dev/zero | tr '\0' 'a'` → `success: true, exitCode: 0, stdout.length: 8000000`, no error — 8 MB returned whole.
  - Same shape on stderr: 4,000,000 chars returned whole, `success: true`.
  - Control `printf 'hello'` → `{ success: true, stdout: 'hello', stderr: '', exitCode: 0 }` as expected.
- The codebase already treats unbounded command output as a defect elsewhere: the web environment runner caps at 4 MiB (`packages/web/server/lib/environment/runtime.js:52`, enforced `:91-95`), the VS Code managed-OpenCode launcher retains only a 32 KiB tail of server output (`packages/vscode/src/managed-opencode-process.ts`, `capture` slices to `-32 * 1024`), and the web twin is #737.

## Why it matters

`api:fs:exec` is a living surface: the shared UI drives git reads and workspace commands through the bridge in the VS Code runtime, exactly as it drives `/api/fs/exec` on web. One runaway command — a verbose test/build run, or a simple `yes`/`cat` mistake — can OOM or badly pressure the extension host that every VS Code session depends on, instead of failing cleanly with a bounded, marked result.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `runCommand` in the `api:fs:exec` handler enforces a documented stdout cap and stderr cap (per-stream or combined); exceeding a cap terminates the child and resolves with a clear `output-too-large` / truncated result instead of unbounded growth.
- [ ] The result shape stays compatible for normal commands (`command`, `success`, `exitCode`, `stdout`, `stderr` unchanged under the cap); a capped result is distinguishable (explicit flag/error text, not silent truncation alone).
- [ ] Tests in `packages/vscode/src/bridge-fs-runtime.test.js` / `bridge-fs-runtime.spawn.test.js` (or a sibling suite) pin: output under the cap is returned whole; output over the cap stops the child and does not return the full stream; stderr is bounded the same way.
- [ ] The cap size is a named constant in one place, at least as generous as the environment runner's 4 MiB precedent unless a smaller bound is justified in the PR, and the git-read cache behaviour for cacheable commands is unchanged.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues 2026-10-28: `fs exec output cap vscode bridge`, `unbounded stdout`, `bridge-fs-runtime output` — the only hit is #737, which is scoped to the web server (`packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.js` `runCommandInDirectory`) and explicitly does not cover this VS Code bridge handler. Sibling, not duplicate: the two fixes should use the same cap semantics, so the worker should read #737 (and its fix, if landed) before choosing constants.

body:
## Problem

The `openchamber quota` CLI judges its two numeric environment variables with bare `Number.parseInt`, so non-decimal spellings are silently reinterpreted instead of falling back to the documented defaults — the same defect class the server-side readers were fixed for (#689/#696/#697 and siblings), in the one CLI file those fixes did not reach.

## Evidence (verified on main `e0487b3f1`, 2026-10-28)

File: `packages/web/bin/lib/commands-quota.js`

1. **Per-provider timeout** — `:226-228`:
   ```js
   const resolveQuotaTimeoutMs = (env) => {
     const parsed = Number.parseInt(env.OPENCHAMBER_QUOTA_TIMEOUT_MS ?? '', 10);
     return Number.isInteger(parsed) && parsed > 0 ? parsed : DEFAULT_QUOTA_TIMEOUT_MS; // 10_000
   };
   ```
   `parseInt` stops at the first non-digit, so:
   - `'1e3'` → **1 ms** (not 1000, not the default): every provider fetch races a 1 ms deadline, so `openchamber quota` reports timeout rows for all providers.
   - `'10000junk'` → 10000 (junk silently honoured).
   - `'10.9'` → **10 ms**; `'250ms'` → 250 ms.
   - The existing tests (`packages/web/bin/lib/commands-quota.test.js:655-659`) pin `''`-absent, `'250'`, `'0'`, `'-5'`, and `'nope'` — but no trailing-junk / exponent / fractional spelling, which is exactly where `parseInt` diverges.

2. **OpenCode port** — `:55-56`:
   ```js
   const port = Number.parseInt(env.OPENCODE_PORT ?? '', 10);
   return `http://127.0.0.1:${Number.isInteger(port) && port > 0 ? port : DEFAULT_OPENCODE_PORT}`;
   ```
   - `'1e3'` → port **1** instead of the 4096 default (CLI talks to the wrong port and falls back to the credential store, masking the misconfiguration).
   - `'4096junk'` → 4096 (junk honoured).
   - `'99999'` → accepted (`> 0` is the only check), producing `http://127.0.0.1:99999` — an out-of-range port the CLI's own `--port` flag rejects (`cli-args.js:205-211` validates 1–65535 with a whole-text `/^-?\d+$/` test).

## The house standard this file missed

- `packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.js:128-137` documents it verbatim: "Only a plain decimal spelling counts: a bare Number(...) would silently honour '' and ' ' as 0, '1e3' as 1000, '0x10' as 16, and '5.9' as a fractional value", via `parsePlainDecimalInt` (`/^\d+$/` + safe-integer).
- `packages/web/bin/lib/cli-args.js` already judges `--port`, `--lines`, `--limit`, and `--timeout` whole-text with explanatory comments saying `parseInt` alone would misread them.
- `packages/web/bin/lib/cli-goal.js` (`parseGoalTokenBudget`) and `cli-tunnel-utils.js` (`parseTtlMsOrThrow`) likewise validate whole-text before converting.

## Why it matters

Quota is a living surface — this CLI is the terminal read of the same provider quota the Usage page shows, used to decide model-pool placement. A typo'd or unit-suffixed value (`250ms`, `1e3`) currently produces an all-timeout run or a silent wrong-port fallback instead of the documented default, with no warning naming the bad value.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `resolveQuotaTimeoutMs`: only a plain decimal positive integer is honoured; `'1e3'`, `'10000junk'`, `'10.9'`, `'250ms'`, `'0x10'` all fall back to 10_000. Tests extend `commands-quota.test.js:655-659` with those spellings.
- [ ] `resolveOpenCodeBaseUrl` (exported or tested through its caller): `OPENCODE_PORT` is honoured only as a plain decimal integer in 1–65535; `'1e3'`, `'4096junk'`, `'99999'`, `'0'` fall back to 4096.
- [ ] Valid values behave exactly as today (`'250'` → 250 ms; `'4097'` → `http://127.0.0.1:4097`); `OPENCODE_HOST` precedence is unchanged.
- [ ] No other quota CLI behaviour changes.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues 2026-10-28: `QUOTA_TIMEOUT`, `commands-quota`, `quota timeout parseInt` — no hits. Open quota issue #736 is about splitting the OpenCode Go row per workspace, unrelated. The server-side env-parsing issues (#689/#696/#697/#704/#705/#725) never covered `packages/web/bin`.

  - `packages/web/server/lib/fs/workspace-file-names.js:14` caps output at 16 MiB.
  - `packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.js` itself caps uploads (`createUploadMaxBytes`, 100 MiB) and served files (`MAX_SERVE_BYTES`, `:207`).
  - The git-read cache in the same file is byte-capped (`GIT_READ_CACHE_MAX_BYTES`, `:245`) — but only cacheable `git rev-parse` commands go through it; arbitrary exec output is never bounded before it is stored in the job result.

## Why it matters

`/api/fs/exec` is a living surface: the UI drives git reads and workspace commands through it (e.g. `packages/ui/src/lib/worktrees/worktreeStatus.ts` notes bursts of `/api/fs/exec` calls). One runaway command — a test suite with verbose logging, a build that spews warnings, or a simple `yes`/`cat` mistake — can OOM or badly pressure the managed server that every session depends on, instead of failing cleanly the way the environment-command runner already does.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `runCommandInDirectory` enforces a documented stdout cap and stderr cap (per-stream or combined); exceeding a cap terminates the child and resolves with a clear `output-too-large` / truncated result instead of unbounded growth.
- [ ] The result shape stays compatible for normal commands (`command`, `success`, `exitCode`, `stdout`, `stderr` unchanged under the cap); a capped result is distinguishable (explicit flag/error text, not silent truncation alone).
- [ ] Tests in `packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.test.js` (or a sibling suite) pin: output under the cap is returned whole; output over the cap stops the child and does not return the full stream; stderr is bounded the same way.
- [ ] The cap size is named in one place (constant, optionally env-overridable using the existing strict `parsePlainDecimalInt` helper in the same file) and is at least as generous as the environment runner's 4 MiB precedent unless a smaller bound is justified in the PR.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues 2026-10-28: `runCommandInDirectory` (only hit was the unrelated, now-closed vscode double-shell #732), `unbounded stdout`, `fs exec output`, `exec output limit` — no existing issue covers a size cap for the web `/api/fs/exec` runner.

title: fix(vscode): revertGitFile recursively deletes files — and the whole directory for '.' — when git cannot confirm the file is untracked (non-repo fallback falls through to fs.rm)

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/high
labels.description: Important and time-sensitive

labels.name: app/vscode
labels.description: Package: vscode (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`revertGitFile` in the VS Code extension deletes files with a recursive `fs.rm` whenever git cannot confirm the file is tracked — including when the directory is not a git repository at all, and, for the path `.`, it deletes the entire directory tree. It reports success in every one of these cases.

## Evidence (verified at main `ef646726b`)

`packages/vscode/src/gitService.ts:2770-2788`:

- `:2776` — `ls-files --error-unmatch` is the tracked check. It fails non-zero for an untracked file, but also for **any** other failure: not a repository, corrupt index, git error. The stderr is discarded, so the branches are indistinguishable.
- `:2778` — on that failure it tries `git clean -f -d`. Outside a repository that fails too.
- `:2779-2785` — on clean failure it falls back to `fs.promises.rm(target, { recursive: true, force: true })`. The only guard (`:2782`) rejects targets *outside* the directory — the directory itself passes, because `target !== root` is false for `filePath === '.'`, so `revertGitFile(dir, '.')` recursively deletes `dir`.
- `:2787` — the function then returns normally; the bridge wraps it as success (`packages/vscode/src/bridge-git-runtime.ts:302-311`, `api:git/revert` — it validates only that `directory` and `path` are non-empty strings).

The web counterpart does not have this hole: `revertFile` (`packages/web/server/lib/git/service.js:3997-4005`) first resolves the repository root (throws for a non-repository) and resolves a validated file context inside that repo, and only then uses the same `clean` → `rm` fallback for a file git has actually shown to be untracked in a real repository.

### Laptop probe (real `revertGitFile`, temp dirs, `~/git/fleet/probe-vscode-revert-rm/probe.test.ts`, 1 pass)

- Non-repo dir + `precious.txt` → **NO THROW, `precious.txt` deleted**.
- Non-repo dir + path `.` → **NO THROW, the whole temp directory (including its marker file) deleted**.
- Control, real repo + untracked file → deleted (the intended revert-untracked behaviour).
- Control, real repo + tracked modified file → content restored to the committed version (intended).

## Why it matters

Revert/discard is already a destructive action; this fallback makes it destructive in exactly the cases where git gave no authoritative answer — a stale or wrong directory, a directory whose repo is broken, or a `.`/directory path — and it does so silently, with a success response, and recursively. The discarded `ls-files`/`clean` errors mean no log records why the deletion happened. This is the "fetch failure masquerading as authoritative empty success" pattern (AGENTS.md invariant) in its most dangerous form: a *read* failure becomes an irreversible *write*.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `revertGitFile` throws (and deletes nothing) when the directory is not inside a git repository, mirroring the web service's repository-root validation before any mutation.
- [ ] `revertGitFile` throws (and deletes nothing) when `filePath` resolves to the directory/repo root itself or to a directory that is not a validated untracked path; `.` and equivalent spellings are rejected explicitly.
- [ ] The `clean` → `fs.rm` fallback only runs for a path git has affirmatively shown to be untracked inside a validated repository (as in the web `revertFile` flow), never on an ambiguous `ls-files` failure.
- [ ] Regression tests cover: non-repo file (no deletion, throws), `.` path (no deletion, throws), real-repo untracked file (deleted), real-repo tracked modified file (restored).
- [ ] Existing VS Code git tests still pass.

title: fix(vscode): fs exec runs every command through two shells — single-quoted $() is executed by the outer shell and shell variables set in the command are lost, unlike the web spawn form

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/vscode
labels.description: Package: vscode (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Bug

The VS Code bridge's `api:fs:exec` handler runs each command through **two** shells, while the web server runs it through exactly one — so the same command string produces different results (and, in one case, executes code the caller had single-quoted as literal text) depending on which runtime serves the shared UI.

### Evidence (main `8e78d2881`)

VS Code — `packages/vscode/src/bridge-fs-runtime.ts:412` (case starts `:388`):

```ts
const { stdout, stderr } = await execAsync(`${shell} ${shellFlag} "${cmd.replace(/"/g, '\\"')}"`, { cwd: resolvedCwd, env: augmentedEnv, windowsHide: true, timeout: 300000 });
```

Node's `child_process.exec` already spawns a shell (`/bin/sh -c <string>` on POSIX) to run that string. The outer shell parses the double-quoted argument **before** the inner shell ever sees it: `$VAR`, `$(...)` and backticks inside the double quotes are expanded/executed by the outer shell, and the inner shell then parses the *result* as code.

Web counterpart — `packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.js:551-557` (`runCommandInDirectory`): `spawn(shell, [shellFlag, command], …)` — argv form, no outer shell, the command is parsed exactly once by the intended shell.

Caller: `packages/vscode/webview/api/files.ts:123-134` implements the shared `execCommands` API (`packages/ui/src/lib/api/types.ts:1344`) over this bridge, so shared UI code written against the web semantics reaches this handler.

### Verified divergence (laptop probe, real construction vs real web form)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-vscode-fs-exec-double-shell/probe.mjs` (Node, `/bin/sh`, same cwd/env for both forms):

| command | web (`spawn` argv) | VS Code (exec string) |
|---|---|---|
| `printf '%s' '$HOME'` | `$HOME` (literal, as quoted) | `/home/user` (expanded by outer shell despite single quotes) |
| `printf '%s' '$(echo SUBSTITUTED)'` | `$(echo SUBSTITUTED)` (literal) | `SUBSTITUTED` — **the single-quoted substitution was executed by the outer shell**, and its output became part of the inner command |
| `X=hello; printf '%s' "$X"` | `hello` | *(empty)* — outer shell expanded `$X` before the inner shell ran the assignment |
| `printf '%s' 'a"b'` | `a"b` | `a"b` (control, same) |
| `printf '%s' "double $HOME"` | `double /home/user` | `double /home/user` (control, same) |

### Why it matters

- Correctness: any command relying on single-quote protection, shell variables it sets itself, or literal `$`/backtick text (git format strings, grep patterns, paths containing `$`) silently misbehaves in VS Code while working on web.
- Safety: a fragment the caller deliberately quoted as data — e.g. a filename or format string containing `$(...)` — is executed by the extension host's outer shell, then its output is re-parsed as code by the inner shell.
- The 300 s `exec` timeout also only signals the outer shell; the inner shell is a grandchild and can outlive it (the web form's timeout kills the only shell).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `api:fs:exec` in `bridge-fs-runtime.ts` launches the command the web way: `spawn(shell, [shellFlag, cmd], …)` (or an equivalent argv form), with no string interpolation of the command into an outer shell command line.
- [ ] Result shape is preserved: per-command `{ command, success, exitCode, stdout, stderr, error? }`, trimmed output, non-zero exit reported (not thrown), and the git-read cache / in-flight dedupe behaviour unchanged.
- [ ] Timeout still bounds a command at 300 s and terminates the shell that is running it.
- [ ] Regression tests in `bridge-fs-runtime.test.js` style (mocked child process) pin the argv launch form, plus a behaviour test (or documented probe) showing the three divergent cases above now match the web form: single-quoted `$HOME` stays literal, single-quoted `$(...)` is not executed, and a variable assigned earlier in the same command is visible later in it.
- [ ] Windows behaviour is considered explicitly (`cmd.exe /c` via argv spawn) and noted in the PR, even if only POSIX is behaviour-tested.

title: fix(vscode): ensureOpenCodeProjectId writes the project ID to <worktree>/.git/opencode — creates a stray .git dir inside bare repos and never caches for separate git dirs (#720 twin)

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/vscode
labels.description: Package: vscode (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

The VS Code port of `ensureOpenCodeProjectId` has the exact defect filed for the web service in #720 — it always places the OpenCode project-ID file at `<primaryWorktree>/.git/opencode`, which is only correct for a plain primary checkout. #720's fix (PR #722) touches only `packages/web/server/lib/git/service.js` and its test, so the VS Code twin in `packages/vscode/src/gitService.ts` remains broken for the two layouts its own caller explicitly supports:

- **Bare repository:** it creates a stray `.git/` directory *inside* the user's bare repository and writes the ID there, a location that is not the repository's git dir at all.
- **Separate git dir** (where `<worktree>/.git` is a pointer file, not a directory): the write fails, the failure is swallowed, and the project ID is re-derived from a full `rev-list` on every worktree-context resolution.

## Evidence (verified on main `4ab427b37`)

- `packages/vscode/src/gitService.ts:1311-1338` — `ensureOpenCodeProjectId(primaryWorktree)`:
  - `:1312` `const gitDir = path.join(primaryWorktree, '.git');`
  - `:1313` `const idFile = path.join(gitDir, 'opencode');`
  - `:1336-1337` `fs.promises.mkdir(gitDir, { recursive: true }).catch(() => undefined)` and `fs.promises.writeFile(idFile, projectId, 'utf8').catch(() => undefined)` — both failures silently swallowed.
- Its only caller, `resolveWorktreeProjectContext` (`gitService.ts:1353ff`, ID call at `:1381`), deliberately supports these layouts:
  - `:1364-1366` comment: "A bare repository has no work tree, so `--show-toplevel` fails there; the bare directory itself still answers the object-level commands worktree creation runs against it."
  - `:1377-1379` comment: "`<root>/.git` resolves to the primary checkout; any other layout (a bare repository, a separate git dir) has no primary worktree, and the sandbox directory is the closest thing to one." — so for a bare repo, `primaryWorktree` **is the bare directory itself**, and `:1312` resolves to `<bare>/.git`.
  - The same function already resolves the real common dir at `:1371-1376` (`rev-parse --git-common-dir`) — `ensureOpenCodeProjectId` is the one place in the flow that still assumes the plain layout. The file also already has a portable `resolveGitDir` helper at `:527ff` (added for #648/#655/#656).
- Callers of `resolveWorktreeProjectContext`: `validateWorktreeCreate` (:1817), `previewWorktreeCreate` (:1965), `createWorktree` (:2225), `removeWorktree` (:2441), `canonicalizeWorktreeState` (:4316) — so the separate-git-dir case pays a `rev-list --max-parents=0 --all` re-derivation (`:1319-1323`) on every call, and the bare case mutates the user's repository with a directory git never asked for.
- The derived ID keys the legacy worktree root (`:1385`, `path.join(getOpenCodeDataPath(), 'worktree', projectID)`), so an ID cached in the wrong place also risks the VS Code runtime and any reader of the real `<git-common-dir>/opencode` (including the web service after #720's fix) disagreeing about the project's identity.

### Laptop probe (this run)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-vscode-projectid/probe.test.ts` on the laptop against the real exported `validateWorktreeCreate` from `gitService.ts` at `4ab427b37` (vscode module mocked per the existing `gitService.bare-repository.test.js` pattern; temp repos; bun test 3 pass):

- **Plain repo control:** validation ok; ID file at `<root>/.git/opencode` contains exactly the root commit hash — current behaviour correct here.
- **Bare repo** (`git clone --bare` into a directory that is itself the git dir): before the call, no `.git` entry and no `opencode` file in the bare repo; after `validateWorktreeCreate(bare)` returned ok, a stray `.git/` **directory** existed inside the bare repo containing the `opencode` ID file, while `<bare>/opencode` (the real git-common-dir location) still did not exist.
- **Separate git dir** (`git init --separate-git-dir <sepdir> <work>`; `rev-parse --git-common-dir` in the worktree prints `<sepdir>`): after validation returned ok, `<sepdir>/opencode` still did not exist — the ID is never cached anywhere readable — and the worktree's `.git` remained a pointer file (the mkdir/write through it failed silently).

## Why it matters

Worktree flows from bare clones are a supported, commented code path in the VS Code runtime (hub-style bare repos are a common way to drive multiple worktrees), and the VS Code extension is where worktree create/remove/validate actually run for desktop users. Today that path silently (a) writes a stray `.git/` directory and ID file into the user's bare repository where nothing will ever read them back as a git dir, and (b) for separate-git-dir layouts, silently never caches the ID at all. Both failures are invisible because the write errors are swallowed. After #720 lands, the web service will read/write the ID at the real git common dir while the VS Code runtime keeps using the wrong path, so the two runtimes can also diverge on where a project's cached ID lives.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] VS Code `ensureOpenCodeProjectId` resolves the repository's real git common dir (e.g. via the `--git-common-dir` value `resolveWorktreeProjectContext` already computes, or the existing `resolveGitDir` helper) and reads/writes the `opencode` ID file there, for plain, bare, linked-worktree, and separate-git-dir layouts alike.
- [ ] No `.git` directory is created inside a bare repository, and no write is attempted through a `.git` pointer file.
- [ ] A failed ID-file write is no longer silently swallowed without trace (at minimum a `console.warn` naming the path), or the caching is dropped deliberately with a comment saying so — matching whatever #720's landed fix does on the web side, so the two runtimes stay in parity.
- [ ] Tests in `packages/vscode/src/` (e.g. a sibling of `gitService.bare-repository.test.js`) cover: bare repository (ID file lands at `<bare>/opencode`, no `<bare>/.git` created) and separate-git-dir layout (ID persisted at the real git dir and re-read, not re-derived).
- [ ] Existing plain-checkout behaviour is unchanged: ID still read from / written to `<root>/.git/opencode`.

## Related

- #720 — the web-service original of this defect (fix PR #722 touches only `packages/web/`; this issue is the VS Code remainder, filed separately because #720 is already claimed/in-progress with a web-only PR).
