- `packages/web/server/lib/ui-auth/ui-auth.js:259-283` — `parseCookies` wraps `decodeURIComponent` in `try/catch` and falls back to the raw value.
- `packages/web/server/lib/security/request-security.js:86-90` — `getUiSessionTokenFromRequest` does the same.

`tunnel-auth.js` is the one parser that was missed.

## Evidence (verified on main `17966b1d3`)

- `tunnel-auth.js:424` — `getTunnelSessionFromRequest` calls `parseCookies(req.headers.cookie)`, which decodes **every** cookie on the request, not just `oc_tunnel_session`.
- Callers that reach it on ordinary requests:
  - `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/core-routes.js` (~:681) — the API auth middleware calls `requireTunnelSession` (tunnel-auth.js:449-465) for every `tunnel` / `unknown-public` scope request.
  - `core-routes.js` (~:689) — `GET /auth/session` calls `getTunnelSessionFromRequest` directly in an async handler.
  - `core-routes.js:48` — `isRequestAuthorized` calls it for tunnel/unknown-public scopes.
- **Laptop probe vs the real module** (fork at main `17966b1d3`, probe at laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-tunnel-cookie-20261031/probe.mjs`, calling `createTunnelAuth().getTunnelSessionFromRequest` with a stub request):
  - `Cookie: other=%` → **THREW `URIError: URI malformed`**
  - `Cookie: other=%E0%A4%A` → **THREW `URIError: URI malformed`**
  - `Cookie: oc_tunnel_session=abc; other=%zz` → **THREW** — a malformed *unrelated* cookie breaks the request even alongside a tunnel session cookie
  - `Cookie: session=plainvalue` → returned `null` (normal path unaffected)
- Cookies are shared across ports on the same host (the request-security parser's own comment at `request-security.js:76-79` calls this out for LAN/loopback hosts), so a malformed cookie set by any other local app or an earlier experiment rides along on tunnel requests. An unauthenticated remote caller can also send one deliberately.

## Why it matters

For tunnel / unknown-public scope requests, one malformed cookie value turns the expected `401 Tunnel authentication required` into a thrown `URIError` out of the auth middleware / `/auth/session` handler — a 500-class failure (or an unhandled rejection, depending on the handler) instead of a clean auth answer, for every request that browser makes. Tunnel access is the remote-access path for the whole UI; a stray cookie on the host permanently wedges it until the cookie expires or is cleared, with nothing in the error pointing at the cause. The guarded behaviour already exists twice in the same codebase; this parser just diverges from it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `parseCookies` in `tunnel-auth.js` never throws on a malformed percent-encoded value: it falls back to the raw value, matching `ui-auth.js`'s parser (or the two parsers are unified so they cannot diverge again).
- [ ] A request carrying a valid `oc_tunnel_session` cookie plus an unrelated malformed cookie still resolves its tunnel session; a request with only a malformed cookie gets the normal `401` tunnel-locked answer, not a 500.
- [ ] Regression tests (new `tunnel-auth.test.js` or the existing tunnel wiring tests) pin: malformed value in an unrelated cookie, malformed value in the session cookie itself, and truncated UTF-8 percent sequences (`%E0%A4%A`) — none throw.
- [ ] No behaviour change for well-formed cookies: session lookup, expiry, and revocation paths behave byte-identically.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for `cookie`, `decodeURIComponent`, `URIError`, `tunnel-auth`, and `malformed cookie`: no issue covers the tunnel-auth parser (the guarded ui-auth / request-security parsers are in-tree code, not issue-tracked work).

title: fix(web): contributor post-checkout hook is read whole with no size gate — inspectPostCheckoutHook stats the file but never checks stat.size before readFile

body:
## Summary

`inspectPostCheckoutHook` stats the contributor worktree's `post-checkout` hook — it already holds `stat` and checks `isFile()` and the execute bit — but **never checks `stat.size`** before `handle.readFile()` buffers the whole file. The content is then retained on the returned action (`content` + sha256 `contentDigest`) for the life of the inspection/plan, and read a second time whole by the snapshot verification in `network-operations.js`. This read runs during *inspection of contributor checkout actions* (`inspectContributorCheckoutActions`, called from `git/routes.js:387/425`) — i.e. on the trust path for someone else's repository, before any trust decision has been made. A contributor repo carrying an oversized `post-checkout` hook (a plain file in `.git/hooks`, not a script anyone would ever execute at that size) grows the web server's memory by the file's size, twice over, before the user is even shown what would run.

## Evidence (verified on main `3337f3b91`)

- `packages/web/server/lib/git/service.js:1435-1437` — `const stat = await handle.stat();` → `if (!stat.isFile() || (…exec bit…)) return null;` → `const content = await handle.readFile();` — no `stat.size` comparison anywhere in `inspectPostCheckoutHook` (:1426-1453).
- The same file already stat-gates a sibling read: `service.js:3304` refuses `stat.size > MAX_NEW_FILE_STAT_SIZE` (1 MiB, :3275) before reading a new file for the diff path; the project-icon discover route was stat-gated for the same read-before-cap shape in #1053.
- The retained content is load-bearing downstream, which is why a size gate (not a streaming rewrite) is the right shape: `network-operations.js` `snapshotCheckoutHook` (:2260) writes `action.content` to the snapshot file and re-reads it whole (:2282 `handle.readFile()`) to verify `contentDigest(bytes) === action.contentDigest` — an oversize hook is therefore buffered whole at least twice per execution.
- **Laptop probe vs the real module** (fork at main, `service.js` md5 `d8ce430f766faeceb7579a372d0c8296` identical to sandbox main; probe at laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-hook-read-cap-20261031/probe.mjs`): a scratch git repo whose `.git/hooks/post-checkout` is a 268,435,475-byte executable file — `inspectContributorCheckoutActions` returned the hook action with **`contentBytes: 268435475`** retained in full and a computed digest; RSS **+258 MB** for the single inspection.
- Existing git service tests cover the hook's presence/digest/trust flow with small scripts only; nothing pins an oversize hook.

## Why it matters

The contributor-checkout flow exists precisely to handle repositories whose content is not yet trusted: it inspects what a checkout would run (the post-checkout hook, the project start command, the setup command), digests it, and only executes after the digest is approved. An inspection step that buffers an unbounded file from that untrusted tree — before the digest/trust UI can intervene — is a memory-exhaustion hole in the guard itself. Real hooks are shell scripts of a few KiB; a named cap in the low MiB range loses nothing legitimate and closes the hole at the stat the code already performs.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `inspectPostCheckoutHook` refuses (returns `null`, exactly as for a missing/non-executable hook) when `stat.size` exceeds an explicit named cap sized for hook scripts (order of MiB; rationale recorded), checked from the already-fetched `stat` before `handle.readFile()` is called — an over-cap hook is never buffered.
- [ ] The refusal composes with the trust flow: an over-cap hook yields the same inspection result shape as an absent hook, so routes/digest computation in `inspectContributorCheckoutActions` and the snapshot path in `network-operations.js` need no compensating changes (or any needed change is included and explained).
- [ ] At-cap and ordinary hooks behave byte-identically: content, `contentDigest`, digest, and the snapshot/execute flow are unchanged.
- [ ] Regression tests pin: an over-cap executable post-checkout hook is treated as absent with `readFile` never consuming it whole (or the file's bytes never retained); an at-cap hook is still inspected with the correct digest.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for `post-checkout hook` and contributor-checkout read terms: no issue covers this read (only unrelated hits — #861 closed is the worktree start-command timeout; #46 is UI test isolation). The stat-gate precedents #1053 (project-icon discover) and the in-file `MAX_NEW_FILE_STAT_SIZE` gate at `service.js:3304` cover different reads; the VS Code twin does not have this inspection (its `gitService.ts` post-checkout handling at :1279 runs the hook directly in the worktree flow, a different mechanism — if a worker finds a shared read there, note it on this issue rather than filing a second one).

body:
## Unaddressed PR review finding — worktree start-command process group is not registered for server shutdown

**Source finding (CodeRabbit Minor — Stability & Availability, merged PR #880):**
- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/openchamber/pull/880 — "fix(web,vscode): terminate the worktree start-command process tree on timeout" (merged)
- Comment: https://github.com/developing-today/openchamber/pull/880#discussion_r4421275873 — coderabbitai[bot], 2026-10-30T07:11:46Z, on `packages/web/server/lib/git/service.js:2182`
- Reviewer, in essence: "Register the detached start-command process for server shutdown. `execWorktreeStartCommand` creates a separate POSIX process group, but it does not register the child with the existing live-tree cleanup. The shutdown path closes server resources and then exits; it does not kill this detached group. A running start command can therefore survive the web server and outlive its timeout. Add this child to the server's process-tree registry, and kill its process group during shutdown and on process exit."
- Note: the sibling Codex P2 findings on this PR (process-group escalation, bounded pipe cleanup) were all fixed with replies; this CodeRabbit finding received no reply.

**No-response evidence:**
- GraphQL `reviewThreads` for PR #880 (checked 2026-10-31): the CodeRabbit threads are `isResolved=false` and contain no replies; no commit after 2026-10-30T07:11:46Z on the PR addressed shutdown registration.

**Still live on current main (e60d22a06, verified 2026-10-31 by reading origin/main):**
- `packages/web/server/lib/git/service.js:2209-2219` — `execWorktreeStartCommand` still spawns the child directly with `detached: process.platform !== 'win32'` and never registers it anywhere; its only kill path is the in-process timeout/escalation timers, which die with the server process.
- `packages/web/server/lib/spaces/run-command.js:27,38-73` — the live-tree registry (`liveTrees`, `killLiveTrees`, the `process` exit listener, `liveTrees.add(child)`) exists and is used by `runCommand`, but `service.js` does not use it for the start-command child, so shutdown/exit cleanup cannot reach this process group.

**Dedupe:** searched open + closed issues 2026-10-31 for "start-command shutdown", "execWorktreeStartCommand shutdown", and PR #880 references; no issue tracks this.

## Acceptance criteria
- A worktree start command still running when the web server shuts down (or the process exits) has its process group killed — no detached start-command process survives the server.
- Normal completion and the existing timeout/escalation behaviour (PR #880 / #868) are unchanged; git service tests still pass, with coverage for the shutdown path where practical.
- Resolve by fixing the registration/cleanup, or by a documented decision on this issue explaining why the survival behaviour is acceptable.

title: fix(web): dev-tunnel WebSocket server has no maxPayload — a single frame up to the ws default 100 MiB bypasses the tunnel's 256 KiB pending and 1 MiB held caps

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

The dev-tunnel's WebSocket server is created with **no `maxPayload`**, so the `ws` default of **100 MiB per message** applies — while every byte cap the tunnel advertises (`MAX_PENDING_BYTES` 256 KiB before connect, `MAX_HELD_BYTES` 1,000,000 after connect) is checked only inside the `message` handler, i.e. *after* the `ws` layer has assembled the whole frame in the server process's memory. A single frame therefore bypasses both caps completely: on the connected path it is handed to `upstream.write(data)` in one write regardless of size (the socket buffers it in process memory and only then marks the connection backed-up), and the held-cap check at `runtime.js:194-196` only ever runs for frames that arrive *after* that. This is the exact whole-stream-in-memory failure #961 added the caps to prevent, reintroduced at frame granularity — and the module's own DOCUMENTATION claims the opposite ("bytes are held only up to a bounded cap and the connection is dropped past it").

## Evidence (verified on main `e60d22a06`)

- `packages/web/server/lib/dev-tunnel/runtime.js:81` — `new WebSocketServer({ noServer: true })`, no `maxPayload`. The bundled `ws@8.21.0` default is `maxPayload: 100 * 1024 * 1024` (`node_modules/ws/lib/websocket-server.js:74`; JSDoc: `options.maxPayload=104857600`).
- The caps are per-message and post-assembly: `MAX_PENDING_BYTES = 256 * 1024` (`runtime.js:43`) is checked at `:207` after the frame was pushed; `MAX_HELD_BYTES = 1_000_000` (`runtime.js:51`) is checked at `:194-196` only on the already-backed-up branch; the normal connected path at `:202` is `if (!upstream.write(data)) upstreamBackedUp = true;` with no size check on `data` at all.
- Sibling WebSocket servers in the same codebase all set the bound explicitly: `terminal/runtime.js:199` (`TERMINAL_WS_MAX_PAYLOAD_BYTES` 64 KiB), `dictation/runtime.js:126` (512 KiB), `guests/surface.js:585` (`VIEWER_MESSAGE_MAX_BYTES`), and the relay's upstream client at `relay/tunnel-host.js:518`. The dev-tunnel server is the one that was missed.
- `packages/web/server/lib/dev-tunnel/DOCUMENTATION.md` states the invariant this breaks: piping is back-pressured in every direction, "bytes are held only up to a bounded cap and the connection is dropped past it".
- **Laptop probe vs the real module** (fork at `e60d22a06`, `runtime.js` md5 `80a5d141d41ec1f622d0f79fad280930` identical to main; probe at laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-devtunnel-frame-20261031/`): the real runtime with a dev server that accepts but never reads; one single **16 MiB** WebSocket frame (16× the held cap, 64× the pending cap) — the client connection stayed **open** (`openSocketCount: 1`, no teardown, no warn), and when the dev server resumed reading it received **all 16,777,216 bytes**: the tunnel had held/forwarded the entire frame. (Probe note: under Bun a plain-`ws` control connection dies at 32 MiB for unrelated Bun/ws interop reasons, so the probe used 16 MiB; under Node the applicable ceiling is the full 100 MiB `ws` default.)
- Existing tests pin the streamed-chunk behaviour from #961 but nothing about frame size: `tunnel.test.js` has no `maxPayload` or single-oversize-frame case.

## Why it matters

The tunnel's clients are the desktop shell and the E2EE-relay renderer path — authenticated, but exactly the "client that can send large pastes / automated reconnecting client" surface the caps exist for, and the bytes land in the long-lived web server process that hosts every other session. #961's fix bounded the *stream*; without a frame bound, one message of up to 100 MiB is assembled whole by `ws`, then buffered whole again by the upstream socket write, before any cap in the file gets a chance to fire. The documented invariant is false as written.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The dev-tunnel `WebSocketServer` is created with an explicit, named `maxPayload` consistent with the tunnel's byte budget (at most `MAX_HELD_BYTES`, or a named constant with the rationale recorded); a frame past it is refused by the `ws` layer (close 1009) instead of being assembled and forwarded.
- [ ] The pending and held caps hold per-frame as well as per-stream: no single frame larger than the held cap is ever passed whole to `upstream.write` or retained whole in the pending/held queues.
- [ ] Regression tests in `dev-tunnel/tunnel.test.js` pin: a single frame over the cap closes the connection and the dev server receives none of it; a frame at/under the cap forwards byte-identically; the existing pending/held/backpressure tests pass unchanged.
- [ ] The receive path in `dev-tunnel/client.js` is checked in the same pass: apply the matching bound there, or record in the code/docs why host-generated chunk frames make it unnecessary.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for `maxPayload` (only #1017, the closed dictation reorder-buffer issue — different mechanism) and for `dev-tunnel` (#961 closed added the post-connect held/pending caps for streamed piping — this issue is the single-frame hole in those caps; #1018 closed is a test-infra flake; #233 closed is port validation). No open or closed issue covers the dev-tunnel server's missing `maxPayload` or single-frame cap bypass. Related: #1059 (open) covers the persistent-pty proxy's pre-open queue — a different module; if a worker fixes both, the `maxPayload` question for `persistent-pty/runtime.js:47` and `realtime-proxy.js:202` (also created without one) is worth the same one-line check, but they are not this issue's scope.

title: fix(web): dev-server scanner buffers lsof/netstat output with no byte cap — an oversize stream is retained whole and parsed into an authoritative empty result

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/triage

body:
## Problem

The dev-server discovery scanner in `packages/web/server/lib/dev-servers/routes.js` accumulates the spawned command's stdout with no byte cap. It is the one spawn-stdout accumulator in the web server that has only a time deadline and no size bound — every sibling runner caps output explicitly:

- `packages/web/server/lib/environment/runtime.js:52` — `MAX_COMMAND_OUTPUT_BYTES = 4 MiB`; at `:91-96` an over-cap stream kills the child and resolves `output-too-large`.
- `packages/web/server/lib/fs/workspace-file-names.js:14` — `DEFAULT_MAX_OUTPUT_BYTES = 16 MiB` for the `git ls-files` spawn; over-cap kills and resolves `null`.
- `packages/web/server/lib/guests/clone.js:185` — `MAX_CAPTURED_STDOUT_BYTES = 4 MiB`; over-cap kills and resolves `output-too-large`.

## Evidence (verified on main `e60d22a0601424dc4aa851fc6a01b18dee32a8be`)

- `packages/web/server/lib/dev-servers/routes.js:26-53` — `runCommand` spawns `lsof`/`netstat` and at `:46` does `child.stdout?.on('data', (chunk) => { stdout += String(chunk); })` with no length check. The only bound is `SCAN_TIMEOUT_MS = 2_500` (`:22`), which limits time, not bytes: a fast producer streams arbitrarily much inside 2.5 s.
- The Windows path (`:77`) runs `netstat -ano -p TCP`, which lists **every** TCP connection, not only listeners — output volume is a property of the host's network state, not of anything this module controls.
- The module's own header (`:9-12`) states the contract the overflow breaks: "A failed scan reports failure; it never reports an empty list, because a caller cannot tell 'nothing is running' from 'the scan broke'." An over-long stream is instead parsed whole and can resolve as an authoritative `ok: true` result.

### Laptop probe against the real module

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-devserver-cap-20261031/probe.mjs` on the laptop (`~/git/openchamber-fork` at `e60d22a06`), importing the real `createDevServerScanner` with an injected fake spawn that emits 64 MiB of chunk data and then closes with code 0:

```
{"command":"lsof-fake-64MiB","resultOk":true,"serversReturned":0,"killCalls":1,"rssGrowthMiB":129}
```

The whole 64 MiB was retained (RSS grew ~129 MiB — the `stdout +=` string concatenation copies as it grows), the child was never killed for size (the single `kill()` call is `finish()`'s own cleanup after close), and the garbage stream parsed into `ok: true, servers: []` — an authoritative empty success for input that was neither a scan nor empty.

There is also no test file for this module's scanner/runner: `packages/web/server/lib/dev-servers/` contains only `parse.js`, `parse.test.js`, and `routes.js`, so the fallback chain (lsof → /proc → failure) and the output handling are unpinned.

## Why it matters

Dev-server discovery runs on the machine OpenChamber serves from, including shared/dev hosts and Windows machines where `netstat -ano -p TCP` output scales with total connection count. An unbounded in-memory accumulation in a long-lived server process is the exact failure shape the sibling caps exist to prevent, and the silent `ok: true` empty result on garbage/overflow contradicts the module's documented never-report-empty-on-failure contract.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `runCommand` enforces a named byte cap on accumulated stdout (suggested: 4 MiB, matching `MAX_COMMAND_OUTPUT_BYTES` / `MAX_CAPTURED_STDOUT_BYTES` in the sibling runners, or a documented equivalent); on overflow it kills the child and resolves `null` — it never parses a truncated stream as a scan result.
- [ ] Overflow on the `lsof` path falls through to the existing `/proc/net/tcp` fallback, and overflow with no fallback left reports `{ ok: false, ... }`, never `ok: true` with an empty/partial listener list.
- [ ] Normal scans are unchanged: valid `lsof`/`netstat` output within the cap parses exactly as before, and the 2.5 s timeout behavior is preserved.
- [ ] Regression tests (new `routes.test.js` in the existing dev-servers test style, using the injected `spawn` seam) pin: over-cap output resolves as failure/fallback with the child killed, at-cap output parses normally, and the timeout path still resolves `null`.

## Dedup

Searched open and closed issues for dev-server / lsof / netstat / scanner: #264 (closed) covers parser port validation in `parse.js`, #274 (closed) covers preview announced-port range checks — neither touches `runCommand`'s output accumulation in `routes.js`. No open issue covers this.

Evidence:

## Still live on current main (verified 2026-10-31)

`packages/web/server/lib/environment/vault.js` on current main still serves the cache on a refresh request whenever the entry is fresh:

```js
const cached = values.get(reference);
const fresh = cached && now() - cached.at < ttlMs;
if (cached && (fresh || !refresh)) {
  resolved[name] = cached.value;
  ...
  return;
}
```

With `refresh: true` and a <5-minute-old cache entry, the cached value is returned and `op read` never runs — so Restart OpenCode right after a secret rotation launches with the stale secret, exactly what the reviewer flagged.

## Acceptance criteria

- A resolution with `refresh: true` (at least on the OpenCode launch path) re-reads the reference instead of serving a cached value.
- Non-refresh resolutions keep the TTL cache behaviour.
- A test pins: rotate-then-restart within the TTL picks up the new value.
- Or: resolve by a documented decision on this issue explaining why the TTL window is acceptable for launches.

title: fix(vscode): bridge api:fs:read has no byte cap — handleFsBridgeMessage reads the whole file while the web and local-fs-proxy twins cap at 16 MiB

labels.name: task/triage

labels.name: effort/s

body:
## Problem

The VS Code bridge's direct file-read handler has no byte cap. `handleFsBridgeMessage`'s `api:fs:read` case in `packages/vscode/src/bridge-fs-runtime.ts:285-303` resolves the path and then runs a bare `fs.promises.readFile(resolution.resolvedPath, 'utf8')` at `:297`, returning the whole content in the bridge response. There is no `stat` before the read and no size check anywhere in the case — its sibling `api:fs:stat` case in the same file (`:305+`) stats the file, so the information was always one case away.

Both twins cap this exact read at 16 MiB:

- Web: `GET /api/fs/read` — `packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.js:221` `MAX_READ_BYTES = 16 * 1024 * 1024`, stat gate at `:1321-1324` answering `413 { error: 'File too large to read' }` before any read (the #1026 fix).
- VS Code local-fs proxy: `packages/vscode/src/bridge-localfs-proxy-runtime.ts:45` `LOCAL_FS_READ_MAX_BYTES = 16 * 1024 * 1024`, stat gate at `:127-129` answering 413 before reading (the #1027 fix).

The direct bridge handler is the copy both passes missed — the same missed-twin pattern as #1027/#1051/#1061. Its caller is the VS Code webview's own file API: `packages/vscode/webview/api/files.ts:101` sends `api:fs:read` and expects `{ content, path }`, so a large file is materialized as one string in the extension host and again as the serialized bridge payload to the webview.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `e60d22a06`)

- `packages/vscode/src/bridge-fs-runtime.ts:285-303` — the full case: path check, `deps.resolveFileReadPath`, then bare `readFile` at `:297`; no stat, no cap constant in the file for reads (the file's only caps are for fs:exec output and the git-read cache).
- Caller/wiring: `packages/vscode/src/bridge.ts:109` dispatches to `handleFsBridgeMessage`; `packages/vscode/webview/api/files.ts:101` is the webview caller.
- Twins: web `fs/routes.js:221,1321-1324` (16 MiB, 413 before read); vscode proxy `bridge-localfs-proxy-runtime.ts:45,127-129` (16 MiB, 413 before read).
- Laptop probe against the real module (bun test, `vscode` mocked in the repo's test-harness shape; laptop fork file md5 `22813ee8c70df0b57816ee3cd9cda2f6`, identical to sandbox main `e60d22a06` for this file): a 64 MiB file on disk was returned whole — `success: true`, `contentLength: 67108864` — with a small-file control (`hello`) reading normally. Probe: laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-bridge-fs-read-20261031/probe.test.mjs`.
- Dedup: `gh search issues` for `bridge-fs-runtime` returned no issue covering this handler; #1027 (closed) is scoped to the local-fs proxy copy in `bridge-localfs-proxy-runtime.ts`, and #1026 (closed) to the web route. Neither touches `handleFsBridgeMessage`.

## Why it matters

The Files view and every other webview consumer of `readFile` in VS Code mode go through this handler. Opening a large file in a workspace — a generated bundle, a data dump, a log, a minified asset — loads it whole into the long-lived extension host and then copies it across the bridge, instead of failing fast with the same 16 MiB / too-large answer both twins already give. The cap is not a new policy decision: two implementations of this read already settled it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `api:fs:read` stats the resolved file before reading and refuses a file over an explicit named cap (16 MiB, matching `MAX_READ_BYTES` / `LOCAL_FS_READ_MAX_BYTES`, or a documented equivalent) with a `{ success: false, error }` bridge failure that names the size limit — the file is never read whole first.
- [ ] A non-file (directory) target fails the way the twins fail it, instead of surfacing a raw `readFile` error.
- [ ] At-cap and ordinary files return `{ content, path }` exactly as before; a missing file keeps its current error behavior.
- [ ] Regression tests pin: over-cap file rejected without being read whole, at-cap file still returns its content, and the small-file path is unchanged.

title: fix(quota): Antigravity local-store fallback reads OpenChamber's process.env database, not the managed OpenCode's launch-environment database (PR #860)

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/pr-diff-review
labels.description: Filed by the pr-diff-review job

labels.name: priority/normal

labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Finding

PR #860 added an Antigravity fallback: when the served OpenCode credential projection yields no candidate, the provider reads this machine's OpenCode credential store directly — but only when `credentialSourceUsesLocalStore()` says the connected OpenCode is known to use this machine's store. That gate returns `true` for any managed (OpenChamber-launched) OpenCode. The direct read, however, resolves the database path from OpenChamber's own `process.env`, while the managed OpenCode runs with a launch environment that can carry different `OPENCODE_DB` / `XDG_DATA_HOME` values (user/saved environment overlaid at launch). When they differ, the fallback reads the wrong database: it can miss the connected runtime's real Google login, or surface an unrelated Google login from the default-location store and refresh/report that account's quota as the connected one.

Codex raised this on PR #860 (comment 4420160018, P2) and it was not addressed in-PR or filed afterward; the merged code and current main still have the shape below.

## Evidence

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/openchamber/pull/860 (merged 6c5faca7f814b49548cfbcc6cf2e81960797fe77, for #858). Codex P2 comment 4420160018: "Resolve the fallback database from the managed launch environment."
- Current main `163f002d3627a39c47b694ad36ed13e47159b430`:
  - `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/auth.js:351-352` — `readLocalOpenCodeCredentials()` calls `openCodeLocalCredentialSource()` with no options, so `env` defaults to `process.env` (`auth.js:218`); the DB path is resolved from that env by `resolveOpenCodeDbPath` (`auth.js:147-149`, honouring `XDG_DATA_HOME` / `OPENCODE_DB`).
  - `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/auth.js:120-125` — `usesLocalStore()` returns `true` whenever `getLaunchEnvironment()` is non-null (any managed launch), with no check that the launch environment's database location matches the reader's.
  - `packages/web/server/index.js:1652` — the source is wired with `getLaunchEnvironment: () => openCodeLifecycleRuntime.getManagedOpenCodeProcessEnv()`.
  - `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/lifecycle.js:1084-1105` — the managed process env is built as shell env + `process.env` + `resolveUserEnvironment()` (the user's saved variables) + managed additions, and stored as `managedProcessEnv`; a saved `OPENCODE_DB` / `XDG_DATA_HOME` therefore reaches the managed OpenCode but not the fallback reader.
  - Sole caller: `packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/antigravity/index.js:62` — `pushStoreAuth(await readLocalOpenCodeCredentials())` under the `credentialSourceUsesLocalStore()` gate.

## Why it matters

The fallback exists to stop a signed-in user reading as "Not configured" (#858). Reading a different database than the connected runtime's reintroduces that failure in one direction (the real login is in the managed DB, the default-location DB is absent/empty) and creates a worse one in the other: an unrelated Google login sitting in the default-location store is refreshed and reported as the connected account's Antigravity quota — a wrong-account surface in a credential path.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The direct local-store read resolves its database from the connected runtime's environment: for a managed OpenCode, the launch environment (`getManagedOpenCodeProcessEnv()`) supplies `OPENCODE_DB` / `XDG_DATA_HOME` / `HOME` to the reader; for a loopback external OpenCode, the fallback is disabled when the runtime's database location cannot be established (per the Codex remedy on PR #860).
- [ ] A test pins the divergence: managed launch env points at a store holding a Google login while `process.env` points elsewhere (and vice versa) — the fallback reads the launch-env store, and does not surface a login that exists only in the `process.env` store.
- [ ] Existing Antigravity credential-resolution tests (served projection, store-read failure state, external-host exclusion) still pass.

## Problem

The VS Code bridge's update-check read has no byte cap on either branch. In `packages/vscode/src/bridge-system-runtime.ts` (`api:openchamber:update-check`, fetch at `:308`), the success path returns `await response.json()` (`:323`) and the error path returns `await response.text()` (`:319`) — both buffer the whole body in the extension host. The only bound is `AbortSignal.timeout(10_000)`, which limits time, not bytes.

The endpoint is operator-configured: `packages/vscode/src/bridge.ts:67` sets `updateCheckUrl: process.env.OPENCHAMBER_UPDATE_API_URL || 'https://api.openchamber.dev/v1/update/check'` — the same env override and the same default endpoint as the web server's update check.

The web twin was already fixed for exactly this: #1047 capped all of `package-manager.js`'s update-check reads, and `packages/web/server/lib/package-manager.js:31,45` now reads via `readBoundedResponseText` with `UPDATE_RESPONSE_MAX_BYTES = 1 MiB`. The vscode copy was missed — the same missed-twin pattern as #1051 (vscode upgrade-status registry read).

## Evidence (verified this run, main `163f002d3`)

- `packages/vscode/src/bridge-system-runtime.ts:308-324`: `fetch(deps.updateCheckUrl, { method: 'POST', signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10_000) })`; `:319` error branch `await response.text()`, `:323` success branch `await response.json()` — no bounded-read helper, no size check.
- `packages/vscode/src/bridge.ts:67,153`: the URL is the operator-configured `OPENCHAMBER_UPDATE_API_URL` override or the api.openchamber.dev default, passed in as `deps.updateCheckUrl`.
- Web twin: `packages/web/server/lib/package-manager.js:28` (same env/default URL), `:31` `UPDATE_RESPONSE_MAX_BYTES = 1 * 1024 * 1024`, `:45` bounded read.
- Laptop probe against the real module (bun test, `vscode` mocked; fork at `163f002d3`, file md5-identical to sandbox main): `handleSystemBridgeMessage({ type: 'api:openchamber:update-check' })` with a stubbed fetch streaming a 32 MiB JSON body with no `content-length` — pulled all 33,554,432 bytes, returned `success: true` with `latestVersion: "9.9.9"` and the full 33,554,375-char `pad`, RSS +105 MB. Probe: laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-vscode-updatecheck-cap-20261031/probe.test.mjs`.
- Dedup: `gh search issues` for vscode update-check / bridge-system terms returned no covering issue; #1047 is scoped to `packages/web/server/lib/package-manager.js` only.

## Why it matters

An operator-configured endpoint is exactly the class #1047 treated as untrusted-size: a misconfigured or hostile update server can push an arbitrarily large body into the long-lived extension host on a routine, automatic surface (the update check runs without a user click in the loop). The error branch is the same bug with extra reach — an error page of any size is also buffered whole and then handed back as the bridge error string.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Both update-check branches read through a bounded read with an explicit named cap (1 MiB, matching the web twin's `UPDATE_RESPONSE_MAX_BYTES`, or a documented equivalent).
- [ ] An over-cap success body (including chunked, no `content-length`) never parses whole; the handler returns its existing `{ success: false, error }` shape.
- [ ] An over-cap error body is truncated/bounded before it becomes the bridge error string.
- [ ] Normal behavior is unchanged: a valid at-cap update-check response returns the same `data`; a small error body returns the same error text; the 10 s deadline is preserved.
- [ ] Regression tests pin over-cap rejection on both branches and at-cap success.

## Summary

The VS Code bridge's per-file diff view has **no size limit on the working-tree side**: `getGitFileDiff` reads the entire modified file into the extension host with `vscode.workspace.fs.readFile` and converts it whole to a UTF-8 string, with no stat, no size check, and no binary sniff beforehand. Every sibling read around it is bounded — the staged side goes through the bridge git exec runtime, which caps output at 20 MiB and fails closed — so this is the one uncapped copy, and it is the exact twin of the web defect tracked in #1054 (`getFileDiff`'s working-tree branch), which is scoped to `packages/web` only.

## Evidence (verified on main `bfc55dd93`)

- `packages/vscode/src/gitService.ts:2833-2834` — unstaged branch: `const modifiedBytes = await vscode.workspace.fs.readFile(fileUri); modified = Buffer.from(modifiedBytes).toString('utf8');`. There is no `fs.stat` anywhere in `gitService.ts` (grep-verified), so nothing consults the file's size before the read.
- The bridge adds no guard: `packages/vscode/src/bridge-git-runtime.ts:291-300` (`api:git/file-diff`) passes `directory`/`path`/`staged` straight to `getGitFileDiff` and returns `original` + `modified` verbatim.
- The git-show sides are bounded and fail closed: `packages/vscode/src/bridge-git-process-runtime.ts:109` sets `GIT_EXEC_DEFAULT_MAX_OUTPUT_BYTES = 20 MiB`, and on overflow `execGit` returns `exitCode: 1` with an `output-too-large` stderr (`:196`) — the staged branch of `getGitFileDiff` (`gitService.ts:2828-2830`) then yields an empty `modified` rather than a truncated one. Only the `fs.readFile` side has no bound at all.
- No test pins this function: `getGitFileDiff` has zero references in `packages/vscode/src/*.test.*` (grep-verified).
- **Laptop probe vs the real module** (bun, mock `vscode` module in the same shape as the repo's own `gitService.*.test.js` harness, fork at `bfc55dd93` with `gitService.ts` md5-identical to main; probe at laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-vscode-gitdiff-20261031/probe.test.mjs`): temp git repo with a 64 MiB text file committed, then modified in the working tree; `getGitFileDiff(repo, 'big.txt', false)` returned `modifiedLength: 67108878` — the whole file — with RSS **+304 MB** in the host process for one diff view of one file.

## Why it matters

The diff view is a routine UI surface: the git panel renders per-file diffs on click, and when the UI is backed by the VS Code bridge this function serves it. Repos routinely contain large tracked text files (generated code, data snapshots, vendored bundles), and a single click on a modified one allocates its full size several times over in the extension host (bytes + UTF-8 string + bridge payload). The web server got this exact fix queued as #1054; the extension host — a process whose memory pressure destabilizes the whole editor — was missed because #1054 is web-scoped.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `getGitFileDiff`'s working-tree branch checks the file size before reading (e.g. `vscode.workspace.fs.stat`) and refuses or truncates above an explicit named cap, returning a shape the UI can render as "file too large to diff" rather than the whole content or a silent empty diff; triage picks the cap (guidance: align with the web fix in #1054 or the bridge exec runtime's 20 MiB).
- [ ] Small-file diff behavior is unchanged (original/modified/path/submodule shapes, staged and unstaged).
- [ ] Regression tests in the vscode gitService test family pin: an over-cap modified file is not read whole, an at-cap file still diffs normally, and the staged path is unaffected.
- [ ] Cross-link #1054 both ways so the web and vscode copies land with one consistent cap story.

## Dedup

## Summary

`POST /api/projects/:projectId/icon/discover` enforces its 5 MB icon limit **after** buffering the whole file: the handler reads the selected favicon from the project directory with a bare `fsPromises.readFile()` and only then checks `bytes.length > projectIconMaxBytes`. The size limit therefore does not bound memory at all — a favicon-named file of any size in a project the user opens is read into the web server's memory in full before being rejected. The house pattern elsewhere in this codebase is stat-before-read (e.g. the fs preview route rejects on `stats.size` before `readFile`, and #1026 pinned stat-before-read for `/api/fs/read`).

## Evidence (verified on main `5f8281596`)

- `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/project-icon-routes.js:415` — discover handler: `const bytes = await fsPromises.readFile(selected.path);` with no preceding `stat` or size gate. The 5 MiB check is at `:419-421`, after the buffer exists: `if (bytes.length > projectIconMaxBytes) return 400 'Discovered icon exceeds size limit (5 MB)'`.
- `selected.path` is a file inside the user's project tree, found by `fsSearchRuntime.searchFilesystemFiles(project.path, { query: 'favicon', ... })` (`:390-395`) and filtered only by the name pattern `favicon.(ico|png|svg|jpg|jpeg|webp)` (`:398-403`) — content and size are whatever the repository contains. Any cloned/opened repo can carry a multi-GB `favicon.png`.
- Contrast in the same repo: `packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.js:1532-1538` stats first and returns 413 when `stats.size > MAX_SERVE_BYTES`, and only then calls `readFile`.
- The sibling upload path in the same file (`:106`) checks decoded bytes from a data URL — that body is already in memory by construction, so post-check is correct there; the discover path is the one that reads from disk unbounded.
- **Laptop probe vs the real module** (bun, `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-icon-discover-cap-20261031/probe.mjs`, module copied verbatim from main `5f8281596`): routes registered with the real `registerProjectIconRoutes`, `fsPromises.readFile` stubbed to materialize a 512 MiB buffer and `fsPromises.stat` stubbed to record calls, search stubbed to return one `favicon.png` entry. Result: `fsCalls` contained exactly one call — `readFile` (stat was **never called**) — process RSS grew **514 MiB**, and only then did the handler return `400 {error: "Discovered icon exceeds size limit (5 MB)"}`. The rejection works; the memory spike the limit exists to prevent happens anyway.
- Trigger: the UI's `discoverProjectIcon` store action (`packages/ui/src/stores/useProjectsStore.ts:967-973`) POSTs to this route when a project icon is (re)discovered.

## Why it matters

The web server is a long-lived process serving the whole UI. One discovery click on a project containing an oversized favicon-named file (a bloated asset, a renamed archive, a hostile repo) allocates the file's full size in server memory before the 5 MB limit gets a say — a 2 GB `favicon.png` is a 2 GB allocation, repeated per click. Every other file-serving surface in this server stats before it reads; this route is the odd one out, and its own limit constant shows the intent was to bound exactly this.

## Acceptance criteria

- The discover handler rejects a selected favicon whose on-disk size exceeds `projectIconMaxBytes` (5 MiB) **before** reading its contents — e.g. `fsPromises.stat(selected.path)` size gate ahead of `readFile`, returning the same `400 {error: 'Discovered icon exceeds size limit (5 MB)'}` shape; the zero-byte case keeps returning the existing empty-icon 400.
- Regression tests in `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/project-icon-routes.test.js` pin: an over-cap favicon is rejected with `readFile` never called (or never called for the selected path), and an at-cap favicon is still discovered and stored successfully.
- Behavior for normal favicons is unchanged (discovery, scoring, persistence); the upload (data-URL) path is out of scope — its check is already as early as possible.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for `project icon`, `favicon`, and icon/readFile size terms: no hits. The bounded-read series (#1006/#1015/#1021/#1026/#1040/#1047/#1051) covers network bodies and `/api/fs/read`; none covers the project-icon discover route's read-before-check.

Its URL is **operator-configured**: `UPDATE_CHECK_URL` at `package-manager.js:27` is `process.env.OPENCHAMBER_UPDATE_API_URL || 'https://api.openchamber.dev/v1/update/check'`, so this is not a fixed trusted endpoint — the same exposure class as #1040 (user-configured npm registry).
- `package-manager.js:156` — `fetchLatestForkRelease()` does `await response.json()` on the GitHub releases list (`?per_page=30`).
- `package-manager.js:113` — `resolveAndroidApkUrl()` does `await response.json()` on the GitHub release-by-tag response (mobile update path).

## Evidence (probe, this run)

Probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-oc-pkgmgr-cap-20261031/probe.mjs`) against the **real** `package-manager.js` at `4a68d6a28`, with `fetch` stubbed to stream a >32 MiB JSON body in 64 KiB chunks and a byte counter on the stream:

- Env-configured API mode (`postUpdateCheck`): `pulledBytes: 33554489`, result version `9.9.9` parsed and returned — the whole body was consumed.
- Fork-release mode (`fetchLatestForkRelease`): `pulledBytes: 33554537`, result version `9.9.9` — likewise uncapped.

The sibling update-notes reader in the same feature area already does this right: `packages/web/server/lib/changelog/update-notes.js` caps its (fixed-URL) index fetch at `CHANGELOG_INDEX_MAX_BYTES` = 1 MiB via `readBoundedResponseText` (`packages/web/server/lib/shared/response-body.js:13`), with the comment "The deadline bounds time, the cap bounds memory." The package-manager paths were missed by the #1006 / #1040 bounded-read series.

## Why it matters

The update check runs in the long-lived web server. A compromised, misconfigured, or simply wrong operator-configured update endpoint (or an oversized GitHub response) can grow server memory without bound on a routine, automatically triggered check — the exact failure mode the bounded-read series (#1006, #1015, #1021, #1040) has been closing endpoint by endpoint.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] All three reads in `package-manager.js` (`postUpdateCheck`, `fetchLatestForkRelease`, `resolveAndroidApkUrl`) go through `readBoundedResponseText` (or the shared bounded-call primitive) with an explicit per-call byte cap (1 MiB is the house size for JSON of this shape; justify any larger value in code).
- [ ] An over-cap body fails the check the same way other failures already do: `checkForUpdates()` resolves to `null` / the helper returns `undefined` — no throw escapes to callers, and the body stream is cancelled rather than drained.
- [ ] Regression tests in `package-manager.test.js` pin the over-cap behavior for at least the env-configured API path and the fork-release path (chunked/streamed oversize body, not just a large `content-length`), mirroring the existing bounded-read tests elsewhere.
- [ ] Existing `package-manager.test.js` update-check tests still pass unchanged in behavior for normal-sized responses.

title: fix(ui): mobile release comparator folds prereleases into releases — an installed beta is never offered the matching stable release

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/ui
labels.description: Package: ui (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

The mobile direct release check's version comparator folds a prerelease into its release, so an installed prerelease build is treated as already running the stable release and is never offered it. This is the one copy the #180–#188 version-parser series missed: that series established the fleet contract (and #185 named this exact defect in the Electron copy — "a prerelease part is silently folded into the release number"), and the web server copy now implements it, but the UI mobile copy still strips the prerelease away.

## Evidence (verified on main `0d3a8b34b`)

- `packages/ui/src/lib/mobileReleaseUpdate.ts:43-51` — `versionParts()` does `version.trim().replace(/^v/, '').split('-')[0]`, discarding any prerelease suffix before parsing, and `compareReleaseVersions` (:57-68) therefore has no prerelease notion at all:
  - `compareReleaseVersions('2.3.3', '2.3.3-beta.1') === 0` — the stable release reads as *equal to* its own prerelease.
  - `compareReleaseVersions('2.3.4', '2.3.3+45') === 0` — a `+build` suffix is not stripped (the server copy strips it), so part `'3+45'` fails the `/^\d+$/` test, `versionParts` returns `null`, and the comparator answers 0 for *every* comparison against such an installed version.
- `packages/ui/src/lib/mobileReleaseUpdate.ts:99` (in `fetchLatestMobileRelease`) — `if (compareReleaseVersions(version, currentVersion) <= 0) return null;`, so both cases above settle as "no update".
- The contract this diverges from: `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/routes.js` `parseVersionForComparison` strips `+build`, records a `prerelease` flag, and orders a prerelease below its release; the behavior is pinned in `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/routes-upgrade.test.js:149-151` ("Parseable versions still compare normally, prerelease included": current `2.0.2` vs latest `2.0.2-beta.1` → not available, i.e. prerelease < release). The routes.js comment even cites `versionParts` as its strictness reference — for digit parsing only; the prerelease semantics were never carried over.
- `packages/ui/src/lib/mobileReleaseUpdate.test.ts` pins digit strictness and equality but has no prerelease or `+build` case, so the divergence is unpinned, not a tested design choice.
- Laptop probe vs the real module (file byte-identical to main, sha256 `963861d6…`; probe `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-mobile-version-20261031/` on the laptop, bun test): `stable vs installed beta of same version: 0`, `next stable vs installed beta: 1`, `build-metadata installed ('2.3.4' vs '2.3.3+45'): 0`.

## Why it matters

`fetchLatestMobileRelease` exists for exactly the phones the server check cannot reach — its header comment: a phone that "has not connected yet — or whose server predates the fork's update route — never hears about a new release. This check needs nothing but the app itself." A null from the comparator is the only answer those phones get. A user who sideloaded a prerelease APK (or runs a build whose versionName carries `+build` metadata) is silently stranded on it: the direct check never offers the matching stable release, and in the `+build` case never offers any release at all. The four other copies were all fixed to one contract in #180–#188; this surface still answers differently for the same two version strings.

Scope notes: GitHub's `/releases/latest` never returns a prerelease tag, so the left-hand side is always a stable release in this flow — the defect bites through the *installed* version string (right-hand side). The fix is comparator-local.

## Acceptance criteria

- `compareReleaseVersions` orders a prerelease below the same numeric release (`compareReleaseVersions('2.3.3', '2.3.3-beta.1') > 0`, and the mirror comparison `< 0`), matching the semantics pinned for the server copy in `routes-upgrade.test.js`.
- A `+build` suffix on either side is ignored for ordering instead of making the version unparseable (`compareReleaseVersions('2.3.4', '2.3.3+45') > 0`).
- Existing pinned behavior is unchanged: strict digit parsing (an unparseable version still never claims an update — `compareReleaseVersions('2.4.0', 'dev') === 0`), `v` prefix, missing-part padding (`'2.3'` vs `'2.3.0'` equal).
- New unit tests in `mobileReleaseUpdate.test.ts` pin the prerelease and `+build` cases above; the existing suite passes.
- No change to the fetch, deadline, or response-schema behavior of `fetchLatestMobileRelease`.

body:
## Finding

The quota surface exposes a `google` provider that reads as a separate Google/Gemini-API quota pool (per-model `daily` windows). It is not a separate pool. Verified 2026-10-31 against the source:

- `packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/google/api.js` calls `POST https://cloudcode-pa.googleapis.com/v1internal:retrieveUserQuota` with an `antigravity/1.11.5` user-agent — the Code Assist / Antigravity subscription backend, not the Gemini API (generativelanguage).
- `providers/google/auth.js` resolves the Gemini CLI OAuth entry (`google`/`google.oauth`) — the same Google account subscription the Antigravity provider reads via `v1internal:retrieveUserQuotaSummary` on the same hosts.
- `providers/google/transforms.js` stamps every returned bucket with a synthetic `daily` window regardless of the bucket's real window — which is why, in the 2026-10-31 08:14 CDT snapshot, the 'google daily' Claude rows reset at exactly the Antigravity Claude weekly reset (Sun Nov 1 3:23 AM) and the Gemini rows at the Antigravity 5h boundary (1:04 PM).

## Why it matters

Quota accounting treats 'google daily' as independent headroom (it appears as its own line in fleet quota summaries), double-counting the one Pro-plan subscription. There is no separate Gemini API quota in play — the `google` routing provider sits in `disabled_providers`, and no AI Studio API-key quota is read anywhere. The mislabel has already caused operator confusion about whether a second Google pool exists.

## Acceptance criteria

- The quota UI/API no longer presents the `google` read as an independent pool: either merge it into the antigravity surface, or label it explicitly as the same Code Assist subscription viewed per-model.
- The synthetic `daily` window label is replaced with each bucket's real window/reset semantics (or the projection is removed).
- Fleet-facing quota summaries derived from this surface stop listing 'google' as separate capacity.

Found via: operator question + source verification in chat, 2026-10-31.

title: fix(web): upgrade-status latest-version read has no byte cap — fetchLatestOpenCodeVersion buffers the whole registry body from a user-configured npm registry

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`GET /api/opencode/upgrade-status` resolves the latest OpenCode version by fetching the `@opencode/cli/latest` document from the **user-configured npm registry** — and reads the body with a bare, uncapped `response.json()`.

Evidence on main `ef162e6be`:

- `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/routes.js:94-103` — `fetchLatestOpenCodeVersion` builds the request with `resolveNpmRegistryRequest('@opencode/cli', 'latest')`, applies only a 10 s deadline (`AbortSignal.timeout(10_000)` at :98), then does `const payload = await response.json()` at :103 with no byte cap.
- The registry is not a fixed endpoint: `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/npm-registry-config.js` (`registryFor`) takes it from `npm_config_registry` / `NPM_CONFIG_REGISTRY`, scoped env vars, or the user's `~/.npmrc` — including private mirrors — and `authFor` attaches npmrc credentials to the request. The route's own test (`routes-upgrade.test.js`, "uses the configured registry for the v2 package version…") pins a mirror at `mirror.example.com` as a supported configuration.
- It runs on every upgrade-status call: `routes.js:204` invokes it in `Promise.all` for `GET /api/opencode/upgrade-status`.

This is the one registry read the earlier caps missed:

- #1006 capped the three public-internet JSON reads, and `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/npm-registry.js:122` now reads its packument through `readBoundedResponseText(response, NPM_PACKUMENT_MAX_BYTES)` (16 MiB, `npm-registry.js:16`). `fetchLatestOpenCodeVersion` in `routes.js` uses the same registry resolver but not the bounded reader.
- #1021 established the same principle for GitLab: a body read from a user-configured instance gets a byte cap even though the document is normally small, because the server on the other end is not under OpenChamber's control.

## Reproduction (verified this run)

Laptop probe against the real route module (`registerOpenCodeRoutes` from `routes.js` on main `ef162e6be`, harness mirroring `routes-upgrade.test.js`, global `fetch` stubbed):

- `/api/info` answered `{version: '2.0.21'}`.
- The registry `/@opencode%2Fcli/latest` request answered a **streaming (no `Content-Length`) JSON body of 32 MiB**: `{"version":"2.0.22","padding":"<~32 MiB of x>"}` served in 64 KiB chunks.
- Result: `GET /api/opencode/upgrade-status` returned **200** with `latestVersion: '2.0.22'`, and the server consumed **all 33,554,432 bytes** — the whole body was buffered and parsed. A streaming body defeats any declared-length check, so only a streaming cap (`readBoundedResponseText`) bounds this.

Probe: laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-upgrade-registry-cap-20261031/probe-upgrade-cap.test.js` (vitest, 1 passed).

A compromised, misconfigured, or merely pathological mirror registry can therefore grow web-server memory without bound on a routine UI status poll, and a slow-drip body is only bounded by the 10 s deadline's byte rate, not by size.

## Why it matters

- The `/latest` document is a few hundred bytes in practice; there is no legitimate need to buffer megabytes for it, and every sibling registry/JSON read in this codebase now carries an explicit cap — this is the remaining outlier on the same resolver.
- The endpoint is polled by the UI to announce updates, so the exposure is on a hot, unauthenticated-registry path rather than a rare admin action.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The registry `/latest` body in `fetchLatestOpenCodeVersion` is read through a bounded reader (e.g. `readBoundedResponseText` from `lib/shared/response-body.js`) with a named cap appropriate to a single-version document (suggested 1 MiB; anything ≤ the 16 MiB packument cap is acceptable if justified in the change).
- [ ] An over-cap body (including a chunked body with no `Content-Length`) fails the lookup with a clear error surfaced as the route's existing 500 error shape — it is never parsed, and no partial/`latestVersion` result is produced.
- [ ] Regression tests in `routes-upgrade.test.js` (or a sibling test file) pin: over-cap streaming body → error shape and the body stream is cancelled/stops being consumed; a normal small `{version}` body still resolves `latestVersion` exactly as before.
- [ ] No behavior change for the `/api/info` half of upgrade-status or for `lookupNpmPackage` in `npm-registry.js`.

title: docs(web): shared DOCUMENTATION.md still describes self-handoff's timeout parser as the isInteger variant — #832 changed it to isSafeInteger bounded at 2^31-1

labels.name: kind/docs

labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator

body:
## Problem

`packages/web/server/lib/shared/DOCUMENTATION.md` — the contract doc the shared-primitive modules point readers at — still describes `opencode/self-handoff.js`'s `resolveHandoffTimeoutMs` as the deliberate `Number.isInteger` variant of the strict parser. That stopped being true when #832 was fixed (commit `485beac90`, "bound timer-feeding env readers at 2^31-1 ms").

What the doc says (`DOCUMENTATION.md:159-167`, "What stays out"):

> It checks `Number.isInteger`, where the shared spellings check `Number.isSafeInteger`, so a digit string beyond the safe-integer range (26 digits, say) yields that huge value there and the fallback here. … It stays local under design rule 5 — a copy that answers differently for a real input is recorded, not silently redefined — until the design owner rules the difference a bug or a feature.

What the code does now (`packages/web/server/lib/opencode/self-handoff.js:31-41`, main `2cf060b20`):

```js
return Number.isSafeInteger(value) && value > 0 && value <= 2_147_483_647 ? value : DEFAULT_HANDOFF_TIMEOUT_MS;
```

So on current main:

- The check is `Number.isSafeInteger`, exactly like the shared spellings — the claimed difference no longer exists.
- A beyond-safe-integer digit string yields the **fallback** there too, not "that huge value".
- The parser additionally bounds at 2^31-1 ms (a larger configured timeout falls back to the default rather than collapsing to a ~1 ms timer) — a real, deliberate difference from the unbounded shared positive parser that the doc never mentions.
- The "until the design owner rules" framing is stale: the difference was ruled on and fixed in #832.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `2cf060b20`)

- `packages/web/server/lib/shared/DOCUMENTATION.md:159-167` — the stale entry, quoted above.
- `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/self-handoff.js:40` — `Number.isSafeInteger(value) && value > 0 && value <= 2_147_483_647`.
- `git log` for self-handoff.js: `485beac90 fix(web,vscode): bound timer-feeding env readers at 2^31-1 ms (#832)` is the change that replaced the `isInteger` spelling.
- The shared spellings the doc contrasts against: `packages/web/server/lib/shared/parse-int.js:22,34` (`Number.isSafeInteger`).
- Dedup: `gh search issues` for "DOCUMENTATION self-handoff" and "isInteger documentation stale" over open + closed returned nothing; the open list was reviewed fresh this run. (Found earlier as a review-finding in the fleet backlog, never filed.)

## Why it matters

This DOCUMENTATION.md is the recorded contract for the shared-primitives design (#802/#804): modules link to it as the spec, and its "What stays out" section is where future consolidation work decides which local copies may be migrated and which must not be touched. As written, it tells the next agent that self-handoff's parser (a) behaves differently from the shared one for huge inputs — it doesn't — and (b) is frozen pending a design ruling that already happened. Both errors point future work in the wrong direction: either preserving a difference that is gone, or re-litigating #832.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The `self-handoff.js` entry in `packages/web/server/lib/shared/DOCUMENTATION.md` matches the code on main: `Number.isSafeInteger` check, fallback for beyond-safe-integer spellings, and the 2^31-1 ms upper bound with its ~1 ms timer-collapse rationale.
- [ ] The entry's disposition is accurate: if the parser stays local, the stated reason is the real remaining one (the 2^31-1 timer bound the shared positive parser does not impose), not the retired `isInteger` difference or a pending design ruling.
- [ ] No other statement in the doc changes meaning; no code changes.

body:
## Finding

The quota deadline fixes in PRs #846 (Kimi) and #831 (NanoGPT) added the right 15 s `AbortSignal.timeout` to the providers' fetches, but their tests neither pin the value nor can run the stall case quickly: `fetchQuota` has no timeout seam, so each stalled-fetch test waits for the real 15 s signal (both test files carry a 25 s test timeout), and the assertions would pass with a materially different timeout. CodeRabbit's nitpick on PR #846 said exactly this — "Assert the exact timeout value… the current assertions would pass with a materially different timeout" — and was never replied to or dispositioned.

## Evidence (current main `2cf060b20647507f736fada283e3f649d787262c`)

- `packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/kimi.js:158` — `signal: AbortSignal.timeout(15_000)` added by PR #846; `kimi.test.js:76-88` asserts only that the captured signal is an `AbortSignal` and not yet aborted; `kimi.test.js:91-101` is the stalled-fetch test with a real 15 s wait (test timeout 25_000 at :101). PR #846's body itself notes "The new stalled-fetch test took the real 15s".
- `packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/nanogpt.js:70` — same pattern from PR #831; `nanogpt.test.js` carries the same 25_000 test timeout at :125 for its real-15 s stall test.
- Sibling fixes in the same sweep did provide seams: PR #839's speech calls take an injectable `timeoutMs`, PR #841's startup wrapper takes `options.timeout` — these two providers are the outliers.
- Dedupe: #844 and #827 (both closed) are the origin deadline issues for Kimi and NanoGPT; searches for the test gap ("kimi test 15 seconds", "AbortSignal timeout assertion") find no covering issue.

## Why it matters

Two unit tests that each burn a real 15 s run on every suite execution and can flake under load, and the 15 s contract these PRs exist to add is not actually protected: a future edit changing 15_000 to 1_500_000 (or 15) passes both suites. The fix is the seam the sibling PRs already used.

## Acceptance criteria

- Both providers expose the deadline as a named constant and/or an injectable option (following the `timeoutMs` pattern of PR #839), defaulting to 15_000.
- Tests assert the exact deadline value passed to the fetch (or spy on `AbortSignal.timeout`), and the stalled-fetch tests run at a short injected bound — no real 15 s waits and no 25 s test timeouts remain in `kimi.test.js` / `nanogpt.test.js`.
- Provider behavior is unchanged: a genuinely stalled production fetch still settles as an error at 15 s.

title: fix(web): speech deadline is not the whole budget — the body phase gets a second full timeout after create settles

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/pr-diff-review
labels.description: Filed by the pr-diff-review job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Finding

PR #839 set the speech deadline as a single budget — the code states it outright: "the deadline here is the whole budget: 60 s, no retries" (`packages/web/server/lib/tts/service.js:13-17` on main). But the body phase gets a second, full budget: `readSpeechBody` starts a fresh `setTimeout(timeoutMs)` when it is invoked, which is only after the SDK create call settles. A server that answers just inside the deadline and then stalls the body holds the voice route for up to ~2× the budget (~120 s at the default), not the promised 60 s.

## Evidence (current main `2cf060b20647507f736fada283e3f649d787262c`)

- `service.js:16-18` — policy comment: "the deadline here is the whole budget: 60 s, no retries"; `SPEECH_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS = 60_000`.
- `service.js:35-45` — `readSpeechBody(response, timeoutMs)` arms its own `setTimeout(..., timeoutMs)` at :39, rejecting with "Speech request timed out after ${timeoutMs} ms".
- `service.js:220-222` — `generateSpeechStream`: `client.audio.speech.create(speechParams, { timeout: timeoutMs })` settles first, then `readSpeechBody(response, timeoutMs)` starts a new full interval.
- `service.js:263-265` — `generateSpeechBuffer` repeats the same two-phase pattern.
- PR #839's tests exercise each phase in isolation at 250 ms (never-responds settles at the deadline; answers-then-stalls settles at the body deadline) — no test measures total elapsed time across both phases, so the doubling is unpinned.
- Dedupe: #824 (closed) is the origin deadline issue; #925/#930 (closed) added the speech body byte cap and did not touch this timing structure; searches for "readSpeechBody" / "speech whole budget" find no covering issue.

## Why it matters

The 60 s bound exists so a wedged local speech server cannot hold a synchronous voice route; the current structure silently doubles that hold in exactly the answer-then-stall case PR #839 added a body-phase deadline for. The behavior contradicts the policy the code itself documents, so either the implementation or the documented contract is wrong.

## Acceptance criteria

- One deadline covers create + body together: pass a deadline instant (or the remaining budget) into `readSpeechBody` so a request that answers at T and stalls the body fails at the original `timeoutMs` from the start of the call, in both `generateSpeechStream` and `generateSpeechBuffer`.
- A regression test pins total elapsed time across both phases (answer near the deadline, then a stalled body settles at ~1× the configured timeout, not ~2×).
- Existing #839/#930 tests (never-responds, body stall with connection close, byte cap) still pass; the "whole budget" comment and the behavior agree.

title: fix(web): routing model download stall deadline does not cover the write-side awaits — a stalled local write still wedges the download

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/pr-diff-review
labels.description: Filed by the pr-diff-review job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Finding

PR #829 gave `downloadModel` a 60-second stall deadline described in its own comment as a "stall bound for the whole transfer" (`route-local-model.js:75-79` on main), and the fetch and every body read are raced against it — but the two write-side awaits are not raced, so a stall there outlives the deadline and the download never settles.

## Evidence (current main `2cf060b20647507f736fada283e3f649d787262c`)

- `packages/web/server/lib/routing/route-local-model.js:88-98` — the stall timer callback can only reject the current `raceStall` promise (`rejectStalled?.(error)`) and abort the fetch controller.
- `:112` the fetch is raced (`raceStall(fetchImpl(...))`) and `:124` each `reader.read()` is raced — the network side is covered.
- `:139` — `if (!out.write(chunk)) await new Promise((resolve) => out.once('drain', resolve));` is NOT raced. While it pends, the current `raceStall` promise has already settled, so when the timer fires `rejectStalled?.()` is a no-op and `controller.abort()` does nothing to a filesystem write.
- `:142` — the `out.end(...)` callback await is likewise unraced.
- Consequence: if the local write stalls past `stallTimeoutMs` (hung or wedged filesystem — the class of stall this PR exists to bound), `downloadModel` never resolves or rejects: the inner catch never runs, the `.part` file is not discarded, and the route layer's `download.active` flag (`route-rules-routes.js:109`) stays set, so Settings reports `downloading: true` forever and refuses retries until a server restart — the exact permanent wedge #828/#829 set out to eliminate, moved to the write side.
- PR #829's tests cover a never-arriving response, a mid-stream silent body, a slow-but-delivering body, and oversize cancellation — no case stalls the write side. Origin issue #828 is closed; searches for "route-local-model stall drain" / "downloadModel stall" find no covering issue.

## Why it matters

The deadline's contract, per the code's own comment, is the whole transfer. A download that can still hang forever — and wedge the Settings surface with it — on a stalled local write is a hole in that contract, in the same hang class as the network stalls the PR fixed.

## Acceptance criteria

- The drain await (`:139`) and the `out.end` await (`:142`) settle at the stall deadline like the read side: when the stall fires during either, `downloadModel` rejects with the existing timed-out 502, the fetch is aborted, the write stream is destroyed, and the `.part` file is removed (the inner catch's existing cleanup).
- A regression test pins a stalled write side (an injectable write stream or an equivalent seam, following the module's existing `fetchImpl` injection pattern) settling at a short `stallTimeoutMs` with no model file and no `.part` left behind.
- Existing #829 tests (never-arrives, mid-stream silence, slow-but-alive, oversize cancel) still pass; healthy-download behavior and progress reporting unchanged.

title: fix(web): bound the OpenCode health-check timeout and interval readers at 2^31-1 ms — oversized values collapse to ~1 ms

labels.name: source/pr-diff-review
