labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Finding

Two timer-feeding env readers in `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/lifecycle.js` still accept any positive safe integer, so a value above Node's timer maximum (2,147,483,647 ms) collapses to ~1 ms at the timer — the exact failure #832 was filed to eliminate and PR #836 fixed for the handoff, fs-exec, git check-ignore, and relay batch-window readers. These two readers were named in CodeRabbit's outside-diff Minor on PR #836 ("Bound the health timer readers at 2,147,483,647 ms", `lifecycle.js:56-61`), which was never replied to or dispositioned, and #832 is closed — so the residual has no owner.

## Evidence (current main `2cf060b20647507f736fada283e3f649d787262c`)

- `lifecycle.js:57` — `HEALTH_CHECK_TIMEOUT_MS = parsePositiveInt(process.env.OPENCHAMBER_OPENCODE_HEALTH_TIMEOUT_MS, 5000)`; `parsePositiveInt` is the shared `parsePositiveIntWithDefault` (spelling + safe-integer only, no upper bound).
- `lifecycle.js:62` — `HEALTH_CHECK_INTERVAL_OVERRIDE_MS = parsePositiveInt(process.env.OPENCHAMBER_OPENCODE_HEALTH_INTERVAL_MS, 0)`, same unbounded reader.
- The timeout feeds timers directly: `setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), HEALTH_CHECK_TIMEOUT_MS)` at `lifecycle.js:1432` (readiness wait) and `AbortSignal.timeout(HEALTH_CHECK_TIMEOUT_MS)` at `:475` and `:898`. Above 2^31-1 the setTimeout fires after ~1 ms, so every health probe aborts immediately and OpenCode is judged unhealthy.
- The interval feeds `setInterval(..., effectiveIntervalMs)` at `lifecycle.js:1966-1969` (`startHealthMonitoring`). Above 2^31-1 it fires ~every 1 ms, so the health-check cycle hammers the local OpenCode `/api/info` endpoint in a busy loop.
- PR #836 (merged, fixes #832): https://github.com/developing-today/openchamber/pull/836 — its covered list is the handoff timeout, fs exec timeout, git check-ignore timeout (web + both VS Code copies), and the relay batch window; CodeRabbit's review on that PR explicitly noted these two health readers "are not in the PR's covered list" and asked for the same bound. No reply/disposition on the PR; no later issue covers it (searched open + closed for the env names and "timer maximum": only #832).

Out of scope (verified non-timer uses, leave unchanged, as PR #836 did for its non-timer readers): `HEALTH_CHECK_MAX_CONSECUTIVE_FAILURES` (`lifecycle.js:58-61`, a count), `HEALTH_CHECK_RESULT_CACHE_MS` (`lifecycle.js:63`, only an elapsed-time comparison at `:1853`), and the drain-grace reader (elapsed-time arithmetic).

## Why it matters

An operator who raises `OPENCHAMBER_OPENCODE_HEALTH_TIMEOUT_MS` or `OPENCHAMBER_OPENCODE_HEALTH_INTERVAL_MS` past ~24.8 days to debug a slow OpenCode gets the opposite: health checks that abort after ~1 ms (OpenCode perpetually "unhealthy") or a ~1 ms health-check busy loop against the local server. It is the same operator-intent inversion #832 documented, left behind in the one file #832's own text pointed at ("every timer-feeding environment reader in `packages/web` to be bounded or listed").

## Acceptance criteria

- `OPENCHAMBER_OPENCODE_HEALTH_TIMEOUT_MS` and `OPENCHAMBER_OPENCODE_HEALTH_INTERVAL_MS` values above 2,147,483,647 fall back to their existing defaults (5000 and 0 respectively); 2,147,483,647 itself is accepted — the same bound shape PR #836 applied (e.g. via the shared bounded parser with max 2,147,483,647).
- Tests pin the boundary for both readers (at-max accepted; 3,000,000,000 and 9,007,199,254,740,993 fall back), following the per-reader test pattern PR #836 added.
- `HEALTH_CHECK_MAX_CONSECUTIVE_FAILURES`, `HEALTH_CHECK_RESULT_CACHE_MS`, and the drain-grace reader are unchanged.

title: fix(vscode): bridge local-fs proxy buffers every file whole plus base64 with no size cap — both /api/fs/read and /api/fs/raw ignore the stats.size they already fetched

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/vscode
labels.description: Package: vscode (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

The VS Code bridge's local-fs proxy (`packages/vscode/src/bridge-localfs-proxy-runtime.ts`, `tryHandleLocalFsProxy`) buffers every file whole — and then base64-encodes it — with no size cap, for both of its read routes:

- `:96` — the handler stats the file (`stats.isFile()` check) but never checks `stats.size`.
- `:115-126` — `/api/fs/read`: `fs.promises.readFile(resolvedPath, 'utf8')`, then `base64EncodeUtf8(content)` — the file exists three times in extension-host memory (string, Buffer, base64 string).
- `:127-137` — `/api/fs/raw`: `fs.promises.readFile(resolvedPath)` whole, then `Buffer.from(raw).toString('base64')`.

The web server's `/api/fs/raw` was deliberately changed to stream because "a recording or a PDF can be hundreds of megabytes the server would otherwise hold in memory" (`packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.js:1399`), and its preview path caps at `MAX_SERVE_BYTES` = 100 MiB (`routes.js:214`). The bridge defeats both protections for VS Code users: opening or previewing a large media/PDF file in a workspace makes the extension host allocate the whole file plus ~33% base64 overhead, in a payload type (`ApiProxyResponsePayload.bodyBase64`) that cannot stream — so the honest fix here is a cap with a clear error, not streaming.

Related but separate: #1026 covers the web server's `/api/fs/read`, which has the same missing `stats.size` check; this issue is the VS Code bridge surface, whose payload shape and fix differ.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `2cf060b20`)

- Code read above: no size check anywhere in `tryHandleLocalFsProxy` between the `stat` and the two `readFile` calls.
- Laptop probe reusing the existing test harness shape (`packages/vscode/src/bridge-localfs-proxy-runtime.test.js`: `bun:test` + mocked `fs`/`vscode` modules) against the real module (probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-vscode-bridge-cap-20261031/probe-bridge.test.js`, fork at the same `2cf060b20`): mock `stat` reported a **500 MiB** file, mock `readFile` returned 32 MiB. Result: `/api/fs/raw` → **200, `bodyBase64` length 44,739,244**; `/api/fs/read` → **200, same body length**; `readFile` called for both. No cap, no error.
- Dedup: `gh search issues` for "bridge-localfs-proxy" and "bridge local fs proxy raw base64" over open + closed returned only #1026 (filed this run, which explicitly scopes the bridge out).

## Why it matters

The extension host is a shared, memory-sensitive process; a single large-file preview can balloon it by 1.33× the file size on top of the raw buffer and destabilize every extension. The web side already decided this trade-off (stream or cap); the bridge never got either.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Both bridge read routes reject a file whose `stats.size` exceeds a named cap with a clear proxy error (status 413, matching the web preview shape) *before* calling `readFile`; triage picks the cap value(s) — e.g. align raw with the web `MAX_SERVE_BYTES` (100 MiB) and give the text read a smaller named cap, or one shared named cap — the decision and its rationale are recorded on this issue.
- [ ] Files at or under the cap return exactly as today (status, headers, base64 body).
- [ ] Tests in `packages/vscode/src/bridge-localfs-proxy-runtime.test.js` pin: over-cap → 413 and `readFile` never called, for both `/api/fs/read` and `/api/fs/raw`; at-cap → 200.
- [ ] Existing bridge tests pass unchanged; no change to the web server's fs routes (#1026 owns those).

title: fix(web): /api/fs/read has no size cap — the one unbounded read path in fs/routes.js buffers the whole file, unlike streamed /raw and the 100 MiB-capped preview

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`GET /api/fs/read` (`packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.js:1281`) reads the whole file into server memory with no size cap — even though the handler already has the file's size in hand before reading, and both sibling read paths in the same file are bounded:

- `:1310-1313` — the handler stats the file (`stats.isFile()` check) but never checks `stats.size`.
- `:1315` — `let content = await fsPromises.readFile(canonicalPath, 'utf8')`, then the whole string is returned via `res.send(content)`. The empty-read retry loop below it can re-read the whole file up to 3 more times.
- Contrast `:1347` `/api/fs/raw`: streamed from disk, with the comment at `:1399` explaining exactly why — "a recording or a PDF can be hundreds of megabytes the server would otherwise hold in memory".
- Contrast `:1497` preview serving: `MAX_SERVE_BYTES = 100 * 1024 * 1024` (`:214`), enforced at `:1522` with a 413 before any read.

So the one read path used for text files is the only unbounded one. Its callers do not protect the server: the UI's own "too large" guard (`packages/ui/src/lib/contextFileOpenGuard.ts`, `MAX_OPEN_FILE_LINES = 20_000`) runs only *after* the full content has been read by the server and downloaded, and other callers (`FilesView.tsx:1835`, `gitApi.ts:372`, `PlansSection.tsx:158`, `detectDevServer.ts:174`) read whatever path they are given. Opening — or polling with `fresh` — a large file in a workspace (a multi-hundred-MB log, a generated JSON dump, a database file with a text-like name) makes the long-lived web server allocate the whole file as a UTF-8 string (plus the response copy), repeatedly if the file is re-opened.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `2cf060b20`)

- Code read above: no size check anywhere in the `/api/fs/read` handler between the `stat` and the `readFile`.
- Laptop probe against the real `registerFsRoutes` from `packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.js` (probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-fs-read-cap-20261031/probe-fs-read.mjs` on the laptop, fork at the same `2cf060b20`): mock `stat` reported a 500 MiB file and mock `readFile` returned 32 MiB; the handler returned **200 with the full 32 MiB body, `readFile` called once, no 413** — i.e. a file five times the preview cap is read whole and served.
- Dedup: `gh search issues` for `fs/read` and a search for "read file size cap" over open + closed issues returned the fs/exec, upload, and installer cap issues (#737, #704, #834) but nothing covering the `/api/fs/read` response path.

## Why it matters

The web server is the long-lived managed process every session depends on. An unbounded whole-file read is a memory-amplification footgun reachable from ordinary UI actions (open a big file, external-change polling re-reads it), and the fix shape is already established twice in the same file — this path was simply missed.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `GET /api/fs/read` rejects a file whose `stats.size` exceeds a named cap with **413** (matching the preview path's shape) *before* calling `readFile`; the cap value is a named constant in `routes.js` (triage picks the value: a text-oriented cap well under `MAX_SERVE_BYTES`, or `MAX_SERVE_BYTES` itself — but it must be named and tested).
- [ ] A file at or under the cap is read and returned exactly as today, including the empty-read retry behaviour.
- [ ] Tests in `packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.test.js` pin: over-cap → 413 and `readFile` never called; at-cap → 200 with content.
- [ ] Existing fs route tests pass unchanged; no change to `/api/fs/raw` streaming or preview behaviour.
- [ ] Out of scope: the VS Code bridge's local-fs proxy (`packages/vscode/src/bridge-localfs-proxy-runtime.ts:115-137`), which buffers whole files for both read and raw — that is filed/tracked separately if pursued.

title: fix(web,ui): relay fragment reassembler has no aggregate bound — partial messages on unlimited distinct streams are retained for the life of the connection

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/ui
labels.description: Package: ui (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

The relay tunnel's fragment reassembler bounds each message but not the aggregate: a peer can park just-under-the-cap partial messages on unlimited distinct streams and grow the host's (and the client's) memory without bound, for as long as the connection lives.

`createFragmentAssembler` (`packages/web/server/lib/relay/tunnel-codec.js:164-165`) keeps a `pending` Map keyed by `${streamId}:${frameType}`. The only bound is per key: a single key's `totalBytes` may not exceed `maxMessageBytes` (16 MiB, `:180`). There is no cap on the number of pending keys, no aggregate byte budget, and no expiry for a partial message that never completes.

Both call sites feed the assembler before any stream check:

- Server: `createTunnelHost` creates one assembler (`packages/web/server/lib/relay/tunnel-host.js:147`) and `handleFrame` calls `assembler.push(frame)` for every `WsText`/`WsBinary` frame (`:637`) — only afterwards does `handleWsMessage` (`:595`) check that the stream exists. Fragments addressed to a stream that was never opened are therefore retained too, and `dropStream` (`:164`) is only ever invoked from the lifecycle of a stream present in the `streams` map, so those orphan partials are never dropped.
- Client: the mirrored assembler (`packages/ui/src/lib/relay/tunnel-codec.ts:132`) is pushed at `packages/ui/src/lib/relay/tunnel-client.ts:634` before the stream-handler lookup (`:645`), so a relay/host peer can park the same unbounded partials in the UI process.

Stream ids are a 4-byte field, so distinct keys are effectively unlimited; each can hold up to just under 16 MiB.

## Evidence (verified this run, main 2cf060b20)

- Code read above: per-key cap only; no aggregate cap, key-count cap, or timeout anywhere in either assembler copy; `dropStream` unreachable for never-opened streams.
- Laptop probe against the real modules (`~/git/fleet/probe-oc-fragment-assembler-20261031/probe.mjs`, node `--expose-gc`):
  - Assembler: 64 partial fragments (1 MiB each, `hasMoreFragments: true`) on 64 distinct never-completed streams → 64/64 returned `null` (retained); buffer memory grew by the full pushed amount and kept growing with more streams. A single key pushed past 16 MiB threw `fragmented message exceeds maximum size` as designed — the per-key cap works, the aggregate does not exist.
  - Host: driving the real `createTunnelHost.handleFrame` with 512 fragmented `WsText` frames (60 KiB each, under the 64 KiB tunnel frame max) addressed to never-opened stream ids → 0 frames sent back (no abort, no error), and all ~30 MiB stayed buffered in the host.

## Why it matters

The relay is the remote-access path for the managed server: one authenticated-but-buggy or hostile tunnel peer (or a malfunctioning client that restarts messages across fresh stream ids) can OOM the long-lived web server process without ever completing a message, opening a socket, or tripping the per-message cap or the downstream scheduler's queue limits (`downstream-scheduler.js` bounds its own queues at 4 MiB / 4096 frames — the assembler sits in front of it with no equivalent budget). The same hole exists in the UI client against a malicious/buggy host. Sibling shapes already fixed: #962 (realtime-proxy unbounded pre-open queue), #1017 (dictation reorder buffer).

## Acceptance criteria

- The assembler enforces an aggregate bound across all pending keys (total buffered bytes and/or pending-key count), in both copies (`packages/web/server/lib/relay/tunnel-codec.js`, `packages/ui/src/lib/relay/tunnel-codec.ts`); exceeding it fails the offending message/connection loudly (existing `TunnelCodecError` semantics or stream abort), never silently drops a completable message.
- Fragments for streams the receiver has never opened (or has already dropped) do not accumulate: either the host/client rejects them before assembly or orphan partials are reaped (e.g. `dropStream` coverage / bounded pending lifetime) — the chosen mechanism is named in the fix.
- Tests pin the bound in both copies: many distinct streams each parking a partial fragment are refused/reaped at the aggregate limit while a legitimate multi-fragment message still reassembles; the host-level test covers a fragmented frame for a never-opened stream.
- Existing tunnel-codec / tunnel-host / tunnel-client tests pass unchanged.

title: fix(web): GitLab auth-path JSON reads have no byte cap — device-flow and verify buffer the whole answer from a user-configured instance

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

The GitLab **auth-path** JSON reads have a deadline but **no byte cap**: `packages/web/server/lib/gitlab/device-flow.js` and `packages/web/server/lib/gitlab/verify.js` parse bodies with bare `response.json()` from the same user-configured, possibly self-managed GitLab instance whose API answers #1015 just capped at 16 MiB in `client.js`. #1015's triage scoped the fix to `client.js` `parseBody` only; these sibling reads were explicitly left to that triage's scope decision (creator run 2026-10-31 01:50 CDT) and remain unbounded after #1015 closed. The answers here are tiny and fixed-shape — a version probe, a device authorization, OAuth token answers, and one user profile — so they need a far smaller cap than the API client's 16 MiB.

## Evidence (verified on main `f73fd500e`, this run)

- `device-flow.js:4-10` — `readJson()` is `return await response.json()` with no size check and no bounded reader; it is used at `:59` (`probeGitLabAuth` → `GET /api/v4/version`), `:81` (device-authorization probe), `:91` (`startGitLabDeviceFlow` → `POST /oauth/authorize_device`), `:106` (`exchangeGitLabDeviceCode` → `POST /oauth/token`), and `:135` (`refreshGitLabAccessToken` → `POST /oauth/token`).
- `verify.js:15` — `verifyGitLabToken` returns `parseGitLabUser(await response.json())` for `GET /api/v4/user`, also uncapped.
- The 10 s bound does not help: `network.js:20-27` `fetchWithTimeout` delegates to `fetchWithDeadline`, whose deadline stays armed until the body is read — that bounds **stalls**, not bytes. A fast instance (or a compromised/misbehaving one) can deliver gigabytes inside the window; `response.json()` buffers all of it before any field is looked at. This is exactly the threat model `client.js` now documents for its capped read ("a user-configured, possibly self-managed instance").
- The bounded primitive already exists in-tree: `lib/shared/response-body.js` `readBoundedResponseText` (used by the #849 error path at 1 KiB and the #1015 success path at 16 MiB).
- **Laptop probe** (`~/git/fleet/probe-oc-gitlab-auth-bodycap-20261031/probe.mjs`, run on the laptop against the real modules at `f73fd500e` with an injected fetch returning a 32 MiB JSON body): `verifyGitLabToken` accepted the whole body (parsed `name` length 33,554,432), `startGitLabDeviceFlow` accepted the whole body (padding field length 33,554,432), and `probeGitLabAuth` read the whole 32 MiB `version` string and confirmed the instance. No read was refused or truncated.

## Why it matters

- These are sign-in paths: they run before any session exists, against an origin the user typed in — the least-trusted moment in the GitLab integration, and the one #1015's rationale already established as in-scope for byte caps.
- Unbounded buffering in the long-lived web server process is this fleet's recurring failure shape (#802 design, #849, #925, #1006, #1015); this is the remaining GitLab surface with that shape.
- The payloads are among the smallest in the integration (version string, device code, token answer, user profile), so a tight cap costs nothing legitimate.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every auth-path JSON read in `device-flow.js` (`readJson` and all five call sites) and `verify.js` goes through a bounded reader (`lib/shared/response-body.js`) with one named cap, sized for these fixed-shape answers (far below the API client's 16 MiB; sizing reasoning in a comment next to the constant, in the style of `client.js`'s `SUCCESS_BODY_MAX_BYTES` comment).
- [ ] An over-cap body surfaces as a classifiable `GitLabRequestError` (e.g. `provider-error` / `unreachable` per the existing `classifyGitLabFailure` vocabulary), never as a parsed result and never as a raw JSON parse error leaking through; the stream is cancelled when the cap is crossed instead of being read to the end.
- [ ] Behaviour for legitimate answers is unchanged: `device-flow.test.js` and the verify paths in the existing GitLab tests pass unmodified in shape (device flow start/exchange/refresh, token verification, instance probe confirm/not-gitlab outcomes).
- [ ] New tests pin the bound: an over-cap body is refused on at least the verify path and one device-flow path (including a streamed/chunked body with no `content-length`, so the cap is enforced while reading, not only from the header), and an at-cap body still parses.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for GitLab body caps / device-flow / verify: #1015 (closed) covers `client.js` `parseBody` only — its triage explicitly scoped out these modules; #849 covers the `client.js` error path; #781 covers deadlines. No issue covers the auth-path reads in `device-flow.js` / `verify.js`.

title: fix(web): dictation stream reorder buffer is unbounded — one missing seq makes receivedChunks retain every later chunk for the life of the connection

labels.name: kind/performance
labels.description: Performance problem or optimization

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

The dictation stream manager's reorder buffer has **no bound**: `DictationStreamManager.handleChunk` (`packages/web/server/lib/dictation/stream-manager.js`) stores every out-of-order chunk in `state.receivedChunks` until the missing earlier `seq` arrives — with no cap on entry count or buffered bytes, and no gap/idle timeout. One chunk that never arrives (a dropped or garbled WebSocket message, a buggy or non-stock client) turns every later chunk of that dictation into permanently retained server memory for the life of the connection, the ack stays pinned, and no error is ever emitted. The per-message WebSocket payload is capped (`DICTATION_WS_MAX_PAYLOAD_BYTES` in `runtime.js`), but the aggregate across messages is not.

## Evidence (verified on main `e0d9f2292`, this run)

- `stream-manager.js:271` — per-stream state creates `receivedChunks: new Map()`; `:314-324` `handleChunk` inserts any `seq >= nextSeqToForward` into it; `:327-330` entries are deleted only while the contiguous prefix advances. There is no size/byte check anywhere in `handleChunk` (grep: `receivedChunks` appears only at :271, :314, :324, :327-330, :369).
- The only timeout in the manager is the finalization timeout, and it is armed only by `handleFinish` (`:388-397`). A stream whose gap never closes and which is never finished has no expiry; cleanup otherwise happens on `handleCancel`, stream error, or socket close (`runtime.js` `cleanupAll()` on `close`).
- The reorder behaviour itself is intentional and tested (`stream-manager.test.js` "reorders out-of-order chunks before appending") — but no test pins a bound, because none exists.
- **Laptop probe** (`~/git/fleet/probe-oc-dictation-reorder-20261031/probe.mjs`, run on the laptop against the real `stream-manager.js` at `e0d9f2292` with a stub STT session): after `handleStart`, sending seq 1..5000 (0.5 s PCM16 chunks, 16,000 bytes each) with seq 0 withheld left `receivedChunks` holding **5,000 entries / 80,000,000 bytes (76.3 MiB)**, `nextSeqToForward = 0`, `ackSeq = -1`, **zero** error events, and the stream still present. Control: 10 in-order chunks buffered 0 entries and advanced `ackSeq` to 9.

## Why it matters

- The stock UI sender (`packages/ui/src/lib/dictation/dictation-stream-sender.ts`) sends strictly in order over one WebSocket, so a gap requires a lost/garbled message or a non-stock client — but the server is the authoritative side of this state machine (its own header says so), and every sibling streaming surface in this codebase bounds exactly this shape: the realtime proxy's pending queue (#962), the dev-tunnel caps (#961), the relay's `MAX_PENDING_WS_BYTES`. This buffer is the remaining unbounded one.
- Dictation chunks are ~16–32 KB each and arrive several per second, so a wedged stream grows at roughly 0.5–2 MB/s of audio the user believes is being transcribed, while the UI receives acks pinned at the pre-gap value and no failure signal.
- It also silently eats the finalization path: `estimateFinalizationTimeout` prices missing seqs into the finish timeout, but with no finish message there is no timeout at all.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The reorder buffer is bounded by a named cap (buffered bytes and/or entry count, sized generously above any legitimate reorder window — chunks arrive in order over a single ordered WebSocket, so the window should be small), with the sizing reasoning in a comment next to the constant.
- [ ] Crossing the cap fails the stream with a clear retryable error via the existing `failAndCleanupStream` path (STT session closed, stream state deleted) instead of buffering further chunks.
- [ ] In-order and small-gap out-of-order behaviour is unchanged: the existing reorder test and the rest of `stream-manager.test.js` pass unmodified.
- [ ] New tests in `stream-manager.test.js` pin the bound: chunks past a withheld seq accumulate only up to the cap and then the stream errors and is cleaned up; a gap that closes before the cap still reorders and forwards normally.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for dictation reorder / `receivedChunks` / stream buffer: dictation hits are #417/#814/#828/#824 (model download and STT/TTS call deadlines) and #428 (archive-pin test coverage). No issue covers the stream manager's reorder buffer.

title: fix(web): GitLab client success-path body read has no byte cap — parseBody buffers the whole JSON/text/blob answer from a user-configured instance

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

The GitLab API client's success-path body read has a deadline but **no byte cap**: `parseBody` in `packages/web/server/lib/gitlab/client.js` buffers the whole response via `response.json()` / `response.text()` / `response.blob()`. A user-configured, possibly self-managed GitLab instance that answers quickly with an oversized body grows web-server memory by the full body size before any parsing or validation runs — the 10s deadline only bounds slow/stalled bodies, not fast large ones.

## Evidence (verified on main `7b1fdc380`, this run)

- `packages/web/server/lib/gitlab/client.js:52-58` — `parseBody(response, asStream)`: JSON → `(await response.json()) || {}`, text → `(await response.text()) || ''`, anything else → `response.blob()`. No size check, no `content-length` pre-check, no use of the shared bounded reader.
- Same file, `:22-27` and `:63-65` — the **error** path in the same module was already hardened for exactly this reason (#849): `ERROR_DETAIL_MAX_BYTES = 1_024` with the comment that the read is capped "instead of buffering the whole answer from a user-configured, possibly self-managed instance", using `readBoundedResponseText` from `lib/shared/response-body.js`. The success path never got the same treatment.
- Same file, `:16-20` — `GITLAB_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS = 10_000` bounds each attempt's deadline; a local/LAN self-managed instance can deliver gigabytes well inside 10s.
- Call site `:131-140` — every GitBeaker request (`get/post/put/patch/delete`) for every GitLab resource routes its success body through `parseBody`; reads retry up to 3 attempts, so a huge body can be buffered repeatedly.
- **Laptop probe** (`~/git/fleet/probe-oc-gitlab-bodycap-20261031/probe.mjs`, run on the laptop against the real module at the same main commit, stubbed `fetch`): a 32 MiB JSON body was accepted whole (`username length = 33554432`), and a 32 MiB `text/plain` body was likewise accepted whole (`string 33554432`). No cap exists at any size the probe tried.

## Why it matters

- The instance origin is user-configured (including self-managed instances), so the body size is not controlled by a trusted first-party server — the exact threat model the module itself names for its error path.
- This is the remaining uncapped member of the body-read family: models.dev/npm/changelog reads are tracked in #1006, TTS in #925 (fixed), and the GitLab error path in #849 (fixed). The success path is the largest surface of the set — it carries every GitLab API answer.
- Memory pressure on the long-lived managed web server is the fleet's recurring failure shape (cf. the unbounded-cache filings #967–#999).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Success-path JSON and text body reads in `parseBody` are bounded by a named byte cap (per content type if justified), enforced while streaming (e.g. via `lib/shared/response-body.js`), not by a post-read length check alone; an over-cap body cancels the stream and surfaces a clear, classifiable error instead of a parsed result.
- [ ] The binary/`blob()` branch is either capped the same way or explicitly documented as streaming-only with its callers audited (`asStream` downloads must keep working unchanged, including Range/video paths in `createGitLabDownloader`).
- [ ] The cap is sized for legitimate large GitLab list/file answers, with the reasoning recorded in a comment next to the constant, in the style of `ERROR_DETAIL_MAX_BYTES`.
- [ ] New tests in `packages/web/server/lib/gitlab/client.test.js` style pin the bound: an over-cap JSON body and an over-cap text body are refused (not returned whole), and an at-cap body still parses.
- [ ] Existing `client.test.js` behaviour (credentials, no-redirect, retry/deadline semantics) is unchanged.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for GitLab body/cap/`parseBody`: #849 covers only the **error** path, #781 added the deadlines, #804 migrated the error-path helper to the shared primitives. No issue covers the success-path read.

title: fix(ui): MessageFreshnessDetector retains every message id forever — seenMessageIds and messageCreationTimes grow for the life of the page, and clearSession is never called

body:
## Problem

The UI's `MessageFreshnessDetector` (a module singleton) retains one entry per assistant message for the entire life of the page, and nothing in production code ever releases them — not even when the session is deleted.

## Evidence (verified on main `7b1fdc380`)

- `packages/ui/src/lib/messageFreshness.ts:4-7` — the detector is a singleton (`getInstance()`); its own comment at `:46-52` says it "outlives ChatViewport remounts". It holds three collections: `sessionStartTimes` (Map), `seenMessageIds` (Set), `messageCreationTimes` (Map).
- Every assistant message a user ever views adds an entry to both `seenMessageIds` and `messageCreationTimes`: `shouldAnimateMessage` writes at `:41` and `:53`, `markMessageAsAnimated` at `:73`. The write path is hot — `packages/ui/src/components/chat/ChatMessage.tsx:353-355` calls `shouldAnimateMessage` for every rendered assistant message.
- `clearSession(sessionId)` at `:59-62` deletes **only** `sessionStartTimes` — the seen-id set and the creation-times map are keyed by message id with no session association, so they cannot be pruned per session at all. Worse, `clearSession` has **no production caller**: the only calls in the tree are the detector's own test (`messageFreshness.test.ts:20`, `clearAll()` in `beforeEach`).
- `packages/ui/src/sync/session-deletion-cleanup.ts` is the established hook that releases per-session UI state when a session is deleted (message queue, folders, multi-select, inline comment drafts, input history, chat drafts) — the freshness detector is not wired into it.
- `messageCreationTimes` is write-only in production: its values are read only by `getDebugInfo()` (`:82-93`), which itself has no production caller. The page retains a number for every message ever seen purely for a debug snapshot nobody takes.

## Why it matters

The OpenChamber web UI is a long-lived page — fleet users keep it open for days across hundreds of sessions and tens of thousands of messages. Two collections grow monotonically for that whole lifetime with no cap, no TTL, and no deletion path, on the app's hottest render path. This is the same never-evicted shape the fleet has been fixing on the server side (#972, #974, #987, #998); the UI singleton was missed because its `clear*` methods exist but are never called outside tests, which makes the leak look handled at a glance.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `seenMessageIds` / `messageCreationTimes` are bounded (e.g. a named entry cap with oldest-first eviction, consistent with the capped-cache precedents in this codebase) **or** pruned when their session is deleted via `cleanupPersistedSessionState` — either way, retention no longer grows with total messages viewed over the page lifetime.
- [ ] `messageCreationTimes` is either removed (if truly unused) or its production reader is named; no write-only retained state remains.
- [ ] The animate-at-most-once behaviour pinned by `messageFreshness.test.ts` (including the #2124 regression test: no re-animation when returning to a session) still passes — eviction must not resurrect entry animations for messages in the visible/recent working set.
- [ ] New tests pin the bound: after more distinct messages than the cap, the collections' sizes stay at the cap, and (if deletion pruning is chosen) a deleted session's entries are gone.
- [ ] Existing `packages/ui/src/lib/messageFreshness.test.ts` tests pass unmodified in behaviour.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for `freshness`, `MessageFreshness`, `seenMessageIds`, and unbounded-UI-memory terms on 2026-10-31: no existing issue covers this detector (nearest hits are the server/vscode cache filings #972/#974/#987/#998 and the unrelated transcript-blanking #52).

title: fix(web): three public-internet JSON reads have a deadline but no byte cap — models.dev catalog, npm packument and changelog index buffer the whole body via response.json()

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: status/parked
labels.description: Work parked, resumes later

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: priority/normal

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Finding

Three web-server reads of public-internet JSON carry a deadline but no byte cap: each calls the global `fetch` with `AbortSignal.timeout(...)` and then buffers the entire body via `response.json()`. A deadline bounds *time*, not *memory* — a fast or hostile endpoint can deliver an arbitrarily large body well inside the deadline, and the parsed result is then retained (the models.dev catalog is cached in process memory). This is the exact gap design #802's shared bounded-body primitive (`lib/shared/response-body.js`, `readBoundedResponseText` / `readBoundedResponseBytes` — cap enforced during the read, stream cancelled the moment the cap is crossed) exists to close, and the same deadline-but-no-cap shape was already filed and fixed for the TTS speech read (#925). These three call sites were never migrated.

## Evidence (verified on main `8f3bad9b2`, 2026-10-31)

1. **models.dev catalog** — `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/models-metadata.js:1` sets `MODELS_DEV_API_URL = 'https://models.dev/api.json'`; `fetchCatalog` (lines 13–24) fetches with `signal: AbortSignal.timeout(timeoutMs)` (default 8000 ms, line 15) and reads `await response.json()` at line 20 with no size bound. The result is kept in the module-level `cachedMetadata` cache, so an oversized body is retained for the TTL, not just transiently buffered. The catalog is legitimately large (multi-MB), so the cap must be generous — but today there is none at all.
2. **npm registry packument** — `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/npm-registry.js:101` `lookupNpmPackage` fetches the registry with `AbortSignal.timeout(NPM_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS)` (`NPM_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS = 5_000`, line 9) and reads `await response.json()` at line 114. Only `dist-tags` and the `versions` keys are consumed, yet the full packument is buffered whole; full packuments for long-lived packages run to tens of MB, and nothing stops a registry (or a mirror/proxy in between) from sending far more.
3. **Changelog index** — `packages/web/server/lib/changelog/update-notes.js:13` sets `CHANGELOG_INDEX_URL = 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/developing-today/openchamber/main/changelog/index.json'`; `fetchUpdateNotes` fetches it with `AbortSignal.timeout(options.timeoutMs ?? 10_000)` (line 77) and reads `await response.json()` at line 79 with no cap. This index is small by design, so an unbounded read here is pure exposure.

None of the three composes `readBoundedResponseText`/`readBoundedResponseBytes` from `packages/web/server/lib/shared/response-body.js`, the primitive sibling call sites were migrated to in #804.

## Why it matters

The managed OpenChamber server is a long-lived process that also brokers sessions and quota for the whole fleet. An oversized or malicious response from any of these three endpoints (compromised CDN/mirror, a registry serving an anomalous packument, a redirected fetch) inflates server memory with no bound short of OOM — the failure mode #802/#925 already established as in-scope for this codebase. The npm read is the worst of the three: it fires on package lookups, and the useful payload is a tiny fraction of the body it buffers.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] All three reads enforce a named per-site byte cap enforced *during* the read (compose the shared `lib/shared/response-body.js` readers or an equivalent streaming cap — not a post-buffer `length` check).
- [ ] Caps are sized to each payload's legitimate scale and named as constants at the call site (models.dev catalog generously; changelog index tightly; npm read either capped generously or switched to the abbreviated install-v1 metadata it actually needs — triage decides, behaviour for real packages unchanged).
- [ ] An over-cap response fails the read the same way a network failure does today (models-metadata falls back to stale cache / propagates; npm lookup returns its `ok: false` shape; update notes return `null`) — no partial JSON is ever parsed or cached.
- [ ] Tests pin the over-cap behaviour for each site (the existing suites `models-metadata.test.js`, `update-notes.test.js`, and the npm-registry tests are extended, following the bounded-reader test precedent in `lib/shared/response-body.test.js`).
- [ ] No behaviour change for within-cap responses: existing tests pass unchanged.

title: fix(vscode): session-activity watcher never prunes sessions — session.deleted is ignored and reconcile marks absent sessions idle, so the v1 snapshot reports deleted sessions forever

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: priority/normal

body:
## Problem

The VS Code extension's session-activity watcher retains every session it has ever seen for the life of the extension host, and its v1 observability snapshot keeps reporting deleted sessions as `idle` forever.

- `packages/vscode/src/sessionActivityWatcher.ts:53` — module-level `sessionActivityPhases = new Map<string, { phase, updatedAt }>()`.
- `setSessionActivityPhase` (:107-145) only ever `set`s an entry (busy / cooldown / idle transitions); no code path deletes a per-session entry. Grep across `packages/vscode/src` finds exactly one removal: `sessionActivityPhases.clear()` in `stopGlobalEventWatcher` (:302), which runs only when the watcher is stopped.
- `deriveSessionActivity` (:165-184) handles `session.status`, `session.execution.*`, and `session.idle` — `session.deleted` falls into the `default` case and is ignored, so a deleted session's entry is never pruned even though the event stream delivers the deletion. The web server's own surfaces handle the same event explicitly (e.g. `packages/web/server/lib/session-warming/runtime.js:58`, `lib/opencode/session-runtime.js:124`).
- `reconcileSessionActivityFromStatus` (:86-99) makes it worse, not better: sessions absent from the authoritative active set are marked `idle` and kept, never removed — so even a session that ended before a reconnect is retained as an idle ghost.
- The retained map is exactly what `getSessionActivitySnapshot()` serializes (`buildSessionActivityV1Snapshot`, :36-52), served to consumers via `packages/vscode/src/bridge-system-runtime.ts:250-251` (`api:session-activity:get`). This is the external observability contract v1 from design #612 — consumers see a `sessions` record that grows monotonically and asserts deleted sessions still exist with `type: "idle"`.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `fc5beaf35`)

Read of `sessionActivityWatcher.ts` at HEAD (lines above): `set` sites at :129 and :137 (cooldown→idle), `clear()` only at :302 in the stop path, no `.delete(` on the phases map anywhere in the package, and no `session.deleted` case in the event switch. The extension host is long-lived (one per VS Code window, typically days), so the map and every snapshot payload grow with every session ever run.

## Why it matters

Two harms, not just memory: (1) unbounded retention in a long-lived host, the same class as #987 (web session-warming map) and #903; (2) contract correctness — the v1 snapshot is an observability surface other tools read to decide what is running; ghost `idle` entries for deleted sessions make "is this session still alive?" unanswerable from the snapshot and inflate every poll response.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A `session.deleted` event prunes that session's phase entry (and any pending cooldown timer for it).
- [ ] Retention is otherwise bounded or reconciled: entries for sessions the authoritative active/status read no longer knows about are eventually removed, not kept as idle forever — or an explicit cap/TTL is enforced and documented in the module.
- [ ] `stopGlobalEventWatcher` behaviour unchanged; live busy/cooldown/idle transitions and the 2s cooldown still work as today.
- [ ] Tests pin: a session that goes busy → deleted disappears from `buildSessionActivityV1Snapshot` output; a live idle session remains.

title: fix(vscode): skills-catalog cache never evicts expired entries — TTL is checked only on re-lookup of the same source, so every catalog ever browsed is retained for the life of the extension host

body:
## Problem

The VS Code extension's skills-catalog cache never evicts expired entries and has no size bound — the VS Code twin of the web cache fixed under #968, which was never ported to this surface.

- `packages/vscode/src/skillsCatalog.ts:592` — module-level `catalogCache = new Map<string, { expiresAt: number; items: SkillsCatalogItem[] }>()`, with `CATALOG_TTL_MS = 30 * 60 * 1000` (:593).
- `packages/vscode/src/skillsCatalog.ts:621-623` — the only expiry deletion: when `getSkillsCatalog` is called for a key whose cached entry has expired, that single key is deleted. An expired entry for a source that is never requested again is never removed.
- `packages/vscode/src/skillsCatalog.ts:637` — `catalogCache.set(cacheKey, …)` inserts with no entry cap, no byte bound, and no sweep/prune on insert or access. Grep for `catalogCache` in the whole VS Code package returns only :592/:621/:623/:637 — there is no other eviction path and no test-only clear either.
- The cache key is `repo[#ref]::subpath` (:618), so every distinct catalog source (built-in curated sources plus every user-configured `additionalSources` entry, passed through from `packages/vscode/src/bridge-config-runtime.ts:749`) ever browsed in this extension host adds a retained `items` array for the life of the host process.
- Contrast: the web twin (`packages/web/server/lib/skills-catalog/cache.js`) had exactly this shape and was filed/fixed as #968 ("expiry is enforced only for the key being read, so every catalog ever scanned is retained"); the VS Code npm cache in the same repo already does it right (`packages/vscode/src/opencodeConfig.ts`, `pruneNpmInfoCache` sweeps expired entries and enforces `NPM_CACHE_MAX_ENTRIES = 500` on access/insert).

## Evidence (verified this run, main `fc5beaf35`)

Read of `skillsCatalog.ts` at HEAD (lines above) plus a full-package grep for `catalogCache` (4 hits, listed above — no sweep, cap, or clear exists). The extension host is long-lived (one process per VS Code window, typically days), so retention is effectively unbounded across every distinct source/ref/subpath combination ever requested.

## Why it matters

Same grow-forever class as #968/#967/#903, on the one catalog surface those sweeps missed. The 30-minute TTL bounds freshness, not retention: memory creep is proportional to every catalog ever browsed, and the stale `items` arrays are the heavy part (full skill listings per source).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Expired `catalogCache` entries are actually removed without requiring a re-read of the same key (sweep/prune on access or insert, mirroring `pruneNpmInfoCache` in `opencodeConfig.ts`), and/or a max-entries bound with eviction is enforced.
- [ ] Behavior unchanged for live entries: cache hit within TTL, `refresh: true` bypass, and per-source failure isolation in `getSkillsCatalog`.
- [ ] Tests pin that expired entries for never-re-read keys are gone after the sweep/bound runs, and that live entries survive it.
- [ ] Existing VS Code skills-catalog tests pass (`opencodeConfig.skills.test.js` / skills catalog test surface).

title: refactor(web): export the shared abort-signal compose helper — PRs #809/#811 copied it instead of reusing it (three divergent copies, plus a fourth in vscode)

body:
## Finding

The abort-signal composition helper from design #802 phase 1 was never exported from `lib/shared`, so each later bounded-call PR copied it instead of reusing it. There are now three divergent copies in the web server plus a fourth in the VS Code bridge:

- `packages/web/server/lib/shared/bounded-fetch.js:16` — the original `combineAbortSignals` (returns `{ signal, detach }`), private to the module, used only by `fetchWithDeadline` (line 116).
- `packages/web/server/lib/message-search/indexer.js:91` — a byte-for-byte copy of the same helper, added by PR #809 (fix for #807), used at indexer.js:153.
- `packages/web/server/lib/scheduled-tasks/runtime.js:24` — a third variant, `composeAbortSignals`, added by PR #811 (fix for #808). It diverges: it filters falsy signals and returns a bare signal with no `detach`, so its `{ once: true }` forwarding listeners are never removed if the composed signal never aborts.
- `packages/vscode/src/bridge-proxy-runtime.ts:98` — a fourth, TypeScript variant with the bare-signal shape (separate package; align if the shared export's shape allows, otherwise document why it stays separate).

Verified on current main (668935927): all four definitions present as above; no issue tracks this (searched `combineAbortSignals`, `composeAbortSignals`, abort-signal compose/duplication — design #802's phase 2, #804, covered parsers, the GitLab helper and bounded readers only).

## Why it matters

The copies have already drifted in contract (detach vs no detach, falsy filtering vs not). A fix to the composition semantics — e.g. listener cleanup, already-aborted handling, reason propagation — now has to be made in up to four places, and the scheduled-tasks variant's un-removed listeners are exactly the kind of quiet divergence the shared-primitive design (#802) was created to prevent.

## Acceptance criteria

- `lib/shared` exports one signal-composition helper (the `{ signal, detach }` shape from bounded-fetch.js, or a documented successor shape).
- `message-search/indexer.js` and `scheduled-tasks/runtime.js` import it and their private copies are deleted; existing indexer and scheduled-tasks tests pass unchanged.
- The vscode copy is either migrated or a comment in bridge-proxy-runtime.ts records why it intentionally stays separate.
- A shared test pins the composed helper's behaviour: any-source abort, already-aborted source, and detach removing the forwarding listeners.

Found by the pr-diff-review job reviewing PRs #806/#809/#811 (commits d34e7eb8e1, 171fd44774, b5616bac49).

body:
## Finding

In the APNs relay send path added by PR #801, a relay that sends response headers but stalls during its body has its deadline abort swallowed: `res.json().catch(() => null)` converts the abort into `null`, the caller treats that as an empty results list, and the send finishes silently — no warning, and any token-drop results the relay did send are lost.

Filed from PR diff review lane B. CodeRabbit raised this as a Minor finding on PR #801 (inline comment at `apns-runtime.js:472`); the thread is still unresolved with no reply, and the code is unchanged on current main.

## Evidence

- Source PR: #801 "fix(web): add deadlines to the APNs push runtime" (merged, head `d2fc9b94bf55726d97d13a5ddf4abb3ab0153a2d`, fixes #798). Its PR body promises: "Expiry lands in the existing warn-and-continue paths."
- Current main `fc5beaf35ae5b5d0842ab40d18ec92fe7a7b2ffd`, `packages/web/server/lib/notifications/apns-runtime.js`, `sendViaRelay`:
  - `:548` the send uses `createTimeoutSignal(APNS_RELAY_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS)` (10 s), and `:570-572` the comment states the signal "stays live until res.json() above has been read: the body read is part of the stall surface."
  - `:560` `const data = await res.json().catch(() => null);` — the catch does not distinguish a malformed-JSON `SyntaxError` from the deadline's abort error.
  - `:561` `results` then defaults to `[]`, the drop-token loop at `:562-566` no-ops, and the function returns normally. The outer catch's warning at `:567-568` (`[APNs relay] request failed:`) is never reached for a body stall.
- Contrast with the pattern the fleet adopted in PR #792 (Meta quota provider): preserve the body-read error and classify it, instead of collapsing every `response.json()` failure to `null`.

## Why it matters

A timed-out relay body is a transport failure, but it is reported as a successful send with zero results: dead tokens the relay asked to drop stay registered, and operators get no log line to diagnose the stall. That is the repo's named correctness invariant — never let a fetch failure masquerade as an authoritative empty success.

## Acceptance criteria

- An abort/timeout raised while reading the relay response body reaches the outer catch and logs `[APNs relay] request failed:` like other relay failures.
- A genuinely malformed JSON body keeps the current null/empty-results fallback (no throw, no spurious warning class change beyond what the fix documents).
- Regression test: relay fetch returns headers, then a body that only settles via the caller's abort signal; the send logs the request-failed warning and does not treat the result as a successful empty send.

title: fix(web): direct APNs send never settles when APNs closes the stream (RST_STREAM CANCEL) — PR #801's 30s deadline destroys an already-destroyed request and the fanout stalls

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/pr-diff-review
labels.description: Filed by the pr-diff-review job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Finding

PR #801's 30-second deadline for the direct APNs send does not settle the send when APNs closes the HTTP/2 stream with `RST_STREAM (CANCEL)`. The send promise settles only on the stream's `end` or `error` events; a peer `CANCEL` can close the stream with neither. When the deadline timer then fires, it calls `req.destroy(...)` on a stream that is already destroyed — a no-op — so no `error` is emitted either, and the promise never resolves.

Filed from PR diff review lane B. CodeRabbit raised this as a Major finding on PR #801 (inline comment at `apns-runtime.js:393`); the thread is still unresolved with no reply, and the gap is still present on current main.

## Evidence

- Source PR: #801 "fix(web): add deadlines to the APNs push runtime" (merged, head `d2fc9b94bf55726d97d13a5ddf4abb3ab0153a2d`, fixes #798). Its stated contract: expiry lands in the existing warn-and-continue paths and every outbound APNs path settles.
- Current main `fc5beaf35ae5b5d0842ab40d18ec92fe7a7b2ffd`, `packages/web/server/lib/notifications/apns-runtime.js`:
  - `:445` `sendOne` returns a promise that resolves only inside its event handlers.
  - `:472-474` the deadline timer: `req.destroy(new Error('APNs request timed out after ...'))`.
  - `:485` `req.on('end', ...)` and `:504` `req.on('error', ...)` are the only settling handlers — there is no `close` handler.
  - `:468-471` the comment asserts "Destroying the request routes into the error handler below (warn + resolve)" — true only while the stream is still open; it does not hold for a stream the peer already closed.
  - `:622-624` `sendViaDirectApns` awaits `Promise.all(deviceTokens.map(sendOne))` before closing the HTTP/2 session (`:606-625`), so one unsettled send stalls the whole direct fanout and leaks the session.
- PR #801's own deadline test masks the gap: its fake request's `destroy()` explicitly invokes `listeners.error?.(error)`, which real HTTP/2 streams do not guarantee for an already-closed stream.

## Why it matters

Direct mode is the self-hoster fallback (relay disabled + `OPENCHAMBER_APNS_*` set). One APNs-side stream cancellation wedges the serial push fanout indefinitely — exactly the hang class #798 / PR #801 set out to eliminate — with no warning logged, because the promise never settles and no handler runs.

## Acceptance criteria

- A `close` (or equivalent) settles the direct send exactly once when neither `end` nor `error` fires, using the same warn-and-continue result as the error path; an earlier `end`/`error` keeps precedence.
- Regression test: a fake stream that closes without `end`/`error` (and whose `destroy()` on the closed stream is a no-op) still settles `sendOne` / the fanout at the deadline.
- The existing #801 deadline tests (register stall, relay-send stall, direct stall) still pass.

title: fix(web): dictation model-catalog spec lookup resolves Object.prototype names — 'constructor'/'__proto__' crash with a TypeError instead of the unknown-model error

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Problem

`getLocalSttModelSpec` resolves a model id with a plain bracket lookup on the two catalog object literals, so `Object.prototype` member names — `'constructor'`, `'toString'`, `'hasOwnProperty'`, `'valueOf'`, `'__proto__'` — resolve to inherited values instead of missing. The function's own guard (`if (!spec) throw new Error('Unknown local speech model id: …')`) never fires for them, and the call then crashes with a `TypeError` from `Object.values(spec.files)` instead of the documented unknown-id error. Its sibling id checks in the same file already do this correctly with `Object.hasOwn` — the spec lookup is the inconsistent one.

## Evidence (verified by code read on main `668935927`, 2026-10-30)

`packages/web/server/lib/dictation/local/model-catalog.js`:

- `:18` / `:92` — `LOCAL_STT_MODEL_CATALOG` and `LOCAL_TTS_MODEL_CATALOG` are plain object literals (prototype is `Object.prototype`).
- `:330` and `:338` — `isLocalSttModelId` / `isLocalTtsModelId` guard with `Object.hasOwn(...)`, so `'constructor'` correctly reads as **not** a model id there.
- `:354-355` — `getLocalSttModelSpec` instead does `const spec = LOCAL_STT_MODEL_CATALOG[modelId] ?? LOCAL_TTS_MODEL_CATALOG[modelId];`. For `modelId === 'constructor'` this yields the inherited `Object` constructor (a truthy function, so `??` does not fall through and `!spec` is false); for `'__proto__'` it yields `Object.prototype`.
- `:362` — the return builds `requiredFiles: Object.values(spec.files)`; `spec.files` is `undefined` for every inherited value above, so the call throws `TypeError: Cannot convert undefined or null to object` — not the `Unknown local speech model id` error the function promises at `:357`.
- Unguarded callers of the lookup (no `isLocal*` check in the file): `model-downloader.js:247` (`isLocalSttModelInstalled`), `model-downloader.js:271` (`ensureLocalSttModel`), and the worker process, which takes `modelId` straight from its IPC message with no `isLocal*` guard anywhere in the file — `worker-process.js:59-60` (`getEngine`), `:102-104` (`getTtsEngine`), dispatched at `:117` / `:130`. The dictation service layer happens to sanitize ids before its own calls today (`service.js:79`, `:288`, `:305`), so the reachable surface is the exported downloader/worker path and any future direct caller — the same latent-resolver shape fixed for the agent-tool action resolver in #965 and `getProviderAuth` in #944.
- `model-catalog.test.js` tests the catalog pins and language resolution but has no prototype-name case for `getLocalSttModelSpec`.

## Why it matters

Every consumer of this lookup — install check, download/extract, and both worker engines — trusts it to reject an unknown id with one clean, catchable error. A prototype-named id instead produces an unrelated `TypeError` deep in spec construction, which the downloader and worker surface as a corrupt/failed model rather than "unknown model", and the inconsistency with the file's own `Object.hasOwn` guards means the next caller that forgets to pre-check re-opens the hole. This is the fleet's standing prototype-registry defect class (#939, #944, #965); this is its remaining instance in the dictation subsystem.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `getLocalSttModelSpec('constructor')`, `'toString'`, `'hasOwnProperty'`, `'valueOf'` and `'__proto__'` throw `Error('Unknown local speech model id: <id>')`, exactly like any other unknown id.
- [ ] The lookup uses own-property semantics consistent with `isLocalSttModelId`/`isLocalTtsModelId` in the same file (e.g. `Object.hasOwn` or an equivalent guard).
- [ ] Regression tests in `model-catalog.test.js` cover the prototype names for the spec lookup (and, if touched, for `getLocalSttModelDir` which delegates to it at `:400`); the existing dictation catalog/downloader suites pass.

title: fix(web): session-warming activity map has no cap — one entry per session the event stream ever reports is kept for the life of the server

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: status/in-progress
labels.description: Actively being worked

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Problem

The session-warming runtime keeps a per-session `activity` map that is written for **every** session the global event stream reports a status for — not only sessions the user has chosen to warm — and entries are removed only when that session is explicitly deleted, the stream reconnects, or warming is toggled off. There is no cap, no TTL, and no eviction. In a long-lived managed server the map grows by one entry per distinct session ever seen and never shrinks while the stream stays connected.

## Evidence (verified by code read on main `668935927`, 2026-10-30)

`packages/web/server/lib/session-warming/runtime.js`:

- `:98` — `const activity = new Map(); // sessionId → { busy, idleAt }`, a module-of-the-runtime map with no bound declared anywhere in the file (grep for LIMIT/MAX/cap over the file returns nothing for this map).
- `:325-327` (`processPayload`) — for every well-formed session-status payload, when the busy flag changes, the runtime does `activity.set(sessionId, { busy, idleAt })`. Only after that does it check `const entry = sessions.get(sessionId); if (!entry) return;` (`:329-330`) — so sessions that were never warmed are recorded too.
- The only removals: `:306` `activity.clear()` on `server.connected` (a stream reconnect), `:316` `activity.delete(sessionId)` on an explicit session-deleted payload, and `:348` `activity.clear()` when warming is toggled off. A session that ends, is archived, or simply goes quiet keeps its entry for the remaining life of the process.
- This is the outlier in its neighbourhood: sibling per-session maps in the same server were recently bounded for exactly this defect class — notifications' cooldown/parent caches cap at 500 with oldest-first eviction (`lib/notifications/runtime.js`, #974), and session-work's `seenMessages`/`suggested`/`turnGenerations` maps cap at `SEEN_MESSAGES_LIMIT` (`lib/session-work/runtime.js:121-169`).
- No test pins a bound: `runtime.test.js` covers pinging, windows, reconnect settle and deletion, but grep finds no reference to the activity map's size or eviction.

## Why it matters

The managed server is long-lived and session churn is structural in fleet use: dispatch and subagents create short-lived sessions continuously (see #791, dozens of live/idle sessions at a time). Each one leaves a permanent `{ busy, idleAt }` entry in this map for as long as the event stream stays connected — which, on a healthy server, is the common case, since reconnects are the only wholesale clear. The growth is small per entry but strictly monotonic and unbounded, the same slow-leak shape the fleet has been closing map by map (#967, #968, #972, #974, #979).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The `activity` map is bounded: entries for sessions that are not warmed are evicted past a stated cap (oldest-first, like the 500-entry sibling caps), or non-warmed entries expire after a stated TTL — while an entry for a currently warmed session is never evicted out from under `setSessionWarm`/`settle`.
- [ ] Behaviour is unchanged for warmed sessions: a toggle still consults the last known busy/idle state (`:383`) and starts its window/ping correctly after eviction of unrelated entries.
- [ ] A regression test feeds status payloads for many distinct non-warmed sessions and shows the map's retained state stays within the bound (observable through the runtime's public behaviour), and the existing session-warming suite passes.

title: fix(ui): McpxDashboard fetches have no deadline and no stale-response guard — a stalled /api/mcpx/status leaves Refresh disabled forever, and out-of-order types responses show the wrong namespace's types

labels.name: effort/s

body:
## Problem

The mcpx settings dashboard (`McpxDashboard`) makes all three of its API calls with bare `fetch` — no deadline, no abort, and no stale-response guard. Two user-visible failure modes follow, in the panel whose whole job is showing whether the mcpx daemon is healthy:

1. **A stalled status load wedges the panel for the session.** `fetchStatus` sets `loading` and only clears it in `finally`; the Refresh button is `disabled={loading}`. If the `/api/mcpx/status` or `/api/mcpx/namespaces` request never settles, the spinner runs forever and Refresh can never be clicked again — the user must reload the app to retry a status check on a daemon that may simply have been restarting.
2. **Out-of-order type loads show the wrong namespace's types.** `fetchTypes` records the selected namespace, awaits the fetch, then unconditionally applies the response. Clicking namespace A (slow answer) and then namespace B (fast answer) ends with A's late response overwriting the panel while B is selected — the types shown do not belong to the namespace on screen.

## Evidence (verified on main `6db66f5c2`, 2026-10-30)

`packages/ui/src/components/sections/mcp/McpxDashboard.tsx`:

- `:42` `const res = await fetch('/api/mcpx/status');` and `:47` `const nsRes = await fetch('/api/mcpx/namespaces');` — no `signal`, no timeout, inside `fetchStatus` (`:38`–`:56`), whose `finally` (`:53`–`:55`) is the only place `loading` clears.
- Refresh button: `disabled={loading}` (render, ~`:94`) — so a never-settling load disables the only retry affordance in the panel.
- `fetchTypes` (`:58`–`:71`): `setSelectedNs(ns)` at `:59`, then `const res = await fetch(\`/api/mcpx/types?namespace=…\`)` at `:62`, then unconditional `setTypes(...)` at `:66`. No request token, no `AbortController`, no check that `ns` is still the selected namespace when the response lands.
- The established UI pattern exists in the same package: 20 uses of `AbortSignal.timeout(...)` across `packages/ui/src` (e.g. the pairing redeem calls at `RemoteInstancesPage.tsx:710` and `desktopHosts.ts:158`), and sibling settings pages route API calls through `runtimeFetch` (`@/lib/runtime-fetch`, e.g. `BehaviorPage.tsx`). This component uses neither.
- Dedup: #774 (closed) bounded the **server-side** mcpx daemon client behind `/api/mcpx/*`; it did not touch this component. #851/#854/#855 fixed the same no-deadline class for other UI fetches (gitmoji catalog, URL-token mint, mobile update check) — none covers the mcpx dashboard.

## Why it matters

This dashboard is the surface a user opens precisely when the mcpx daemon looks stuck. A panel that can itself stick in "loading" with its Refresh button disabled — and that can attribute one namespace's tool types to another — undermines the one screen meant to answer "is the daemon OK, and what does it serve?".

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] All three dashboard fetches carry a deadline (e.g. `AbortSignal.timeout`, consistent with the package's existing uses) so a stalled answer surfaces the existing error state instead of loading forever; Refresh is usable again after a timed-out load.
- [ ] A types response is applied only if its namespace is still the selected one (request token, abort of the superseded request, or equivalent guard) — a late response for a previously selected namespace never overwrites the current selection's types.
- [ ] Normal behavior is unchanged: successful loads render status, namespaces, and types exactly as before.
- [ ] A component test (following the existing `McpPage.test.tsx` patterns in the same folder) pins both behaviors: a never-settling status fetch reaches the error/retry state after the deadline, and an out-of-order types response does not overwrite the current namespace's types.

title: fix(web): git service remote-existence and remote-heads caches never evict — TTL is checked only on re-lookup of the same directory+remote, so every worktree directory ever listed is retained for the life of the server

labels.name: kind/performance
labels.description: Performance problem or optimization

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

Two module-level caches in the web server's git service enforce their 30-second TTL only on re-lookup of the exact same key. Expired entries for keys that are never looked up again are never removed — there is no sweep, no cap, and (for one of them) no delete call anywhere in the codebase. Both keys embed the working directory, so every distinct directory the server ever lists branches for — in fleet use, a steady churn of short-lived worktree directories — leaves a permanent entry in a long-lived server process.

## Evidence (verified on main `6db66f5c2`, 2026-10-30)

`packages/web/server/lib/git/service.js`:

- `remoteExistenceCache` — declared `:31`; TTL `REMOTE_EXISTENCE_CACHE_TTL_MS = 30_000` at `:34`. `hasRemote` (`:1092`–`:1102`) returns the cached value while fresh and otherwise `remoteExistenceCache.set(key, { exists, checkedAt })`. Grep over the whole repo: **1 `set`, 0 `delete`, 0 `clear`** for this map — an entry, once written, is never removed for any reason.
- `remoteHeadsCache` — declared `:4711`; TTL `REMOTE_HEADS_TTL_MS = 30_000` at `:4710`. `readRemoteHeads` (`:4714`–`:4730`) keys entries by `` `${directory}\0${remote.name}\0${remote.refs?.fetch ?? ''}` `` and stores `{ at, localKey, heads }`, where `heads` is a `Set` of every branch name on that remote. The only `delete` (`:4728`) fires when the `ls-remote` promise rejects. A successful entry whose key is never read again stays forever, branch-name set included.
- Key churn is structural, not hypothetical: both keys start with the directory path, and directories are per-worktree. The same file already treats directory-keyed state as needing a bound — `worktreeRepositoryKeyByDirectory` is capped with oldest-first eviction at `MAX_TRACKED_WORKTREE_DIRECTORIES` (`:5053`–`:5058`) and `worktreeTopologyByRepository` at `MAX_TRACKED_WORKTREE_REPOSITORIES` (`:5115`–`:5118`) — and `packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.js` caps its git-read cache at 500 entries / 1 MiB (`:251`–`:252`). These two caches are the outliers in the same subsystem.
- No test references either cache: grep for `remoteExistenceCache` / `remoteHeadsCache` / `REMOTE_HEADS` across `packages/web/server` tests returns nothing outside `service.js` itself.

## Why it matters

The managed server is long-lived and the git panel is a living surface: branch listing runs several times per action (the `readRemoteHeads` header comment at `:4705`–`:4709` says exactly this). Every worktree ever opened contributes one existence entry per remote plus one branch-name `Set` per remote+refspec, retained for the life of the process. This is the same defect class already fixed for the npm-registry caches (#967), the skills-catalog caches (#968), and the Octokit ETag cache (#848), and currently open for the pr-status caches (#972) — a distinct module and subsystem from all of those.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Expired `remoteExistenceCache` and `remoteHeadsCache` entries are removed even for keys never re-read (sweep on insert/access, periodic prune, or a size bound with oldest-first eviction — matching the in-file precedents above).
- [ ] Fresh-hit behavior is unchanged: within the 30 s TTL and with unchanged local remote-tracking refs, `hasRemote` / `readRemoteHeads` serve the cached answer and concurrent listings still share one `ls-remote` round trip; a rejected `ls-remote` is still not cached.
- [ ] Tests pin the eviction: after the TTL passes (or the bound is exceeded), entries for never-re-read directory+remote keys are gone, while live entries survive.
- [ ] No change to the TTL values, key shapes, or the branch-listing results returned to callers.

title: feat(web): one shared durable-store primitive in lib/shared — strict three-state read, preserve-aside, mode-explicit atomic write (design #976, phase 1)

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: New feature or capability request

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/m
labels.description: Medium: expected under 1 day of work

labels.name: source/design-architect
labels.description: Filed by the repo design architect job

body:
## Scope — phase 1 of design #976

Land one shared durable-store primitive in `packages/web/server/lib/shared/`, with **no call-site behaviour change**. This is the consolidation step only; migration of stores is phase 2 (a separate sub-issue of #976).

The primitive codifies the behaviour the per-store fixes of 2026-10-30 (#887/#889/#892/#897/#898/#905/#907) each hand-wrote around the already-shared `atomic-rename.js`:

1. **Strict three-state reader** — returns `missing | valid | malformed` for a JSON file, with a caller-supplied shape check (a parsed non-object is `malformed` for an object-shaped store — the routing stores' rule). Distinct from every lenient read-as-empty reader: callers choose explicitly what each state means. (Design #976 rule 1. Private precedents being generalised: `linear/auth.js:59` `readJsonFileStrict`, the routing stores' reader, `opencode/settings-runtime.js`'s strict read.)
2. **Preserve-aside helper** — renames a malformed file to `` `${file}.corrupt-${Date.now()}-${process.pid}-${random}` `` (the collision-proof spelling the later fixes converged on: `tts/voice-keys.js:64`, `routing/route-settings.js:56`, `tunnels/managed-config.js:73`; the plain `` `.corrupt-${Date.now()}` `` spelling of `client-auth/pairing.js:147` et al. is the anti-pattern — routing needed a follow-up fix, commit `650dce3ed`, to make its preservation collision-proof). Before renaming, it re-validates the on-disk bytes: a valid replacement written concurrently is never renamed away. Its result distinguishes *preserved* from *preservation failed*, and the contract is fail-closed — a caller whose preservation failed must refuse the write (the routing/tunnels/settings behaviour). Raw parse errors are never logged (they can quote file contents).
3. **Mode-explicit atomic writer** — unique temp name in the same directory (pid + time + random, not a bare `.${pid}.tmp`), written with a caller-stated mode (`0o600` for secret-bearing stores), renamed via the existing shared `renameWithRetry` / `renameSyncWithRetry`. Composes `atomic-rename.js`; does not modify it.

Each piece in **async and sync spellings** (the `atomic-rename.js` precedent), fs-injectable where stores inject fs today (e.g. `client-auth/pairing.js` receives `fsPromises`), dependency-free and domain-neutral (platform APIs only — shapes, defaults and domain errors stay with callers).

Plus: behaviour-matrix tests beside the module in the `shared/` test style, and a section in `packages/web/server/lib/shared/DOCUMENTATION.md` stating contract rules 1–5 from #976 and what stays out — the named divergent policies that are **not** this contract: `relay/key-store.js` (throw-and-stop), `agent-memory/runtime.js` (malformed = failure), `walkthrough/store.js` and other caches (corrupt = miss).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] All three pieces exist in `packages/web/server/lib/shared/`, async + sync, importing nothing beyond platform APIs, composing `renameWithRetry`/`renameSyncWithRetry`.
- [ ] Behaviour-matrix tests cover: missing / valid / malformed / non-object-shape reads; two preservations in the same millisecond both surviving (collision-proof naming); preservation failure ⇒ the fail-closed result a caller must honour; a valid replacement landing between judgement and preserve is never renamed away; the stated mode present on the written file; sync and async spellings answering identically across the matrix.
- [ ] `shared/DOCUMENTATION.md` documents the contract (rules 1–5 of #976) and the named divergences that stay out.
- [ ] No existing store changes behaviour in this phase; `bun run check:changed` passes.

Design: #976 (full doc: `files/designs/openchamber-durable-json-store.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace).
