body:
## Problem

`sessionParentIdCache` in `packages/web/server/lib/notifications/runtime.js` (verified on main `ec3ce9888`) grows by one entry per session for the life of the server and is never capped:

- The map is declared at `runtime.js:215` with a 60s TTL (`SESSION_PARENT_CACHE_TTL_MS`, `:216`).
- Every event payload the notification trigger sees populates it: `maybeSendPushForTrigger` calls `maybeCacheSessionParentFromPayload` first (`:524`), which caches `{ parentID, at }` for every `session.created` record (`:327-335` → `setCachedSessionParentId`, `:253-255`).
- The TTL is only evaluated in `getCachedSessionParentId` (`:242-251`), which deletes the entry **only when that same session is read again after expiry**. A finished session is never read again, so its entry is retained forever. There is no max-entries cap and no sweep.

The same factory bounds its sibling stores, so the pattern is established in-place: `assistantStepMeta` and `lastAssistantStepBySession` are capped at 500 with oldest-eviction (`ASSISTANT_STEP_CACHE_LIMIT`, `:276`, evictions `:294-299`), and the per-session cooldown maps are capped via `rememberSessionNotificationAt` (`:205-212`). #875 pruned `notifiedPermissionRequests` and the cooldown maps in this file, and its inventory noted this cache has a `.delete` (the expired-read path above) — but no cap or expiry sweep was ever filed for it. This is also the same defect class as #903 (template-runtime session caches) and #972 (pr-status.js caches), in a different store.

## Verification (this run)

Laptop probes against the real module (laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-notif-parent-cache-20261030/`, fork at `ec3ce9888`, `node --expose-gc`), driving the exported `maybeSendPushForTrigger` with `session.created` payloads and stub deps (the `trigger-runtime.test.js` construction):

- Instrumented copy (only change: a `sessionParentIdCache.size` accessor next to the setter): after 200,000 distinct sessions the cache size was exactly **200,000** and heapUsed grew 7.0 → 41.4 MB.
- Unmodified module, 200,000 payloads: distinct sessions → heapTotal 16 → 136 MB, RSS 67.7 → 170.3 MB; control (same session repeated 200,000 times) → heapTotal 16 → 24 MB, RSS 68.4 → 85.6 MB. The growth tracks distinct sessions, not call volume.

## Why it matters

The notification trigger runs in the long-lived OpenChamber server and sees every session created on the host — including every subagent session, which fleet dispatch creates in large numbers. Each one leaves a permanent entry. The growth is slow per session (~170 B retained) but unbounded and invisible: no cap, no metric, and no path that ever removes a finished session's entry.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `sessionParentIdCache` is bounded: a max-entries cap with oldest/LRU eviction (following the in-file 500-entry precedent) and/or a sweep that drops expired entries without requiring a same-key read.
- [ ] Lookup behavior is unchanged for live entries: a parent cached from a `session.created`/`session.updated` payload or a lineage fetch still answers within the 60s TTL, and an expired entry still re-fetches.
- [ ] Regression tests show entries for sessions that are never read again are evicted under cap pressure / after expiry, and the existing `trigger-runtime.test.js` suite passes.

title: fix(web): pr-status.js caches never evict — repoPulls, repo metadata, default-branch and search-disabled maps keep one entry per distinct repo for the life of the server

labels.name: app/web

body:
## Problem

Four module-level caches in `packages/web/server/lib/github/pr-status.js` (verified on main `ec3ce9888`) are checked against a TTL only when the **same key** is read again, and none of them has an entry cap or a sweep. An entry for a repo that is never revisited stays in memory for the life of the server process:

- `defaultBranchCache` (`pr-status.js:18`) — read at `:177`; an expired entry is only overwritten by a successful refetch of the same key, and the fetch-error path (returns `null`) leaves the stale entry in place.
- `repoMetadataCache` (`pr-status.js:19`) — read at `:219`; same pattern, and each value retains the **full** `repos.get` response object (`data` at `:236-241`), the heaviest payload of the four.
- `repoPullsCache` (`pr-status.js:359`, TTL 45s at `:358`) — read at `:448`; each value retains the repo's pull-request list (up to 100 PR objects, `:466`).
- `_searchApiDisabledRepos` (`pr-status.js:497`, retry window 5 min at `:498`) — read at `:525`; an entry is deleted only when a later search for the same repo-set key succeeds (`:545`). A repo set that 403s once and is never searched again is retained forever.

The same file already bounds its other two caches, so the pattern is established in-place: `_historicalPrCache` is capped at 500 entries with oldest-eviction (`:371`, `:386-392`) and `_searchMissCache` is capped at 500 (`:504`, `:511-517`). The four caches above were missed. This is also the same defect class fixed this week in sibling modules: npm-registry metadata caches (#967/#969) and the skills-catalog / github-meta caches (#970) got sweep + cap for exactly this "TTL-on-read only, expired entries never evicted" shape.

Keys are scoped per repo **and per Octokit identity** (`scopedCacheKey`, `:33-36`), so distinct users/tokens multiply the entries per repo.

## Verification (this run)

Laptop probe against the real module (laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-prstatus-cache-20261030/probe.mjs`, fork at `ec3ce9888`, `node --expose-gc`), driving the exported `findBranchPrCandidates` with a fake Octokit whose `pulls.list` returns a fresh 20-PR page:

- 20,000 **distinct** repos: heap 9.4 MB → 102.2 MB (+92.8 MB); after simulating TTL expiry (`Date.now` +10 min, past the 45s TTL), touching 5 fresh repos and forcing GC twice, heap was still 102.2 MB — no expired entry was released.
- Control, same repo repeated 20,000 times: 6 `pulls.list` calls total, heap flat at 9.5 MB — the growth is per-distinct-repo retention, not per-call churn.

## Why it matters

The OpenChamber web server is long-lived (managed-server layer, runs for days). PR status is polled for every worktree/session branch, and a fleet machine touches many repos, forks and identities over that lifetime — parents and sources are folded in by `expandRepoNetwork`, so one checkout can seed several repo keys. Retention is unbounded and invisible: no metric, no cap, and the retained payloads (full repo metadata, up-to-100-PR lists) are the largest objects this module handles. It is a slow, certain memory leak in the exact shape the repo has already decided to fix three times this week.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every cache in `pr-status.js` is bounded: expired entries are actually evicted (sweep on write/read or equivalent) and a maximum-entries cap with oldest/LRU eviction applies, following the in-file `_historicalPrCache`/`_searchMissCache` precedent or the #969/#970 sweep+cap shape.
- [ ] Behavior is unchanged for live entries: TTL freshness semantics, `invalidateRepoPullsCache` invalidation (including pending-write tokens), and the search-disabled retry window all keep working.
- [ ] Regression tests show that entries for repos that are never revisited are evicted after expiry/cap pressure, and that a fresh entry for the same key still hits the cache.
- [ ] Existing `pr-status.test.js` suite passes.

title: fix(ci): ci-policy.md and workflow headers still describe a PR tier that commit 4478502bb removed — docs claim lint/type-check gate every PR, but no workflow runs on pull_request

labels.name: kind/ci

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator

labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: area/ci

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

Since commit `4478502bb` ("ci: main-only workflow triggers, cancel-in-progress everywhere", Drew's order 2026-10-30: "CI runs only on the main branch"), no workflow in this repo runs on `pull_request`. That part is deliberate. But the in-repo documentation and workflow comments still describe a live PR tier that can never fire, so anyone (human or fleet agent) reading the policy surface is misled about what gates a merge and keeps working around the gap by hand (`gh workflow run oc-review.yml --ref <branch>`).

## Evidence (verified on main `cf5011987`, 2026-10-30)

- `.github/workflows/oc-review.yml` `on:` block (lines ~16–26) contains only `push: branches: [main]`, `schedule`, and `workflow_dispatch`. The removed trigger is visible in `git show 4478502bb -- .github/workflows/oc-review.yml`: `pull_request: types: [opened, synchronize, reopened, ready_for_review]` deleted.
- The same file's header still says: "PR tier = lint + type-check only", "Dedup: push is restricted to branches: [main], so a PR branch push fires pull_request only — a commit never runs the same suite twice", and states a "MERGE REQUIREMENT (Drew, 2026-10-29): the basic tier only" for jobs that now never run pre-merge.
- The `tests` and `build` jobs still carry dead guards `if: github.event_name != 'pull_request'` (oc-review.yml:81, :108) — an event that can no longer occur — and the concurrency group still keys on `github.event.pull_request.number || github.run_id` (:32).
- `.github/ci-policy.md` tier map (lines 58–63) still marks `lint` and `type-check` as "✅ runs" on PR (`pull_request`), presents the basic tier as the merge requirement, and states (line ~66) "`nix-eval.yml` stays paths-gated on PRs to `flake.nix`, `flake.lock`, and `nix/**`" — but nix-eval.yml's `on:` is now `workflow_dispatch` only.
- `.github/workflows/nix-eval.yml` header (lines 13–14) likewise still claims "Triggers are pull_request / workflow_dispatch only".
- Live confirmation: `gh run list --workflow "pr checks"` shows only `push` (main) and `workflow_dispatch` events — no `pull_request` run exists since the change; queue workers already hand-dispatch the workflow per branch as a workaround (see backlog note, Lane A shift 2026-10-30 16:37 CDT).

## Why it matters

The CI policy file is the fleet's contract for what "green" means before merge. With the docs claiming a PR tier that does not exist, reviewers and queue workers cannot tell from the repo whether the main-only shape is intended (it is, per 4478502bb) or a regression, and the merge-requirement wording points at checks no PR will ever produce. Stale policy text in exactly the file meant to be the adjustable policy surface invites the next agent to "fix" the workflows instead of the docs, or vice versa.

## Acceptance criteria

- `.github/ci-policy.md` describes the actual trigger set: main-only (`push` to main + nightly schedule + manual dispatch), with the merge-requirement section rewritten to match (or the PR tier restored by an explicit policy change — one direction, applied consistently).
- `oc-review.yml` header comments no longer claim a PR tier, a pull_request dedup shape, or a PR-based merge requirement that cannot fire; the dead `github.event_name != 'pull_request'` job guards and the pull_request concurrency key are removed or justified in a comment.
- `nix-eval.yml` header and the ci-policy tier map agree with nix-eval's actual triggers.
- No behavior change to any workflow's triggers or jobs is required by this issue beyond comment/guard cleanup, unless the triage decision is to restore the PR tier instead.

title: fix(web): skills-catalog scan and repo-meta caches never evict expired entries from memory — expiry is enforced only for the key being read, so every catalog ever scanned is retained for the life of the process

labels.name: kind/performance
labels.description: Performance problem or optimization

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

The skills-catalog caches never evict expired entries from memory: expiry is only enforced lazily for the single key being read, there is no sweep and no entry/byte cap, and the reset functions have no production caller.

- Scan cache: `packages/web/server/lib/skills-catalog/cache.js` — module-level `cache` Map (line 8). `setCachedScan` (lines 76-80) stores `{ expiresAt, value }` per key (`repo[#ref]::subpath::identity`, line 57-63) with a 3-hour default TTL; `getCachedScan` (lines 65-74) deletes a key only when that exact key is read after expiry. Expired entries for keys never read again stay in the Map for the life of the process. `clearCache()` (line 82) is called only from tests (grep: no production caller). The disk writer already filters expired entries out of the persisted file (lines 37-51) — so on disk they die, in memory they do not.
- Repo-meta cache: `packages/web/server/lib/skills-catalog/github-meta.js` — same shape: `metaCache` Map (line 14), 3-hour TTL checked only in `fetchRepoMeta` for the requested repo, no sweep/cap. Its own documentation (`skills-catalog/DOCUMENTATION.md:36`) calls `clearGitHubMetaCache()` a "Test-only cache reset", confirming there is no production eviction path. Values here are small (stars + timestamp), so this half is minor; the scan cache holds whole catalog scan results and is the real weight.

Callers: `scanWithCache` is used by the skill routes (`packages/web/server/lib/opencode/skill-routes.js:468`, wired in `feature-routes-runtime.js:660`), so every distinct catalog (repo/ref/subpath/identity) a long-lived server ever scans is retained in memory indefinitely, TTL notwithstanding.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `cf5011987`)

Laptop probe against the real module (`~/git/fleet/probe-oc-skills-cache-20261030/probe.mjs`; `cache.js` md5 `7ef44d8c83ecacaa3e604e57819d2f4a`, byte-identical to main; `OPENCHAMBER_DATA_DIR` pointed at a probe temp dir):

- Set 1,500 distinct scan entries (~57 KB value each, 50 ms TTL): heap 4.2 MB → **89.6 MB**.
- After TTL expiry, reading one expired key returns null and deletes only that key; heap stays **89.5 MB** — the other 1,499 expired entries are never released.
- `clearCache()` + GC drops heap to **4.4 MB**, proving it is the only release path — and production never calls it.

Related but distinct: #967 (filed today) covers the npm-registry caches in `lib/opencode` + VS Code; #936 covers the installed-sources store in this same catalog module family (corrupt-read data loss, a different defect). Dedup: `gh` search for the skills-catalog/scan cache across open+closed issues returns no eviction/retention filing.

## Why it matters

Same grow-forever class as fixed #903/#875 and today's #967, in the one catalog surface those sweeps missed: memory creep proportional to every catalog ever browsed, in a server meant to run for weeks. The 3-hour TTL gives a false sense of boundedness — it bounds freshness, not retention.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Expired scan-cache entries are actually removed without requiring a re-read of the same key (sweep on access/insert or periodic prune), and/or a max-entries/max-bytes bound with eviction is enforced; same treatment for the github-meta cache (small values — TTL sweep alone is fine there).
- [ ] In-memory retention and the disk-persisted form agree on expiry (the disk writer already drops expired entries).
- [ ] Tests in `cache.test.js` (and `github-meta` tests if touched) pin that expired entries for never-re-read keys are gone after the bound/sweep runs.
- [ ] Behavior unchanged for live entries: cache hit within TTL, in-flight scan dedupe, concurrency limit, and `scanWithCache` refresh semantics.

title: fix(web): managed-process claim files are never deleted — every orphan handover leaks a claim file the reaper cannot see, and a stale claim answers with a dead holder

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`claimManagedProcess` records an orphan-adoption claim as a file `<pid>.claim-from-<fromOwner>` in the managed-process registry directory — and no code path ever deletes a claim file. Every handover leaks one more file, the orphan reaper cannot see them, and a stale claim keeps answering ownership questions with a long-dead holder pid.

## Evidence (verified on main `f0d3428b8`, 2026-10-30)

Code:

- `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/managed-process-registry.js:89-105` — `claimManagedProcess(pid, fromOwner, claimant)` creates `${pid}.claim-from-${fromOwner}` with flag `wx`; on `EEXIST` it reads and returns the recorded holder. There is no delete, expiry, or liveness check anywhere in the function.
- Repo-wide search: `claim-from` occurs only at creation (registry) and in `managed-process-claim.test.js`. Nothing removes claim files: `unregisterManagedProcess` (`managed-process-registry.js:207-214`) removes only `<pid>.json`, and the reaper's cleanup (`:342`) removes only the `.json` files it iterated.
- `readAllEntries` filters `names.filter((value) => value.endsWith('.json'))` (`:169`), so claim files are invisible to `reapOrphanedProcesses` — they are never inspected, pruned, or counted.
- The stale answer is load-bearing: `lifecycle.js:535-546` (`otherServerOwning`) calls `claimProcess(pid, owner)` and trusts the returned holder — if the holder pid is alive it is treated as the owning server; if dead, the caller gets `'unknown'` and the orphan is not adopted.

Probe (run on the laptop against the real module, `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-claim-leak-20261030/probe.mjs`, registry dir pointed at a temp dir):

- Three successive handovers of pid 500 (owners 100 → 201 → 202 → 203) left `500.claim-from-100`, `500.claim-from-201`, `500.claim-from-202` alongside `500.json`.
- After `unregisterManagedProcess(500)`: all three claim files remained; only the `.json` was removed.
- After `reapOrphanedProcesses(...)`: result `{ inspected: 0, reaped: 0 }` and all three claim files still remained.
- A fresh claim attempt for the same (pid 500, fromOwner 100) pair still returned the stale holder `201` — a pid that may by then have been recycled onto an unrelated process, which `otherServerOwning` would then treat as the live owner (or, if dead, as `'unknown'`, leaving the orphan unadopted).

## Why it matters

Handovers are not rare: every upgrade/self-handoff where a server adopts an orphan whose owner died goes through this claim. The registry directory — whose whole design premise is "one small file per live process, pruned by the reaper" — instead accumulates one permanent file per handover, forever, and the stale records are not inert: they answer future ownership questions for recycled (pid, owner) pairs with wrong, dead, or recycled holder pids.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Claim files have a defined end of life: removed when the claimed process is unregistered/reaped, when the claim is superseded by the winner's re-registration, or swept by the reaper when the named pid/holder is dead — at least one mechanism, applied consistently.
- [ ] A claim whose holder pid is dead no longer blocks or misattributes a later claim for the same (pid, fromOwner) pair (the two-claimant race semantics in `managed-process-claim.test.js` still hold for live holders).
- [ ] Regression tests extend `managed-process-claim.test.js` / the registry tests: handovers followed by unregister and by a reaper pass leave no claim files behind, and a dead-holder claim does not answer for a new claimant.
- [ ] The VS Code parity implementation of the registry (same directory) is checked and kept consistent, per the header comment in `managed-process-registry.js`.

title: fix(web): managed OpenCode log opencode.log grows without bound — no rotation or truncation anywhere, and only the last 32 KiB is ever read

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/m
labels.description: Medium: expected under 1 day of work

labels.name: kind/infrastructure
labels.description: Infrastructure work

body:
## Problem

The managed OpenCode child's stdout/stderr go to one file — `<dataDir>/managed-opencode/opencode.log` — for the whole life of the data dir, and nothing ever rotates, truncates, or caps it. The module's own documentation already admits the gap; this issue tracks fixing it.

## Evidence (verified on main `f0d3428b8`, 2026-10-30)

- `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/managed-opencode-state.js:13` — `logPath: path.join(dir, 'opencode.log')` is the single log for every managed spawn on that data dir.
- `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/lifecycle.js:669-681` — each launch opens it append-only (`openSync(managedPaths.logPath, 'a', 0o600)`), records `logOffset = fstatSync(logFd).size`, and hands the fd to the child's stdout+stderr (`stdio: [..., logFd, logFd]`). The fd/offset design assumes the file only ever grows.
- Repo-wide search: no rotation, truncation, or size cap exists for this file anywhere in `packages/` (the only "rotate" hits in the module are password rotation and an unrelated comment).
- `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/DOCUMENTATION.md:453` — "Known gaps: no log rotation for `opencode.log`".
- Nothing ever reads more than the tail: `MANAGED_STDERR_TAIL_MAX_BYTES = 32 * 1024` (`lifecycle.js:97`), and `readLogTail` (`managed-opencode-state.js:122-129`) only reads the last `maxBytes`. Everything older than 32 KiB is kept on disk forever and never used.
- The growth is structural, not per-run: a managed OpenCode is deliberately left running across OpenChamber restarts and adopted by the next start (same data dir, same log file), so one long-lived install accumulates every spawn's output plus the adopted server's ongoing output, indefinitely.

## Why it matters

A core promise of the managed lifecycle is that OpenCode outlives OpenChamber and is adopted across upgrades — which also means its log outlives every individual run's housekeeping. On a long-lived install the file grows without any bound, silently eating disk on exactly the machines (always-on fleet hosts, user desktops) where nobody watches the data dir. Every other retained-bytes surface in this codebase is capped (bounded response readers, the 32 KiB stderr tail, ETag cache byte budgets); this file is the outlier.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `opencode.log` is bounded by a stated size policy (cap + retained tail, rotation, or equivalent), enforced on a defined trigger (e.g. at spawn, before the new fd is opened).
- [ ] Rotation never loses the bytes current readers depend on: the readiness drain (`readLogSince` from the spawn offset) and `readLogTail`'s 32 KiB tail still work across a rotation, including when a previously spawned, still-running adopted OpenCode holds the old fd open (POSIX rename semantics vs Windows must be handled explicitly, or rotation is restricted to moments when that is safe — say which).
- [ ] The spawn-time `logOffset` bookkeeping stays correct: no other server's "server listening" line is consumed or missed because the file shrank.
- [ ] Regression tests cover: an oversized pre-existing log at spawn time, tail readability after rotation, and the no-rotation-needed case leaving the file untouched.
- [ ] `DOCUMENTATION.md` known-gaps line is updated to match the new behavior.

title: fix(web): GitHub gh-CLI toggles rewrite shared settings.json from an empty base when it is malformed

labels.name: source/creator

body:
# GitHub gh-CLI toggles rewrite the shared settings.json from an empty base when it is malformed — every other setting is erased

## Summary

`packages/web/server/lib/github/auth.js` read-modify-writes the **shared** `settings.json` (the main OpenChamber settings file in the data dir) through a lenient reader that returns `{}` on any parse failure. Toggling the gh CLI on/off while `settings.json` is momentarily malformed (torn write, crash mid-save by another writer, manual edit typo) silently rewrites the whole file containing only the one gh-CLI key — every other user setting is permanently lost, with no error and no preserved copy.

This is the exact failure class fixed for the Linear sibling in #907: `linear/auth.js` now routes settings writes through `readSettingsForUpdate()` / `readJsonFileStrict()` with the comment "a write built on a malformed file would rewrite the whole file from an empty base" (`linear/auth.js:299-303`). The relay key store likewise reads settings strictly (`relay/key-store.js` `readSettingsStrict`). The GitHub module was missed.

## Evidence (main `f0d3428b8c21ea0cb989623bbfe018d8a39f180a`)

- `github/auth.js:309-314` — `readSettingsFile()`: `catch {}` around `JSON.parse(...)` falls through to `return {}` for a malformed file (it also returns a non-object parsed value unchecked).
- `github/auth.js:17` — `SETTINGS_FILE = path.join(OPENCHAMBER_DATA_DIR, 'settings.json')` — the shared main settings file, not a GitHub-private file.
- Write paths built on the lenient reader:
  - `github/auth.js:394-399` — `setGhCliDisabled(disabled)`: `const settings = readSettingsFile(); settings.ghCliDisabled = ...; writeSettingsFile(settings);`
  - `github/auth.js:406-410` — `setGhCliActive(active)`: same shape.
- Reachable from user actions in `github/routes.js`: `setGhCliActive(false)` (:1286, :1669), `setGhCliActive(true)` (:1560 — activating the gh-cli account), `setGhCliDisabled` via `setGhCliDisabledState` (:1359-1367, the disable/enable endpoint).
- The module's own credential store (`github-auth.json`) already does this correctly — atomic temp+rename writes and `invalidState` thrown on malformed JSON (`auth.js:197-214`) — so the settings path is an outlier inside the same file.

## Reproduction (laptop probe vs the real module, fork at `f0d3428b8`)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-gh-settings-20261030/probe.mjs` (imports the real `github/auth.js` with `OPENCHAMBER_DATA_DIR` pointed at a temp dir):

- Control — valid `settings.json` `{theme, ghCliActive, openCodeGoPlan, nested, profileName}` → `setGhCliDisabled(true)` preserves all keys. ✅
- Experiment — torn `settings.json` (`{"theme":"dark","ghCliActive":true,"openCodeGoPlan":"pro","nested":{"a":1` — truncated mid-object) → `setGhCliActive(true)` **does not throw** and the file afterwards is exactly:

  ```json
  {
    "ghCliActive": true
  }
  ```

  Every other setting is gone; no backup, no warning.
- Read side: `isGhCliDisabled()` on the torn file silently answers `false`.

## Why it matters

`settings.json` is the user's main settings document (themes, profiles, provider plans, session preferences, and keys other modules keep there). A single gh-CLI toggle at the wrong moment — e.g. right after a crash tore a settings write, the exact scenario the atomic-write fixes elsewhere guard against — destroys all of it, silently. The fleet has already accepted this severity for the identical Linear path (#907, fixed and merged); the GitHub path is the remaining unguarded writer of the same shared file.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `setGhCliDisabled` / `setGhCliActive` refuse to write when `settings.json` exists but is malformed: they throw (or otherwise surface an error the routes report) and leave the file byte-for-byte untouched — the strict-reader pattern from `linear/auth.js` (`readSettingsForUpdate`) or the settings runtime's strict read.
- [ ] A missing `settings.json` still behaves as today (starts from `{}` and writes the gh-CLI keys).
- [ ] A valid `settings.json` round-trips: toggling either key preserves every unrelated key exactly.
- [ ] A non-object JSON document in `settings.json` (e.g. `42`, `[]`) is treated as malformed for write purposes, not used as the base object.
- [ ] Tests pin all four cases against the real module (the module currently has route-level tests; add store-level coverage for these two setters), and existing GitHub auth tests stay green.

title: fix(web): quota provider registries resolve Object.prototype members — 'constructor'/'toString'/'__proto__' pass as supported providers, fabricate configured:true results, and 500 the credential routes

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

The quota provider registries are plain object literals keyed by a URL-supplied `providerId`, and every lookup resolves inherited `Object.prototype` members. A provider id of `constructor`, `toString`, `hasOwnProperty`, or `__proto__` therefore passes the "is this a supported provider?" checks as if it were a real provider, and the quota API answers with fabricated results, wrong status codes, and 500s — instead of the `404 UNSUPPORTED_PROVIDER` / "Unsupported provider" answers a genuinely unknown id gets.

## Evidence (main `f0d3428b8`, verified this run)

Plain-object registries with unguarded keyed lookups:

- `packages/web/server/lib/quota/credentials/providers.js:5` — `export const normalizers = { 'exe-dev': …, cursor: …, zenmux: …, opendesign: … }`; lookups at `:33` and `:38` (`normalizers[providerId]`).
- `packages/web/server/lib/quota/routes.js:13-19` — `validators` is a plain object literal; `:23` `if (!normalizers[providerId])` is the only supported-provider gate for the credential routes; `:54` calls `normalizers[providerId](req.body)` **outside** the `try`; `:57`/`:70` call `validators[providerId](credential)`.
- `packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/index.js:51` — `const registry = { claude: …, … }`; lookups at `:375`, `:482`, `:500` (`registry[providerId]`).

Reproduced this run with the real modules (lib tree copied verbatim from main to the laptop probe dir `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-proto-provider/`, `registerQuotaRoutes` mounted on express, `OPENCHAMBER_DATA_DIR` pointed at a temp dir):

| Request / call | Actual | Expected (cf. `nonexistent-xyz`) |
|---|---|---|
| `fetchQuotaForProvider('constructor')` / `'toString'` / `'__proto__'` | `{ok:false, configured:true, error:"provider.fetchQuota is not a function"}` | `{configured:false, error:"Unsupported provider"}` |
| `GET /api/quota/credentials/constructor` (and `toString`) | `200 {"configured":false}` + server logs `Failed to read constructor quota credentials` | `404 UNSUPPORTED_PROVIDER` |
| `DELETE /api/quota/credentials/constructor` | `500` — the store's `Unsupported credential provider` throw escapes the handler (`routes.js:91`) | `404 UNSUPPORTED_PROVIDER` |
| `PUT /api/quota/credentials/__proto__` | `500 TypeError: normalizers[providerId] is not a function` at `routes.js:54` (call sits outside the `try`) | `404 UNSUPPORTED_PROVIDER` |
| `PUT /api/quota/credentials/constructor` / `toString` | `400 INVALID_CREDENTIAL` with the store's internal `Unsupported credential provider` message (the inherited `Object`/`toString` functions run as "normalizer" and "validator" and pass) | `404 UNSUPPORTED_PROVIDER` |
| `POST /api/quota/credentials/constructor/validate` | `404 NOT_CONFIGURED` | `404 UNSUPPORTED_PROVIDER` |

Probe facts: `normalizers['constructor'] === Object`, `normalizers['toString']` is `Object.prototype.toString`, `normalizers['__proto__']` is `Object.prototype` (truthy, not callable) — while `normalizers['nonexistent-xyz']` is `undefined` and correctly 404s.

Note the store layer is **not** the hole: `credentials/store.js:8,16` guards file access with a `MANAGED_QUOTA_PROVIDERS` Set, so no credential file is written for these ids. The defect is entirely in the route/dispatcher lookup layer above it.

## Why it matters

`/api/quota/*` is the fleet's measurement-gate surface. A bogus id reporting `configured: true` (with an internal TypeError as its error) can be read by consumers as "a configured provider whose fetch is broken" rather than "no such provider", and the credential routes disagree with themselves about whether these providers exist (200 on read, 500 on delete, 400 with a leaked internal message on write). Any client typo or probe that lands on a prototype name gets misleading state instead of a clean unsupported-provider answer.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Provider-id lookups in the quota layer use own-property semantics (e.g. `Object.hasOwn`, a `Map`, or a null-prototype registry) for `normalizers`, `validators`, and the provider `registry` — including the `registry[id]` filter at `providers/index.js:375`.
- [ ] For `constructor`, `toString`, `hasOwnProperty`, `valueOf`, and `__proto__`: `GET /api/quota/:providerId` returns the same unsupported-provider result as an unknown id (`configured:false`); all `/api/quota/credentials/:providerId` routes return `404 UNSUPPORTED_PROVIDER`; no 500s and no `Failed to read … quota credentials` warnings.
- [ ] Real provider ids (`exe-dev`, `cursor`, `zenmux`, `opendesign`, and every registry provider) behave exactly as before.
- [ ] Tests pin the prototype-name cases at the route and/or dispatcher level, alongside the existing unknown-id cases.

title: fix(web): skills-catalog installed-sources store reads a corrupt file as empty and the next install overwrites it — every skill's provenance is silently lost

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/small-fix

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: app/web

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

The skills-catalog installed-sources store (`skills-installed-sources.json`) reads a corrupt file as "no provenance" and the next unrelated install or delete overwrites the file, permanently destroying every recorded install's provenance. The write itself is atomic (temp + rename) — the loss is in the read-modify-write cycle. This is the same corrupt-read-as-empty pattern fixed for the sibling stores in #887/#891/#892/#898/#905/#907; this store was missed. #907's fix established the house pattern: distinguish missing from MALFORMED on write paths and refuse to overwrite a malformed file in place.

## Evidence

`packages/web/server/lib/skills-catalog/installed-sources.js` (main `f0d3428b8`):

- `readInstalledSources` (:35-52): any `JSON.parse` / read failure is caught at :40 and returns an empty `Map` — indistinguishable from a missing file.
- `appendInstalledSources` (:61-78): seeds its merge from `readInstalledSources()` (:68) and unconditionally persists the result via `writeEntries` (:78). After a corrupt read, the merged map contains only the new entries.
- `removeInstalledSources` (:86-90) has the same shape (no-op on corrupt read, so a delete silently does nothing — the overwrite in `appendInstalledSources` is the destructive path).
- Write callers: `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/skill-routes.js:631` (install) and `:870` (delete).

Reproduced this run with the real module (copied verbatim from main to the laptop probe dir `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-installed-sources-20261030/`, `OPENCHAMBER_DATA_DIR` pointed at a temp dir):

1. `appendInstalledSources([{skillName:'skill-a', sourceId:'src-1', skillDir:'skills/a', scope:'user'}])` → file contains skill-a. ✔
2. File truncated mid-JSON (torn write / disk error / hand edit).
3. `appendInstalledSources([{skillName:'skill-b', …}])` → file now contains **only skill-b**; `skill-a provenance survived: false`.

The existing test (`installed-sources.test.js:53`) pins malformed → empty for *reads*, which is fine for the badge fallback; nothing pins the write path, and that asymmetry is the bug: a read-only fallback became a destructive write.

## Why it matters

Provenance is what lets the Installed badge match a catalog item by source instead of name alone (the fix for the #4756 same-name badging problem, per the module header). One corrupt byte — from a torn write elsewhere, a disk error, or a user hand-editing the JSON — silently reverts every skill to name-only matching the next time any skill is installed, with no error surfaced and no way to recover the lost records. The sibling stores were all judged worth fixing for exactly this failure mode; this one holds user-visible state in the same data directory.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The store distinguishes three read states: missing, valid, malformed (following the strict-reader pattern landed for Linear in #907 / PR #910).
- [ ] `appendInstalledSources` and `removeInstalledSources` refuse to overwrite a malformed file: they surface/skip with the malformed file preserved in place, instead of writing an empty-seeded replacement.
- [ ] Read-only consumers (`readInstalledSources`, `isInstalledFromSource`) keep the current graceful fallback to name matching.
- [ ] Tests: corrupt file + append leaves the file byte-identical; corrupt file + remove leaves it byte-identical; missing file + append still creates it; valid file behavior unchanged.

title: fix(ui): ToolOutputDialog Mermaid remote-URL load has no deadline and no byte cap — a stalled or oversized remote source wedges the dialog in loading and buffers the whole body

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/ui
labels.description: Package: ui (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Problem

The Tool Output dialog's Mermaid source loader fetches a remote http(s) URL with a bare `fetch()` — no deadline and no byte cap — and buffers the whole body with `response.text()`.

Evidence (`packages/ui/src/components/chat/message/ToolOutputDialog.tsx`, main @ e8b70e170):

- Line 705: `sourcePromise = fetch(resolvedUrl.toString())` — no `signal`, no `AbortController` anywhere in the file (verified: the file contains no `AbortController`/`AbortSignal`).
- Line 710: `return response.text();` — the entire body is buffered before any size check; there is no cap constant in the loader.
- Line 677 / 885: the dialog sets `status` to `loading` and only leaves that state when the promise settles, so a stalled server leaves the dialog spinning forever (the request-id guard at the `.then` only discards stale results — it never cancels the fetch).
- The URL comes from tool output (a Mermaid diagram reference), so the remote host is not the user's own OpenChamber server: a slow, hung, or oversized response is a realistic input, not a theoretical one. The sibling branches are safer — `data:` URLs are local, and the `file://` branch goes through `runtimeFetch('/api/fs/raw', …)`.

This is the same failure class as #851 (gitmoji catalog fetch), #854 (URL-auth token mint), and #855 (mobile release update check) — all fixed by adding a deadline — except this one also lacks any byte bound on the buffered body.

## Why it matters

- One stalled remote host wedges the dialog in `loading` for the whole session; the user cannot retry productively because a re-open starts another undeadlined fetch.
- An oversized or endless body is buffered whole into the webview/renderer memory before Mermaid parsing even begins.

## Acceptance criteria

- The remote-URL branch fetches with an explicit deadline (AbortSignal/AbortController), comparable to the deadlines used by the #851/#854/#855 fixes, and aborts the request when the dialog's load is superseded or the dialog closes.
- The body read is byte-capped (streaming read with an early abort, or an equivalent bound); an over-cap response fails with the existing `loadFailed` error state instead of buffering unboundedly.
- A stalled-server regression test (fake fetch that never settles / oversized body) proves the loader reaches the error state within the deadline.
- Existing behavior for `data:`, `file://`, and inline `target.source` is unchanged.

title: fix(web): credential helper delegate timeout kills only 'git credential fill' — the stalled credential helper survives orphaned

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: priority/normal

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
Follow-up to #867 / PR #869 (Codex P2 finding on PR #869, review comment 4420080861):

PR #869 bounded the credential helper's delegate `git credential fill` spawn with `DELEGATE_TIMEOUT_MS = 10_000` + SIGKILL in `packages/web/server/lib/git/repository-credential-helper.js`. That kills only the intermediate `git credential fill` process. When the configured credential helper itself stalls, the actual helper survives orphaned after OpenChamber's helper exits.

Codex reproduced it with real Git configuration (`credential.helper = "!f() { sleep 120; }; f"`): the OpenChamber helper exited after 10 seconds, but the helper shell and `sleep` remained orphaned. A stalled credential manager or GUI prompt can therefore survive the timeout, and retries accumulate more instances.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] On delegate timeout expiry, the owned process tree (the `git credential fill` child and the credential helper it launched) is terminated, not just the direct child.
- [ ] A regression case uses real Git with a stalled child helper (the current stub's `exec sleep` replaces Git itself and misses this behavior) and shows no surviving helper processes after the deadline.
- [ ] The fail-quiet contract from #867 is preserved: the helper still exits 0 promptly with no output beyond what the chain already answered.

Same shape as #868 (the worktree start-command process-tree follow-up from PR #864): the direct-child bound landed first; tree termination is the tracked remainder.

Found by: Codex review on PR #869; dispositioned by queue task 3765 resume (repo-queue-worker-shift-openchamber, lane A, 2026-10-29) after the PR merged with the finding unanswered.

body:
## Finding

`packages/ui/src/components/chat/hooks/useChatTurnNavigation.test.ts` is timing-flaky: the test at line ~96 ("returning to a session restores its turn scroll" scenario: jump to `turn_a`, open `session_2`, reopen `session_1`) expects `scrolledTo` to equal `['turn_a', 'turn_a', 'turn_a']` but intermittently receives a fourth `'turn_a'` scroll.

## Evidence

- CI: `pr checks` run 41687154269 (main @ `d8b8a0d`, 2026-11-03T18:15Z), job `full (main tier): tests` — exactly this assertion failed (received +1 `turn_a`). The same tier failed at `43b04eb` earlier the same day (tracked as #1497; breakage-ID cea2f6b6abc5 groups them).
- Local reproduction (2026-11-03, laptop, current main): `bun test src/components/chat/hooks/useChatTurnNavigation.test.ts` run 5 times in isolation — **2 of 5 runs failed**, 3 passed. Single-file isolation, so this is not the cross-file leakage of #46.
- The extra scroll suggests the navigation effect can fire one more time than the test's model expects (e.g. a late load/ready transition re-triggering the restore scroll after reopen), i.e. either the hook double-fires under slow scheduling or the test synchronizes on too few ticks. Either way the main gate now fails intermittently at unrelated SHAs.

## Acceptance criteria

- The test (or the hook, if the double scroll is real product behaviour) is fixed so the file passes deterministically: 20 consecutive isolated `bun test` runs of the file with zero failures.
- If the hook is at fault, the fix is in the hook and the test keeps asserting the exact scroll sequence; if the test is at fault, the fix synchronizes on the actual completion signal instead of fixed ticks, without weakening the assertion.
- No other test in the file changes behaviour.

Found via: triage of #1497 (queue task 8890, lane A).

title: fix(web): dispatch-results readFile returns [] after exhausting read attempts — a valid replacement file can be clobbered (PR #1390 comment)

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: priority/high
labels.description: Important and time-sensitive

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: source/pr-comment-review
labels.description: Filed by the pr-comment-review job

body:
## Finding (from a PR review comment, never addressed)

On PR #1390 (`refactor(web): migrate dispatch-results store to durable-store primitive (#978)`), CodeRabbit raised a concrete data-loss finding against `readFile` in `packages/web/server/lib/dispatch-results/runtime.js`. It was never replied to, fixed, or tracked; the PR merged as-is.

### Finding — read-loop exhaustion is treated as an empty store
- Comment: https://github.com/developing-today/openchamber/pull/1390#discussion_r4450060668
- Reviewer: `coderabbitai[bot]`, 2026-11-03T01:54:47Z, `packages/web/server/lib/dispatch-results/runtime.js:276`
- Essence: "**Fail closed when the read loop runs out of attempts.** If `readFile` sees a malformed file and then a valid replacement on all three attempts, it returns `[]`. `load()` treats that as success, so the next `register` writes only its new entry and replaces the valid file. Throw instead, as the other read-failure paths do, so writes stay off until a load succeeds."

## No-response evidence
- GraphQL `reviewThreads` for PR #1390: this thread is `isResolved: false` and contains only the single CodeRabbit comment — no replies (verified 2026-11-03; a fresh `gh api .../pulls/1390/comments` re-read confirms exactly 2 inline comments on the PR, both CodeRabbit findings, neither with replies).
- The PR's last commit `d33d17c64` (the main-merge head Codex re-reviewed at 2026-11-03T03:12:45Z) does not change the flagged line — the code on current main is byte-identical in this spot (see below).
- The only later conversation activity is a dezren39 `@codex review` note about merging main and test counts; it does not address this finding.
- Dedupe: `gh issue list --state all` searches (dispatch-results readFile/register/persist; "refusing to treat as empty") on 2026-11-03 return no issue covering this defect — #976/#978 are the parent durable-store design/migration trackers, not this bug.

## Still live on current main (verified 2026-11-03)
- `packages/web/server/lib/dispatch-results/runtime.js:250-277`: `readFile` loops 3 attempts; the malformed-with-`replaced`-preservation path `continue`s, and after the loop the function still ends with `return [];` at line 276.
- `runtime.js:279-294`: `load()` only keeps writes off when `readFile()` throws/rejects; a resolved `[]` is treated as a successful empty load.
- So the flagged sequence still holds: three attempts each superseded by a valid replacement -> `[]` -> next `register`/`persist` writes only the in-memory entries and replaces the valid on-disk file, dropping its pending dispatch results.

## Acceptance criteria
- `readFile` throws (or otherwise fails closed) when the read loop exhausts its attempts without a definitive result, so `load()` rejects and writes stay off until a load succeeds — matching the other read-failure paths in the same function; or
- Resolve by a documented decision on this issue showing the exhaustion path cannot be reached with a valid file at stake (cite the primitive's guarantees).
- A regression test covering the replaced-on-every-attempt sequence is expected with the fix.

Found via: unaddressed PR comment review (pr-comment-review job), PR #1390.

title: fix(web): walkthrough prune reads pointer files whole with no size gate — the one store read that ignores MAX_FILE_BYTES (4 MiB)

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`pruneMissingRepositories` in the walkthrough store reads every pointer file whole with no size gate, while the sibling read in the same file is capped.

- `packages/web/server/lib/walkthrough/store.js:222` — `const value = JSON.parse(await fsp.readFile(full, 'utf8'));` inside the prune loop: no `stat`, no byte cap, for up to `PRUNE_LIMIT` (500) pointer files per housekeeping run.
- Same file, `store.js:75-83` — `readJson` judges the store's own cap first: `if (!stat.isFile() || stat.size > MAX_FILE_BYTES) return null;` with `MAX_FILE_BYTES = 4 * 1024 * 1024` at `store.js:31`. The prune path never applies it.

Pointer files are small JSON records the server itself writes (`{ repoRoot, ... }`), so a pointer that has grown or been replaced by something large is exactly the input the cap exists for in `readJson` — the prune path is the one read of this store that does not honour it. This is the design #1254 ("read it bounded") residual class, in the same shape as #1436 (guest serve stat/read) and #1410 (stat-gated reads): a store read that buffers whole past the store's own named cap.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe against the real module)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-walkthrough-prune-20261103/probe.mjs` (laptop) — sets `OPENCHAMBER_DATA_DIR` to a scratch dir, plants two pointers in `walkthroughs/pointers/`, and calls the real `pruneMissingRepositories()` from current main (987e53c99):

- `small.json` — a normal pointer to a missing repo (control).
- `huge.json` — a valid pointer JSON to a missing repo padded to **67,108,911 bytes** (16× the store's 4 MiB `MAX_FILE_BYTES`).

Result: `removed: 2`; both files gone. The 67 MB pointer was buffered whole, parsed, and acted on — had the prune read applied the store's own cap the way `readJson` does, the oversized pointer would have been skipped and left in place. Housekeeping runs off the request path on a timer, and the Electron desktop app hosts this server in its main process (the file's own comment at `store.js:~195-205` calls out exactly this stall risk), so an unbounded whole-file read here is on the surface that comment is protecting.

## Why it matters

- One oversized/corrupt pointer file turns routine housekeeping into a whole-file buffer + `JSON.parse` of arbitrary size, repeated for up to 500 files, in the desktop main process.
- It is an inconsistency inside one file: every other read of this store honours `MAX_FILE_BYTES`; this one was missed, so the store's stated bound is not actually a bound.

## Acceptance criteria

- `pruneMissingRepositories` applies the store's size bound before reading a pointer file (stat-gate on `MAX_FILE_BYTES`, matching `readJson`, or an equivalent bounded read): an oversized pointer is skipped (left in place, not parsed, not deleted on the basis of an unread file), a normal pointer behaves exactly as today.
- A regression test plants an oversized pointer (over `MAX_FILE_BYTES`) pointing at a missing repo and asserts it survives a prune run while a normal missing-repo pointer next to it is still removed.
- Existing walkthrough store tests still pass.

Found by: new-issue-creator-openchamber run, 2026-11-03. Related: #1254 (design umbrella), #1410, #1436 (same residual class, other stores).

title: observability: expose queue task/issue binding on session-activity entries

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: New feature or capability request

labels.name: task/triage

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: effort/m
labels.description: Medium: expected under 1 day of work

labels.name: meta/enriched

body:
## Problem

The external observability contract v1 (`GET /api/session-activity`, `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/DOCUMENTATION.md`) exposes exactly five keys per session entry: `type`, `lastActivityAt`, `status`, `model`, `toolInFlight`. There is **no queue/task/issue binding**, so the babysitter poller — the contract's first consumer — cannot distinguish a queue-spawned session from a dispatcher-launched or interactive one, and cannot report which task/issue a supervised session belongs to.

This is the concrete in-repo gap behind `developing-today/code#1656` acceptance criterion 1 ("Babysitter round output identifies queue-spawned sessions with their task/issue binding for 100% of sessions launched under the executor mode"). The launch-side binding already exists on the code side: `pm-stack/opencode-claimant` binds `session_id` ↔ task id ↔ issue atomically at launch (migration 0021, `repo-queue.py bind`, `progress.session_id`). What is missing is the projection of that binding onto the observability surface the babysitter reads.

## Proposed change

Add one additive key to each `sessions` entry — contract rule 1 is additive-only within v1, so no version bump is needed:

- `queue`: object | null — `null` when the session has no known queue binding (interactive/dispatcher sessions), otherwise `{ taskId, issueNumber, queue, lane }` with explicit `null`s for any component the source cannot verify (rule 2: never fabricate).
- Source: the authoritative queue binding for the session (the task ledger row bound to that session id), not inferred from the process table (rule 5).
- Update the allowlist projection and `observability-contract.test.js` key-set assertions, plus a case pinning `queue: null` for an unbound session and the binding shape for a bound one.
- Document the key in `DOCUMENTATION.md` (v1 entry table).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `GET /api/session-activity` entries carry `queue` (`null` for unbound sessions), additively within contract v1.
- [ ] Conformance fixture pins the new key set, the `null` case, and the bound-session shape.
- [ ] `DOCUMENTATION.md` v1 entry table documents `queue`.
- [ ] No secret/auth material appears in the new field (rule 4).

## Context

- Parent: `developing-today/code#1656` (OpenCode-half step 3, keeper/babysitter binding-aware supervision).
- Related: `developing-today/code#2132` (session conductor design — the babysitter-facing half lands there after cutover; this contract key is what makes either consumer able to see the binding).

title: nix: node_modules FOD hash does not reproduce on amd-6 (x86_64-linux entry baked in another environment)
body:
Found 2026-11-03 while deploying the service-cascade migration (developing-today/code#4880): the home-manager activation build for the laptop fails on exactly one derivation, `openchamber-node_modules-2.5.0` at pin e1ad0521:

```
specified: sha256-WJn5Zv0wh4KAhTVl2yUCgzcsAglR6GjBgDGjMASOx34=
     got:  sha256-H2NGcbn/5V9dWLnMXEd0xLufNuYkpFV6obHOP7OScVo=
```

Facts:

- The mismatch reproduced **identically in two independent full builds** on amd-6 (same "got" hash both times), so the recorded `x86_64-linux` entry in `nix/hashes.json` is reproducibly wrong in this environment — not a transient fetch error.
- The fetched tree is genuine e1ad0521 (its `nix/modules/` is present; its lock pins opencode 2d912e02 and the aligned nixpkgs f9887a8a), and the failing hash is exactly the one recorded in that tree.
- Everything else in the ~890-derivation activation closure built or substituted cleanly — including the fork opencode's own node_modules FOD at 2d912e02 — so this is specific to openchamber's packaging, not the machine or the pin set.
- This looks like the #449 disease: bun's install tree is environment-sensitive, and the recorded hash evidently only reproduces in the environment that baked it.

Fix path: re-bake the `x86_64-linux` entry on amd-6 with `nix/update-hashes.sh` (the "got" above is stable across builds here), then bump code's openchamber pin and re-run the deploy. Longer term, the hash needs a baking environment that matches where the package is actually built, or the FOD needs the same environment-hardening the package already applies to `.bun/**/.bin` links.

title: fix(web): GitHub /pulls/context ?diff=1 has no size cap at all — Octokit buffers the whole PR diff and the route serves and caches it whole, past the walkthrough's 50 MiB cap

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Finding

The GitHub `/pulls/context` route's `?diff=1` branch fetches the pull request's entire diff through Octokit and serves it whole, with **no size cap at all** — not on the read, not on the response, and the oversized payload is then retained in the route's response cache. Its walkthrough sibling caps the same read at 50 MiB (judged after buffering — that residual is #1456); this route does not even judge it afterwards.

## Evidence (verified on main `0f32d5a11`, 2026-11-03)

`packages/web/server/lib/github/routes.js:3493-3505` — the complete diff handling for the context route:

```js
let diff = undefined;
if (includeDiff) {
  const diffResp = await octokit.request('GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{pull_number}', {
    owner: repo.owner,
    repo: repo.repo,
    pull_number: number,
    headers: { accept: 'application/vnd.github.v3.diff' },
  });
  if (!isProviderString(diffResp?.data)) {
    throw invalidProviderPayload('GitHub returned an invalid pull request diff');
  }
  diff = isProviderString(diffResp?.data) ? diffResp.data : undefined;
}
```

- No byte-length check anywhere in the branch (contrast `packages/web/server/lib/walkthrough/pull-request.js:113`, `MAX_PATCH_BYTES = 50 * 1024 * 1024`, and the 5 MiB `MAX_FULL_FILE_BYTES` for single-file contents in the same module).
- The response (including `diff`) is stored in `prContextCache` at `routes.js:3187`, so an oversized diff is not just transiently buffered and serialized into the JSON response — it is retained in server memory for the cache TTL, once per cache key.
- The UI requests this shape: `packages/web/src/api/source-control.ts` sends `diff: '1'` for the PR context (see its test at `source-control.test.ts:784`), so any large PR a user opens in the checks/comments view triggers it.
- The GitLab twin is not affected the same way: its context diffs arrive as a per-file array through `readCollection` with a page cap that throws past the bound (`packages/web/server/lib/gitlab/resources.js:980-982`).

## Reproduction (laptop probe vs the real route, this run)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-context-diff-cap-20261103/` registers the real `registerGitHubRoutes` with a stubbed fetch whose pulls endpoint returns a 60 MiB diff body (`62,914,560` bytes plus header) for the `vnd.github.v3.diff` accept:

```
PROBE status= 200
PROBE diffBytesServed= 62914583
PROBE walkthroughCap= 52428800
```

The route answered 200 and served all 62,914,583 bytes — 10 MiB past the cap the walkthrough route would have rejected with a 413 — and cached the payload.

## Why it matters

This is the unbounded-read class the repo has been systematically closing (#1254 contract, #1373, #1410, #1436, #1456): one oversized or adversarial PR diff on a connected account spikes the shared OpenChamber server's memory (buffer + JSON serialization + cache retention), with no bound and no error. The walkthrough route got a cap in PR #1271 because #1267 showed this read "had no total byte bound"; the context route — the one the everyday PR view uses — was left with none.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The `/pulls/context` GitHub diff read enforces a named byte cap (the walkthrough's 50 MiB `MAX_PATCH_BYTES`, or a deliberately chosen context-route cap): an over-cap diff is never served or cached whole — the route either rejects with a clear error (413-style, matching `patch-too-large`) or omits `diff` with an explicit truncation/too-large signal in the payload.
- [ ] Ideally the cap is judged during the read (streamed bounded read via the shared `readBoundedResponseText`-style primitive, as #1456 asks for the walkthrough), not only after Octokit has buffered the body; if this fix lands post-buffer only, the issue or PR states that explicitly and leaves the during-read part to #1456's pattern.
- [ ] At/under-cap diffs return byte-identically to today; the invalid-payload guard (`isProviderString`) behavior is preserved.
- [ ] A regression test drives the real route handler with an over-cap diff body and asserts it is not served/cached whole (not only a mock resolving a pre-materialized string at the cap boundary).
- [ ] Existing `routes.test.js` GitHub context tests pass.

## Related

- #1456 — walkthrough patch cap judged after buffering (different route, post-buffer residual; this route has no cap at all).
- #1375 (closed) — this same route's files/comments pagination, fixed.
- #1254 — the bounded-read contract this route's diff branch sits outside.

body:
# workflow-audit.yml is the only workflow with no `permissions:` block — it executes checked-out scripts on `pull_request` with whatever token the repo default grants

## Evidence (verified on origin/main `e1ad052118956b95550a0d9a7c3dbc57bc49ed72`, 2026-11-03)

- `.github/workflows/workflow-audit.yml` contains **zero** occurrences of `permissions:` — no top-level block and no job-level block (the `caller-jobs` job at lines 23–30 declares `runs-on` and `timeout-minutes` only).
- It is the sole outlier: each of the other 26 files in `.github/workflows/` declares permissions at the top level or on its jobs (e.g. `.github/workflows/oc-review.yml:34-35` carries top-level `permissions: contents: read`; `bot-help.yml`, `pr-review.yml`, `mobile-release.yml` carry job-level blocks).
- The workflow triggers on `pull_request` (paths: `.github/workflows/**`, `.github/scripts/audit-workflow-caller-jobs.py`, `.github/scripts/test-audit-workflow-caller-jobs.sh`) and on push to `main`. Its steps check out the PR head (`actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1`, line 26) and then **execute scripts from that checkout**: `bash .github/scripts/test-audit-workflow-caller-jobs.sh` (line 28) and `python3 .github/scripts/audit-workflow-caller-jobs.py .github/workflows` (line 30). Both scripts are inside the trigger paths, so a PR can change the very code this workflow runs.
- Today the exposure is latent, not live: `gh api repos/developing-today/openchamber/actions/permissions/workflow` reports `default_workflow_permissions: "read"` (checked 2026-11-03), so the job's token is currently read-only by repo default rather than by anything the workflow declares.

## Why it matters

Every other workflow in this repo pins its token to the least privilege it needs; this one silently inherits the repo default. If that default is ever flipped to permissive (GitHub's legacy default is read/write, and the setting is one admin toggle), the one workflow that runs PR-supplied shell and Python code becomes a write-token execution path — the classic pwn-request shape — with no diff in this repo to review. The fix is two lines, and it is doubly appropriate here: workflow-audit.yml exists to guard the repo's workflow correctness (it is the #1399 recurrence guard), so it should model the declaration standard the rest of the repo already follows.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `.github/workflows/workflow-audit.yml` declares `permissions: contents: read` (top-level, matching oc-review.yml's shape, or on the `caller-jobs` job).
- [ ] The workflow still runs green on a workflows-path PR and on push to main (checkout + audit self-test + audit all execute unchanged under the read-only token).
- [ ] No other workflow's permissions change in the same PR.

Related: #1399 (the invalid caller-job class this workflow guards against), #628 (least-privilege/pinning hygiene precedent in branch-cleanup.yml).

body:
## Problem

`startCloudflareQuickTunnel` never settles its startup promise when `cloudflared` exits cleanly (code 0) or dies by a signal (code `null`) before printing a trycloudflare URL — starting a quick tunnel hangs forever instead of failing.

## Evidence (verified on origin/main 91ce18e74, file blob identical at laptop HEAD)

`packages/web/server/lib/cloudflare-tunnel.js`, `startCloudflareQuickTunnel` (:361):

- The startup promise (:411) settles three ways: the 30 s timeout rejects when no URL arrived (:412-417), the 100 ms `checkReady` interval resolves when `publicUrl` is set (:419-425), and the child `exit` handler rejects — but only for a non-zero exit code (:427-434):

```js
child.on('exit', (code) => {
  clearTimeout(timeout);
  clearInterval(checkReady);
  cleanupTempDir();
  if (code !== null && code !== 0) {
    reject(new Error(`Cloudflared exited with code ${code}`));
  }
});
```

The exit handler clears the timeout and the interval first, so on exit code 0 — or code `null` when the process is killed by a signal (OOM killer, an operator, a supervisor) — every remaining settlement path is dismantled and the promise is left pending forever. The caller (`packages/web/server/lib/tunnels/providers/cloudflare.js:252`, via `startCloudflareTunnel` :610) awaits it, so the tunnel-start request never returns an error and the UI waits indefinitely.

The managed modes in the same file do this correctly: `waitForManagedTunnelReady`'s `onExit` rejects on **any** exit while starting. The quick path is the odd one out.

### Reproduction (laptop probe, fake `cloudflared` on PATH, real `startCloudflareQuickTunnel`)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-cf-quick-exit-20261103/` (`probe.mjs` + `bin-<mode>/cloudflared` fakes; `--version` answers normally so the availability check passes):

| fake `cloudflared` behavior | result |
|---|---|
| exits 0 immediately, no URL | **NEVER SETTLED after 4000 ms** |
| kills itself with SIGTERM, no URL | **NEVER SETTLED after 4000 ms** |
| exits 1 (control) | rejected promptly: `Cloudflared exited with code 1` |
| prints a trycloudflare URL, keeps running (control) | resolved with that URL |

`packages/web/server/lib/cloudflare-tunnel.test.js` covers only `checkCloudflaredAvailable` — no test exercises the quick-tunnel exit paths.

## Why it matters

A quick tunnel is started from the UI on demand. A `cloudflared` that exits cleanly before announcing a URL (misconfiguration, an interrupted update, a wrapper script) or is killed externally leaves the start request hung with no error, no timeout, and no log line naming the cause — the user can only reload and retry into the same hang. Every other tunnel mode in the same file reports this exact event as a failure.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The quick-tunnel startup promise rejects promptly when the child exits before a URL is seen, for exit code 0 and for signal deaths (code `null`) alike, with an error that names the exit (code or signal).
- [ ] Exit code non-zero and the 30 s no-URL timeout keep their current error behavior; a URL printed before exit still resolves with that URL.
- [ ] An exit after the promise has resolved (normal tunnel shutdown) does not throw or change the returned handle's behavior.
- [ ] New tests in `cloudflare-tunnel.test.js` (or a sibling) cover exit-0-before-URL and signal-death-before-URL settlement, alongside the existing exit-1 and URL controls.

Top layer of Drew's cascade design (2026-11-03): each level offers an option handling its service creation as a single enable switch. Setting services.openchamber.enable = true must create all three services — openchamber, the standing opencode server, and the mcpx daemon — with the consumer writing nothing but the switch (no package overrides, no unwrapped, no hand-wired drop-ins).

This repo's slice: author services.openchamber platform modules (nixosModules / homeManagerModules / darwinModules.openchamber, beside the mcpx pass-throughs from #1431):
- services.openchamber.enable, .package (default: this flake's build), .port (default 3000), plus an upstream group: .opencode.hostname/.port defaulting to the standing server (127.0.0.1:13420).
- Cascade: services.opencode.enable = lib.mkDefault true and services.mcpx.enable = lib.mkDefault true (the opencode module originates in the fork; the mcpx module originates in code; both already pass through this flake).
- ONE-PROCESS RULE baked in (Drew, standing): the openchamber service ATTACHES to the standing opencode server — OPENCODE_HOST set from the upstream options, OPENCODE_SKIP_START=true — and never starts its own opencode. This is the durable form owed since the live drop-in (openchamber#766): the service's start wrapper reads the current server password from ~/.local/state/opencode/service-prod.json AT START and exports OPENCODE_PASSWORD (never in the store), replacing the unmanaged drop-in and the password-sync watcher hack for fresh provisions.
- Escape hatch: an option (e.g. services.openchamber.opencode.manage = false semantics or attachExisting) for consumers who genuinely want openchamber to spawn its own server — off the default path.
- systemd user unit (NixOS / home-manager Linux) + launchd user agent (darwin), mirroring the mcpx/opencode module shapes.

Verification: eval a config with ONLY services.openchamber.enable = true and assert all three services render — the openchamber unit with the attach env + password-reading start wrapper, the opencode serve unit, and the mcpx daemon — with package defaults from this chain.

## Acceptance criteria

- `services.openchamber` exposes a single enable option that brings up OpenChamber with its opencode + mcpx dependencies wired (cascade), matching the pattern Drew specified 2026-11-03.
- Enabling only `services.openchamber` evaluates cleanly on the module's supported platforms.
- The cascade does not force-enable the dependencies when openchamber itself is disabled.

title: fix(web): guest asset serve path still judges its 2 MB cap from the resolver stat, then readFile whole — a file grown after the stat is buffered and served past the cap (#1254 residual, guest twin of #1410)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

body:
## Finding

The guest asset serve path is the one guest file read that still judges its byte cap from a stat taken before the read, instead of from the bytes actually read — the stat-then-read spelling design #1254 rule 2/3 forbids, and the same module's other reads have already been migrated off it.

- `packages/web/server/lib/guests/catalog.js:139-159` — `resolveGuestServedFile` returns `size: await fileSizeOrNull(filePath)` (a path stat at :41-47) alongside the path.
- `packages/web/server/lib/guests/routes.js:887-895` — `GET /api/guests/:id/{*filePath}` refuses with 413 only when that earlier stat size is a number over `GUEST_ASSET_MAX_BYTES` (2,000,000, catalog.js:39), then does `raw = await fs.readFile(filePath)` whole, with no post-read or during-read cap. A file that grows (or is swapped) between the resolver stat and this read is buffered and served whole past the cap. When the stat failed (`size: null` — e.g. the compiled `.ts`→`.js` branch at catalog.js:159, where the compiled path may not exist at stat time), the 413 gate is skipped entirely and the read is judged by nothing.
- Same-module contrast: the guest manifest read (catalog.js `readGuestManifest`) opens a handle and enforces the cap during the read, and the entry-HTML read in `guestBuiltScriptsReady` (catalog.js:193) uses the shared `readBoundedFile` — its comment states the reason verbatim: "The shared bounded read (design #1254) enforces the cap during the read, where the previous stat-then-read left a grow-between gap."
- Related second site, same pattern: `packages/web/server/lib/guests/files.js:181-193` (`readOperation`, the guest file-API read) stat-gates on `stat.size > GUEST_FILE_CONTENT_MAX`, then `readFile(absolute, 'utf8')` whole; its post-read length check runs only after the whole file is already in memory, so a grown file is still buffered whole before being refused.

Guest packages are third-party code installed into the server; their files are exactly the "files whose size the server does not control" class the bounded reader in `lib/shared/bounded-file-read.js` exists for. Precedents: #1116 added this serve cap as a stat gate; #1305 (closed) filed the identical stat→read race for project icons; #1410 tracks the same residual for parseMdFile/config/plugin/AGENTS.md reads but does not list the guest serve or guest file-API paths.

## Evidence (verified this run on main 392c3e2c69947c63b9dc7888921ac9ee5127468a)

Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-oc-guest-serve-20261103/probe.mjs`, run with bun against the real `resolveGuestServedFile` from the laptop primary at origin/main): a 100-byte `big.js` resolves with `size: 100`; after appending to 2,500,000 bytes before the route's read step, replicating routes.js:887-895 verbatim serves status 200 with 2,500,000 bytes — 500,000 bytes over the 2,000,000 cap. The existing test `packages/web/server/lib/guests/asset-cap.test.js` covers only the static over-cap case ("refuses an over-cap asset with 413 before reading it whole"); no grows-after-stat case exists.

## Why it matters

The 2 MB cap (#1116) exists so one oversized asset in any installed guest cannot be loaded whole into the server on every request. As spelled today, that protection holds only as long as nothing touches the file between two path-based operations — a guest that updates itself, a sync tool, or any local writer appending to the asset defeats it, and the response then also *serves* the over-cap bytes, not merely buffers them. The fix is the already-landed shared primitive, not a new mechanism.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The guest asset serve path reads through `readBoundedFile` (or an equivalent handle-bounded read that enforces the cap during the read): a file grown or swapped past `GUEST_ASSET_MAX_BYTES` after resolution is refused with the existing 413 `{ error: 'file-too-large' }` shape, and at most cap+1 bytes are read.
- [ ] A stat failure / missing size no longer bypasses the cap: the bytes actually read are judged in all branches, including the compiled `.ts`→`.js` branch.
- [ ] `readOperation` in guests/files.js likewise enforces its cap during the read instead of buffering whole before the post-read length check (existing `FILE_TOO_LARGE` shape preserved).
- [ ] Existing contracts preserved: at-cap files serve byte-identically, in-cap HTML still gets token propagation and style injection, missing files and tools-only frame content still 404 (asset-cap.test.js and files.test.js pass).
- [ ] A grows-after-resolve regression test in the style of the descriptor-growth tests used for the #1410 sites: grow/append after the size check, assert 413/refusal and that the over-cap bytes are not served.

title: fix(web): /pulls/context check-run annotations silently cap at 150 — hand-rolled page<=3 loop (per_page 50, catch-break) was left behind when sibling collections moved to readTotalCountCollection, with no truncation signal in the output

labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests
