body:
## Problem

In the `/pulls/context` handler, every sibling collection was moved to the named-cap pagination discipline — check runs and workflow jobs are read with `readTotalCountCollection`, which paginates to the end, probes one page past its cap, and **throws rather than return a partial list** (#1375/#1405). The check-run **annotations** fetch was left behind as a hand-rolled loop with a silent hard cap:

Evidence (main `f56726108`, verified this run; blob identical between the laptop primary and `origin/main`), `packages/web/server/lib/github/routes.js`:

- :3306–:3322 — `for (let page = 1; page <= 3; page += 1)` with `per_page: 50`: at most **150 annotations per check run**, hardcoded and unnamed (the sibling caps are named constants, e.g. `GITHUB_CHECK_RUN_MAX_PAGES`, with a documented probe-past-the-cap contract at :156).
- A page error is swallowed by `catch { break; }` — a failure on page 2 returns page 1's annotations as if complete.
- The output mapping (~:3385) emits `annotations: [...]` with **no count, no truncation flag, no completeness marker**, so neither the server log nor the UI can tell a 150-annotation partial list from a complete one.
- Contrast in the same handler: check runs at :3235 and workflow jobs at :3272 both go through `readTotalCountCollection` (:156), whose header comment states the rule this loop breaks: "a partial list is never summarised as complete".

## Verified behavior (laptop probe, real source)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-annotations-cap-20261103/probe.mjs` — extracts the actual annotations block and output mapping from `routes.js` on main and asserts their properties:

- Loop bound `page <= 3`: true. `per_page: 50`: true. Silent `catch { break; }`: true. Any mention of total/truncation in the block: false.
- Output mapping segment carries any truncation/count/complete field: false.
- Sibling check-runs and jobs in the same handler use `readTotalCountCollection`: true for both.

A check run with 151+ annotations (linters, code scanners and coverage tools routinely emit hundreds) loses every annotation past 150 — often the later files' warnings — and a mid-pagination API error silently shortens the list further. The annotations are the actionable part of a failing check in the preview; dropping them silently is worse than dropping the run's summary line.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Annotations are read under the same named-cap discipline as the sibling collections: paginate until a short page under a named page/total cap constant, probe or otherwise detect overflow, and never return a partial list as complete — on overflow, surface an explicit error or an `annotationsTruncated`-style flag on the check run's output.
- [ ] A page error after page 1 is not silently swallowed into a partial result: it follows the same explicit path as overflow (error or truncation flag).
- [ ] Tests: a mocked `listAnnotations` returning three full pages plus a fourth returns the full set or a marked truncation (never a silent 150); a page-2 error produces the explicit path, not page 1's annotations alone.
- [ ] Existing `routes` github tests pass.

## Not this issue

- #1375/#1378 (closed): files, issue comments and review comments in this same route — already paginated under named caps.
- #1405 (closed): check runs for a ref in the checks summary — already paginated via `readTotalCountCollection`.
- #1418: GraphQL `contexts(first: 100)` truncation in the summaries/detail queries — different API surface.

body:
## Problem

The GitHub reference-detail query signals truncation for two of its collections and silently truncates the rest. In the same query, in the same function, a reader can tell whether comments and commits were cut — but not whether reviews, review threads, or a thread's replies were.

Evidence (main `f56726108`, verified this run; blob identical between the laptop primary and `origin/main`), `packages/web/server/lib/github/reference-search.js`:

- Comments: `comments(last: 50) { totalCount nodes … }` (:138/:164) → returned as `commentTotal` (:461).
- Commits: `commits(last: 50) { totalCount nodes … }` (:165) → returned as `commitTotal` (:486).
- Reviews: `reviews(last: 30) { nodes … }` (:169) — **no `totalCount` requested**, and the zod detail schema's `reviews` object has no `totalCount` field, so even a returned count would be stripped.
- Review threads: `reviewThreads(last: 50)` (:173, `DETAIL_THREAD_LIMIT`) — **no `totalCount`**, none in the schema, none in the result.
- Per-thread replies: thread `comments(first: 50)` (`DETAIL_THREAD_COMMENT_LIMIT`) — **no `totalCount`**; replies past 50 in a long thread are dropped with the thread still presented as complete.
- `fetchReferenceDetail` (:423–:486) merges reviews and thread openers into the returned `comments` array, so the dropped reviews/threads are indistinguishable from a PR that simply has fewer of them.

## Verified behavior (laptop probe, real code)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-detail-totals-20261103/probe.mjs` — drives the real `fetchReferenceDetail` with a stub `octokit.graphql` returning a schema-valid PR payload (30 reviews, 50 threads, `comments.totalCount: 75`, `commits.totalCount: 75`):

- Returned top-level keys: `number, comments, commentTotal, pull`; pull keys include `commitTotal` — and **no review or thread total anywhere** (`reviewTotal`/`threadTotal` absent from the serialized result).
- The captured query text contains `reviews(last: 30)` and `reviewThreads(last: …)`; neither segment contains `totalCount`.

## Why it matters

The detail preview is what a user reads to judge a PR's discussion: whether reviewers have weighed in and whether line-comment threads remain open. Past 30 reviews or 50 threads — reachable on long-lived, heavily reviewed PRs — the preview silently presents a partial discussion as the whole thing, with none of the completeness signals the same payload already carries for comments and commits. The fix pattern exists in-file; these three connections were simply left out of it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `reviews`, `reviewThreads`, and per-thread `comments` in `DETAIL_QUERY` request `totalCount` (thread comments may use `totalCount` on the connection), and the zod detail schema carries the new fields.
- [ ] `fetchReferenceDetail`'s result exposes the truncation state for reviews and threads alongside `commentTotal`/`commitTotal` (e.g. `reviewTotal`, `threadTotal`, and a per-thread reply total or a thread-level truncated flag), so the UI can mark a partial discussion.
- [ ] Tests: a mocked payload with more reviews/threads than the returned nodes surfaces the totals/truncation in the result; a payload within the limits reports no truncation.
- [ ] Existing `reference-search` tests pass.

## Not this issue

- #1418: the `contexts(first: 100)` checks truncation in this file's detail query and in `pr-summaries.js` — a different connection and consequence (wrong check state vs missing discussion).
- #1377: board picker label/reviewer lists truncating at 100 on the references endpoints — different routes.

body:
## Problem

The two GraphQL check-status surfaces fetch a PR head commit's check contexts with `contexts(first: 100)` and request **no `pageInfo` and no `totalCount`**, so a context past the first 100 is silently dropped and the summary is computed from a partial list — a failing or pending context beyond position 100 reads as **success**.

Evidence (main `f56726108`, verified this run; file blobs identical between the laptop primary and `origin/main`):

- `packages/web/server/lib/github/pr-summaries.js:35` — `SUMMARY_FIELDS`: `statusCheckRollup { contexts(first: 100) { nodes { … } } }`, no `pageInfo`/`totalCount` in the connection. The result feeds `summarizeCheckContexts` (:129, called :207), which trusts the nodes array as complete; the zod schema for the connection likewise carries only `nodes`.
- `packages/web/server/lib/github/reference-search.js:149` — the detail query repeats the same `contexts(first: 100)` shape with no completeness field, feeding the same summarizer (:473) for the PR preview's checks.

## Verified behavior (laptop probe, real code)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-gql-contexts-20261103/probe.mjs` (laptop, against the real `summarizeCheckContexts` from `pr-summaries.js`):

- 100 successful CheckRun contexts (exactly what `contexts(first: 100)` returns when the 101st context is a failure): `{"state":"success","total":100,"success":100,"failure":0}`.
- The same 101 contexts including the failing one: `{"state":"failure","total":101,"failure":1}`.
- Source scan in the same probe: both query sites contain `contexts(first: 100)`; the surrounding segment contains neither `pageInfo` nor `totalCount`.

So the truncation is invisible end-to-end: GitHub is never asked whether more contexts exist, and no layer downstream can tell the list was cut.

## Why it matters

This is the GraphQL twin of #1405, which fixed the REST checks summary reading only the first 100 check runs ("a failing or pending run past page 1 is silently dropped and the summary reports success"). The REST path now paginates under a named cap and errors rather than summarizing a partial list; the sidebar summaries (`pr-summaries.js`) and the reference/PR preview (`reference-search.js`) still report a definitive `state` from a silently partial context list. PRs with >100 check contexts are routine on matrix-heavy repos — exactly the PRs whose status a user most needs to trust.

## Not this issue

- #1405 (closed): REST `checks.listForRef` in the checks summary — fixed by pagination.
- #1408 (open): `dedupeCheckRuns` ranking of re-runs — orthogonal; it operates on whatever list it is given.
- The REST `/pulls/context` collections (#1375/#1378) — already paginated under named caps.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Both GraphQL queries request a completeness signal for the contexts connection (`totalCount` and/or `pageInfo { hasNextPage }`), through their zod schemas.
- [ ] When the connection reports more contexts than were returned, the summary does not present a definitive success: it either pages to completion under a stated cap (with an explicit error/signal past the cap, per the #1405 discipline) or marks the checks summary as incomplete/unknown.
- [ ] The same treatment applies to both call sites (sidebar summaries and reference detail), so the surfaces cannot diverge.
- [ ] Tests: a mocked GraphQL payload whose contexts connection reports `totalCount > nodes.length` (or `hasNextPage: true`) does not yield `state: "success"` from the partial list; a complete ≤100-context payload is unchanged.
- [ ] Existing `pr-summaries` / `reference-search` tests pass.

body:
## Finding

The Linear issue read silently truncates comments at 50, with no truncation signal anywhere in the chain — the GraphQL query never even asks for the information that would reveal it.

In `packages/web/server/lib/linear/issues.js` (main `751a4eeab`):

- `GET_QUERY` (:129) and `ISSUE_UPDATE` (:165) both fetch `comments(first: 50) { nodes { id body createdAt user {...} } }` — **no `pageInfo`**, so the server cannot know whether a 51st comment exists.
- `readIssue` (:366-380) maps `node.comments.nodes` into `comments` and returns it bare. There is no `commentsMore` / `commentsComplete` field.

The same file handles the identical shape correctly for sub-issues, which makes comments the odd one out:

- `SUB_ISSUES_FIELDS` requests `pageInfo { hasNextPage }`, and `readIssue` returns `subIssuesMore: readPageInfo(node.subIssues).hasMore` (:378).
- `readSubIssueProgress` returns a `more` flag for the children connection, and the file's own comment documents the cap-and-signal convention ("more reads as N+").

Secondary site, same file, same shape: `STATES_QUERY` (:148-156) fetches `states(first: 50)` with no `pageInfo`, and `listLinearIssueStates` returns `{ connected, states }` with no truncation signal — a team with more than 50 workflow states silently loses the tail of its state list.

## Evidence

- Code verified on origin/main `751a4eeab1a5` via two channels (laptop tree read + `gh api` raw read of the file at main): `comments(first: 50)` at :129 and :165, no `pageInfo` in either comments block; `subIssuesMore` present at :378; no comments-truncation field anywhere (`grep commentsMore|commentsComplete` over `packages/` returns nothing).
- Laptop probe against the real module (real `issues.js` + `parse.js` copied from the laptop tree, `auth.js`/`client.js` stubbed to return exactly the fields `GET_QUERY` requests — 50 comment nodes, no pageInfo, because the query never asks for it; probe at laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-linear-comments-20261103/`):
  - `getLinearIssue("ENG-1")` → `comments returned: 50`
  - issue keys: `assignee, comments, description, id, identifier, labels, parent, priority, state, subIssueProgress, subIssues, subIssuesMore, team, title, updatedAt, url` — no comments-truncation field
  - same payload's sub-issues DO surface the signal: `subIssuesMore: true`, `subIssueProgress.more: true`
- Consumer impact: `packages/ui/src/components/references/resolveComposerReferences.ts:49` builds the agent's context for an attached Linear issue from `issue.comments` via `packages/ui/src/lib/linearIssueContext.ts` ("What an agent receives for an attached Linear issue: the issue and its comments as JSON"). Linear's comments connection returns oldest first, so on an issue with 51+ comments the **newest** discussion — usually the part that supersedes the rest — is exactly what never reaches the agent, and nothing in the payload says anything is missing. The issue preview reads the same `readIssue` shape.

## Why it matters

This is the same silent-truncation class the repo has been eliminating provider by provider (#1375/#1383 GitHub PR context and issue comments, #1405 checks summary, #1377 board pickers): a page-1-only read presented as complete. Here the cost lands on agent context quality — an attached Linear issue with a long thread gives the model a confidently incomplete picture, with the most recent comments missing.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `GET_QUERY` and `ISSUE_UPDATE` request `pageInfo { hasNextPage }` for the comments connection (or paginate comments to completion under a stated cap), and `readIssue` exposes the result (e.g. `commentsMore`, mirroring `subIssuesMore`).
- [ ] The composer-reference context (`linearIssueContext.ts` / `resolveComposerReferences.ts`) marks the context as truncated when the flag is set, so an agent can tell its picture is partial — or the truncation is otherwise surfaced to the user.
- [ ] `listLinearIssueStates` gets the same treatment (signal or pagination) for `states(first: 50)`, or a documented reason 50 is a safe bound for workflow states.
- [ ] Tests cover an issue whose comments connection reports `hasNextPage: true`: the flag reaches the payload, and a ≤50-comment issue reports no truncation.

body:
## Problem

`.github/workflows/pr-review.yml` (634 lines, the workflow that mints GitHub App tokens and posts bot reviews) still carries a complete `pull_request_target` execution path that can never run. The trigger was removed deliberately — commit `4478502bb` ("ci: main-only workflow triggers", Drew's order 2026-10-30) deleted `pull_request_target: types: [opened, synchronize, reopened, ready_for_review, converted_to_draft]`, and commit `0a4f9ee2c` (Drew, 2026-11-02) reaffirmed the policy: "CI never runs on pull requests". This issue does **not** ask to restore the trigger. It asks for the dead path and the comments that describe it as live to be removed or explicitly marked dormant — the #971 cleanup covered `oc-review.yml`, `nix-eval.yml` and `ci-policy.md` for the same commit, but `pr-review.yml` was left out, and its residue is executable code, not just header text.

## Evidence (verified on main `06d07f0214`, 2026-11-02, via laptop tree and `gh api` raw read — two channels)

- Triggers, `pr-review.yml:3-8`: `on:` is only `issue_comment`, `pull_request_review_comment`, `workflow_dispatch`. There is no `pull_request_target`.
- Live confirmation: the last 100 Actions runs of this workflow are 98 `issue_comment` + 2 `pull_request_review_comment`, 0 `pull_request_target` (`gh api repos/developing-today/openchamber/actions/workflows/pr-review.yml/runs?per_page=100`, grouped by event).
- Dead executable branches (11 mentions of `pull_request_target` in the file):
  - `:37` gate job `if:` leads with `github.event_name == 'pull_request_target' ||` — never true.
  - `:64` "Generate access-check token" is conditioned on `github.event_name != 'pull_request_target'` — vacuously true.
  - `:84-87` "Check commenter access" shell branch: on `pull_request_target` it writes `allowed=true` and exits, skipping the collaborator-permission check every comment command goes through.
  - `:205` "Throttle push-burst reviews" branches on `pull_request_target` + `synchronize`; `:320-321` "Debounce new commits" (`sleep 30`) is gated solely on that combination. Both are unreachable.
  - `:242` / `:271` ("Resolve manual command", "Acknowledge manual review command") carry vacuous `!= 'pull_request_target'` conditions.
  - `:28` concurrency group still branches on the event for its key.
- Comments that describe the dead path as live behaviour:
  - `:32` jobs comment: "Every PR event gets a review." No PR event triggers this workflow; reviews start only from `/oc-review` / `@openchamber-bot review` comments or manual dispatch.
  - `:13-27` concurrency comment explains, in present tense, Phase 1 `pull_request_target` run sharing/cancelling semantics that no run can exercise (and `cancel-in-progress` is now the literal `true`, not the event expression the comment narrates).

## Why it matters

This is a trust-boundary file: it generates GitHub App tokens and posts reviews as the bot. A dormant `allowed=true` shortcut in its access step is safe only for exactly as long as nobody re-adds a `pull_request_target` trigger for an unrelated reason (a `ready_for_review` hook, say) — at which point the whole unreviewed path, throttle and debounce included, silently reactivates under a policy that has since changed twice. Until then, the present-tense comments mislead anyone debugging "why did this PR get no review" or editing the gate: the file claims PR events are its primary input, when its real input is comment commands.

## Acceptance criteria

- One direction, applied consistently: either (a) remove the dead `pull_request_target` branches/conditions (gate disjunct, access shortcut, throttle branch, debounce step, vacuous `!=` conditions, concurrency key branch) and rewrite the `:13-27` and `:32` comments to describe the comment-command + dispatch operation that actually exists, or (b) keep the code and add an explicit header block stating the `pull_request_target` path is dormant by policy, citing `4478502bb` and `0a4f9ee2c`, so no reader mistakes it for live behaviour. Option (a) is preferred: dormant code in a token-minting workflow is the hazard itself.
- Do **not** restore the `pull_request_target` trigger (or any PR trigger): the no-PR-trigger policy (Drew, 2026-10-30, reaffirmed 2026-11-02) is deliberate and out of scope here.
- The comment-command path is behaviourally unchanged: an `issue_comment` `/oc-review` run still passes the gate's permission check and reaches the review job.
- The edited workflow still validates (e.g. actionlint or a `workflow_dispatch` run that reaches the gate and skips cleanly when the review app is unconfigured, per #61's behaviour).

Residual of #971 (same root commit, different file; #971's scope was `oc-review.yml` / `nix-eval.yml` / `ci-policy.md`).

title: fix(vscode,web): stat-then-read size gates still buffer whole past the cap if the file grows after the stat — parseMdFile, config, plugin and AGENTS.md reads (design #1254 phase 3)

labels.name: task/triage

labels.name: effort/m

body:
## Finding

Design #1254's contract (rule 2/3: open once, judge from the handle, enforce the cap during the read — never stat-by-path then read-by-path) is landed for the web server's shared primitive (`lib/shared/bounded-file-read.js`, PR #1258) and the web modules migrated in PRs #1263/#1269. It was never extended to the VS Code extension host, and two web sites from the same size-gate batch still use the stat-then-read spelling. At those sites a file that grows (or is swapped) between the stat and the read is buffered whole past the cap, and a non-regular file is not refused from the handle. Design #1254 names this exactly: "VS Code modules (design #1254 phase 3, deliberately unfiled)" — phases 1–2 have since landed, so phase 3 is now the unfiled remainder.

Found by pr-diff-review while reviewing the size-gate batch PRs #1137–#1251: in that same batch, the web twins that got it right are handle-bounded (PR #1145 web `parseMdFile`, PR #1147 web skill supporting files, PR #1153 guest manifest, PR #1160 VS Code skill supporting files), while the sites below got the stat-only spelling.

## Evidence (all verified on current main `06d07f0214acaa45adb28490e7820e315f9f84f6`, contents-API reads, 2026-11-02)

VS Code (`packages/vscode/src/`):

- `opencodeConfig.ts:2053-2062` — `parseMdFile` (landed in PR #1212, cap from issue #1157): `fs.statSync` size check, then `fs.readFileSync(filePath, 'utf8')` whole. No regular-file check either: the web twin (PR #1145) opens `O_NONBLOCK` and refuses non-regular files from the handle precisely so a FIFO cannot block the read.
- `opencodeConfig.ts:653-677` — `readConfigFileContent` (landed in PR #1248, cap from issue #1154): stat gate, then `readFileSync` whole; the post-read byte-length check runs **only when the stat failed** (`statSize === null`), so the grows-after-a-successful-stat case is the one case never re-checked.
- `opencodeConfig.ts:1492-1502` — `readPluginDirFile` (landed in PR #1251, cap from issue #1156): `fs.statSync(...).size` gate, then `fs.readFileSync(target.filePath, 'utf8')` whole.
- `bridge-config-runtime.ts:197-204` — `api:behavior/agents-md:get` (landed in PR #1159, twin of web PR #1137): `fs.promises.stat` gate at 1 MiB, then `fs.promises.readFile(AGENTS_MD_PATH, 'utf8')` whole.

Web (`packages/web/server/lib/`):

- `opencode/routes.js:664-676` and `:698-702` — Behavior AGENTS.md GET and the PUT expectedContent conflict check (landed in PR #1137, cap from issue #1132): stat gate at 1 MiB, then `readFile` whole, both handlers.
- `opencode/shared.js:350-358` (`assertConfigFileWithinCap`) + `:400-401` (`readConfigFile`) (landed in PR #1155, cap from issue #1150): stat-only gate, then `fs.readFileSync(filePath, 'utf8')` whole. (`writeConfig`'s pre-read in the same module uses the same gate.)
- `fs/routes.js:1607-1613` — `POST /api/fs/write` identical-content pre-read (landed in PR #1140, issue #1127): the stat-equality gate decides `canCompare`, then `readFile` whole; a file grown between the stat and the read is buffered past both the equality length and `MAX_READ_BYTES` (16 MiB).

Precedent that this race is a filed defect class in this repo: issue #1305 (closed) — "project-icon discover: stat→readFile race can buffer an unbounded favicon before the 5 MiB check".

## Why it matters

These are the extension host and the web server reading project/user-controlled files (agent/command/skill markdown, OpenCode configs, plugin files, the user-managed AGENTS.md) synchronously in several cases. The caps exist to keep one oversized file from loading into the host/server whole; the stat-then-read spelling keeps the cap only as long as nothing touches the file mid-read, and the fleet has already paid this down site-by-site on the web side. One issue tracks the whole set so it is fixed once, through the shared bounded reader (the VS Code tree already cross-imports from `packages/web/server/lib/shared/`, e.g. `readBoundedResponseText` at `opencodeConfig.ts:19`), instead of being rediscovered per site.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every site listed above reads through a handle-bounded read (open once, `fstat` from the handle, at most cap+1 bytes read) or an equivalent that re-judges the bytes actually read against the same cap — no stat-by-path-then-read-by-path remains at these sites.
- [ ] Existing over-cap contracts preserved per site: `ERR_MD_FILE_TOO_LARGE` (parseMdFile), `CONFIG_FILE_TOO_LARGE` (config reads), `PLUGIN_FILE_TOO_LARGE` (plugin files), the AGENTS.md 413 / `{success:false}` shapes, and the fs/write fall-through-to-write behaviour.
- [ ] Missing-file behaviour unchanged at every site (e.g. AGENTS.md get still returns `{content:'', exists:false}`; plugin read still returns null).
- [ ] `parseMdFile` refuses a non-regular file (FIFO/device/directory) without blocking, matching the web twin in PR #1145.
- [ ] A grows-after-stat regression test per migrated site, in the style of PR #1147's descriptor-growth test (append after the size check; assert refusal and that at most cap+1 bytes were read).
- [ ] At-cap and ordinary files load byte-identically (existing site tests pass).

title: fix(web): checks summary dedupe drops a not-yet-started re-run — dedupeCheckRuns ranks solely by started_at (missing = epoch 0), so a queued/waiting re-run loses to the previous completed run and the summary reports the stale conclusion

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`dedupeCheckRuns` (`packages/web/server/lib/github/checks-summary.js:8-25`) decides which of several same-name check runs is "the latest" **solely by `started_at`**, mapping a missing or unparseable `started_at` to epoch 0 (`Date.parse(previous?.started_at || '') || 0`, lines 17-18). The run `id` — GitHub's monotonic creation order — is only a tiebreak when the two timestamps are exactly equal (line 19-20).

A re-run that has not started yet has no `started_at`: a check run is created with `status: queued` (or `waiting`/`requested`) and `started_at` is only set when execution begins (the GitHub create-check-run API takes `started_at` as an optional field supplied when a run starts; queued runs are created without it). So when a user re-requests a check, the payload for a ref contains the previous **completed** run (real `started_at`, conclusion `success`/`failure`) alongside the new **queued** run (`started_at: null`, larger `id`) — the exact co-existence the function's own header comment describes ("A re-run leaves the previous completed check run in the listForRef payload alongside the new in-progress one"). The queued re-run can never displace the completed one: `0 > T` is false and `0 === T` is false. The stale completed run wins in either payload order.

Result: every surface that summarizes checks — `pr/status` and `/pulls/context` (`packages/web/server/lib/github/routes.js:1885` and `:3235`, summary at `:1897`/`:3406`) and `pr/summaries` (`packages/web/server/lib/github/pr-summaries.js:147`) — reports the **old conclusion** while GitHub shows the check as queued/pending. A re-requested check that previously passed reads `state: success` in OpenChamber until the re-run actually starts (and a previously failed one reads `failure` instead of `pending`). That is the merge-confidence surface reporting a state GitHub itself does not show.

This is distinct from #1405 (closed): that was page-1 truncation of `listForRef`; pagination is now complete under `readTotalCountCollection`, so the full set reaches the dedupe — and the dedupe picks the wrong member of it.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `ef33ecfc0`)

Laptop probe against the real `dedupeCheckRuns`/`summarizeCheckRuns` imported from the laptop primary (`~/git/fleet/probe-oc-checks-dedupe-20261102/probe.mjs`):

- A: `[completed success id 100 started_at 2026-11-02T10:00:00Z, queued id 101 started_at null]` → kept id **100**, summary `{state: success, total: 1, success: 1, pending: 0}`.
- B: same pair in reverse payload order → kept id **100**, summary `success` (order-independent).
- C: `waiting` re-run (id 102, `started_at: null`) after the completed run → kept id **100**, summary `success`.
- Control D: `in_progress` re-run (id 103, later `started_at`) → kept id 103, summary `pending` — the started re-run path works today; only the not-yet-started re-run is dropped.
- Control E: the queued run alone → summary `pending`/`queued: 1` — `summarizeCheckRuns` handles it correctly once it survives dedupe; the loss is entirely in the dedupe ranking.

Code grounding: `checks-summary.js:17-20` (ranking), `:36-40` shows the codebase already treats `started_at` as optional on non-completed runs (earliest-start tracking guards `typeof run?.started_at === 'string'`). There are no direct unit tests for `checks-summary.js` — existing route tests only exercise runs that all carry `started_at`.

## Why it matters

The checks summary is what a user reads to decide a PR is green. During the window between re-requesting a check and the runner picking it up — exactly when someone is watching the summary after pushing a fix or re-running a flake — OpenChamber shows the previous run's verdict as current: green stays green even though the check is about to re-run (and may fail), and a fixed failure stays red with no sign a re-run is pending.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `dedupeCheckRuns` ranks a not-yet-started re-run (`queued`/`waiting`/`requested`, `started_at` null) above the previous completed run for the same (app, name): the kept run is the one with the larger `id` when either side lacks a parseable `started_at`, or an equivalent rule that is provably recency-correct for all status combinations.
- [ ] Summary for [completed success + queued re-run] is `pending` with `queued: 1`; for [completed failure + queued re-run] is `pending`, not `failure` — in either payload order.
- [ ] Existing correct behavior preserved: an `in_progress` or newer completed re-run still wins; runs that both carry `started_at` keep the current latest-start (then larger-id) ordering.
- [ ] New unit tests for `checks-summary.js` cover the mixed started_at present/absent pairs (queued and waiting), both payload orders, plus the control cases above.
- [ ] Existing GitHub routes / pr-summaries tests pass.

title: fix(web): GitHub checks summary reads only the first 100 check runs for a ref — a failing or pending run past page 1 is silently dropped and the summary reports success (probe: 250 runs, sole failure on page 3 → state success, total 100)

labels.name: effort/s

body:
## Problem

The GitHub checks summary reads only the first page of check runs for a ref and presents it as the complete picture — no pagination, no `total_count` check, no truncation signal:

- `packages/web/server/lib/github/routes.js:1845` — branch/PR status endpoint: one `octokit.rest.checks.listForRef({ ..., per_page: 100 })` call, then `dedupeCheckRuns` + `summarizeCheckRuns` over that page alone.
- `packages/web/server/lib/github/routes.js:3191` — `/pulls/context`: the identical single call; its summary (`:3349`) and the returned `checkRuns` list are built from page 1 only.
- Secondary site, same shape: `routes.js:3223` — with check details on, `actions.listJobsForWorkflowRun({ per_page: 100 })` is also page-1-only per workflow run, so a run with >100 jobs loses its job mapping for the remaining check runs.

`dedupeCheckRuns` (`lib/github/checks-summary.js`) keeps the latest run per (app, name) **within the fetched page**. GitHub returns check runs newest-first, so the page fills with the 100 newest runs: on a busy ref, re-trigger and re-run duplicates of a few names can evict the latest instance of a real check past the page boundary, and any distinct check whose newest run is older than the 100 newest runs is invisible. Its failure or pending state never reaches the summary — the surface reports green.

This is the page-1-only pattern the repo has already fixed elsewhere in the same file: PR-context files/comments paginate under a named cap and throw rather than return a partial list as complete (`readPullContextCollection`, #1375), branches paginate with a cap probe (#1313), and the board pickers' page-1 truncation is filed as #1377. The checks reads were missed.

## Evidence (verified 2026-11-02 on main `4960b05e6`)

- Live count: `GET /repos/developing-today/openchamber/commits/4960b05e6e7d897b11e0e4e912b280000e140258/check-runs` reports `total_count: 133` — this repo's own main head already exceeds one page (the overflow there is duplicate bot-workflow runs, which is exactly the eviction mechanism: 100 newer duplicates of 5 names fill page 1).
- Laptop probe against the real `registerGitHubRoutes` (vitest, stubbed GitHub REST): 250 distinct check runs for the head SHA, pages 1–2 all success, the only failure (`critical-tests`) and the only in-progress run (`slow-e2e`) on page 3. The route answered `checks = {"state":"success","total":100,"success":100,"failure":0,"pending":0,"inProgress":0,"queued":0}`, returned 100 of 250 check runs, and made exactly **one** check-runs request (`.../check-runs?per_page=100`, no `page`). Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-checkruns-pagination-20261102/` on the laptop.

## Why it matters

The checks summary is the merge-confidence surface: it colours the PR/branch status the UI shows and feeds `canMerge`-adjacent decisions. A summary that silently drops a failing or still-running check and reports `success` is worse than no summary — it manufactures confidence. Refs cross 100 runs in ordinary use (matrix jobs, re-runs, re-triggered bot workflows — this repo's main head is already at 133).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Both `listForRef` sites read all pages under a named cap (the `readPullContextCollection` discipline: paginate to a short page, probe past the cap, and error — never silently summarise a partial list as complete), or return an explicit truncation signal the UI can show.
- [ ] `total_count` from the first response is honoured: when it exceeds the runs actually read, the summary is not reported as a plain `success`.
- [ ] Dedupe runs over the complete fetched set, so the latest instance of each (app, name) wins regardless of which page it landed on.
- [ ] The `listJobsForWorkflowRun` read gets the same treatment (paginate under a cap or signal truncation).
- [ ] Regression tests: a stubbed ref with >100 runs where the only failure / only pending run sits past page 1 yields a `failure` / `pending` summary; a >cap ref yields the explicit error or truncation signal, not `success`.
- [ ] Audit the GitLab twin while here: `lib/gitlab/resources.js` `loadCI` reads pipeline jobs with `maxPages: 1, perPage: 100` for the detail view — paginate it or signal truncation the same way.

title: fix(quota): quota CLI combined source passes its own env off as the connected server's launch environment — Antigravity direct store read can read a different opencode.db than the live loopback server uses (#1142)

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/pr-diff-review
labels.description: Filed by the pr-diff-review job

labels.name: priority/normal

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Finding

PR #1142 made the quota CLI's combined credential source report the **CLI process's own environment** as the connected server's launch environment whenever the server source merely claims `usesLocalStore()` — which, for the CLI's server source, reduces to "the URL is loopback" (it is wired with no `getLaunchEnvironment`, so that half of the check is always null). That re-opens, for the CLI wiring, the exact wrong-store bug #1063 fixed for the OpenChamber-server wiring: `auth.js`'s own contract says a process's own env is **not** evidence of the store a running OpenCode resolves its database from, because the server may have been started with a different `OPENCODE_DB`, `XDG_DATA_HOME`, or `HOME` than the CLI process.

Concretely: a live loopback OpenCode started with a different data dir than the CLI → the server projection withholds the Antigravity refresh token → `resolveAuthCandidates` finds no candidates → the gate `credentialSourceUsesLocalStore()` passes → `readLocalOpenCodeCredentials()` resolves the store from the CLI's env and reads a **different `opencode.db`** → an unrelated local Google login can be added as a candidate, refreshed, and its quota reported as the connected server's Antigravity pool — with the CLI output labeling the run `credentialSource: 'server'`, because the direct read never goes through `list()` and never flips `servedBy()` to `'local'`.

Codex raised exactly this on PR #1142 (P2, comment 4435236086, "Establish the connected server's database before reading locally"). The reply (4442704624) declined it, arguing the CLI env "is the established store location by construction" because the server-down transport fallback resolves the store from the same env. That conflates two different reads: the server-down fallback has no connected server whose store must match, and its reads are honestly labeled `servedBy() === 'local'`; the live-server direct read claims to speak for the connected OpenCode's store and is labeled `'server'`. The PR's own header comment states the contract it breaks: "`servedBy()` reports which source the run's reads came from, so the output never presents a store read as a live server read. Writes and the launch environment always stay with the server source."

## Evidence

- Source PR: #1142 MERGED 2026-11-02, head c97a4ac8ef58e8230d8660a413cbabdf77d1ee91, merge 99bd9fa02e — https://github.com/developing-today/openchamber/pull/1142 (closes #1141). Codex P2 4435236086 on `commands-quota.js:232`; disposition reply 4442704624 ("Not applied, with reasoning"); the change shipped as-is.
- Current main 4960b05e6e7d897b11e0e4e912b280000e140258, `packages/web/bin/lib/commands-quota.js`:
  - :224-233 — `createFallbackCredentialSource(primary, fallback, localEnvironment)`: `getLaunchEnvironment()` returns `localEnvironment` whenever `primary.usesLocalStore()` is true and the primary has no launch environment of its own.
  - :413 — the CLI wires it with its own process env: `createFallbackCredentialSource(serverSource, runtime.openCodeLocalCredentialSource(), env)`.
  - :227, :435-436 — `servedBy()` is `'server'` unless `list()` transport-fell back; every result is stamped `credentialSource: credentialSource.servedBy()`. A direct store read inside a provider does not touch `list()`, so it is stamped `'server'`.
  - :205-222 — the header comment asserting the launch environment "always stays with the server source" and that output "never presents a store read as a live server read".
- `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/auth.js` (current main):
  - :118-131 — the server source's `usesLocalStore()` is true when `getLaunchEnvironment()` is non-null **or the URL is loopback**; the CLI's server source supplies no launch environment, so loopback alone decides.
  - :343-350 — `wiredLaunchEnvironment` doc: "Without it the local store's location cannot be established: OpenChamber's own process.env is not the environment the running OpenCode resolves its database from, and resolving against it can read a different store than the one the connected OpenCode uses."
  - :368-377 — `readLocalOpenCodeCredentials()` throws when no launch environment is established; PR #1142's substitution is what now supplies one for the CLI.
- `packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/antigravity/index.js` (current main): :47-65 — with no candidates and `credentialSourceUsesLocalStore()`, `resolveAuthCandidates` pushes `resolveAntigravityStoreAuth(await readLocalOpenCodeCredentials())` as a store candidate; `fetchQuota` then refreshes the first working candidate and reports its quota.
- Precedent: #1063 (CLOSED) — "Antigravity local-store fallback reads OpenChamber's process.env database, not the managed OpenCode's launch-environment database (PR #860)". The launch-environment contract exists because this mismatch already bit once; #1142 bypasses it for the CLI source.

## Why it matters

The quota CLI is the fleet's diagnostic for "which Google account / pool is this OpenCode actually using". Reading a different store than the connected server's can present a healthy quota for the wrong account (masking a dead pool) or a "Not configured"/wrong-account result for a healthy one — silently, and stamped as server-sourced. It also spends a refresh of an unrelated account's token. The mismatch needs a server started under a different env than the CLI shell (a long-running desktop/managed OpenCode plus a terminal CLI run is the ordinary shape), not an exotic setup.

## Acceptance criteria

- The combined source never presents the CLI's own env as the connected server's launch environment: the Antigravity direct store read through the CLI runs only when the store location is established for the connected server (the primary's own launch environment, forwarded), or the CLI establishes the server's actual database location some other verifiable way.
- The #1141 case still works where it is sound: a test pins the CLI combined source with a primary that has a real launch environment (forwarded, direct read resolves that store), and a test pins that a loopback-only primary with no established launch environment does **not** enable the direct read against the CLI env's store.
- Output labeling stays honest: any result whose credentials came from a local store read is not stamped `credentialSource: 'server'`.
- Existing commands-quota tests keep passing, including the server-down transport-fallback cases (that fallback is unchanged and keeps resolving from the CLI env, labeled 'local').

## Dedupe

Searched open + closed issues 2026-11-02 for the CLI combined source / launch-environment mismatch ("1142", "getLaunchEnvironment", "usesLocalStore", "launch environment", "OPENCODE_DB combined"): only #1141 (the origin issue, CLOSED by #1142) and #1063 (the closed server-wiring precedent). Open #766 (standing server / one database) is about server-process uniqueness, not this CLI read path. No issue covers the CLI combined source supplying its own env as the server's launch environment.

body:
# fix(web): realtime-proxy WebSocket-bounds tests OOM the test worker on main — at-cap frame forwarding times out and the over-cap frame escapes as an uncaught ws RangeError

## Evidence (verified this run, main `ad4efe6ed0d03ae98de607670630339072f8cd12`)

Running the realtime-proxy test file alone on the laptop reproduces a hard failure — three consecutive reproductions (one full-suite run + two isolated runs), same failure shape each time:

```
cd packages/web && bunx vitest run server/lib/realtime-proxy.test.js
```

- `realtime proxy WebSocket bounds > forwards a single frame at the maxPayload cap byte-identically` — **test timed out in 10000ms** (`realtime-proxy.test.js:414`).
- The vitest worker then **dies with a V8 heap OOM**: `FATAL ERROR: Reached heap limit Allocation failed - JavaScript heap out of memory` (Mark-Compact at 4096 MB), followed by `[vitest-pool]: Timeout terminating forks worker` — 2 of the file's 17 tests never complete (1 failed | 14 passed | 2 errors).
- During the sibling test `refuses a single frame over the maxPayload cap with 1009 and forwards nothing upstream`, an **uncaught exception** escapes: `RangeError: Max payload size exceeded` (`code: WS_ERR_UNSUPPORTED_MESSAGE_LENGTH`) thrown from `ws/lib/receiver.js` `Receiver.haveLength` via `Socket.socketOnData` — it is not surfaced as a socket `error`/close on any socket the proxy owns.

Full-suite run for context (same main): `Test Files 1 failed | 503 passed`, `Tests 3 failed | 9553 passed` — the only product-code failure file was `realtime-proxy.test.js` (the other 2 failures are the known environment-bound `spaces/tools-filler` tar tests); the suite summary also showed the same unhandled `RangeError` against this file.

## Why it matters

These tests are the regression net for the proxy's frame bounds (#1109 client-side cap, #1249 upstream cap — `REALTIME_PROXY_WS_MAX_PAYLOAD_BYTES = 1 MiB` at `realtime-proxy.js:24`, upstream `MAX_BUFFERED_BYTES = 16 MiB` at `:40`, handler-side checks at `:298` and `:330`). On current main that net is broken in the worst way: instead of a clean assertion failure, the run burns a worker to the 4 GiB heap limit. Something in the at-cap/over-cap frame path — proxy forwarding, the recorded-echo test harness, or their interaction — amplifies or loops a 1 MiB frame instead of forwarding/refusing it once, and the over-cap refusal leaks an uncaught exception out of the `ws` receiver instead of settling as the documented 1009 close. If the amplification is in the proxy path rather than the harness, the same shape is a live memory-amplification surface on the session event stream, not just a test problem — triage needs to determine which side of the socket it is on.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `bunx vitest run server/lib/realtime-proxy.test.js` passes all tests on a clean checkout with no worker OOM, no unhandled errors, and no pool timeout terminating the worker.
- [ ] The root cause is identified and recorded on this issue: which side (proxy forwarding path vs test harness echo) amplifies the at-cap frame, and where the over-cap `RangeError` escapes handling.
- [ ] A single frame at exactly `REALTIME_PROXY_WS_MAX_PAYLOAD_BYTES` is forwarded byte-identically exactly once; a frame one byte over is refused with close code 1009 and nothing is forwarded — both asserted by the existing tests passing as written (test bodies changed only if the harness itself is the defect, with the reason recorded).
- [ ] No uncaught `WS_ERR_UNSUPPORTED_MESSAGE_LENGTH` escapes during the bounds tests.
- [ ] The full `packages/web` vitest suite no longer reports `realtime-proxy.test.js` as its failed file.

Phase 2 of design #1391 (walk it bounded, or not at all). **Dependency: sequences after phase 1** — the `lib/shared/traversal-budget.js` primitive (phase 1 sub-issue of #1391) must land first; if it has not, this issue waits rather than re-inventing a local budget.

## Problem

Two web walks already carry caps whose fixes have landed and settled, each in a private spelling the #1391 contract replaces:

- `packages/web/server/lib/fs/search.js` — BFS file search; the directory cap test reads the `visited` Set's own size (`directoryVisitCapReached`, :141; `FILE_SEARCH_MAX_VISITED_DIRS = 50_000`, :7; files capped separately at `FILE_SEARCH_MAX_VISITED_FILES = 10_000`, :6). The Set itself is load-bearing for dedupe and must stay.
- `packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.js` — `findGitDirectories` takes its caps as function parameters (`maxDepth: GIT_DIRS_MAX_DEPTH = 3`, `maxDirs: GIT_DIRS_MAX_DIRS = 100`, :438-439; called from the `/api/fs/git-dirs` route at :2220).

## Scope

Migrate both walks onto the shared traversal budget from phase 1, **behaviour-identical**:

- search.js: the budget takes over the directory-cap test (and the visited-files count where the budget's entries dimension fits it); the `visited` Set remains for dedupe/cycle protection only. Same values (50,000 dirs / 10,000 files), same partial-result behaviour (candidates found so far are returned at the bound — the #1332 acceptance behaviour).
- routes.js: `findGitDirectories` builds its budget from the same parameters its caller already passes (depth 3 / 100 dirs); signature, route behaviour, and the repositories-found-so-far result at the bound are unchanged.

Explicitly out of scope: the agents walks (`opencode/agents.js` — their cap landed under #1388, which is still in flight with its VS Code half; migrating them is a #1391 phase-3 question), the still-open walks #1357 / #1365 / #1366 (their own queue lifecycles), and every VS Code twin.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Both walks consult the shared budget; neither keeps a private cap mechanism (no visited-set-size cap test in search.js, no hand-rolled depth/dir counting in `findGitDirectories`).
- [ ] Cap values are unchanged: search 50,000 dirs / 10,000 files; git-dirs depth 3 / 100 dirs.
- [ ] Existing tests for both walks pass with unchanged expectations, including at-bound and directory-heavy cases from #1332 (a directory-only tree stops at the bound with partial results).
- [ ] The `visited` Set in search.js is retained for dedupe; a tree with repeated/linked directories behaves exactly as before.

body:
Phase 1 of design #1391 (walk it bounded, or not at all — one traversal-budget contract for directory walks). This phase lands the shared primitive and changes **no call-site behaviour**; phase 2 (the migration of the settled capped walks) sequences after it.

## Problem

Three capped directory walks on current main (`ad4efe6ed0`) use three different budget mechanisms, and three more walks (#1357, #1365, #1366) have no bound at all:

- `packages/web/server/lib/fs/search.js` — the cap test reads the BFS `visited` Set's own size (`FILE_SEARCH_MAX_VISITED_DIRS = 50_000`, :7, :141).
- `packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.js` `findGitDirectories` — caps passed as function parameters (`GIT_DIRS_MAX_DEPTH = 3` / `GIT_DIRS_MAX_DIRS = 100`, :438-439).
- `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/agents.js` — one constant (`AGENT_WALK_MAX_DIRS = 5000`, :43) consulted two ways in one file: a per-root local counter in `buildUserAgentIndex` (:94) and a shared mutable `budget = { visitedDirs: 0 }` object threaded through `collectAgentIds` (:555).

`packages/web/server/lib/shared/` holds the bounded-read/store/fetch primitives (#802, #976, #1254) but no traversal primitive, so every new walk invents its own spelling — and mirrors it by hand into VS Code.

## Scope

Add `packages/web/server/lib/shared/traversal-budget.js` implementing the #1391 contract's counting core:

- `createTraversalBudget({ maxDirs, maxEntries?, maxDepth?, deadlineMs? })` returning a budget object a walk consults **before descending** into a directory (the consultation counts the directory when it is allowed).
- `maxDirs` (directories visited) is the mandatory dimension — the lesson of #1332, whose files-only counter was vacuous on a directory-only tree.
- The budget exposes whether it has been exhausted and a `truncated` flag the caller reads afterwards (the *enumerate* disposition's signal; wiring it into any caller's result shape is explicitly not this phase).
- A followed link's directories count against the same budget as the root's — the budget is consulted per directory entered, regardless of how the walk reached it.
- `deadlineMs` is an optional dimension consulted by async walks; sync callers use counts alone and stop at the bound.
- Record the contract (the five rules from #1391, the budget's dimensions, the two named dispositions) in `packages/web/server/lib/shared/DOCUMENTATION.md`, following the existing sections' shape.

No call site changes in this phase. No cap value is introduced for any real walk — values stay at call sites when walks migrate (phase 2 keeps 50,000 / 100 / depth 3 exactly).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `lib/shared/traversal-budget.js` exists with the semantics above; it imports nothing domain-specific (the `lib/shared` admission rule in `DOCUMENTATION.md`).
- [ ] Conformance tests (probe matrix) cover: a directory-only tree stops at `maxDirs` with `truncated` set and no further consultations allowed; a tree exactly at the bound completes with `truncated` unset; `maxEntries` and `maxDepth` dimensions stop independently; directories reached through a followed link count against the same budget; the deadline dimension reports exhaustion to an async caller; repeated consultation after exhaustion keeps answering "stop" (no counter drift past the bound).
- [ ] `shared/DOCUMENTATION.md` gains a traversal-budget section stating the contract and the two dispositions (enumerate = partial + signal; copy = abort, no partial destination).
- [ ] No existing test changes expectation; no call site is modified.

body:
## Problem

Agent discovery walks agent directories recursively with no directory-visit cap, no depth cap, and no deadline — in both runtimes, and synchronously in both:

- Web: `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/agents.js:83` `buildUserAgentIndex` walks every directory under the user agent dirs (`agents/`, `agent/`, `modes/`, `mode/` under the OpenCode config dir) with an unbounded `dirsToVisit` stack (`readdirSync` at :92). It runs on any single agent lookup via `getIndexedUserAgentPath`, not just on list requests.
- Web: `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/agents.js:545` `collectAgentIds` recurses into every subdirectory of each project ancestor's `.opencode/{agents,agent,modes,mode}` with no bound. `listDisabledAgents` (:567) calls both walks and is served per-request at `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/config-entity-routes.js:70` — a fresh lookup cache is built per call, so the walk repeats on every request.
- VS Code twin: `packages/vscode/src/opencodeConfig.ts:201` `buildUserAgentIndex` (same unbounded stack, `readdirSync` at :213-238) and `:2158` `collectAgentIds` (unbounded recursion), called by `listDisabledAgents` (:2180) and served by `packages/vscode/src/bridge-config-runtime.ts:271`. There the synchronous walk blocks the extension host.

The project-side walk is over project-controlled content: opening a cloned repository whose `.opencode/agents` tree is directory-heavy (nested group folders are a supported layout, so the recursion is by design) makes the Settings disabled-agents listing — and any agent lookup that builds the user index — traverse the whole tree before answering.

This is the same unbounded-walk class as #1357 (skill discovery) and #1365 (skill supporting-files), but a different surface: those issues cover `walkSkillMdFiles` / `listSkillSupportingFiles` only. The sibling file-search walk was already capped after #1332 (`FILE_SEARCH_MAX_VISITED_DIRS` in `fs/search.js`).

## Evidence (verified this run, main `b86ac21a845e9bcbe6a04b76a2ee634b81fd82b8`)

Laptop probe calling the real exported `listDisabledAgents` from the laptop primary (`~/git/openchamber-fork`), with an isolated `HOME` and a project tree of 30,000 empty directories (200 groups × 150 subgroups) under `project/.opencode/agents`, `readdirSync` counted by patching the shared `fs` module:

- Run 1: **30,204 `readdirSync` calls, 534 ms** for one `listDisabledAgents(projectDir)` call, 0 agents found, no bound fired.
- Run 2 (reproduction): **30,204 `readdirSync` calls, 296 ms**.

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-agent-walk-20261102/probe.mjs` on the laptop. Because the walks are synchronous, that time is pure event-loop block in the web server and pure extension-host block in VS Code; cost scales linearly with directory count, so a 150k-directory tree (the scale probed for #1332) blocks for seconds.

## Why it matters

- A project the user merely opens can stall the managed server's event loop and freeze VS Code's extension host when Settings asks for disabled agents — no malicious payload needed, just a directory-heavy `.opencode/agents` tree (generated/vendored content can do this accidentally).
- The walk repeats per request (no shared cache across `listDisabledAgents` calls), so the cost is paid on every Settings visit, not once.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Both walks (`buildUserAgentIndex`, `collectAgentIds`) in web `agents.js` and VS Code `opencodeConfig.ts` stop at a named directory-visit cap (and/or depth cap) sized well above legitimate grouped agent layouts, following the `fs/search.js` precedent (`FILE_SEARCH_MAX_VISITED_DIRS`).
- [ ] Hitting the cap returns the agents found so far (partial results) instead of failing or walking on; the truncation is visible in code/tests, not silent in a way that hides real agents without a trace.
- [ ] Regression tests in both runtimes build a directory-heavy agents tree past the cap and assert the call returns promptly with the in-cap agents (existing suites: `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/config-entity-v2.test.js`, VS Code config tests).
- [ ] Normal nested layouts (`group/name.md` agents) are still discovered in full under the cap.

title: flake outputs rejects the new fleet input (missing ...), breaking all flake evaluation on main
body:
Since #1386, the flake declares a `fleet` input but the outputs function signature is still `{ self, nixpkgs, opencode, }` with no `...`. Nix passes every input to outputs, so evaluating any output (packages, devShells) fails. Surfaced by the fleet-build warm-export (dezren39/fleet run 41555313761): `error: flake 'git+file:///.../openchamber' does not provide attribute 'devShells.x86_64-linux.fleet'` — the attr exists in the source; the outputs call itself is what fails. `nix flake lock` does not call outputs, which is why the pin PR's lock regeneration did not catch it.

Fix: add `...` to the outputs formals.

body:
## Problem

The GitHub issue-comments route (`GET /issues/comments`, `packages/web/server/lib/github/routes.js:2718`) reads a single first page and returns it as if it were the complete discussion:

- `routes.js:2758` — `issues.listComments({ owner, repo, issue_number: number, per_page: 100 })` — page 1 only; no `page` is ever sent and no second page is followed.
- The response (`routes.js:~2775`: `{ connected, repo, comments }`) carries no total, no `complete`/`hasMore` flag, and no truncation signal.
- The web client (`packages/web/src/api/source-control.ts:1825`, `issueComments`) returns `payload.comments` as the issue's full comment list, so comments 101+ are invisible in the UI with no indication anything is missing.

This is a distinct endpoint from `/pulls/context` (#1375, in flight as PR #1378): that issue and PR cover the pull-context route's files/issue-comments/review-comments reads, not this standalone `/issues/comments` route, which the issue view uses.

## Evidence (verified this run, main 3194bcffc)

Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-oc-issue-comments-pagination-20261102/probe-issue-comments.test.js`) driving the **real** `registerGitHubRoutes` handler (the `routes.auth.test.js` harness pattern) with a stubbed GitHub fetch serving a page-aware 130-comment issue:

- `commentsReturned= 100 of 130` — exactly one request: `/repos/team/project/issues/3/comments?per_page=100`
- Response body keys: `[connected, repo, comments]` — no truncation/`complete`/`hasMore` field.

The route never asks for page 2.

## Why it matters / parity

- Long-lived issues — exactly the kind used for tracking, discussion, and fleet coordination in this repo — routinely exceed 100 comments. Their later discussion (often the newest decisions) is silently cut off in the issue view, presented as complete.
- The GitLab twin refuses this: `issueComments` in `packages/web/server/lib/gitlab/resources.js:1161` reads notes through `readCollection` (`resources.js:49`, cap `COLLECTION_MAX_PAGES = 20` at `:22`) and **throws** `'GitLab issue has more comments than OpenChamber reads'` rather than returning a partial list. The two providers currently diverge in completeness semantics for the same UI surface.
- The GitHub branches route in this same file paginates under a named cap (`GITHUB_BRANCH_PAGE_SIZE`/`GITHUB_BRANCH_MAX_PAGES`/`GITHUB_BRANCH_MAX_COUNT`, `routes.js:21-23`, loop at `:2094`, #1313) and throws when the cap is crossed. `/issues/comments` is the outlier.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `/issues/comments` paginates beyond the first page (following pages until a short page), under a named page/item cap in the style of `GITHUB_BRANCH_MAX_PAGES` / GitLab's `COLLECTION_MAX_PAGES`.
- [ ] Crossing the cap is never silent: the route either fails with an explicit error (the GitLab twin's `'has more … than OpenChamber reads'` shape) or returns a machine-readable truncation/`complete` signal that the web client surfaces — a partial list presented as complete is the bug.
- [ ] New tests in the github routes test suite stub multi-page comment answers (full first page + second page) and assert the route returns the merged set, plus a test for the over-cap behavior chosen above.
- [ ] Existing github routes tests pass; issues with ≤100 comments behave exactly as today.

## Problem

The board pickers' label and reviewer-candidate reads silently truncate at the first 100 entries on **both** source-control providers, and neither response carries a truncation signal:

GitHub (`packages/web/server/lib/github/routes.js`, main `3194bcffc`):
- `:2349` — the wrapper comment states the design plainly: "one page of 100 is what the pickers show"
- `:2384` — `/references/labels`: `issues.listLabelsForRepo({ ..., per_page: 100 })` — page 1 only, no `page` ever sent
- `:2392` — `/references/reviewers`: `issues.listAssignees({ ..., per_page: 100 })` — page 1 only
- `:2370` (wrapper `readRepositoryChoices`) — response is `{ connected: true, items }`: no total, no `complete`/`hasMore`, no truncation flag

GitLab (`packages/web/server/lib/gitlab/resources.js`):
- `:628` `listLabels` — `ProjectLabels.all(id, { perPage: 100, maxPages: 1 })`, comment "One page of the project's labels"
- `:650` `listReviewerCandidates` — `ProjectMembers.all(id, { includeInherited: true, perPage: 100, maxPages: 1 })`, comment "One page of the project's active members"

## Evidence (verified this run, main 3194bcffc)

- **This is not hypothetical — the fleet's own repos already exceed the cap.** Live counts via `gh api repos/<repo>/labels --paginate` on 2026-11-02: `developing-today/openchamber` **120 labels**, `developing-today/opencode` **141**, `developing-today/code` **209**. The label picker for openchamber's own repo already silently drops 20 labels; for code it drops 109.
- **Laptop probe vs the real handlers** (`~/git/fleet/probe-oc-picker-pagination-20261102/`, vitest, both probes pass):
  - GitHub `registerGitHubRoutes` with page-aware stubbed fetch (250 labels, 130 assignees): `labelsReturned=100 of 250`, `reviewersReturned=100 of 130`, exactly one request per collection (`/labels?per_page=100`, `/assignees?per_page=100`), response body keys `[connected, items]` only.
  - GitLab `createGitLabResourceService` with a recording fake client: `listLabels` called the client once with `{perPage: 100, maxPages: 1}` and returned 100; `listReviewerCandidates` once with `{includeInherited: true, perPage: 100, maxPages: 1}` and returned 100.

## Why it matters / parity

- A user picking labels or reviewers on a repo with >100 labels (or >100 assignable people / project members) cannot select — or even see — entries past the first page, and nothing tells them the list is incomplete. On the fleet's own repos this already bites for labels today.
- The codebase's sibling patterns refuse silent truncation: the GitLab twin for MR context reads collections through `readCollection` (`resources.js:49`, cap + throws `'has more … than OpenChamber reads'`); the GitHub branches route paginates under `GITHUB_BRANCH_MAX_PAGES` (#1313); #1375 tracks the same defect for `/pulls/context` files/comments. These picker reads are the remaining outliers, on both providers at once.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] GitHub `/references/labels` and `/references/reviewers` paginate beyond page 1 (following pages until a short page) under a named page/item cap in the style of `GITHUB_BRANCH_MAX_PAGES`, **or** return a machine-readable truncation/`complete` signal the picker surfaces.
- [ ] GitLab `listLabels` and `listReviewerCandidates` get the same treatment (paginate via `readCollection`-style bounded reading, or an explicit over-cap error/signal) — the two providers must not diverge in completeness semantics.
- [ ] Crossing the cap is never silent on either provider: explicit error (the GitLab `readCollection` shape) or a surfaced truncation signal.
- [ ] New tests: github routes tests stub multi-page label/assignee answers and assert the merged set (plus the chosen over-cap behavior); gitlab resources tests do the same for labels/members.
- [ ] Existing github routes and gitlab resources tests pass; repos with ≤100 labels/members behave exactly as today.

body:
## Problem

The GitHub pull-request context route (`GET /pulls/context`, `packages/web/server/lib/github/routes.js:2972`) reads three collections with a single first-page request each and returns them as if they were complete:

- `routes.js:3108` — `issues.listComments(..., per_page: 100)` — issue comments, page 1 only
- `routes.js:3124` — `pulls.listReviewComments(..., per_page: 100)` — review comments, page 1 only
- `routes.js:3143` — `pulls.listFiles(..., per_page: 100)` — changed files, page 1 only

None of the three follows a second page, and the response (`routes.js:~3353`: `{ connected, repo, pr, issueComments, reviewComments, files, ... }`) carries no total, no `complete` flag, and no truncation signal — the mapped `pr` object does not even carry GitHub's `changed_files` count. A PR with more than 100 changed files, 100 issue comments, or 100 review comments is silently shown with exactly the first 100 of each: files missing from the changed-files view (and from the `diff` assembled from file patches when `diff=1` consumers use `files`), and discussion/review history cut off with no indication anything is missing.

## Evidence (verified this run, main a768956f6)

Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-oc-pr-context-pagination-20261102/probe-context-pagination.test.js`) driving the **real** `registerGitHubRoutes` handler (the `routes.auth.test.js` harness pattern) with a stubbed GitHub fetch that serves page-aware results — 250 files, 130 issue comments, 120 review comments:

- `filesReturned= 100 of 250` — exactly one request: `/repos/team/project/pulls/5/files?per_page=100`
- `issueCommentsReturned= 100 of 130` — exactly one request: `/repos/team/project/issues/5/comments?per_page=100`
- `reviewCommentsReturned= 100 of 120` — exactly one request: `/repos/team/project/pulls/5/comments?per_page=100`

The route never asks for page 2 of any of the three collections.

## Why it matters / parity

- This is the PR surface users review from: a large PR (dependency bumps, generated code, lockfile + source changes — this repo's own PRs regularly exceed 100 files) presents an incomplete file list and incomplete review discussion as complete. Reviewers can merge believing they have seen every file and every comment.
- The codebase's own sibling patterns all refuse silent truncation:
  - The GitLab twin, `changeRequestContext` in `packages/web/server/lib/gitlab/resources.js:957`, reads notes and diffs through `readCollection` (cap `COLLECTION_MAX_PAGES = 20`, :22) and **throws** `'GitLab merge request has more changed files than OpenChamber reads'` rather than returning a partial list.
  - The branches route in this same file paginates with `GITHUB_BRANCH_MAX_PAGES` (`routes.js:2094`, #1313).
  - The annotations reader in this same route paginates pages 1–3 (`routes.js:3223`).
  - `pr-status.js`'s repo-pulls cache explicitly tracks `complete: prs.length < 100` so a first-page miss is never treated as authoritative.
  The `/pulls/context` collections are the outliers.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `/pulls/context` paginates files, issue comments, and review comments beyond the first page (following pages until a short page), under a named page/item cap in the style of `GITHUB_BRANCH_MAX_PAGES` / GitLab's `COLLECTION_MAX_PAGES`.
- [ ] Crossing the cap is never silent: the route either fails with an explicit error (the GitLab twin's `'has more … than OpenChamber reads'` shape) or returns a machine-readable truncation/`complete` signal that the web client surfaces — a partial list presented as complete is the bug.
- [ ] New tests in the github routes test suite stub multi-page GitHub answers (full first page + second page) for all three collections and assert the route returns the merged set, plus a test for the over-cap behavior chosen above.
- [ ] Existing github routes tests pass; single-page PRs behave exactly as today.

title: fix(web): Octokit ETag fetch buffers the whole body before its 2 MiB cache cap when Content-Length is absent or understated — chunked responses are materialized whole by response.arrayBuffer() (#848 residual)

body:
## Problem

The Octokit conditional-fetch wrapper in `packages/web/server/lib/github/octokit.js` only enforces its 2 MiB ETag-cache entry cap (`ETAG_CACHE_MAX_ENTRY_BYTES`, :37) **before** buffering when the response declares an oversize `Content-Length`, and **after** buffering otherwise:

- `octokit.js:91-93` — a declared length over the cap passes the response through unbuffered (covered by the test at `octokit.test.js:60`).
- `octokit.js:95` — every other ETag-bearing GET response goes through `await response.arrayBuffer()`, which materializes the **entire** body in memory; only then does `:96` check `body.byteLength <= ETAG_CACHE_MAX_ENTRY_BYTES` to decide whether to *retain* it in the cache.

So a response with no `Content-Length` (chunked transfer encoding) — or one that understates its length — is buffered whole no matter how large it is, defeating the stated intent at `octokit.js:89-90` ("Oversized answers are returned whole but never retained") and the #848 byte bounds: the peak memory cost the cap exists to prevent is paid before the cap is consulted. The 8 s request timeout (`OCTOKIT_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS`, :20) bounds duration, not bytes — a fast endpoint can deliver far more than 2 MiB inside it.

This is the undeclared-length residual of #848: that fix added the declared-length gate and the post-hoc retention check, and its test suite covers only the declared case.

## Evidence (verified this run, main e5cbd4539)

Probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-oc-octokit-etag-20261102/probe2.mjs`) driving the real `createOctokit()` with a stubbed `fetch` returning a streamed 32 MiB JSON body with an `etag` header, instrumenting `Response` construction to observe what the wrapper materializes:

- **No `Content-Length` (chunked):** the wrapper constructed a `Response` from a single **32,505,868-byte ArrayBuffer** — the whole body, 16× the 2 MiB cap — before discarding it from the cache.
- **Declared `Content-Length` over the cap:** the wrapper passed the response through — **no ArrayBuffer materialized** (`arrayBuffersWrappedByWrapper: []`).

## Why it matters

Every GitHub poll through `createOctokit` (PR status, checks, repo data) flows through this wrapper. One unexpectedly large or chunked GitHub answer (large tree/contents/release payloads, a proxy that strips `Content-Length`, a gzip/chunked hop) spikes the managed server's memory by the full body size as an extra copy on top of Octokit's own parse — in the process that must stay up to serve every session. The codebase's other readers (e.g. `readBoundedResponseBytes` in `lib/shared/response-body.js`, the theme catalog, the guest surface reader) all judge size *while* streaming; this wrapper is the outlier.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] When an ETag-bearing GET response has no `Content-Length`, or one at/under the cap, the wrapper never materializes more than `ETAG_CACHE_MAX_ENTRY_BYTES` (+ one chunk) before deciding: bodies that cross the cap while streaming are passed through unbuffered (or the stream is handed onward untouched), never fully buffered and then dropped.
- [ ] Bodies at/under the cap are still cached and replayed on 304 exactly as today; declared-oversize pass-through behavior is unchanged.
- [ ] New tests in `octokit.test.js` cover the undeclared-length oversize case (streamed body, no `Content-Length`) and an understated `Content-Length`, alongside the existing declared-oversize test.
- [ ] Existing octokit tests pass.

title: fix(ui): session-goal save writes the objective file before the guarded metadata write — a concurrent save loses its objective file to an aborted save (PR #1094's named follow-up)

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

body:
## Finding

`setSessionGoal` (packages/ui) protects the goal **metadata record** against concurrent edits — `nextGoalRecord` re-checks `isSameGoal` inside the metadata write — but the **objective file** is written before that write, unconditionally. Between the pre-check and the metadata write, a save made elsewhere can lose its objective file to this one: this save overwrites the shared objective file, its own metadata write then correctly aborts as `changed`, and the surviving goal record (the other window's, including its `objectiveRevision`) now points at a file whose text is this save's objective. The stored revision hash no longer matches the file content, and the goal silently runs with the wrong objective text.

PR #1094's body named this explicitly — "The save-path check-then-write race is a separate finding and is not touched" — and the code on current main documents the same window. It was never filed as its own issue (dedupe below).

## Evidence

- Source PR: #1094 MERGED 2026-11-01, head c148d5ef967559966bef1a15081cba1bc77f8f18 — https://github.com/developing-today/openchamber/pull/1094 (fixes #1075; its body scopes this race out).
- Current main 5d465222dc5a1d075ca610face16acfbb7ca7476, `packages/ui/src/lib/sessionGoalActions.ts`:
  - doc comment on `setSessionGoal` (~:226-233): "The stored goal is read before the objective file is written and again inside the metadata write; between those two a change made elsewhere can still lose its objective file to this one, a window of one request."
  - :254 — the pre-check `isSameGoal(getSessionGoal(await opencodeClient.getSession(sessionId, directory)), existing)`.
  - :258 — `writeGoalObjectiveFile(sessionId, objective)` runs next, before any metadata write.
  - :270 / :182 — `writeGoal(...)` → `nextGoalRecord` re-checks `isSameGoal(currentGoal, existing)` and aborts the record write on mismatch — but nothing restores the objective file already overwritten at :258.
- The revision mechanism added by #1094 makes the corruption detectable after the fact (stored `objectiveRevision` = hash of the other save's text ≠ hash of the file's current text) but nothing checks it on read.

## Why it matters

Two windows (or a window plus a rewrite finishing) editing the same session goal inside one request window can leave the goal running an objective nobody's record describes — the exact class of silent overwrite #1075/#1094 set out to eliminate for the record itself. The window is narrow ("one request") but the failure is silent and self-concealing: the conflict is reported as correctly refused while the file has already been replaced.

## Acceptance criteria

- A save whose metadata write aborts as `changed` leaves the previously stored objective file byte-identical (e.g. write the objective file inside/after the guarded metadata write, stage it per-save and promote only on success, or restore the prior file content on abort).
- A regression test in `sessionGoalActions.test.ts`: an intervening save between the pre-check and the write keeps its objective file content, and the aborted save reports `changed`.
- The doc comment on `setSessionGoal` is updated to describe the closed window.
- Existing session-goal tests keep passing (accounting-bump and revision conflict cases from #1094 included).

## Dedupe

Searched open + closed issues 2026-11-02 for "session goal race", "check-then-write", and "goal save conflict": only #1075 (the parent finding, CLOSED by #1094) and unrelated race/store issues (#659, #978, #942). No issue covers the objective-file write window.

title: fix(web): message-stream WS cap relies on maxPayload alone — no handler-side guard, so under Bun over-cap frames are assembled and never refused with 1009 (#1118 missed the #1117/#1082 pattern)

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/pr-diff-review
