body:
## Finding

PR #1118 capped the message-stream WebSocket server at 64 KiB by passing `maxPayload` alone — but every sibling WebSocket server in this codebase pairs `maxPayload` with an in-handler frame-size check, because under Bun the bundled `ws` does not enforce `maxPayload`. The message-stream runtime has no such check, and no `message` handler at all, so under Bun an over-cap frame is never refused with 1009: it is assembled in server memory and silently discarded, and the connection stays open to repeat that indefinitely. That is exactly the unbounded-assembly exposure #1108 was filed to close; the fix only holds under Node.

## Evidence

- PR #1118 (merged 173d56235b9fc47cf01ae08c2b2e2b6e5bac3792, closes #1108): diff touches only `protocol.js` (new `MESSAGE_STREAM_WS_MAX_PAYLOAD_BYTES`), `runtime.js` (+2 lines: import + `maxPayload:`), tests, and docs. No handler-side size check.
- Current main, `packages/web/server/lib/event-stream/runtime.js:75-78`: `new WebSocketServer({ noServer: true, maxPayload: MESSAGE_STREAM_WS_MAX_PAYLOAD_BYTES })` — and the file contains no socket `message` handler and no 1009 close path (verified by grep of the file at main 5d465222d).
- Current main, `packages/web/server/lib/event-stream/DOCUMENTATION.md:29` documents the outcome as: "an over-cap frame is refused by the ws layer (close 1009) instead of being assembled in server memory up to the 100 MiB ws default" — not true under Bun.
- The Bun caveat is established in-repo, three times over:
  - `packages/web/server/lib/dev-tunnel/runtime.js:58-59` (comment) and `:205-212` (handler check closing 1009, #1082 precedent): "under Bun the bundled ws does not enforce maxPayload, so the message handler below ALSO checks…"
  - `packages/web/server/lib/realtime-proxy.js` (#1117, merged minutes before #1118 for sibling issue #1109): handler check `data.length > REALTIME_PROXY_WS_MAX_PAYLOAD_BYTES` → `closePair(1009, …)` before forwarding or queueing.
  - `packages/web/server/lib/persistent-pty/runtime.js` (#1117): same pattern, `client.close(1009, 'Persistent PTY frame too large')`.
- PR #1118's regression tests run under vitest/Node, where the ws layer does enforce `maxPayload`, so they pass while the Bun path stays unguarded — the gap is invisible to the test suite as written.

## Why it matters

The message-stream endpoints (`/api/global/event/ws`, `/api/event/ws`) are browser-facing and long-lived. Under a Bun-run server, a single client can repeatedly send frames up to the 100 MiB ws default; each is fully assembled in server memory before being discarded, and because nothing closes the connection with 1009, there is no bound on how often it can repeat. The other three WS servers were all hardened against precisely this runtime behaviour; this one was missed because its PR landed in the same batch as #1117 and only copied the `maxPayload` half of the pattern.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The message-stream runtime refuses an over-cap inbound frame with close 1009 even when the ws layer does not enforce `maxPayload` (handler-side check in the dev-tunnel / realtime-proxy / persistent-pty style, or an equivalent runtime-independent guard).
- [ ] A test exercises the over-cap path in a way that does not depend on Node ws enforcement (e.g. drives the handler/guard directly), and the at-cap / ready-flow behaviour is unchanged.
- [ ] `event-stream/DOCUMENTATION.md` describes the enforcement accurately for both runtimes.
- [ ] In-cap behaviour unchanged: no legitimate client frame is affected (the stream is receive-only; 64 KiB cap value itself is not in question).

Found by: pr-diff-review job, 2026-11-02 run reviewing PRs #1106–#1136. Source PRs: #1118 (the incomplete fix), #1117 and #1082 (the established pattern it missed).

title: fix(web,vscode): skills-catalog install copies a skill directory with no file-count or byte cap — copyDirectoryNoSymlinks copies every file in a cloned repo's skill dir (probe: 20,000 dirs + 256 MiB file → 35s, 268,435,456 bytes written)

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator

body:
## Problem

Installing a skill from the skills catalog copies the selected skill directory with no file-count cap, no total-bytes cap, and no per-file size cap in either runtime:

- `packages/web/server/lib/skills-catalog/install.js:73` — `copyDirectoryNoSymlinks(srcDir, dstDir, cloneRoot)` walks the source recursively (`install.js:102-141`) and `copyFile`s every regular file it finds. Its guards are all traversal/symlink guards (reject symlinks, real-parent-inside-clone checks); nothing counts entries, sums bytes, or bounds any single file. It is called from `installSkillsFromRepository` at `install.js:356`.
- VS Code twin: `packages/vscode/src/skillsCatalog.ts:445` `copyDirectoryNoSymlinks` is the same walk with the same guards and the same absence of caps, called at `skillsCatalog.ts:629`.
- The source is third-party content by design: the catalog installs skills from arbitrary GitHub repositories the user browses, cloned at `install.js:143` (`--depth 1`). A repository can place an arbitrarily large tree inside the skill directory it offers for install — many directories, many files, or one huge file — and one install click copies all of it into the user's skills directory.
- Contrast in the same surface: the catalog scan caps a `SKILL.md` read at 4 MiB (`SKILL_MD_MAX_BYTES`, vscode `skillsCatalog.ts:20`; #1103 capped the clone-controlled SKILL.md read on both surfaces), and supporting-file *reads* cap at 1 MiB (#1139/#1158) — only the install copy has no bound at all.

`copyFile` streams, so memory is not the issue; the unbounded quantities are disk written, entry count, and wall time (the walk also does an `lstat` + `realpath` per entry, so directory-heavy trees are slow as well as unbounded).

## Evidence (verified on main 910cfa65f)

Laptop probe against the real exported `copyDirectoryNoSymlinks` (probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-skill-install-copy-20261102/probe.mjs` on the laptop; `install.js` sha256 `29629466…` and `skillsCatalog.ts` sha256 `50ee81d3…` both identical between the laptop fork and origin/main), source skill dir = 20,000 empty directories + 1,000 small files + 1 `SKILL.md` + one 256 MiB file:

- **20,202 `readdir` calls** — every directory visited.
- **34,963 ms** wall time for one install copy.
- **1,002 files copied**, including the 256 MiB file copied whole (**268,435,456 bytes**) — no cap objected at any point.

## Why it matters

The skills catalog is a one-click install path for third-party repository content. Without any count/size bound, a bloated or hostile catalog repository can fill the user's disk and stall an install for tens of seconds or more, in the managed server (web) or the extension host (VS Code). Every neighboring read on this surface has been capped; the copy is the remaining unbounded one.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Both `copyDirectoryNoSymlinks` implementations (web `install.js:73`, VS Code `skillsCatalog.ts:445`) enforce named caps: a maximum entry/file count and a maximum total copied bytes (and/or a per-file maximum), sized generously relative to legitimate skills, aborting the install with a clear error when a cap is crossed.
- [ ] A failed/over-cap install leaves no partial skill directory behind (the destination is cleaned up or the copy goes to a staging dir that is only moved into place on success).
- [ ] Tests cover: a directory-heavy source aborts at the count cap; a source whose total or per-file bytes exceed the cap aborts; a normal skill (at/under caps) installs byte-identically, and the existing symlink/traversal rejections still hold.
- [ ] Re-probe after the fix with the probe tree above: the copy aborts at the bound instead of running ~35 s and writing 256 MiB+.

Related: #1103 (catalog SKILL.md read cap — same surface), #715 (install-copy symlink/traversal guards — the guards this walk does have), #1326 (clone copy/verify streaming hash — a different copy path).

body:
## Problem

The supporting-files listing walk has no directory-visit cap, no file-count cap, and no deadline in either runtime — it is a different walk from the skill-discovery walk filed as #1357, and that filing does not cover it:

- `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/shared.js:1054` — `listSkillSupportingFiles(skillDir)` recurses via its inner `walkDir` (`shared.js:1061-1080`) over **every** directory under one skill's directory, sequentially (`await` per directory, not even the concurrency limiter the discovery walk has), pushing one result object per non-`SKILL.md` file into an array that is returned whole. No cap constant, no deadline, no partial/truncated marker.
- It runs on the skill-detail path: `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/skills.js:326` `getSkillSources(...)` defaults `includeSupportingFiles = true`, and at `skills.js:473-474` calls `listSkillSupportingFiles(mdDir)` — so opening one skill's detail walks that skill's entire directory tree, however large.
- VS Code twin: `packages/vscode/src/opencodeConfig.ts:3129` `listSupportingFiles` is the same walk **synchronously** (`fs.readdirSync` at `:3131`, recursion at `:3137-3148`), so the unbounded walk blocks the extension host's event loop for its whole duration.
- Contrast inside the same module: reading one supporting file's *contents* is capped at 1 MiB (`SKILL_SUPPORTING_FILE_MAX_BYTES`, `shared.js:915`, enforced in `readSkillSupportingFile`), and the discovery walk's missing cap is #1357 — only this listing walk remains unbounded.

A skill directory is user/project content (skills are commonly vendored, generated, or checked into a project), and a directory that happens to contain a bundled `node_modules`, `.venv`, or generated tree makes one detail request walk all of it.

## Evidence (verified on main 910cfa65f)

Laptop probe against the real exported `listSkillSupportingFiles` (probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-supporting-files-walk-20261102/probe.mjs` on the laptop; the laptop fork's `shared.js` is sha256-identical `c788f386…` to origin/main's), with `fs.promises.readdir` instrumented, skill dir = 30,000 empty directories (300 × 100) + 2,000 small files + 1 `SKILL.md`:

- **30,302 `readdir` calls** — every directory visited.
- **9,537 ms** wall time for one listing call (slower than the #1357 discovery-walk probe's 6.3 s on the same tree shape, because this walk is fully sequential).
- All **2,000 files returned** — the result array grows without any count bound; growth is linear in tree size with nothing to arrest it.

## Why it matters

This is the same unbounded-traversal class the repo has been closing walk by walk (#1332 file-search directory cap, #1357 skill-discovery walk), on the one skills walk those filings missed. Existing cap tests pass while a single skill-detail request can still be made to do unbounded filesystem work, and in VS Code the same tree freezes the extension host synchronously.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The web walk in `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/shared.js` stops at a named directory-visit and/or returned-file cap (a `SKILL_SUPPORTING_FILES_MAX_*`-style constant sized generously relative to legitimate skills), returning the files found so far (partial results, the established pattern for this repo's capped walks) instead of walking to exhaustion.
- [ ] The VS Code twin (`packages/vscode/src/opencodeConfig.ts:3129`) gets the same bound, and the synchronous walk stops at the bound rather than merely recording that it passed it.
- [ ] The capped behavior is observable to the caller (e.g. a truncation signal or a documented partial-result contract), so the UI does not present a truncated list as complete.
- [ ] Tests cover: a directory-heavy skill dir (many empty directories) terminates at the bound with files found before it still returned; an at-bound tree returns complete results; existing skills tests (`shared.test.js`, `skills.test.js`) still pass.
- [ ] Re-probe after the fix with the 30,000-empty-directory tree: `readdir` calls and wall time stay near the bound, not linear in tree size.

Related: #1357 (skill-discovery walk — same class, different walk), #1332 (file-search walk directory cap).

title: fix(web): ngrok readiness poll reads the agent-API body with a deadline but no byte cap — fetchNgrokPublicUrl buffers the whole body via response.json() every 250 ms (probe: 128 MiB body consumed whole in 664 ms, +521 MiB RSS)

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

The ngrok readiness poll reads the local agent API's response body with a deadline but no byte cap — the one tunnel-path body read that missed the repo's bounded-read sweep:

- `packages/web/server/lib/ngrok-tunnel.js:255-259` — `fetchNgrokPublicUrl` fetches `http://127.0.0.1:4040/api/tunnels` (`:15`) and does `const payload = await response.json()`, buffering and parsing the whole body. The only bound is the abort deadline (`NGROK_POLL_TIMEOUT_MS = 2000`, `:19`); the function's own comment (`:242-245`) is careful that the deadline also aborts an in-flight body read — but a body that *arrives* inside the deadline is consumed without limit, and loopback delivers a lot in 2 s (probe below: 128 MiB in 664 ms).
- The poll repeats every 250 ms during tunnel startup (`pollNgrokPublicUrl`, `:274`), so a body near the deadline is re-read again and again through the startup window.
- The bounded pattern already exists in the same server: `packages/web/server/lib/shared/response-body.js:47` exports `readBoundedResponseJson(response, maxBytes)`, and the sibling body reads this repo has capped use it or an equivalent (changelog index 1 MiB at `lib/changelog/update-notes.js:19`, quota response-body helper, session-list 16 MiB in `lib/opencode/proxy.js`). A tunnels payload is a handful of small objects — kilobytes, not megabytes.
- History in this exact file: #819 added the deadline and the in-flight guard to this poll; #820 bounded its `spawnSync` probes. The byte cap is the remaining third of that set.

The endpoint is loopback, but the server does not control what answers on port 4040: a wedged or hostile local process (or an ngrok agent in a bad state) that floods the API makes the managed server allocate the full body on every poll.

## Evidence (verified on main 5e759ec0c)

Laptop probe against the real exported `fetchNgrokPublicUrl` (probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-ngrok-body-cap-20261102/probe.mjs` on the laptop; the laptop fork's `ngrok-tunnel.js` is sha256-identical `78d5a516…` to origin/main's), with an injected `fetchImpl` returning a streamed valid-JSON body — one https tunnel followed by 128 MiB of padding inside a tunnel name:

- **134,217,812 body bytes generated and consumed** before the function returned — no early stop at any bound.
- **664 ms** elapsed — comfortably inside even the production 2 s poll deadline, so the deadline does not arrest this in practice.
- **+521 MiB RSS** in the reading process for a payload whose useful content is one short URL.
- The function returned the correct `https://demo.ngrok-free.app` — behavior is right; the read is just unbounded.

## Why it matters

This is the same deadline-but-no-byte-cap class closed across the server in #1282/#1285/#1291/#1293/#1303 (and in this file's own history, #819/#820), on the one poll that runs repeatedly — every 250 ms — while a tunnel starts. The fix is small and the bounded helper already exists in the same tree.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `fetchNgrokPublicUrl` reads the agent-API body through a bounded read (e.g. `readBoundedResponseJson` from `lib/shared/response-body.js`) with a named cap sized generously for a tunnels payload (the repo's usual 1 MiB is far above any real `/api/tunnels` answer); over-cap settles as `null`, like every other failure in this function.
- [ ] The deadline/abort behavior is unchanged: a never-answering fetch and a stalled body still settle as `null` within the deadline, and a caller abort still settles promptly (the existing tests at `ngrok-tunnel.test.js:158-196` pass unmodified in behavior).
- [ ] Tests cover: a body over the cap settles as `null` without being consumed whole (a streamed/chunked body whose generator is not exhausted); a normal tunnels payload still returns the preferred https URL and the fallback.
- [ ] Re-probe after the fix with the 128 MiB streamed body: bytes consumed stay near the cap and RSS stays flat.

Related: #819 / #820 (this file's deadline and spawnSync bounds), #1291 / #1303 (deadline-only body reads capped elsewhere in the server).

title: fix(web,vscode): skill-discovery walk has no directory cap or deadline — walkSkillMdFiles walks every directory under a skills root (probe: 30,000 empty dirs → 30,302 readdir calls, 6.3s, +185 MiB RSS)

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/vscode
labels.description: Package: vscode (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

Skill discovery's directory walk has no visit cap and no deadline in either runtime — the only bounds are a concurrency limiter (web) and an ancestor-cycle check (web). A skills root that contains a large directory tree is walked to the end on every discovery:

- `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/shared.js:935` — `walkSkillMdFiles(rootDir)` recurses over every directory under the root. Its only limits are `SKILL_WALK_CONCURRENCY = 8` (`shared.js:928`, bounds parallelism, not total work) and the `ancestors` real-path set (`shared.js:962-967`, stops a link that points back to one of its own ancestors only).
- `shared.js:986-991` — links are followed at any depth (`stat` on a symlink entry makes it a directory entry and it is walked), so a link inside a skills root that points at a large tree outside it (e.g. a project tree or a home directory) is walked in full too; two links to the same large target are both walked, per the function's own comment.
- The roots are not all trusted: `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/skills.js:154` `discoverSkills(workingDirectory)` walks `~/.claude/skills` and `~/.agents/skills`, the same roots at **every project ancestor** (`skills.js:184-193`), every config directory's `skill`/`skills` subdir, and any `config.skills.paths` entries — project-controlled content. It runs on request from the skills routes (`packages/web/server/lib/opencode/skill-routes.js:318`) and the control surface (`integration-actions.js:379`).
- VS Code twin: `packages/vscode/src/opencodeConfig.ts:863` `walkSkillMdFiles` is the same walk **synchronously** (`fs.readdirSync` at `:870`, recursion at `:890-898`), called from `discoverSkills` at `:3152` — so the unbounded walk blocks the extension host's event loop for its whole duration, and it has no cycle protection beyond not following non-root links.

Contrast: the file-search walk's missing directory cap was filed as #1332 with the in-repo precedent `GIT_DIRS_MAX_DIRS` in `fs/routes.js`; this walk is a different walk (skills roots, not project search) and was missed by that filing.

## Evidence (verified on main 5e759ec0c)

Laptop probe against the real exported `walkSkillMdFiles` (probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-skill-walk-20261102/probe.mjs` on the laptop; the laptop fork's `shared.js` is sha256-identical `c788f386…` to origin/main's), with `fs.promises.readdir` instrumented to count directory visits, root = 30,000 empty directories (300 × 100) + 1 real `SKILL.md`:

- **30,302 `readdir` calls** — every directory visited, plus the root and the skill dir.
- **6,280 ms** wall time and **+185 MiB RSS** for a tree containing exactly one skill and nothing else.
- The 1 `SKILL.md` was found — the walk is correct, it is just unbounded: no cap, no deadline, and no partial-result return until the whole tree is exhausted.

Growth is linear in directory count with nothing to arrest it. A project that vendors a large tree under a `.claude/skills` / `.agents/skills` root (generated files, a bundled `.venv`/`node_modules` — the function's own header comment at `shared.js:931-934` already anticipates "tens of thousands of entries"), or a symlink in a skills root pointing at a large tree, makes one skills-list request walk all of it in the managed server; in VS Code the same tree freezes the extension host synchronously for the duration.

## Why it matters

This is the same unbounded-traversal class the repo has been closing walk by walk (#1315/#1317/#1320 cursor page caps, #1332 file-search directory cap), on a walk those filings did not cover — so all existing cap tests pass while skill discovery still has no bound on the total work one request can trigger, on roots a project controls.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The web walk in `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/shared.js` stops at a named directory-visit (and/or entry) cap — a `SKILL_WALK_MAX_*`-style constant sized generously relative to legitimate skills collections — and/or a deadline, returning the `SKILL.md` paths found so far (partial results, the established pattern for this repo's capped walks) instead of walking to exhaustion.
- [ ] The VS Code twin (`packages/vscode/src/opencodeConfig.ts:863`) gets the same bound, so the two walks stay in agreement; the synchronous walk must also stop at the bound rather than merely recording that it passed it.
- [ ] A link inside a skills root that points at a large external tree cannot expand the walk past the same bound.
- [ ] Tests cover: a directory-heavy skills root (many empty directories, few/no `SKILL.md`) terminates at the bound with the skills found before it still returned; an at-bound tree returns complete results; the existing `walkSkillMdFiles` tests in `shared.test.js` (link-following, ordering, cycle cases) still pass unchanged in behavior.
- [ ] Re-probe after the fix with the 30,000-empty-directory tree: `readdir` calls, wall time, and RSS stay near the bound, not linear in tree size.

Related: #1332 (file-search walk directory cap — same class, different walk), #1317 / #1320 (cursor-walk page caps).

title: fix(web): streamed git ls-files decode corrupts non-ASCII untracked filenames split across pipe chunks — pending += chunk.toString('utf8') at git/service.js:3070 turns a straddling multi-byte character into U+FFFD, so getStatus returns a path that does not exist (probe: 1 of 12 boundary-aligned é filenames corrupted, twice)

body:
## Problem

The streamed `git ls-files` reader that expands untracked directories in a status read decodes each pipe chunk independently, so a multi-byte UTF-8 character in a filename that straddles a chunk boundary is corrupted into U+FFFD replacement characters — and the corrupted path is what the status response returns:

- `packages/web/server/lib/git/service.js:3067-3070` — `listUntrackedFilesBounded` (spawned at `:3036` as `git ls-files --others --exclude-standard -z -- <dir>`) does `pending += chunk.toString('utf8')` per chunk, then splits `pending` on `\0`. `Buffer.toString` on a chunk that ends mid-character emits U+FFFD for the partial sequence, and the following chunk's continuation bytes become a second U+FFFD — the original character is unrecoverable.
- `service.js:3106-3131` — `expandUntrackedDirectories` substitutes these decoded paths into `status.files`; `readStatus` (`:3270`) applies it to every `getStatus` result, so the corrupted name propagates to every client surface that lists untracked files (diff/status views then reference a path that does not exist on disk).
- The codebase already knows this pattern: `packages/web/server/lib/fs/content-search.js:11,179` decodes its streamed ripgrep output with `StringDecoder` (`node:string_decoder`), which holds partial sequences across chunks. This reader — and two sibling accumulators below — missed that treatment.

Same-pattern sites to audit in the same fix (whole-output accumulators, corrupted only if a boundary splits a character, after which the name no longer matches):

- `packages/web/server/lib/fs/search.js:178` — `stdout += data.toString()` for `git check-ignore` output, split on `\n` at `:187-192` and matched against real entry names: a corrupted ignored name means an ignored non-ASCII file is *not* filtered out of file search.
- `packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.js:2112` — the identical `check-ignore` accumulator for the file-tree route, matched at `:2124-2127`.

## Evidence (verified on main 3f10c28e2)

Laptop probe against the real module (probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-lsfiles-utf8-20261102/probe.mjs`; the laptop fork's `service.js` is sha256-identical `d498d95a…` to origin/main's). The probe builds a git repo whose untracked directory `newdir/` holds 781 files (under the 1,000-file expansion limit at `service.js:2996`), with 12 target filenames placing a `é` (U+00E9, 2-byte UTF-8) so its first byte lands exactly on successive 16 KiB output offsets in the `ls-files -z` stream, then calls the real `getStatus(repo)`:

- `git ls-files` ground truth: 781 entries, 12 with intact `é`, 0 with U+FFFD.
- `getStatus`: 781 expanded entries, 11 with intact `é`, **1 with U+FFFD replacement characters** — `newdir/0259zz��qqq…` — i.e. the target aligned to a real pipe-chunk boundary came back corrupted.
- Reproduced identically on a second run (same file corrupted both times).

Any sufficiently large untracked directory (total `ls-files` output over one pipe chunk, ~64 KiB — a few hundred files) with a non-ASCII filename in the wrong position triggers this in ordinary use: CJK/accented filenames in an untracked folder are common, and which file is hit depends only on the cumulative byte offset of its name.

## Why it matters

Status is the most-polled read in the product, and the expanded untracked paths are identifiers, not display text: clients use them to open diffs and files. A corrupted path silently points at a file that does not exist — the file appears in status but its diff/open fails or 404s, with no error anywhere pointing at the decode. ASCII-only trees are unaffected, which is why it survives: every existing test uses ASCII names and small listings that never cross a chunk boundary.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `listUntrackedFilesBounded` decodes the `ls-files` stream with a `StringDecoder` (the `content-search.js` pattern) or equivalent byte-level buffering, so a multi-byte character split across any chunk boundary round-trips intact; the trailing partial record on `close` keeps working.
- [ ] The two `check-ignore` accumulators (`fs/search.js:178`, `fs/routes.js:2112`) get the same treatment, or are explicitly verified/fixed so an ignored non-ASCII name still matches after a split chunk.
- [ ] Regression test: a listing whose total output crosses a pipe-chunk boundary with a multi-byte character straddling it returns the exact on-disk path (no U+FFFD) — e.g. an untracked directory with enough padded filenames to push a `é`/CJK target name across the boundary, asserting `getStatus` (or the bounded reader) returns it verbatim.
- [ ] Existing behavior unchanged for ASCII listings, the 1,000-entry truncation bound, and the stall timeout in the same reader.

Related: `packages/web/server/lib/fs/content-search.js:179` (the in-repo `StringDecoder` precedent).

body:
## Problem

The filesystem search walk that backs project-icon discovery (and the VS Code bridge's directory search) bounds only the **files** it inspects — the directories it visits are unbounded, and the web version has no deadline of any kind:

- `packages/web/server/lib/fs/search.js:4` — the only ceiling is `FILE_SEARCH_MAX_VISITED_FILES = 10_000`.
- `search.js:121-122` — the walk keeps a BFS `queue` and a `visited` Set of directory paths.
- `search.js:130-134` — `reachedSearchStop()` stops on `candidates.length >= limit` (empty query) or `inspectedFiles >= FILE_SEARCH_MAX_VISITED_FILES` (query) — and `inspectedFiles` is only incremented for files at `search.js:227`. A directory increments nothing: it is added to `visited`/`queue` at `search.js:215` and walked, forever, until the tree runs out.
- `search.js:116` — the web runtime's `searchFilesystemFiles(rootPath, options)` does not even accept a time budget. Its one production caller is the project-icon discover route, `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/project-icon-routes.js:429`, which searches the whole project tree for `favicon` on request.
- VS Code twin: `packages/vscode/src/bridge-fs-helpers-runtime.ts:305-332` has the identical file-only stop. It accepts a `timeBudgetMs` deadline (`:315`), but only the query fallback passes one (1500 ms, `:523`); the empty-query `searchDirectory` path (`:449`) calls it with no budget, so it has the same unbounded directory walk.

Contrast inside the same web file's sibling: `findGitDirectories` in `packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.js` walks a tree with explicit `GIT_DIRS_MAX_DEPTH = 3` and `GIT_DIRS_MAX_DIRS = 100` caps (`routes.js:437-438`, enforced at `:527`) — the house pattern this walk missed.

## Evidence (verified on main 0ffe7442b)

Laptop probe against the real `createFsSearchRuntime` (probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-fs-search-dir-cap-20261102/probe.mjs` + `probe2.mjs` on the laptop; the laptop fork's `search.js` is sha256-identical `1df3bb3d…` to origin/main's), with `readdir` instrumented to count directory visits, query `zzzz` (no matches), `respectGitignore: false`:

- **30,000 empty directories + 2 files:** 30,001 `readdir` calls — every directory visited — 2,109 ms, RSS +38 MiB, 0 results. The 10,000 ceiling never fired because only 2 files were inspected.
- **150,000 empty directories:** 150,001 `readdir` calls, **15,877 ms**, RSS **+190 MiB** (the `visited` Set + queue), 0 results, no early stop, no error, no deadline.

The growth is linear in directory count with nothing to arrest it: a project containing a large generated/vendored directory tree (deep `target/`, build farms, snapshot trees — none of them in `FILE_SEARCH_EXCLUDED_DIRS`) makes one icon-discover request walk the entire tree in the managed server, growing memory the whole way. With `respectGitignore: true` (the production caller's setting) each non-empty directory listing additionally runs a `git check-ignore` child (2.5 s timeout each, batches of 5), so wall time is worse, not better.

## Why it matters

This is the same unbounded-traversal class the repo has been closing walk by walk (cursor page caps #1315/#1317/#1320, the git-dirs depth/visit caps already in `routes.js`), but on directory count rather than bytes or pages — so every existing cap test passes while the walk itself has no bound. The trigger is an ordinary request (project icon discovery) against a project tree the server does not control.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The web walk in `packages/web/server/lib/fs/search.js` stops at a named directory-visit cap (a `FILE_SEARCH_MAX_VISITED_DIRS`-style constant, sized generously relative to the 10,000-file ceiling) and/or a deadline, so a directory-only tree cannot keep it walking or growing `visited`/`queue` without bound.
- [ ] Hitting the new bound is indistinguishable-safe for callers: the search returns the candidates found so far (partial results, the established pattern for this walk's file ceiling) — project-icon discovery still finds a favicon that appears before the bound.
- [ ] The VS Code twin (`bridge-fs-helpers-runtime.ts`) gets the same directory bound, including on the empty-query `searchDirectory` path that passes no `timeBudgetMs` — keep the two walks in agreement, as their comments already require for the file ceiling.
- [ ] Tests cover: a directory-heavy tree (many empty directories, few/no files) terminates at the bound with partial results; an at-bound tree returns complete results; existing `search.test.js` / bridge search behavior for ordinary trees is unchanged.

Related: #1317 / #1320 (cursor-walk page caps — same class, different walk), `packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.js:437` (`GIT_DIRS_MAX_DIRS` — the in-repo precedent for a directory-visit cap).

title: fix(web): clone copy/verify buffers every checked-out file whole to hash it — copyCheckout and checkoutMatches readFile each file with no streaming hash or size bound (probe: 256 MiB repo file → +279 MiB server RSS)

body:
## Summary

Cloning a repository through the managed git network operations buffers **every checked-out file whole in server memory — twice on the paths that verify the copy** — just to compute its SHA-256 digest. `copyCheckout` copies each file with `copyFile` (which does not buffer), but then reads the entire destination file back with `readFile` to hash it; `checkoutMatches` later reads the entire file again the same way. There is no size threshold and no streaming hash anywhere in the module. A repository containing one large file — a model weight, a video, a database dump, a vendored binary — spikes the managed server's memory by at least the file's size during an otherwise routine clone, and a multi-GB file can OOM the server outright.

## Evidence (main `6e6d5e5fb`)

- **Digest helper takes a whole buffer** — `packages/web/server/lib/git/network-operations.js:104`: `contentDigest = (value) => crypto.createHash('sha256').update(value)...`. Callers must materialise the full contents before hashing.
- **Copy path reads every file whole** — `network-operations.js:1911-1918` (`copyCheckout`, file branch): inside the `copyFile` mutation's completion callback, `contentDigest: contentDigest(await fsImpl.readFile(destinationPath))`. `sourceStats` is already in hand at that point, but no size is consulted and no cap exists.
- **Verify path reads every file whole again** — `network-operations.js:1943` (`checkoutMatches`): `contentDigest(await fsImpl.readFile(entryPath)) !== entry.contentDigest`. `checkoutMatches` is the ownership verifier used when a retained checkout is quarantined/cleaned (`:2118`), so a retained large checkout is re-buffered on cleanup checks too.
- **Reachable from a normal clone** — `executeClone` (`:1990`) runs `git clone --no-checkout`, `checkout --force`, hydration, then `copyCheckout(plan.temporaryDirectory, plan.destination, ...)` at `:2060`. Every regular file in the hydrated checkout — working-tree files, not just `.git` objects — goes through the whole-file digest read.
- **Contrast in the same codebase** — the post-checkout hook reader in `git/service.js:1466-1478` judges `stat.size` against a 1 MiB cap on an opened handle before reading; the bounded file-read primitive (design #1254, phase 1 #1256) exists precisely so callers hash/read without buffering whole files. The clone copy path uses neither pattern.

## Reproduction (laptop probe vs the real module, main `6e6d5e5fb`)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-clone-digest-20261102/probe.mjs` (laptop) — drives the real `createNetworkOperations` exactly as the module's own scale test does (`network-operations.test.js`, "clones a regular repository at scale"): `service.plan({operation:'clone', transportMode:'system', unverifiedConfirmed:true})` + `service.execute(...)` against a local fixture repository, with peak RSS sampled every 10 ms.

```
{"sizeMiB":0,   "state":"succeeded", "baselineMiB":63.7, "peakMiB":71.5,  "peakDeltaMiB":7.8}
{"sizeMiB":256, "state":"succeeded", "baselineMiB":65.3, "peakMiB":343.9, "peakDeltaMiB":278.6, "destBigBytes":268435456}
```

Control clone (README only): peak RSS +7.8 MiB. Same clone with one 256 MiB incompressible file committed: peak RSS **+278.6 MiB** — the whole file (plus overhead) held in memory by the digest read — while the clone itself succeeds and the destination file is byte-complete (268,435,456 bytes). Memory cost scales linearly with the largest file in the repo; nothing in the path bounds it.

## Why it matters

Clone is a first-run, user-facing operation, and repository contents are not trusted input: public and third-party repos routinely carry files of hundreds of MB or more. The managed server is a long-lived process serving the whole UI; a single clone of such a repo can spike it by gigabytes or kill it mid-operation, taking every session with it. The digest's purpose — proving the copied bytes are the bytes that were checked — does not require holding them all at once: a streamed hash over the already-open copy, or hashing while copying, preserves the guarantee at O(1) memory.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Clone copy/verify digests are computed without buffering a whole file: stream the file through the hash (e.g. `createReadStream` + `hash.update` per chunk, or hash during the copy), in both `copyCheckout` (`:1916`) and `checkoutMatches` (`:1943`).
- [ ] Digest values for unchanged files are byte-identical to today's whole-buffer SHA-256 (`base64url`), so existing `copiedEntries` snapshots and retained-checkout verification keep matching.
- [ ] Clone behaviour is otherwise unchanged: ownership/identity checks, `checkoutMatches` semantics, cancellation/deadline handling (`awaitPhase`/`awaitMutation` wrapping preserved or equivalently applied to the streamed read), and the success/partial result shapes.
- [ ] A test in `network-operations.test.js` clones a repository containing a file well above a small threshold (tens of MB is enough with a memory or read-size assertion, or a fake `fsImpl` that fails on any whole-file `readFile` of a large file) and passes with the streamed implementation; the existing clone-at-scale tests still pass.

Found by: new-issue-creator-openchamber, 2026-11-02 run. Deduped against open + recently closed issues: `gh issue` search for clone / copyCheckout / contentDigest / network-operations returns no filing for this path (#715 covers skill-install copy traversal, #1103 skills-catalog reads, #1272 file-diff git show — different code). The stat-gated hook read in `git/service.js` was checked and is capped; it is not part of this filing.

## Summary

`loadSessionTitleTurns` in `packages/ui/src/sync/session-title-context.ts` is a fifth UI cursor walk with the exact shape filed in #1320 — a repeated-cursor guard but **no page cap** — and it is not one of the four walks #1320 lists. An OpenCode server that keeps returning a fresh cursor (buggy build, proxy rewiring cursors, or a hostile local/remote endpoint) makes the AI session-rename path loop indefinitely, fetching and committing one history page after another, with no deadline on the caller side.

This is a residual of #1320 in the same sense as earlier residuals (#1304 of its sibling path, #1277 of #1133): the class was filed, and this walk in a separate file was missed.

## Evidence (main `82a92eabe`)

- **`loadSessionTitleTurns`** — `packages/ui/src/sync/session-title-context.ts:20-31`. The `while (true)` loop exits only when `collectSessionTitleTurns(...)` reaches 3 turns, when `state.complete` is true, or when the cursor is missing/repeated (`:29` throws "Session history pagination made no progress"). There is no page counter and no cap. Each iteration awaits `loader.loadOlder(target)` (`:30`), which fetches a page and commits it into the retained session history — so renderer memory grows with every page, not just CPU/network.
- **Caller has no deadline** — the sole caller is the AI-rename prepare step, `packages/ui/src/sync/use-session-ai-rename.ts:32`. Its signal comes from `runSessionTitleGeneration` (`packages/ui/src/sync/session-title-generation.ts:52-70`), whose `AbortController` is aborted only on a runtime-endpoint change or an explicit manual-save cancellation — there is no timeout. A looping walk therefore runs until the user navigates away / the runtime switches.
- **#1320 does not cover it** — #1320 lists `listGlobalSessionPages`, `SessionMessageLoader.loadComplete`, the `loadOlderPage` turn-alignment loop, and `findSessionMessageById`. `session-title-context.ts` is a separate walk in its own file, driving the loader from outside, and appears nowhere in #1320's evidence, scope, or acceptance criteria.
- **House pattern** — comparable walks carry an explicit page cap: server session-activity `CHILDREN_MAX_PAGES = 8`, session-assist `MAX_PAGES = 8`, GitHub branches `GITHUB_BRANCH_MAX_PAGES = 20` (#1313). #1320 asks for the same on its four UI walks.
- **Existing tests pin only terminating cases** — `packages/ui/src/lib/sessionTitle.test.ts` covers a 2-page walk reaching 3 turns, a failed loader, and a retry after failure. Nothing covers ever-new cursors.

## Reproduction (laptop probe vs the real module, main `82a92eabe`)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-title-cursor-20261102/` (laptop worktree of the repo at `82a92eabe`) — a `bun test` case importing the real `loadSessionTitleTurns` with a fake loader in the shape `sessionTitle.test.ts` itself uses: every `loadOlder` returns a brand-new cursor, never `complete`, and records never yield a turn. The walk called `loadOlder` 20,000 times and only ended because the probe dropped the cursor at that point (which surfaces as the existing no-progress error):

```
PROBE loadOlderCalls=20000 elapsedMs=80 rssMB=58.9 endError=Session history pagination made no progress
(pass) probe: ever-new cursor > loadSessionTitleTurns has no page cap
```

20,000 pages is ~2,500× the house page-cap pattern (8 pages), for a feature that only needs the newest 3 completed turns.

## Why it matters

AI rename is a user-facing action: the user clicks rename and waits. With a looping or hostile endpoint (the UI also connects to remote/relayed servers, not only a trusted loopback build), the rename spinner never resolves, the renderer keeps fetching and retaining history pages without bound, and no error is ever surfaced. The repeated-cursor guard proves the codebase already treats pathological cursors as a real failure mode; ever-new cursors are the same failure with a fresh string.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `loadSessionTitleTurns` stops after a named page cap in the house style (`MAX_PAGES`-style constant; triage pins the value — it must sit far above the pages a legitimate 3-turn search could need, as a pathology guard, not a product limit).
- [ ] Hitting the cap has explicit behaviour, never a silent partial result presented as complete: either reject with a "pagination exceeded" style error like the existing no-progress error, or return the turns collected so far only if triage decides a partial title is acceptable — the choice must be documented in the code/PR.
- [ ] In-cap behaviour is unchanged: 3-turn early stop, `complete` stop, generation/status checks, abort-signal handling, and the existing repeated-cursor/no-progress error all keep working.
- [ ] A test in `sessionTitle.test.ts` (or a new `session-title-context` test) pins the ever-new-cursor case: a loader that always returns a fresh cursor stops at the cap instead of looping.

Deduped against open + recently closed issues: #1320 (four UI walks — this file not among them), #1317 (server control-service walks, open), #1315 (message-search indexer, open), #1313 (GitHub branches, closed); `gh issue` search for `loadSessionTitleTurns` / `session-title-context` / `extendWindow` returns no filing for this walk.

## Summary

Four cursor walks in `packages/ui` guard against a *repeated* cursor but have **no page cap**, so an OpenCode server that keeps returning a fresh `cursor.next` (buggy build, proxy rewiring cursors, or a hostile local endpoint) makes each walk loop indefinitely. This is the UI twin of open issue #1317 (the same shape in the web control service) and open issue #1315 (the indexer, which had neither guard) — those cover `packages/web/server`; no issue covers the UI walks.

## Evidence (main `d0bb42f0d`)

1. **`listGlobalSessionPages`** — `packages/ui/src/stores/globalSessions.ts:55`, walk at `:70-114`. The only exits are no next cursor, `next === cursor`, or a page that added no new session ids (`:111`). It accumulates every accepted record into `all` (`:99-105`) and streams each page to `onPage`, so an ever-new-cursor server grows renderer memory without bound on the global session bootstrap path (callers: `useGlobalSessionsStore`, `sync-context`).
2. **`SessionMessageLoader.loadComplete`** — `packages/ui/src/sync/session-message-loader.ts:644`, loop at `:653-664`. Guarded only by `visitedCursors` (`:652-661`); each iteration commits another page of history into the store via `loadOlderPage(..., "complete")`. Used by session export (`useSessionMessageRecordsForExport`, `packages/ui/src/sync/use-sync.ts:284`): an ever-new cursor hangs the export forever while the retained history grows.
3. **`loadOlderPage` turn-alignment loop** — `packages/ui/src/sync/session-message-loader.ts:610-622`. The `HISTORY_TURN_ALIGNMENT_EXTRA_PAGES = 2` bound (`:30`) only breaks the loop when the accumulated batch already holds a user message (`:613`); a batch with no user prompt at all keeps reading — the code comment at `:605-609` states this is unbounded by design — accumulating `[...older.session, ...page.session]` in memory per interactive scroll step, guarded only against a repeated cursor (`:614`).
4. **`findSessionMessageById`** — `packages/ui/src/sync/session-actions.ts:543-555`. `for (;;)` with a `seenCursors` guard (`:551`) and no page cap; it discards each page, so the failure mode is an infinite fetch loop (renderer CPU/network) on the revert path (`revertToMessage`, `:2959`) when the target message is never found and cursors never repeat.

## House pattern these break

Every comparable walk elsewhere in this repo carries an explicit page cap:

- Server session-activity children walk: `CHILDREN_MAX_PAGES = 8` (`packages/web/server/lib/opencode/session-activity.js:19`), returning `null` (unknown) when the cap is hit instead of spinning.
- Session-assist context walk: `MAX_PAGES = 8` (`packages/web/server/lib/session-assist/context.js:3`), with the same repeated-cursor guard these UI walks have.
- GitHub branch pagination: `GITHUB_BRANCH_MAX_PAGES = 20` (landed in #1313/#1314).
- Open issue #1317 asks for the same cap on the two server control-service walks.

Existing UI tests pin only the terminating cases: `globalSessions.test.ts` covers normal and repeated/empty termination, `session-message-loader.test.ts:281` covers the repeated-cursor "made no progress" error for `loadComplete`. Nothing covers ever-new cursors for any of the four walks.

## Reproduction (laptop probe vs the real module, main `d0bb42f0d`)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-ui-cursor-cap-20261102/` (laptop worktree of the repo at `d0bb42f0d`) — a `bun test` case importing the real `listGlobalSessionPages` with an injected lister that always returns a full page of two brand-new sessions and a brand-new `cursor.next`. The probe itself had to drop the cursor at page 50,000 to end the walk; the walk never decided to stop:

```
PROBE calls=50000 sessions=100000 streamed=100000 elapsedMs=592 rssMB=105.7
```

50,000 pages is ~6,250× the house page-cap pattern (8 pages). Walks 2–4 share the exact guard-without-cap shape and were verified by code reading above.

## Why it matters

These walks run in the renderer on core paths — global session bootstrap, session export, history scrolling, and message revert. A looping or hostile local OpenCode endpoint (the UI also connects to remote/relayed servers, not only a trusted loopback build) turns any of them into an unbounded memory/CPU/network loop with no error surfaced to the user: the bootstrap spinner, export, scroll, or revert simply never completes. The repeated-cursor guard proves the codebase already treats pathological cursors as a real failure mode; ever-new cursors are the same failure with a fresh string.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Each of the four walks stops after a named page cap (per-walk constants in the house style of `CHILDREN_MAX_PAGES`/`MAX_PAGES`; triage pins the values — they must sit far above any legitimate history/list size, as a pathology guard, not a product limit).
- [ ] Hitting the cap has explicit, per-caller behaviour, never a silent partial result presented as complete: `listGlobalSessionPages` surfaces an error or a clearly-marked partial result to its store callers; `loadComplete` rejects with a "pagination exceeded" style error like its existing no-progress error; the alignment loop commits what it has (the turn simply starts mid-turn, as it already can at the extra-pages bound); `findSessionMessageById` returns `null` (target not found within the bounded walk).
- [ ] In-cap behaviour is unchanged: page order, dedup by session/message id, `onPage` streaming, retry behaviour in `listGlobalSessionPages`, and the existing repeated-cursor/no-progress errors all keep working.
- [ ] Tests pin the ever-new-cursor case for each walk: `globalSessions.test.ts` (lister that always returns a fresh cursor stops at the cap), `session-message-loader.test.ts` (`loadComplete` and the alignment loop), and a `session-actions` revert test or an extracted-helper test for `findSessionMessageById`.

Deduped against open + recently closed issues: #1317 (server control service walks, open), #1315 (message-search indexer, open), #1313 (GitHub branches, closed) — no issue covers the `packages/ui` walks; `gh issue search` for `listGlobalSessionPages` and `session-message-loader` returns no filing for this.

## Summary

Two cursor walks in the OpenChamber control service (`packages/web/server/lib/openchamber-control/service.js`) guard against a *repeated* cursor but have **no page cap**, so an OpenCode server that keeps returning a fresh `cursor.next` (buggy build, proxy rewiring cursors, or a hostile local endpoint) makes the walk loop indefinitely — accumulating every page in memory — until V8 kills it when the seen-cursor `Set` itself overflows at 2^24 entries.

## Evidence (main `d0bb42f0d`)

- `service.js:624` `sessionMessages(client, sessionID, role, limit)` — the `for (;;)` walk at :633-650 breaks only on an empty page, a missing `cursor.next`, or a repeated cursor. When `limit === undefined` there is no early stop, and `collected.push(...raw)` at :640 buffers every record of every page in memory.
- Reachable with `limit === undefined` from the agent-facing action: `service.js:1327-1328` — `session.messages` with `input.all === true` calls `sessionMessages(client, sessionID, role, undefined)`.
- `service.js:681` `resolveSessionDirectory(sessionID)` — the same shape over `client.session.list` (:686-697): no page cap, and it does not even break on an empty page (only on a missing/repeated cursor or finding the session). It runs on the session-scoped path for many control actions (`service.js:852`, `:1108`, `:1223`, `:1239`, `:1261`).
- Contrast inside the same file: the `session.list` walk at `service.js:1272-1299` stops as soon as `collected.length >= limit`. The message-search indexer had neither guard and was filed as #1315; these two walks have the guard but not the cap.
- Existing tests pin only the terminating cases: `service.test.js:1008-1025` covers a repeated cursor and an empty page. Nothing covers ever-new cursors.

## Reproduction (laptop probe vs the real module, main `d0bb42f0d`)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-control-cursor-cap-20261102/probe.mjs` (laptop) — builds the real `createOpenChamberControlService` with a fake client whose `message.list` always returns one text message plus a brand-new cursor (`cursor-N`), then calls `execute('session.messages', { sessionId: 'ses_1', directory: '/repo', all: true })` raced against 3 s.

Observed:

```json
{"settled":"rejected: Set maximum size exceeded","messageListCalls":16777217,"rssDeltaMB":3476}
```

The call never returned a result: it made **16,777,217** `message.list` calls and grew RSS by **+3,476 MB** before V8 threw `Set maximum size exceeded` from the `seenCursors` guard itself. Against a real server each iteration is also an HTTP round trip, so the practical shape is an unbounded request loop plus unbounded memory growth in the managed server.

## Why it matters

`session.messages` with `all: true` is an agent-facing control action: an agent (or a wedged OpenCode build) triggers it and the OpenChamber server process — the same process serving the UI and routing — spins on upstream requests while its heap grows by gigabytes. `resolveSessionDirectory` sits in front of ordinary session actions, so the same pathological cursor behaviour can wedge routine control calls, not just history reads.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `sessionMessages` stops after an explicit named page cap (a module constant, sized generously above any legitimate history — compare the indexer's cap in #1315) and returns the messages collected so far instead of looping; the bounded-`limit` path is unchanged.
- [ ] `resolveSessionDirectory` gets the same page cap (returning `null` past it, matching its existing not-found result), and also stops on an empty page.
- [ ] Regression coverage in `service.test.js`: a fake client that always returns a fresh cursor makes `session.messages` with `all: true` terminate with a bounded number of `message.list` calls (assert the call count, not just the result), and the directory-resolution walk terminates the same way; the existing repeated-cursor and empty-page tests still pass.
- [ ] The cap is a named constant with a comment saying what happens past it (partial history / unresolved directory), in the style of the neighbouring `MESSAGE_PAGE_LIMIT`.

## Scope notes

- Sibling, not duplicate: #1315 is the message-search indexer (`lib/message-search/`), a different module with neither guard nor cap; this issue is the control service, which has the guard but no cap. The two fixes should use the same pattern.
- Out of scope: the `session.list` walk at `service.js:1272-1299` (already stops at its limit) and the bounded response-body reads (covered by #1285/#1291).

body:
## Problem

The message-search indexer walks OpenCode cursor pagination in two loops with no repeated-cursor guard and no page cap. A server (or proxy) that keeps answering full pages with the same `cursor.next` makes both loops run forever — each individual read has the 5 s deadline from #807, but the loop as a whole has no bound.

`packages/web/server/lib/message-search/indexer.js` (main `b536d0b2b`):

1. Per-session message walk, `syncSession` at `:213-260`:
```js
for (;;) {
  page = messagePageSchema.parse(await readWithDeadline((options) => client.message.list({
    sessionID: sessionId, limit: pageSize, type: role,
    ...(cursor ? { cursor } : { order: 'asc' }),
  }, options)));
  // ...rows collected...
  if (!next || records.length < pageSize) break;
  cursor = next;
}
```
The only exits are "no next cursor" or "short page". There is no check that `next` differs from the cursor just used, and no maximum page count.

2. Backfill session-list walk, `startBackfill` at `:325-333`:
```js
for (;;) {
  const page = sessionPageSchema.parse(await readWithDeadline((options) => client.session.list({ parentID: null, limit: SESSION_PAGE_SIZE, ...(cursor ? { cursor } : { order: 'desc' }) }, options)));
  // ...sessions collected into `listed`...
  if (!next || page.data.length < SESSION_PAGE_SIZE) break;
  cursor = next;
}
```
Same shape: no repeated-cursor guard, no page cap. Because the queueing code sits after the loop, a looping backfill never queues anything and `backfill` state never advances.

## House pattern it breaks

Every other cursor walk in this codebase guards against exactly this:

- UI global session list: `if (!next || next === cursor || accepted.length === 0) break;` (`packages/ui/src/stores/globalSessions.ts:111`)
- OpenChamber control service: `seenCursors` set checked in both `sessionMessages` (`packages/web/server/lib/openchamber-control/service.js:640`) and `resolveSessionDirectory` (`:695`), with a regression test for the looped-cursor case (`service.test.js:1015`)
- UI session message loader: `visitedCursors` set, throws "pagination made no progress" (`packages/ui/src/sync/session-message-loader.ts:653-665`)
- Server page-number paginations are capped by named constants (GitLab `COLLECTION_MAX_PAGES = 20`, Linear `MAX_PAGES = 20`, session children `CHILDREN_MAX_PAGES = 8`, spaces `SESSION_MAX_PAGES = 10`; the GitHub branches loop is tracked separately in #1313)

The indexer is the remaining unguarded walker.

## Verification (this run, laptop probe vs the real module)

Probe: laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-indexer-cursor-loop-20261102/probe2.mjs` — imports the real `createMessageSearchIndexer` from the laptop clone at the same main (`b536d0b2b`, indexer.js sha256 `80443137…` identical on both clones), with an in-memory stub store and a fake OpenCode client whose reads yield 1 ms (like real network I/O) and always answer a full page with the same next cursor (`loop-cursor`).

- Case A (backfill): `session.list` was called **1,593 times in 3 s**; after 3 s the backfill state was still `{state: "idle", total: 0, done: 0, queued: 0}` — the walk never finished, so no session was ever queued for indexing.
- Case B (per-session sync): `message.list` (user role) was called **1,345 times in 3 s** and `syncSession` never settled. Inside `drain()` (`indexer.js:280-297`) one such sync blocks the drain loop, so every later live/backfill session waits behind it.
- A zero-latency variant of the same probe (`probe.mjs`) never even reached its 3 s timer: with instantly-resolving reads the loop spins on microtasks and starves the event loop's timers entirely.

Control behavior is covered by the existing fake in `indexer.test.js`, whose pages advance the cursor and terminate — normal finite pagination works today and must keep working.

## Why it matters

- Message search is a background indexer: a wedged backfill silently means search never catches up (status stays `idle` with nothing queued), and a wedged live sync stalls the single drain loop for all sessions.
- The trigger does not require a hostile server: any OpenCode/proxy bug or version skew that repeats a cursor on a full page (the exact failure the sibling guards were written for) turns a 5 s-per-read deadline into an infinite, CPU- and request-burning loop.
- #807 fixed the per-read deadline for this same module; this is the loop-level residual it did not cover.

## Acceptance criteria

- Both walks terminate on a repeated/unchanged cursor: the message walk and the backfill session-list walk stop (with a `logger.warn` naming the session/role or the backfill, matching the module's existing warning style) when `next` equals a cursor already used in that walk.
- Both walks are also bounded by a named page cap in the house order (a named constant in `indexer.js`, e.g. aligned with the existing page-size constants), so even an endless stream of *distinct* cursors cannot loop forever; hitting the cap logs a warning and treats the walk as complete-with-what-was-read where that is safe (for backfill: only replace the known-session set when the list actually completed — the existing "a failed page is not an empty list" rule at `indexer.js:313-317` must not be weakened into deleting sessions after a capped partial list).
- A wedged sync cannot block the drain forever: after the fix, `syncSession` for a looping-cursor session settles (returns or throws) and `drain()` proceeds to the next queued session.
- Regression tests in `indexer.test.js` style: (a) a fake whose `message.list` always returns a full page with the same cursor — sync completes/settles with a bounded number of calls; (b) a fake whose `session.list` does the same — backfill finishes and queues the sessions it did read; (c) existing multi-page tests still pass unchanged.
- No change to the per-read deadline (#807), the revert/start-over logic, or what gets indexed — pagination bounds only.

body:
## Problem

`GET /api/source-control/github/repo/branches` paginates the GitHub branch list with no page cap, no total cap, and no deadline — it is the only uncapped pagination loop in the web server.

`packages/web/server/lib/github/routes.js:2090-2104` (main `b536d0b2b`):

```js
const branches = [];
let page = 1;
while (true) {
  const response = await octokit.rest.repos.listBranches({ owner: selectedRepo.owner, repo: selectedRepo.repo, per_page: 100, page });
  const payload = requireProviderArray(response?.data, 'GitHub returned an invalid branch list');
  if (payload.length === 0) break;
  for (const branch of payload) { /* ... */ branches.push(branch.name); }
  if (payload.length < 100) break;
  page++;
}
return res.json({ branches });
```

The loop breaks only when a page comes back empty or short. Every result is accumulated in memory and nothing is answered until the last page, so the request's duration, memory, and GitHub API consumption are all proportional to the repository's branch count with no bound at all.

## House pattern it breaks

Every sibling pagination in this codebase is capped:

- GitLab collections: `COLLECTION_MAX_PAGES = 20` (`packages/web/server/lib/gitlab/resources.js:22`), most reads `maxPages: 1`
- Linear teams: `MAX_PAGES = 20` (`packages/web/server/lib/linear/teams.js:14`)
- Session children: `CHILDREN_MAX_PAGES = 8` (`packages/web/server/lib/opencode/session-activity.js:19`)
- Spaces session list: `SESSION_MAX_PAGES = 10` (`packages/web/server/lib/spaces/host.js:49`)
- Same file, check-run annotations: `for (let page = 1; page <= 3; page += 1)` (`packages/web/server/lib/github/routes.js:3206`)

## Verification (this run, laptop probe vs the real route)

Probe: laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-branches-pagination-20261102/probe.mjs` — real `registerGitHubRoutes` + real auth storage, global `fetch` stubbed exactly as in `routes.auth.test.js`, fake GitHub endpoint with a 20 ms/page delay.

- Control (finite repo, 2 full pages + one short page): `200`, 250 branches, exactly 3 `listBranches` calls — normal behavior confirmed.
- Always-full pages (every page returns 100 branches): after 6 s the route had fetched **255 pages** (25,500 branch names accumulated), the request was **still unresolved**, and RSS had grown **+27.6 MiB** and kept growing. No cap at or below the GitLab house cap (20 pages) ever fired; the probe had to abort the request itself.

Real-world shape: large repositories legitimately carry thousands of branches, so even a well-behaved GitHub makes this route issue hundreds of sequential API calls before answering anything; a GitHub Enterprise / proxy endpoint that keeps returning full pages makes it loop indefinitely, burning the account's rate limit the whole time.

## Why it matters

- One branch-picker request against a big repo can hold a server request slot and consume GitHub rate limit for minutes, with the UI showing nothing until every page lands.
- The accumulated array is unbounded memory growth driven by a remote endpoint's answers.
- It is a lone exception to a cap discipline the rest of the server already follows, so it will keep being copied as the "example" pagination if left.

## Acceptance criteria

- The branches loop stops at a named page/total cap in line with the house pattern (e.g. GitLab's `COLLECTION_MAX_PAGES = 20` order: 20 pages × 100 = 2,000 branches), or is otherwise bounded by a named limit plus a deadline.
- When the cap is hit, the route's behavior is explicit and tested: either it returns the branches gathered so far (with the truncation visible to the caller, e.g. a flag) or it fails with a clear error — silently returning a partial list as if complete is not acceptable if the UI treats it as authoritative; the chosen behavior is documented on this issue.
- Repos at or below the cap behave exactly as today (all branches, same response shape unless the truncation flag design adds an optional field).
- Regression test in `routes.auth.test.js` style: a stubbed endpoint that always returns full pages terminates at the cap with the documented behavior; a finite multi-page repo still returns all its branches.
- No change to the route's auth/binding/network validation (`validateReadContext`, exact-account, fork-network constraint) — pagination bound only.

## Problem

The direct-mode APNs send (self-hoster path: relay disabled + `OPENCHAMBER_APNS_*` set) accumulates the HTTP/2 response body with no byte cap. Only the 30 s wall-clock deadline bounds it — a deadline bounds time, not bytes.

`packages/web/server/lib/notifications/apns-runtime.js` (main `36422fb50`):

- `:485` `let responseBody = '';`
- `:490-492` `req.on('data', (chunk) => { responseBody += chunk; });` — unbounded string concatenation, no size check, no destroy on overflow
- `:503` the whole accumulated string is `JSON.parse`d on `end`, only to read `.reason`

The sibling relay path in the same file was capped by #1304: `APNS_RELAY_RESPONSE_MAX_BYTES = 1 MiB` (`:41`) read via `readBoundedResponseText` (`:585`), with the code comment at `:579` stating exactly this rationale ("deadline bounds time, not bytes"). The direct path was not given the same treatment. APNs error bodies are tiny JSON documents (`{"reason": "..."}`); nothing in the direct path needs an unbounded buffer.

## Verification (this run)

Laptop probe against the real module (`createApnsRuntime` with the test-suite's fake-`http2` dependency pattern, relay disabled, real P-256 key): the fake APNs stream answered status 400 with a 64 MiB valid-JSON body (`{"reason":"BadDeviceToken"}` + whitespace padding). The send resolved normally after buffering the entire body — process RSS rose 55 MiB → 184 MiB (+129 MiB). Probe: laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-apns-direct-cap-20261102/probe.mjs`.

Dedup: #798 (deadlines), #992 (stream-close settle), #993/#1304 (relay body) cover the relay path and the direct path's timing/settle behaviour; no open or closed issue covers a byte cap on the direct-mode response body.

## Why it matters

Direct mode is the fallback for self-hosters who disable the relay. A misbehaving or compromised endpoint/proxy in that path — or any peer that can answer the HTTP/2 session — can grow server memory without limit inside the deadline window, once per token in the fanout. The relay sibling proves the intended contract: read it bounded, or not at all.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Direct-mode response body accumulation is bounded by a named cap of the same order as `APNS_RELAY_RESPONSE_MAX_BYTES` (1 MiB); on overflow the request is destroyed/settled through the existing terminal handlers and the send resolves without parsing a partial body as authoritative.
- [ ] Behaviour for well-formed small bodies is unchanged: 200 resolves silently; dead-token reasons (410 / `DEAD_TOKEN_REASONS`) still trigger token removal; other errors still warn with status + reason.
- [ ] Regression test in `apns-runtime.test.js` style: an over-cap response body settles the send without unbounded buffering (e.g. fake stream emitting >cap bytes; assert resolve + no dead-token removal from a truncated reason).
- [ ] No change to the relay path, JWT signing, or the 30 s direct deadline.

body:
## Problem

#931 capped the Tool Output dialog's Mermaid **remote-URL** load (deadline + 1 MiB streaming cap, `toolOutputDialogMermaid.ts`), and its body called the sibling `file://` branch "safer" because it goes through the user's own server. That branch was never capped, and the server route it reads from serves far more than a Mermaid source should ever be:

- `packages/ui/src/components/chat/message/ToolOutputDialog.tsx:703-711` (current main `b16d37041`) — the `file://` branch does `runtimeFetch('/api/fs/raw', { query: { path: normalizedPath } }).then((response) => … return response.text())`. No byte cap, no `signal`: the load is not wired to `remoteLoadAbortRef`, so superseding or closing the dialog does not cancel it either (the remote branch passes an `AbortController` signal through `getMermaidRemoteSourcePromise`).
- `packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.js:214,1532-1540` — `/api/fs/raw` rejects only files over `MAX_SERVE_BYTES` = 100 MiB, and otherwise reads and returns the whole file. So this branch buffers up to **100 MiB** into the renderer as a UTF-8 string (plus the Mermaid parse on top) — 100× the 1 MiB cap the remote branch enforces on the same dialog (`MERMAID_REMOTE_MAX_BYTES`, `toolOutputDialogMermaid.ts:45`).
- The path comes from a `file://` reference in tool output, so the referenced file is not necessarily a small hand-written diagram: any readable local file up to 100 MiB (a log, a data dump, a binary) that a tool output points at is buffered whole when the user opens the diagram preview.

## Why it matters

Same failure class as #931 and #1275 (guest binary editor judged its 20 MB cap only after buffering): a size judgement that happens after — or never, here — does not bound renderer memory. The inconsistency is the tell: the dialog's three source branches are `data:` (inline, bounded by the message), remote http(s) (1 MiB cap + 15 s deadline), and local file (no cap, no deadline, no abort). The local branch is the only unbounded one left.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The `file://` branch reads the `/api/fs/raw` body through a bounded reader with an explicit named cap consistent with the remote branch (1 MiB, `MERMAID_REMOTE_MAX_BYTES`, or a documented local-source cap of the same order); an over-cap file fails with the existing `loadFailed` error state instead of buffering whole.
- [ ] The file-branch fetch carries the load's abort signal (supersede/close cancels it), like the remote branch.
- [ ] Regression tests (extending `ToolOutputDialog.test.ts` / the mermaid loader tests): an over-cap local file reaches the error state without being fully buffered, and an at-cap file renders byte-identically to today.
- [ ] No behaviour change for `data:`, remote http(s), or inline `target.source` loads, and no change to `/api/fs/raw` itself (other consumers legitimately serve up to 100 MiB).

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for `mermaid` (2026-11-02): only #931 (closed — remote-URL branch only; its acceptance criteria explicitly left `file://` behaviour unchanged) and #1264 (unrelated catalog fetches). No open or closed issue covers the `file://` branch read.

Filed by new-issue-creator-openchamber, run 2026-11-02 00:50 CST. Verified this run by reading both sides of the read on current main `b16d37041`: the uncapped `response.text()` at `ToolOutputDialog.tsx:709` and the 100 MiB serve gate at `fs/routes.js:1532`.

title: project-icon discover: stat→readFile race can buffer an unbounded favicon before the 5 MiB check

labels.name: task/triage

body:
## Finding (from a PR review comment, never addressed)

The project-icon discover route's 5 MiB size gate is a check-then-read race: it stats the selected favicon and then reads it through a second, independent path resolution, so the size it checked is not the size it buffers.

Reviewer **coderabbitai[bot]** (CodeRabbit, **Major** · Stability & Availability), 2026-10-31T17:18:02Z, on PR #1056, `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/project-icon-routes.js:418`:
https://github.com/developing-today/openchamber/pull/1056#discussion_r4432579193

> "Read the selected favicon through a bounded file handle. `stat(selected.path)` and `readFile(selected.path)` resolve the path independently. If a user or build process replaces or grows the favicon after `stat`, `readFile` can buffer the new file before the length check rejects it. Open the file once, inspect its size through the handle, and read no more than `projectIconMaxBytes + 1` bytes. Close the handle in all paths. Preserve the empty-file rejection and the 5 MiB limit behavior."

Source PR: https://github.com/developing-today/openchamber/pull/1056 — "fix(web): stat-gate the project-icon discover read at 5 MiB (#1053)"

## No-response evidence

- The CodeRabbit review thread is **unresolved** (GraphQL `reviewThreads` checked 2026-11-02) and has **no replies** — the single comment in the thread is the finding itself.
- No commit on PR #1056 after the comment addressed it.
- PR #1056 was closed unmerged as a duplicate of PR #1055, which merged the same stat-gate fix for issue #1053 — so the flagged pattern is exactly the code that landed on main, and the race came with it. Issue #1053 is closed; no open issue tracks this race (searched 2026-11-02: "project-icon", "favicon", "stat-gate", "bounded file handle", "projectIconMaxBytes", "1056").

## Still live on current main (verified 2026-11-02)

`packages/web/server/lib/opencode/project-icon-routes.js` (blob `5ce95cb3df77b9835095bd7865a120975fa2c4bc`, identical in the local clone and via the GitHub contents API):

- L415: `const stats = await fsPromises.stat(selected.path);` — size checked on the path
- L419: rejects when `stats.size > projectIconMaxBytes`
- L423: `const bytes = await fsPromises.readFile(selected.path);` — the path is resolved again and the **whole file is buffered**
- L427: the length check runs only after that unbounded buffer exists

A favicon replaced or grown between L415 and L423 is therefore read into server memory without bound before any check can reject it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The discover route opens the selected favicon once and reads it through that handle: size inspected via the handle, at most `projectIconMaxBytes + 1` bytes read, handle closed on every path.
- [ ] Existing behavior preserved: empty discovered icons rejected (400), icons over 5 MiB rejected (400), supported-format handling unchanged.
- [ ] Regression coverage: a test in which the file grows or is replaced after the size check (or an fs fake whose stat and read disagree) proves the read stays bounded.
- [ ] Or: resolve by a documented decision on this issue explaining why the race is acceptable.

body:
## Problem

The APNs relay send reads the relay's response body whole with no byte cap: `sendViaRelay` in `packages/web/server/lib/notifications/apns-runtime.js:573` does `await res.json()`, bounded only by the 10 s deadline (`APNS_RELAY_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS`, :36, via `createTimeoutSignal`). The endpoint is a remote server — the default relay at `https://api.openchamber.dev/v1/push/send` (:26), overridable via `OPENCHAMBER_PUSH_RELAY_URL` — and this runs in the long-lived web server on every push fanout.

A deadline bounds time, not memory: a fast, misbehaving, or compromised relay response path can deliver arbitrarily many bytes inside 10 s, and `res.json()` buffers all of them before the code picks the only thing it needs — the small `results` array of `{ token, drop }` entries (:582-587). Prior APNs work gave this path its deadlines (#798) and fixed the body-read abort semantics so a deadline abort during `res.json()` is rethrown rather than swallowed as `null` (#993) — neither change bounds the bytes.

## Evidence (verified on main f61875ebb, this run)

- Code read: `apns-runtime.js:561-593` — the send fetch carries the timeout signal; the body read at :573 is a bare `res.json()` with no size check before, during, or after. No bounded reader is used in the module for this read.
- Laptop probe against the real module (byte-identical copy of main, md5-verified; probe at `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-apns-relay-cap-20261101/` on the laptop): with `fetch` stubbed per the module's own test harness, the relay send answered a valid 64 MiB JSON body (`results` with one `drop: true` entry + an ignored padding field). The send completed normally — the whole body was parsed — and process RSS grew +257 MiB during the read.
- The consumed payload is tiny by construction: only `data.results[].drop === true` tokens are acted on (:582-587); a legitimate relay answer for at most 100 tokens (:546, `deviceTokens.slice(0, 100)`) is a few KB at most.

## Why it matters

This is the same deadline-only pattern the fleet has been closing across the server (#1292 GitHub device-flow, #1293 Linear GraphQL). The relay path was missed because its earlier issues were about deadlines and abort semantics, not bytes. The fix is small and local once triage confirms the cap value (suggested 1 MiB, the fleet's auth/small-JSON precedent — two orders of magnitude above any legitimate relay answer) and preserves the #993 contract exactly: a deadline abort during the bounded read still rethrows as a transport failure, and only a malformed (or over-cap) body keeps the null fallback that drops no tokens.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `sendViaRelay` reads the relay response body through a bounded reader (e.g. `readBoundedResponseJson`/`readBoundedResponseText` from `lib/shared/response-body.js`) behind a named cap constant in `apns-runtime.js`, enforced while streaming, not after buffering.
- [ ] The #993 semantics are preserved: an abort from the still-live deadline signal during the body read rethrows (outer catch reports it); a malformed or over-cap body resolves to the null fallback — no tokens dropped, no partial `results` acted on.
- [ ] In-cap behaviour unchanged: `drop: true` tokens are removed via `removeApnsTokenFromAllSessions`, non-OK statuses still only warn, and the register-token path is untouched.
- [ ] Tests: an over-cap relay response drops no tokens and does not throw into the caller; a normal response with a `drop: true` result still removes that token; a body-read deadline abort still surfaces as a request failure (the #993 regression test still passes); existing apns-runtime suites pass.
- [ ] No change to the relay URL resolution, signing, request body, timeout value, or exported signatures.

Filed by new-issue-creator-openchamber (fleet role map: developing-today/code#2131; implementation #2152). Dedup: searched open + closed for "apns relay body" — #798 (closed) added the deadlines, #993 (closed) fixed body-read abort swallowing, #1200 is a preserved-branch decision for #993's PR; no issue covers a byte cap on the relay send response read in `apns-runtime.js`.
