## Problem

The skills catalog's GitHub repo-meta fetch reads the response body whole with no byte cap: `fetchRepoMeta` in `packages/web/server/lib/skills-catalog/github-meta.js:121` does `parseMeta(await response.json())`, bounded only by the 1.5 s deadline (`FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS`, :7, applied via `AbortSignal.timeout` at :108). The endpoint is the public GitHub API (`https://api.github.com/repos/<owner/repo>`, :3) — an external response path — and this runs in the long-lived web server every time the skills catalog enriches a repo with stars / last-push data.

A deadline bounds time, not memory: a fast, misbehaving, or compromised response path can deliver arbitrarily many bytes inside 1.5 s, and `response.json()` buffers all of them before `parseMeta` picks the two fields it actually needs (`stargazers_count`, `pushed_at`). Sibling catalog reads in this codebase already made the opposite choice: the models.dev catalog caps at 16 MiB (`lib/opencode/models-metadata.js`, `MODELS_DEV_CATALOG_MAX_BYTES`), the theme catalog reads through `readBoundedResponseBytes`, and the changelog index reads through `readBoundedResponseText` behind `CHANGELOG_INDEX_MAX_BYTES`.

## Evidence (verified on main f61875ebb, this run)

- Code read: `github-meta.js:104-121` — the fetch carries only `AbortSignal.timeout(FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS)`; the body read at :121 is a bare `response.json()` with no size check before, during, or after. No bounded reader is imported in the module.
- Laptop probe against the real module (byte-identical copy of main, md5-verified; probe at `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-github-meta-cap-20261101/` on the laptop): stubbed `fetch` returned a valid 64 MiB repo-meta JSON (real fields + an ignored padding field). `fetchGitHubRepoMetas(['owner/repo'])` accepted it whole and returned `{ stars: 42, repoUpdatedAt: '2026-01-01T00:00:00Z' }`; process RSS grew +266 MiB during the read.
- The parsed payload is tiny by construction: `parseMeta` (:84-92) consumes exactly two scalar fields, so a generous cap loses nothing real.

## Why it matters

This is the same deadline-only pattern the fleet has been closing across the server (#1292 GitHub device-flow, #1293 Linear GraphQL, #1264 public catalog fetches). The repo-meta path was missed because it lives in the skills catalog rather than an auth/quota package. The fix is small and local once triage confirms the cap value (the auth-read precedent is 1 MiB; repo-meta answers are a few KB, so 1 MiB is generous) and the over-cap shape (the function's existing contract is best-effort: failures cache a null meta briefly and return null — an over-cap body should take that same path, never throw into catalog loading).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `fetchRepoMeta` reads the response body through a bounded reader (e.g. `readBoundedResponseText`/`readBoundedResponseJson` from `lib/shared/response-body.js`) behind a named cap constant in `github-meta.js`, enforced while streaming, not after buffering.
- [ ] An over-cap body follows the existing failure path: brief failure-cache entry and a `null` meta result — catalog loading is never blocked or thrown into by an oversized meta response.
- [ ] In-cap behaviour unchanged: stars / `pushed_at` extraction, success and failure cache TTLs, in-flight dedup, disk-cache persistence, and the 1.5 s deadline.
- [ ] Tests: an over-cap response resolves to the null/failure-cache path without being parsed whole; a normal repo-meta response still returns stars and `repoUpdatedAt`; existing skills-catalog suites still pass.
- [ ] No change to the endpoint, headers, timeout value, or exported function signatures.

Filed by new-issue-creator-openchamber (fleet role map: developing-today/code#2131; implementation #2152). Dedup: searched open + closed for "github-meta", "skills catalog github" — #968 (closed) covers cache eviction for this module, not the body read; #1103 (closed) capped the SKILL.md file read; no issue covers the `api.github.com` response-body read in `github-meta.js`.

body:
## Problem

The web server's local git diff reads buffer the entire diff output in memory with no byte cap, while every sibling diff/content read in the same surfaces is capped:

- `packages/web/server/lib/git/service.js:505` — `createGit` builds the shared simple-git instance with no output bound (simple-git 3.36 accumulates stdout unbounded; there is no maxBuffer anywhere in the executor path).
- `service.js:3606` — `readDiff` returns `git.raw(['diff', ...])` whole. Reached from `getDiff` (`service.js:3534`, whole-tree when no path is given), `getPathDiff`/`getPathDiffs`, and routes `GET /api/git/diff` (`lib/git/routes.js:919`) and `POST /api/git/diffs` (`routes.js:951`, up to 1000 paths, all results held in one array/response).
- `service.js:3812` — `getRangeDiff` returns `git.raw(['diff', base...head])` whole; `service.js:3747` — the working-tree range variant does the same. Served by `GET /api/git/range-diff` (`routes.js:1013`).
- `service.js:6994` — `getCommitDiff` returns `git.raw(['show', ...])` whole.

The walkthrough feature consumes exactly these functions for its local sources — `lib/walkthrough/sources.js:114/:119` (`getDiff`, working-tree), `:129` (`getRangeDiff`, branch), `:137` (`getCommitDiff`, commit) — while the same feature's remote pull-request source caps its patch at `MAX_PATCH_BYTES = 50 MiB` (`lib/walkthrough/pull-request.js:109`, enforced at `:122`, landed for #1267). Local sources bypass that cap entirely. Other in-repo precedents: `getFileDiff` caps file contents at 50 MiB, and the execFile-based `runGitCommand` (`service.js:1219`) caps stdout at 20 MiB.

## Evidence (verified on main 4246fcfe3)

Laptop probe against the real `createGit`-backed exports (probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-local-diff-cap-20261101/probe.mjs` on the laptop, module sha256 identical to origin/main): a scratch repo whose one text file changes on every one of its 800,000 lines produces a ~161.6 MB diff, and

- `getRangeDiff(repo, {base:'HEAD~1', head:'HEAD'})` returned a string of length **161,600,115**
- `getCommitDiff(repo, {hash})` returned **161,600,115**
- `getDiff(repo, {})` (whole-tree unstaged) returned **161,600,181**
- process RSS grew **+346.5 MiB** across the three reads; no error, no truncation, no cap.

A user opening a changeset/range/commit view (or a walkthrough) on a repo with a large generated-file change, a vendored import, or a line-ending flip pays this in server memory per request, and `/api/git/diffs` multiplies it across paths.

## Why it matters

Unbounded in-memory accumulation on a request path is the same failure class this repo has been closing one read at a time (#1054, #1267, #1272). The diff endpoints are user-triggerable against any opened repository, whose contents the server does not control; one oversized diff can OOM or stall the managed server for every connected client.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Local diff output (`getDiff`/`readDiff`, `getRangeDiff` incl. the working-tree variant, `getCommitDiff`) is bounded at a named constant, consistent with the in-repo precedent (50 MiB `MAX_PATCH_BYTES` / file-diff cap, or a justified alternative).
- [ ] Over-cap behavior is explicit and tested: either a typed `diff-too-large`-style error the routes surface as a clear 4xx/413-style response, or documented truncation the UI can distinguish from an empty diff — never a silent empty/`''` result and never an unbounded buffer.
- [ ] Walkthrough local sources (working-tree, branch, commit) respect the same bound as the PR source.
- [ ] Tests cover at-cap and over-cap behavior for at least the range and whole-tree paths (a small injected cap in tests is fine, following the existing bounded-read test patterns).
- [ ] Small diffs are byte-identical to today, including the untracked/no-index fallback and submodule handling in `readDiff`.

Related: #1267 (walkthrough PR patch cap — the precedent this extends to local sources), #1272 (getFileDiff `git show` blob cap — different function, same file), #742 (the VS Code executor twin, fixed there).

title: fix(vscode): four extension-host OpenCode fetchers still read bodies with a deadline but no byte cap — /api/skill and /api/info probes buffer the whole body via response.json()

labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.description: Package: vscode (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

Four VS Code extension-host fetchers that read from the configured OpenCode server still buffer the whole response body via bare `response.json()` with only an `AbortSignal.timeout` deadline and no byte cap. The web surface closed this exact shape in #1285/#1287 and #1291 (internal OpenCode fetchers), and the VS Code surface closed it for the bridge proxy (#1279/#1281), the npm packument (#1250) and models.dev — but these four sites were in none of those lists. The configured OpenCode server is user-chosen (`manager.getApiUrl()` — it can be a remote/shared server, not only the local managed one), and one of the endpoints returns every skill's full file content, so a large or misbehaving server can push hundreds of MiB into the extension host on a routine panel refresh.

## Evidence (main `7961a1a29`, verified this run)

- `packages/vscode/src/bridge-settings-runtime.ts:137` — `fetchOpenCodeSkillsFromApi` does `const payload = await response.json()` on `GET /api/skill` (deadline 8 s at :131). The payload carries each skill's full `content` (:154/:165), so the body is unbounded by construction. Called from the bridge config runtime (`bridge-config-runtime.ts:137`) whenever the skills panel refreshes.
- `packages/vscode/src/bridge-system-runtime.ts:255` — the `api:opencode/version` handler does `await response.json()` on `GET /api/info` (deadline only). The same file's update-check read a few hundred lines below *is* capped (`readBoundedResponseText`, `UPDATE_RESPONSE_MAX_BYTES`, :360-379) — this probe was missed.
- `packages/vscode/src/opencode-upgrade-runtime.ts:113` — `getOpenCodeUpgradeStatus` does `await healthResponse.json()` on `GET /api/info`. The npm-registry read in the *same function* was capped at 1 MiB (`OPENCODE_LATEST_VERSION_MAX_BYTES`, :66-91, #1250-era fix); the `/api/info` read beside it was not.
- `packages/vscode/src/extension.ts:724` — the connection-diagnostics `safeFetch` does `await resp.json()` on the configured server (6 s deadline) just to summarise keys.

No file imports the surface's bounded reader (`packages/vscode/src/bounded-response-body.ts`, used by `bridge-proxy-runtime.ts`, `bridge-fs-helpers-runtime.ts`, `bridge-system-runtime.ts` update check, `opencode-upgrade-runtime.ts` registry read) at these four sites.

Laptop probe against the real module (file md5-identical to main `7961a1a29`; `vscode` module mocked, local HTTP server streaming a chunked body): `fetchOpenCodeSkillsFromApi` consumed a 67,108,950-byte `/api/skill` body whole and returned the skill with `content` length 67,108,864 chars; extension-host RSS +70 MiB. Probe: laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-vscode-residual-caps-20261101/probe-skill.mjs`.

## Why it matters

A deadline bounds time, not memory — the principle behind #1006, #1250, #1285 and #1291. The skills fetch is the sharpest site: skill contents are legitimately non-trivial, the list is fetched on panel refresh, and the server answering it is user-configured (remote/shared OpenCode servers are a supported configuration), so the body source is not a trusted local process by construction. The three `/api/info` / diagnostics reads are small-shape endpoints where a named cap costs nothing, exactly like the capped registry and update-check reads sitting in the same files.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] All four sites (`bridge-settings-runtime.ts` `/api/skill`, `bridge-system-runtime.ts` `/api/info`, `opencode-upgrade-runtime.ts` `/api/info`, `extension.ts` diagnostics `safeFetch`) read through the VS Code surface's bounded reader (`bounded-response-body.ts`) with explicit named caps — generous for `/api/skill` (skill contents; the 16 MiB bridge-proxy/session precedent is a reasonable anchor), small for `/api/info` (1 MiB precedents in the same files).
- [ ] Over-cap answers preserve today's failure semantics: `fetchOpenCodeSkillsFromApi` returns `null` (panel falls back to the local disk scan), the version probes return their existing `{ version: null, error }` / `{ available: null, error }` shapes, diagnostics report a failed probe — never a hang, an OOM, or an authoritative empty success where today it is a failure.
- [ ] Tests per site (or per module where a test file already exists): an over-cap streamed body is rejected without being fully buffered; an at-cap body parses byte-identically, including the `{ data }` envelope unwrap for `/api/skill`.
- [ ] No behaviour change for bodies under the caps.

Dedup: searched open + closed issues for vscode body caps / `api/skill` / `fetchOpenCodeSkillsFromApi` — #1285/#1287/#1291 cover `packages/web/server` only; #1279 covers the bridge proxy forwards; #1250 covers the npm packument. No issue covers these four reads.

Filed by new-issue-creator-openchamber, run 2026-11-01 21:50 CST.

title: fix(web): PR #1066 carries an unrelated bun.lock rewrite to registry.npmmirror.com in its rescue commit — drop it before merge

body:
## Finding

Open PR #1066 (the persistent-pty proxy bounds fix for #1059) carries a second commit that rewrites `bun.lock` wholesale to a third-party npm mirror. The fix commit itself is clean; the contamination is entirely in the rescue commit on top of it. If the PR merges as-is, the repo's lockfile switches every package's tarball source to `registry.npmmirror.com`.

## Evidence

- PR #1066, head `3dc8765cda97d5aea0215209ef0c13294114e323`, OPEN (checked 2026-11-02T03:30Z).
- Commit `031f95037` "fix(web): bound persistent-pty proxy pre-open queue, handshake, and slow peers (#1059)" touches only `packages/web/server/lib/persistent-pty/runtime.js` (+67/-1) and `runtime.test.js` (+129/-2) — no lockfile change.
- Commit `3dc8765cd` "rescue: preserve uncommitted work from worktree cleanup 2026-11-01" touches ONLY `bun.lock` (+1877/-1875): every package entry's resolved URL is rewritten from the default (empty) registry to `https://registry.npmmirror.com/...` — 1,875 `npmmirror` occurrences in the PR diff, 0 `registry.npmjs.org`.
- Current main carries no mirror URLs: code search for `npmmirror` in this repo returns nothing, and main's `bun.lock` blob is `2df6d11e958292822a821c523e9b27e97120cf0e`.
- The `sha512` integrity hashes are unchanged by the rewrite, so this is not a content compromise — it is registry provenance churn, the same machine-registry-config leak class as #1289 (closed; a machine whose `~/.npmrc` sets a non-default registry leaking into repo artifacts, isolated for tests in PR #1290).

## Why it matters

- Merging would make every future install resolve tarballs through a third-party mirror instead of the default registry: an availability and supply-chain-provenance change nobody chose, introduced by a worktree-cleanup rescue, not by the PR's author intent.
- The ~3,750-line lockfile diff also buries the real 2-file fix, making the PR effectively unreviewable as a whole.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] On PR #1066's branch, `bun.lock` is restored to main's version (the rescue commit's lockfile change is dropped/reverted); the PR diff then contains only `packages/web/server/lib/persistent-pty/runtime.js` and `runtime.test.js`.
- [ ] `grep -c npmmirror` over the PR diff is 0.
- [ ] The #1059 fix itself is byte-unchanged (commit `031f95037`'s changes intact) and PR #1066 remains open, ready for its normal shepherd/merge path.
- [ ] No other file changes ride along with the cleanup.

Found by the pr-diff-review job (run 2026-11-01 21:24 CST), reviewing PRs #1041–#1072 in developing-today/openchamber.

title: fix(web): Linear GraphQL client reads response bodies with a deadline but no byte cap — fetchLinearGraphql buffers the whole body via response.json() while the package's OAuth reads cap at 1 MiB

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

The Linear GraphQL client reads every response body whole with no byte cap: `fetchLinearGraphql` in `packages/web/server/lib/linear/client.js:151` does `payload = await response.json()`, bounded only by the 10 s deadline (`LINEAR_GRAPHQL_TIMEOUT_MS`, :15). Every Linear surface in the server flows through this one function — viewer identity (:178) and all of `lib/linear/issues.js` (get/search/list/summary/states/update, :421-599) — inside request handlers and background tracked-item refreshes.

Its sibling in the same package already made the opposite choice for the auth path: `lib/linear/oauth.js:24-26` caps broker and token JSON reads at `LINEAR_JSON_RESPONSE_MAX_BYTES = 1 MiB`, with a comment explaining that a deadline does not stop an endpoint "from buffering an unbounded body via .json()" and naming the GitLab auth cap as the model. The broker half of that lesson was filed and fixed as #1102/#1111; the GraphQL data path was only ever given a deadline (#778).

## Evidence (verified on main 2b5e51c28, this run)

- Code read: `client.js:136-167` — the fetch carries `AbortSignal.timeout(LINEAR_GRAPHQL_TIMEOUT_MS)`; the body read at :151 is a bare `response.json()` with no size check before, during, or after; the parsed payload's `data` subtree is returned to callers whole.
- No bounded reader is imported anywhere in `client.js` (the module imports only auth/oauth/parse helpers), while `oauth.js:10` imports `readBoundedResponseText` from `lib/shared/response-body.js`.
- A deadline bounds time, not memory: a fast or misbehaving endpoint (or a compromised response path for `https://api.linear.app/graphql`) can deliver arbitrarily many bytes inside 10 s, and each concurrent handler/refresh holding one multiplies the long-lived server's memory.

## Why it matters, and the honest sizing question

Real GraphQL answers here are issue lists and summaries — legitimately far bigger than the few-hundred-byte token answers the 1 MiB auth cap was sized for, so this is NOT a copy-the-constant fix. The triage must pick a cap sized from the real queries in `issues.js` (the fleet's other data-catalog reads use 16 MiB, e.g. the models.dev catalog cap in #1009) and an over-cap behaviour that fits the existing error contract (`LinearApiError` with a 502-class status, like the "response was not JSON" path at :167-169). What is not defensible is the current state: no bound at all on the package's highest-volume external read.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `fetchLinearGraphql` reads the response body through a bounded reader (e.g. `readBoundedResponseText`/`readBoundedResponseJson` from `lib/shared/response-body.js`) behind a named cap constant in `client.js`, enforced while streaming, not after buffering; the cap's value is justified in a comment from the queries actually sent (list/search payload shapes in `issues.js`).
- [ ] An over-cap body surfaces as a `LinearApiError` (no partial `data` returned, no silent null treated as an empty result), consistent with the existing not-JSON error path.
- [ ] In-cap behaviour unchanged: 401 handling, GraphQL error extraction (`readGraphqlError`), timeout mapping (`isTimeoutAbort` → `graphqlTimeoutError()`), and BOM/parse semantics.
- [ ] Tests: an over-cap response is rejected without being parsed whole; a normal viewer/issues response still returns `data`; existing linear suites (`issues.test.js`, `oauth.test.js`, `routes.test.js`) still pass.
- [ ] No change to the endpoint, headers, timeout value, or the exported function signatures.

Filed by new-issue-creator-openchamber (fleet role map: developing-today/code#2131; implementation #2152). Dedup: searched open + closed for "linear graphql cap", "linear client body cap" — #775/#778 gave this path deadlines only, #1102/#1111 capped the OAuth broker/token reads in oauth.js; no issue covers the GraphQL data read in client.js.

title: fix(web): GitHub device-flow reads token responses with a deadline but no byte cap — postForm buffers the whole body via response.json() while the GitLab twin caps auth bodies at 1 MiB

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: priority/normal

labels.name: app/web

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

The GitHub device-flow module reads OAuth token-endpoint responses with a 10 s deadline but no byte cap: `postForm` in `packages/web/server/lib/github/device-flow.js:28` does `await response.json().catch(() => null)`, buffering the whole body before any field is looked at. Both device-flow calls go through it — `startDeviceFlow` (device code) and `exchangeDeviceCode` (access token) — and on the error path the whole parsed payload is also attached to the thrown error (`error.payload`, :33).

The GitLab twin of this exact module was capped for this exact shape in #1021 / #1023: `packages/web/server/lib/gitlab/device-flow.js:6` and `verify.js:16` read auth bodies through `readBoundedResponseText` behind `AUTH_BODY_MAX_BYTES = 1 MiB` (`packages/web/server/lib/gitlab/network.js:22`), throwing a provider error when the body crosses it. The Linear OAuth module made the same choice (`LINEAR_JSON_RESPONSE_MAX_BYTES = 1 MiB`, `packages/web/server/lib/linear/oauth.js:26`, with a comment naming the GitLab cap as the model). The GitHub module is the remaining auth-path reader with no cap.

## Evidence (verified on main 2b5e51c28, this run)

- Code read: `device-flow.js:15-38` — the only bound on the read is `AbortSignal.timeout(timeoutMs ?? 10_000)`; no `readBoundedResponse*` import, no size constant in the module.
- Laptop probe against the real module (file md5 `d79700e0b5c8b98633a47783de474a95`, identical to sandbox main): `startDeviceFlow` with an injected fetch returning a 128 MiB JSON body (valid fields plus a padding field) accepted and parsed the whole body — result carried the full 134,217,728-char padding field and process RSS grew +525 MiB during the call. Probe: laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-gh-device-flow-20261101/`.
- A deadline bounds time, not memory: a fast endpoint (or a compromised/MITM'd response path — the module posts to `github.com/login/device/code` and `github.com/login/oauth/access_token`) can deliver arbitrarily many bytes inside the 10 s window, and the long-lived server process holds all of them, plus the parsed object, plus the error-path copy.

## Why it matters

Device flow is the sign-in path for GitHub accounts in OpenChamber; it runs in the shared server process that serves every connected client. An oversized token-endpoint body is a memory-amplification vector (probe: ~4x the body size in RSS) with no benefit — real device-flow answers are a few hundred bytes. The repo has already decided this contract three times (GitLab auth, Linear auth, quota/internal fetchers in #1282/#1285); this module simply missed the sweep.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `postForm` in `packages/web/server/lib/github/device-flow.js` reads the response body through a bounded reader (e.g. `readBoundedResponseText` from `lib/shared/response-body.js`) behind a named cap consistent with the other auth readers (1 MiB, as `AUTH_BODY_MAX_BYTES` / `LINEAR_JSON_RESPONSE_MAX_BYTES`), enforced while streaming, not after buffering.
- [ ] An over-cap body fails the same way an unreachable/invalid endpoint does today (thrown error with status where available); no partial payload is returned or attached to the error.
- [ ] BOM/parse semantics preserved for in-cap bodies: a leading UTF-8 BOM does not break parsing (the shared bounded reader does not strip it — see the note in `lib/gitlab/device-flow.js`), and non-JSON bodies still yield the current `payload = null` error shape.
- [ ] Regression tests in `packages/web/server/lib/github/device-flow.test.js`: over-cap body rejected without being parsed whole; a normal device-code and access-token exchange still succeed; an error response still surfaces `error_description`/`error`.
- [ ] No change to the endpoints, form encoding, timeouts, or the exported function signatures.

Filed by new-issue-creator-openchamber (fleet role map: developing-today/code#2131; implementation #2152). Dedup: searched open + closed issues for "device-flow", "github device", "device code response" — #1021/#1023 cover the GitLab module only; no issue covers the GitHub module's read.

title: fix(web): three internal OpenCode fetchers missed by #1285 still read bodies with a deadline but no byte cap — session-warming, permission-auto-accept and pwa-manifest buffer the whole body via response.json()

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

#1285 listed seven internal OpenCode fetch modules that read the upstream JSON body whole via `response.json()` with only an `AbortSignal.timeout` deadline, and PR #1287 capped those plus the lifecycle/compatibility/routes health probes. Three more modules with the exact same shape were not in #1285's list and were not touched by #1287 — each still buffers the whole body from the user-chosen (possibly remote) OpenCode server, with no byte cap and no bounded reader imported:

- `packages/web/server/lib/session-warming/runtime.js:200` — `readBusy` fetches `GET /api/session/active` (10 s deadline, `STATUS_TIMEOUT_MS`) and does `unwrapOpenCodeResponse(await response.json())`. This is the **same endpoint** #1285's probe verified against `session-activity.js`; session-activity is now capped at 16 MiB (`SESSION_ACTIVITY_RESPONSE_MAX_BYTES`, via `readBoundedResponseJson`), session-warming is not.
- `packages/web/server/lib/permission-auto-accept/runtime.js:206` — the shared `request()` helper (5 s deadline, `REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS` at `:7`) ends in `return response.json().catch(() => null)`. It serves `GET /api/session/:id` (session-record fetch in `getSession`, :209-215), the pending-permission list (`/api/permission/request` in `reconcilePending`), and permission replies — session records are the same shape notifications' capped fetches read in #1285.
- `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/pwa-manifest-routes.js:121` — `listSessions` fetches `GET /api/session` (2.5 s deadline) and does `await response.json().catch(() => null)`. The session **list** is the largest shape OpenCode serves (the #776 proxy caps the same list at 16 MiB); the manifest route runs on every `/manifest.webmanifest` fetch for authorized callers.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `2b5e51c28a48`)

Laptop probe against the real modules (files md5-identical between the laptop fork and sandbox main at `2b5e51c28`; injected fetch returning a counting `ReadableStream` body; probe: laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-opencode-residual-caps-20261101/probe.mjs`):

- **session-warming**: a 67,108,907-byte valid `/api/session/active` body was pulled **whole** (`bytesPulled=67108907`, 1 fetch), process RSS **+234 MiB**. Control with a small body where the target session is absent correctly parsed and set `warmUntil` — the parse path is the one probed.
- **permission-auto-accept**: a 67,108,940-byte valid session record was pulled **whole** (`bytesPulled=67108940`); the runtime then walked the lineage to the record's parent (2 fetches total), proving the oversized record was parsed, not rejected.
- **pwa-manifest**: a 67,109,112-byte valid session-list body was pulled **whole** (`bytesPulled=67109112`); the manifest came back with 4 shortcuts (1 static + 3 sessions parsed from the oversized list).

Grep on current main: none of the three files imports `lib/shared/response-body.js`; after #1287 they (plus the fixed-SaaS/local classes already dispositioned in earlier runs — github device-flow, Linear, APNs, ngrok, github-meta — and the already-filed guest OAuth reads in #1085) are the only bare `response.json()` reads left in `packages/web/server`.

## Why it matters

Same reasoning as #1285: the OpenCode server these calls target can be an external/remote instance the user connected to, and session payloads are the largest shapes it serves. These three run on hot paths — session-warming polls `/api/session/active` per warmed session on every settle/retry, permission-auto-accept fetches a session record per permission lineage walk, and the PWA manifest lists all sessions per manifest fetch — so one oversized or hostile upstream answer is buffered and parsed whole in the OpenChamber server's memory, repeatedly, with no bound but the clock.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] All three sites read the body through a bounded reader (e.g. `readBoundedResponseJson` from `lib/shared/response-body.js`) with an explicit named byte cap per module, consistent with the #1287 precedent (16 MiB for session shapes).
- [ ] Over-cap answers preserve today's failure semantics exactly: session-warming's `readBusy` returns `null` ("could not ask", never an authoritative idle), permission-auto-accept's `request()` keeps its current null/throw behaviour for its callers, and pwa-manifest's `listSessions` falls back to `[]` shortcuts — an over-cap body must never become an authoritative empty success where today it is a failure, nor vice versa.
- [ ] Tests: for each module, an over-cap streamed body is rejected without being fully buffered (reader cancelled / stream not drained), and an at-cap body parses byte-identically to today, including the `{ data, cursor }` envelope unwrapping.
- [ ] No behaviour change for bodies under the cap.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for `pwa-manifest`, `permission-auto-accept`, `session-warming`, `session/active`, `manifest`, and "byte cap": #1285 (closed, fixed by #1287) lists seven modules — none of these three — and its acceptance was scoped to the listed sites; #987/#1202 concern session-warming's activity-map cap, not its fetch body; #875 concerned permission-auto-accept's in-memory maps, not its fetch body. No open or closed issue covers these three reads. This is the residual set of #1285, filed separately per the fleet's one-finding-one-issue practice (cf. #1277, the residual of #1133).

title: fix(web): routes-upgrade bundled-binary test reads the machine's npm registry config — fails on any machine whose ~/.npmrc sets a non-default registry

labels.name: kind/test
labels.description: Test coverage, test infrastructure, or test-only fixes

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Summary

One test in `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/routes-upgrade.test.js` — "never announces a newer version for a bundled binary: it updates with the desktop app" (`:110-132`) — is not isolated from the machine's npm configuration. Its fetch mock only recognises `registry.npmjs.org` and `api.github.com` URLs and returns the `/api/info`-shaped payload (`{ version: '1.18.8', pid: 1, ... }`) for **any other URL**. But the route under test resolves the registry through `resolveNpmRegistryRequest` (`packages/web/server/lib/opencode/npm-registry-config.js`), which reads `npm_config_registry` / `NPM_CONFIG_REGISTRY` from the environment and the `registry=` value from the user npmrc (`npm_config_userconfig`, else `~/.npmrc` — resolver `:6-12`, `:47-60`). On any machine whose npmrc or environment names a different registry (a corporate mirror, npmmirror, a local Verdaccio), the upgrade-status handler fetches `<that-registry>/@opencode%2Fcli/latest`, the mock's fallback answers it with the info-shaped payload, and the test sees `latestVersion: "1.18.8"` instead of the expected `"2.0.3"`. The sibling test in the same file (`:40-58`) already shows the isolation pattern — it sets `npm_config_registry` and points `npm_config_userconfig` at a missing file, restoring both afterwards — but the bundled-binary test does not.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `534e3ded8`)

- Laptop (fork clone at the same main commit, `~/.npmrc` contains `registry=https://registry.npmmirror.com`): `bunx vitest run server/lib/opencode/routes-upgrade.test.js` → 1 failed / 15 passed. Failure diff: expected `latestVersion: "2.0.3"`, received `latestVersion: "1.18.8"` (assertion at `routes-upgrade.test.js:123`); every other field matched.
- Control, same machine, same checkout: `npm_config_registry=https://registry.npmjs.org npm_config_userconfig=/nonexistent.npmrc bunx vitest run server/lib/opencode/routes-upgrade.test.js` → **16/16 passed**. The only variable is the machine's registry configuration, which proves the dependence.
- `npm-registry-config.js` `configPath()`: falls back to `path.join(os.homedir(), '.npmrc')` when no userconfig env is set, and `registryFor()` consults env registries and the npmrc values before the `https://registry.npmjs.org` default — so the un-pinned test inherits whatever the developer's machine says.

## Why it matters

The test guards a real behaviour — a bundled OpenCode must never be announced as upgradable — and it passes in CI only because CI machines happen to use the default registry. Any contributor (or fleet machine) with a mirror in `~/.npmrc` gets a red suite on clean main and a failure message that points at the route's version logic, not at the test's environment leak; the natural response is to distrust or "fix" correct route code. This is the same class as #1280 (vscode quota tests failing on clean main for a config reason): environment-dependent tests erode the signal of the whole suite.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The bundled-binary test (and any other test in `routes-upgrade.test.js` whose mock keys on a specific registry host) pins its npm configuration the way the sibling test at `:40-58` does — e.g. sets `npm_config_registry` and a missing-file `npm_config_userconfig` for the test's duration and restores both — or the mock matches the resolved registry URL structurally instead of by host name.
- [ ] `routes-upgrade.test.js` passes in full (16/16) on a machine whose `~/.npmrc` sets `registry=https://registry.npmmirror.com`, with no change to the route code's behaviour.
- [ ] The suite still passes with the default registry configuration (CI conditions).

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for routes-upgrade / upgrade-status registry terms: #1040/#1051 (registry body byte cap — fixed), #796/#789 (info-probe deadlines — fixed), #184 (version parsing — fixed), #1250 (vscode packument cap — fixed). None covers test isolation from the machine's npm registry config. #1280 is the analogous clean-main test failure in the vscode quota suite, a different file and cause.

body:
## Problem

The web server's internal OpenCode-session fetches read the upstream JSON body whole with `response.json()` — each has an `AbortSignal.timeout` deadline (2–15 s) but no byte cap. The shared bounded readers (`lib/shared/response-body.js`: `readBoundedResponseText`/`readBoundedResponseBytes`) exist and are used elsewhere, but not here. The OpenCode server these calls target can be an external/remote instance the user connected to, and session/message payloads are the largest shapes it serves — a huge or hostile body is buffered and parsed whole in the OpenChamber server's memory before any field is looked at.

Verified sites on main `7c158496b` (all `await response.json()` after a deadline-only fetch):

- `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/session-activity.js:33` — `openCodeGet` behind the session-activity probe (active statuses, children pages)
- `packages/web/server/lib/context-obligatory/runtime.js:81` — `openCodeFetch` (session record, message pages, pinned-message fetches)
- `packages/web/server/lib/dispatch-results/runtime.js:306` — same helper shape
- `packages/web/server/lib/message-queue/runtime.js:462` — same helper shape
- `packages/web/server/lib/session-goal/runtime.js:395` — same helper shape
- `packages/web/server/lib/notifications/runtime.js:370` and `:1010` — session record fetches (2 s deadline)
- `packages/web/server/lib/notifications/template-runtime.js:179` and `:248` — message page + session fetches (2–3 s deadlines)
- `packages/web/server/lib/markdown-image-grants/routes.js:251` — single-message fetch (10 s deadline)

Same pattern, smaller fixed shapes (fix in the same pass if cheap, or explicitly disposition): `lib/opencode/lifecycle.js:925` (`/api/info`) and `:1516` (`/api/agent`), `lib/opencode/routes.js:210/:256/:302` (health/info).

## Evidence (this run)

Laptop probe against the real module (`createSessionActivityProbe` from `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/session-activity.js`, injected `fetchImpl` streaming a 67,108,931-byte JSON body for `/api/session/active`):

- Returned all 659,020 keys — the whole body was buffered and parsed.
- Server-process RSS grew +186.6 MiB for the single call.
- Probe: laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-session-body-cap-20261101/probe.mjs`.

This is the internal-helper twin of #776 (session-list proxy, capped at 16 MiB) and the same defect class as #1282 (quota providers): deadline present, byte cap missing, on an endpoint that is not a fixed trusted SaaS — the directory's OpenCode server is user-chosen and may be remote.

## Why it matters

These helpers run on hot paths — notification fan-out, message-queue delivery, goal audits, context re-injection — so one oversized upstream answer multiplies: several of them fetch per session event. A remote OpenCode server that is compromised, misconfigured, or simply carrying a very large session can push the OpenChamber server's memory up by hundreds of MiB per call with no bound but the clock.

## Acceptance criteria

- Every site listed above reads the body through a bounded reader (e.g. `readBoundedResponseText` from `lib/shared/response-body.js`) with an explicit byte cap; over-cap answers fail the fetch the same way a non-OK status does today (callers already treat fetch failure as "could not look" / null — that behavior must be preserved, never converted into an authoritative empty success).
- The cap is sized for legitimate session/message pages (the #776 proxy cap precedent is 16 MiB) and named as a constant next to each module's existing `FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS`.
- Tests: an over-cap streamed body is rejected without being fully buffered (reader cancelled / stream not drained), and an at-cap body parses byte-identically to today.
- No behavior change for bodies under the cap, including the `{ data, cursor }` envelope unwrapping via `unwrapOpenCodeResponse`.

title: fix(web): content search buffers a whole ripgrep line with no byte cap — one match in a 256 MiB single-line file peaks server RSS at +1.6 GiB for a 374-char result

body:
## Summary

Find-in-files (`fs/content-search.js`) caps everything downstream — 500 matches max, 200-char previews, 64 KiB stderr — but the unfinished-line accumulator that feeds it has no byte cap. A single ripgrep match event for a match inside a very long line is buffered whole, joined, and `JSON.parse`d before any cap applies, so one search over a workspace containing a large single-line file (minified bundle, generated data file) grows server memory by roughly 6× the line size.

## Evidence (main `8c4dac677`, verified this run)

Code — `packages/web/server/lib/fs/content-search.js`:

- :223-236 the stdout handler accumulates an unfinished line into `pending` (list of string pieces) with no size check; on the newline it runs `consume(pending.join(''))`, and :208-219 `consume` `JSON.parse`s the whole line before `readRipgrepMatch` / preview capping (`PREVIEW_MAX_CHARS` :25, `buildPreview` slicing) ever see it.
- The caps that do exist are all downstream or beside the point: `CONTENT_SEARCH_MAX_LIMIT` 500 (:16), `STDERR_MAX_BYTES` 64 KiB (:27), and the 30 s deadline (:18) — which bounds time, not bytes; ripgrep emits the giant line in well under a second.
- The module's own comment (:221-222) acknowledges the shape: "A single line can be tens of megabytes (a minified file)." There is no constant bounding it.

Laptop probe against the real module (file md5 `027726e4e6cdf86a10903f93cc0f333e`, identical in the sandbox clone at main and the laptop fork; probe `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-content-search-line-20261101/probe.mjs`):

- Fixture: one file, a single line of 268,435,467 bytes (`ZZTOKENZZ ` + 256 MiB of `a`).
- `searchFileContents` returned `{ status: 'ok', matches: 1 }` with a 374-char first-match JSON — the useful result is tiny.
- Server-process RSS went from 21 MiB to a peak of 1,643 MiB (**+1,622 MiB, ~6.3× the line size**: pending pieces + join + the parsed event object holding the full line text) in 6.4 s.

## Why it matters

Content search runs against arbitrary user workspaces, which routinely contain minified or generated single-line files far larger than 256 MiB (bundles, sourcemap-adjacent data, ML/data dumps). One find-in-files request can OOM or swap-thrash the long-lived OpenChamber server for every connected client — triggered by an ordinary search for a common token, no hostile input required. Every sibling accumulator in this codebase is byte-capped (stderr in this same function, dev-servers scanner, fs/exec output); the line buffer is the remaining hole.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The unfinished-line accumulator in `content-search.js` is bounded by a named byte cap; a line past the cap is abandoned (the search continues with later lines / ends with an explicit stopped reason) instead of being joined and parsed whole.
- [ ] Peak memory for the probe fixture (256 MiB single line, one match) stays within a small multiple of the cap — no whole-line string or parsed event is ever materialized.
- [ ] Regression tests in `content-search.test.js`: an over-cap line does not produce a match from that line and does not stall the search; normal multi-line and long-but-under-cap line searches are unchanged.
- [ ] The chosen cap and the over-cap behavior are named in the module comment / `fs/DOCUMENTATION.md` if it documents search limits.

Filed by new-issue-creator-openchamber, run 2026-11-01 16:50 CST. Dedup: searched open + closed issues for content-search / ripgrep line caps — #554 (query-param parsing), #1026/#1127 (fs read/write routes) are different paths; no issue covers the content-search line accumulator.

body:
## Summary

Every quota provider on both surfaces fetches with a 15 s deadline but reads the response body with no byte cap. The deadlines were added by #782/#827/#844; the body reads were never bounded. A fast endpoint — compromised, misconfigured, or user-configured — can stream an arbitrarily large body inside the deadline window and the server (web) or extension host (VS Code) buffers all of it before `JSON.parse`.

## Evidence (main `8c4dac677`, verified this run)

Web — `packages/web/server/lib/quota/`:

- 39 bare `response.json()` / `response.arrayBuffer()` success-path reads across 27 provider modules; `grep -rn readBoundedResponse packages/web/server/lib/quota/` returns **0** — no quota module uses the shared bounded reader (`lib/shared/response-body.js`, `readBoundedResponseText` :13 / `readBoundedResponseBytes` :48).
- Representative sites: `providers/deepseek.js:60` (`await response.json()` after `AbortSignal.timeout(15_000)` at :36), `providers/codex.js:88`, `providers/copilot.js:151` and `:217`, `providers/openrouter.js:102`, `providers/zai.js:85` and `:139`, `providers/opencode-go.js:141`/`:168`/`:199`, `providers/antigravity/api.js:56` and `:83`, `providers/google/api.js:41` and `:64`, `providers/xai.js:281` (`new Uint8Array(await response.arrayBuffer())`).
- Two of the endpoints are caller-controlled, so the body source is not even a fixed first party: OpenRouter uses a configured base (`providers/openrouter.js:28` `resolveQuotaBase()`, fetch at :81); Copilot builds its URL from the login's `enterpriseUrl` (`providers/copilot.js:93-94`, fetches at :130/:196).

VS Code twin — `packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.ts`:

- 31 bare `response.json()` reads (e.g. :1051 Codex, :1247 Google, :1456 Antigravity, :2750 OpenRouter, :3257 NanoGPT), all behind the same 15 s `AbortSignal.timeout` pattern, with no byte cap anywhere in the file.

## Why it matters

The fleet has already closed this exact shape on every other outbound surface — #1006 (models.dev / npm / changelog), #1047 (package-manager update checks), #1102 (Linear OAuth broker), #1250 (VS Code npm packument) — each time on the principle that a deadline bounds time, not memory. The quota surface is the largest remaining cluster of unbounded body reads, it runs on a recurring poll against third-party endpoints with the user's credentials, and quota payloads are small JSON documents, so a generous named cap (e.g. 1 MiB, matching the changelog-index precedent in `changelog/update-notes.js`) costs nothing.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every success-path body read in `packages/web/server/lib/quota/**` goes through the shared bounded reader (or an equivalent named-cap helper) with a named per-surface cap; an over-cap body produces the provider's normal failure result, not a buffered parse.
- [ ] The VS Code twin `packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.ts` gets the same treatment with a named cap (its own helper is fine; the surfaces do not share code today).
- [ ] Error-path body reads are either bounded the same way or explicitly discarded (`discardResponseBody`).
- [ ] Regression tests: a stubbed fetch returning an over-cap body yields a failed quota result (not an OOM/parse of the whole body) for at least one web provider and the VS Code provider set; existing quota tests stay green.
- [ ] `quota/DOCUMENTATION.md` (or the providers' owning docs) names the cap and the rationale.

Filed by new-issue-creator-openchamber, run 2026-11-01 16:50 CST. Dedup: searched open + closed issues for quota body caps — #782/#827/#844 cover deadlines only; #1006/#1047/#1102/#1250 cover other surfaces; no open or closed issue covers quota-provider body reads.

title: fix(web): gh CLI account removal reconciles bindings before setGhCliActive, which now throws on malformed settings.json and strands them

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

body:
## Finding

In `packages/web/server/lib/github/routes.js`, `removeAccount`'s gh-CLI branch reconciles the account's bindings **before** the settings update that can now fail:

```js
// routes.js:1668-1669 (main aa631af77)
await options.onAccountRemoved?.(accountIdentity(requestedAccountId));
setGhCliActive(false);
```

`onAccountRemoved` is wired in `packages/web/server/lib/source-control/routes.js:146` to `accountUnavailable(...)`: matching providers lose authority and matching managed remotes / auxiliary credentials are marked as requiring confirmation. Since PR #990 (merged 2026-10-31T04:38:16Z, head `6dc3b4fc8`, fixes #940), `setGhCliActive` reads settings through the strict `readSettingsFileForUpdate()` in `github/auth.js`, which **throws `MALFORMED_SETTINGS`** when `settings.json` is malformed or a non-object — where the old lenient read never threw.

So with a malformed `settings.json`, removing the gh CLI account now:
1. invalidates the account's bindings (step 1 succeeds),
2. throws at `setGhCliActive(false)` → the DELETE route answers 500,
3. leaves `ghCliActive` still true in the (untouched) settings file — the account remains available while its bindings are stranded until the account is reconnected or the bindings are repaired.

Flagged in-PR by CodeRabbit as a Minor (comment 4430192823 on PR #990, `auth.js:441` thread) with the suggested reorder; it was never replied to or fixed — PR #990 merged as a single commit `6dc3b4fc8` without the reorder, and the order is unchanged on current main `aa631af77b0fb60b782188462ae9d5bd19c15845`.

## Evidence

- PR #990: https://github.com/developing-today/openchamber/pull/990 — strict settings read for the gh-CLI setters (`readSettingsFileForUpdate`, `MALFORMED_SETTINGS`, tests pin the throw + byte-identical preservation).
- CodeRabbit Minor 4430192823 (PR #990): "Run the settings update before invalidating bindings… If settings.json is malformed, setGhCliActive(false) throws after onAccountRemoved has already reconciled the bindings."
- Main `routes.js:1668-1669`: `onAccountRemoved` still precedes `setGhCliActive(false)` in the `github.com#cli:` branch of `removeAccount` (the function's own header comment states bindings are "reconciled first").
- Main `source-control/routes.js:146`: `onAccountRemoved: (identity) => accountUnavailable(identity, …)`.
- No test pins the failure order: `routes.auth.test.js` mocks the GitHub libraries, so its `setGhCliActive` never throws (existing expectations at :129-142 and :1188-1193 cover success/validation paths only).

## Why it matters

#990 deliberately made settings writes fail closed to stop silent settings loss — the right call — but on this one path the fail-closed throw lands *after* an irreversible side effect on a different store. A user with a damaged `settings.json` who disconnects the gh CLI account gets a 500, a still-active account, and bindings that no longer work — the worst of both states, and hard to diagnose because the error message points at the settings file, not the bindings.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] In `removeAccount`'s gh-CLI branch, the settings update (`setGhCliActive(false)`) runs before `onAccountRemoved` is invoked — or an equivalent ordering/guard ensures bindings are only reconciled once the account state change has succeeded.
- [ ] A regression test pins it: with `setGhCliActive` throwing (malformed-settings simulation), `onAccountRemoved` is not called and the route surfaces the settings error; the success path still calls `onAccountRemoved` with the same identity and returns `removed: true`.
- [ ] Existing `routes.auth.test.js` and `github/auth.test.js` suites stay green; #990's strict-read behaviour (throw + file preserved byte-identical) is unchanged.

Found by pr-diff-review lane B (run 2026-11-01 13:18 CST, gap-correction batch: PRs #982–#990 reviewed after a discovery-listing miss). Evidence: goal hidden_files `pr-review-b-2026-11-01-1318/` (pr-990.diff, comments-gap.txt).

body:
## Problem

In `getFileDiff`, the two `git show` reads that supply the committed/index side of a file diff have no byte cap at all, while every sibling read in the same function is capped at 50 MiB.

`packages/web/server/lib/git/service.js`:

- The working-tree side is capped: `MAX_FILE_DIFF_WORKING_TREE_BYTES = 50 * 1024 * 1024` (:3971), enforced by a stat gate before any read (:4125) and by the bounded reader `readFileDiffWorkingTreeFile`. The comment at :3969-3971 states the cap is "the same limit the image `git show` reads in getFileDiff already carry".
- The image `git show` reads are capped the same way: `maxBuffer: 50 * 1024 * 1024` at :4152 (HEAD) and :4175 (index).
- The non-image `git show` reads are not: `original = await git.show([`HEAD:${repoPath}`])` (:4161) and, for staged diffs, `modified = await git.show([`:${repoPath}`])` (:4181) go through simple-git. `createGit` (:504) configures no `maxBuffer`, and simple-git's executor accumulates every stdout chunk into an array with no limit — so a committed blob of any size is buffered whole in the managed server and returned as the diff's `original`/`modified` string.
- The gates that exist do not cover these paths: the working-tree stat gate runs only when `!staged` (:4118-4128), so a staged diff never stats anything before the index `git show`; and when the working-tree file has been deleted, the stat is null and the HEAD `git show` still runs ungated.

VS Code twin (`packages/vscode/src/gitService.ts` `getGitFileDiff`): the working-tree side is capped at `MAX_FILE_DIFF_WORKING_TREE_BYTES = 20 MiB` (:2797, gates :2837/:2871-2879), but `original` comes from `repo.show('HEAD', …)` / `repo.show(':0:' + …)` (:2853-2860) with no size gate on the committed/index blob (the staged `modified` read at :2866 at least passes through the git-exec 20 MiB output cap and fails empty rather than returning `file_too_large`).

## Verified evidence (main `55570dcd3`, 2026-11-01)

Laptop probe against the real `getFileDiff` (probe: laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-filediff-show-cap-20261101/probe.mjs`, run against the laptop clone at the same main):

- Case A (staged): a 64 MiB plain-text file staged over a small committed version → `modified` returned whole: 67,108,864 chars, RSS +194 MB. No `file_too_large`, no error.
- Case B (unstaged, working copy deleted): the same 64 MiB file committed at HEAD → `original` returned whole: 67,108,864 chars, RSS +193 MB.
- The cap both cases bypass is 50 MiB = 52,428,800 bytes.

## Why it matters

File size here is clone-controlled: any repository the user opens can contain a huge committed text file (generated code, vendored fixtures, data files — all pass the binary sniff, which only samples the working-tree file). Opening its diff — a routine review action, including for a file the user just deleted or staged — buffers the entire blob (plus the string copies the response makes) in the managed server that every session depends on. The working-tree and image paths were deliberately capped for exactly this failure mode; the `git show` paths are the uncapped remainder in the same function. This is the #1254 bounded-read class, in a read those designs did not name.

## Acceptance criteria

- Web: both non-image `git show` reads in `getFileDiff` (HEAD original at :4161, index modified at :4181) enforce the 50 MiB file-diff cap, rejecting over-cap blobs with the existing `file_too_large` coded error (`FILE_DIFF_TOO_LARGE_CODE`, HTTP 413 at the route) instead of returning the content — mirroring the working-tree and image behaviour in the same function.
- VS Code: `getGitFileDiff`'s `repo.show` original reads (:2853-2860) get an equivalent gate against its 20 MiB cap, returning the existing `fileDiffTooLarge` result (`kind: 'unavailable', reason: 'file_too_large'`) for over-cap committed/index blobs, staged and unstaged.
- Tests: web `git/service.test.js` — staged diff of an over-cap staged blob and deleted-working-tree diff of an over-cap HEAD blob both reject/return `file_too_large`; an at-cap blob still diffs byte-identically. VS Code gitService tests cover the over-cap `repo.show` original.
- No change to `getCommitFileDiff` (already bounded via `runGitCommand`'s 20 MiB `maxBuffer`) or to the image paths (already capped).

body:
Follow-on from developing-today/opencode#1140 (nested routes conversion).

opencode now treats `experimental.routes.*` as the canonical routing shape (models/providers/windows/schedules/tuning/log/settings) and folds the flat `experimental.model_routes` / `provider_routes` / `model_route_*` keys into it at load via a normalize compat shim. The flat keys remain accepted in the file, so `validateModelRoutes` — which reads the flat keys directly — keeps validating existing configs unchanged today.

Owed work here: teach `validateModelRoutes` to ALSO validate `experimental.routes.models` (and the rest of the routes.* family) so a config file written in nested-only form is validated instead of silently validating nothing. The flat shim in opencode must not be removed until this lands (and the route-proxy follow-on in developing-today/code lands).

## Acceptance criteria

- `validateModelRoutes` also validates `experimental.routes.models` and the rest of the `routes.*` family (providers/windows/schedules/tuning/log/settings as applicable): a nested-only config is actually validated, not silently passed.
- Flat-key configs validate exactly as before.
- Tests cover nested-only, flat-only, and mixed configs, mirroring opencode's normalize compat shim semantics.
- opencode's flat-key shim is NOT removed by this change — removal waits on this and the route-proxy follow-on (developing-today/code issue #3889) both landing.

title: fix(quota): CLI misses the local-store fallback when a live server withholds the refresh token — forward usesLocalStore through the combined source (code#2490 phase 2)

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: source/queue-worker
labels.description: Filed or worked by the queue/worker pilot

labels.name: priority/high
labels.description: Important and time-sensitive

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: meta/enriched
labels.description: Intake review done: acceptance criteria, links, and normalized labels added

body:
## Problem

The `openchamber quota` CLI can still report Antigravity as "Not configured" for a healthy, signed-in pool in the one case the server endpoint no longer can: **the OpenCode server is up and answering, but its served credential projection withholds the refresh token** the Antigravity resolver must present.

Evidence at openchamber main `04e6a7e4` (2026-11-01), from triage of developing-today/code#2490:

- The endpoint path is fixed: `packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/antigravity/index.js:47-67` falls back to `readLocalOpenCodeCredentials()` when the projected read yields no candidates **and** `credentialSourceUsesLocalStore()` is true; a store read failure surfaces as its own error state (`Failed to read OpenCode credential store`, PR #860, #858 closed).
- The CLI wires a combined source: `packages/web/bin/lib/commands-quota.js:392` — `createFallbackCredentialSource(serverSource, openCodeLocalCredentialSource())`. That fallback switches to the local store **only on transport failure** (`isTransportFailure`, commands-quota.js:~195-232). A live server answering with a withholding projection is not a transport failure, so the CLI never reaches the store at the source level.
- The provider-level fallback cannot rescue the CLI either: the combined source declares no `usesLocalStore`, and `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/auth.js` (`credentialSourceUsesLocalStore`, ~line 63-73) treats a source that does not say — its own comment names "the quota CLI's combined source" — as **not** known-local, so the direct-store read is never enabled there.

Result: three surfaces, still two semantics for this case — endpoint reads the pool, CLI says "Not configured", the aggregator hub (direct store read) reads the pool. This is phase 2 of the code#2490 unification ruling.

## Fix shape

Forward the primary source's locality through the CLI's combined source: when the server source is `openCodeCredentialSource`, its `usesLocalStore()` already knows the truth (managed launch, or loopback URL — auth.js:~115-130). `createFallbackCredentialSource` should expose `usesLocalStore: () => primary.usesLocalStore?.() ?? false` so the Antigravity resolver's existing, Codex-guarded fallback (PR #860 / #1063 semantics: never substitute this machine's store for a remote OpenCode) activates in the CLI exactly as it does on the endpoint.

## Acceptance

- CLI + endpoint return the same Antigravity result in the same tick for: (a) server up, projection withholding refresh token, local store holding the login → both read the pool; (b) server up via a non-loopback `OPENCODE_HOST` → CLI does **not** substitute the local store (the #860 guard holds); (c) server down → CLI reads via the local store as today (transport fallback unchanged).
- A credential-store read failure in the CLI surfaces as its own error, distinct from "Not configured" (endpoint parity).
- Existing commands-quota tests pass; add coverage for the forwarded `usesLocalStore` and case (a)/(b).

Refs: developing-today/code#2490 (triage ruling, 2026-11-01), #858, PR #860, #1063.

body:
## Finding (from PR review)

CodeRabbit Minor (Functional Correctness) on PR #938 — "Preserve the shared-auth origin in xAI results":

> `readOpenCodeCredentials()` propagates failures from the configured OpenCode credential source. When it rejects with `Authentication required`, `readXaiAuth()` replaces that error with `Failed to read xAI OAuth credentials`. The dispatcher then cannot add `errorKind: 'opencode_upstream_auth'` or show the shared OpenCode password guidance. Carry an explicit credential-read source marker through the xAI result and classify that marker. Do not pass through the raw `Authentication required` text alone, because the dispatcher would also classify an identical provider API error as a shared-auth failure.

- Source PR: https://github.com/developing-today/openchamber/pull/938 (OPEN; parent issue #894)
- Review comment: https://github.com/developing-today/openchamber/pull/938#discussion_r4425554381 — coderabbitai[bot], 2026-10-30T15:49:26Z, `packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/index.js:570`
- Flagged code: `packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/xai.js` — `readXaiAuth()` catches any credential-read failure and returns `{ entry: null, error: 'Failed to read xAI OAuth credentials' }`, discarding the original error and its origin.

## No-response evidence

- The review thread is unresolved (GraphQL `reviewThreads`: isResolved=false) and its only author is CodeRabbit — no reply from the PR author or any maintainer.
- The PR head is unchanged since the review: single commit `045b38bee17a` (2026-10-30T15:34:54Z); no fix commit followed. The comment is >24h old and the PR is still open, so the open-PR grace rule is passed.

## Still live on the PR head (verified 2026-11-01, head `045b38bee`)

- `providers/xai.js`, `readXaiAuth()`: the catch returns the generic `Failed to read xAI OAuth credentials` error with no marker and no preserved cause.
- The dispatcher's classifier in `providers/index.js` matches only the exact text `Authentication required`, so a shared credential-path failure surfaced through xAI leaves the module unclassified — no `errorKind: 'opencode_upstream_auth'`, no shared-failure guidance — one of the ten-provider identical-failure shapes #894 exists to eliminate.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `readXaiAuth` preserves an explicit marker (or the original error) when the configured OpenCode credential source fails, and the dispatcher classifies that marker so the xAI result carries `errorKind: 'opencode_upstream_auth'` for shared-path failures only.
- [ ] A test covers the xAI credential-read shared-auth failure case, and provider-API `Authentication required` errors remain unclassified.
- [ ] Or: resolve by a documented decision on this issue.

body:
## Summary

The guest OAuth module reads token-endpoint and account-endpoint answers with **bare `response.json()` and no byte cap** — only the 20 s `GUEST_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS` deadline bounds them. Both endpoints are **declared by the guest package itself** (`integration.oauth.tokenUrl`, and the integration's `apiOrigin` + `account.path`, resolved via `resolveIntegrationApi` / `credentialTarget` in `packages/web/server/lib/guests/oauth.js:234-242`), i.e. third-party extension code names the server that answers. This is not the fixed-SaaS-endpoint class and not the loopback own-server class: a guest-declared (or compromised / misbehaving) endpoint that streams a chunked body with no `Content-Length` is buffered whole in the long-lived web server process before `JSON.parse` ever runs.

Every sibling read in the same subsystem is capped while streaming:

- `guests/request.js:40` — the guest API proxy reads via `readBoundedResponseText(response, GUEST_REQUEST_RESPONSE_MAX)` (8,000,000 bytes, `packages/sdk/src/contract.ts:402`) and throws `RESPONSE_TOO_LARGE` past it.
- `guests/service.js:753` — the panel proxy reads via `readBoundedResponseText(response, responseMax)`.
- `guests/surface.js:438/467` — resize/clipboard answers capped at schema-sized maxima; frames via `readBoundedResponseBytes`.
- `spaces/login-keeper.js` — the other token exchange in the codebase caps the issuer's answer at 64 KiB, enforced *while streaming*, with the comment (citing #842) that a chunked answer with no declared length must not grow server memory past the cap before being refused.

`oauth.js` is the one guest read path that was missed.

## Evidence (verified on main `3337f3b91`)

- `packages/web/server/lib/guests/oauth.js:130` — `postForm`: `const payload = await response.json().catch(() => null);` after a POST to the guest-declared `tokenUrl`. Called by `exchangeAuthorizationCode` (:154, authorization-code exchange) and directly by `refreshGuestAccessToken` (:469, token refresh).
- `packages/web/server/lib/guests/oauth.js:147` — `postJson`: same bare `response.json()`; the JSON fallback leg of `exchangeAuthorizationCode`.
- `packages/web/server/lib/guests/oauth.js:225` — `fetchAccountLabel`: same bare `response.json()` on `GET <apiOrigin><account.path>`; called from `saveGuestAccessToken` (:336) and `consumeGuestAuthorization` (:432). Only the single account-name string is consumed from the payload.
- The only bound on all three is `signal: AbortSignal.timeout(GUEST_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS)` (20 s, `packages/sdk/src/contract.ts:403`) — a deadline is not a byte cap: a fast endpoint can deliver hundreds of MiB inside it.
- **Laptop probe vs the real module** (fork at main, `oauth.js` md5 `7c485b8c9ec9f13e7b093cfde5264798` identical to sandbox main; probe at laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-guest-oauth-cap-20261031/probe.mjs`, stubbed `fetch` returning a streamed 32 MiB JSON body with no `Content-Length`):
  - Leg 1 — `refreshGuestAccessToken` → `postForm`: **pulled all 33,554,432 bytes**, refresh succeeded (`storedAccess: "access-new"`), RSS **+110 MB**.
  - Leg 2 — `saveGuestAccessToken` → `fetchAccountLabel`: **pulled all 33,554,432 bytes**, returned `{connected: true, account: "ada"}` — the whole body was buffered to extract one short string.
- Existing tests (`guests/oauth.test.js`) stub small JSON answers only; nothing pins an over-cap token or account answer.

## Why it matters

Guest packages are third-party extensions; their integration manifests name the OAuth token endpoint and the API origin the host sends credentials to and reads tokens from. Token answers are a few hundred bytes and an account label is one short string — there is no legitimate answer anywhere near even 1 MiB. Today one guest-declared endpoint can grow the web server's memory without bound (up to what it can push in 20 s) on every connect, token paste, and refresh, in the process that hosts every session. The subsystem's own contract — bounded reads via `lib/guests/response-body.js` — is already established everywhere else in `guests/`; this is the remaining hole in it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] All three reads in `guests/oauth.js` (`postForm`, `postJson`, `fetchAccountLabel`) read the body through the bounded reader (`readBoundedResponseText` from `guests/response-body.js`, as `request.js`/`service.js` do) with an explicit named cap sized for token/account answers (the 64 KiB token-answer precedent in `spaces/login-keeper.js`, or `GUEST_REQUEST_RESPONSE_MAX` with the rationale recorded); the cap is enforced while streaming, so a chunked body with no declared length cannot exceed it in memory.
- [ ] Over-cap behaviour preserves the existing error shapes: a token answer over the cap fails the exchange/refresh with a `GuestOAuthError` (never a stored token, never a silent `null` payload treated as an empty-token error); an account answer over the cap leaves `fetchAccountLabel`'s contract intact (account label empty / probe not-ok as the callers already handle).
- [ ] At-cap and ordinary answers behave byte-identically to today: authorization-code exchange (form leg and JSON fallback leg), refresh, and account-label probing all keep working, including the non-OK error path that reads `error` / `error_description` from the payload.
- [ ] Regression tests in `guests/oauth.test.js` pin: a streamed over-cap token answer (no `Content-Length`) is refused without being buffered whole; a streamed over-cap account answer does not connect with a fabricated account; an at-cap token answer still exchanges successfully.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for `guest oauth` and for guest body-cap terms: no issue covers the `guests/oauth.js` reads (the only hit, #304 closed, is about Linear 1Password references — unrelated). The bounded-read fixes in this subsystem (`request.js`, `service.js`, `surface.js`) landed without an issue covering the OAuth paths; #842's streaming-cap precedent is in `spaces/login-keeper.js`, a different module. Related but distinct: the quota/GitLab/GitHub bare-`response.json()` reads previously dispositioned as fixed-SaaS endpoints do not apply here — these endpoints are guest-declared.

title: fix(web): persistent-pty proxy pre-open queue is unbounded and its upstream handshake has no deadline — a stalled OpenCode connect buffers every client byte forever (realtime-proxy twin fixed in #962)

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

The persistent-PTY WebSocket proxy buffers client input with **no bound and no handshake deadline**: while its upstream WebSocket to OpenCode is `CONNECTING`, every client message is pushed onto a `pending` array that is only drained if the upstream `open` event fires. If the upstream handshake stalls (OpenCode wedged during startup, a half-open connection, a remote that accepts TCP but never answers the upgrade), the queue — and the long-lived web server's memory — grows for as long as the client keeps sending, and nothing ever closes the pair. The sibling realtime proxy had exactly this defect and was fixed in #962 with a 256 KiB pending bound plus a handshake timeout; this proxy, which shares the same `pending`/`flush` structure, was missed.

## Evidence (verified on main `bfc55dd93`)

- `packages/web/server/lib/persistent-pty/runtime.js:61-80` — `const pending = []`, `client.on('message', ...)` pushes `[data, isBinary]` whenever `upstream.readyState === WebSocket.CONNECTING`; `flush` on upstream `open` is the only drain. No byte/count accounting, no `bufferedAmount` check on the `OPEN` forwarding path either, and no timer anywhere in the 139-line file — the upstream `new WebSocket(...)` at `:52` is created with no handshake timeout.
- The established in-repo pattern, `packages/web/server/lib/realtime-proxy.js`: `MAX_PENDING_BYTES = 256 * 1024` (`:8`), `MAX_BUFFERED_BYTES = 16 MiB` (`:10`), pending-byte accounting that terminates the upstream and closes the client with 1013 when the bound is exceeded (`:267-280`), a `closeIfPeerTooSlow` backpressure check on the open forwarding path, and a `handshakeTimeoutMs` parameter — all from #962.
- The existing tests pin none of this: `packages/web/server/lib/persistent-pty/runtime.test.js` covers framed proxying and the 401 upgrade rejection only.
- **Laptop probe vs the real module** (bun, fork at `bfc55dd93`, `runtime.js` md5-identical to main; probe at laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-pty-pending-20261031/`): the real runtime in a child process, upstream pointed at a TCP server that accepts the connection and never answers the WS upgrade (upstream stuck `CONNECTING`); a client sent 48 × 1 MiB binary frames. Server-process RSS went **27 MB → 85 MB (+58 MB)** and the client connection was still open afterwards (`readyState: 1`, never closed by the proxy). Under the realtime proxy's bound the pair would have been closed after 256 KiB.

## Why it matters

This proxy fronts terminal input for persistent PTY sessions — a surface where a client legitimately sends large pastes and where automated clients (reconnecting UIs, replayed input) can send continuously. OpenCode restarts and slow starts are routine in the managed-server layer, so the `CONNECTING` window is not exotic; a stall inside it converts directly into unbounded memory growth in the server process that hosts every other session, with no log, no metric, and no recovery short of the client disconnecting on its own.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The persistent-pty proxy bounds its pre-open queue the way #962 bounded the realtime proxy: pending bytes are accounted, and past an explicit named cap the pair is closed (queued bytes never flushed) instead of buffering further.
- [ ] The upstream handshake gets a deadline: if `open` has not fired within a named timeout, the pair is closed and the queue dropped.
- [ ] Forwarding to a slow peer is bounded (a `bufferedAmount` check on the `OPEN` path, mirroring the realtime proxy) or the omission is explicitly justified in the code.
- [ ] Regression tests in `persistent-pty/runtime.test.js` pin: a stalled handshake plus over-cap input closes the client and retains nothing, a slow-but-successful handshake still flushes queued input in order, and normal framed proxying is unchanged.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for persistent-pty / pty proxy / pending-queue terms: #962 covers `realtime-proxy.js` only, #961 covers dev-tunnel piping, #1017 the dictation reorder buffer. No issue covers `persistent-pty/runtime.js`.
