body:
## Scope — phase 2 of design #976

Migrate the web server's convergent JSON state stores onto the shared durable-store primitive landed in phase 1 (the sibling sub-issue of #976), module by module — each module is an independently landable step. This phase sequences **after** phase 1 lands.

The fifteen preserve-and-proceed stores whose private implementations are semantics-identical (they differ only in spelling — preserve-name uniqueness, temp-name shape, stated vs omitted write mode, presence of revalidation):

`client-auth/pairing.js`, `client-auth/remote-clients.js`, `magic-prompts/runtime.js`, `ui-auth/ui-passkeys.js`, `notifications/apns-runtime.js`, `notifications/push-runtime.js`, `routing/route-overrides-store.js`, `routing/route-settings.js`, `tunnels/managed-config.js`, `tts/voice-keys.js`, `dispatch-results/runtime.js`, `message-queue/runtime.js`, `openchamber-sessions/archive-store.js`, `openchamber-sessions/session-metadata-store.js`, `session-warming/runtime.js`

(file:line for each store's private copy is in #976's grounding list; all line refs are main `ec3ce98889`.)

Per module: the private `.corrupt-` preservation, temp-name and write code is replaced by the shared primitive; the store keeps its shape, defaults, domain error surface, serialization/locking (e.g. pairing's persist queue, routing's write queue — the primitive composes with them) and its fs-injection seam. A store whose callers cannot tolerate rule 2's fail-closed refusal surfaces that in its own step rather than silently keeping a divergent spelling.

### Excluded by name

- `opencode/settings-runtime.js` — the multi-writer shared `settings.json` with its own migration semantics (#899); folding it in is a settings-file decision, not a spelling migration (open question on #976).
- Stores with an open fix issue at migration time — today #936 (skills-catalog installed-sources) and #940 (GitHub settings toggles) — they land on their own PRs and adopt the primitive afterwards; this phase never races an in-flight fix (the #802 phase-2 rule).
- The named divergent policies of #976 rule 5 (`relay/key-store.js`, `agent-memory/runtime.js`, `walkthrough/store.js`, other caches) — not migrated, not redefined.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Each of the fifteen listed stores uses the shared primitive for its strict read, preservation and atomic write; no store's shape, defaults or domain error surface changes.
- [ ] Stores that previously passed no write mode now state one explicitly through the primitive (the value is the store's current effective behaviour unless its own step records a deliberate tightening, e.g. `0o600` for a secret-bearing store).
- [ ] Completion is grep-checkable: `.corrupt-` and the private temp-name spellings survive only in `packages/web/server/lib/shared/` and in the documented divergences named in `shared/DOCUMENTATION.md`.
- [ ] Each migrated store's existing tests pass unmodified in behaviour; any test that pinned a private spelling (exact preserved-file name, exact temp name) is updated to pin the contract instead.
- [ ] `bun run check:changed` passes per module step.

Design: #976 (full doc: `files/designs/openchamber-durable-json-store.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace).

title: refactor(web,electron,ui): outside-file grants are minted and threaded but never validated — remove the dead grant machinery left by a91777602

labels.name: kind/refactor
labels.description: Code restructuring with no behavior change

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Problem

The outside-file grant is dead security machinery: tokens are still minted, stored, threaded through the UI, and sent on every outside-workspace file request — but no server code has validated one since a91777602 ("fix(files): open outside-workspace files without grants") deliberately removed the validator. The remaining code misleads readers into believing outside-workspace reads are grant-bound when they are auth-only by design.

This issue does **not** propose restoring grant enforcement — that was a settled maintainer decision (a91777602: "Read outside files under normal server authentication and OS permissions"). It proposes removing (or explicitly deprecating) the leftover machinery so the code says what it does.

## Evidence (verified this run, on current `main` adc00f640)

- `packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.js:22-31,86-126` — `outsideFileGrants` Map, `pruneOutsideFileGrants`, and the exported `mintOutsideFileGrant` (realpath + stat, 10-minute TTL, scopes) still exist and still run.
- No consumer remains: `grep -rn "outsideFileGrant" packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.js` finds only the mint side. `resolveReadPathFromContext` (routes.js:536-546) returns `{ ok: true, … }` for any path when `allowOutsideWorkspace === 'true'` and never reads `req.query.outsideFileGrant`; the `scope` argument its callers pass is unused on that branch. a91777602's diff (verified via `git show`) deleted `resolveOutsideFileGrant` — the only validator — and removed the client grant cache in the UI.
- Minters still mint: `packages/web/server/lib/markdown-image-grants/routes.js:362-370` mints a `['raw']` grant for every outside-workspace assistant image, under the comment at :361 "Reuse the existing path-bound raw-file grant instead of creating another asset lifecycle" — the grant is not path-bound in effect, because nothing checks it. `packages/electron/main.mjs:6102,6130` mints `['stat','read','raw']` grants for picked/target files and returns the token to the renderer.
- Threading still threads: the token is returned to the UI and attached to file requests in `packages/web/src/api/files.ts:232,261,394`, `packages/ui/src/components/chat/markdown/markdownImageAssets.ts:269-283`, and `packages/ui/src/components/session/project-context/PlansSection.tsx:155-156` — and ignored on arrival.
- Tests encode the deadness without naming it: `packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.test.js` — "ignores legacy grants when reading another outside file" expects a read of a *different* path with a mismatched grant to succeed (200), and the adjacent tests show `allowOutsideWorkspace: 'true'` alone reading `/etc/passwd` from the fixture. The word "legacy" in that one test title is the only place the deprecation is recorded.
- Retention wart: expired grants are only pruned when a new grant is minted (routes.js:101), so the Map holds dead tokens indefinitely in a server that never mints again — small, but it is state kept for a check that never happens.

## Why it matters

A maintainer reading `markdown-image-grants` or the Electron picker today reasonably concludes outside-workspace reads are capability-bound to an exact path and scope; they are not, by deliberate design. Security-relevant dead code is worse than ordinary dead code: it invites changes built on a false boundary (e.g. a future route "protected" by requiring a grant parameter that is never validated), and every mint costs a realpath+stat on the image-preparation path for nothing.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The grant machinery is removed end-to-end, or explicitly deprecated with a pointer to a91777602: `mintOutsideFileGrant` + `outsideFileGrants` + `pruneOutsideFileGrants` in fs/routes.js; the mint in markdown-image-grants/routes.js (results return path/status only); the Electron mints in main.mjs:6102,6130; the token threading in packages/web/src/api/files.ts, markdownImageAssets.ts, PlansSection.tsx, and the `outsideFileGrant` fields in shared API/desktop types.
- [ ] The misleading comment at markdown-image-grants/routes.js:361 is replaced with the actual rule: outside-workspace reads are allowed under normal server authentication and OS permissions (a91777602), and image sources must be referenced by the assistant message (the `referenced` check above it is the real gate).
- [ ] fs `DOCUMENTATION.md` and any docs describing grant-bound outside reads are updated to match.
- [ ] Tests updated: the mint/grant tests in fs/routes.test.js and markdown-image-grants/routes.test.js are removed or rewritten to assert the auth-only behavior directly; the "legacy grants" test title's implicit deprecation is no longer the only record.
- [ ] No behavior change for clients: outside-workspace stat/read/raw with `allowOutsideWorkspace=true` behave exactly as today, with or without an `outsideFileGrant` parameter (old clients sending one keep working).

## Dedup

`gh issue list --search "outside file grant"` and `--search "grant dead"` (open + closed) return no covering issue. a91777602 is a merged commit, not an issue, and it removed the validator + UI cache but left the server minters and threading in place (the markdown-image minter was re-added afterwards in fe644985a, citing the by-then-dead grant).

title: fix(ci): agents.yml has no concurrency group — overlapping scheduled/manual runs launch duplicate bolt/palette/suggestions sessions with no dedupe

labels.name: kind/ci

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.description: Needs a user-look: Muse reviews first and handles what it can

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: area/ci
labels.description: CI, workflows, and build infrastructure

body:
## Problem

`agents.yml` — the thin caller that runs this repo's scheduled agents (added 2026-10-30 in f6473d92a / 6ccd9093f, converting to the central `pm-scheduled` reusable in developing-today/code#2672) — is now the only workflow in this repo with **no concurrency group at all**, and neither the reusable callee nor the dispatch action compensates for non-`ci-fix` tasks. Overlapping runs therefore launch duplicate live agent sessions for the same scheduled task.

This is the same failure class as #923 (pm-dispatch-smoke, fixed in PR #927), in the workflow that replaced/augmented that dispatch surface the same day.

## Evidence (verified this run, on current `main` adc00f640)

- `.github/workflows/agents.yml` (whole file, 40 lines): triggers are `schedule: '0 2 * * *'` + `'0 14 * * *'` and `workflow_dispatch` with `task` ∈ all/bolt/palette/suggestions. `grep -c concurrency .github/workflows/agents.yml` = **0**. Every other workflow in `.github/workflows/` (25 files, 29 `concurrency:` occurrences across the set) defines a group.
- The callee defines none either: `developing-today/code:.github/workflows/pm-scheduled.yml@main` (bd5896fa) has no `concurrency:` — its single job runs one `pm-dispatch-task` step per resolved task (bolt, palette, suggestions).
- `pm-dispatch-task` (code repo, `.github/actions/pm-dispatch-task/action.yml@main`): the dedupe step is gated `if: inputs.task == 'ci-fix'` — it searches for an existing open tracking issue **only for ci-fix**. For bolt/palette/suggestions the dispatch step is unconditional: `Dispatch via pm-dispatch-start (launch a session now)`, `if: inputs.task != 'ci-fix' || …`, with `wait: "true"`. Each invocation creates a new queue task, a new OpenCode session, and a new tracking issue (outputs `task_id` / `session_id` / `issue_number`).
- Overlap is reachable in normal use: a manual `workflow_dispatch` (e.g. `task: all`) while a scheduled run is in flight, two manual dispatches minutes apart, or a dispatch retried after an apparent stall. Scheduled slots are 12 h apart, but a `wait: "true"` dispatch session can run long, and nothing serializes a dispatch against the next slot either.

## Why it matters

Bolt and palette are work-performing agents: two concurrent instances of the same scheduled task on the same repo duplicate pool burn, can open duplicate PRs/issues for the same improvement, and race each other on the same files — exactly what #923's concurrency group and #916's serialization were filed to stop on sibling surfaces. The dedupe that exists in the dispatch action does not cover these tasks at all.

## Cross-repo set (one issue, handled as a set)

The identical thin caller, also with no `concurrency:` (verified via `gh api repos/<repo>/contents/.github/workflows/agents.yml`, 0 matches each), exists in:

- developing-today/code — `agents.yml`, schedule `0 1 * * *` (+ suggestions slot)
- developing-today/opencode — `agents.yml`, schedule `0 0 * * *` (+ suggestions slot)
- dezren39/nix — `agents.yml` (thin caller, same shape)
- developing-today/zettel — `agents.yml` (same pattern; outside the four-repo fleet, listed for completeness — the fix there is the caller's owner's call)

Fixing only this repo leaves the same duplicate-dispatch window open in the other callers; the per-repo fix is the same few lines in each caller (a reusable workflow cannot impose caller-job concurrency).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `agents.yml` in this repo gains a workflow-level concurrency group that serializes runs of this workflow (e.g. group `agents`, `cancel-in-progress: false`, `queue: max` — matching the main-broken watcher / pm-dispatch-smoke pattern in this repo), so a second trigger queues instead of launching duplicate sessions; a running dispatch is never cancelled mid-session.
- [ ] The group choice is reasoned in the PR: why not `cancel-in-progress: true` (dispatch steps run with `wait: "true"`; cancelling the caller does not reliably stop an already-launched session), and why one group for all task selections rather than per-task groups (per-task groups would still let `task: all` overlap `task: bolt`).
- [ ] The same change is applied to the callers in developing-today/code, developing-today/opencode, and dezren39/nix (PRs there reference this issue), or a SET-REMAINDER note records which callers remain.
- [ ] No schedule, task-list, or prompt changes: triggers and the `pm-scheduled` inputs are byte-identical apart from the added concurrency block.

## Dedup

`gh issue list --search "agents.yml concurrency"` and `--search "agents workflow concurrency scheduled"` (open + closed) return nothing. #923 covered `pm-dispatch-smoke.yml` only; that workflow now has a group (verified above). #916/#918/#927 are sibling serialization fixes, not this workflow.

body:
## Problem

Since sometime between 02:48 and 03:02 CDT on 2026-10-30, the laptop OpenChamber server's `/api/quota/*` endpoint returns `Authentication required` for most providers, while a minority still succeed. The fleet's measurement gate (dispatcher + babysitter + quota steward) depends on this endpoint; with it broken, most pools cannot be verified and dispatch degrades to the hourly hub export until that goes stale.

## Evidence (2026-10-30, laptop server, OpenChamber 2.5.0, pid 1694045, startedAt 2026-10-30T06:39:47Z, serverId LgSj5VlhWhEdG-5AgZ5DNY5twgI_0CGm8HXdpI_SYe8 — server NOT restarted)

- 02:45–02:48 CDT dispatcher run: full `/api/quota/*` read succeeded for all 14 providers (raw saved in goal hidden_files `dispatch-packets/quota-2026-10-30-0245.json.txt`).
- 03:02 CDT, dispatcher + babysitter (independent, concurrent reads, fetchedAt 1793347337–1793347338): `{"error":"Authentication required"}` or `ok:false, error:"Authentication required"` for opencode-go, meta, cline-pass, codex, openai.alternate, google, github-copilot, openrouter, deepseek, command-code. claude still fails separately with "Rate limited. Retrying soon."; openai still "Unsupported provider" (both pre-existing).
- Still failing on re-reads at 03:03 and 03:06 CDT.
- Unaffected in the same reads: antigravity ok:true, opendesign ok:true (5h 0% / 7d 2.71%); `/api/version` and `/api/session-activity` answer normally (17 sessions enumerated).
- The hourly hub export (`quota-hub-2026-10-30-0215.json.txt`, generatedAt 2026-10-30T07:15:19Z) still shows all providers ok — it was generated before the failure.

## Impact

- Dispatcher measurement gate: live per-pool verification unavailable for meta / codex / opencode-go / cline-pass / openai.alternate / google / github-copilot / openrouter / command-code; runs fall back to the ≤60-min hub picture and must close those pools once it stales.
- Any consumer of `/api/quota/*` (quota steward, babysitter pool-effectiveness checks) is blind on the same providers.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Root cause identified: what authentication expired / became unavailable between 02:48 and 03:02 CDT with no server restart, and why antigravity + opendesign are unaffected while the other providers share one error string.
- [ ] `/api/quota/*` returns ok:true with fresh windows for the previously failing providers (or a specific, actionable per-provider error instead of one shared string).
- [ ] A regression test or health check covers the shared-auth failure mode so one credential-path failure is surfaced as such, not as N identical provider errors.

Filed by the openchamber-dispatcher run 2026-10-30 03:00 CDT, which also recorded the failure in hidden_files/dispatcher-log.md.

body:
DREW DIRECTION (2026-10-29, main chat): the scheduled-tasks subsystem's hard 30-minute run cap is a top-priority fix.

Requirements:
- REMOVE the hard cap as a fixed product limit. We are in full control of this code; a fleet queue-lane run legitimately needs far longer (the Muse lane shifts it mirrors run ~90 minutes).
- Make the limit CONFIGURABLE in two places: per scheduled task (a field on the task) and server-wide (a global setting that applies when a task doesn't set its own).
- Set the server-wide value VERY HIGH as the shipped default posture for our deployment (effectively unbounded for practical purposes), so existing and new tasks are not silently strangled; per-task values remain available where a bound is genuinely wanted.
- A run that does hit a configured limit must SAY so in its run record (distinguishable from a failure), so the watchdog can tell a capped run from a crashed one.

Context: the first two fleet queue lanes went live as OpenChamber scheduled tasks on 2026-10-29 (code#2174) with prompts that self-limit to ~30 min only because of this cap. Once this lands, the lane prompts' self-limit can be raised to match the lane discipline instead.

## Acceptance criteria

- The hard 30-minute run cap is gone as a fixed product limit: a scheduled task with no per-task limit and no server-wide override runs past 30 minutes without being killed.
- A per-task limit field exists and is honored, and a server-wide default setting exists that applies when a task sets none; the shipped server-wide default is very high (effectively unbounded for practical purposes), as directed.
- A run terminated by a configured limit records that fact distinctly in its run record (capped, not failed), so the watchdog can tell a capped run from a crashed one.

body:
## Summary

Two external-consumer feature requests filed the same day by the fleet babysitter program — #524 (session-activity API) and #525 (managed-server registry) — each presuppose a contract neither defines: payload versioning, empty-vs-unknown semantics, and what may never be exposed. Built independently they will diverge in exactly the ways external consumers cannot tolerate. This design is the shared contract, in five rules, with each issue landing as one phase under it:

1. **Additive-only, versioned in the payload** — every response carries `version: 1` + `serverTime`; fields may be added in v1, never redefined. The existing `{ type }` field of `/api/session-activity` is frozen (shared UI and the VS Code bridge consume it today).
2. **Explicit unknowns, never fabricated values** — an unknown field is `null`, never `0` / "now" / silently dropped; an unreadable upstream marks the read unavailable instead of returning a partial read dressed as complete (the session-activity probe's null-means-unknown convention, applied at the HTTP boundary).
3. **Empty vs unknown is distinguishable** — session activity carries `watcherReady`; registry entries carry a `status` where an unverifiable server is `"unknown"`, not dropped and not `"ready"`.
4. **Allowlist projection, no auth material, ever** — `state.json` holds the managed password and agent-tool token (`managed-opencode-state.js`: the file "is 0600 and never logged"); the registry exposes an explicit field allowlist, and a test pins the key set.
5. **Authoritative sources only** — the registry is served from lifecycle/registry state via the existing validated readers, the activity read from the session runtime's tracked maps. No process scanning: ownership inferred from `ps` is the fragile path the managed-process registry exists to replace.

Evidence for the gaps, from current main:

- `packages/web/server/lib/notifications/routes.js:287` — `/api/session-activity` returns `getSessionActivitySnapshot()` and nothing else.
- `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/session-runtime.js:366` — the snapshot projects only `data.phase`; the phase map already records `updatedAt` (`session-runtime.js:176`) and the snapshot **drops it**. No last-activity, no model/provider, no tool-in-flight — the babysitter's stall detector (developing-today/code#1192) is blocked on last-activity specifically.
- `packages/web/server/lib/notifications/runtime.js:266` — the notifications runtime already remembers per-message `agent` + `modelID` (`assistantStepMeta`), the precedent/data source for the model/provider fields.
- `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/managed-process-registry.js:179` — registry records carry pid, ownerPid, port, binary, runtime, startedAt; `managed-opencode-state.js` carries pid/port/binary/fingerprint plus secrets. There is no API read of either; external tools scrape `ps` or files that were never an interface (#525).

## Phased breakdown

1. **Phase 1 — Session-activity v1 fields** → lands as the existing **#524** (linked as a sub-issue below, enqueued): additive `lastActivityAt` (the already-recorded phase `updatedAt`), `status`, `model`/`provider` (`{ modelID, providerID } | null`, remembered from the latest assistant message info), `toolInFlight: boolean | null`, plus top-level `version` + `watcherReady`, and the route shape documented where API consumers will find it.
2. **Phase 2 — Managed-server registry read** → lands as the existing **#525** (sub-issue, enqueued): new `GET /api/managed-servers`; the hosting instance's own server is the complete entry (directory, port, version, status incl. `draining`, `startedAt`, live session count), other instances' entries carry what the registry record actually has with `null` for the rest; stopped servers leave the list with their records (no zombies, verified against process ground truth).
3. **Phase 3 — Contract documentation + consumer conformance fixture** → new sub-issue filed with this design (enqueued): one external-consumer doc (both reads, the five rules, empty-vs-unknown semantics, model/provider documented as *observed* not configured) and a paired-client conformance fixture pinning key sets, `version`, readiness semantics, and secret-field absence.

Alternatives considered and why they lose, full risk analysis, and the open questions (spawn-time registry enrichment incl. the VS Code parity writer; push vs poll; snapshot retention semantics) are in the design doc — they stay questions, not issues, until answered.

## Links

- Design doc: `files/designs/openchamber-external-observability-contract.md` in the fleet goal workspace (`keep-the-four-repos-healthy`), registered in `files/potential-projects.md`
- Implementation vehicles: #524, #525 (sub-issues), phase 3 (sub-issue, filed with this design)
- Consumers: developing-today/code#1185 (babysitter), developing-today/code#1192 (stall detector)
- Non-goals: no control surface (reads stay read-only), no change to `/api/sessions/snapshot` or `/api/sessions/status`, no durable-cursor work (that is #2), no change to the registry on-disk format or the reaper safety model in v1

🤖 **Agent note** · state: filed
- **Agent:** repo-design-architect job
- **Session / ID:** repo-design-architect cron run 2026-10-27 20:33 CDT (split rotation: opencode / openchamber / nix; openchamber's first pass)
- **Found via:** design pass over ROADMAP.md, TODO.md, planning/, docs/, and the open issue list; #524/#525 read in full; code evidence verified against the local clone on current main
- **Task:** Design issue — the contract above is the deliverable; phases 1–2 land as #524/#525, phase 3 as its own sub-issue, all enqueued to repo-health-openchamber-pilot
- **Expectation:** effort/l across the three phases; this issue closes when all three sub-issues land or are explicitly retired
<!-- agent-note:v1 agent=repo-design-architect state=filed at=2026-10-28T01:33:00Z -->

## Acceptance criteria

- Phase 1 (#524) lands: `/api/session-activity` returns the additive v1 fields (`lastActivityAt`, `status`, `model`/`provider`, `toolInFlight`) plus top-level `version: 1`, `serverTime`, and `watcherReady`; the existing `{ type }` field is unchanged.
- Phase 2 (#525) lands: `GET /api/managed-servers` serves registry entries projected through the explicit field allowlist — a test pins the exposed key set and proves no auth material (managed password, agent-tool token) can appear.
- Phase 3 (#614) lands: the external-consumer contract doc and the paired-client conformance fixture pin key sets, `version`, and empty-vs-unknown semantics for both reads.
- Unknown values are explicit `null` / `"unknown"` everywhere in both reads — never fabricated `0`, "now", or silently dropped fields.
- This issue closes only when all three sub-issues have landed or been explicitly retired.

body:
## Finding

PR #488 (merged, merge commit `8711e6d56a4ead379926f4ca59e39f71cf54ad4d`) made the `openchamber-node_modules` fixed-output tree deterministic by deleting the store-internal `.bin` directories in the derivation's install phase — on **every** system. It only re-baked the `x86_64-linux` hash. The `aarch64-darwin` pin in `nix/hashes.json` is unchanged, so a darwin build now produces the new (stripped) tree but is checked against the pre-#488 (unstripped) hash and fails with a fixed-output hash mismatch.

This is distinct from #275: that issue tracks the `aarch64-linux` pin, which was already stale before #488. The darwin pin was **not** stale — #275's evidence records that after PR #269 "the darwin build works", and the competing fix PR #491 deliberately exempted Darwin for exactly this reason ("Darwin is exempt: its pin was measured on a Mac and reproduces there, and the variance has only been observed on Linux"). #488 took the opposite choice (strip on all systems) but shipped no darwin re-measurement.

## Evidence

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/openchamber/pull/488 — diff changes `nix/hashes.json` only on the `x86_64-linux` line (`sha256-UTeYcuNWiTMZiOHzLoGNmRj8L0Kf3CJcmr/nytukvtM=` → `sha256-OifIHp4OC4AdtZfxozHwQD/s9OzgTLpEF/QHBCf+K5k=`); `aarch64-darwin` stays `sha256-2TrjBeUL2y50CzQ/QPOB8O91wkGYKptqB3x8KJn6BVU=`.
- Current `main` (verified this run via `git show origin/main:nix/package.nix`): the install phase strips unconditionally, with no platform guard —
  ```nix
  if [ -d $out/node_modules/.bun ]; then
    find $out/node_modules/.bun -mindepth 3 -maxdepth 3 -type d -name .bin -exec rm -rf {} +;
  fi
  ```
  and `git show origin/main:nix/hashes.json` still carries the same pre-#488 `aarch64-darwin` value above.
- Current `main`'s own `nix/update-hashes.sh` (rewritten by #488) can only bake the **current** system's hash and explicitly logs that the other systems' hashes "were NOT re-measured — no builder for them here", so this gap cannot close itself from a Linux host.
- Cross-check that the x86_64 half works: the post-#488 opencode-update failures tracked in #490 fail at `bun run test`, past the nix build step — the rebaked x86_64-linux pin verifies in CI.
- Dedupe: searched open/closed issues for `488 darwin`, `aarch64-darwin stale`, and `node_modules hash` — the only hits are #275 (Linux pins only; its 2026-10-26 intake comment confirms the aarch64-linux remainder and does not mention darwin), #422 and #449 (both closed, x86_64/#449-class). No issue tracks the darwin pin after #488.

## Why it matters

`aarch64-darwin` is a supported build target (the macOS app is built from this flake). Since #488 merged, a clean darwin build of `.#openchamber` fails before any package code compiles, and nothing in CI exercises darwin — so the breakage is silent until a Mac builder next tries it. This is the same failure class as #422/#275, this time introduced by a merged fix that changed the output tree for a system it did not re-measure.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] On an `aarch64-darwin` builder, `nix build .#openchamber.node_modules` (or `bash nix/update-hashes.sh` / `nix run .#update-hashes` from a committed tree) measures the post-#488 tree hash and `nix/hashes.json`'s `aarch64-darwin` entry is updated to that value.
- [ ] A subsequent clean `nix build .#openchamber` on `aarch64-darwin` succeeds through the node_modules fixed-output derivation (no hash mismatch).
- [ ] The `x86_64-linux` entry is unchanged by the fix, and the already-tracked `aarch64-linux` remainder stays with #275 (do not fold it into this issue).

body:
## Finding

PR #269 updated only the `aarch64-darwin` entry in `nix/hashes.json` after the upstream sync (#203) changed `bun.lock`. Its body and commit message state that the two Linux hashes are stale too but could not be measured on the author's Mac, and no issue was filed for that follow-up. PR #269 has now merged (merge commit `341e63bb282445091cdf6c146868a5e795598939`), so on current `main` the Linux nix builds fail with a fixed-output hash mismatch while the darwin build works.

## Evidence

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/openchamber/pull/269 (1 commit `1983c87671f9cd1e5652e95df70ce6f4170c2be4`), diff touches only the `aarch64-darwin` line of `nix/hashes.json`.
- PR body: "The two Linux hashes are stale too. They can't be measured on this Mac." / Risks: "The Linux builds stay broken until their hashes are measured."
- `nix/hashes.json` on current `main` (341e63bb2):
  - `x86_64-linux`: `sha256-j0XUH0wUrFK8y6dNQJVR9Hk51iQV89MGFTZqzWAFliE=`
  - `aarch64-linux`: `sha256-5E7Q+yRx5unuRZt7Z25yGsvVW1ACZT4qBR/uQNAW+Z0=`
  - `aarch64-darwin`: `sha256-2TrjBeUL2y50CzQ/QPOB8O91wkGYKptqB3x8KJn6BVU=` (updated by #269)
- The hash is consumed by the fixed-output `openchamber-node_modules` derivation in `nix/package.nix` (`outputHash = nodeModulesHash`, per-system via `bun install --cpu/--os`), so a stale entry fails the build before any package code compiles.
- **x86_64-linux measured this run** on an x86_64-linux host, building PR #269's base `b5f69e084` (whose `bun.lock` and package manifests PR #269's validation table confirms are identical to `main`'s):

  ```
  $ nix build .#packages.x86_64-linux.openchamber --no-link
  error: hash mismatch in fixed-output derivation '...-openchamber-node_modules-2.5.0.drv':
           specified: sha256-j0XUH0wUrFK8y6dNQJVR9Hk51iQV89MGFTZqzWAFliE=
              got:    sha256-l/YLyGlVTz60KAD9ylwVqKaN+DMxP+gAE2ba0ROvaIc=
  ```

- The `aarch64-linux` value has **not** been measured yet — it needs an aarch64-linux builder/host (the review sandbox is x86_64-linux). It is stale by the same reasoning PR #269 gives for darwin: the same `bun.lock` sync changed the install output, and both Linux entries predate it.

## Why it matters

Anyone building this fork's nix package on Linux — the package's primary server platform — hits a hard hash-mismatch failure on `main` today. The darwin fix in #269 makes the breakage easy to miss: the repo looks "fixed" while two of its three pinned systems still cannot build.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `nix/hashes.json` `x86_64-linux` is updated to `sha256-l/YLyGlVTz60KAD9ylwVqKaN+DMxP+gAE2ba0ROvaIc=` (re-measure to confirm before committing).
- [ ] `aarch64-linux` is measured on an aarch64-linux host/builder and its entry updated.
- [ ] `nix build .#packages.x86_64-linux.openchamber` and `nix build .#packages.aarch64-linux.openchamber` each complete (at minimum, their `openchamber-node_modules` derivations build without a hash mismatch) on `main` with the updated hashes.

body:
A place to choose how much a session row shows: two lines or one, and which elements appear on it.

Today the row's shape comes from fixed rules. List rows have two lines (title, then branch and badges); Tree rows and Chats have one; "Detailed rows" turns Tree's zone rows into two lines; "One line per session" (#20) turns List rows into one. Which elements a row carries is fixed per shape, and some are dropped on one-line rows (the branch, the provider logo, the PR number).

Wanted: one control, separate from the view mode and the section layout, that sets:

- **Lines:** two or one, for each kind of row (zone rows, rows under a project, chats), or one setting for all.
- **Elements:** which of these appear, and on which line:
  - title
  - time or elapsed turn counter
  - live status
  - pin marker
  - done hint
  - project icon
  - branch or space name
  - PR / issue badge
  - permission and question badges
  - goal glyph
  - provider logo
  - directory action indicator

Things to settle before building:

- **Where the control lives.** The display menu is already long, so this is probably a small Settings page (Appearance → Sidebar rows) with a live preview row, plus a shortcut from the display menu.
- **What can't be hidden.** The live status and the permission/question badges are how a row says it needs you, so they probably stay, or at least stay on by default.
- **Defaults.** Today's shapes become the default, so nothing changes until someone opts in.
- **Layout stability.** Rows of one kind keep one height (the virtualizer estimates by kind), and hover actions cover the right end of the first line, so the element picker has to keep rows the same height whatever they contain.
- **Which existing options this replaces.** Detailed rows and One line per session would become presets of this control; decide whether to keep them as shortcuts.
- **Phone.** Whether the phone sheet follows (its rows are separate components).

Code pointers: `components/session/sidebar/sessions/SessionTimelineRowBody.tsx` draws every row's lines and clusters; `SessionNodeItem.tsx` and `RunSidebarRow.tsx` decide what goes in them per render context.

## Acceptance criteria

- A single control (separate from view mode and section layout) sets row lines (two or one) per row kind or globally, and which elements appear on each line.
- Defaults reproduce today's row shapes exactly; nothing changes until a user opts in.
- Live status and permission/question badges cannot be fully hidden (or stay on by default), per the issue's design constraint.
- Rows of one kind keep a uniform height regardless of chosen elements, and hover actions still cover the first line's right end.
- "Detailed rows" and "One line per session" are either preserved as presets/shortcuts of the new control or removed with a documented migration.

body:
### Context & Background
In OpenChamber upstream PR #4582 / commit `390dc4a0fe`, plans in the Project Context sidebar have "Implement" and "Improve" actions (`KnowledgeActions.tsx` and `PlansSection.tsx`). Clicking "Implement" creates or opens a session to work on the plan. Currently, this creates a session with whatever default model is configured, with no awareness of model tiers or cost tracking.

In our fork (`developing-today`), we introduced:
1. Standardized model tiers: `cheap`, `standard`, and `frontier`.
2. Execution cost accounting using official `models.dev` catalog pricing, storing calculated USD cost in `cost_usd` per `route_attempt`.
3. Action button send mode toggle (`openchamber.routing.plans.actionSendMode`: `prefill` vs `auto-send`, default `prefill`).

### Feature Objective
Enhance Project Knowledge Plans with tier-aware session dispatching and plan-level accumulated cost/token metrics:
1. **Tier-Aware Dispatching**: Allow users to click "Implement" with a selected model tier (`Cheap`, `Standard`, or `Frontier`), respecting the prefill vs auto-send preference.
2. **Plan Cost Tracking**: Aggregate and display total USD cost and token usage accumulated across all sessions linked to a specific plan.

---

### Specifications

#### 1. Tier-Aware Dispatch Menu in `PlansSection.tsx` & `KnowledgeActions.tsx`
- Replace or expand the single "Implement" button in the plan row / menu with a tiered dispatch action:
  - Default action: "Implement" (uses currently active or configured default tier).
  - Dropdown / split button options:
    - `Implement with Cheap Tier` (e.g., Haiku 3.5 / 4o-mini for straightforward tasks/boilerplate)
    - `Implement with Standard Tier` (e.g., GPT-4o for balanced tasks)
    - `Implement with Frontier Tier` (e.g., Claude 3.5 Sonnet / O1 for complex architecture/refactoring)
- Respect `openchamber.routing.plans.actionSendMode` (`localStorage`):
  - If `prefill`: Prefills the prompt input with `/route <tier> Implement the plan at <plan_path>` so the user can inspect/edit before dispatching.
  - If `auto-send`: Dispatches the new session immediately with the prompt and pre-selected model tier.

#### 2. Plan Accumulated Cost & Token Metrics
- In the plan store / `project-knowledge.js`:
  - When returning `knowledge.list` or `knowledge.show` for `kind: 'plan'`, look up the session IDs associated with the plan.
  - Query the session routing metrics store (`route_attempt` records for those session IDs).
  - Sum the `cost_usd`, input tokens, and output tokens.
  - Return aggregated stats:
    ```json
    {
      "id": "plan-slug",
      "title": "Refactor Database Layer",
      "progress": { "done": 3, "total": 4 },
      "metrics": {
        "costUsd": 0.428,
        "inputTokens": 142000,
        "outputTokens": 8900
      }
    }
    ```
- In the frontend `PlansSection.tsx`:
  - Next to the progress badge (`3/4`), display the accumulated cost badge (e.g. `$0.43` or `<$0.01` with a tooltip breaking down token usage and model tiers used).

#### 3. i18n & Localization

## Summary

Found by the #1656 phase-2 inventory audit (design #1655) on main `8cc23ba52d`. `packages/web/server/lib/gitlab/auth-storage.js` `readState` (:193) reads its credential-bearing state file whole with no size gate at all: `encoded = await fsImpl.readFile(filePath, 'utf8')` — no stat, no cap, no regular-file check, so an oversized file is buffered entire and a FIFO at the path wedges the store's serialized transaction queue.

## Both halves (design #1655 rule 2)

- **Bound:** missing — no open issue covers this reader (#1021 capped this module family's network-response reads, not this file read; #1663 covered the `lib/source-control/` stores, not this one).
- **Disposition:** private three-state spelling already — missing → empty state, malformed / wrong version → coded invalid-state throw, never read as empty. No preserve-aside; the file stays in place.

## Ask

Give `readState` one gated read: open once, judge from the handle, state a byte cap derived from the store's own write-side shape (versioned credential records, mode `0600` writes) and enforce it in flight (cap+1), keeping the existing disposition, lock, and fs seam unchanged. No behaviour change for any file at or under the cap.

Filed only because no open issue covers either half for this store — see the inventory table on #1656. Do not let this pre-empt the #1655 phase-3 migration-shape question.

body:
# fix(ui): Settings search for pool schedules opens the Routing page on the wrong tab — `routing.pools-schedules` is missing from the routing tab map, so its target is never rendered

## Summary

PR #1661 (merged 2026-11-05, main `0155b9a710`) split the Routing settings page into tabs and added `routingTabForSearchTarget` so a Settings search result opens the tab that holds its target before the highlight effect looks for it. The map covers the Pools section's advanced, targets and tuning targets — but not its schedules target. `routing.pools-schedules` falls through to the `routing.` prefix default (`'auto'`), while the element it names is rendered only inside the Pools tab. In tabbed mode (the default; `showAllOnOnePage` off) the target is never rendered, so choosing the "Pool schedules" search result lands the user on the Auto tab with no highlight and no way to see the thing they searched for short of guessing the tab.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `0155b9a710efe701b14f1fef38b6e346f9f03be5`)

- The map: `packages/ui/src/components/sections/routing/routingTabs.ts:8-14` — `SEARCH_TARGET_TABS` contains `routing.add-category`, `routing.pools-advanced`, `routing.pools-targets`, `routing.pools-tuning`, `pools.add-pool`. No `routing.pools-schedules`.
- The fallthrough: `routingTabs.ts:17-21` — an unmapped id starting with `routing.` returns `'auto'`.
- The target element: `packages/ui/src/components/sections/routing/ModelPoolsSection.tsx:680` — `settingsItem="routing.pools-schedules"` on the global schedules field row inside `ModelPoolsSection`.
- The gating: `packages/ui/src/components/sections/routing/RoutingPage.tsx:326` — `shows(section) = showAllOnOnePage || tab === section`; `:576` renders `ModelPoolsSection` only when `shows('pools')`.
- The search entry: `packages/ui/src/lib/settings/search.ts:1141-1148` — id `routing.pools-schedules`, page `routing`, keywords schedule / peak hours / weekdays / timezone / weight.
- The consumer: `packages/ui/src/components/views/SettingsView.tsx:508-511` sets the routing tab from `routingTabForSearchTarget(result.id)`; the reveal effect (`SettingsView.tsx:624-660`) polls for `[data-settings-item="routing.pools-schedules"]` for a bounded number of frames and silently gives up — the element is not in the DOM on the Auto tab, and the effect does not re-run when the tab later changes (its deps are `pendingSearchItemId` + `settingsSlug`).

### Probe (laptop, real module, run twice with identical output)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-routing-tabs-20261105/probe.ts` imports the real `routingTabs.ts` from the laptop primary at main `0155b9a710` and judges every Routing-page search-catalog id against the tab that actually renders its element:

```
routing.enabled -> auto (element tab: auto)
routing.preserve-cache -> auto (element tab: auto)
routing.fallback-model -> auto (element tab: auto)
routing.add-category -> categories (element tab: categories)
routing.pools-advanced -> pools (element tab: pools)
routing.pools-targets -> pools (element tab: pools)
routing.pools-tuning -> pools (element tab: pools)
routing.pools-schedules -> auto (element tab: pools)  <<< MISMATCH
pools.add-pool -> pools (element tab: pools)
```

Exactly one mismatch in the whole catalog. The projects-page twin (`projectSettingsTabs.ts`) was checked the same way and is complete by design — its unmapped catalog ids (`projects.name`, `projects.icon`, `projects.close`) are header items rendered above every tab.

## Why it matters

Settings search is the discovery path for exactly the kind of rarely-touched setting pool schedules are (peak-hours weights, timezone). A search result that opens the wrong tab and highlights nothing reads as "the setting does not exist" — the user searched, the app said it found the setting, and then showed them a page where it is absent. This is a regression introduced by the tab split in #1661: before it, every Routing section was on one page and the highlight always found its target.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `routingTabForSearchTarget('routing.pools-schedules')` returns `'pools'`.
- [ ] A regression test enumerates every Routing-page entry in the settings search catalog (`lib/settings/search.ts`, page `routing`) plus every `settingsItem` rendered by the Routing page's sections, and asserts the returned tab is the tab that renders that element — so the next section added to a non-Auto tab cannot silently fall through to `'auto'` again. (Oracle: the rendered element's owning section, per `RoutingPage`'s `shows()` gating.)
- [ ] Choosing the pool-schedules result in Settings search (tabbed mode) lands on the Pools tab with the schedules row scrolled into view and highlighted, as the other Pools targets already do.
- [ ] The `routing.` prefix fallthrough is either removed in favour of the exhaustive test above or documented as Auto-only-by-construction, so a future non-Auto `routing.*` target is a deliberate decision, not a default.

Filed by the new-issue-creator fleet run (agent `new-issue-creator-openchamber`) after verification against the code on main; not a hunch filing.

title: fix(web): source-control stores read their state files whole with no size gate — mutation, audit and binding readState buffer their files entire inside the serialized write chain (and a FIFO wedges every later operation), unlike the shared bounded reader

body:
## Problem

All three source-control state stores in `packages/web/server/lib/source-control/` read their own state files with a plain unbounded `readFile`, and every read runs **inside the store's serialized write chain**, so one bad file wedges the whole store:

- `mutation-storage.js:182` — `readState()`: `parseState(JSON.parse(await fsImpl.readFile(filePath, 'utf8')))`. Every public operation (`claim`, `complete`, `read`, `list`) is funnelled through `enqueueWrite` (`:175-180`), which awaits `readState()` under the file lock.
- `audit-storage.js:211` — the identical `readState()` pattern; `plan` / `start` / `finish` / `read` / `list` all run through its `enqueue` chain (`:204`).
- `binding-storage.js:54` — `readState()`: `encoded = await fsImpl.readFile(filePath, 'utf8')`; `read`, `listRemoteGrants` and `compareAndSwap` all run through `enqueueWrite` (`:35`).

No byte cap and no regular-file check anywhere: an oversized file is buffered and parsed entire before `parseState`'s record-shape checks (which cap nothing by size — e.g. the mutation record's `inputDigest` is any non-empty string) can reject anything, and a FIFO at any of the three paths makes the read never settle — which, because the read sits inside the serialized chain, blocks **every later operation on that store forever**, not just one request.

These stores are the idempotency/audit/binding records for source-control mutations (change-request and issue writes against GitHub/GitLab): wedging or OOM-ing them takes down the mutation-safety layer itself. The legit files are self-bounded — the mutation store caps at 500 records (`DEFAULT_MAX_RECORDS`, `mutation-storage.js:9`), the audit store at 1,000 (`audit-storage.js:9`), each record a small fixed-shape object — so a named cap derived from those bounds loses nothing real. This is the same ungated-reader class the shared bounded reader (`lib/shared/bounded-file-read.js`) exists to prevent.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe vs the real modules, x2 identical)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-source-control-20261105/probe.mjs` on the laptop, importing the real `createMutationStore` and `createBindingStore` from main `b1f25606a`:

1. Control (mutation): a small valid state file → `read('k1')` returned the record (`inputDigest` `d1`).
2. Oversize (mutation): a schema-valid state file whose record's `inputDigest` is a 33,554,432-character pad → `read('k1')` returned it with `inputDigest` length **33,554,432** — buffered and parsed whole, accepted.
3. FIFO (mutation): the state path replaced by a FIFO → `read('k1')` **never settled** within 3 s, and `list()` queued behind it in the serialized chain **also never settled** — the store is wedged, not just one call.
4. Control (binding): a small valid `{version: 2, repositories: {}}` file → `read('r1')` returned `{revision: 0, binding: null}`. (Audit and binding oversize/FIFO behaviour is code-verified: the identical unbounded `readState()` inside the identical serialized-chain shape.)

## Why it matters

- Total store wedge from one bad file: a FIFO or a swapped path doesn't fail one read — the serialized chain means no claim, completion, binding check or grant listing for that store ever runs again until restart (and restart hits the same file).
- Memory: an inflated/corrupted state file is parsed whole on every operation.
- These records are the safety layer for external mutations; their storage should fail closed and promptly (the stores already throw a typed invalid-state error for bad shapes — an over-cap / non-regular read should land in a defined outcome triage chooses, never a hang or an unbounded buffer).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] All three stores (`mutation-storage.js`, `audit-storage.js`, `binding-storage.js`) read their state files through the shared bounded reader (or an equivalent gated read) under named byte caps justified from each store's own record bound (500 / 1,000 records of fixed-shape entries).
- [ ] A FIFO / non-regular file at any of the three paths is refused promptly and does **not** wedge the serialized chain: the operation settles with the triage-chosen defined outcome and a subsequent operation on the same store can still run.
- [ ] Missing file still yields each store's current empty state; malformed JSON still produces the current invalid-state error; valid at-cap files behave exactly as today.
- [ ] Regression tests per store: oversize valid file is refused without parsing the pad whole; FIFO path settles promptly and the next operation proceeds; control files unchanged.

body:
## Problem

`readSpaceSettingFile` judges its safety gate on one file and reads another. `packages/web/server/lib/spaces/space-setting-file.js`:

- `:17` `const stat = await fs.promises.lstat(filePath);`
- `:18` `if (!stat.isFile() || stat.size > MAX_SETTING_BYTES) return null;` — `MAX_SETTING_BYTES = 1024` (`:8`)
- `:19` `JSON.parse(await fs.promises.readFile(filePath, 'utf8'))` — a fresh by-path read of whatever the path points to *now*

The module's own header (`:1-3`) states why this reader exists and who the adversary is: the files live in a space's HOME, "the agent owns these files and can make them anything, a FIFO among them, which a plain read would wait on forever". The two consumers are the in-space server's permission default (`space-permission-default.js:26`, via `readSpacePermissionDefault`) and idle-stop (`idle-stop.js:68`) — a file that is missing / not plain / over 1 KiB / not schema-valid must give the agent "nothing the user did not choose" (`:10-13`).

Because the judgement and the read are two separate by-path operations, an agent (or any process able to rename in that directory) that swaps the file between them defeats both halves of the gate at once:

- **Cap defeat:** `lstat` judges a 34-byte file; the `readFile` that follows buffers a 200,000-byte payload whole — the 1 KiB cap never applies to the bytes actually parsed.
- **FIFO defeat:** `lstat` judges a plain small file; the `readFile` opens a FIFO and waits forever for a writer that never comes — exactly the hang the header says this module prevents. Enough swapped-in FIFOs exhaust the libuv threadpool (default 4 threads), after which *every* fs operation in the server stalls, not just this read.

The repo's house standard judges from the handle it reads: `lib/shared/bounded-file-read.js` `readBoundedFile` (`:73`) opens once (`O_NONBLOCK`), stats the handle, refuses non-regular files, and enforces cap+1 in flight as it reads. #1605 fixed this same stat→read pattern in `fs/routes.js` and the VS Code bridge fs proxy; #1305 fixed it for project icons. This reader — in the spaces surface, against the explicitly adversarial writer — was not covered by either.

## Evidence (this run, main `c11726d32e12230ccd5353a85a0c852dfca3ad36`)

Laptop probes against the real `readSpaceSettingFile` (probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-space-setting-race-20261105/` on the laptop — `probe.mjs`, `swapper.mjs`, `reader.mjs`, `reader-fifo2.mjs`; pass-through schema so only the read behaviour is judged):

Controls (no swapper):

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| small valid file (`{"v":1}`, 8 bytes) | `{v:1}` |
| 200,000-byte valid JSON file | `null` (cap works when nobody swaps) |
| FIFO at the path | `null` in 0 ms (gate works when nobody swaps) |
| missing file | `null` |

Race A — a separate swapper process alternately hardlink-renames a 200,000-byte file and the small file over the target path while 64-wide batches of real reads run:

- Run 1: 384 reads → **11 cap defeats** (returned the 200,000-byte payload that `lstat` had judged ≤ 1 KiB), 108 `null` (lstat saw the big file), 265 small.
- Run 2: 320 reads → **9 cap defeats**, 98 `null`, 213 small.

Race B — same swapper alternating a FIFO and the small file, 32-wide batches, per-call 600 ms timeout:

- First batch: **15 of 32 calls never settled within 600 ms** (their `readFile` had opened the FIFO); the reader process then wedged completely — subsequent fs calls stopped settling as the blocked FIFO opens exhausted the threadpool — and had to be killed at 120 s. The un-swapped FIFO control above returns `null` in 0 ms, so the hangs are the swap, not the shape.

## Why it matters

- The permission-default consumer decides what mode a new chat in the space starts in. The gate is the only thing standing between an agent-writable file and that decision; a reader whose judgement can be detached from the bytes it parses does not provide it. (The parsed value still has to pass the caller's zod schema — the exposure today is the unbounded buffer and the hang, plus any future schema field that trusts file size.)
- The hang is the worse half: it needs no valid payload at all, it converts the module's stated worst case (a FIFO) from "refused in 0 ms" back into "waits forever", and at threadpool scale it stalls the whole in-space server's filesystem work, not one setting read.
- The fix pattern is already the house standard and already applied to this exact pattern twice (#1605, #1305); this is the remaining by-path stat→read site in the spaces lib.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `readSpaceSettingFile` reads through the shared bounded reader (`lib/shared/bounded-file-read.js` `readBoundedFile` with the existing `MAX_SETTING_BYTES = 1024`), judging regularity and size from the opened handle and enforcing the cap in flight — no by-path `lstat`-then-`readFile` sequence remains in `space-setting-file.js`.
- [ ] Outcome semantics preserved exactly: missing, non-regular (incl. FIFO and symlink-to-anything), over-cap, unparseable, and schema-rejecting files all return `null`; a valid ≤ 1 KiB file returns the schema-parsed value. Both consumers (`space-permission-default.js:26`, `idle-stop.js:68`) keep their current behaviour on every non-race input.
- [ ] Regression tests pin the race, not just the shapes: a file that grows past 1 KiB after being opened is refused having read at most cap+1 bytes, and a FIFO (or a handle judged non-regular) is refused promptly without a writer — following the bounded reader's existing test patterns, so the swap cases fail on the pre-fix implementation.
- [ ] Existing spaces suites stay green (idle-stop, space-permission-default consumers, hardening).

Related: #1605 (same stat→read class: web fs routes + VS Code bridge proxy), #1305 (project-icon stat→readFile race, fixed), #1655 design rule 2 (a state-file read owes the bound judged from the handle), `lib/shared/bounded-file-read.js:73` (the shared reader to reuse).

title: fix(web): spaces host-providers loopback judge is a hand-rolled string test — /^127\./ judges public DNS names like 127.evil.example as this machine (rewriting key-bearing provider windows to host.docker.internal) and misses *.localhost and ::ffff:-mapped loopback, unlike the shared bind-host judge

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

body:
## Problem

The spaces host-providers loopback judge is a hand-rolled string test that diverges from the repo's shared, range-correct judge in both directions: it judges public DNS names as "this machine", and it misses two loopback spellings the shared judge accepts.

`packages/web/server/lib/spaces/host-providers.js`:

- `:32` `LOOPBACK_HOSTS = new Set(['localhost', '[::1]', '0.0.0.0'])`
- `:53` `isLoopback = (url) => LOOPBACK_HOSTS.has(url.hostname.toLowerCase()) || /^127\./.test(url.hostname)` — the regex runs against the parsed hostname **string**, never testing that the host is actually an IPv4 address in 127.0.0.0/8.

Two consumers trust this judge:

- `windowUpstreamOf` (`:39-44`): a "loopback" base URL has its hostname rewritten to `host.docker.internal` (`HOST_NAME`, `lib/spaces/hardening.js:81`), and `lib/spaces/journey.js:475-483` (`customWindowOf`) attaches the custom provider's **key** to that window (`{ upstream, header, secret: definition.key }`) — the gatekeeper forwards the space's requests to `upstream` with the provider's credential in its SDK header.
- `list()` (`:154`): the `loopback` flag the Settings dialogs use to warn that a provider address names the machine the space runs on (`packages/ui/src/components/session/spaces/spaceModelKeys.ts`).

The repo already owns the correct judge: `isLoopbackUrl` / `isLoopbackBindHost` in `packages/web/server/lib/security/bind-host.js:33-55` parse the URL, accept `localhost` / `*.localhost`, test all of 127.0.0.0/8 numerically, and unwrap `::ffff:`-mapped forms (including the hex form URL parsing produces). #1551 moved three other hand-rolled judges onto it; this fourth copy was not covered.

## Evidence (this run, main `c11726d32e12230ccd5353a85a0c852dfca3ad36`)

Laptop probe against the real `isLoopbackUrl` / `windowUpstreamOf` from `host-providers.js` (probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-hostproviders-loopback-20261105/probe.mjs` on the laptop), run twice with identical output:

| Base URL | `loopback` | `windowUpstreamOf` | Correct? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `http://127.0.0.1:11434` | true | `http://host.docker.internal:11434/` | Yes (control) |
| `http://127.0.0.2:11434` | true | `http://host.docker.internal:11434/` | Yes (control) |
| `http://localhost:11434` | true | `http://host.docker.internal:11434/` | Yes (control) |
| `http://[::1]:11434` | true | `http://host.docker.internal:11434/` | Yes (control) |
| `http://127.evil.example:11434` | **true** | `http://host.docker.internal:11434/` | **No — a public DNS name is judged this machine** |
| `http://127.0.0.1.evil.example:11434` | **true** | `http://host.docker.internal:11434/` | **No — same prefix flaw** |
| `http://myapp.localhost:5173` | **false** | unchanged | **No — `*.localhost` is this machine (the shared judge and the repo's own portless docs use it)** |
| `http://[::ffff:127.0.0.1]:11434` | **false** | unchanged (`[::ffff:7f00:1]` after URL normalization) | **No — mapped loopback missed** |
| `https://api.example.com` | false | unchanged | Yes (control) |
| `http://192.168.1.10:11434` | false | unchanged | Yes (control) |

The module's own tests already pin the intent that a DNS name is not this machine — `host-providers.test.js:93` expects `http://localhost.example.com/v1` NOT to be rewritten — but the `/^127\./` regex lets the `127.`-prefixed spelling of the same trick through.

## Why it matters

- **False positive (public judged local):** a custom provider whose base URL is a public DNS name beginning `127.` (e.g. a hosted gateway at `127.<something>`) has its window silently retargeted to `host.docker.internal`: the space's requests — carrying the provider's API key in the window's secret header — go to whatever listens on the user's own machine at that port/path instead of the configured provider, and the provider is simply unusable from the space. The `list()` flag also misreports it as a this-machine provider.
- **False negative (local judged remote):** a host model server addressed as `*.localhost` (the portless spelling the repo's docs teach, `packages/docs/content/docs/project-actions.mdx`) or via a `::ffff:`-mapped address is left pointing inside the gatekeeper container, where that name/address is the container itself or unresolvable — the space cannot reach a server that is in fact on the host, with no diagnostic pointing at the judge.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `host-providers.js` judges loopback by parsing and range-testing — ideally by reusing `security/bind-host.js`'s `isLoopbackUrl`/`isLoopbackBindHost` rather than a fifth copy: `localhost` / `*.localhost`, all of 127.0.0.0/8, `::1`, and `::ffff:`-mapped forms are loopback; DNS names that merely start with `127.` (or any other prefix shape) are not.
- [ ] Triage decides the `0.0.0.0` case explicitly: the current tests pin it as this-machine (`host-providers.test.js:90`), while the shared bind-host judge treats `0.0.0.0` as a wildcard bind, not loopback. Whichever way it lands, the decision and its reason are recorded in the code/tests.
- [ ] Regression tests in `host-providers.test.js` pin the probe cases: `127.evil.example` and `127.0.0.1.evil.example` are NOT rewritten and report `loopback: false`; `myapp.localhost` and `[::ffff:127.0.0.1]` ARE rewritten; all existing pinned cases (`:86-99`, including `127.1.2.3` and `localhost.example.com`) keep their outcomes except any deliberately re-decided `0.0.0.0` case.
- [ ] Existing spaces suites (host-providers, journey, gatekeeper consumers) stay green.

Related: #1551 (the same hand-rolled-judge class; three sites moved to the shared judge), #1517 (guests SSRF judge fixed to judge IPv6 numerically), `packages/web/server/lib/security/bind-host.js` (the shared judge this site should reuse).

body:
## Summary

Phase 2 of design #1655 (bounded, and judged — one gated read for the server's own state files). An inventory audit only — no production behaviour changes: disposition every remaining hand-rolled state-file reader in `packages/web/server/lib` against **both** halves of the design's rule 2, and file per-site follow-up issues for any store no open issue covers on both halves.

## Background

Design #1254 bounded project/user files and explicitly excluded the server's own state files; design #976 gave fifteen migrated stores a three-state disposition (missing / valid / malformed-preserved) but no bound. The second "no size gate" wave — 27 filings in three days, ~20 still open (#1490, #1608, #1609, #1610, #1613, #1614, #1621, #1622, #1624, #1627, #1628, #1631, #1632, #1635, #1636, #1638, #1645, #1651, plus the VS Code readers #1641/#1643/#1644) — fixes the bound half store by store. What nobody has is the table: which stores remain hand-rolled, which have the bound, which have a #976-shaped disposition, and which have neither. Hand-rolled readers invent both halves privately (e.g. `lib/routing/store.js` `readJsonFile` :147 / `readJsonFileSync` :171 on main `c11726d32e`: whole read; ENOENT → null, empty → null, malformed → uncoded throw, no preserve). Phase 1 of the design (#1649, adopted) gives the durable store both halves; this audit covers everything that is **not** on the durable store.

## Scope

- Enumerate every private store reader in `packages/web/server/lib` that reads a state file whole (private `readJsonFile`-style helpers, direct `readFile`/`readFileSync` of store paths, store modules not on `lib/shared/durable-json-store.js`). Re-grep on current main at audit time — do not reuse this issue's filing-day list as the inventory.
- For each reader, record: store file(s), bound? (reader used, cap value, cap derivation from the store's write-side clamps per design rule 4 — or "no write clamp exists"), judged? (disposition shape: durable three-state / private spelling / read-as-empty hazard), sync or async, and which open issue (if any) covers it on each half.
- Name the three VS Code readers (#1641/#1643/#1644) as the mirror inventory section — dispositioned as mirror rows, not audited as web code.
- Name append-only log readers (plan-notes #1638, replay #1632, route-feedback in #1624) as their own kind in the table — the design leaves their answer (tail/window vs rotation vs exception) open; the audit records the kind, it does not decide it.
- File a per-site follow-up issue for any store no open issue covers on **both** halves (a store whose open filing covers the bound only gets a disposition follow-up naming this audit and design #1655 — do not edit or supersede the open filing).
- Record the table in `lib/shared/DOCUMENTATION.md` alongside the bounded-read and durable-store contract sections.

## Out of scope

- Any production code change, migration, or cap change.
- The durable store's own readers — phase 1 (#1649) owns them.
- Deciding phase 3 (migration shape, log semantics, VS Code mirror, ratchet) — the audit feeds those questions; it does not answer them.
- The open per-site filings' queue lifecycles — cited and cross-referenced, never pre-empted.

## Acceptance criteria

- A disposition table exists in `lib/shared/DOCUMENTATION.md` covering every hand-rolled state-file reader found in `packages/web/server/lib` on the audit-day main, each row dispositioned: migrated / conforming-on-both-halves / covered-by-open-issue (named, per half) / follow-up-filed (named) / excepted (reason named) — with the VS Code mirror rows and the append-only-log kind named as their own sections.
- Every store with no open issue covering both halves has a filed follow-up issue linked from the table and from this issue.
- No production behaviour changed by this issue (docs + filed issues only).

🤖 Filed by the repo-design-architect job as phase 2 of design #1655, design pass 2026-11-05.

body:
## Problem

The web server's async settings runtime buffers the shared `settings.json` and `preferences.json` whole, with no size gate and no regular-file check — the async twin of the sync reader filed as #1631 (`settings-files.js` `readMergedSettingsSync`), in a different module that #1631 does not cover:

- `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/settings-runtime.js:590-605` — `readInstanceSettingsFromDisk` does `await fsPromises.readFile(SETTINGS_FILE_PATH, 'utf8')` (:593) and parses the whole buffer; every failure except ENOENT degrades to `{}`.
- `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/settings-runtime.js:613-640` — `readPreferenceFields` does `await fsPromises.readFile(PREFERENCES_FILE_PATH, 'utf8')` (:616); a read failure marks the profile `failed` (writes paused), a parse failure does the same — the failure mapping a bounded read must land in.
- `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/settings-runtime.js:676-693` — `readSettingsFromDiskStrict` does the same whole read (:679). This is the strict variant whose contract is deliberate: only a genuinely missing file means "no settings", every other failure throws, because its callers regenerate persisted relay identity when a key looks absent. A bounded-read rejection must throw here, never degrade to `{}`.
- Same module, code-verified sibling: the generic `readJsonFile` helper (:105-107) whole-reads the per-project config/context files used by the migration and orphan-recovery paths (:140, :322-323, :365, :478).

These readers are the merged-settings path every settings consumer uses (`readSettingsFromDisk` / `readSettingsFromDiskMigrated`, :649/:1109, exported :1261-1263; the runtime is constructed by `packages/web/server/index.js`). The house standard exists in the same server, in both spellings: `lib/shared/bounded-file-read.js` — `readBoundedFile` (:73, async) and `readBoundedFileSync` (:117) — handle read with a named cap plus a regular-file check. The sync twin's triage (#1631) already picked the cap family for this exact pair of files: settings.json at the 8 MiB `linear/auth` precedent, preferences.json at 8 MiB or a documented 4 MiB.

## Why it matters

`settings.json` is the shared file at the centre of the server: the VS Code bridge, the sync web reader (#1631/#1644/#1651), and this async runtime all read it. A FIFO at either path makes the settings read never settle — every settings consumer waits forever (persist, relay identity, project migration). An oversized but well-formed file is buffered and parsed whole on every read. And the strict reader is the dangerous one to get wrong in a fix: if an over-cap read ever degraded to `{}` there, callers would mint a new relay identity and orphan every paired device — the exact failure the strict contract exists to prevent.

## Evidence (this run, laptop probe against the real module)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-settings-runtime-ungated-20261105/probe.mjs` on the laptop, plain `node`, importing the real `createSettingsRuntime` from the laptop primary at `c11726d32e12230ccd5353a85a0c852dfca3ad36`, constructed with the same stub deps as `settings-runtime.test.js`, `SETTINGS_FILE_PATH` pointed at a scratch dir. Run twice, identical results:

- Control: a small `settings.json` read back normally through both readers (`CONTROL_MARKER ctl-value`, `CONTROL_STRICT_MARKER ctl-value`).
- Oversize: a 33,554,432-char padding field was parsed whole by both the lenient and the strict reader (`OVERSIZE_PAD_LEN 33554432`, `OVERSIZE_STRICT_PAD_LEN 33554432`) — no rejection at any size.
- FIFO: with the settings path replaced by a FIFO, `readSettingsFromDisk` never returned (timeout exit 124, ×2).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `readInstanceSettingsFromDisk`, `readPreferenceFields`, and `readSettingsFromDiskStrict` read `settings.json` / `preferences.json` through the shared bounded reader (or an equivalent handle-based bounded read) under named caps consistent with the #1631 triage for the same two files (settings 8 MiB; preferences 8 MiB or documented 4 MiB).
- [ ] An over-cap or non-regular file lands in each reader's existing failure semantics exactly: lenient instance read → `{}` as a read failure does today; preferences → the `failed` status (file left alone, writes stay paused); strict read → throws (never `{}`), so no caller can mistake it for a missing file and regenerate identity.
- [ ] The same-module `readJsonFile` helper (:105) is either bounded under a named cap appropriate to per-project config files or explicitly dispositioned in the PR as out of scope with a reason.
- [ ] Regression tests in `settings-runtime.test.js` (or a sibling suite) pin the over-cap and FIFO/non-regular behaviour for all three readers, including the strict-throws case.
- [ ] No behaviour change for files within the caps: existing settings-runtime tests pass.

body:
## Summary

`packages/web/server/lib/github/auth.js` reads both of its local files whole with no size gate or regular-file check, in three places:

- `readState` (:207) — `await fsImpl.readFile(filePath, 'utf8')` buffers `github-auth.json` entire. Every store operation funnels through it: `read`/`mutate` run inside a single serialized transaction queue (:222-231), so one blocked or bloated read wedges every GitHub-auth operation behind it.
- `readSettingsFile` (:311) — lenient sync reader: `JSON.parse(fsSync.readFileSync(SETTINGS_FILE, 'utf8'))` of the shared `settings.json`, called from `setGitHubAuth` (:393), `activateGitHubAuth` (:400), `getGitHubClientId` (:410), `getGitHubScopes` (:418), `isGhCliDisabled` (:425) and `isGhCliActive` (:436).
- `readSettingsFileForUpdate` (:333) — strict sync reader for the write paths (:429, :441): same whole `readFileSync`. Because it is synchronous, a non-regular file at the settings path blocks the whole server event loop, and an oversized file is fully parsed before any validation can reject it.

The same package's house standard already exists and is used by the sibling fixes: `lib/shared/bounded-file-read.js` (`readBoundedFile` / `readBoundedFileSync` — O_NONBLOCK + fstat regular-file check + in-read byte cap). The shared `settings.json` half of this exposure was flagged as a code-verified cross-reference in #1645; this filing covers the github/auth.js readers themselves, including the module's own auth store.

Not covered elsewhere: #1615 fixed the linear/auth.js readers of the same shared file (different module, different functions); #940 (closed) was the malformed-settings rewrite-from-empty-base bug in these same functions — a correctness defect, not the read-gate defect.

## Evidence (main c11726d32e, verified this run)

Code (laptop primary `~/git/openchamber-fork`, origin/main c11726d32e12230ccd5353a85a0c852dfca3ad36):

- `packages/web/server/lib/github/auth.js:207` — `encoded = await fsImpl.readFile(filePath, 'utf8')`, no cap, no stat/fstat.
- `packages/web/server/lib/github/auth.js:311` — `JSON.parse(fsSync.readFileSync(SETTINGS_FILE, 'utf8'))` inside the lenient reader.
- `packages/web/server/lib/github/auth.js:333` — `raw = fsSync.readFileSync(SETTINGS_FILE, 'utf8')` inside the strict reader.
- `SETTINGS_FILE` (:16) is the shared `<OPENCHAMBER_DATA_DIR>/settings.json`; `STORAGE_FILE` (:15) is `github-auth.json` in the same directory.

Laptop probe against the real module (scratch `OPENCHAMBER_DATA_DIR` per process; probe at laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-github-auth-ungated-20261105/probe.mjs`), run ×2 with identical results:

- Control: small `settings.json` → `getGitHubClientId()` returns the stored id.
- Oversize lenient: `settings.json` carrying a 33,554,432-char pad → stored client id still returned (whole file parsed).
- Oversize strict: `setGhCliActive(true)` on the padded file → rewrite preserves the pad at full length 33,554,432 (whole file parsed by `readSettingsFileForUpdate` before rewrite).
- Oversize store: legacy-format `github-auth.json` with a 33,554,432-char `accessToken` → `createGitHubAuthStore({filePath}).getActive()` returns the token at full length 33,554,432 (schema caps no field length; the whole file is buffered and parsed first).
- FIFO at `settings.json` → `getGitHubClientId()` never returns; killed at 5s (exit 124, ×2 clean runs).
- FIFO at `github-auth.json` → `store.listAccounts()` never settles; killed at 5s (exit 124, ×2) — and because all store operations serialize behind the one transaction queue, every later GitHub-auth call wedges behind it.

## Why it matters

`settings.json` is the shared, multi-writer file at the centre of the settings fixes (#907/#940/#1615/#1631/#1644/#1645): any writer or external tool that grows or corrupts it — or replaces it with a non-regular file — takes down GitHub auth reads with it, and the two sync readers freeze the whole server while doing so. `github-auth.json` holds the user's GitHub credentials; its reader is the one path where a FIFO does not just block one request but permanently wedges the serialized store queue for the life of the process.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] All three reads go through a bounded, regular-file-checked path (the shared `lib/shared/bounded-file-read.js` readers or an equivalent), under named per-file caps documented in code.
- [ ] Failure mapping preserves today's semantics exactly: lenient settings read over-cap/non-regular → `{}` (as a read failure today); strict read over-cap/non-regular → propagates as a read failure (never parsed-as-empty — the #907/#940 rule: a writer that cannot see the current contents must not replace them); store read over-cap/non-regular → the existing `INVALID_GITHUB_AUTH` / read-failure path, never a silently empty state.
- [ ] FIFO at either path is refused promptly (no event-loop block, no wedged transaction queue).
- [ ] Within-cap behaviour unchanged: existing github auth tests pass, plus new over-cap and FIFO regression cases for the store read and both settings readers.
