body:
## Problem

The web server's shared durable JSON store — the one strict reader/preserve primitive that fifteen server modules are built on (design #976, built in #977, migration #978) — reads its files whole with no size gate and no regular-file check, in every spelling:

`packages/web/server/lib/shared/durable-json-store.js` (main `c11726d32e`):

- `:90-100` `readDurableJsonFile` — `await fs.readFile(filePath, 'utf8')` buffers the whole file before `judgeRaw` parses it.
- `:103-113` `readDurableJsonFileSync` — `fs.readFileSync(filePath, 'utf8')`, same, synchronously.
- `:132+` `preserveMalformedJsonFile` and `:220+` `preserveMalformedJsonFileSync` — the preserve path reads the file whole again (`:136` async / `:224` sync), re-reads it inside the attempt loop (`:163` / `:240`), and reads the preserved candidate whole after the rename (`:187` / `:256`): up to three whole-file buffers per attempt, `PRESERVE_ATTEMPTS = 10`.

There is no cap, no `fstat`/`isFile()` check, and no `O_NONBLOCK` open anywhere in the module. A FIFO at any store path blocks the read indefinitely (the sync spellings freeze the whole server event loop); an oversized file is buffered and parsed whole before any judgement can reject it.

Callers of the readers/preserve helpers (grep `readDurableJsonFile|preserveMalformedJsonFile` in `packages/web/server/lib`, excluding the primitive and tests): `client-auth/pairing.js`, `client-auth/remote-clients.js`, `dispatch-results/runtime.js`, `magic-prompts/runtime.js`, `message-queue/runtime.js`, `notifications/apns-runtime.js`, `notifications/push-runtime.js`, `openchamber-sessions/archive-store.js`, `openchamber-sessions/session-metadata-store.js`, `routing/route-overrides-store.js`, `routing/route-settings.js`, `session-warming/runtime.js`, `tts/voice-keys.js`, `tunnels/managed-config.js`, `ui-auth/ui-passkeys.js`. Several of these files hold credentials or tokens (voice keys, APNs tokens, push subscriptions, passkeys, paired clients).

This is the primitive-level remainder of the per-store bounded-read series (#1607–#1645): those filings bounded stores that hand-roll their reads; the stores that were migrated onto this shared primitive in #978 inherit its uncapped read instead. `lib/shared/bounded-file-read.js`'s header scopes itself to "files whose size the server does not control … as opposed to … the server's own state files (durable-json-store.js, #976)" — but the confirmed per-store filings established that server state files get caps too, because the FIFO/oversize hazard is about the path, not about who normally writes the file.

## Evidence (this run, laptop probe against the real module)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-durable-json-ungated-20261105/` on the laptop, importing `durable-json-store.js` from the laptop primary at `c11726d32e`, run twice per case:

- Control: a small valid store file → `{ state: 'valid' }` from both spellings.
- Oversized: a store file holding one 33,554,432-char string → both `readDurableJsonFileSync` and `readDurableJsonFile` returned `{ state: 'valid', raw }` with `raw.length === 33,554,443` — the whole file buffered and parsed, no gate.
- FIFO: a FIFO at the store path → `readDurableJsonFileSync`, `readDurableJsonFile`, and `preserveMalformedJsonFileSync` all blocked and were killed by `timeout 5` (exit 124), both runs, all three spellings.

## Why it matters

One fix here bounds fifteen stores at once, including credential-bearing ones; per-store filings cannot reach these, because the read lives in the primitive. The preserve path is the sharp edge: it runs exactly when a store file is already malformed/suspicious, and it multiplies the whole-file read by up to three reads × ten attempts — and a FIFO there wedges the fail-closed write path itself, so the store can neither read nor safely write.

## Acceptance criteria

- All four entry points (`readDurableJsonFile`, `readDurableJsonFileSync`, `preserveMalformedJsonFile`, `preserveMalformedJsonFileSync`) read through a bounded, regular-file-checked path (e.g. the shared `readBoundedFile`/`readBoundedFileSync` in `lib/shared/bounded-file-read.js`, O_NONBLOCK + fstat + cap enforced during the read), with a named cap (per-caller `options` override with a stated default sized above the largest legitimate store, in the spirit of the caps chosen in the per-store fixes).
- Failure semantics preserved and stated: over-cap / non-regular must land in the existing fail-closed branches — for the readers, the "read failure other than absence throws" rule (never `malformed`, so an over-cap file is never preserve-renamed or overwritten on a misjudgement); for preserve, `{ preserved: false, outcome: 'failed' }`. Missing/empty behaviour is unchanged.
- The injected-`fs` test seam (`options.fs`) keeps working or is deliberately re-specified, and the existing `durable-json-store.test.js` suite passes with new cases: over-cap file, FIFO at the path (prompt refusal, no block) for both reader spellings and the preserve path, and a valid-at-cap file still reading as `valid`.
- No caller changes behaviour for within-cap files: the fifteen caller modules' existing tests pass unmodified.

body:
## Problem

One more reader of the shared OpenChamber settings file in the VS Code
extension buffers it whole, synchronously, with no size gate and no
regular-file check — in the single-threaded extension host:

- `packages/vscode/src/opencode.ts:112-125` — `readOpenChamberSettings`
  does `fs.readFileSync(settingsPath, 'utf8')` (:115) on
  `~/.config/openchamber/settings.json` and `JSON.parse`s the whole
  buffer; every failure degrades to `{}` in the bare catch.
- It is called from the OpenCode CLI resolution paths (:266 and
  `resolveOpencodeCliPath` :313), which run from `getDebugInfo()`,
  `getCompatibility()`, `isCliAvailable()` and the managed-server launch
  path — so it is read repeatedly, not once at startup.

This is the third ungated reader of this same settings file: the web
server's merged-settings reader is #1631 and this package's bridge
settings runtime is #1641 (whose filing already cross-referenced this
site as code-verified only). The same package already has the bounded
pattern: `opencodeConfig.ts:665` `readCappedFileSync` reads through a
handle with `O_NONBLOCK` + fstat under `MAX_CONFIG_FILE_BYTES` = 4 MiB
(:636).

## Why it matters

A synchronous `readFileSync` that blocks blocks the whole extension
host. A FIFO (or device, or pathologically grown file) at the shared
settings path freezes CLI resolution, the debug/compatibility surfaces
and managed-server launch — not one request. An oversized but
well-formed settings file is buffered and parsed whole in
extension-host memory on every resolution. The failure mode should be
a bounded, named rejection that lands in the existing `{}` degradation,
not unbounded buffering.

## Evidence (this run, laptop probe against the real module)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-creator-20261105-0450/probe-vscode-settings.test.js`
on the laptop, `bun test`, importing the real
`packages/vscode/src/opencode.ts` from the laptop primary at
origin/main `c11726d32e12230ccd5353a85a0c852dfca3ad36`, with `vscode`
mocked and `HOME` pointed at a scratch dir so
`~/.config/openchamber/settings.json` is the probe's file; the reader
is exercised through the real `createOpenCodeManager(...).getDebugInfo()`
→ `resolveOpencodeCliPath` → `readOpenChamberSettings` chain. Run
twice, identical results:

- Control: a small settings file with `opencodeBinary` pointing at a
  scratch executable resolved normally (`CONTROL_CLIPATH <scratch>/fake-opencode`).
- Oversize: a settings file with a 33,554,432-char padding field placed
  before `opencodeBinary` was parsed whole and the binary after the
  padding still extracted (`OVERSIZE_CLIPATH <scratch>/fake-opencode`) —
  no rejection at any size.
- FIFO: with `settings.json` replaced by a FIFO, `getDebugInfo()` never
  returned — the probe was killed by `timeout` (exit 124), twice.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `readOpenChamberSettings` goes through a bounded,
      regular-file-checked read with a named byte cap sized from the
      settings file's legitimate shape (the same file is capped at
      4–8 MiB by the readers fixed under #1631/#1641 — stay consistent).
- [ ] Over-cap and non-regular files degrade exactly as a read failure
      does today (`{}`), and no path parses a too-large file whole.
- [ ] Normal small settings files behave byte-for-byte as today,
      including `opencodeBinary` resolution through both call sites.
- [ ] Regression tests pin an over-cap settings file and a FIFO at the
      settings path returning promptly instead of blocking; the
      existing vscode suites stay green.
- [ ] `packages/vscode/src/DOCUMENTATION.md` notes the cap alongside
      the existing bounded-read entries.

Found by: new-issue-creator-openchamber run, 2026-11-05 04:50 CST.
Related: #1641 (same package's bridge settings readers — this site was
its cross-referenced third reader), #1631 (web-server twin reader of
the same settings.json), #1643 (same package's quota local-file readers).

body:
## Problem

The spaces chat-archive reader in `packages/web/server/lib/spaces/space-archive.js` reads every archive entry file whole, synchronously, with no size gate and no non-regular-file protection:

- `readEntries` (:76) loops over every `*.json` in `<dataDir>/spaces/archive/` and does `JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(path.join(root, name), 'utf8'))` at :88, feeding the result to `archiveEntrySchema.parse`.
- It runs at construction: `createSpaceArchive` (:70) executes `const entries = readEntries()` (:97), and the server constructs the archive in `packages/web/server/index.js:2347` — so this read is on the server-startup path, and because it is **synchronous**, a FIFO at any entry path blocks in `open()` and freezes startup (and the event loop) outright.

Unlike the shared bounded reader (`lib/shared/bounded-file-read.js`, `readBoundedFileSync` :117) that sibling stores were migrated to (#1607-#1615, #1620-#1628), this reader buffers each entire file before the schema gets to judge it.

One aggravating fact: the reader does not enforce the module's own write-side bound. The write path caps a space at `ARCHIVE_MAX_CHATS = 1000` chats, but `archiveEntrySchema`'s `chats` is an unbounded `z.array(chatIdSchema)` — an entry claiming hundreds of thousands of chats is accepted whole on read, and every id lands in the in-memory entries map and the `relock()` set derived from it.

Related site for triage to disposition (not the headline): the restore path in the same file reads each exported chat file whole at :267 (`JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(path.join(incoming, `${id}.json`), 'utf8'))`) before `hostOpenCode.importChat`. Chat exports can be legitimately large, so that site needs its own stated bound/streaming decision rather than the entry cap.

## Evidence (verified this run, main f80ffdb893795fbd44fdddf85cf22b0a5c74da3b)

Laptop probe against the real module from origin/main (probe worktree `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-creator-20261105/`, `probe.mjs` importing the real `lib/spaces/space-archive.js`, `createSpaceArchive` with a stub host), each case run ×2 with identical results:

- **Control:** a small valid entry (`spaceId abcdef012345`, one chat) constructed normally.
- **Oversized:** a schema-valid entry of 34,840,098 bytes — 520,000 chat ids, 520× the module's own 1000-chat write cap — was read, parsed, and accepted whole; construction completed with the entry in the map, no size or count rejection.
- **FIFO:** with the entry path replaced by a FIFO, construction printed its pre-read marker and never returned — the probe had to be killed by an external 5 s timeout (exit 124) both runs. Synchronous at server construction, so in production this is a server that never starts serving.
- The spaces tests contain no oversized / FIFO / bounded-read case for `readEntries`.

## Why it matters

The archive is the read-only guard for deleted spaces' chats: it is constructed unconditionally at startup whether or not the spaces feature is in use, per the module header. A single grown, corrupted, or planted file in the archive directory therefore takes down the whole managed server before it serves anything — worse placement than a per-request reader. The entries are small by construction (name ≤200 chars, one project path, ≤1000 chat ids on the write side), so a generous named cap loses nothing legitimate.

## Acceptance criteria

- `readEntries` judges each entry file's size and type from an opened handle (the shared bounded reader's sync spelling), with a named, documented cap sized from the legitimate entry shape (schema-bounded fields plus the 1000-chat write cap, with headroom stated).
- Semantics preserved: a missing archive directory still reads as an empty map; an unreadable/malformed entry is still skipped with the existing `logger.warn` line and never aborts construction — over-cap and non-regular entries join that same skip-and-log path, promptly (a FIFO must not block construction).
- The read side enforces a chat-count bound consistent with `ARCHIVE_MAX_CHATS` (or the schema gains a stated larger read bound with the reason documented) — an entry past the bound is skipped-and-logged like any other malformed entry, not silently ingested.
- Triage dispositions the restore-path read at :267 explicitly: a stated bound or a documented reason it stays whole-read, recorded on this issue.
- Regression tests: oversized entry, over-cap chat count, and FIFO entry cases; ordinary, missing-directory, and malformed-entry behaviour unchanged.
- Existing spaces suites pass.

Out of scope: space records (#1628, `spaces/space-records.js`), the archive write/save flow and its timeout, the guard's route matching, and the entry schema's field shapes other than the chat-count bound.

body:
## Problem

One routing reader in `packages/web/server/lib/routing/plans.js` was left out of the routing bounded-read filings (#1608 store.js, #1624 plans.json / pool-plan-links.json / route-feedback.jsonl):

- `readNotes` (:205) does `fs.readFileSync(file, 'utf8').split('\n')` at :210 for `plan-notes.jsonl`, then JSON-parses and schema-validates **every line**, filters, sorts, and only at the very end applies the caller's `limit` (`matching.slice(-filter.limit)`, :227). There is no size gate and no non-regular-file protection, and the read is **synchronous**.

Unlike the shared bounded reader (`lib/shared/bounded-file-read.js`, `readBoundedFileSync` :117) that sibling stores were migrated to, this reader buffers the entire file before judging anything — and because it is synchronous, a FIFO at `plan-notes.jsonl` blocks in `open()` and freezes the whole server event loop.

Two aggravating facts:

- `plan-notes.jsonl` is **append-only**: `addNote` (:182-201) appends one line per note and nothing in `plans.js` or `plan-routes.js` rotates, prunes, or compacts it. The whole-read cost therefore grows monotonically with use, forever.
- `readNotes` is on request paths: `plan-routes.js:56` calls it with `{ limit: 20 }` on every `GET /api/routing/plans`, and `plan-routes.js:97` serves `GET /api/routing/plans/notes` from it. Asking for 20 notes still reads and parses the entire history first. The note schema (:81-91) also puts no length bound on a note's `text`, so a single legitimate-shaped note can be arbitrarily large.

Scope note: #1624 covers `readPlanStore` (plans.json), `readPoolPlanLinks`, and `readFeedback` (route-feedback.jsonl in route-overrides-store.js). `readNotes` / `plan-notes.jsonl` is a different function over a different file and is named in none of them.

## Evidence (verified this run, main f80ffdb893795fbd44fdddf85cf22b0a5c74da3b)

Laptop probe against the real module from origin/main (probe worktree `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-creator-20261105/`, `probe.mjs` importing the real `lib/routing/plans.js`), each case run ×2 with identical results:

- **Control:** a one-line valid `plan-notes.jsonl` returned 1 note, skipped 0.
- **Oversized:** a schema-valid `plan-notes.jsonl` of 34,603,097 bytes (one note whose `text` is 34,603,008 chars) was read and parsed whole — `readNotes({ limit: 20 })` returned the note with its full 34,603,008-char text. The limit did not bound the read or the parse.
- **FIFO:** with `plan-notes.jsonl` replaced by a FIFO, `readNotes` printed its pre-read marker and never returned — the probe had to be killed by an external 5 s timeout (exit 124) both runs. Synchronous, so in the server this is an event-loop freeze, not a hung request.
- `plans.test.js` exercises `readNotes` for filtering/limit behaviour but contains no oversized / FIFO / bounded-read case for it.

## Why it matters

The Plans surface is a living routing surface: every plans-page load pays a full-history read whose cost only grows, and one planted or corrupted non-regular file at the notes path freezes the managed server outright. The fix is the house pattern already adopted by the neighbouring routing readers — the remaining work is the retention/read-bound decision for an append-only log, which is exactly what triage is for.

## Acceptance criteria

- `readNotes` judges size and file type from an opened handle (the shared bounded reader's sync spelling), with a named, documented bound; a FIFO or other non-regular file at `plan-notes.jsonl` is refused promptly instead of blocking the event loop.
- The append-only growth is addressed explicitly: either a bounded tail read (the callers only ever want the newest `limit` matching notes — state how filtering interacts with a tail bound) or rotation/pruning on append in `addNote`; the chosen behaviour is documented where `readNotes` / `addNote` live, so the request path stops scaling with total history.
- Semantics preserved: missing file → `{ notes: [], skipped: 0 }`; damaged lines are still skipped and counted in `skipped`; filter fields (providerID / planID / modelID / poolID / kind / since), oldest-first sort, and newest-`limit` slicing unchanged for files within the bound.
- Over-cap behaviour is stated and tested — never a silently truncated answer presented as complete history (if a tail read can drop matching older notes, that is visible in the result or the docs).
- Regression tests: oversized and FIFO cases for `readNotes`; ordinary, missing, damaged-line, and limit behaviour unchanged.
- Existing routing suites pass.

Out of scope: `readPlanStore` / `readPoolPlanLinks` / `readFeedback` (#1624), `routing/store.js` (#1608), the note schema's field shapes, and the write path's atomicity (append-only is the design; only its unbounded growth is in scope).

body:
## Problem

The git identity store reads `git-identities.json` whole, synchronously, with no size gate — every other hardened store in this server has adopted a bounded read or an explicit cap, and this one was missed.

`packages/web/server/lib/git/identity-storage.js` (main `6b3b879219`):

- `:148-166` — `readFile()` opens the target with `O_NOFOLLOW` and rejects non-regular files via `fstatSync`, but then calls `fsImpl.readFileSync(handle, 'utf8')` and `JSON.parse`s the entire contents with **no byte cap judged at any point** — not from the already-available `fstatSync` size, and not during the read.
- `:121-131` — the only size-ish validation, `parseState`'s `profiles.length > 256` check, runs **after** the whole file has been buffered and parsed. `parseState` also places no length cap on the stored fields themselves (`userName`/`userEmail` are only checked `isString` + non-empty at `:127`), unlike the public-profile parser in the same file, which caps text fields at 512 chars.

The read runs under the store's file lock on request paths: `loadProfiles` / `getProfiles` / `getProfile` and every mutation transact through `readState()`, and `packages/web/server/lib/git/routes.js:488` calls `getProfiles()` per request (identity provisioning at `lib/git/identity-provisioning.js:80,131` likewise). A bloated or corrupted store file therefore costs a full synchronous buffer + parse of its entire size, under lock, on each of those calls — the store's own writes can never produce such a file (≤256 profiles of ≤512-char fields is a few hundred KB at most), so anything larger is pure unhandled surface: disk corruption, a hand-edited file, or another writer in the data dir.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe against `origin/main` `6b3b879219`)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-05-creator-oc/probe-identity.mjs` (laptop): a `git-identities.json` containing one profile whose `userName` is a single 2 MiB string is accepted — `store.getProfiles()` returns it with `userName.length === 2097152`. No cap fires at read time, at parse time, or in `parseState`.

Dedup: `gh issue list --state all` searches for "identity store", "git identity", "credential helper" return only feature/test issues (#3457-era work, #117, #877); no open or closed issue covers this store's read path. Sibling unbounded-read filings (#1608–#1632) name other stores; this file is not among them.

## Why it matters

This store is otherwise the most carefully hardened reader in the git lib (O_NOFOLLOW, mode checks with migration, atomic rename-with-retry writes) — the missing size gate is the one gap in that posture, and it sits on a synchronous, lock-holding, per-request path. The fix is small because the handle and its `fstatSync` result are already in hand.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An over-cap `git-identities.json` is rejected as an invalid store (`GIT_IDENTITY_STORE_INVALID`, the existing behaviour for malformed content) **without** buffering/parsing the whole file — e.g. a size judgement from the opened handle's `fstatSync` before `readFileSync(handle)`, or adoption of the shared bounded reader (`lib/shared/bounded-file-read.js`) with the store's injected-`fsImpl` test contract preserved or deliberately migrated.
- [ ] The cap is documented in the module and is comfortably above the largest legitimate store (256 profiles × the public parser's 512-char fields); 1 MiB matches the shared-config precedent (#1247).
- [ ] Existing behaviour is unchanged for: missing file (empty state), legacy-file migration, shipped-mode migration, non-regular file rejection, symlink rejection.
- [ ] Regression tests cover the over-cap file and keep the existing `identity-storage.test.js` suite green.

## BLOCKED ON: the Mistral sign-in lane's data-path outcome

A parallel lane is performing Drew's Mistral sign-in (RustDesk session on the laptop, `vibe --setup` → keyring `ai.mistral.vibe`). Which data path this adapter treats as primary depends on what that lane finds, per Drew's directive (2026-11-04 ~23:18 CST): he believes the **Vibe plan token has true usage access**; if it does not, there is a console endpoint to read (via the live session, or a cookie extracted from it). **Do not start the producer build until the sign-in lane records which of these is true** (its record lands on the provider registry's Mistral section / openchamber#1146 thread). The adapter file's `dataPaths` order is the only thing that changes with the answer; everything else here can be designed now.

## Context

- #1619 adds the Mistral **key-validity** quota provider: the API key we hold (Bitwarden `mistral.api-key`, verified live) cannot read usage — `/v1/usage` and `/v1/billing` return 404, and the Admin usage API is Enterprise-only. Usage/credits are **console-only** (Mistral Studio) for this credential class, and the Vibe plan's usage has the same property.
- The design for reading such sources is developing-today/code#6031 (browser-dependent quota watchdog): per-provider **producers** in the code#1301 file-export convention (atomic `~/atlas/<provider>-export/latest.json` + `history.jsonl`, failure-class documents, gatherer ingestion via `FILE_EXPORTS` with code#1268 retention), watched by a generic self-repairing watchdog core (developing-today/code#6032) with escalation to a browser-enabled agent (developing-today/code#6033).
- The producer implementation forks the retired Meta producer (`~/atlas/meta-quota-export/meta-quota-export.mjs` on the laptop): CDP against the laptop's Helium session (:19222), **in-page fetch so the session cookie never leaves the browser**, tab ownership, failure classes with exit codes.

## What to build (adapter #1: Mistral)

1. **Adapter file** `mistral` for the watchdog core: origins allowlist (Mistral Studio console origin(s) only), CDP port 19222, cookie names for presence checks, login flow (console origin → Google SSO via the browser's standing session), class map (401 / redirect-to-login → `session-expired`; 404 / shape-check failure → `endpoint-changed`; 429 → `rate-limited`), thresholds (escalate after 3 consecutive failures; rate-limit cooldown cap 6 h).
2. **Producer** `mistral-quota-export` in the #1301 convention, data paths in the order the sign-in lane's outcome dictates:
   - `token-api` (if the Vibe token reads usage): call it with the token resolved by name (keyring `ai.mistral.vibe` / fleet credential path) — no browser involved on the happy path.
   - `console-fetch`: in-page fetch through CDP of the usage endpoint(s) the signed-in Studio session actually calls; map the response to quota windows (plan usage %, API credits if the console exposes them).
   - `cookie-extract` (last resort): session value → fleet secrets as `mistral.console-session`, then direct fetch. Value never logged or written anywhere else.
3. **Fetcher integration:** the gatherer's `FILE_EXPORTS` gains the mistral entry (registry line + stale threshold 30 min per the convention) so the row lands in `quota-current.json` beside #1619's key-validity row — the two are complementary: validity from the API, plan usage from this adapter. If the module-side marker from #1619 ("console-only") needs updating once real windows exist, note it on #1619 rather than changing its contract silently.
4. **Windows honesty:** emit only figures the console/token actually reports, mapped to the quota module's window shape; anything the source shows that has no window equivalent (e.g. a raw credit balance) goes in as a labeled value, never forced into a percentage. Absence stays absence (no zeros), per the fleet's retention/honesty conventions.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The sign-in lane's data-path outcome is recorded (comment on this issue) naming the primary path, before the producer build starts.
- [ ] With a live signed-in session, a producer tick writes a fresh `latest.json` whose windows match what the Mistral console shows for the same moment (verified side-by-side once).
- [ ] Killing the session (logout in a scratch profile / cookie removed) produces a `session-expired` failure document — not zeros, not silence — and the watchdog's re-login rung can recover it without human help when the browser's Google session is intact.
- [ ] The gatherer ingests the producer document: `quota-current.json` carries a mistral plan-usage row; a stale document (>30 min) ingests as an error entry with the last-good row retained.
- [ ] No secret value (token, cookie) appears in the producer's documents, logs, or this repo at any point.

Related: #1619 (key-validity provider), developing-today/code#6031 (design), #6032 (watchdog core), #6033 (escalation), developing-today/code#5928 (cross-tick state lesson), developing-today/code#4889 (history pipeline).

## Problem

The session-folders routes in `packages/web/server/lib/session-folders/routes.js` read `sessions-directories.json` whole, with no size gate and no non-regular-file protection, at both read sites:

- `readCurrent` (:148) does `fsPromises.readFile(filePath, 'utf8')` at :150 — and `readCurrent` runs inside the store's serialized write queue (`serialize`, :176) on the POST/PATCH save paths
- the `GET /api/session-folders` handler does `fsPromises.readFile(filePath, 'utf8')` at :190 and returns the parsed snapshot verbatim

Unlike the shared bounded reader (`lib/shared/bounded-file-read.js`, `readBoundedFile`) that sibling stores were migrated to (#1607–#1610, #1613–#1615, #1620, #1622), these readers buffer the entire file before judging it. The write side of this very module knows the bound — writes refuse a serialized snapshot over `MAX_BODY_BYTES` = 4 MiB (:5, enforced at :226 and :268) — but the read side enforces nothing: a file grown past the cap by anything else (an older build, a hand edit, a sync tool, corruption) is buffered, parsed, and served whole, and a FIFO at the path never settles.

## Why it matters

The FIFO case wedges more than one request: because `readCurrent` runs inside `serialize`, one never-settling read stalls every later folder save behind it in the queue, silently — the client that caused it and every client after it just hang. The oversized case is served back to every connected client on every GET. This is the same failure shape as the model-choices store in #1610 (read inside a serialized queue), one store over.

## Evidence (verified this run, main 57e2319b76ef041597a7a6e752a9c661d339fb72)

Laptop probe against the real `registerSessionFoldersRoutes` from origin/main (`~/git/fleet/probe-oc-stores-20261104/probe.mjs`, worktree at origin/main, injected `fs.promises` + temp data dir), run x2 with identical results:

- A schema-valid snapshot with a 33 MiB folder name (34,603,008-byte file — 8x the module's own 4 MiB write cap) was served whole by the GET handler (`foldersMap.s1[0].name.length === 34603008`).
- A FIFO at `sessions-directories.json`: the GET handler never settled — still unsettled after 2.5 s both runs.
- `routes.test.js` for session-folders contains no oversized / FIFO / bounded-read test.

## Acceptance criteria

- Both read sites judge size and file type from an opened handle (the shared bounded reader), with a named, documented cap at or modestly above the module's own 4 MiB write cap, so every file the writer can produce stays readable.
- Semantics preserved exactly: missing file → `EMPTY_SNAPSHOT` / `{ exists: false }` as today; malformed → the existing `null` / 500 answers; over-cap and non-regular files follow those same existing malformed paths — never a false-empty snapshot (a false empty read inside the save queue would let a merge overwrite the real folders).
- FIFO / non-regular targets are refused promptly, so the serialized save queue can never be wedged by one bad read.
- Regression tests in the session-folders routes tests: oversized file, FIFO at the path (both the GET and the save-path read), and ordinary / at-cap / missing files unchanged.
- Existing session-folders suites pass.

Out of scope: the write paths and the 4 MiB write cap (correct as they stand), the merge/tombstone logic, and the durable-json-store stores (deliberate #976/#1254 design split).

body:
## Summary

The two guest (extension) stores read their JSON files whole with no size gate and no non-regular-file protection — the residual class fixed for the routing store (#1608), the environment store (#1609), the model-choices store (#1610), the quota credential store (#1613), the relay key-store (#1614) and the Linear auth reader (#1615), in a subsystem none of those fixes touched:

- `packages/web/server/lib/guests/persist.js` — `readExtensionStore` (:139) does `const raw = await fs.readFile(persistPath, 'utf8')` (:141) and parses whatever comes back. It serves `{dataDir}/extensions.json` (`extensionsPersistPath`, :115-121): the installed-guest catalog — install paths, git origins, capability grants and their approved scopes, disabled flags, socket overrides, storage ids.
- `packages/web/server/lib/guests/auth-store.js` — `readGuestAuthStore` (:60) does the same ungated `fs.readFile` (:62) for `{dataDir}/guest-auth.json` (`guestAuthPersistPath`, :38-44): per-guest OAuth client ids/secrets, access and refresh tokens, and settings.

Neither reader uses the house standard that already exists for exactly this: `readBoundedFile` in `packages/web/server/lib/shared/bounded-file-read.js` (:73) — open once with `O_NONBLOCK`, judge from the opened handle, refuse non-regular files, buffer at most cap + 1 byte. The guests subsystem knows the discipline: its per-guest storage reader (`lib/guests/storage.js`) at least stat-gates on `GUEST_STORAGE_TOTAL_BYTES` before reading. These two stores have no gate at all — not even a stat.

## Verified this run (laptop probe against the real modules, main 68c9f11c54)

Code read on `origin/main` 68c9f11c54f25fcff7e2f7c69a71d16725ac9e1f (laptop `git show origin/main:`, cross-checked with `gh api`), plus a probe on the laptop (probe dir `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-guests-ungated-20261104/`) running the real `persist.js` / `auth-store.js` extracted from `origin/main`, each case run ×2 with identical results:

- **Oversized:** a 34,603,008-byte schema-valid `extensions.json` (one 33 MiB path entry) was returned whole by `readExtensionStore` — first path length 34603008, no size rejection. A 34,603,008-byte schema-valid `guest-auth.json` (one 33 MiB access token) was likewise returned whole by `readGuestAuthStore`.
- **FIFO:** with either store path replaced by a FIFO, the reader never settled within 3,000 ms in either run (the blocked `open()` kept the probe process alive until an external 30 s timeout killed it). The reads are async, so this does not freeze the event loop — it wedges the caller permanently (below).
- **Control:** ordinary small files of both shapes read back exactly.
- Neither test suite has a bounded case: `persist.test.js` and `auth-store.test.js` contain no oversized / FIFO / non-regular / bounded test (grep-verified).

## Why it matters

- **The wedge is serialized, so it is total for that store.** Both stores run their reads inside per-path write locks: every guest-auth mutation (`patchGuestAuth` :125, `forgetGuestAuth` :177, via `withAuthStoreLock` :88) first awaits `readGuestAuthStore`, and every extension-store mutation (`updateExtensionStore`, persist.js :276) first awaits `readExtensionStore` under `withStoreWriteLock`. A FIFO (or a writer that never finishes) at either path blocks the lock's promise chain in the read, and every later guest-auth or extension-catalog operation for that path queues behind it forever — token refreshes, grant changes, installs — with no error and no recovery short of removing the file by hand. The plain catalog/install reads (`catalog.js:553`, `install.js:43` and `:121`) hang the same way.
- **Memory:** the schema validators run only *after* the whole file is in memory, so they bound what is kept, not what is read. One oversized file at either path is buffered and parsed whole on every read — and `guest-auth.json` holds OAuth tokens and client secrets.
- **Semantics that must not flip:** today a missing file reads as the empty store (`emptyStore()` / `{ guests: {} }`), an empty auth file reads as `{ guests: {} }`, and a malformed file throws (`Invalid extensions store` / `Invalid guest auth store`). An over-cap or non-regular file must follow the malformed/throw path — never the empty path: reading a bloated `guest-auth.json` as empty would let the next locked patch overwrite the real token file with a fresh store, silently destroying every guest's credentials (the same false-first-run hazard #1614 pins for the relay identity).

## Why the caps are safe (write-side clamps)

Everything both stores write is small, bounded records keyed by installed guest: paths are filesystem paths; git origins are a URL plus a ref ≤ 256 chars and an identity id ≤ 128 (persist.js `gitOriginSchema`); scopes are short pattern/origin/URL lists checked per entry; auth entries carry tokens and settings whose values are ≤ 2,000 chars with account ≤ 200 (`guestAuthEntrySchema`). Even a pathological 1,000 installed guests at a few KB of records each stays in the low single-digit MB. A named cap per file in that range (the shared reader's 8 MiB default class, or a smaller cap whose comment carries this computation) loses nothing legitimate.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `readExtensionStore` (persist.js) and `readGuestAuthStore` (auth-store.js) read through a bounded, handle-judged read (`readBoundedFile` in `lib/shared/bounded-file-read.js`, or equivalent): at most cap + 1 byte is ever buffered, and a FIFO / directory / other non-regular file at either path is refused promptly instead of blocking the read — including the reads taken under both stores' write locks.
- [ ] Each cap is a named constant documented in code with its headroom over the legitimate maximum from the write-side clamps above, the way the sibling fixes document theirs.
- [ ] Existing semantics preserved exactly: missing file still reads as the empty store for both readers; an empty `guest-auth.json` still reads as `{ guests: {} }`; malformed, over-cap, and non-regular files follow the existing throw path (`Invalid extensions store` / `Invalid guest auth store`) — an over-cap file never silently reads as a valid empty store anywhere.
- [ ] Regression tests in `persist.test.js` and `auth-store.test.js` (or the guests suites): oversized file refused without being parsed whole, FIFO/non-regular target refused without hanging, at-cap and ordinary files read unchanged, missing file unchanged.
- [ ] No other guest behaviour changes; the write paths, schemas, per-entry tolerant parsing (unknown capabilities / malformed scope entries drop out per entry), and atomic writes are untouched. Per-guest storage (`storage.js`) is out of scope — it already stat-gates.

## Dedup

## Gap

The quota module has no `mistral` provider, so Mistral never appears in `quota-current.json` even though the fleet now holds a live Mistral credential (provider audit, 2026-11-04):

- Bitwarden `mistral.api-key` (created 2026-11-04T21:20:19Z) + active OpenCode credential row `Mistral (drewrypope)` (`cred_1a1a91e057d001wNEjIGIbKN5x`).
- Verified live: `GET https://api.mistral.ai/v1/models` with that credential → **200, 64 models** (codestral-2508, mistral-large-latest, ministral line, …).

## What a mistral quota provider can and cannot read (probed, not assumed)

- `GET /v1/usage` → **404**; `GET /v1/billing` → **404**. There is no usage/balance endpoint for a standard API key.
- Mistral's Admin API (`/v1/admin/usage`, `/v1/admin/analytics/vibe`, spend/rate limits) does expose usage, but per Mistral's docs it is **Enterprise-plan only** and needs a separate **Admin API key** (`x-api-key` header, created in the Admin Panel) — a standard key does not work with admin endpoints. The fleet does not hold one.
- So usage percentages and the API credit balance are **console-only** (Mistral Studio / admin console) for the credential class we hold. The Vibe plan's usage has the same property (the legacy vibe field on the admin usage response is documented "Always 0; use the Vibe usage API instead" — itself behind the Admin API).

## Ask

Add a `mistral` provider to the quota module in the key-validity class (like the providers that report credential state rather than windows):

- Configured when an OpenCode `mistral` credential resolves.
- Read = `GET /v1/models` with the credential: 200 → `ok: true` with the credential label and a usage object that states plainly `windows: {}` plus a machine-readable marker that usage is not API-readable on this credential class (so the board shows "tracked, console-only" instead of another ok-but-null mystery); 401/403 → unauthorized class; transport failure → error class.
- Register it in `providers/index.js` so `listConfiguredQuotaProviders` picks it up automatically (the gatherer then emits a mistral entry every tick with no aggregator change).
- Tests in the house style (cf. `meta.test.js`, `codex.test.js`): 200 validity, 401 class, malformed body.

When/if the fleet ever holds an Enterprise Admin API key, a follow-up can add real windows from `/v1/admin/usage` behind it. Until then this closes the "Mistral is invisible to the quota system" gap honestly — presence + validity tracked, percentages explicitly not measurable.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A `mistral` provider exists in the quota module and appears in `quota-current.json` under the key-validity class.
- [ ] No usage/balance figures are emitted for Mistral (the standard-key endpoints return 404 — verified in the issue); absence of data is represented honestly, not as zero.
- [ ] A valid key reports valid; an invalid/revoked key reports invalid, using the existing provider contract and tests.
- [ ] The provider reads its credential from the fleet's existing credential store path, like the other providers.

body:
## Problem

`packages/web/server/lib/linear/auth.js`'s strict JSON reader reads its files whole, synchronously, with no size gate and no regular-file check — and one of the files it reads is the shared `settings.json`:

- `auth.js:59-62` — `readJsonFileStrict(filePath)` does `raw = fs.readFileSync(filePath, 'utf8')`, then trims and `JSON.parse`s the whole buffer. No cap, no `stat` judgement, no use of the shared bounded reader.
- It is the reader for both Linear files: `readAuthForUpdate` reads `linear-auth.json` (the token store) through it at `:277`, and the settings reader returns `readJsonFileStrict(settingsFile()) || {}` at `:302` — i.e. the same ungated sync read is applied to `<data-dir>/settings.json`, the large shared settings file that other subsystems already read through gated readers.
- It also backs the lenient reader (`:111-114`) and `jsonFileState`/`getLinearStorageState` (`:85-105`), so the ungated read runs on status/diagnostic paths as well as every Linear write path ("Used by every write path", comment at `:55-58`).

Unlike the house standard: `packages/web/server/lib/shared/bounded-file-read.js` (`readBoundedFile`, `:41-70`) opens with `O_NONBLOCK`, judges the handle's stat (rejecting non-regular files), and reads in chunks up to an explicit cap (default 8 MiB). Sibling stores in this series: #1607, #1608, #1609, #1610, #1490.

## Verified this run (main `9cef4f4c1e95`)

Code read ×2 independent routes (`gh api` raw read and laptop `git grep`/`git show` on `origin/main`), plus a laptop probe against the real `lib/linear/auth.js` extracted from `origin/main` (probe dir `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-linear-auth-ungated-20261104/` on the laptop), run ×2 each, via the exported `getLinearStorageState()` with `OPENCHAMBER_DATA_DIR` pointed at the probe dir:

- Oversized: a 33,554,443-byte `linear-auth.json` was judged `{"authFile":"valid", …}` — parsed whole, no size rejection.
- FIFO: with `linear-auth.json` replaced by a FIFO, `getLinearStorageState()` never returned within 3 s in either run (killed by timeout). The read is **synchronous**, so this blocks the server's event loop, not just the Linear surface.

## Why it matters

- Availability: a non-regular or runaway file at either path stalls the whole managed server (sync read on write, read, and diagnostic paths).
- Blast radius is larger than the sibling stores: the settings arm applies the ungated read to `settings.json`, a file whose size is driven by every other subsystem's settings, not by Linear.
- Memory: oversized content is buffered and parsed whole with no bound, on a file pair that holds OAuth tokens.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `readJsonFileStrict` (or its replacement) judges the file before/while reading: non-regular files (FIFO, device, directory) are refused promptly instead of blocking, and content past an explicit named cap is refused rather than buffered whole — for both the `linear-auth.json` and `settings.json` call sites (per-file caps may differ; both must be named in code).
- [ ] Existing semantics preserved exactly: missing/empty file reads as `null`, malformed JSON throws the existing `MALFORMED` `LinearAuthError` without quoting file contents, non-object JSON is malformed, and `getLinearStorageState` still distinguishes missing/valid/malformed/unreadable (`auth.test.js` behaviour).
- [ ] The gated read must not leak file contents into errors or logs (the current reader's no-quote discipline, `auth.js:46-53`, is preserved).
- [ ] Regression tests cover: oversized file refused on both call sites, FIFO/non-regular path refused promptly (no hang), and normal auth + settings files still read.

Filed by the new-issue-creator fleet run (agent `new-issue-creator-openchamber`), 2026-11-04. Sibling filings in the same ungated-read series: #1607, #1608, #1609, #1610, #1490.

## Problem

`packages/web/server/lib/quota/credentials/store.js` reads each managed quota credential file whole, synchronously, with no size gate and no regular-file check:

- `store.js:20-22` — `readQuotaCredential` does `JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(credentialPath(providerId), 'utf8'))`. There is no cap, no `stat`/`fstat` regular-file judgement, and no use of the shared bounded reader.
- The files are per-provider secrets (`<data-dir>/quota/<provider>.json`, written `0600` by `writeQuotaCredential` at `store.js:37-40`) for the allowlisted providers at `store.js:6` (`exe-dev`, `cursor`, `zenmux`, `opendesign`). A legitimate file is a single token object — a few hundred bytes.
- Call path: `quota/credentials/providers.js:39` returns `readQuotaCredential(providerId, normalize)` from the credential read used by the quota providers, i.e. this synchronous read runs on the quota surface's normal operation.

Unlike the house standard: `packages/web/server/lib/shared/bounded-file-read.js` (`readBoundedFile`, `:41-70`) opens with `O_NONBLOCK`, judges the handle's stat (rejecting non-regular files), and reads in chunks up to an explicit cap (default 8 MiB). Every sibling store filed in this series (#1607 agent-memory/project-context, #1608 routing, #1609 environment, #1610 model-choices, #1490 projects config) is being moved to that standard; this store was noted as checked-not-filed in the 2026-11-04 17:50 CST creator run and is filed now with probe evidence.

## Verified this run (main `9cef4f4c1e95`)

Code read ×2 independent routes (`gh api` raw read and laptop `git grep`/`git show` on `origin/main`), plus a laptop probe against the real `store.js` extracted from `origin/main` (probe dir `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-quota-cred-ungated-20261104/` on the laptop), run ×2 each:

- Control: a normal `{"usageToken":"secret"}` file reads back correctly.
- Oversized: a 33,554,462-byte `exe-dev.json` was parsed whole and returned (pad field of 33,554,432 chars present in the result) — no size rejection.
- FIFO: with `exe-dev.json` replaced by a FIFO, `readQuotaCredential` never returned within 3 s (both runs killed by timeout). Because the read is **synchronous**, a FIFO at that path does not just wedge one request — it blocks the server's event loop entirely.

## Why it matters

- Availability: one non-regular or runaway file at a predictable data-dir path stalls the whole managed server (sync read), not just the quota surface.
- Memory: an oversized credential file is buffered and parsed whole with no bound.
- Consistency: this is the same ungated-read class the fleet has been closing store by store; leaving the secrets-bearing quota store ungated keeps the pattern alive as a copy source.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The credential read judges the file before/while reading: non-regular files (FIFO, device, directory) are refused promptly instead of blocking, and content past an explicit named cap is refused rather than buffered whole.
- [ ] The cap is sized to the legitimate shape (a single provider token object) and named in code, mirroring `readBoundedFile`'s discipline or reusing it where the store's sync call shape allows (converting the read to the bounded async reader is acceptable if callers are updated).

- [ ] Regression tests cover: oversized file refused, FIFO/non-regular path refused promptly (no hang), and the normal small credential still reads.

body:
## Summary

The environment store — the web server's store for the user's environment variables and per-project environment commands, a file that holds API tokens (mode 0600) — reads its JSON file whole with no size gate and no non-regular-file protection, and it reads **synchronously**. It is the residual class fixed for the project config (#1490), the session-goal objective (#1582), agent-memory + project-context (#1607) and the routing store (#1608), in a store none of those touched:

- `packages/web/server/lib/environment/store.js` — `readFromDisk` (:99) does `raw = fs.readFileSync(filePath, 'utf8')` (:101) and `JSON.parse`s whatever comes back. There is no byte cap, no `stat`/`isFile` judgement, and no use of `readBoundedFile` or the durable-store primitive anywhere in the file (full-file read: :101 is the only read).
- The read is on a hot path by the module's own design: "Git reads the environment on every command, polling included, so the parsed document is kept in memory" (store.js :91–93). The first read — and every retry, because "a failed read is not kept and is retried on the next call" (:92) — goes through `read()` (:94) from `userVariables()`, `projectEntry()`, `hasProjectEntries()` and the describe/update paths, consumed by `lib/environment/runtime.js` (`store.userVariables()` :137, `store.projectEntry(projectId)` :146, :264–278) whenever a command's environment is assembled.
- Because the read is synchronous, a FIFO or other non-regular file at the store's path does not hang one request: `readFileSync` blocks in `open()` on the event loop's only thread and freezes the whole server, indefinitely, with no error. An oversized regular file is buffered whole and parsed whole before the zod schema ever runs — the schema bounds what is *kept*, not what is *read*.

The house standard for exactly this already exists: `readBoundedFile` in `packages/web/server/lib/shared/bounded-file-read.js` — open once with `O_NONBLOCK`, judge from the opened handle, refuse non-regular files, buffer at most cap + 1 byte — in both async and sync spellings. The environment store was not one of the fifteen stores migrated to the durable-store primitive in #976.

## The cap needs one deliberate choice (unlike the sibling stores)

The sibling fixes could mirror a small computed legitimate maximum from tight write-side clamps. Here the write side clamps each *entry* — `MAX_VARIABLES = 200`, `MAX_VARIABLE_VALUE_LENGTH = 32_000`, `MAX_COMMAND_LENGTH = 4_000` (`lib/environment/variables.js` :9–11), enforced per user/project entry by `storeSchema` — but the number of project entries in the `projects` record is itself unbounded, so there is no small fixed legitimate maximum to copy. Triage should pick and document the disposition: a generous fixed cap with headroom (a single entry's worst case is ≈ 200 × (256-char name + 32,000-char value) ≈ 6.5 MB), a per-entry accounting read, or a cap paired with a project-count bound on write. Any of them beats buffering an arbitrary file whole on a polling path; what is not acceptable is the status quo.

## Verified this run (code-verified on origin/main 41c124c7c, read ×2 via `gh api`)

- `readFromDisk` and the :101 `readFileSync` re-read independently twice on main `41c124c7ca7c82fbca59d866c43cb76961bfcba8` (contents API by ref and by blob `f8644222f3e602891d2189ee4a204a97523f65e3`); the line numbers above are from the second read. Full-file grep: :101 is the only read in `store.js`; no cap, no handle judgement, no bounded reader.
- Consumers verified in `lib/environment/runtime.js` (:137, :146, :264–278) on the same main.
- The store's own test suite (`environment/store.test.js`, 103 lines) contains no oversized-file, FIFO, or non-regular-file case (grep: no `fifo`/`oversiz`/`bounded`/`MAX` case).
- `fs.readFileSync` on a FIFO with no writer blocks in `open()` before any judgement can run — the identical ungated pattern was probe-confirmed on the laptop for #1607 (FIFO never settled within 3,000 ms; 33 MB files buffered whole). A runtime probe of this store was **not** run this run: the laptop SSH tunnel was down for the entire run (repeated `laptop-agent: HTTP 502 … proxy closed during CONNECT` from `~/tools/laptop-ssh.sh`, plus the real-SSH fallback failing), and probes are never run on the sandbox. The defect is fully determined by the code above; a triage probe against `createEnvironmentStore` with an oversized file and a FIFO is a reasonable first confirmation step.

## Why it matters

The file lives in the user's config/data directory, which other tools, sync jobs and agents also write, and it holds secrets the server must never lose: the module header (:21–22) is explicit that an unreadable file is an error, never an empty store, because "a write on top of it would erase every stored secret". One oversized or non-regular file at that path either buffers unboundedly on the git/command polling path or freezes the entire server synchronously with no error and no recovery short of finding and removing the file by hand. The strict malformed semantics must stay exactly as they are: an over-cap file must follow the existing `EnvironmentStoreError` path, never read as an empty store.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `readFromDisk` in `lib/environment/store.js` reads through a bounded, handle-judged read (`readBoundedFile`'s sync spelling in `lib/shared/bounded-file-read.js`, or equivalent): at most cap + 1 byte is ever buffered, and a FIFO / directory / other non-regular file at the store path is refused promptly instead of blocking the event loop.
- [ ] The cap (or per-entry accounting) is documented in code with its reasoning from the write-side clamps above — per-entry maxima in `variables.js`, the unbounded project count — the way the sibling fixes document theirs.
- [ ] Existing read semantics are preserved exactly: missing file still reads as `{ version: 1 }`; a malformed or over-cap file still throws `EnvironmentStoreError` (never silently reads as an empty store, so no later write can erase stored secrets); the success-only cache and failed-read retry behaviour are unchanged.
- [ ] Regression tests in `environment/store.test.js`: oversized file refused via the error path without being parsed whole, FIFO/non-regular target refused without hanging, at-cap and ordinary files read unchanged.
- [ ] No other store changes behaviour; the write path, schemas, 0600 mode handling and atomic rename are untouched.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for `environment.json`, `environment store`, `model-choices`, `quota credential`, `relay-identity` and the full open-issue list: #117 (closed) covers this store's rename-retry on writes — a different defect; #1553 covers environment *command output* decoding; #1607 covers agent-memory + project-context, #1608 the routing store, #1490 the project config, #1582 the session-goal objective. The environment store's read is covered nowhere.

## Summary

Two of the web server's own JSON state stores read their files whole with no size gate and no non-regular-file protection — the exact residual class fixed for the project config (#1490), the session-goal objective (#1582), the walkthrough pointer files (#1482) and the project-icon serve path (#1537), in the two stores those fixes did not touch:

- `packages/web/server/lib/agent-memory/runtime.js` — `readJson` (:231) does `raw = await fsPromises.readFile(filePath, 'utf8')` (:234) and `JSON.parse`s whatever comes back. It serves both `memory.json` files: global (`<userConfigRoot>/memory.json`) and per-project (`<projectsDir>/<stem>/memory.json`).
- `packages/web/server/lib/project-context/runtime.js` — an identical private `readJson` (:284, `readFile` :287) serves `context.json` (and the legacy `<stem>.json` read through the same helper).

Neither store uses the house standard that already exists for exactly this: `readBoundedFile` in `packages/web/server/lib/shared/bounded-file-read.js` (:73) — open once with `O_NONBLOCK`, judge from the opened handle, refuse non-regular files, buffer at most cap + 1 byte.

## Why the caps are safe (write-side clamps)

Everything these stores write is tightly clamped, so a generous read cap loses nothing legitimate:

- agent-memory: at most 60 (global) / 200 (project) entries; title ≤ 60 chars, body ≤ 2,000 chars (writes reject over-limit bodies, `runtime.js:45-49`, `:148`). A legitimate project `memory.json` is ≲ 0.5 MB.
- project-context: notes ≤ 200 × 3,000 chars, todos ≤ 500 × 1,000 chars, plan links ≤ 500 × (title ≤ 160 + file name + ids) (`runtime.js:25-31`). A legitimate `context.json` is ≲ 1.3 M chars. (Plan *bodies* live in separate `.md` files, already read through the capped `readPlanFile`/`readBoundedUtf8` path in the same module, :766-791.)

## Verified this run (laptop probe vs the real runtimes from origin/main 41c124c7c, run ×2)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-jsonstores-ungated-20261104/` (`probe.mjs`, `probe2.mjs`; modules exported verbatim from `origin/main`).

- Control: a small valid `memory.json` / `context.json` reads back normally (1 entry / 1 note).
- Oversized: a 33,554,534-byte valid `memory.json` was buffered and parsed whole — the read settled in ~32 ms, returned the entry with its body silently clamped to 2,000 chars, **no size rejection at any point**. Same for a 33,554,527-byte `context.json` (note body clamped to 3,000). A file 60× the largest legitimate size is not refused; a 1 GiB file would be buffered the same way.
- FIFO: with `memory.json` (resp. `context.json`) replaced by a FIFO with no writer, the read **never settled within 3,000 ms** — `readFile` blocks in `open()` before any `isFile` judgement can run. `readBoundedFile`'s `O_NONBLOCK` open + handle stat is the pattern that refuses this (its own tests pin the FIFO case).

## Why it matters

These files sit in the user's config/projects directories, which other tools and agents also write (agent memory is written by agents unprompted, by design of that module). One oversized or non-regular file at either path makes every memory/context read buffer unboundedly or hang the request path indefinitely. The sanitizers only run *after* the whole file is in memory, so they bound what is kept, not what is read.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Both `readJson` helpers read through a bounded, handle-judged read (`readBoundedFile` from `lib/shared/bounded-file-read.js`, or equivalent): at most cap + 1 byte is ever buffered, and a FIFO / directory / other non-regular file at either path is refused promptly instead of blocking the read.
- [ ] Each cap is documented in code with its headroom over the computed legitimate maximum (write-side clamps above), the way `PLAN_FILE_READ_MAX_BYTES` is documented in `plan-progress.js`.
- [ ] Existing read semantics are preserved exactly: missing file still reads as authoritative empty; an unparseable or over-cap file follows the current malformed path (agent-memory `read()` throws "Stored agent memory is malformed"; project-context keeps its current malformed handling) — an over-cap file must never silently read as empty.
- [ ] Regression tests in `agent-memory/runtime.test.js` and `project-context/runtime.test.js` (or their existing suites): oversized file refused without being parsed whole, FIFO/non-regular target refused without hanging, at-cap and ordinary files read unchanged.
- [ ] No other store changes behaviour; the plan-file reads in project-context (already capped) are untouched.

## Dedup

body:
## Problem

This repo moved from `developing-today/openchamber` to `developing-today-forks/openchamber` on 2026-11-04. Three workflows gate their jobs on the OLD full name with an equality test against `github.repository`, which now always returns `developing-today-forks/openchamber` — so the guards can never pass again and the jobs skip silently on every run:

- `.github/workflows/repo-sweeper.yml:60` — job "Sweep PR intake (size + parking labels)"
- `.github/workflows/repo-sweeper.yml:277` — job "Sweep merge-conflict labels"
- `.github/workflows/repo-sweeper.yml:316` — job "Collect un-intaked open issues" (the intake matrix job downstream of it skips with it)
- `.github/workflows/main-broken.yml:63` — the watcher's only job: `github.repository == 'developing-today/openchamber' && (...)`
- `.github/workflows/stale.yml:29` — the stale-labelling job

Each guard is `github.repository == 'openchamber/openchamber' || github.repository == 'developing-today/openchamber'` (main-broken has only the second arm). Including the old fork name is what proves these jobs were meant to run HERE — unlike the deliberate upstream-only gates listed under Out of scope.

## Observed behaviour (verified 2026-11-04, main `41c124c7c`)

- repo-sweeper run 41879988834 (2026-11-04T17:44:08Z, schedule): run conclusion **skipped**; all four jobs skipped — "Sweep PR intake", "Sweep merge-conflict labels", "Collect un-intaked open issues", "Intake issue".
- The previous sweeper run 41810444450 (2026-11-04T09:52:30Z, schedule, before the move): conclusion **success**, the three guarded jobs succeeded.
- main-broken workflow_run runs since the move (e.g. 41846008429, 2026-11-04T14:17:03Z) conclude **skipped**; independently of its failure-conclusion arm, its repository arm can now never be true.
- stale.yml's next scheduled run (daily 01:30 UTC) will skip the same way; its last scheduled run (41793711912, 2026-11-04T07:38:44Z, pre-move) succeeded.

## Why it matters

The repo-sweeper is this repo's intake automation (PR size/parking labels, merge-conflict labels, un-intaked issue collection every 15 minutes) and main-broken is the watcher that files main-breakage issues. Both have been silently dead since the move — a skipped run looks like a quiet day, so nothing alerts. Stale labelling is dead too. Every day this stands, intake and breakage detection drift further behind.

## Also audit (same move, redirect-dependent — disposition each, fix or record why it is safe)

These still name the old repo but currently work only through GitHub's transfer redirect, which disappears if the old name is ever re-registered:

- `packages/web/server/lib/package-manager.js:19` — `GITHUB_RELEASES_API_URL = 'https://api.github.com/repos/developing-today/openchamber/releases'` (the fork update check).
- `.github/workflows/jules-daily-upstream-sync.yml:70` — the sync prompt instructs `gh issue create --repo developing-today/openchamber`.
- `.github/scripts/test-require-main-gate.sh:45` — `GH_REPO=developing-today/openchamber` fixture.

## Out of scope (deliberate upstream-only gates — do NOT change)

- `.github/workflows/nix-eval.yml:31` and `nix-hashes.yml:23` gate to `openchamber/openchamber` only, by design.
- `.github/workflows/release.yml:117` publish gate to `openchamber/openchamber`, by design.
- Cosmetic old-name links in README/nix/About UI that follow the web redirect.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] repo-sweeper.yml, main-broken.yml and stale.yml guards name `developing-today-forks/openchamber` (replacing or extending the old-name arm), with no other behaviour change.
- [ ] A scheduled repo-sweeper run after the fix shows the three guarded jobs running (success), not skipped.
- [ ] A workflow_dispatch of stale.yml (dry conditions as configured) runs its job instead of skipping.
- [ ] Each audit-list reference above is either updated to the new name or carries a comment/recorded reason it intentionally keeps the old one.
- [ ] The workflow-audit checks still pass on the edited workflows.

body:
## Problem

PR #1584 (2026-11-04, Drew's ruling: no commit- or PR-triggered CI) removed the `push: tags: ['v*']` trigger from both release workflows. Its body states the scope plainly: every push entry removed, "nothing outside the `on:` blocks is touched." The rest of both files still describes — and in one place still depends on — the tag-push world, and one release step can now never run.

Verified on main `78037f1e5ddbfe62ecebe280583d5ac9047482d1`:

### `.github/workflows/release.yml`

- `on:` (from :3) is now `workflow_dispatch` only, with a required `version` input.
- Header comment (:32-37) still says: "Tag pushes and manual dispatches each get a per-run group (run_id)… Triggers are push/workflow_dispatch only".
- Concurrency group (:39) still carries a dead push arm: `(github.event_name == 'push' && (github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' || startsWith(github.ref, 'refs/tags/')))`.
- Input descriptions still warn about tag pushes: `build_macos` (:21) "a tag push never builds macOS unless this is chosen", `build_windows` (:26) likewise — a tag push now builds nothing at all.
- `get_version` (:80-81) still derives the version from `refs/tags/v*` when no input version is given; with `version` required on the only remaining trigger, that arm is unreachable.

### `.github/workflows/vscode-extension.yml`

- `on:` (:3-4) is now `workflow_dispatch` only.
- Header comment (:8-13) and concurrency group (:14) repeat the same false "Tag pushes… / Triggers are push/workflow_dispatch only" text and dead push arm.
- **"Attach VSIX to GitHub Release" step (:62-63) is gated `if: startsWith(github.ref, 'refs/tags/')`** — a dispatch run's ref is a branch, so this step can never execute again. The VSIX is still built and uploaded as a workflow artifact, and the marketplace/Open VSX publish steps were updated to fire on `workflow_dispatch`, but nothing attaches the VSIX to the GitHub Release any more. The step's own comment says "The release workflow publishes the release once every platform is on it; uploading here must not publish the draft early" — that handoff is silently broken.

## Why it matters

- A maintainer reading either header will believe pushing a `v*` tag releases. It does nothing: no run starts. The first symptom would be a "missing" release discovered by hand.
- The dead VSIX-attach step fails silently — every dispatched extension publish looks successful while the GitHub Release ships without the VSIX that the release workflow's flow expects to find there.
- This is the same stale-contract class as #1585 (oc-review/ci-policy, fixed by PR #1588) and #1586 (workflow-audit), in the two files of the #1584 set those issues did not cover.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `release.yml` and `vscode-extension.yml` header comments and concurrency groups describe the dispatch-only reality (no tag-push claims, no dead `push` arms), OR the tag-push trigger is deliberately restored with the decision recorded — Drew's 2026-11-04 no-push-trigger ruling is the default assumption.
- [ ] The VSIX reaches the GitHub Release again on the dispatch path (e.g. the attach step takes an explicit release tag/version input or is owned by the release flow), OR the step is removed and the place the VSIX is published from is documented in the workflow.
- [ ] `release.yml`'s `get_version` tag arm and the `build_macos`/`build_windows` "tag push" input descriptions are removed or rewritten to match how a release is actually started now.
- [ ] A grep over `.github/workflows/` for `refs/tags` event claims matches only steps/triggers that can actually fire.

Found by the #1530 phase-2 inventory (design #1528). Surface: `packages/web/server/lib/linear/teams.js`, team list.

## The read

`listLinearTeams` paginates `teams(first: 50, after:)` up to `MAX_PAGES = 20`, following `pageInfo.hasNextPage`. If the connection still has a next page after the 20th page, the loop simply ends and the function returns `{ connected: true, teams }` — the prefix is returned as the whole, with no error and no `hasMore`/incomplete signal in the result shape. That is exactly the silent-cap shape #1528's contract forbids ("hitting a cap is explicit").

## What done looks like

- Past the cap, the read either errors (verdict-style) or returns its incompleteness with the teams (display-style `teamsMore`), matching the shape Linear results already use elsewhere in this codebase (`commentsMore`, `statesMore`, `subIssuesMore` in `lib/linear/issues.js`).
- A test pins the cap-hit case.

## Acceptance criteria

- Past the `MAX_PAGES = 20` cap, `listLinearTeams` either errors (verdict-style) or returns its incompleteness with the teams (display-style `teamsMore`), matching the `*More` shape Linear results already use in this codebase.
- A test pins the cap-hit case.

body:
## Problem

`repo-sweeper.yml` once again carries a workflow-level concurrency block that can cancel a running issue intake — the exact failure closed #758 was filed and fixed to eliminate. Two governing texts in the same tree still state the opposite design, so either the workflow regressed or a deliberate reversal was never documented.

On current main (`78037f1e5ddbfe62ecebe280583d5ac9047482d1`):

- `.github/workflows/repo-sweeper.yml:33-35` — a workflow-level block sits directly under `on:`:

  ```yaml
  concurrency:
    group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
    cancel-in-progress: true
  ```

- `.github/workflows/repo-sweeper.yml:40-54` — the #758 concurrency audit comment, a few lines below in the same file, says the opposite: "this workflow deliberately has NO workflow-level concurrency block. A workflow-level cancel-in-progress cancels the whole run, intake legs included… issue-intake legs carry a per-issue job-level group with `cancel-in-progress` as the literal false, so a tick can never cancel a running intake, however long it takes."
- `.github/ci-policy.md:143-152` — the policy doc repeats the design as current fact: "The sweeper has no workflow-level concurrency block (#758): the label passes carry per-job groups with `cancel-in-progress: true`, and each issue-intake leg carries a per-issue group with the literal `cancel-in-progress: false`… so a tick can never cancel a running intake."
- The job-level design the audit describes is still in place: label passes at `:60-62`, `:277-279`, `:316-318` carry per-job groups with `cancel-in-progress: true`; the `issue-intake` job at `:369-377` has `timeout-minutes: 35` and a per-issue group with `cancel-in-progress: false`.

## How it regressed

- `d515a71d0` (2026-10-29, "fix(ci): repo-sweeper ticks can no longer cancel a running issue intake (#758)") removed the previous workflow-level block, added the audit comment and the per-job groups, and updated `ci-policy.md` to match.
- `4478502bb` (2026-10-30, "ci: main-only workflow triggers, cancel-in-progress everywhere") then re-added a workflow-level block to this file — its message notes "concurrency block added where missing (repo-sweeper)" as part of a blanket every-workflow change. It did not touch the #758 audit comment or the `ci-policy.md` statement, and its message gives no sign the #758 intake-cancellation trade-off was considered.

## Why it matters

The sweeper ticks every 15 minutes (`:30-32`) while an issue-intake leg may run for up to 35 minutes (`:369`). With a workflow-level `cancel-in-progress: true` group, a new tick entering the group cancels the whole in-progress run — the per-issue job-level `cancel-in-progress: false` cannot shield a job from a workflow-level cancellation. That is precisely the #758 failure mode ("a slow intake can never finish and blocks the oldest-first queue"): the oldest un-intaked issues are re-selected first on every sweep, so an intake that needs more than one tick interval can be cancelled repeatedly, burn its compute each time, and starve the intake queue behind it. No existing guard catches this: the workflow audit (`workflow-audit.yml`, the #1399 recurrence guard) only checks reusable-workflow caller-job keys, not concurrency semantics.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A decision is recorded on this issue: restore the #758 design (remove the workflow-level block at `repo-sweeper.yml:33-35`), OR ratify the blanket cancel-everywhere behaviour for this workflow explicitly, knowing it re-opens the #758 intake-cancellation trade-off.
- [ ] If the #758 design is restored: the workflow-level block is gone, the per-job groups (`:60-62`, `:277-279`, `:316-318`, `:375-377`) are unchanged, and the YAML still parses / the workflow still starts.
- [ ] If the blanket behaviour is ratified instead: the audit comment at `repo-sweeper.yml:40-54` and the statement at `ci-policy.md:143-152` are rewritten to match reality, and the intake-cancellation mitigation (how a >15-minute intake can ever finish) is stated in both places.
- [ ] Either way, workflow file, audit comment, and `ci-policy.md` agree afterwards — no remaining text claims the sweeper has no workflow-level concurrency block while one is present (or vice versa).

Related: #758 (the original fix this regresses), #1399 / #1586 (the workflow-audit guard — it does not cover concurrency semantics), commit `4478502bb` (the blanket change that re-added the block), commit `d515a71d0` (the #758 fix).

title: fix(vscode): VS Code fs-exec bridge decodes output per pipe chunk — a multi-byte character split across chunks is silently corrupted in returned (and git-read-cached) output

body:
## Problem

The VS Code extension's fs-exec bridge decodes command output one pipe chunk at a time, so a multi-byte UTF-8 character that straddles a chunk boundary is silently corrupted — and this is the one site #1558 explicitly left open ("triage confirms whether the bridge fs-exec accumulator … is in scope here or filed separately"). It is filed separately here.

`packages/vscode/src/bridge-fs-runtime.ts` (`api:fs:exec` handler, `runCommand`):

- `:525` `appendCapped` accumulates each stream's output.
- `:531` `value: current + buffer.toString()` — each `Buffer` chunk is decoded independently. A character split across two chunks becomes U+FFFD replacement characters on both sides of the split.
- `:533` the overflow-kept prefix is also decoded standalone (`buffer.subarray(0, remaining).toString()`), so a split at the cap boundary corrupts the same way.
- `:563/:570` both stdout and stderr feed through this accumulator; the results are returned to the bridge caller at `:583-584` / `:594-595` (trimmed, but the corruption is already in the string).
- There is no `StringDecoder` anywhere in `packages/vscode/src`.

This is the extension-side twin of the `/api/fs/exec` command runner: the web version (`packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.js`, `runCommandInDirectory`) already decodes incrementally with per-stream `StringDecoder`s feeding its `appendCapped`. The vscode copy kept the older per-chunk shape when the cap was added (#747).

Consumers treat this output as data, not just display text: `runCommandWithGitReadCache` in the same file caches cacheable git-read results produced by this runner, so a corrupted decode can be cached and replayed for the cache TTL; the UI's terminal/project-action surfaces likewise consume the returned stdout/stderr verbatim. Git output carries user data — non-ASCII directory paths (rev-parse), filenames, branch names.

## Evidence (this run, main `15c0ab90d61e95815a1d050b23881b45eed803e1`)

Laptop probe against the real `handleFsBridgeMessage` from `bridge-fs-runtime.ts` (probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-vscode-fsexec-chunksplit-20261104/probe.test.js` on the laptop; `child_process`/`vscode` mocked exactly as the module's own `bridge-fs-runtime.test.js` mocks them; the fake child emits the UTF-8 bytes of `café 🔑 end\n` in controlled chunks), run twice with identical results:

- Single chunk (control): stdout `café 🔑 end`, exact match.
- Split inside the é (1 byte | 1 byte): stdout `caf�� 🔑 end` — corrupted, exit 0, no error reported.
- Split inside the 🔑 (2 bytes | 2 bytes): stdout `café ��� end` — corrupted, exit 0, no error reported.

Pipe chunk boundaries are chosen by the OS and the producing program, not by OpenChamber, so corruption is nondeterministic from the user's point of view: the same command can return correct or mangled output depending on total output size and where a boundary happens to land.

## Why it matters

A silently mangled path or filename in exec output produces wrong behavior downstream (lookups for U+FFFD names that do not exist, wrong git-dir paths) with no error anywhere — the result reports success. Because cacheable git reads cache this runner's result, one unlucky chunking can stick for the cache TTL instead of being a one-off. This is the last known per-chunk decode site in the #1553/#1558 class: the web environment runner (#1553), the vscode git executor (#1558), and the web fs-exec runner (already decoder-based) are all covered elsewhere.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `runCommand`'s accumulator in `packages/vscode/src/bridge-fs-runtime.ts` decodes stdout and stderr incrementally (e.g. `StringDecoder` per stream, flushed at close) or accumulates buffers and decodes once, so a multi-byte character split across any chunk boundary round-trips exactly; the byte cap (`FS_EXEC_OUTPUT_LIMIT_BYTES`), overflow termination, and timeout behavior from #747 are unchanged.
- [ ] The overflow-kept prefix path (`:533`) does not introduce a split-character corruption beyond the intended truncation.
- [ ] Regression tests in `packages/vscode/src/bridge-fs-runtime.test.ts` (the existing mocked-spawn harness) emit command output in chunks split inside a 2-byte and a 4-byte character and assert stdout/stderr match the single-chunk control exactly.
- [ ] Existing bridge-fs-runtime suites (exec cache, spawn launch, output-cap env reader) stay green.

Related: #1558 (same decode class, vscode git executor — this site was its open triage question), #1553 (web environment runner), #1336 / #1540 (web git/fs readers and their chunk-boundary tests), #747 (this runner's output cap — decode was not part of that fix).
