body:
## Problem

`.github/workflows/workflow-audit.yml` is the recurrence guard for issue #1399 (and #118 before it): a reusable-workflow caller job carrying a key GitHub does not allow (the classic case is `timeout-minutes` on a caller job) invalidates the whole workflow file, and every run of that workflow fails at startup with zero jobs. The audit exists so that class of breakage "fails a PR check instead of merging to main" (its own header).

PR #1584 (commit `9d1616f5e`, merged 2026-11-04) removed its `pull_request` and `push` triggers — its only automatic triggers — and added `workflow_dispatch` so it "stays reachable", flagging it for review in the PR body. This issue is that flagged review. As it stands on main:

- The workflow has **no automatic trigger at all** — no `push`, no `pull_request`, and no `schedule`. Unlike `oc-review.yml` it has no nightly backstop, so the guard runs only if a human remembers to dispatch it by hand.
- Its header (`.github/workflows/workflow-audit.yml:3-7`) still claims it "runs on any change that could reintroduce one, so it fails a PR check instead of merging to main" — neither is true now.
- The audit itself is healthy: verified this run on main `2b71228642c0bc5296ce7fd6ce7a3be9ac336992` — `python3 .github/scripts/audit-workflow-caller-jobs.py .github/workflows` reports "28 workflow files, no invalid caller jobs" and `bash .github/scripts/test-audit-workflow-caller-jobs.sh` passes. The machinery works; it is simply never invoked.

## Why it matters

The failure mode this guards against is silent and total for the affected workflow (startup failure, zero jobs), and it is introduced exactly by editing workflow files — the one change class that now has no automatic audit coverage at all. A guard that only runs on manual dispatch will, in practice, be discovered to have been needed only after a workflow has already broken on main.

## Acceptance criteria

- The audit regains an automatic trigger that covers workflow-file changes without reintroducing PR-tier CI contrary to the 2026-11-04 ruling — e.g. a `schedule` (nightly, alongside `pr checks`) and/or a path-filtered `push: branches: [main]` on `.github/workflows/**` + `.github/scripts/audit-workflow-caller-jobs.py` + its test script — OR a decision is recorded on this issue that dispatch-only is accepted, with the reasoning.
- The workflow header comment is rewritten to describe the trigger model that actually ships (it must not claim PR-check behaviour that no longer exists).
- `bash .github/scripts/test-audit-workflow-caller-jobs.sh` and the audit over `.github/workflows` still pass after the change.

Related: PR #1584 (which flagged this workflow for review); sibling filing for `oc-review.yml`'s lost push-to-main trigger and the stale `ci-policy.md` main-gate contract.

body:
## Problem

PR #1584 (commit `9d1616f5e`, merged 2026-11-04) removed the `push: branches: [main]` trigger from `.github/workflows/oc-review.yml` (`pr checks`, this repo's designated main-gate). The workflow now runs automatically only on its nightly schedule (`37 5 * * *`) or by manual dispatch. Everything that documents or consumes the main-gate still assumes a per-merge run on push to main, so the repo's main-breakage detection and release-gate default path silently changed shape:

- A merge that breaks main is no longer verified at merge time. The next automatic verification is the nightly run, which batches every merge since the previous night into one run — the `main-broken` watcher (`main-broken.yml:18-20`, `workflow_run` on `pr checks` completions on main) can then only file a breakage against the batched nightly failure, not the merge that caused it, and detection is delayed by up to ~24 h.
- The release gate (`require-main-gate.sh`, called by `release.yml` / `mobile-release.yml`) requires a successful `pr checks` run for the exact release SHA. For any freshly merged SHA that the nightly has not run on, no such run exists, so every release now falls onto the documented manual workaround (dispatch `oc-review.yml` on the exact SHA and wait) — the policy doc presents that as a hotfix override, not the normal path.

This may be the intended end state of the 2026-11-04 "no commit- or PR-triggered CI" ruling — but the ruling's PR applied the trigger removal to the main tier as well as the PR tier, and none of the in-repo contracts were updated to match. One of the two has to give: either restore the main-push trigger for the main-gate, or amend the policy/watcher/release contracts to state nightly-only verification and own the consequences.

## Evidence (verified on main `2b71228642c0bc5296ce7fd6ce7a3be9ac336992`, 2026-11-04)

- `.github/workflows/oc-review.yml:15-23` — `on:` is now only `schedule` + `workflow_dispatch`; the `push:` block is gone (diff in PR #1584, commit `9d1616f5e`).
- `.github/workflows/oc-review.yml:6-10` — the header still says triggers are "push to main, the nightly schedule below, and workflow_dispatch" and "Dedup: push is restricted to branches: [main]"; `:16-17` leaves the orphaned comment "Merged code gets the same verification on main itself: without this, a merge that breaks main is only discovered by the next PR's run" directly above `schedule:`; job comments at `:74` and `:97` still say "Runs on push to main, on the nightly schedule, and on manual…".
- `.github/ci-policy.md:24` — "All four run automatically only after merge, on push to `main` and on the nightly schedule"; `:37` "Main tier — everything, once per merge. On push to `main`, `pr checks` runs its full suite"; `:67-72` the tier map marks every job ✅ for `main (push to main)`.
- `.github/ci-policy.md` Release gate section (~`:90-102`) — requires a successful `pr checks` run for the exact release SHA and describes dispatching on the exact SHA as "the hotfix override path for a missing run".
- `.github/workflows/main-broken.yml:18-20,65-69` — the watcher fires on `pr checks` completions on main (it does accept `schedule` events, so nightly failures still file — batched and delayed, not per-merge).

## Why it matters

The main-gate + watcher chain (fleet design developing-today/code#1779/#1782) exists so a red main produces exactly one owned breakage issue per failure, promptly, attributed to the merge that broke it. Nightly-only runs break attribution (several merges, one failure), delay detection by hours, and quietly convert the release gate's normal path into its exception path. The stale policy doc makes it worse: a reader of `.github/ci-policy.md` will believe per-merge verification still happens.

## Acceptance criteria

- A decision is recorded on this issue: restore `push: branches: [main]` for `oc-review.yml`, OR adopt nightly-only main verification explicitly.
- If restored: `oc-review.yml` runs on push to main again and the header/policy text is accurate as written.
- If nightly-only is adopted: `.github/ci-policy.md` (merge-requirement section, main-tier description, tier map, release-gate section) and the `oc-review.yml` header/job comments are rewritten to say nightly + dispatch only; the release-gate section names the exact-SHA dispatch as the normal pre-release step; and the `main-broken` expectations (batched attribution) are stated in `main-broken.yml` or the policy doc.
- Either way, no file in `.github/` still claims `pr checks` runs on push to main if it does not (or vice versa).

Related: PR #1584; sibling filing for `workflow-audit.yml`, which lost its only automatic triggers in the same PR.

title: fix(web): session-goal objective is read whole with no size gate — readObjective buffers any goals-dir file whole (and blocks on a FIFO); the 1M-char hard cap is applied only after the read

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

The session-goal objective **read** path buffers the objective file whole, with no size gate during the read and no regular-file check — the 1,000,000-character hard cap is applied only *after* the whole file is already in memory. An objective file on disk that exceeds the cap (replaced or grown outside the write path, a legacy file, or a symlink target) is buffered whole into server memory on every read; a non-regular file at the objective path blocks the read forever.

## Evidence

`packages/web/server/lib/session-goal/objectives.js` (main @ 709ce4b05):

- `:74` — `readObjective` reads the file whole, no stat, no cap during the read, no regular-file check:
  ```js
  const raw = await fs.promises.readFile(objectiveFilePath(sessionId), 'utf8');
  return clampContent(raw);
  ```
- `:54` — `clampContent` slices to `GOAL_OBJECTIVE_HARD_CAP` (1,000,000 chars, `:16`) — but only after `readFile` has already buffered the entire file, however large it is on disk.
- The write path does clamp before writing (`writeObjective`, `:61`), so an over-cap file can only arrive out-of-band — the exact assumption #1537 (project-icon serve) and #1490 (project config) already falsified for sibling paths: the file lives in the user's data dir (`<openchamberDataDir>/goals/<sessionId>.md`, `goalsDir()`/`objectiveFilePath()`), outside the server's control between writes.
- Contrast in the same repo: `readBoundedUtf8` in `packages/web/server/lib/project-context/plan-progress.js` reads through one handle at most `maxBytes + 1` bytes and returns null over cap, and `readDiscoveredIcon` (project-icon-routes.js) enforces its cap during the read — the bounded-read pattern this reader does not use.
- Readers affected: `session-goal/routes.js:45` (goal GET), `session-goal/runtime.js:577` (progress check — which only needs the first `check` chars, default 20,000), and fork inheritance via `openchamber-sessions/routes.js:1289`. Every one pays the whole-file buffer.

## Reproduction (probe, this run)

Laptop probe driving the real `readObjective` from `objectives.js` on main 709ce4b05 with `OPENCHAMBER_DATA_DIR` pointed at a temp dir (probe dir: laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-goal-objective-20261104/`):

- **Oversize:** planted a 20 MiB file at `goals/ses_big1.md` → `readObjective` returned the clamped 1,000,000 chars in 71 ms — i.e. all 20,971,520 bytes were read and buffered first, and the clamp discarded 95% of them after the fact. A 1 GiB planted file would be buffered the same way.
- **FIFO:** replaced the objective path with a FIFO → `readObjective` **never settled after 3000 ms** (`fs.readFile` blocks opening a FIFO with no writer; there is no timeout), hanging the caller indefinitely.

## Why it matters

- Memory/DoS surface on a long-lived server: one oversized (or hostile, via a symlink planted in the goals dir) file is buffered whole per read, and the progress check reads objectives repeatedly.
- A FIFO/device at the path wedges the read with no deadline — the same failure class the bounded readers elsewhere in this repo were built to close (design #1254).
- The hard cap exists and is documented as the runaway-size guard ("the file only refuses runaway sizes" — write-side comment); the read side simply never enforces it where it counts, during the read.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `readObjective` enforces a byte bound **during** the read (e.g. a handle read capped at the hard cap's maximum UTF-8 size, in the `readBoundedUtf8` / `readDiscoveredIcon` style), so an over-cap file on disk is never buffered whole; the returned text stays clamped to `GOAL_OBJECTIVE_HARD_CAP` chars exactly as today.
- [ ] Non-regular files at the objective path (FIFO, device, directory) are rejected promptly (returning null, like a missing objective) instead of blocking the reader.
- [ ] Objectives within the cap — including the raised-limit case in the existing test (12,000 chars) and a goal at exactly the hard cap — read back byte-identical.
- [ ] Regression tests in `objectives.test.js` cover: over-cap file on disk returns the clamped text without a whole-file buffer (or is refused per the chosen contract), FIFO/non-regular target settles promptly, at-cap file reads fully.

Related: #1537 / #1490 (same read-whole-then-trust pattern in sibling paths), design #1254 (bounded-read contract — this is a specific residual site).

title: fix(electron): SSH runSshOutput decodes stdout per pipe chunk — a multi-byte character split across chunks is silently corrupted in the output callers parse (ssh -G config, status --json registry, system-info probe)

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/electron
labels.description: Package: electron (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

The Electron SSH manager's output runner decodes remote-command stdout one pipe chunk at a time, so a multi-byte UTF-8 character that straddles a chunk boundary is silently corrupted in the output its callers parse as data.

`packages/electron/ssh-manager.mjs`, `runSshOutput` (`:563`), the runner behind every remote SSH command the desktop app makes:

- `:596` `const text = chunk.toString()` — each `Buffer` chunk is decoded independently. A character split across two chunks becomes U+FFFD replacement characters on both sides of the split.
- `:597` the byte cap (`MAX_SSH_OUTPUT_BYTES`, 4 MiB, from #745) is charged `Buffer.byteLength(text)` — the length of the *decoded* string, not the bytes received — so a split sequence is also mis-accounted (each replacement char re-encodes to 3 bytes).
- `:603` `stdout += text` — the corrupted string is what resolves.
- `:533` and `:606` the stderr/diagnostic captures use the same per-chunk decode; those feed error text only (secondary — same fix pass).

The stdout is parsed as data, not just displayed:

- `resolveSshConfig` (`:1083`) runs `ssh -G` through it and splits the output into a config map (hostnames, identity paths — non-ASCII possible).
- `listRemoteServers` (`:1402`) runs `status --json` through `runRemoteCommand` and `JSON.parse`s the stdout into the remote server registry.
- `probeRemoteServer` (`:1270`) runs a script whose stdout carries the status lines plus the `/api/system/info` JSON body, parsed by the caller.
- `probeRemoteSystemInfo` / tool-resolution / `uname` probes (`:1166`, `:1199`, `:1600`) consume the same stdout.

#745 gave this runner its byte cap and execution timeout; the decode was not part of that fix, and no open or closed issue covers it (search: `ssh-manager`, `runSshOutput`, `electron decode chunk` — only #745/#817 and the SSH parser issues #241–#316).

## Evidence (this run, main `fbeef40a8f20f417395fa5149f397a8cbe0d804e`)

Laptop probe against the real `ElectronSshManager.runSshOutput` from `packages/electron/ssh-manager.mjs` (probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-ssh-chunksplit-20261104/probe.mjs` on the laptop; fake `spawn` in the same injected shape the module's own `ssh-manager.test.mjs` uses, writing raw byte chunks to a PassThrough stdout), run twice with identical results. The child emits `{"name":"café 🔑 end"}\n` as raw bytes:

- Single chunk (control): stdout exact match with the payload.
- Split inside the é (first byte of the 2-byte sequence alone in chunk 1): stdout `{"name":"caf�� 🔑 end"}` — 2 U+FFFD, no error.
- Split inside the 🔑 (2 bytes | 2 bytes): stdout `{"name":"café ��� end"}` — 3 U+FFFD, no error.

## Why it matters

This runner is the desktop app's only channel for remote SSH work: resolving the user's SSH config, listing remote OpenChamber servers, and probing remote system info. A corrupted character in a hostname, a home-directory path, or a server name in the `status --json` registry silently becomes U+FFFD while the command reports exit 0 — the app then connects to, or lists, something that does not exist. The failure is chunking-dependent (pipe boundaries are chosen by the OS and `ssh`, not by OpenChamber), so it presents as flaky, hard-to-reproduce corruption, most likely exactly on the large outputs where chunk splits are common.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `runSshOutput` in `packages/electron/ssh-manager.mjs` decodes stdout incrementally (e.g. `StringDecoder`, flushed at close) or accumulates buffers and decodes once, so a multi-byte character split across any chunk boundary round-trips exactly.
- [ ] The `MAX_SSH_OUTPUT_BYTES` cap is charged on bytes received, not on the decoded string length; cap and timeout behavior from #745 otherwise unchanged.
- [ ] The stderr/diagnostic captures (`:533`, `:606`) get the same decode treatment, or triage records why they stay diagnostic-only.
- [ ] Regression tests in `packages/electron/ssh-manager.test.mjs` emit output split inside a 2-byte and a 4-byte character (the fake-spawn pattern the file already uses) and assert stdout matches the single-chunk control exactly.
- [ ] Existing ssh-manager suite stays green.

Related: #745 (this runner's cap + timeout — decode not covered), #1553 / #1558 / #1567 (same per-chunk decode class in the web environment runner, the VS Code git executor, and the fs/exec runners — different modules, this is the Electron SSH twin).

labels.name: source/dispatch
labels.description: Filed by pm-dispatch

body:
Perform the daily upstream sync of OpenChamber from upstream openchamber/openchamber (branch `main`) into `main`.
Follow these strict requirements and principles:
### 1. UPSTREAM TRACKING POLICY - Track upstream `main` into our `main` branch: `git fetch upstream main && git merge --no-ff upstream/main`.
### 2. CONFLICT RESOLUTION & CAPABILITY PRESERVATION RULES - **Preserve All Features**: Keep all features, tools, custom settings, and routes from BOTH sides:
  - Retain fork-specific controls (`openchamber.routing.plans.actionSendMode`, `autoCreateWorktree`, `agentTerminalsPlacement`, persistent terminal keys, and JIT secrets).
  - Retain custom release channels, draft release uploads, and worktree-by-default session creation.
- **No Deprecations**: If upstream removed an API, feature, parameter, or route that our fork uses or provides, DO NOT remove it on our side. We want more capabilities and features in general. - **Reduce Future Conflicts**: Where appropriate, isolate fork additions and extensions into separate/modular files (`packages/web/server/lib/routing/`, `packages/ui/src/lib/routing/`, dedicated i18n modules) so future merges conflict less often. - **Complete i18n & RTL Parity**: Ensure full key parity across all 15 locales (including Arabic `ar` and Hebrew `he` RTL). If new keys were added upstream or in fork features, provide valid English fallback entries across dictionaries so `src/lib/i18n/messages.test.ts` passes with zero missing keys.
### 3. FEATURE OPPORTUNITY TRIAGE & ISSUE CREATION - Inspect the newly merged upstream commits (`git log ... --grep="^feat"`). - Identify if any new upstream capabilities, refactors, or UI surfaces could be adopted or built upon by our fork's additions (such as interactive render pages, project knowledge plans, model routing tiers, or plan cost tracking). - For each identified high-value synergy, create a comprehensive GitHub issue using `gh issue create --repo developing-today/openchamber` containing:
  - Clear title and summary
  - Upstream commit references
  - Architectural context and user story
  - Concrete technical specifications and relevant file paths
  - Complete acceptance criteria
  (Ensure enough detail that a brand-new agent with zero prior context can implement it).

### 4. VALIDATION & TESTING - Run UI typecheck: `bun run type-check:ui`. - Run i18n key parity test: `bun test src/lib/i18n/messages.test.ts` (in `packages/ui`). - Run Plans UI tests: `env NODE_ENV=development bun test src/components/sections/routing/PlansSection.test.tsx` (in `packages/ui`). - Run routing server vitest suite: `npx vitest run server/lib/routing/` (in `packages/web`). - Verify that all tests that weren't already failing continue to pass, and all newly merged tests pass.
### 5. PULL REQUEST & SAFE MERGE - Update the `README.md` fork notice with the latest upstream commit SHA and timestamp. - Open a clean, conflict-free Pull Request detailing all merged upstream commits and resolved conflicts. - Merge the PR into `main` only when you are reasonably certain it is correct: tests pass cleanly, there are no regressions, and the sync is conflict-free. Merging is permitted, never required — when any of that is uncertain, leave the PR open and state your confidence and what a human should check in the description.

title: fix(web,vscode): fs/exec command runners decode output per pipe chunk — a multi-byte character split across chunks is silently corrupted in the command result

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.description: Package: vscode (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

Both `/api/fs/exec` command runners — the web route and its VS Code bridge twin — decode command stdout/stderr one pipe chunk at a time, so a multi-byte UTF-8 character that straddles a chunk boundary is silently corrupted in the command result the caller receives.

Web: `packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.js`, `runCommandInDirectory` (`:536`), the runner behind `POST /api/fs/exec`:

- `:604` `appendCapped` accumulates each stream as a string.
- `:611` `current + buffer.toString()` — each `Buffer` chunk is decoded independently. A character split across two chunks becomes U+FFFD replacement characters on both sides of the split.
- `:613` the overflow-kept prefix is also decoded standalone (`buffer.subarray(0, remaining).toString()`), so a split at the 4 MiB cap boundary corrupts the same way.
- `:631-645` the stdout/stderr `data` handlers feed every chunk through `appendCapped`; the byte accounting beside it (`stdoutBytes`/`stderrBytes`, cap from #737) is byte-honest — only the decode is per-chunk. The resolved result's `stdout`/`stderr` (`:647+`, trimmed) is returned verbatim in the API response.
- The same runner also serves the cached git-read path (`runCommandWithGitReadCache`, `:806+`): `git rev-parse --absolute-git-dir/--git-common-dir/--show-toplevel` output — repository paths, which can themselves contain non-ASCII characters.

VS Code twin: `packages/vscode/src/bridge-fs-runtime.ts` carries the identical implementation — `appendCapped` at `:525`, full-chunk decode `:531`, cap-boundary subarray decode `:533`, data handlers `:565`/`:572` — behind the extension bridge's fs-exec (cap from #747).

This is the #1553 decode class in a different runner: #1553/#1554 cover the environment command runner (`lib/environment/runtime.js`); #1558 covers the VS Code git executor and its final acceptance item explicitly leaves this fs-exec accumulator to be confirmed in scope *or filed separately*. This issue is that separate filing, for both twins — the web twin is not named in any open issue (search: `appendCapped`, `runCommandInDirectory`, and `fs exec decode` return only the #737/#741/#747 cap issues and #1553/#1558).

## Evidence (this run, main `794e5f5c260ee4de1d8d9c4a29b330b009fde5aa`)

Laptop probe against the real `registerFsRoutes` from `packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.js` (probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-fsexec-chunksplit-20261104/probe.mjs` on the laptop; fake `spawn` in the same injected-dependency shape the module's own `routes.test.js` uses, emitting timed separate byte writes; command result read from the route's response `results[0]`), run twice with identical results. The child emits `café 🔑\n` as raw bytes on both streams:

- Single chunk (control): stdout and stderr `café 🔑`, exact match, `success: true`.
- Split inside the é (first byte of the 2-byte sequence alone in chunk 1): stdout and stderr `caf�� 🔑`, `success: true` — both halves corrupted, no error reported.
- Split inside the 🔑 (2 bytes | 2 bytes): stdout and stderr `café ���`, `success: true`.

## Why it matters

`/api/fs/exec` is the server's general command-execution surface: its results are shown to the user and consumed by agent/UI flows as the command's actual output. A corrupted character in a filename, a path from `git rev-parse`, or any non-ASCII command output silently becomes U+FFFD — a name that does not exist on disk — while the result still reports success. The failure is chunking-dependent (pipe boundaries are chosen by the OS and the child, not by OpenChamber), so it presents as flaky, hard-to-reproduce output corruption, most likely on the large outputs where the runner is used hardest. The VS Code bridge twin has the same defect for extension-side command execution.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `runCommandInDirectory` in `packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.js` decodes stdout and stderr incrementally (e.g. `StringDecoder` per stream, flushed at close) or accumulates buffers and decodes once, so a multi-byte character split across any chunk boundary round-trips exactly; the per-stream byte cap, overflow termination, and timeout behavior from #737/#932 are unchanged.
- [ ] The overflow-kept prefix path (`:613`) does not introduce a split-character corruption beyond the intended truncation.
- [ ] The VS Code twin `appendCapped` in `packages/vscode/src/bridge-fs-runtime.ts` (`:525`/`:531`/`:533`) gets the same treatment, or triage records why it is handled under #1558 instead.
- [ ] Regression tests emit command output in chunks split inside a 2-byte and a 4-byte character (the fake-spawn pattern `routes.test.js` already uses; the bridge twin's test file likewise) and assert stdout/stderr match the single-chunk control exactly.
- [ ] Existing fs routes / bridge fs suites stay green.

Related: #1553 / PR #1554 (same decode class, environment runner), #1558 (same decode class, VS Code git executor — its final acceptance item is the origin of this separate filing), #737 / #741 / #747 (these runners' caps — decode was not part of those fixes), #932 (fs/exec tree kill).

title: test(ci): PR #1382's release-gate test script is run by nothing — test-require-main-gate.sh has no CI wiring

labels.name: kind/test

labels.name: source/pr-diff-review
labels.description: Filed by the pr-diff-review job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: area/ci
labels.description: CI, workflows, and build infrastructure

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Finding

PR #1382 added `.github/scripts/test-require-main-gate.sh` — a 75-line, 6-case test for the release gate — but no workflow, package script, or other automation ever runs it. The gate script it tests (`.github/scripts/require-main-gate.sh`) is the only thing standing between a red main and a published release, and its test has been dead since the day it landed.

## Evidence

- PR #1382 (commits `2f505485a4`, `a60d83e0b2`, merged 2026-11-03) added `.github/scripts/require-main-gate.sh` (+31), `.github/scripts/test-require-main-gate.sh` (+75, 6 cases: green push SHA accepted, green dispatch SHA accepted, failed rejected, pending rejected, wrong-SHA rejected, empty rejected), `.github/workflows/require-main-gate.yml`, and wired the gate into `release.yml` / `mobile-release.yml`.
- Verified on current main `794e5f5c260ee4de1d8d9c4a29b330b009fde5aa` (2026-11-04): a grep for `test-require-main-gate` across all 27 files under `.github/workflows/` and the root `package.json` returns zero references. The script is referenced only by itself.
- The sibling pattern exists in-repo: `.github/scripts/test-audit-workflow-caller-jobs.sh` IS wired into `.github/workflows/workflow-audit.yml` (line 35, with `paths:` filters on the script and the workflows it audits) — the shape this test never got.
- Dedupe (2026-11-04): issue searches for `test-require-main-gate` and for the release-gate test returned no covering issue; #139 is a closed precedent for the same class (a test suite run by nothing) in a different area.

## Why it matters

`require-main-gate.sh` decides releases by parsing `gh api` output with a `jq` `any(.workflow_runs[]?; .head_sha == $sha and .conclusion == "success")` expression. A regression in that logic either blocks every release or — worse — lets a release ship from a red main, which is exactly the failure #1382 was filed to prevent. Today nothing would catch such a regression: the test exists, passes when run by hand, and is executed by no automation.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A workflow runs `bash .github/scripts/test-require-main-gate.sh` when `.github/scripts/require-main-gate.sh`, `.github/scripts/test-require-main-gate.sh`, or `.github/workflows/require-main-gate.yml` changes — e.g. a job in `workflow-audit.yml` following the `test-audit-workflow-caller-jobs.sh` pattern, or a step in the `oc-review.yml` main tier.
- [ ] The test passes on current main.
- [ ] Red/green shown on the implementing PR: a deliberately broken gate script (e.g. conclusion check inverted) fails the new job.

title: fix(vscode): VS Code git executor decodes output per pipe chunk — a multi-byte character split across chunks is silently corrupted in parsed status, branch and diff output

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/vscode
labels.description: Package: vscode (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

The VS Code extension's git executor decodes git's stdout/stderr one pipe chunk at a time, so a multi-byte UTF-8 character that straddles a chunk boundary is silently corrupted — and that output is parsed structurally (filenames, branch names, diffs), not just displayed.

`packages/vscode/src/bridge-git-process-runtime.ts` (`execGit`, the single executor behind the extension's git surface):

- `:152` `appendChunk` accumulates each stream.
- `:174` `stderr += chunk.toString();` and `:177` `stdout += chunk.toString();` — each `Buffer` chunk is decoded independently. A character split across two chunks becomes U+FFFD replacement characters on both sides of the split.
- `:157` the overflow-kept prefix is also decoded standalone (`chunk.subarray(0, remaining).toString()`), so a split at the cap boundary corrupts the same way.
- The byte accounting beside it (`stdoutBytes`/`stderrBytes`, `:147-148`, cap from #742/#743) is byte-honest — only the decode is per-chunk. There is no `StringDecoder` anywhere in `packages/vscode/src`.

Consumers parse the returned string as data, e.g. `packages/vscode/src/gitService.ts`:

- `:322-324` the `execGit` wrapper used by the whole git service.
- `:618` `git status --porcelain=v1 -b -uall` output is split into lines and parsed into status files/paths (`getGitStatusRaw`, `:632+`).
- `:773` branch listing parsed from `--format=` output; `:2901` `git show :<file>` content; `bridge-git-special-runtime.ts` status/diff collectors and `scmCommitMessage.ts` likewise consume `execGit` output.

Git output carries user data — non-ASCII filenames, branch names, commit subjects. Pipe chunk boundaries are chosen by the OS and git, not by OpenChamber, so corruption is nondeterministic from the user's point of view: the same repository can read correctly or with mangled names depending on total output size and where a boundary lands (in practice, large outputs — exactly the busy repositories where status/diff correctness matters most).

Sibling readers already do this correctly with `StringDecoder` / `Buffer.concat` (web `lib/git/service.js` readers, fixed for #1336; the vscode worktree start-command runner in `gitService.ts` itself collects chunks and decodes once via `Buffer.concat(stdoutChunks).toString('utf8')`). This executor is a remaining per-chunk decode site — the #1553 class (web environment runner), in the vscode git path.

## Evidence (this run, main `794e5f5c260ee4de1d8d9c4a29b330b009fde5aa`)

Laptop probe against the real `execGit` from `bridge-git-process-runtime.ts` (probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-vscode-gitexec-20261104/probe.ts` on the laptop; `execGit(['-e', script], tmpdir, { binary: process.execPath })`, the same binary-override pattern the module's own tests use; the child emits `café 🔑\n` as raw bytes), run twice with identical results:

- Single chunk (control): stdout `café 🔑\n`, exact match, exit 0.
- Split inside the é (1 byte | 1 byte) and inside the 🔑 (2 bytes | 2 bytes) across timed separate writes: stdout `caf�� ���\n`, exit 0 — both characters corrupted, no error reported.

## Why it matters

A corrupted filename in porcelain status parsing means the extension shows/goes looking for a path that does not exist (U+FFFD names) while the real file's status is lost; corrupted branch names and diff content mislead the same way. The failure is silent (exit 0, no log) and chunking-dependent, so it presents as flaky, hard-to-reproduce git state in the editor for repositories with non-ASCII names and large outputs.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `execGit` in `packages/vscode/src/bridge-git-process-runtime.ts` decodes stdout and stderr incrementally (e.g. `StringDecoder` per stream, flushed at close) or accumulates buffers and decodes once, so a multi-byte character split across any chunk boundary round-trips exactly; the byte cap, overflow termination, and timeout behavior from #742/#743 are unchanged.
- [ ] The overflow-kept prefix path (`:157`) does not introduce a split-character corruption beyond the intended truncation.
- [ ] Regression tests in `packages/vscode/src/bridge-git-process-runtime.test.ts` emit command output in chunks split inside a 2-byte and a 4-byte character (the binary-override pattern the file's tests already use) and assert stdout/stderr match the single-chunk control exactly.
- [ ] Existing vscode git/process suites stay green.
- [ ] Triage confirms whether the bridge fs-exec accumulator in `packages/vscode/src/bridge-fs-runtime.ts:531/:533` (same per-chunk `current + buffer.toString()` shape, capped under #747) is in scope here or filed separately.

Related: #1553 (same decode class, web environment runner), #1336 / #1540 (web git/fs readers and their chunk-boundary tests), #742/#743 (this executor's cap/timeout — decode was not part of that fix).

title: fix(quota): Codex quota reads Not configured when ChatGPT credentials live under provider instances

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: meta/enriched

body:
## Symptom

`GET /api/quota/codex` answers `{"ok":false,"configured":false,"error":"Not configured"}` even though both ChatGPT accounts are signed in and healthy — the quota board's Codex line is dark.

## Diagnosis

The Codex quota fetch reads the credential projected under the bare `openai` integration (`getAuthEntry(auth, ['openai', 'codex', 'chatgpt'])`, in `packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/codex.js` and its twin `packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.ts` `fetchCodexQuota`). The per-credential dispatch (`fetchQuotaForProviderInstances`) likewise only enumerates stored rows under those bare integration ids.

Since the 2026-11-02/03 provider re-seat, no credential lives under the bare `openai` integration. Both ChatGPT accounts are stored under provider-instance integrations declared in the merged OpenCode config:

- `openai.main` (`instanceOf: openai`, drewrypope, chatgpt-browser OAuth)
- `openai.alternate` (`instanceOf: openai`, popesdrew, chatgpt-headless OAuth)

The instance rows themselves work — verified live 2026-11-04:

- `GET /api/quota/openai.main` → `ok:true`, account drewrypope@gmail.com, weekly window present
- `GET /api/quota/openai.alternate` → `ok:true`, account popesdrew@gmail.com, 5h + weekly windows present
- `GET /api/quota/providers` lists both instances, but not `codex`

So the base Codex row and its single-credential fetch are the only dark surface: they never look at the instance integrations where the credentials actually live now.

## Fix

- `fetchQuotaForProviderInstances('codex')` folds in the stored rows of configured instances of the Codex base (opt-in per registry entry), so `/api/quota/codex` returns one labeled result per account.
- The single-credential Codex fetch (web `codex.js` and the VS Code twin) falls back to the first usable instance credential when the bare integration holds none, keeping both runtimes in sync per the quota DOCUMENTATION.md parity note.
- `listConfiguredQuotaProviders` lists `codex` when one of its folded instances is listed.

No credential storage, routing, or provider changes — quota projection only.


## Acceptance criteria
- `GET /api/quota/codex` returns one labeled result per configured ChatGPT account (the `openai.main` and `openai.alternate` provider instances), instead of `{"ok":false,"configured":false}`.
- The single-credential Codex fetch falls back to the first usable instance credential in both runtimes (web `packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/codex.js` and the VS Code twin `packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.ts`), keeping parity per the quota DOCUMENTATION.md note.
- `listConfiguredQuotaProviders` / `GET /api/quota/providers` lists `codex` when one of its folded instances is configured.
- No credential storage, routing, or provider changes — quota projection only.

title: fix(web): environment command output is decoded per pipe chunk — a multi-byte character split across chunks is silently corrupted in the variables applied to OpenCode, Git and terminals

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: status/needs-triage
labels.description: Not yet triaged; needs a first look

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: queue/queued
labels.description: Has a queued task in the Supabase agent queue

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

The project environment command's output is decoded one pipe chunk at a time, so a multi-byte UTF-8 character that straddles a chunk boundary is silently corrupted — and the corrupted variable is applied to every process OpenChamber starts in that directory.

`packages/web/server/lib/environment/runtime.js`:

- `:65` `runCommand` collects the command's stdout.
- `:90` `stdout += chunk.toString();` — each `Buffer` chunk is decoded independently. A character split across two chunks becomes U+FFFD replacement characters on both sides of the split.
- `:91` the output cap is also judged on the decoded string: `stdout.length > MAX_COMMAND_OUTPUT_BYTES` (`:52`, 4 MiB) counts UTF-16 code units, not bytes, so the byte cap the constant names is not the cap enforced for non-ASCII output.
- `:226-227` the collected string goes straight to `parseEnvironmentOutput(outcome.stdout, env)`, and the parsed variables layer into the managed OpenCode, Git, the terminal, and project actions (module header, `:9-14`).

Sibling readers already do this correctly with `StringDecoder` (e.g. `lib/git/service.js` untracked listing, fixed for #1336; `lib/fs/search.js`; `lib/fs/routes.js:2093` check-ignore reader). The environment runner is a remaining per-chunk decode site.

## Evidence (this run, main `26048025531867723a51a72064058f6c6f331922`)

Laptop probe against the real `createEnvironmentRuntime` + `createEnvironmentStore` (probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-env-chunksplit-20261104/probe.mjs` on the laptop; fake child emitting controlled `Buffer` chunks; project command output `{"GREETING":"café 🔑 end"}`), run twice with identical results:

- Single chunk (control): `GREETING="café 🔑 end"`, status `applied`.
- Split inside the 🔑 emoji (2 bytes | 2 bytes): `GREETING="café ��� end"`, status still `applied` — corruption is silent, no failure is reported.
- Split inside the é (1 byte | 1 byte): `GREETING="caf�� 🔑 end"`, status still `applied`.

Pipe chunk boundaries are chosen by the OS and the producing program (direnv/devenv-style commands), not by OpenChamber, so any environment value containing non-ASCII text — a path, a name, a token with UTF-8 content — can be corrupted depending on where the boundary happens to fall, and the result is cached (`commandCache`, TTL 5 min) and reused.

## Why it matters

Environment variables from the project command are an input to credential-bearing processes: a silently mangled value (e.g. a path or key material with non-ASCII content) produces wrong behavior that no log or status surfaces — the project status reports `applied` with the right variable count. The failure is nondeterministic from the user's point of view because it depends on pipe chunking.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `runCommand` in `packages/web/server/lib/environment/runtime.js` decodes stdout incrementally (e.g. `StringDecoder`) so a multi-byte character split across any chunk boundary round-trips exactly; the decoder is flushed at close.
- [ ] The output cap is enforced on bytes received (or the constant/behavior is otherwise made honest), without changing the 4 MiB limit or the `output-too-large` outcome.
- [ ] Regression tests in `packages/web/server/lib/environment/runtime.test.js` emit the command output in chunks split inside a 2-byte and a 4-byte character and assert the parsed variables match the single-chunk control exactly.
- [ ] Existing environment runtime/variables suites stay green.

Related: #1336 (same decode class in the git ls-files reader, fixed), #1540 (chunk-boundary decode tests for the check-ignore readers). The `/api/fs/exec` accumulator (`lib/fs/routes.js` `appendCapped`) shows the same per-chunk `toString()` shape on code read — triage should confirm whether it is in scope here or filed separately.

title: fix(web): loopback is judged by string prefix / exact match in three places — the push VAPID judge accepts localhost.evil.example and localhost@evil.example as loopback and misses 127.0.0.2, and the OpenCode-URL and pairing-candidate judges miss the rest of 127/8

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

Three loopback judges in the web server decide "is this address this machine?" by string shape instead of by parsing the address and testing the loopback range. One is wrong in both directions; the other two share the narrower exact-match miss. The repo already has a range-correct judge — `isLoopbackBindHost` in `packages/web/server/lib/security/bind-host.js` (parses the address, treats all of 127.0.0.0/8 as loopback, unwraps `::ffff:`-mapped IPv4) — but these three sites do not use it.

Verified on main `5a9c8807e355070ab014b455a105bca96197906f` (laptop primary `~/git/openchamber-fork`, ff'd to origin/main this run).

## 1. Push VAPID subject: prefix match (wrong in both directions)

`packages/web/server/lib/notifications/push-runtime.js:12-20`:

```js
const isLoopbackHttpOrigin = (value) => {
  if (typeof value !== 'string') return false;
  return value.startsWith('http://localhost')
    || value.startsWith('http://127.0.0.1')
    || value.startsWith('http://[::1]');
};
```

Its only caller is `resolveVapidSubject` (`push-runtime.js:407`, call sites :416 and :427): a "loopback" origin is replaced with `mailto:openchamber@localhost`; anything else is used verbatim as the VAPID subject passed to `webPush.setVapidDetails` in `ensurePushInitialized` (:441-448).

Probe against the real `createPushRuntime` (fake web-push module capturing `setVapidDetails`, settings stubbed with existing VAPID keys, `OPENCHAMBER_PUBLIC_ORIGIN` varied; laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-vapid-loopback-20261104/probe.mjs`):

| Origin | Subject chosen | Correct? |
|---|---|---|
| `http://localhost.evil.example:3000` | `mailto:openchamber@localhost` | No — public host judged loopback (prefix) |
| `http://localhost@evil.example` | `mailto:openchamber@localhost` | No — host is `evil.example` (userinfo trick), judged loopback |
| `http://127.0.0.1.evil.example` | `mailto:openchamber@localhost` | No — public DNS name judged loopback |
| `http://127.0.0.2:3000` | `http://127.0.0.2:3000` | No — 127.0.0.2 is loopback (127/8), judged public and used verbatim as the VAPID subject |
| `http://[::1]:3000` | `mailto:openchamber@localhost` | Yes (control) |
| `http://localhost:3000` | `mailto:openchamber@localhost` | Yes (control) |
| `https://chat.example.com` | `https://chat.example.com` | Yes (control) |

Consequences: a real public origin that merely starts with one of the prefixes silently loses its VAPID subject (push services get the placeholder `mailto:openchamber@localhost` contact, plus a misleading "No public origin configured for VAPID" warning even though one is configured); a loopback origin on any 127.x other than 127.0.0.1 is handed to the push service as the subject.

## 2. OpenCode credential source: exact-match list

`packages/web/server/lib/opencode/auth.js:54-62` — `isLoopbackOpenCodeUrl` accepts only `localhost`, `*.localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `::1`. It gates `usesLocalStore()` (:119-131), whose only production consumer is the Antigravity quota provider's local-store fallback (`packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/antigravity/index.js:52`, via `credentialSourceUsesLocalStore()`). An OpenCode reached at `http://127.0.0.2:<port>` or `[::ffff:127.0.0.1]` is on this machine but is judged remote, so the fallback silently never applies. (Fail-closed direction, but a silent feature loss — the same class the bind-host judge already handles correctly.)

## 3. Pairing candidates: exact-match list

`packages/web/server/lib/opencode/core-routes.js:591-599` — `isLoopbackCandidateUrl` accepts only `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `::1`, `[::1]`. At :626 it decides whether the request origin is loopback and must be skipped as a direct pairing candidate (loopback is unreachable from the paired device). An origin on `127.0.0.2` (or another 127/8 address) is judged non-loopback and advertised to another device as a direct candidate that can never connect, wasting the candidate race before the relay fallback.

## Why it matters

Loopback judgement is a recurring source of subtle bugs in this codebase precisely because each site hand-rolls it (compare the guests SSRF judge, fixed to judge IPv6 by numeric range in #1517 / PR #1547). Three more hand-rolled copies have now diverged from the one range-correct judge the repo already owns. The push-runtime copy is the worst shape — a raw prefix test on an unparsed string — and it misjudges attacker-shaped strings (`localhost@…`, `localhost.evil…`) as local.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] All three sites judge loopback by parsing the URL/address and testing the range: `localhost` / `*.localhost`, all of 127.0.0.0/8, `::1`, and `::ffff:`-mapped forms of the above — ideally by reusing or extending the `security/bind-host.js` judge rather than adding a fourth copy.
- [ ] Regression tests pin the probe cases: `http://localhost.evil.example:3000`, `http://localhost@evil.example`, and `http://127.0.0.1.evil.example` are NOT loopback; `http://127.0.0.2:3000` IS loopback; `[::1]` and `localhost:3000` controls stay loopback.
- [ ] `resolveVapidSubject` behaviour for a genuine public origin and a genuine loopback origin is unchanged (controls above).
- [ ] No change to `parseLoopbackUrl` in `core-routes.js` (:16-40) — that one is a deliberate allowlist parser, not a range judge, and is out of scope.

title: test(web): #881 createWorktree oversized-timeout test races its bootstrap status — marker is polled, status is asserted once

labels.name: kind/test
labels.description: Test coverage, test infrastructure, or test-only fixes

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: app/web

labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Summary

The #881 regression test `falls back to the default bound for an oversized start-command timeout` in `packages/web/server/lib/git/service.test.js` races its own bootstrap status. It polls the start command's marker file with `expect.poll` (`:2325`), but then asserts the worktree bootstrap status with a **single** `.resolves.toMatchObject` (`:2326-2330`). The marker and the status are written by different steps: the marker is written by the start command itself, while the `ready`/`setup-ready` status is only recorded after the command process exits and the bootstrap store is updated. There is a real, measurable lag between the two, so on a slow runner the single assertion reads `pending`/`git-ready` and fails a test whose production behavior is correct.

This already failed on main: `pr checks` run 41771073647 (recorded on the #1497 main-broken tracker) failed the web segment on exactly this test — 9,743 passed / 1 failed — with the bootstrap status still `pending`/`git-ready` when the single assertion polled it, in a segment that took 323 s under runner backlog.

## Evidence

`packages/web/server/lib/git/service.test.js` (main @ bb1c05b36):

- `:2325` — `await expect.poll(() => fs.existsSync(marker), { timeout: 15_000 }).toBe(true);` (the marker is polled, correctly)
- `:2326-2330` — immediately after:
  ```js
  await expect(getWorktreeBootstrapStatus(created.path)).resolves.toMatchObject({
    status: 'ready',
    phase: 'setup-ready',
    error: null,
  });
  ```
  One read, no poll, no retry.
- The same file does it correctly elsewhere: `:1568`, `:1607`, `:1647` poll `(await getWorktreeBootstrapStatus(created.path)).status` with `expect.poll` before asserting; the sibling suite `network-operations.test.js:2241` also polls the bootstrap status (`expect.poll(async () => (await getWorktreeBootstrapStatus(created.path)).status, { timeout: 10_000 })`).

## Reproduction (probe, this run)

Laptop probe replicating the test's exact setup against the **real** `createWorktree`/`getWorktreeBootstrapStatus` from the laptop primary (main bb1c05b36; probe dir: laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-bootstrap-poll-20261104/`; two identical runs):

- Tight-poll the marker (1 ms interval, as `expect.poll` finds it as early as possible), then read the status **once, immediately** — both runs: `{"status":"pending","phase":"git-ready","error":null}` — the single assertion in the test would **fail**.
- The status became `ready`/`setup-ready` only **14 ms / 17 ms later** (3rd read). On an idle laptop the window is milliseconds; under CI runner load (323 s segment in run 41771073647) it widens past the assertion.

## Why it matters

- The test guards a real timer-overflow regression (#881: an oversized start-command timeout must fall back to the default bound instead of overflowing to ~1 ms). A flaky guard produces false main-red, feeds the #1497 main-broken tracker, and trains everyone to ignore failures in this suite — the next real #881-class regression would hide in the noise.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The #881 test polls the bootstrap status itself (e.g. `expect.poll(async () => { const s = await getWorktreeBootstrapStatus(created.path); return [s.status, s.phase, s.error]; }, { timeout: 15_000 })` or the status-poll pattern already used at `:1568`/`:1607`/`:1647` in the same file), instead of a single `.resolves` read after the marker poll.
- [ ] The oversized-timeout semantics stay asserted: the command still runs to completion under the fallback bound (marker written) and the final status is `ready`/`setup-ready` with `error: null`.
- [ ] No production-code change is needed; if the fix touches `service.js` at all, it must be justified separately.
- [ ] The git service test file passes repeatedly (e.g. 5 consecutive runs) including under load.

Related: #881 (the regression this test guards), #1497 (main-broken tracker where run 41771073647's failure is recorded).

title: fix(ui): layoutAnimation calls requestAnimationFrame unguarded — throws at entry and as an uncaught error at settle time when rAF is unavailable

labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

`beginLayoutAnimation` in `packages/ui/src/lib/layoutAnimation.ts` guards only on `document` existing (`:63`), then calls the bare globals `requestAnimationFrame` (`:70` and, nested inside the settle `setTimeout`, `:74`) and `cancelAnimationFrame` (`:66`) with no check that they exist. In any DOM environment where `document` exists but `requestAnimationFrame` does not — test environments (happy-dom/jsdom teardown), embedded/non-browser DOMs — this throws:

- at entry (`:70`): a synchronous `ReferenceError: requestAnimationFrame is not defined` to the caller (e.g. `ContextPanel.tsx:1074` toggling the context panel);
- worse, at settle time (`:74`): the first frame runs while rAF exists, the environment changes before the settle timer fires, and the timer callback throws an **uncaught** `ReferenceError`. `settle()` is only ever reached through that rAF call, so when it throws the pending `runWhenLayoutSettled` tasks never run and the `data-panel-animating` root attribute is never removed.

This is not hypothetical: it already failed a main `pr checks` run — run 41710136292 (recorded on the #1497 main-broken tracker) failed `packages/ui` segment file `contextPanelEscapeClosesTerminal.test.tsx` with 5/5 tests passing but 1 unhandled error: `ReferenceError: requestAnimationFrame is not defined at packages/ui/src/lib/layoutAnimation.ts:74`, from the nested rAF scheduled by a `setTimeout` callback.

## Evidence

`packages/ui/src/lib/layoutAnimation.ts` (main @ bb1c05b36):

- `:62-63` — the only environment guard is `if (!globalThis.document) return;`
- `:66` — `cancelAnimationFrame(settleFrame)` unguarded.
- `:70` — `settleFrame = requestAnimationFrame(() => { ... })` unguarded.
- `:72-75` — inside that frame, `settleTimer = setTimeout(() => { settleTimer = null; settleFrame = requestAnimationFrame(settle); }, delay)` — the `:74` call happens a full animation duration after the environment was first checked, in a fresh timer context where nothing revalidates rAF.
- Sibling code in the same package does guard: `prefersReducedMotion` (`:41-42`) uses `globalThis.matchMedia?.(...)`, and `device.ts:213/:435` calls `window.requestAnimationFrame` in browser-only paths.
- The module's own tests (`layoutAnimation.test.ts:34-37`) always stub `requestAnimationFrame`/`cancelAnimationFrame` in `beforeEach` — there is no test where rAF is absent.

## Reproduction (probe, this run)

Laptop probe against the **real** module from the laptop primary (main bb1c05b36; probe dir: laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-layout-raf-20261104/`; two identical runs):

- **Scenario A (rAF absent at entry):** `document` stubbed, `requestAnimationFrame` deleted → `beginLayoutAnimation(5)` **threw** `ReferenceError: requestAnimationFrame is not defined`.
- **Scenario B (rAF removed after the first frame — the CI shape):** rAF stub captures the first frame; frame runs (scheduling the settle timer); rAF is then deleted before the timer fires → **uncaught** `ReferenceError: requestAnimationFrame is not defined` recorded via `uncaughtException`, exactly matching run 41710136292's failure at `:74`.

## Why it matters

- It flakes main CI: an unhandled error fails an otherwise-green test file and feeds the #1497 main-broken tracker, costing a full re-triage to attribute.
- In a real non-browser DOM (or a test harness that tears the environment down mid-animation), queued layout-settled work is stranded silently — no error surfaces to the caller, the work simply never runs, and the document root keeps `data-panel-animating`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `beginLayoutAnimation` does not throw when `requestAnimationFrame`/`cancelAnimationFrame` are unavailable: it settles immediately (or via the settle timer alone) so pending `runWhenLayoutSettled` tasks still run and the root attribute is removed.
- [ ] The settle path (`:74`) cannot raise an uncaught error if rAF disappears between the first frame and the timer firing.
- [ ] New regression tests in `layoutAnimation.test.ts`: (a) rAF absent at entry — no throw, tasks run; (b) rAF removed after the first frame — no uncaught error, tasks run, `isLayoutAnimating()` returns to false.
- [ ] Existing layoutAnimation tests and the context-panel test files stay green; behavior in a normal browser (rAF present throughout) is unchanged, including the frame-then-duration settle timing.

Related: #1497 (main-broken tracker where run 41710136292's failure is recorded), #46 (ui tests cross-file state — a different failure class; this one reproduces in a single module with no cross-file state).

title: fix(web): ngrok tunnel URL is extracted per pipe chunk — a split URL is accepted truncated (https://abcd1234.ngrok) or lost, and the captured URL beats the agent-API poll

labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

`startNgrokQuickTunnel` extracts the public tunnel URL from ngrok's stdout/stderr **per pipe chunk, with no accumulation or line carry-over** — the same chunk-boundary class as #1542 (cloudflared), but with a worse failure mode: depending on where the chunk boundary lands, a split URL is either **lost entirely** or **accepted in truncated form**.

- Split after the substring `ngrok` has arrived (e.g. first chunk ends `...https://abcd1234.ngrok`): the regex matches the fragment, `normalizeNgrokPublicUrl` accepts it because the hostname merely has to *contain* `ngrok`, and startup resolves with the non-existent host **`https://abcd1234.ngrok`**.
- Split anywhere earlier (inside `https://`, or inside `ngrok` before the substring completes): neither fragment matches, so the stdout path never learns the URL.
- The truncated URL actively **wins over the correct one**: the readiness poller checks the captured stdout URL *before* fetching the agent API (`pollNgrokPublicUrl`, with a comment saying child output must resolve startup promptly), so once the fragment is captured, the correct URL the local agent API (`127.0.0.1:4040/api/tunnels`) would have returned is never consulted.

Pipe chunk boundaries are arbitrary (write size, pipe-buffer pressure, scheduling), so this is intermittent in exactly the loaded conditions where tunnels are used.

## Evidence

`packages/web/server/lib/ngrok-tunnel.js` (main @ 0882feb7f):

- `captureOutput` (`:350-368`), wired to `child.stdout.on('data')` (`:371`) and `child.stderr.on('data')` (`:375`): each chunk is decoded and extracted alone —
  ```js
  const text = chunk.toString('utf8');
  const parsedUrl = extractNgrokPublicUrlFromText(text);   // :352
  if (parsedUrl) { publicUrl = parsedUrl; }
  ```
  Nothing accumulates between chunks.
- `extractNgrokPublicUrlFromText` (`:133-161`): per line it first tries `JSON.parse(line)` (a split JSON log line never parses), then falls back to `NGROK_PUBLIC_URL_REGEX` (`:28`, `/https:\/\/[^\s"']+/i`), which happily matches a *prefix* of the real URL at end-of-chunk.
- `normalizeNgrokPublicUrl` (`:~118-131`): acceptance is `parsed.protocol === 'https:' && parsed.hostname.includes('ngrok')` — a truncated hostname like `abcd1234.ngrok` passes.
- `pollNgrokPublicUrl` tick (`:290-297`): "Check the captured URL before the in-flight guard: child output can supply the URL while a poll fetch is stalled, and it must resolve startup promptly" — the captured (possibly truncated) URL is delivered via `onPublicUrl` and settles startup in `startNgrokQuickTunnel` before any API fetch result is used.
- Secondary: `captureOutput` also splits each chunk into `recentOutput` lines (`:358-367`), so a split log line is stored as two fragments and `summarizeNgrokOutput`'s per-line `JSON.parse` diagnostics degrade the same way.

## Reproduction (probe, this run)

Laptop probe against the **real** exported `extractNgrokPublicUrlFromText` from the laptop primary (main 0882feb7f), replaying `captureOutput`'s per-chunk, first-non-null-wins logic (probe dir: laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-ngrok-chunksplit-20261104/`; two identical runs):

- **full line (control):** `{"lvl":"info","msg":"started tunnel","url":"https://abcd1234.ngrok-free.app"}` in one chunk → `https://abcd1234.ngrok-free.app` ✓
- **split after `ngrok`:** first chunk ends `..."url":"https://abcd1234.ngrok` → captured URL is **`https://abcd1234.ngrok`** — truncated, wrong, and accepted.
- **split inside `ngrok`:** → `null` from both fragments (stdout URL lost).
- **split inside `https://`:** → `null` from both fragments (stdout URL lost).

## Why it matters

- A user starting an ngrok tunnel can be handed a **confidently wrong public URL** — startup reports success, the URL does not resolve to their tunnel, and the failure surfaces later detached from its cause. The agent-API poll that exists precisely as a reliable source is pre-empted by the bad capture.
- When the split lands earlier, the stdout fast-path silently does nothing and startup depends entirely on the API poll — inconsistent behavior for identical ngrok output, decided by pipe scheduling.
- The repo has fixed this exact per-chunk class twice in the sibling tunnel file (#1542 cloudflared, filed; #1443 exit settlement); ngrok is the remaining per-chunk tunnel parser.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] URL extraction operates on text accumulated across chunks (bounded rolling buffer or `StringDecoder` line buffer, consistent with the fix direction in #1542): a tunnel URL straddling a chunk boundary resolves startup with the **complete, correct** URL.
- [ ] A partial URL fragment at end-of-chunk is never accepted: extraction only matches a URL terminated by whitespace/quote/end-of-line on a complete line, or `normalizeNgrokPublicUrl` otherwise rejects hostnames that are a strict prefix fragment of a plausible ngrok hostname.
- [ ] The agent-API poll remains able to correct/override: a captured stdout URL must not settle startup if it is a fragment (see above), and existing poll-priority behavior for *complete* captured URLs is preserved.
- [ ] `recentOutput` line accumulation carries a partial line across chunks, so error summaries see complete log lines.
- [ ] Regression tests in `ngrok-tunnel.test.js` (or the existing tunnel test file): split-after-`ngrok` chunk pair yields the full URL (not the truncation), split-inside-scheme yields the full URL once the second chunk arrives, single-chunk control unchanged.

Related: #1542 (same per-chunk class in cloudflared — distinct file, distinct failure mode: there a split pattern is *missed*, here it is *accepted truncated*), #819 / #1359 (ngrok poll deadline / body cap, fixed), #820 (tunnel availability spawnSync timeout, fixed).

title: fix(web): cloudflared output is matched per pipe chunk — a split trycloudflare URL fails quick-tunnel startup after 30 s, and a split fatal line makes a managed tunnel report ready

body:
## Summary

Both cloudflared output parsers in `cloudflare-tunnel.js` match against **each pipe chunk in isolation** — there is no rolling buffer and no line carry-over — so any pattern that straddles a chunk boundary is never seen. Pipe chunk boundaries are arbitrary (write size, pipe-buffer pressure, scheduling), so this is a real failure mode, not a theoretical one:

- **Quick tunnel:** if the `*.trycloudflare.com` URL is split across two chunks, startup never detects it, waits the full 30 s, kills a healthy cloudflared, and reports "Tunnel URL not received within 30 seconds".
- **Managed tunnels:** if a fatal log line (e.g. `error parsing the config file…`) is split across two chunks, the fatal check never fires — and the 6 s liveness fallback then **resolves startup as successful** because it only requires *some* output, handing callers a live controller for a tunnel that failed to start.

This is the same chunk-boundary class as #1336 (git ls-files decode, fixed with a `StringDecoder`) and #1540 (untested sibling readers), in the one consumer that was left per-chunk.

## Evidence

`packages/web/server/lib/cloudflare-tunnel.js` (main @ 371371a31):

- Quick tunnel `onData` (`:378-388`): each chunk is decoded and matched alone —
  ```js
  const text = chunk.toString('utf8');
  if (!tunnelReady) {
    const match = text.match(TRY_CF_URL_REGEX);   // :382, regex at :15
    ```
  Nothing accumulates between chunks. On no match the startup promise only settles via the 30 s `DEFAULT_STARTUP_TIMEOUT_MS` (`:17`) rejection, which also kills the child.
- Managed readiness `waitForManagedTunnelReady` (`:297`): `inspectChunk` (`:315-334`) splits **the chunk** into lines (`:320`) and tests each fragment against the ready/fatal patterns; a line split across chunks is tested as two fragments and matches neither. The fallback timer (`:349-355`, `MANAGED_TUNNEL_LIVENESS_FALLBACK_MS` = 6000, `:23`) resolves whenever `sawOutput` is true, so the missed fatal line degrades into a false success instead of the 20 s hard timeout.
- Both paths also decode per chunk (`chunk.toString('utf8')` at `:316` and `:379`), so a multi-byte character straddling a boundary becomes U+FFFD — cosmetic for logs, but it shows no decoder state is kept at all.

## Reproduction (probe, this run)

Laptop probe driving the **real** exported `startCloudflareQuickTunnel` / `startCloudflareManagedRemoteTunnel` with a fake `cloudflared` on PATH (probe dir: laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-cf-chunksplit-20261103/`; fake prints `--version` normally, tunnel output to stderr like real cloudflared):

- **quick-single (control):** URL printed in one write → resolved, `getPublicUrl()` = `https://happy-tunnel.trycloudflare.com`.
- **quick-split:** the same URL printed as `https://split-tun` + (1 s) + `nel.trycloudflare.com\n` → **never settled within 6 s** (and per the code can only settle at the 30 s timeout, as a failure, after killing the healthy process).
- **fatal-single (control):** `error parsing the config file: bad` in one write, process stays alive → **rejected promptly** with `Cloudflared failed to start managed-remote tunnel: error parsing the config file: bad`.
- **fatal-split:** the same line split as `error parsing the con` + (1 s) + `fig file: bad` → **resolved successfully** (`getPublicUrl()` = `https://example.com`) via the liveness fallback — a false-ready managed tunnel.

## Why it matters

- Quick tunnels intermittently fail to start for no user-visible reason: a 30 s hang, a killed healthy cloudflared, and an error message that blames the tunnel service. Chunk splits become *more* likely exactly when output is heavy or the machine is loaded.
- Managed tunnels are worse: a fatal configuration error that happens to split is reported as success, so the user is told their named tunnel is up when cloudflared rejected its config — the failure then surfaces later, detached from its cause.
- The repo already fixed this exact class twice (#1336, #1358/#1540); this is the remaining per-chunk parser.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Quick-tunnel startup detects the trycloudflare URL even when it straddles chunk boundaries (accumulate a bounded rolling buffer of recent output and match against it, or buffer by lines with a `StringDecoder`); a split URL resolves startup with the correct `getPublicUrl()`.
- [ ] `waitForManagedTunnelReady` evaluates ready/fatal patterns against complete lines carried across chunks: a split fatal line rejects startup with the fatal-line error, and a split ready line resolves via the ready path (not the liveness fallback).
- [ ] The accumulated buffer is bounded (a named cap, consistent with the repo's bounded-buffer precedents) so a chatty or hostile child cannot grow it without limit.
- [ ] Regression tests in `cloudflare-tunnel.test.js` using the existing fake-cloudflared harness: split-URL quick tunnel resolves with the right URL; split fatal line rejects; single-write controls keep their current behavior (including #1443's exit-before-URL settlements).

Related: #1443 (quick-tunnel exit-before-URL hang, fixed — different mechanism), #1336 / #1540 (same chunk-boundary class in the git readers), #820 (tunnel availability spawnSync timeout, fixed).

body:
## Finding

PR #1358 (merged 2026-11-02, fixes #1336) switched three streamed git-output readers from per-chunk `chunk.toString('utf8')` to `StringDecoder`, so a multi-byte UTF-8 character split across pipe chunks no longer corrupts to U+FFFD:

1. `packages/web/server/lib/git/service.js` — the `git ls-files` reader in `listUntrackedFilesBounded`.
2. `packages/web/server/lib/fs/search.js` — the `git check-ignore` reader in `createFsSearchRuntime`.
3. `packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.js` — the `git check-ignore` reader in `registerFsRoutes` (file-tree listing).

Only reader 1 got a regression test (the boundary-aligned é filename test added to `git/service.test.js` in the same PR). Readers 2 and 3 — the exact same bug class, fixed in the exact same PR — have no test that feeds them check-ignore output split across chunk boundaries, or any non-ASCII check-ignore output at all.

## Evidence

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/openchamber/pull/1358 (head 977037ec04, merged 2026-11-02T17:49Z). Its diff touches `search.js` and `routes.js` decode logic but adds tests only in `packages/web/server/lib/git/service.test.js`.
- Verified on current main 68bdf7ab9f0abe796bd821e1636c98f965d268bc:
  - `packages/web/server/lib/fs/search.js:177` — `const stdoutDecoder = new StringDecoder('utf8')`, used at :197-198. Its suite `search.test.js` (215 lines) contains exactly one check-ignore test, "kills a stuck git check-ignore instead of hanging the search", whose fake child never emits any stdout data — decode is never exercised.
  - `packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.js:2083` — `const stdoutDecoder = new StringDecoder('utf8')`, used at :2103-2104. Its suite `routes.test.js` (3054 lines) contains no check-ignore test at all (no `check-ignore`/`checkIgnore` reference).
- Dedupe: issue search for "check-ignore decoder chunk" and "StringDecoder" returns only #1336 (closed, the ls-files bug this PR fixed). No open or closed issue covers test coverage for the two check-ignore readers.

## Why it matters

The failure mode #1358 fixed is silent: a corrupted ignored-path name simply fails to match, so an ignored non-ASCII file or directory stays visible in file search and in the file tree — no error anywhere. If either reader is later refactored back to per-chunk decoding (the pattern still exists elsewhere in the codebase's history), nothing fails. The ls-files reader is pinned; its two siblings from the same fix are not.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A test feeds the `search.js` check-ignore reader stdout in chunks that split a multi-byte character in an ignored non-ASCII path, and asserts the path is treated as ignored (the fake-spawn EventEmitter harness already used in `search.test.js` can emit chunked data).
- [ ] An equivalent chunk-split test covers the `routes.js` check-ignore reader, or the routes reader is routed through the same tested helper as search so one test covers both.
- [ ] Both tests fail if the reader is reverted to per-chunk `data.toString()` decoding (red/green verified by the implementer).

body:
## Summary

The project-icon **serve** path reads the stored icon file whole, with no size gate of any kind — while every other path in the same file enforces the 5 MiB cap, including one that enforces it *during* the read. An icon file on disk that exceeds the cap (replaced or grown outside the upload path, a legacy file, or a symlink target) is buffered whole into server memory and served in full; a non-regular file at the icon path blocks the request forever.

## Evidence

`packages/web/server/lib/opencode/project-icon-routes.js` (main @ 68bdf7ab9):

- `:288` — the GET handler serves from disk with a bare whole-file read, no stat, no cap, no regular-file check:
  ```js
  const data = await fsPromises.readFile(iconPath);
  ```
  The result is then `res.send(data)` at `:316`/`:322`-ish (and stringified whole for SVG theming).
- Contrast in the same file:
  - `readDiscoveredIcon` (`:36-70`) opens a handle, stats, and reads in 64 KiB chunks, refusing as soon as the running total passes `projectIconMaxBytes` (5 MiB, `:30`) — the bounded-read pattern landed for #1305.
  - `parseProjectIconDataUrl` (`:146`) rejects uploads over the cap before anything is written.
- So the cap is enforced at write time and at discover time, but never at serve time. The serve path trusts that the file on disk can only be what the writers allowed — the exact assumption #1436 (guest assets) and #1490 (project config) already falsified for sibling serve/read paths: the file lives in the user's data dir (`<openchamberDataDir>/project-icons/project-<sha1>.<ext>`, `:15`/`:88-100`), outside the server's control between writes.

## Reproduction (probe, this run)

Laptop probe driving the real `registerProjectIconRoutes` handler with real `fs/promises` (probe dir: laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-icon-serve-20261103/`):

- **Oversize:** planted a 6 MiB file at the icon candidate path → handler returned **status 200 with all 6,291,456 bytes served** (cap is 5,242,880).
- **FIFO:** replaced the icon path with a FIFO → handler **never settled after 3000 ms** (`fs.readFile` blocks opening a FIFO with no writer; there is no timeout), hanging the request indefinitely.

## Why it matters

- Memory/DoS surface on a long-lived server: one oversized (or hostile, via a symlink planted in the icons dir) file is buffered whole per request, and the immutable-cache response invites repeat hits.
- A FIFO/device at the path wedges the request handler with no deadline — the same failure class the bounded readers elsewhere in this repo were built to close.
- It is the last uncapped reader in this file; closing it makes the icon surface consistent with the repo's bounded-read contract (design #1254).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The GET `/api/projects/:projectId/icon` serve path enforces the 5 MiB cap **during** the read (e.g. reuse the `readDiscoveredIcon`-style chunked handle read), so an over-cap file is refused (4xx/5xx with no body bytes served) without ever being buffered whole.
- [ ] Non-regular files at the icon path (FIFO, device, directory) are rejected promptly instead of blocking the handler.
- [ ] Normal icons (all five extensions, SVG theming variants) still serve byte-identical with the existing headers.
- [ ] Regression tests in `project-icon-routes.test.js` cover: over-cap file on disk is refused, FIFO/non-regular target does not hang, at-cap file serves fully.

Related: #1305 / #1053 (discover path, fixed), #1436, #1490 (same stat/trust pattern in sibling paths), design #1254.

title: fs save identical-content check rethrows non-ENOENT open errors, failing saves over write-only files (PR #1415 CodeRabbit finding)

body:
## Finding (from PR review)

CodeRabbit (coderabbitai[bot]) raised this finding on merged PR #1415 and it was never fixed or replied to:

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/openchamber/pull/1415 — "fix(web): surface Linear comments truncation via commentsMore (#1414)" (the PR also carried the fs save-flow change CodeRabbit reviewed)
- Comment: https://github.com/developing-today/openchamber/pull/1415#discussion_r4451883308 (2026-11-03T07:19:46Z, on `packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.js:1616`)
- Essence: "Skip the identical-content read when the open fails. The save route now opens the existing target with mode `'r'` before it checks the byte length. For any non-`ENOENT` open error, the route rethrows. A file that the process can write but not read, such as mode `0222`, returns 403 with `Access denied`, so the requested content is not saved. The previous code skipped the read for a length mismatch and treated a failed `readFile` as \"not identical\", so the write succeeded. Let the open failure fall through to the atomic write, as the earlier code did."

## No-response evidence

- The review thread contains only the CodeRabbit comment; no reply followed it (reviewThreads check 2026-11-04: thread unresolved, sole author coderabbitai).
- PR #1415 merged with the finding unaddressed; the code is unchanged on current main (below).

## Still live on current main (verified 2026-11-04 by gh api raw read)

`packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.js`, save route identical-content check (~lines 1573-1577):
```js
handle = await fsPromises.open(writePath, 'r');
} catch (error) {
  if (!error || typeof error !== 'object' || error.code !== 'ENOENT') throw error;
}
```
The rethrown error reaches the route's outer catch, where permission errors are answered with 403 `Access denied` — so saving over an existing write-only (unreadable) file fails even though the atomic write itself (temp file + rename) does not need to read the target. This is a regression against the pre-change behaviour described in the comment.

## Acceptance criteria

- An open failure in the identical-content check (any error, not just `ENOENT`) skips the read and falls through to the atomic write; the shortcut still applies when the file opens successfully.
- A test covers saving over an existing unreadable/write-only target, or the limitation is documented on this issue as an accepted decision with reasoning.
- Existing fs route tests still pass.
