## Finding (from PR review)

CodeRabbit (coderabbitai[bot]) raised this Major finding on merged PR #1415 and it was never fixed or replied to:

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/openchamber/pull/1415 — "fix(web): surface Linear comments truncation via commentsMore (#1414)" (the PR also carried the fs save-flow change CodeRabbit reviewed)
- Comment: https://github.com/developing-today/openchamber/pull/1415#discussion_r4451883300 (2026-11-03T07:19:46Z, on `packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.js:1614`)
- Essence: "Avoid a blocking `open` on FIFO targets in the identical-content check. `fsPromises.open(writePath, 'r')` runs before the `isFile()` check. A FIFO with no writer blocks that open, so the save never reaches the atomic write. The pre-PR stat gate skipped the read for a size-0 FIFO. Open with `O_NONBLOCK`, as `readBoundedFile` in `packages/web/server/lib/shared/bounded-file-read.js` does, or reuse that reader."

## No-response evidence

- The review thread contains only the CodeRabbit comment; no reply followed it (reviewThreads check 2026-11-04: thread unresolved, sole author coderabbitai).
- PR #1415 merged with the finding unaddressed; the code is unchanged on current main (below).

## Still live on current main (verified 2026-11-04 by gh api raw read)

`packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.js`, save route identical-content check:
- Line 1574: `handle = await fsPromises.open(writePath, 'r');` — plain blocking open, no `O_NONBLOCK`.
- The `isFile()` judgement happens only afterwards, on the opened handle's stat (~line 1582).
On POSIX, opening a FIFO read-only blocks until a writer appears, so a save targeting a FIFO path hangs instead of falling through to the atomic write. The established in-repo pattern is `packages/web/server/lib/shared/bounded-file-read.js:28-29`: `openFlags()` = `O_RDONLY | O_NONBLOCK` on non-Windows.

## Acceptance criteria

- The identical-content check no longer blocks on FIFO targets: it opens with `O_NONBLOCK` (or reuses `readBoundedFile`), and a FIFO target proceeds to the atomic write without waiting for a writer.
- The regular-file identical-content shortcut still works (existing fs route tests pass, plus a FIFO/non-regular case is covered or documented).
- Or: the finding is resolved on this issue by a documented decision with reasoning recorded.

body:
Phase 2 of design #1528 (complete, or say so — one collection-completeness contract for provider collections). This phase is an **inventory audit only**: it changes no behaviour and fixes nothing; phase 1 (the shared `lib/github/collections.js` readers + the contract in `lib/github/DOCUMENTATION.md`) should land first so dispositions can name the shared shape.

## Problem

Nine per-site filings in two days (#1375, #1377, #1383, #1405, #1414, #1418, #1419, #1420, #1427 — all closed) each found one provider collection read that presented a prefix as the whole: REST page-1 reads, GraphQL `first:`/`last:` connections without `totalCount`, GitLab `maxPages: 1`, Linear `first:` without a `*More` signal. Three were explicitly residuals or twins of a sibling fix (#1383 ex-#1375, #1418 ex-#1405, #1420 "left behind when sibling collections moved to `readTotalCountCollection`"). Nobody has enumerated the *remaining* fixed-size collection reads, so the family's next residual is currently undiscoverable except by another incident.

## Scope

Enumerate every fixed-size collection read in:

- `packages/web/server/lib/github/` — REST reads that stop at page 1 or a `per_page` bound without a total check or a shared reader; GraphQL connections bounded by `first:`/`last:` that do not request `totalCount`.
- `packages/web/server/lib/gitlab/` and `packages/web/server/lib/linear/` — the same shapes in their transports (`maxPages`, `first:`, hand-rolled page loops).
- Web routes outside those modules that read provider collections directly.

Disposition each read in an inventory table posted as a comment on this issue, one row per read (file:line, collection, consumer), with exactly one disposition:

- **exhausts** — names the reader it goes through (a `collections.js` reader after phase 1, a cursor/page loop with a cap, a provider `*More` walk).
- **signals** — names the completeness flag/total its result carries (rule 1 of #1528).
- **verdict-guarded** — names the error or unknown/incomplete path that an incomplete set reaches (never the affirmative verdict).
- **justified cap** — a recorded one-line reason the prefix *is* the product (a deliberate top-N, a preview, a hard provider limit the UI already presents as such).

For every read with no disposition: file ONE per-site issue per surface (route/module + collection), stating the read, the consumer it feeds, and which #1528 disposition it should take; link it from the inventory. Do not fix any site inside this audit.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The inventory comment covers all four scopes above; every fixed-size collection read found has exactly one disposition or a linked per-site issue.
- [ ] The search method is recorded in the inventory (the grep/search patterns used per transport), so a later re-audit can repeat it.
- [ ] No production code changes in this issue's PR (test-only additions are out of scope too); the deliverable is the inventory + any filed per-site issues.
- [ ] Reads already covered by an open issue at audit time (e.g. #1496's search fallback) are dispositioned as "covered by #<n>", not re-filed.

body:
Phase 1 of design #1528 (complete, or say so — one collection-completeness contract for provider collections). This phase extracts the shared readers and records the contract; it changes **no call-site behaviour** and adopts no new call site. Phase 2 (the inventory audit) sequences after it.

## Problem

The GitHub module's completeness discipline exists only as three private functions inside `packages/web/server/lib/github/routes.js` (3,655 lines on current main `158df18debd9`):

- `readPullContextCollection` (:143) — pull-context files/comments (#1375/#1383 fixes).
- `readTotalCountCollection` (:169) — check runs for a ref, jobs for a run (#1405 fix): paginate to a short page, probe one page past the cap, error when the probe is non-empty; `total_count` honoured both ways (stop when covered; a short page that leaves runs unread is an explicit error).
- `readCheckRunAnnotations` (~:203) — annotations (#1420 fix): plain-array payload with no `total_count`; page errors propagate instead of returning the pages read so far as if complete.

Because they are private to `routes.js`, no other module can adopt them — `pr-summaries.js` re-derived the GraphQL form privately (`contexts(first: 100)` with `totalCount` :35-36; `summarizeCheckContexts` returning `{ state: 'unknown', incomplete: true, contextsTotal }` :156-157), and `lib/gitlab/` / `lib/linear/` have no shape to adopt at all. The contract they embody is stated only in a code comment ("a partial list is never summarised as complete").

## Scope

- Create `packages/web/server/lib/github/collections.js` and move the three readers there **behaviour-identical**: same page sizes and caps, same probe-one-page-past-the-cap discipline, same error messages, same `total_count` handling. `routes.js` imports them from the new module; no other file changes.
- State the #1528 contract in `packages/web/server/lib/github/DOCUMENTATION.md`, following the file's existing shape: rule 1 (complete, or say so), the two named dispositions (*verdict* — error, or explicit unknown/incomplete, never the affirmative verdict; *display* — items plus the completeness signal), the shared-shape rule across providers, and the GraphQL reference shape (`pr-summaries.js` contexts: bounded connection + `totalCount` + incomplete flag).

No cap value changes. No call site is added, removed, or altered in behaviour. The GitLab/Linear adoption and the audit of remaining fixed-size reads are phase 2 / phase 3 of #1528, not this issue.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `lib/github/collections.js` exists exporting the three readers with the semantics above; `routes.js` imports them and contains no private copies.
- [ ] Existing tests covering check runs, workflow-run jobs, annotations and pull context pass unchanged in expectation (CI is the judge).
- [ ] `lib/github/DOCUMENTATION.md` gains a collection-completeness section stating the contract, the two dispositions, and the GraphQL `totalCount` reference shape.
- [ ] No other module or call site is modified.

title: fix(web): idle-session reaper batch-archives linked btw/review sessions with no partner unlink — parents keep dangling btwSessionID links and live forks are orphaned

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/small-fix

labels.name: source/creator

labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s

body:
## Problem

The idle-session reaper added in PR #1515 (`packages/web/server/lib/openchamber-sessions/idle-session-reaper.js`, current main `158df18debd9`) archives finished idle sessions in one server-side batch through the archive store — but it has no handling for **linked sessions**, the one class the rest of the codebase treats as unsafe to archive in a batch:

- A **btw fork** (`metadata.openchamber.kind === 'btw'`, `originalSessionID` → parent) and a **review session** (`kind === 'review'`) point at a parent that must be unlinked when they are archived.
- A **parent carrying `metadata.openchamber.btwSessionID`** has an active btw fork that must be dealt with when the parent is archived.

The UI's archive path states this explicitly and routes exactly these sessions off the batch path:

- `packages/ui/src/sync/session-actions.ts:1708-1713` — "review sessions, btw forks, sessions with an active btw fork … keep the per-session path, because unlinking a partner is UI-owned work that reads and rewrites another session's metadata."
- `packages/ui/src/sync/session-actions.ts:1792-1794` — `hasLinkedSessionCleanup(session) = isReviewSession(session) || isBtwSession(session) || Boolean(getBtwSessionID(session))`.
- The UI retention sweep also protects btw parents outright: `packages/ui/src/sync/session-retention.ts` (`buildSessionRetentionCandidates`) adds any session with `getBtwSessionID(session)` to `protectedIds`.

The reaper (idle-session-reaper.js:52-58, `isKeptByUser`) mirrors only the pin / In-work protections. It never reads `btwSessionID`, `kind`, `originalSessionID`, or `reviewSessionID`, and it is constructed (routes.js:557-602) with no metadata store at all — so it cannot unlink a partner even in principle. Its only guards are idle status, age, pin/In-work, scheduled-task targets, archive-store membership, and working descendants via OpenCode `parentID` lineage — a btw fork is created by `forkSession` and linked by metadata, not by `parentID`, so `hasWorkingDescendants` does not cover it.

## Verified behavior (probe vs the real module, reproduced twice)

Laptop probe importing the real `createIdleSessionReaper` from main `158df18de` (`~/git/fleet/probe-oc-reaper-linked-20261103/probe.mjs`), stub archive store / status map (all idle), `hasPendingWork: false`:

- Scenario 1 — parent live (updated 1 min ago) carrying `btwSessionID: fork-old`; `fork-old` (kind `btw`) and `review-old` (kind `review`) idle for 3 h: **reaped = `["fork-old", "review-old", "plain-old"]`**. The forks are archived while their parent stays live, and the parent's `btwSessionID` / review link is never unlinked — the parent's btw panel is derived from that link (`packages/ui/src/lib/sessionBtwMetadata.ts:9-10,40-41`), so it now points at an archived fork.
- Scenario 2 — parent old/idle carrying `btwSessionID: fork-live`, fork updated 1 min ago: **reaped = `["parent-old"]`**. The parent is archived out from under its live btw fork, which the interactive path deletes/unlinks with the parent; the orphaned fork stays live and is hidden from session lists (`packages/ui/src/components/session/sidebar/list/sessionCollection.ts:45` skips btw sessions), so it also keeps counting against the live-set cap the reaper exists to bound (#791).

Both scenarios ran twice with identical results.

## Why it matters

The reaper runs unattended every 15 minutes on the real server (routes.js:603). Btw forks are side questions that normally finish long before their parent does — exactly the idle-and-old profile the reaper targets — so the dangling-link case is the common case, not an edge case. Review sessions have the same shape.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The reaper never batch-archives a session with linked-session metadata (`kind === 'btw'` with `originalSessionID`, `kind === 'review'` with `originalSessionID`, or a non-empty `btwSessionID` / `reviewSessionID`) without the partner unlink/cleanup the interactive path performs — either skip such sessions (conservative, matching the retention sweep's protection of btw parents) or perform the unlink; triage picks, the choice is recorded on this issue.
- [ ] Regression tests in `idle-session-reaper.test.js` cover: btw fork skipped/cleaned with a live parent, review fork likewise, btw parent not archived while its fork is live, plain old idle session still reaped (control).
- [ ] The reaper's header comment / `isKeptByUser` documentation names the linked-session rule alongside the pin / In-work / scheduled-target protections, so the protection list stops drifting from the UI's.

title: fix(web): guest install SSRF guard judges most of fe80::/10 link-local as public — clone.js blocks only the literal fe80: prefix

labels.name: kind/security
labels.description: Security issue or security hardening

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

The guest-install SSRF guard `isPublicHostname` in `packages/web/server/lib/guests/clone.js:29` blocks IPv6 link-local addresses only when the address literally starts with `fe80:`. Link-local is **fe80::/10** — the first hextet runs fe80–febf — so fe81:: through febf:: addresses are judged "public", both as literal install-URL hosts and as DNS answers. The server will then pin a git clone to such an address via `http.curloptResolve`.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe against the real module, main 069622f1d, run x2)

`packages/web/server/lib/guests/clone.js:19-31`:

```js
if (version === 6) {
  return !(host === '::1' || host === '::' || host.startsWith('fe80:') || host.startsWith('fc') || host.startsWith('fd') || host.startsWith('::ffff:'));
}
```

Probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-oc-guest-linklocal-20261103/probe.mjs` on the laptop, importing the real `clone.js`):

- `isPublicHostname('fe80::1')` → `false` (control, blocked)
- `isPublicHostname('fe81::1')` → `true`; `fe9a::1` → `true`; `feaf::1` → `true`; `febf::ffff` → `true` (all link-local, all judged public)
- `publicAddressesOf('example.com', stubLookup → [{address:'fe90::1'}])` → returns the fe90::1 address (the same stub returning fe80::1 correctly returns `null`)
- `gitNetworkArgs('https://example.com/x.git', stubLookup → fe90::1)` → `['-c','http.followRedirects=false','-c','http.curloptResolve=example.com:443:fe90::1']` — the clone is pinned to the link-local address

The repo's own sibling guards get the range right, so this is drift, not a policy choice:

- `packages/web/server/lib/linear/status.js:65-67`: comment "fc00::/7 (unique local) and fe80::/10 (link local)", implemented as `/^fe[89ab]/`.
- `packages/web/server/lib/small-model/index.js:230`: `net.BlockList` with `['fe80::', 10]`.

`clone-network.test.js` has no `isPublicHostname`/`publicAddressesOf` cases at all, which is how the gap survived.

## Why it matters

This guard is the only thing standing between a user-supplied guest install URL (or a DNS record its author controls) and the server fetching from its own machine/network — the exact SSRF the module header describes. Three of the four link-local hextet groups pass it. A hostname whose AAAA record is an fe81–febf address, or a literal `[fe90::1]` install URL, reaches the clone path with the address pinned by `curloptResolve`, defeating the DNS-rebinding protection the pinning exists for.

## Acceptance criteria

- `isPublicHostname` returns `false` for the whole fe80::/10 range (fe80–febf first hextets), as a literal and as a resolved address; `publicAddressesOf` returns `null` when any answer is in the range, and `gitNetworkArgs` returns `null` for such a host.
- Regression tests in `clone-network.test.js` (or a sibling) cover fe80/fe81/fe9f/feaf/febf literals plus the stubbed-DNS path; existing public/private controls (fc00::/7, ::1, 10/8, a public IPv4/hostname) still judge as before.
- Triage also judges fec0::/10 (deprecated site-local), which passes today (`fec0::1` → `true` in the same probe): block it too, or record why not on this issue.

## Summary

`packages/vscode/src/bridge-fs-helpers-runtime.test.ts` fails deterministically on main: two source-shape assertions still expect the pre-migration file-search implementation, but `bridge-fs-helpers-runtime.ts` was migrated to the shared traversal budget (#1393, design #1391).

## Evidence

- Test (verified live on main `5da1e2616`, 2026-11-03):
  - line 17: `assert.match(source, /inspectedFiles >= FILE_SEARCH_MAX_VISITED_FILES/)`
  - line 26: `assert.match(source, /visited\.size >= FILE_SEARCH_MAX_VISITED_DIRS/)`
- Runtime now implements the ceilings through the shared budget instead:
  - `budget.visitedEntries >= FILE_SEARCH_MAX_VISITED_FILES` (inspected-file stop)
  - `budget.visitDir()` gating directory admission against `FILE_SEARCH_MAX_VISITED_DIRS`
- CI failures (pr checks, `full (main tier): tests`, `100/101 test files passed, 1 failed` — this file the only failure):
  - run 41693228061 @ `f3ae56e` (tracked by #1497)
  - run 41723145311 @ `9dee9c0` — same two AssertionErrors

This is not a flake and not a runtime regression: the traversal-budget migration preserved the ceilings (10,000 files / 50,000 dirs, asserted at test lines 16/25 and still present), only the counting mechanism changed. The two stale assertions were missed when the vscode twin was migrated.

## Fix

Update the two assertions in `bridge-fs-helpers-runtime.test.ts` to match the budget-based implementation (e.g. `budget.visitedEntries >= FILE_SEARCH_MAX_VISITED_FILES` and the `budget.visitDir()` admission gate), keeping the ceiling-value assertions unchanged. Do not change runtime behavior.

title: fix(web): /health readiness never flips when an external (skip-start) OpenCode server dies

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: priority/high
labels.description: Important and time-sensitive

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: meta/enriched
labels.description: Intake review done: acceptance criteria, links, and normalized labels added

body:
## Problem

For an **external** OpenCode server (skip-start attach via `OPENCODE_HOST` + `OPENCODE_SKIP_START=true`), OpenChamber's `/health` readiness never reflects an outage of the remote server: `openCodeRunning` and `isOpenCodeReady` stay `true` and `lastOpenCodeHealthFailure` stays `null` indefinitely after the remote dies, even though API calls through the proxy correctly fail with `503 {"error":"OpenCode service unavailable"}`.

Found during the live nonlocal-attach validation of #766 (task 8872, 2026-11-03): remote `opencode serve` (v2.0.30, second host, tailnet origin) killed at ~23:47Z; ~60s and several nominal health intervals later, `/health` still reported ready. Sessions recovered immediately when the remote restarted.

## Root cause (verified on main 5da1e2616)

`packages/web/server/lib/opencode/lifecycle.js`:

- `runHealthCheckCycle` (line ~1943) begins `if (!state.openCodeProcess || state.isShuttingDown || state.isRestartingOpenCode) return;` — for an external server `state.openCodeProcess` is always null (nothing was spawned), so the periodic cycle is a complete no-op for external attach.
- `probeExternalOpenCode` (line ~977) exists and works, but its only callers are the bootstrap path (line ~1647) and the restart path (line ~1359) — nothing calls it periodically, and nothing ever clears the bootstrap-time ready state for an external server.

So readiness for external servers is a bootstrap-time snapshot, not live state.

## Acceptance

- With an external (skip-start) server configured, killing the remote flips `/health` to not-ready (`isOpenCodeReady: false`, a recorded `lastOpenCodeHealthFailure`) within one health interval (plus the existing consecutive-failure threshold semantics if applied), without attempting to restart the external process.
- Restarting the remote returns `/health` to ready without restarting OpenChamber.
- Managed (spawned) server health behavior is unchanged; existing lifecycle tests pass and new tests cover the external cycle (external probe failure → not-ready; probe success → ready again).

## Context

- Origin validation: #766 (see the task 8872 results comment there for the full live checklist).
- The API proxy path already surfaces unavailability correctly (503 + PushWatcher disconnect) — this issue is only about the health/readiness state.

- With an external (skip-start) OpenCode server attached, killing the remote makes /health report not-ready (openCodeRunning/isOpenCodeReady false, lastOpenCodeHealthFailure set) within roughly two nominal health intervals.

title: fix(web): pairing store fabricates a fresh expiry for sessions whose expiresAt is missing or unparseable — the secret never expires and stays redeemable

labels.name: kind/security
labels.description: Security issue or security hardening

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

A stored pairing session whose `expiresAt` is missing or unparseable is silently given a **fresh full TTL on every read**, so it never expires and its pairing secret stays redeemable indefinitely — for a credential that creates a new remote client (device pairing).

Verified on main `d61be2b866` (laptop primary at origin/main), all in `packages/web/server/lib/client-auth/pairing.js`:

- `normalizeStore` (:130) maps every stored session through `expiresAt: normalizeTimestamp(session.expiresAt) || new Date(Date.now() + ttlMs).toISOString()`. `normalizeTimestamp` (:35-40) returns `null` for a missing/unparseable value, so the fallback **fabricates** `now + ttlMs` (default TTL 10 min, :10) instead of treating the session as expired.
- Every read goes through this: `readStore` returns `normalizeStore(result.value)`, and `redeemPairingSession` checks expiry (:299) only against the already-normalized session — `Date.parse(session.expiresAt) <= Date.now()` can never fire for a session whose expiry was lost, because normalization just replaced it with a future date.
- The module's own definition disagrees: `isPendingSession` (:76-80) requires a **finite, parseable** `expiresAt` in the future. Normalization defeats that check before any caller sees the session, so `listPendingSessions` and `hasActiveRelaySession` also report such sessions as pending with the fabricated expiry.
- The sweep agrees too: `sweepExpiredSessionsFromStore` (:205-216) keeps never-used sessions whose expiry is unparseable (`!Number.isFinite(expiresAt) || expiresAt > now`) — and after normalization that branch is moot anyway.
- Contrast in the same package: `remote-clients.js:84` normalizes with `expiresAt: normalizeTimestamp(client.expiresAt)` and keeps `null` — it does not fabricate an expiry.

Sessions written by `createPairingSession` always carry a valid ISO `expiresAt`, so the trigger is a store written by another/older version, a hand edit, or partial corruption that leaves the JSON parseable (the exact shape `normalizeStore` exists to tolerate). The existing tests cover a parseable-but-past expiry (`pairing.test.js:77-84`, negative-TTL) — that path works — but no test stores a session with a missing/unparseable `expiresAt`.

## Evidence (laptop probe vs the real runtime, reproduced twice)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-pairing-expiry-20261103/probe.mjs` — imports the real `createClientPairingRuntime` from main `d61be2b866`, seeds `pairing.json` with four sessions (secret hashes of known secrets), stub `createClient`:

- `pair_missing` (no `expiresAt` field): listed pending with fabricated `expiresAt` ≈ now+10 min; **redeemed — a client token was issued**.
- `pair_garbage` (`expiresAt: "not-a-date"`): same — pending with fabricated expiry; **redeemed**.
- `pair_past` (`expiresAt` 2026-01-02, control): rejected with "Invalid or expired pairing session". ✔
- `pair_future` (`expiresAt` 2999-01-01, control): redeemed. ✔

The fabricated stamp is also persisted by the redeem write (`expiresAt` ≈ usedAt + 10 min in the stored file), so the extension looks deliberate in hindsight.

## Why it matters

A pairing secret is a bearer credential: whoever holds it can pair a new device/client against the server within its window. The 10-minute TTL is the control that bounds a leaked or abandoned pairing link. A session whose expiry record is lost — precisely the degraded-store case the tolerant reader is built for — silently escapes that control and stays redeemable until some unrelated store write happens to persist a concrete stamp (and even then it gets a fresh full TTL from that moment, not from creation).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A stored pairing session with a missing or unparseable `expiresAt` is treated as expired: it is not returned by `listPendingSessions`, does not count in `hasActiveRelaySession`, and `redeemPairingSession` rejects it with the generic redeem error — no fabricated expiry is ever substituted or persisted.
- [ ] Sessions with a valid past `expiresAt` stay rejected and valid future ones still redeem exactly once (existing behaviour and tests unchanged).
- [ ] New regression tests in `pairing.test.js` seed a store with a missing-`expiresAt` session and an unparseable-`expiresAt` session and pin both as unredeemable/not pending.
- [ ] The sweep drops never-used sessions whose expiry is missing/unparseable instead of keeping them.

body:
## Problem

`OPENCODE_HOST` accepts a URL with userinfo (`https://user:pass@host:4096`) but silently discards the credentials, so a remote (nonlocal) OpenCode attach configured that way fails authentication with an unexplained 401.

Verified on main `9306f3f1a` during triage of #766 (task 8707):

- `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/env-config.js` — `resolveOpenCodeEnvConfig`'s `configuredOpenCodeHost` parses with `new URL(raw)` and returns `{ origin: url.origin, port }`; `url.origin` strips userinfo, and the written-port regex explicitly tolerates an `@` userinfo segment (`(?:[^@/?#]*@)?`). No warning is emitted.
- The only credential surface is `OPENCODE_SERVER_PASSWORD`, rendered as Basic `opencode:<password>` by `getOpenCodeAuthHeaders` (`packages/web/server/lib/opencode/auth-state-runtime.js:49-60`).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `OPENCODE_HOST` with URL userinfo produces an explicit logger warning (or rejection) naming that URL credentials are ignored and `OPENCODE_SERVER_PASSWORD` is the credential surface — never silent acceptance.
- [ ] No behaviour change for userinfo-free `OPENCODE_HOST` values; existing env-config tests pass.
- [ ] New env-config test pins the userinfo behaviour.
- [ ] Do NOT start sending URL userinfo as credentials: `OPENCODE_SERVER_PASSWORD` stays the one credential surface.

Found by: queue triage task 8707 (lane B) while verifying the #766 nonlocal-attach credential path.

title: fix(web): dispatch-results register resolves an ID when persist refuses the write — entry silently dropped on restart (PR #1390 comment)

labels.name: app/web

labels.description: Filed by the pr-comment-review job

body:
## Finding (from a PR review comment, never addressed)

On PR #1390 (`refactor(web): migrate dispatch-results store to durable-store primitive (#978)`), CodeRabbit raised a concrete data-loss finding against `register` in `packages/web/server/lib/dispatch-results/runtime.js`. It was never replied to, fixed, or tracked; the PR merged as-is.

### Finding — register reports success for a write that was refused
- Comment: https://github.com/developing-today/openchamber/pull/1390#discussion_r4450060697
- Reviewer: `coderabbitai[bot]`, 2026-11-03T01:54:48Z, `packages/web/server/lib/dispatch-results/runtime.js:307`
- Essence: "**Make `register` reject when its write is refused.** When preservation fails, `persist` logs a warning and skips the write. `register` still resolves with an ID, so the service reports the result as pending. A restart before delivery drops that entry. Remove the entry from memory and throw from `register` when the write fails."

## No-response evidence
- GraphQL `reviewThreads` for PR #1390: this thread is `isResolved: false` and contains only the single CodeRabbit comment — no replies (verified 2026-11-03; a fresh `gh api .../pulls/1390/comments` re-read confirms exactly 2 inline comments on the PR, both CodeRabbit findings, neither with replies).
- The PR's last commit `d33d17c64` (the main-merge head Codex re-reviewed at 2026-11-03T03:12:45Z) does not change the flagged behavior — the code on current main is unchanged in this spot (see below).
- The only later conversation activity is a dezren39 `@codex review` note about merging main and test counts; it does not address this finding.
- Dedupe: `gh issue list --state all` searches (dispatch-results register/persist; readFile) on 2026-11-03 return no issue covering this defect — #976/#978 are the parent durable-store design/migration trackers, not this bug.

## Still live on current main (verified 2026-11-03)
- `packages/web/server/lib/dispatch-results/runtime.js:295-317`: `persist()` chains onto `writePromise` and its `.catch(...)` only logs `[dispatch-results] failed to persist pending results:` — a preservation failure (`preservation.outcome === 'failed'` -> throw inside the chain) is swallowed and the returned promise resolves.
- `runtime.js:500-527`: `register` does `entries.set(entry.id, entry)`, then `await persist();` (line 523), then returns `{ id: entry.id }` unconditionally — so a refused write still yields a successful registration, and the entry exists only in memory. A restart before delivery drops it while the caller was told the result is pending.

## Acceptance criteria
- When the write underlying `register` is refused/fails, `register` removes the new entry from memory and rejects, so the caller does not report an undelivered result as pending; successful writes behave exactly as today; or
- Resolve by a documented decision on this issue explaining an alternative mechanism that guarantees a registered entry survives restart (cite it).
- A regression test covering the preservation-failure path in `register` is expected with the fix.

Found via: unaddressed PR comment review (pr-comment-review job), PR #1390.

title: fix(web): APNs relay send silently drops every device token past 100 — sendViaRelay slices the group and never chunks, unlike the direct path

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Bug

In relay mode (the default APNs path), `sendViaRelay` silently drops every device token past the first 100 in an environment group — no chunking, no warning, no log. Devices past 100 simply never receive the push.

## Evidence (main `9306f3f1a7c6c2247057b18965fa77dca6ed93b5`)

- `packages/web/server/lib/notifications/apns-runtime.js:580-581` — `sendViaRelay` starts with `const tokens = deviceTokens.slice(0, 100);` and posts exactly one relay request. Nothing iterates the remainder.
- `apns-runtime.js:730-731` — the caller, `sendApnsToAllUiSessions`, passes the whole per-environment token group (deduped across all UI sessions) into that single call.
- `apns-runtime.js:33,327` — each UI session may hold up to `MAX_TOKENS_PER_SESSION = 10` tokens, so 11 sessions' worth of devices already crosses the slice.
- The direct-APNs sibling has no such cap: `sendViaDirectApns` (`apns-runtime.js:660,689`) sends to every token in the group via `Promise.all(deviceTokens.map(...))`. The two modes therefore deliver to different device sets for the same notification.
- The only "100" rationale in the file is the response-size comment at `apns-runtime.js:43-45` ("drop tokens for at most 100 tokens"), i.e. 100 is the assumed relay batch size — which makes chunking the natural fix shape, not a reason to drop the rest.

## Reproduction (verified this run, twice)

Laptop probe against the real `createApnsRuntime` (in-memory token store + stubbed relay fetch; probe at `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-apns-relay-100-20261103/`):

- Registered 105 distinct tokens across 11 sessions, then called `sendApnsToAllUiSessions`.
- Result (both runs): exactly **1** relay send call carrying **100** tokens; `tok100`–`tok104` were never sent; missing count 5; no warning emitted.

## Why it matters

Relay is the default mode (direct mode is the self-hoster fallback). On any server with more than 100 registered iOS devices in one APNs environment, the excess devices silently stop receiving "agent finished / needs input" pushes — the exact notifications a phone user relies on when away from the desk. Because dead-token cleanup also runs off the relay `results` array, the dropped tokens are never even judged; they just stay registered and unsent-to forever.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] With more than 100 tokens in one environment group, every token is sent to (chunked relay requests of at most 100, signed per chunk as today), or the truncation is otherwise removed.
- [ ] Dead-token (`drop: true`) results from every chunk are acted on, not just the first chunk's.
- [ ] Regression test in `apns-runtime.test.js`: >100 tokens across sessions → all tokens appear across the relay send calls; tokens past 100 are included.
- [ ] Existing apns-runtime tests pass; sealed per-device sends (one token each) unchanged.

title: fix(web): PR-status search fallback is unscoped — it returns another owner's PR for a same-named repo and loses the real PR past 20 global results

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Bug

The branch PR-status search fallback can return a pull request that belongs to a **different owner** — and can lose the real PR behind unrelated global search results.

`searchFallbackPr` in `packages/web/server/lib/github/pr-status.js` (verified on main `25d0c3dd326f`):

- `:621` — the Search API query is completely unscoped: ``q: `is:pr state:open head:${branch}` `` with `per_page: 20`. No `repo:`, `user:`, or `org:` qualifier, even though the caller (`:931-935`) knows the resolved target owners — it passes only repo **names**: `repoNames: resolvedTargets.map((target) => target.repo.repo)`.
- `:613` + `:644` — results are filtered only by repo name: `normalizedRepoNames.has(normalizeLower(repo.repo))`. The owner parsed from `repository_url` (`:640`) is never compared to a target owner. Every fork shares its upstream's repo name, and unrelated owners routinely have same-named repos.
- The first same-named result whose head ref matches is returned as this checkout's PR (`resolveGitHubPrStatus` returns it with the other owner's repo), with no pagination past the first 20 **global** results and no `total_count` check. A genuine miss is then cached for 10 minutes (`SEARCH_MISS_RETRY_MS`, `:503`).

The fallback runs exactly when the per-repo lists were incomplete (`coverage.authoritative === false`, `:928-948`) — i.e. on large/busy repos, where a wrong or missing answer is most likely.

## Verified (laptop probe, this run)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-prstatus-search-20261103/probe.mjs` on the laptop, driving the real `resolveGitHubPrStatus` with a mocked Octokit (incomplete pulls list to force the fallback; checkout remote `target-owner/app`, branch `feature`). Reproduced twice with identical output:

- **Wrong owner:** search returns only `someone-else/app` PR #77 → resolver returns `{owner: "someone-else", repo: "app"}` PR #77 as this checkout's PR status.
- **Truncation + wrong owner combined:** 20 same-named results from other owners precede the target owner's PR #42 → resolver returns another owner's PR #100; the real PR at global position 21 is never seen.

## Why it matters

PR status drives the work-status / PR surfaces in the UI. Showing a stranger's PR — its state, checks, and links — for the user's branch is a correctness and trust bug, not just a missed lookup; and for common branch names (`feature`, `fix`, `dev`) the real PR is likely to sit beyond the first 20 global hits, so the fallback silently degrades to wrong-or-nothing on exactly the busy repos that trigger it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The search query is scoped to the resolved target repositories (e.g. `repo:owner/name` qualifiers), or results are filtered by owner **and** repo name against the resolved targets before any `pulls.get`.
- [ ] A result from an owner not among the resolved targets is never returned as the checkout's PR (regression test with a same-named different-owner hit).
- [ ] The real PR is still found when same-named results from other owners precede it (regression test), without unbounded Search API spend — the tiny-quota comment at `:618` still applies.
- [ ] Existing pr-status tests pass; new tests cover the fallback path in `pr-status.test.js`.

title: fix(web): plan summary cache never evicts — createPlanSummaryCache's entries Map is unbounded for the server's lifetime, orphaned by every deleted or renamed plan

body:
## Problem

`createPlanSummaryCache` (`packages/web/server/lib/project-context/plan-progress.js:79-119`) memoizes plan summaries in a plain `Map` (`entries`, :80) that **never evicts and has no size bound**:

- Entries are added in three places (:104, :110, :116 — the normal, too-large-at-stat, and grew-past-cap paths).
- The only `entries.delete` in the module is in `summaryOf`'s stat-ENOENT branch (:95) — it fires only when the *exact same path* is queried again after the file disappeared.
- The cache is a **single server-lifetime instance**: `createProjectContextRuntime` creates it once (`runtime.js:254`) and every project shares it.

The eviction branch is unreachable from the real list flow. `listSharedPlans` (`runtime.js:486-493`) calls `summaryOf` only for names `readdir` just returned, and `progressOfLink` (`runtime.js:520`) only for files in the current manifest. A plan file that is deleted, renamed, or unshared is simply never queried again — so its entry (path string + `{ mtimeMs, size, summary }`) is retained for the remaining life of the server process. The shared plans folder is explicitly open to files "written by other tools" (`runtime.js:476-478` comment), so churn there counts too: every distinct plan path ever listed in any project leaves a permanent entry.

## Evidence (verified this run, main e1e8bc3dad)

- Code read in the laptop primary and re-verified via `gh api` raw contents (two channels agree): `plan-progress.js:80` `const entries = new Map();`, sets at :104/:110/:116, the sole delete at :95; no cap, TTL, or prune anywhere in the module.
- Laptop probe against the real `createPlanSummaryCache` (probe `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-plan-summary-cache-20261103/probe3.mjs`, counting-fs wrapper): three plan files listed twice → 3 reads total (cache hits work as documented); after deleting `b.md`, replaying the list flow (readdir → `summaryOf` per surviving name) never re-queries `b.md`, so its entry can never reach the ENOENT delete; only a direct `summaryOf(b.md)` returns null and evicts it — a call the list flow never makes for a missing file.
- House pattern: sibling long-lived caches in this codebase are bounded — notifications runtime caches capped at 500, realpath cache at 256, skills-catalog scan cache with LRU eviction (the #968 fix). This cache, added with the plan-progress feature, has none.

## Why it matters

The managed server is a long-lived process (it supervises the standing OpenCode instance for days). Plan files are high-churn by design — agents create, tick, rename, share, and delete plans across every project — and each churned path leaks one entry forever. The growth is slow and silent: no metric, no bound, and no test pins a limit, so nothing notices until a long-lived instance has accumulated the path history of every plan it ever listed.

## Acceptance criteria

- `createPlanSummaryCache` bounds its entries (e.g. an LRU/size cap in the style of the codebase's other caches, sized and named as a module constant) **or** evicts entries for paths a listing no longer returns; either way an entry for a deleted/renamed plan does not outlive the bound.
- Cache-hit behavior is unchanged for live plans: a second listing of an unchanged file still costs one `stat` and no read (the existing `plan-progress.test.js` cache tests still pass).
- A regression test plants more distinct plan paths than the bound (or deletes/renames a listed plan, per the chosen design) and asserts the stale entries are gone while live entries still hit.
- Existing project-context tests (`plan-progress.test.js`, `runtime.test.js`) still pass.

Filed by the new-issue-creator-openchamber run 2026-11-03 12:50 CST. Probe: laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-plan-summary-cache-20261103/`.

title: perf(web): plan metrics are re-fetched live from OpenCode on every project-context read — no cache or in-flight dedup in createPlanMetricsReader (#1462)

labels.name: kind/performance

labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

Plan metrics (added today in #1462, `packages/web/server/lib/project-context/plan-metrics.js`) are read live from OpenCode on **every** project-context read, with no caching and no in-flight dedup anywhere in the path:

- `createPlanMetricsReader` (plan-metrics.js:124-152) performs a fresh `GET /api/session/:id` fetch (10 s timeout, :131-143) on every single call. There is no memoization, no TTL, and no sharing of concurrent calls for the same session.
- `readContext` (runtime.js:533, :551-564) maps over **all** listed plans and awaits `readPlanMetrics(plan.session.sessionId)` for each one with a linked session, every time the context is read. A project may hold up to 500 plans (`PROJECT_PLAN_MAX_ITEMS`, runtime.js:31).
- `readContext` is not a rare call: it backs `GET /project-context/:projectId` (project-context/routes.js:60), `publicPlanOf` (runtime.js:571-574, used by the single-plan mutation/read paths at :916/:956/:984/:1126/:1155), and the context object returned by most mutations. On the client, `observeProjectContext` (packages/ui/src/lib/projectContextSync.ts:42-48) reloads the context on every `project-context-changed` event, every window focus, and every visibility/online change — so each open client re-triggers the full fan-out, and a mutation broadcasts a fresh fan-out to every watching client.

Session cost/token figures change only when the session runs; re-fetching every linked session's record on every context read is pure repeated load on the managed OpenCode server, and each context read's latency includes the slowest of N session fetches.

## Evidence (verified this run, main b9db267b6)

Laptop probe against the **real** `createPlanMetricsReader` with a counting `fetchImpl` returning a fixed session record (probe: laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-plan-metrics-cache-20261103/`):

- 1 read of `ses_1` → 1 fetch, metrics `{costUsd: 1.25, costSource: 'opencode', tokens: {...total: 150}}`
- 2 more sequential reads of the same session → 3 fetches total (no cache hit)
- 5 concurrent reads of the same session → 5 additional fetches (no in-flight dedup)

Contrast: the catalog half of the same feature already goes through a shared 10-minute TTL cache (`getModelsMetadata`, `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/models-metadata.js:4-16,54-55`) — the per-session record read is the uncached half.

## Why it matters

Project context is a hot, multi-client surface: the panel reloads on change events and focus. As users link more plans to sessions (the feature #16 is built around), every reload costs one live OpenCode request per linked plan per client, forever, for data that is stale-tolerant by design (metrics are a display badge, explicitly "never stored", and a failed read already degrades to no badge). This is avoidable load on the single managed OpenCode server every other surface also depends on.

## Acceptance criteria

- Repeated `readPlanMetrics` calls for the same session within a short TTL (or an equivalent invalidation scheme) do not each issue a `GET /api/session/:id` fetch; concurrent calls for the same session share one in-flight fetch.
- A metrics value may be served stale within the TTL; a failed read still resolves null and does not poison the cache for the full TTL (or failures are not cached at all).
- `readContext` output shape is unchanged: plans with a readable linked session still carry `metrics`, plans without one carry none.
- Tests: reader-level tests prove (a) a second read inside the TTL performs no additional fetch, (b) concurrent reads share one fetch, (c) after TTL expiry a fresh fetch happens; existing plan-metrics and project-context runtime tests still pass.
- The chosen TTL/invalidation is named in code with a comment saying why that freshness is acceptable for a display badge.

## Notes

Filed by the new-issue-creator run; the fix is a design call (TTL length, whether invalidation hooks into session events) so this is filed for triage, not self-solved. Origin feature: #16 stage 1, PR #1462.

title: fix(web): both hand-rolled ZIP readers never verify CRC-32 — guest extract-zip and VSIX theme-archive silently accept length-preserving corruption

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

Both hand-rolled ZIP readers in the web server parse the local/central headers for sizes but **never verify the CRC-32 stored in those headers**, so a length-preserving corruption of an entry is silently accepted as good data:

1. **Guest packages** — `packages/web/server/lib/guests/extract-zip.js`: the local-header parse reads flags (offset +6), method (+8), `compressedSize` (+18, :50) and `uncompressedSize` (+22, :51), caps the inflate at the declared size (:91), and checks only `data.length !== uncompressedSize` (:95) before `fs.writeFile(target, data)` (:103). The CRC-32 field at local-header offset +14 is never read; the word CRC does not appear in the file. For STORE entries there is no other integrity check at all (raw DEFLATE catches some corruptions structurally, stored data catches none). The extracted tree is then installed by `installGuestFromZipBuffer` (`packages/web/server/lib/guests/install.js:285-294`) — package, panel and script files are served/executed from this extraction.
2. **VSIX themes** — `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/theme-archive.js`: the central-directory parse reads `compressed` (cursor+20, :25) and `size` (cursor+24, :26) and stores `{ offset, compressed, size, method }` (:36) — the CRC-32 at central offset +16 is never read. The reader checks only `result.length !== size` (:50) and returns the entry as theme JSON text.

## Evidence (verified this run, main f46050fc0)

Laptop probe against the real `extractZipBuffer` and `openThemeArchive` (probe: laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-zip-crc-20261103/probe.mjs`), using a STORE zip whose header CRC was computed over the original bytes, then flipping one data byte in place (length unchanged):

- Guest zip, entry `panel/data.txt` = `hello world` with first byte flipped to `Hello world`: `extractZipBuffer` returned `{ ok: true }` and the corrupted file was read back from disk as `Hello world`. Stored CRC 222957957 ≠ corrupted-data CRC 2346098258 — never compared.
- VSIX, entry `extension/theme.json` = `{"name":"original"}` with one byte flipped to `{"name":"Original"}` (still valid JSON): `openThemeArchive` returned the corrupted string with no error.

Dedup: no open or closed issue mentions CRC, checksum, or integrity for either reader (searched 2026-11-03).

## Why it matters

These readers exist precisely to distrust the archive: they reject traversal, zip64, encryption, data descriptors, and over-cap expansion. The one standard integrity field ZIP provides is the one check missing, so bit rot, a truncated-then-padded transfer, or a hand-edited archive produces a silently wrong guest install (wrong panel/script bytes pass inspection, which parses only the manifest) or a silently wrong theme, with no error anywhere to diagnose from. The Windows OpenCode installer in the same codebase does verify its download (`v2-install.js` sha512 check) — these two readers are the inconsistent ones.

## Acceptance criteria

- `extractZipBuffer` verifies each extracted entry's CRC-32 against its local header (and, where cheap, the central directory) and returns `{ ok: false, code: 'extract-failed' }` on mismatch, for both STORE and DEFLATE entries, before the file is written (or removes it on mismatch).
- `openThemeArchive`'s reader verifies the entry CRC-32 from the central directory and throws on mismatch, for both methods.
- Regression tests: a STORE entry with a single flipped byte (header CRC of the original) is rejected by both readers; a DEFLATE entry with a corrupted-but-length-preserving payload is rejected by both; the existing valid-archive tests (`extract-zip.test.js`, theme archive tests) still pass.
- No change to the existing caps, traversal, zip64, encryption, or data-descriptor rejections.

title: fix(web): dictation, terminal and guest-surface WebSocket caps are maxPayload-only — no handler-side guard, so under Bun over-cap frames are assembled and parsed, never refused with 1009 (#1371 residual)

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Finding

Three WebSocket servers still rely on `maxPayload` alone, with no handler-side frame-size check — the exact gap #1371 closed for the message-stream server and #1082/#1249 closed for dev-tunnel and realtime-proxy. The in-repo premise (dev-tunnel/runtime.js:54-59, realtime-proxy.js:21-39, event-stream fix for #1371) is that under Bun the bundled `ws` does not enforce `maxPayload`: an over-cap frame is assembled whole in server memory and handed to the message handler, and the connection is never refused with 1009. Under Node the `ws` layer enforces the cap, so the exposure is Bun-only — same as the siblings.

## Evidence (main 984deac17)

- Dictation: `packages/web/server/lib/dictation/runtime.js:31` sets `DICTATION_WS_MAX_PAYLOAD_BYTES = 512 * 1024` and `:126` passes it as `maxPayload`; the `message` handler at `:159` does `JSON.parse(raw.toString('utf8'))` with no byte-length check on `raw` first. No `1009` anywhere in the file. A chunk message's base64 audio is then handed to the stream manager, whose reorder-buffer bound (stream-manager.js, 8 MiB of *decoded* chunks) only applies after the frame has been assembled and parsed.
- Terminal: `packages/web/server/lib/terminal/runtime.js:199` creates the server with `maxPayload: TERMINAL_WS_MAX_PAYLOAD_BYTES` (64 KiB, terminal-ws-protocol.js:3); the handler at `:520` passes `raw` straight to `readTerminalWsControlFrame`, which (terminal-ws-protocol.js:39-58) buffers and `JSON.parse`s the whole frame with no length check. No `1009` in the file. (The `write` branch's `MAX_INPUT_CHARS` check runs only after the full frame is parsed.)
- Guest surface: `packages/web/server/lib/guests/surface.js:585` creates the server with `maxPayload: VIEWER_MESSAGE_MAX_BYTES` (256 KiB, `:62`); `handleViewerMessage` (`:486`) does `JSON.parse(Buffer.from(raw).toString('utf8'))` with no length check on `raw`. No `1009` in the file.
- Contrast — the fixed pattern: event-stream/runtime.js:115-124 checks `messageStreamPayloadByteLength(data)` in the handler and closes 1009; dev-tunnel/runtime.js:205-212 and realtime-proxy.js:303-305 do the same.
- Probe (laptop, real module from the laptop primary at main 984deac17, `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-ws-handler-guard-20261103/probe.mjs`): built a terminal control frame of 262,182 bytes (4x the 65,536 cap) with `createTerminalWsControlFrame`; `readTerminalWsControlFrame` accepted and parsed it in full (`d` length 262,144) — nothing in the handler path rejects an over-cap frame.

## Why it matters

These are authenticated local-server surfaces, but the fleet's own standard — set three times already (#1082, #1249, #1371) — is that a stated frame cap must hold on both runtimes. Right now the dictation (512 KiB), terminal (64 KiB) and guest-surface (256 KiB) caps are fiction under Bun: a buggy or hostile client can make the server assemble and JSON-parse frames up to the 100 MiB `ws` default, repeatedly, on a live connection.

## Acceptance criteria

- Each of the three handlers checks the assembled frame's byte length against its existing cap before parsing, and closes with 1009 on excess — mirroring event-stream/runtime.js:115-124.
- Tests for each server: an over-cap frame under a non-enforcing transport (the #1371/#1394 test approach) is refused with 1009 and not parsed; at-cap frames still work.
- DOCUMENTATION notes for the three surfaces state the cap is enforced handler-side, as the sibling docs do.

title: fix(web): walkthrough GitHub patch cap is judged after Octokit buffers the whole diff — 50 MiB limit bounds the response, not the read (PR #1271)

labels.name: kind/security
labels.description: Security issue or security hardening

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/pr-diff-review
labels.description: Filed by the pr-diff-review job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/m
labels.description: Medium: expected under 1 day of work

body:
## Finding

PR #1271 (fixing #1267) added the 50 MiB `MAX_PATCH_BYTES` cap to walkthrough pull-request patch reads, but on the GitHub path the cap is judged **after** the body has already been buffered whole — so it bounds the size of the patch the route *returns*, not the memory the server *spends* reading it. This is the same "judge before buffering" defect class this repo has filed and fixed elsewhere (e.g. #1275, guest binary editor: "judge the cap before buffering the file").

Found by pr-diff-review while reviewing PR #1271 (merge commit verified via the pulls API; code below verified on current main via contents-API read, 2026-11-03).

## Evidence

`packages/web/server/lib/walkthrough/pull-request.js` — `readGitHubPullRequestDiff` (current main):

```js
const response = await octokit.request('GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{pull_number}', {
  owner: target.owner,
  repo: target.repo,
  pull_number: number,
  mediaType: { format: 'diff' },
});

assert.match(response.data, /^(?:diff --git |\s*$)/, 'GitHub returned an invalid pull request diff');
if (Buffer.byteLength(response.data) > MAX_PATCH_BYTES) {
  throw Object.assign(new Error('This pull request diff is too large to show'), { statusCode: 413, code: 'patch-too-large' });
}
```

- Octokit's diff media type returns the entire diff as one string in `response.data`. By the time `Buffer.byteLength(response.data)` runs, the whole body is already a single in-memory string (plus whatever copies Octokit/fetch made producing it). A diff of any size — hundreds of MiB from a large or adversarial PR on a connected account — is fully buffered before the 413 can fire.
- The PR's own test pins only the return/reject contract with a mocked `request` resolving an already-materialized string; nothing bounds the read itself.
- The GitLab sibling in the same PR (`changeRequestPatch` in `packages/web/server/lib/gitlab/resources.js`) is better but related: it counts `pieces` incrementally and rejects before the final `join('')`, yet `pieces` is `files.map(gitPatchForDiff)` — every file diff is already materialized in the array before counting starts, so peak memory is likewise not bounded by the cap, only the joined result is.

## Why it matters

#1267 was filed because this read "had no total byte bound" while sibling readers cap at 5 MiB; the walkthrough route runs in the shared OpenChamber server, so one oversized PR diff can spike server RSS exactly as the unbounded read could before — the cap merely converts the outcome from a huge successful response into a huge transient allocation followed by a 413. The fix should judge size **during** the read (streamed bounded read of the diff endpoint, aborting past 50 MiB), the way the repo's shared `readBoundedResponseText` primitive already does for other upstream bodies.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The GitHub walkthrough diff read enforces `MAX_PATCH_BYTES` while the body arrives (declared `Content-Length` refused up front when present; streamed read cancelled as soon as accumulated bytes cross the cap) — an over-cap diff is never held whole in memory.
- [ ] The existing contract is preserved: at-cap diffs return byte-identically; over-cap rejects with `statusCode 413`, code `patch-too-large`; the leading `diff --git ` shape assertion still applies to accepted diffs.
- [ ] A regression test proves the read stops early: e.g. a streamed body whose later chunks are never pulled once the cap is crossed (in the style of PR #1266's bounded catalog tests), not only a mock that resolves a whole string.
- [ ] GitLab `changeRequestPatch`: either the same during-read accounting is applied to the `allDiffs` collection (reject as soon as the running total crosses the cap, without first materializing every piece), or the issue documents why its collection read is already bounded upstream.
- [ ] Existing walkthrough and GitLab resource tests pass.

1. **`.github/workflows/jules-daily-upstream-sync.yml`** — the daily upstream sync is dead, and its failure escalation is dead with it.
   - `:48` `uses: developing-today/code/.github/actions/pm-dispatch-start@main`
   - `:109` and `:118` `uses: developing-today/code/.github/actions/pm-dispatch-queue@main`
   - These are the *exact two actions already vendored* by PR #1447 — the local copies exist at `.github/actions/pm-dispatch-start` and `.github/actions/pm-dispatch-queue`, and this workflow's first step is already `actions/checkout`, so the local-action precondition is met.
2. **`.github/workflows/oc-review.yml`** — the best-effort CI-failure dispatch never dispatches.
   - `:137` `uses: developing-today/code/.github/actions/pm-dispatch-ci-fix@main` (the `ci-fix` job, `needs: [type-check, lint, tests, build]`, `if: failure()`)
   - `pm-dispatch-ci-fix` was not vendored by PR #1447. The step's `continue-on-error: true` cannot help: the failure happens in the job's **Set up job** phase, before any step exists to continue past. The `ci-fix` job also has no checkout step, which a local action requires (PR #1447 added one to `pm-dispatch-smoke.yml` for exactly this reason).

Out of scope: `agents.yml:55` calls `developing-today/code/.github/workflows/pm-scheduled.yml@main` as a **reusable workflow** — a different mechanism from a step-level action reference; this issue does not claim it is affected.

## Evidence (verified 2026-11-03, main `ecbf3bc12c76`)

- Jules scheduled run **41633212191** (2026-11-03T12:08Z, `event=schedule`, head `ecbf3bc12` = current main): job `daily-upstream-sync` fails at step 1, **Set up job**. Log:
  - `Download action repository 'developing-today/code@main' (SHA:4372e613d67850fda459f3c7c9a5c65bced50947)`
  - `##[error]Could not find file '/home/runner/work/_actions/_temp_.../_staging/code-4372e613d67850fda459f3c7c9a5c65bced50947/archive'.`
  - The Nov 2 runs (41490307676, 41489543257) failed the same way. Because the job never starts, the workflow's own `failure()` steps that would queue a tracker follow-up (themselves remote-action references) never run either — the sync fails silently.
- oc-review run **41631545897** (2026-11-03T11:56Z): jobs lint/type-check/build succeed, tests fail, and the **`ci-fix` job fails at Set up job** with the identical error:
  - `Download action repository 'developing-today/code@main' (SHA:d1628b4beeec26a0aa55286d748206e7d71a2f6b)`
  - `##[error]Could not find file '/home/runner/work/_actions/_temp_.../_staging/code-d1628b4beeec26a0aa55286d748206e7d71a2f6b/archive'.`
  - Run 41611390668 shows the same `ci-fix` Set up job failure shape. So on every red main-tier run, the pm-dispatch ci-fix task is never queued.
- Precedent in-repo: `main-broken.yml:211-212` already inlined its pm-dispatch call for this exact reason ("the watcher used to call pm-dispatch-queue from developing-today/code at main, which failed…"), and `opencode-update.yml:272/:304` + `pm-dispatch-smoke.yml:39` now use the vendored local actions with the comment "the whole-repo action download fails in runner setup".

## Why it matters

- The daily upstream sync (the fork's upstream intake, including feature-opportunity triage) has not run since the remote references began failing, and its built-in failure escalation is unreachable, so nothing files or queues a tracker when it dies.
- Every failing `oc-review` run is supposed to hand the failure to a pm-dispatch ci-fix task (code#2672); that handoff silently never happens, so main-tier failures rely on someone noticing the red run manually.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `jules-daily-upstream-sync.yml` references no `developing-today/code` action: the dispatch step uses `./.github/actions/pm-dispatch-start` and both failure-queue steps use `./.github/actions/pm-dispatch-queue`.
- [ ] `oc-review.yml`'s `ci-fix` job references no `developing-today/code` action: `pm-dispatch-ci-fix` is vendored byte-identical from `developing-today/code` at a recorded SHA (provenance header, following PR #1447's pattern) with a checkout step added to the job, or the dispatch is inlined like `main-broken.yml`.
- [ ] A `workflow_dispatch` run of `jules-daily-upstream-sync` gets past Set up job and reaches the dispatch step; an `oc-review` run with a failing main-tier job shows the `ci-fix` job starting its steps (not failing in Set up job).
- [ ] No remaining step-level `uses: developing-today/code/.github/actions/...` references in `.github/workflows/` (`grep` clean); the `workflow-audit` coverage is extended or a note records why this class is now checked.

Related: #805 (origin of the vendoring fix, PR #1447), #1446 (workflow-audit permissions gap — different defect in the same audit surface).

body:
## Finding

The size-gate batch capped the WRITE side wherever it capped a read for
config files (PR #1155 web / #1248 VS Code: serialized result checked before
writing), shared project config (PR #1252: both writers refuse over-cap),
snippets (PR #1148: write side refuses past the cap) and behavior AGENTS.md
(PR #1159: save measures UTF-8 bytes against the same cap). Three file kinds
from the same batch got read gates with NO write-side cap, so OpenChamber's
own editors can create a file that OpenChamber then refuses to ever read
back — the file is stranded: every later GET returns the too-large error
and every later PUT fails at its pre-read of the existing file. Only
delete (which does not read) still works.

Verified on current main `91ce18e74f0e5501d6c5fd44d227ac60d896824b`
(contents-API reads, 2026-11-03):

### 1. Plugin files — 1 MiB read cap, uncapped writes (web + VS Code)

- Web read gate: `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/plugins.js:21`
  `MAX_PLUGIN_FILE_BYTES = 1024 * 1024`, enforced in `readPluginDirFile`
  (`:429-432`, bounded read, `PLUGIN_FILE_TOO_LARGE`). Landed by PR #1152.
- Web write: `plugins.js:450-460` `writePluginDirFile` writes
  `file?.content ?? ''` with no size check. Callers:
  `plugin-routes.js:308` (POST create) and `:331` (PUT — pre-reads the
  existing file through the capped reader, then writes `req.body?.content`
  uncapped).
- VS Code read gate: `packages/vscode/src/opencodeConfig.ts:1527` (cap),
  `:1529-1541` `readPluginDirFile`. Landed by PR #1251 (this review batch).
- VS Code write: `opencodeConfig.ts:1543-1557` `writePluginDirFile` writes
  `file.content` with no size check. Callers:
  `packages/vscode/src/bridge-config-runtime.ts:607` (POST) and `:620`
  (PUT, same pre-read-then-uncapped-write shape).

### 2. Skill supporting files — 1 MiB read cap, uncapped writes (web + VS Code)

- Web read gate: `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/shared.js:1167`
  `readSkillSupportingFile` (cap `SKILL_SUPPORTING_FILE_MAX_BYTES`,
  coded `skill_supporting_file_too_large`; GET route maps it to 413 in
  `skill-routes.js:725`). Landed by PRs #1139/#1147.
- Web write: `shared.js:1227` `writeSkillSupportingFile` writes `content`
  with no size check; called from the PUT route at `skill-routes.js:814`
  (the route PR #1246 touched in this batch for the wildcard-path fix).
- VS Code read gate: `packages/vscode/src/opencodeConfig.ts:3487` (cap),
  `:3495-3527` `readSkillSupportingFile` (fd-based cap+1 read). Landed by
  PR #1160 (this review batch).
- VS Code write: `opencodeConfig.ts:3529-3533` `writeSkillSupportingFile`
  writes `content` with no size check.

### 3. Agent/command/skill/snippet markdown — 4 MiB parse cap, uncapped writes (web + VS Code)

- Web parse gate: `MD_FILE_MAX_BYTES` in `shared.js` (PR #1145);
  VS Code parse gate: `parseMdFile` in `opencodeConfig.ts` (PR #1212,
  this review batch).
- Writes: web `shared.js:207` `writeMdFile` and VS Code
  `opencodeConfig.ts:2112` `writeMdFile` build and write the full content
  with no byte check, so an editor save over 4 MiB produces a markdown
  file the parser then refuses (`ERR_MD_FILE_TOO_LARGE` / web twin).

## Why it matters

The read gates exist so a hostile or accidental oversized file is never
buffered whole. A write path that bypasses the same cap defeats the
protection in the worst direction: the oversized file is created BY
OpenChamber, through its normal UI flow (paste a large plugin, skill
script, or agent prompt), and from then on the UI cannot display or edit
it again — the user must find and fix the file outside OpenChamber. The
sibling fixes in the same batch (#1155, #1248, #1252, #1148) all treated
exactly this stranding shape as in-scope and fixed it in-PR; these three
kinds were missed.

Related, not this issue: open #1410 tracks the read-side stat-then-read
growth gap at some of these same sites (design #1254 phase 3); this issue
is only the write side.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Plugin file create/update refuses content over
  `MAX_PLUGIN_FILE_BYTES` (UTF-8 bytes) with the existing
  `PLUGIN_FILE_TOO_LARGE` error shape, on BOTH the web routes
  (`plugins.js` / `plugin-routes.js`) and the VS Code bridge
  (`opencodeConfig.ts` / `bridge-config-runtime.ts`); a refused write
  leaves the existing file byte-identical.
- [ ] Skill supporting-file PUT refuses content over
  `SKILL_SUPPORTING_FILE_MAX_BYTES` with the existing too-large error
  shape (web 413; VS Code bridge `{ success: false, error }`), on both
  surfaces; a refused write leaves the existing file byte-identical.
- [ ] Markdown writes through `writeMdFile` (web + VS Code) refuse a
  serialized result over `MD_FILE_MAX_BYTES` with the existing
  too-large coded error; a refused write leaves the existing file
  byte-identical.
- [ ] Regression tests per surface: over-cap write refused + file
  unchanged; exactly-at-cap write succeeds and reads back
  byte-identically (mirroring the at-cap pins the read gates already
  carry, e.g. PR #1251's POST-at-cap test).

Found by pr-diff-review lane B reviewing PRs #1160, #1212, #1246, #1251
(and the web read gates #1139/#1145/#1147/#1152 they pair with).

body:
## Problem

After #1419/#1423 (reference-detail review/thread/commit totals) and #1418 (GraphQL check `contexts`), two GraphQL connections in `packages/web/server/lib/github/reference-search.js` still truncate silently — they request no `totalCount` and return no truncation signal, unlike every sibling connection in the same queries:

- **Labels (search + lookup):** `COMMON_FIELDS` at :101 requests `labels(first: 6) { nodes { name color } }` with no `totalCount`. The schema at :223 likewise carries only `nodes`, and `toReference` (:369) maps those nodes straight into the result's `labels` — there is no `labelTotal` or truncation key anywhere in the returned reference. This fragment feeds both the reference search (`SEARCH_QUERY`) and the by-number lookup (`buildLookupQuery`), so picker rows and previews present a partial label set as the complete one.
- **Review requests (detail):** `DETAIL_QUERY` at :162 requests `reviewRequests(first: 30)` with no `totalCount`; `fetchReferenceDetail` maps the nodes to `pull.reviewers` (:475) with no total alongside it — while the same result object does carry `commentTotal`, `commitTotal`, `reviewTotal` and `threadTotal` (:470, :495, :499–:500) for its other capped connections.

## Verified behavior (this run, main `516f00c65`)

- **Live GitHub evidence for labels:** this repo's own issue #1414 carries **10 labels**. The exact query shape used at :101 — `labels(first: 6) { totalCount nodes { name } }` run against the live API — returns `totalCount: 10` but only 6 nodes (`kind/bug`, `task/small-fix`, `status/parked`, `source/creator`, `priority/normal`, `queue/parked`); `app/web`, `area/integrations`, `effort/s` and the remaining label never reach OpenChamber. Fleet-filed issues routinely carry 8–10 labels (kind/source/queue/task/status/priority/app/effort), so this truncation hits the repo's own issues by default, not as an edge case.
- **Laptop probe against the real module** (`~/git/fleet/probe-oc-reference-labels-20261103/probe.mjs`; laptop blob `c03c0c5fe1` identical to `origin/main`): feeding `toReference` a node shaped exactly as `labels(first: 6)` returns it returns 6 labels and **no label/truncation key** on the result; capturing the `DETAIL_QUERY` string passed to a mock `octokit.graphql` confirms `reviewRequests(first: 30)` carries no `totalCount`.

A user reading a reference preview cannot tell that labels are missing — the missing ones are often the informative ones (priority, app, effort) — and a PR with more than 30 pending review requests shows an incomplete reviewer list with no sign anything was dropped.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `labels` requests `totalCount` in `COMMON_FIELDS`; the reference result surfaces it (e.g. `labelTotal`) next to `labels`, in the server payload and the shared UI type, so a total above the returned count is visible (the picker/preview shows a "+N more" style indication or equivalent).
- [ ] `reviewRequests` requests `totalCount` in `DETAIL_QUERY`; the detail result surfaces it (e.g. `reviewRequestTotal` on `pull`) alongside `reviewers`, following the `reviewTotal`/`threadTotal` pattern already in the same return object.
- [ ] Schemas (`commonSchema` labels, `detailSchema` reviewRequests) require the new totals, so a response without them fails loudly instead of silently reading as complete.
- [ ] Tests in `reference-search.test.js`: a node with a label total above the returned nodes surfaces the total; a detail payload with a review-request total above 30 surfaces it; at/under-cap payloads are unchanged.
- [ ] Existing github reference-search tests pass.

## Not this issue

- #1418 / PR #1424: GraphQL check `contexts(first: 100)` in the summaries and this file's detail query — different connection, already tracked and in flight.
- #1419 (closed, PR #1423): reviews / review threads / thread replies totals in this same detail query — done; this issue is the two connections that fix left behind.
- #1377 (closed): the board pickers' REST/GitLab label and reviewer lists — different endpoints.

body:
## Finding

PR #1396 ("ci: add timeout-minutes to jobs that lacked one", merged 2026-11-02 as 89c070b7f) put `timeout-minutes` on four **reusable-workflow caller jobs** — jobs whose definition is `uses:` at job level. GitHub allows only a fixed keyword list on a caller job (`name`, `uses`, `with`, `secrets`, `strategy`, `needs`, `if`, `concurrency`, `permissions`); `timeout-minutes` is not in it, so **the whole workflow file is invalid** and every run fails at startup with zero jobs.

This is a recurrence of #118 (closed 2026-10-19), where PR #116 made the exact same mistake on `release.yml`'s mobile-release caller job and the fix removed the line. PR #1396 reintroduced the same placement in `release.yml` and added three more.

## Evidence (all on main 89c070b7ff27c7c76e47a9949202979761f1daa8)

Invalid placements — `uses:` job + `timeout-minutes`:

- `.github/workflows/agents.yml:56` — job `scheduled`, `uses: developing-today/code/.github/workflows/pm-scheduled.yml@main`, `timeout-minutes: 60` (commit bbae58b2f)
- `.github/workflows/mobile-release.yml:88` — job `require-main-gate`, `uses: ./.github/workflows/require-main-gate.yml`, `timeout-minutes: 5` (commit 22bf60744)
- `.github/workflows/release.yml:59` — job `require-main-gate`, `uses: ./.github/workflows/require-main-gate.yml`, `timeout-minutes: 5` (commit acb84dee6)
- `.github/workflows/release.yml:643` — job `mobile-release`, `uses: ./.github/workflows/mobile-release.yml`, `timeout-minutes: 60` (commit acb84dee6; the same caller job #118 was filed over)

Observed behavior:

- `agents.yml` and `mobile-release.yml` trigger on push, and every push since the merge produces a failed run named by file path (GitHub's invalid-workflow symptom) with **zero jobs**: e.g. runs 41567065540 and 41567067034 at 2026-11-03T02:35Z, plus 41567043812 / 41567044851 / 41567030425 minutes earlier. `gh api .../actions/runs/41567065540/jobs` returns 0 jobs. Already tracked as symptoms in #1397 and #1398 — this issue is the root cause for both.
- Control group from the same PR: the other five files got `timeout-minutes` only on ordinary `runs-on` jobs, and they are healthy on the same head — `oc-review.yml` run 415684... pr checks and `require-main-gate.yml` run 41567083737 both **succeeded** on 89c070b7f.
- `release.yml` has not run since 2026-10-21 (its triggers are tag pushes / dispatch), so its two invalid placements are **latent**: the next release attempt will fail before any job starts — the worst possible time to discover it, and exactly the impact #118 documented.

The caps also never had their intended effect on caller jobs: hang protection for the callees already lives in the callee jobs themselves (e.g. `mobile-release.yml`: require-main-gate is the callee `require-main-gate.yml`'s own job at 5 min; android-release 90, ios-testflight 90; `require-main-gate.yml`'s job carries its own valid 5-minute cap added by the same PR).

## Why it matters

Two workflows are down on every push right now (the scheduled-agents dispatcher and the mobile-release gate chain), and the release workflow is silently broken until the next release. This class has now recurred twice (#116 → #118, #1396 → here), so the fix needs a recurrence guard, not just four deleted lines.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `timeout-minutes` is removed from all four caller jobs listed above; the valid caps PR #1396 added to `runs-on` jobs stay.
- [ ] A push to main no longer creates failed zero-job runs for `agents.yml` / `mobile-release.yml` (closes the root cause of #1397 and #1398).
- [ ] A YAML audit of every workflow confirms no job-level `uses:` job carries a keyword outside GitHub's allowed caller-job list.
- [ ] A recurrence guard lands: a lightweight workflow-file validation step (e.g. actionlint or an equivalent audit script) runs in CI on workflow changes, so an invalid caller job fails a PR check instead of merging and breaking main.
- [ ] `release.yml` validity is verified explicitly (e.g. `gh workflow view` / a dispatch dry-run starts jobs), since it has no push-to-main trigger to prove it.

title: design(web): walk it bounded, or not at all — one traversal-budget contract for directory walks over trees the server does not control

labels.name: task/triage

labels.name: effort/m
labels.description: Medium: expected under 1 day of work

labels.name: meta/enriched

labels.name: source/design-architect
