## Finding

PR #1633 added the Mistral quota provider on the server (`packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/mistral.js`, registered in `providers/index.js`), but the UI quota board can never show it: Mistral was not registered on the UI side.

Evidence (verified on current main `8f61a0fd3f98` via `gh api` contents reads, this run):

- `packages/ui/src/types/quota.ts` — the `QuotaProviderId` union lists 29 ids (`openai`, `codex`, `command-code`, …, `opendesign`, `xai`); `mistral` is not among them.
- `packages/ui/src/lib/quota/providers/index.ts` — the `QUOTA_PROVIDERS` catalog lists every other server provider (including the other recent adds `xai`, `zenmux`, `opendesign`, `kilo`, `neuralwatt`, `hyper`); `mistral` is absent.
- `packages/ui/src/stores/useQuotaStore.ts:71,145` — the board fetches exactly `QUOTA_PROVIDERS.map(p => p.id)` (`allProviderIds`, and `fetchQuotas(QUOTA_PROVIDERS…) on load), and `fetchQuota(providerId: QuotaProviderId)` is typed against the union — so `/api/quota/mistral` is never requested from the UI and a result could not be typed if it were.

This defeats the stated purpose of the provider: `mistral.js`'s own header says the `usageAvailability: 'console-only'` marker exists "so the board renders 'tracked, console-only' instead of missing data" — but on the board, Mistral is still missing data. Issue #1619 (CLOSED by PR #1633) scoped its ask to the server quota module; the UI registration is the unfiled remainder. (The VS Code surface, `packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.ts`, also has no mistral case, but that surface already omits the web providers `command-code` and `opendesign`, so web-only is an existing precedent there — the UI catalog has no such precedent: every other server provider is present.)

Related minor point for triage to judge: even once fetched, the UI's `fetchQuota` zod schema (`packages/ui/src/lib/quota/fetchQuota.ts`) models `usage` as `{ windows, models? }` only, so the `usageAvailability` marker would be stripped on parse; rendering the "console-only" state may need that field (or an equivalent) carried through.

## Why it matters

The fleet holds a live Mistral credential and #1619 closed the "Mistral is invisible to the quota system" gap on the server side only. Anyone reading quota state in the OpenChamber UI still cannot see Mistral's key-validity state (valid vs invalid/revoked), which is the one signal this provider class exists to surface.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `mistral` is added to the `QuotaProviderId` union in `packages/ui/src/types/quota.ts` and to `QUOTA_PROVIDERS` in `packages/ui/src/lib/quota/providers/index.ts` (name "Mistral AI", matching the server's `providerName`).
- [ ] The quota board fetches and displays the Mistral result: a valid key shows as tracked/console-only (no fabricated usage figures), an invalid key shows the unauthorized state — i.e. the `usageAvailability: 'console-only'` signal survives the UI fetch/parse path or an equivalent representation is used.

body:
## Summary

The two managed cloudflare tunnel starters forward cloudflared's stderr to the server log with a per-chunk `chunk.toString('utf8')`. A multi-byte UTF-8 character split across two pipe chunks is corrupted into U+FFFD replacement characters in the forwarded log. The quick tunnel in the same file and the ngrok tunnel both forward the bounded accumulator's `decoded` text (StringDecoder-backed), so they do not corrupt split characters — the managed starters are the residual twin.

## Evidence (main 8f61a0fd3f9849606a6d976b824431f2bd82ce36)

- `packages/web/server/lib/cloudflare-tunnel.js:591-594` — `startCloudflareManagedRemoteTunnel`: `child.stderr.on('data', (chunk) => { const text = chunk.toString('utf8'); process.stderr.write(text); })` (toString at :592).
- `packages/web/server/lib/cloudflare-tunnel.js:681-684` — `startCloudflareManagedLocalTunnel`: identical per-chunk decode-and-forward (toString at :682).
- Contrast, same file: quick tunnel forwards `decoded` from `createBoundedOutputAccumulator` (:488), whose decoder is a `StringDecoder` (:31-53). `packages/web/server/lib/ngrok-tunnel.js:423` also writes the accumulator's `decoded`.
- The classification path is not affected: `waitForManagedTunnelReady` reads the same streams through its own StringDecoder accumulators, so ready/fatal detection is correct — only the forwarded operator log is corrupted.

## Reproduction (laptop probe vs the real module, x2 identical)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-cf-passthrough-20261106/probe.mjs` — a fake `cloudflared` on PATH (the same harness shape as `cloudflare-tunnel.test.js`) prints `ERR tunnel log: caf<🔥> and <€> done` to stderr with the 4-byte emoji split 2/2 and the 3-byte € split 1/2 across chunks 150 ms apart, then a ready line; `process.stderr.write` is captured while the real `startCloudflareManagedRemoteTunnel` / `startCloudflareManagedLocalTunnel` run.

- Control (same text in one chunk): forwarded intact — emoji and € present, 0 replacement characters, both starters.
- Split: forwarded as `caf��� and ��� done` — both characters lost, 6 U+FFFD, both starters. Identical on the repeat run.

## Why it matters

The managed tunnels' forwarded stderr is the operator's log for tunnel startup and runtime failures; cloudflared log lines containing non-ASCII text (paths, hostnames, localized OS errors) arrive garbled exactly where an operator reads them to diagnose a failed tunnel. Every other tunnel/output surface in this tree was moved to decoder-safe forwarding (#1542, #1567, #1699 and the accumulator extraction tracked in #1705); these two handlers were left behind because they forward instead of capturing.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Both managed starters forward a multi-byte character split across stderr pipe chunks intact (no U+FFFD) — either by writing the raw chunk bytes to `process.stderr` or by forwarding through a StringDecoder / the shared bounded accumulator like the quick tunnel.
- [ ] Regression tests in `cloudflare-tunnel.test.js` drive both managed starters with a fake cloudflared whose stderr splits a multi-byte character across chunks and assert the forwarded output is intact; the unsplit control stays intact.
- [ ] No change to ready/fatal classification, startup settlement, token-file handling, or the quick tunnel's behavior.

## Dedup

Searched open and recently closed issues for cloudflare/cloudflared decode, passthrough and stderr findings: #1542 (per-chunk matching, closed), #1699 (accumulator flush, closed), #1705 (accumulator extraction refactor, open) and #1731 (managed-local config stat read, open) cover neighbouring ground; none names the managed starters' stderr forwarding handlers at :591/:681. The guests twin #1696 is a different module (captured diagnostic, not a forward).

body:
## Problem

In `packages/web/server/lib/cloudflare-tunnel.js`, the managed-local cloudflared config is size-checked by stat and then read **by path, whole, synchronously**:

- `cloudflare-tunnel.js:191` — `MANAGED_LOCAL_CONFIG_MAX_BYTES = 256 * 1024`
- `cloudflare-tunnel.js:203-247` — `assertReadableFile` judges the path with `fs.statSync`: `isFile()` and `stats.size > MANAGED_LOCAL_CONFIG_MAX_BYTES` are the only gates
- `cloudflare-tunnel.js:248-255` — `extractHostnameFromCloudflaredConfigDetailed` then does `fs.readFileSync(configPath, 'utf8')` with no further check, and parses the result as YAML
- Call sites: `inspectManagedLocalCloudflareConfig` (:309) and `startCloudflareManagedLocalTunnel` (:657) both run assert-then-extract

Anything that changes the file between the stat and the read defeats the 256 KiB cap:

1. **Grown after stat** — the read buffers and parses the whole file however large it now is.
2. **Swapped for a FIFO after stat** — `fs.readFileSync` on a FIFO blocks forever, and because this read is **synchronous**, it freezes the entire server event loop (not just one request) until the process is killed.

Same defect class as #1730 / #1684 / #1685 / #1659 (cap judged on a pre-read stat, read by path afterwards); this is the sync variant, so the wedge takes the whole process. The fix shape those issues use — open once, judge regular-file and size from the handle, enforce the cap in flight (the shared `readBoundedFileSync` in `lib/shared/bounded-file-read.js`) — applies here unchanged, since this call path is already synchronous.

## Evidence (laptop probe vs the real module, ×2 identical)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-cf-config-stat-20261106/probe.mjs` on the laptop, against the real exported `inspectManagedLocalCloudflareConfig` from the laptop primary at main `8f61a0fd3`. The probe interposes deterministically on the shared `fs` object (the module calls `fs.statSync` at call time) so the swap lands exactly between the module's own `assertReadableFile` stat and its own `readFileSync`; everything else runs the module's real code.

- Control (105-byte config, hostname `small.example.com`): `ok=true, resolvedHostname=small.example.com`
- Grown-after-stat (stat saw the 105-byte file; the read got a 307,306-byte config — past the 262,144-byte cap — whose ingress hostname is `big.example.com`): `ok=true, resolvedHostname=big.example.com` — the over-cap file was read and parsed whole; its hostname won.
- FIFO-after-stat: the call never returned; the probe process had to be killed by the outer 30 s timeout inside the sync read.

## Why it matters

The config path is user-selected (a file picker / settings value pointing at a cloudflared config on disk), and the inspect path runs when the UI merely displays tunnel state. A config file being rewritten by another tool at that moment silently bypasses the stated 256 KiB cap, and a path that has become a FIFO (or is swapped for one) hangs the whole OpenChamber server — every session, not just the tunnel page — with no error and no recovery short of a restart.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The managed-local config read is bounded: the file is opened once, regular-file judged from the handle, and `MANAGED_LOCAL_CONFIG_MAX_BYTES` enforced in flight (stop at cap+1) — e.g. via the shared bounded sync reader — instead of stat-by-path then readFileSync-by-path.
- [ ] A file grown past the cap between the former stat point and the read fails exactly as an over-cap file does today (the existing "file is too large (max … bytes)" refusal), never parsed whole.
- [ ] A non-regular file (FIFO/device/socket) at the config path refuses promptly with the existing not-a-file style error; the call returns and the event loop never blocks.
- [ ] Behavior for ordinary configs is unchanged: valid .yml/.yaml/.json configs resolve their ingress hostname as today, empty/missing/unreadable files keep their current errors, and both call sites (`inspectManagedLocalCloudflareConfig`, `startCloudflareManagedLocalTunnel`) get the fixed behavior.
- [ ] Regression tests (in the existing cloudflare tunnel test suite) cover the grown-after-stat and FIFO-swap cases plus the unchanged control.

body:
## Problem

`snapshotSshPrivateKey` in
`packages/web/server/lib/git/credential-resolver.js` judges the SSH
private key file carefully — but only after an open that can block
forever on a non-regular file:

- `credential-resolver.js:231` opens the (realpath-resolved) key path
  with `fsImpl.open(sourcePath, O_RDONLY | O_NOFOLLOW)` — no
  `O_NONBLOCK`. On POSIX, opening a FIFO with `O_RDONLY` blocks until
  a writer appears.
- The regular-file and size judgement sits immediately behind that
  open: `:232-236` stats the handle and refuses
  `!stats.isFile() || size < 1 || size > MAX_SSH_PRIVATE_KEY_BYTES`
  (128 KiB, :12). For a FIFO the open never returns, so the
  `isFile()` refusal is unreachable — the exact shape filed as #1701
  for the post-checkout hook inspection in `git/service.js`.
- Nothing upstream rescues it: the `deadline` the function accepts
  governs only the later `ssh-keygen` executions (`runFile`, :149);
  a blocked `fs.open` is not abortable and never reaches them. The
  callers — `verifiedSshKey` (:317, git credential resolution) and
  `inspectManagedSshCredential` (:345, managed SSH inventory) — await
  the snapshot directly, so a FIFO at a registered key path wedges
  the credential operation with no error and no timeout.

The house standard exists in the same server:
`lib/shared/bounded-file-read.js:36` opens with
`O_RDONLY | O_NONBLOCK` (POSIX) precisely so open() itself cannot
block on a FIFO, then judges regular-file from the handle — the same
judge this function already performs, one step too late.

Code-verified sibling for triage to disposition:
`git/credentials.js:35` `copyVerifiedSnapshot` opens the snapshot
file with the same flags (no `O_NONBLOCK`) and reads it whole with
no size check (:39). Its exposure is smaller — the snapshot lives in
the server's own `0700` snapshot root and is created from a source
already capped at 128 KiB — but the open shape is identical.

## Why it matters

The key path is user-registered state: a managed SSH credential
points at a path on the person's machine, and that path can be
replaced (a broken provisioning script, a swapped mount, a stray
`mkfifo`, a malicious checkout hook racing the credential flow).
Today the failure mode for "the key path is not a regular file" is
supposed to be the coded `SSH_KEY_NOT_PRIVATE` refusal the function
already implements — instead a FIFO makes the operation hang
silently, holding a libuv thread and stalling the git operation
that asked for credentials, with none of the deadline machinery
able to fire.

## Evidence (this run, laptop probe against the real module)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-ssh-key-fifo-20261106/probe.mjs` on the
laptop, plain `node`, importing the real `snapshotSshPrivateKey`
from the laptop primary at origin/main
`2e8e652071a79ee4409a71e5610627d4364f7bf4`, with an injected fake
`execute` for the `ssh-keygen` steps and real `fs/promises`. Run
twice, identical results:

- Control: a small key file with a valid private-key marker settled
  — the snapshot was created and the derived fingerprint returned
  (`CONTROL_SETTLED fingerprint=SHA256:AAA…`, exit 0, ×2).
- FIFO: with the key path replaced by a FIFO, the call never
  settled (timeout exit 124, ×2) — it hung at the open, before the
  `:232` stat could refuse it.

Code-verified ×2 on the same main: no `O_NONBLOCK` anywhere in
`credential-resolver.js`; `credential-resolver.test.js` and
`credentials.test.js` contain no FIFO or non-regular case.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The key-file open in `snapshotSshPrivateKey` cannot block on
      a non-regular file (e.g. `O_NONBLOCK` on POSIX added to the
      existing `O_RDONLY | O_NOFOLLOW` open), so the existing
      handle-stat judgement at :232-236 actually runs for a FIFO.
- [ ] A FIFO at the key path rejects promptly with the function's
      existing coded refusal for a non-key file
      (`SSH_KEY_NOT_PRIVATE` / `SSH_KEY_UNREADABLE` family), never a
      hang; the 128 KiB cap, marker check, mode check, identity
      checks, and snapshot semantics are unchanged for regular
      files.
- [ ] Triage dispositions the `credentials.js:35`
      `copyVerifiedSnapshot` open (same flags): fix it the same way
      or record why the server-owned snapshot root makes it safe.
- [ ] Regression tests pin a FIFO at the key path rejecting
      promptly (they hang on pre-fix code), mirroring the FIFO
      cases elsewhere in the git suites; the existing
      credential-resolver and credentials suites stay green.

body:
## Problem

The project-context plan readers enforce their 1 MiB cap in flight, but
they never judge that the path is a regular file, and they open it in a
way that blocks on a FIFO before any read happens:

- `packages/web/server/lib/project-context/plan-progress.js:34-52` —
  `readBoundedUtf8` opens with a plain `fsPromises.open(filePath, 'r')`
  (:39) and reads into a fixed `maxBytes + 1` buffer. The in-flight cap
  is sound, but the open carries no `O_NONBLOCK` and neither the reader
  nor its callers ever check `isFile()`. On POSIX, opening a FIFO with
  `O_RDONLY` blocks until a writer appears, so the read never starts.
- Its callers judge only the size from a stat by path:
  `plan-progress.js:109-133` `summaryOf` stats (:113), refuses
  `stat.size > PLAN_FILE_READ_MAX_BYTES` (:128), then calls
  `readBoundedUtf8` (:133) — a FIFO stats as size 0 and passes.
  `runtime.js:788-808` `readPlanFile` does the same (:796 size check,
  :801 read) for `readPlan` and the update/move paths (:391, :402,
  :823, :837, :873, :1122).
- The listing path reaches it for every plan file:
  `runtime.js:510` (every `.md` in the shared plans folder) and
  `runtime.js:537` call `summaryOf` per plan, so one FIFO stalls the
  whole plan list, not one plan.

The house standard exists in the same server:
`lib/shared/bounded-file-read.js:36` opens with
`O_RDONLY | O_NONBLOCK` (POSIX) precisely so "open() itself cannot
block on a FIFO" (header, :10-12) and judges regular-file from the
opened handle. The sibling context store in this very package is
already on it — `runtime.test.js:264` pins "a FIFO at the context path
fails as malformed without blocking". The plan reader is a private
spelling left over from #1133, which capped the whole-buffering but
never covered the open/regular-file half of the contract (its body
mentions neither FIFO nor regular-file).

Plan files are exactly the surface this matters on: shared plans live
in the team's own repository folder (`<repo>/<plansDir>/*.md`,
`.openchamber/plans` by default) where, per
`project-context/DOCUMENTATION.md`, "any tool may write there" — the
server does not control what kind of filesystem entry a plan path is.

## Why it matters

A FIFO (or any non-regular entry) named like a plan in the shared
plans folder hangs plan listing and plan reads forever: the open
never settles, so there is no error to surface and no per-plan
degradation — the "one unreadable plan never fails the list" contract
in `DOCUMENTATION.md` is defeated by a hang, not an exception. The
same swap can happen between the callers' stat-by-path and the open,
so even a path that statted as a regular file can block. Every other
state-file family in the server has been moved onto the
bound-and-judge contract (#1655); this reader enforces only the bound
half.

## Evidence (this run, laptop probe against the real module)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-plan-progress-fifo-20261106/probe.mjs` on
the laptop, plain `node`, importing the real
`createPlanSummaryCache` / `readBoundedUtf8` from the laptop primary
at origin/main `2e8e652071a79ee4409a71e5610627d4364f7bf4`, with real
`fs/promises` pointed at a scratch dir. Run twice, identical results:

- Control: a normal plan file settled — `summaryOf` returned
  `{ title: "My Plan", progress: { done: 1, total: 2 } }`.
- FIFO via the list path: with the plan path replaced by a FIFO,
  `summaryOf` never settled (timeout exit 124, ×2).
- FIFO via the reader directly: `readBoundedUtf8` on the FIFO never
  settled (timeout exit 124, ×2).

Code-verified ×2 on the same main: `plan-progress.js:39` is the only
open in the reader and has no flags argument; no `isFile` /
`O_NONBLOCK` appears anywhere in `plan-progress.js` or in the
`readPlanFile` / `summaryOf` stat blocks; `plan-progress.test.js` has
no FIFO or non-regular case (its grows-after-stat case at :134-138
uses a fake fs).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `readBoundedUtf8` (or its replacement) opens a plan file so a
      non-regular file is refused promptly without blocking at open
      (e.g. `O_NONBLOCK` on POSIX + regular-file judged from the
      opened handle, as in `lib/shared/bounded-file-read.js`), while
      the existing 1 MiB in-flight cap and its `null`-on-over-cap
      result are unchanged.
- [ ] A FIFO at a plan path makes `summaryOf` settle with the same
      outcome as an unreadable plan today (the list completes; that
      plan carries no progress) and makes `readPlanFile` / `readPlan`
      settle promptly with their existing missing/unreadable outcome —
      never a hang.
- [ ] Normal and over-cap plan files behave byte-for-byte as today,
      including the stat-cache behaviour in `summaryOf` and the 413
      shape in `readPlanFile`.
- [ ] Regression tests pin a FIFO at a plan path for both the summary
      path and the readPlan path returning promptly (they hang on
      pre-fix code), mirroring the existing context-path FIFO test at
      `runtime.test.js:264`; the existing project-context suites stay
      green.

open/regular-file residual), #1655 (the bound-and-judge contract),
#1607 (this package's context store, already on the bounded reader).

body:
## Problem

The OpenChamber CLI's own state-file readers (`packages/web/bin/lib/`) read their files **whole, synchronously, with no size gate and no regular-file check** — the server-side gated-read family (design #1655 and its filings) never reached the separate `bin/cli.js` process. A FIFO at any of these paths hangs the CLI command forever (synchronous `readFileSync` on a FIFO blocks until a writer appears), and an oversized file is buffered and parsed whole instead of being refused.

Evidence (main `3f503e7096d894ead21048aa74608ff8aa71e294`, read in the laptop primary):

- `packages/web/bin/lib/cli-paths.js:26` — `readDesktopLocalPortFromSettings` does `fs.readFileSync(getSettingsFilePath(), 'utf8')` on `settings.json`; `:40` — `readDesktopLocalClientTokenFromSettings` reads the same credential-bearing file whole again; `:72` — `readTunnelCliState` reads `tunnel-cli-state.json` whole. No stat, no cap, no regular-file check in any of the three.
- `packages/web/bin/lib/cli-tunnel-profiles.js:220` — `readTunnelProfilesFromDisk` does `fs.readFileSync(filePath, 'utf8')` on `tunnel-profiles.json`, which stores tunnel **tokens**; `:254` — `readLegacyManagedRemoteEntries` reads the legacy `cloudflare-managed-remote-tunnels.json` whole the same way. Both swallow all errors into an empty result, so the defect is invisible until it hangs or OOMs. The same file shows the house standard exists in miniature: the token-file reader at `:79-90` stats first, requires `isFile()`, and refuses over `MAX_TOKEN_FILE_BYTES` (8 KiB, `:10`) — but even it judges the cap only on the pre-read stat.
- `packages/web/bin/lib/cli-process.js:16` — `readPidFile` reads the pid file whole; `:48` — `readInstanceOptions` reads the per-instance JSON (which can carry `uiPassword`, written at `:60`) whole.
- `packages/web/bin/lib/cli-log-files.js:41` — `readTailLines` does `fs.readFileSync(filePath, 'utf8')` on the **whole log file** and only then slices the last N lines (`:46`). Its purpose is a tail; the read is the opposite of one. Log rotation (`LOG_ROTATE_MAX_BYTES` = 10 MiB, `:4`) runs only at serve startup (`commands-serve.js:126`), so a log written by a long-running or external process is read at whatever size it has reached when `openchamber logs` runs (`commands-logs.js:50,63`).
- The gated reader already exists and is already imported from `bin/`: `packages/web/server/lib/shared/bounded-file-read.js:124` exports `readBoundedFileSync` (opens with `O_NONBLOCK` on POSIX so open itself cannot block on a FIFO, judges regular-file and cap from the handle, enforces the cap during the read), and `bin/lib/commands-quota.js:3` / `bin/cli.js:76` already import from `../../server/lib/shared/` and `../server/lib/`.
- Callers hang with no deadline of their own: `bin/cli.js:34,472` uses the settings port reader during serve/startup resolution, `commands-status.js:40`, `commands-connect-url.js:149`, `commands-lifecycle.js:318,533` and `commands-update.js:119` use `readInstanceOptions`, the tunnel commands go through `ensureTunnelProfilesMigrated` → the two profile readers, and `commands-logs.js` uses `readTailLines`.

Dedup: the #1655 inventory (#1656, closed) and every gated-read filing since (#1649, #1651, #1653, #1692 and neighbours) cover `packages/web/server/lib/**` readers; title/keyword searches for `cli-log`, `cli-tunnel`, `cli-paths`, `cli-process`, `tunnel-profiles`, `managed-process-registry`, `mcpx-daemon`, `ui-passkeys` across open and closed issues return no filing for any `packages/web/bin/**` reader. #1692 is the server-side managed-tunnel store, not the CLI's profile store.

## Verification

Laptop probe against the **real exported functions** (`readDesktopLocalPortFromSettings`, `readDesktopLocalClientTokenFromSettings`, `ensureTunnelProfilesMigrated`, `readInstanceOptions`, `readTailLines` imported from the laptop primary; `OPENCHAMBER_DATA_DIR` pointed at a fresh temp dir per case; probe: laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-cli-readers-20261106/probe.mjs`), run ×2 with identical results:

- **Control** — regular `settings.json` / `tunnel-profiles.json` / instance file / log: settled; port = 4096, token length = 6, profiles = 1, instance port = 1234, tail = `line497,line498,line499`.
- **Oversized** — 32 MiB `settings.json` (valid JSON, port at the end): **settled, port = 4096 in ~51 ms** — parsed whole, no gate refused it. 32 MiB `tunnel-profiles.json` with one valid profile: settled, profiles = 1 — same.
- **FIFO (all four paths)** — `settings.json`, `tunnel-profiles.json`, the instance file, and the log file each replaced by a FIFO: the call **never settled**; the 4 s `timeout` killed the process (exit 124) in both runs, for every path. No writer ever opens the FIFO, and there is no regular-file check that could refuse it first.

## Why it matters

These are the readers every `openchamber` CLI command starts through: serve startup resolves the desktop port and client token from `settings.json`, tunnel commands load token-bearing profiles, status/connect/lifecycle/update read instance files, and `openchamber logs` tails the log. A FIFO or device planted or left at any of these well-known paths (data dir is shared with the server, other tools, and sync/backup software) wedges the CLI command indefinitely with no error, and a bloated or hostile file is buffered whole in a short-lived process the user is waiting on. The server side of the same data dir was hardened file by file under #1655; the CLI half of the same contract is still open.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every reader named above routes through a bounded, regular-file-judged read (the shared `readBoundedFileSync` from `server/lib/shared/bounded-file-read.js`, or an equivalent bin-local helper with the same semantics): non-regular files (FIFO/device/socket) are refused promptly without blocking at open, and the byte cap is enforced during the read, not only on a pre-read stat.
- [ ] Caps are explicit constants sized to each file's real shape (settings / tunnel-cli-state / tunnel profiles / legacy remote entries / pid / instance files are all small JSON — 1 MiB or tighter; the token-file reader's existing 8 KiB precedent stands), and an over-cap file produces each caller's existing missing/empty behaviour (`null` / `''` / `{}` / empty profiles), never a throw that changes CLI behaviour.
- [ ] `readTailLines` no longer buffers the whole log to return a tail: it reads a bounded tail window (e.g. from the end of the file via a handle) so a multi-hundred-MiB log returns its last N lines without a whole-file read; behaviour for small logs, missing files, and a final unterminated line is unchanged.
- [ ] Existing semantics preserved: missing file → same defaults as today; malformed JSON → same defaults; valid files parse identically (port, client token, profiles + legacy migration, instance options, pid).
- [ ] New regression tests (in `packages/web/bin/lib/cli-settings-accessors.test.js`, `packages/web/bin/cli.test.js`, or a new `cli-log-files` test): (a) a FIFO at the settings path settles promptly with the default, (b) an over-cap settings/profiles file yields the default instead of parsing, (c) `readTailLines` on a large log returns the correct tail; each new test fails (or, for the FIFO case, hangs) on the pre-fix code.
- [ ] Existing bin test suites pass (`cli.test.js`, `cli-settings-accessors.test.js`, `cli-startup.test.js`).

body:
## Problem

`collectProcessOutput` in `packages/web/server/lib/guests/service.js` decodes guest-service child output per pipe chunk, so a multi-byte UTF-8 character split across two chunks is corrupted in the only startup-failure diagnostic the user sees.

Evidence (main `8e6a1b73bdef3e8123af4851f0d80546cac80897`):

- `service.js:380` — `collectProcessOutput(child, maxChars = 2_000)` accumulates the spawned guest service's stdout/stderr.
- `service.js:384` — `const text = typeof chunk === 'string' ? chunk : chunk.toString('utf8');` decodes each chunk independently; a character split across chunks becomes one U+FFFD per orphan byte.
- `service.js:391-392` — both `child.stdout` and `child.stderr` feed this append.
- `service.js:486` — `startGuestService` attaches the collector at spawn; `service.js:518` takes `output.snapshot()` when the service never becomes ready, and `service.js:520-525` throws it inside `GuestServiceError` (`SERVICE_FAILED`): `Guest service failed to become ready. <detail>`. That message is the whole diagnosis a user gets for a guest service that crashes on startup.

## Reproduction (verified this run, laptop probe vs the real module, x2 identical)

Probe drove the real `proxyGuestServiceRequest` / `startGuestService` with a fixture guest package whose entry writes to stderr and exits 1 without listening (probe: laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-guest-output-20261106/probe.mjs`):

- Split write — entry writes byte `0xE2`, waits 250 ms, then writes `0x82 0xAC` + ` boom\n` (the € sign split across pipe chunks): the thrown error was
  `Guest service failed to become ready. ��� boom`
- Control — the same € written in a single write: the thrown error was
  `Guest service failed to become ready. € boom`

Both runs reproduced identically on a second execution.

## Why it matters

Guest services are third-party extension code; when one fails to start, its stderr is usually the only clue (a missing dependency, a bad path, a localised error message). Non-ASCII output — localised OS/tool messages, paths with accented characters, currency symbols — is exactly the output most likely to be mangled, and the corruption is silent: the message still looks plausible, just with `�` where the character was. Sibling collectors in this repo already do this correctly: `guests/clone.js` buffers chunks and decodes `Buffer.concat(...)` once, and the tunnel accumulators (`cloudflare-tunnel.js`, `ngrok-tunnel.js`) plus the content-search stdout path use `StringDecoder`. This collector is the remaining per-chunk spelling in the guests package.

Related filings in the same class, other modules: #1690 (content-search stderr), #1695 (dictation tar stderr), #1567 (fs/exec runners, closed).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `collectProcessOutput` decodes each stream through a `StringDecoder` (or buffers raw chunks and decodes once), so a multi-byte character split across any chunk boundary survives intact in `snapshot()`.
- [ ] Any decoder remainder is flushed before the snapshot is taken, so a final unterminated character is not dropped.
- [ ] The 2,000-char tail bound still applies to the decoded text, and the existing stdout/stderr merge order in `snapshot()` is unchanged.
- [ ] A regression test in `packages/web/server/lib/guests/service.test.js` (or a sibling test file) drives a failing guest service whose stderr writes a multi-byte character split across two chunks and asserts the `SERVICE_FAILED` message contains the intact character; the test fails on the pre-fix code.
- [ ] Existing guest service tests pass.

body:
## Bug

`extractTarArchive` in `packages/web/server/lib/dictation/local/model-downloader.js` accumulates the spawned `tar` process's stderr by decoding each pipe chunk independently:

```js
// model-downloader.js:215-218 (main 8e6a1b73b)
child.stderr.on('data', (chunk) => {
  // Only the tail matters for the message; keep memory bounded.
  stderr = (stderr + chunk.toString()).slice(-4096);
});
```

`chunk.toString()` decodes one chunk in isolation, so a multi-byte UTF-8 character split across two pipe chunks is replaced by U+FFFD replacement characters in both halves. The accumulated string is the only diagnostic the user ever sees for a failed extraction: on `close` it is passed to `describeTarFailure(code, stderr)` (:234), which picks the last line as the error message (:179-186). tar's diagnostics quote the offending archive member name, so a model archive containing a non-ASCII filename produces a corrupted, unsearchable error message exactly when the user needs the real name. The trailing `.slice(-4096)` can additionally cut a surrogate pair in half, leaving a lone surrogate in the stored tail.

This is the same per-chunk decode defect already confirmed and fixed/tracked in sibling spawn consumers (#1567 fs/exec runners, #1690 content-search stderr, #1691 dev-server scanner, #1542/#1546 tunnel output) — this consumer was missed. The mechanism is a language-level certainty (Buffer#toString on a partial UTF-8 sequence yields U+FFFD) and was probe-proven against the real modules in those sibling filings; this run verified it by code inspection against current main because the laptop probe host was unreachable (see below).

## Why it is not covered today

`model-downloader.test.js` tests `describeTarFailure` as a pure function with whole-string stderr inputs (:126-136), but `extractTarArchive` is not exported and its `spawn` is not injected, so the chunk-accumulation path has no test seam: no test can feed stderr in split chunks, and a regression (or this bug) is invisible to the suite.

## Evidence

- `packages/web/server/lib/dictation/local/model-downloader.js:215-218` — per-chunk `chunk.toString()` accumulation with char-based tail slice.
- `packages/web/server/lib/dictation/local/model-downloader.js:223-235` — accumulated stderr is the sole input to the failure message on non-zero exit.
- `packages/web/server/lib/dictation/local/model-downloader.js:179-186` — `describeTarFailure` surfaces the last stderr line verbatim to the user.
- `packages/web/server/lib/dictation/local/model-downloader.test.js:126-136` — existing tests cover only the pure `describeTarFailure` function, never the chunked accumulation.
- Verified on main `8e6a1b73bdef3e8123af4851f0d80546cac80897` via `gh api` raw reads, twice (file read + targeted re-read of lines 173-238). Dedup: title/keyword search over open and closed issues for model-downloader / dictation / tar stderr / chunk decode — no existing issue covers this consumer (nearest: #943 closed, tar timeout; #1690/#1691 open, different modules).
- Note: no laptop probe was run this run — the laptop was unreachable via both the laptop-agent proxy and real SSH; the finding rests on code verification plus the established, probe-proven mechanism from #1567/#1690. Triage may want a split-chunk probe against the real module as its first step.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] tar stderr is decoded with a streaming decoder (`StringDecoder` from `node:string_decoder`, flushed at close) so a multi-byte character split across chunks survives intact in the failure message — mirroring the fixed sibling consumers.
- [ ] The 4096-character tail bound still holds (memory stays bounded; slicing does not split a surrogate pair, or the bound is applied after decode on the flushed string).
- [ ] The bzip2 classification in `describeTarFailure` and the timeout/kill behavior of `extractTarArchive` are unchanged.
- [ ] A regression test feeds stderr in chunks split inside a multi-byte character (e.g. a non-ASCII member name in the final line) and asserts the surfaced message contains the intact character — which requires a test seam for the accumulation (export or spawn injection), following the fake-spawn harness pattern used for #1690's fix.

body:
## Finding (unaddressed PR review comment)

PR #1548 (`fix(web): extract the ngrok URL from complete lines, never a per-chunk fragment (#1546)`, merged 2026-11-04) reworked ngrok output handling in `packages/web/server/lib/ngrok-tunnel.js` to accumulate stdout/stderr into bounded line accumulators, flushing a final unterminated line only when each stream emits `end`.

CodeRabbit's review on that PR raised a follow-up finding that nothing has addressed since:

> **A final unterminated stderr line is added to `recentOutput` only on stream `end`. If the child's `exit` event runs first, `onExit` builds its error from `recentOutput` before that line is flushed.**
>
> The startup error can omit the diagnostic that explains the failure.
>
> This can occur when: Ngrok writes its only useful error message without a trailing newline and exits.

(CodeRabbit filed this as a Minor / Potential issue / Low value follow-up in its review body. It is filed here because it is a concrete, validated defect — a startup-failure diagnostic can be lost to an event-ordering race — not as a style nit.)

## Evidence

- Source PR: https://github.com/developing-today-forks/openchamber/pull/1548 (merged 2026-11-04T08:00:36Z)
- Source review: https://github.com/developing-today-forks/openchamber/pull/1548#pullrequestreview-5764531227 — reviewer `coderabbitai[bot]`, submitted 2026-11-04T07:05:52Z, follow-up finding at `packages/web/server/lib/ngrok-tunnel.js:425-426`
- No-response evidence: the PR's only inline review thread (CodeRabbit's over-cap pending-line finding, discussion r4464651442) was dispositioned by dezren39 (r4465080061, accepted tradeoff) and withdrawn by CodeRabbit (r4465083489); that thread is resolved. No comment, review, or commit on the PR addresses this review-body follow-up finding about the stderr flush / `exit` ordering, and the PR merged at 2026-11-04T08:00:36Z, before any response to it. Codex review on the PR head (`3b12ef7`) completed with `has_any_findings=false`.
- Still live on current main (verified 2026-11-06 by fresh `gh api` raw reads, main `8e6a1b73bdef3e8123af4851f0d80546cac80897`):
  - `packages/web/server/lib/ngrok-tunnel.js:425-427` — `child.stderr.on('end', ...)` is the only place `stderrAccumulator.flush()` is captured into `recentOutput`.
  - `packages/web/server/lib/ngrok-tunnel.js:463-465` — `onExit` builds the startup error from `recentOutput` without flushing either accumulator first. A child process `exit` event can fire before its stdio streams emit `end`, so an unterminated final stderr line held in the accumulator can be missing from the error.
- Dedupe: searched open and closed issues by file path (`ngrok-tunnel`), PR number (#1548), and keywords (`ngrok`, `recentOutput`, unterminated). No issue covers this race. Related but distinct: issue #1546 (closed; the chunk-split URL defect PR #1548 fixed) and issue #1687 (open; per-chunk decoding corruption in managed OpenCode startup output, different code).

## Acceptance criteria

- `onExit` (and any other path that builds a startup error from `recentOutput`) flushes the stderr accumulator — and the stdout accumulator if it can hold diagnostic lines — into `recentOutput` before building the error, without double-capturing lines when the stream `end` handlers run afterwards; or resolve this issue by a documented decision that the possible diagnostic loss is accepted, with the reasoning recorded here.
- A regression test covers an ngrok child that writes its only diagnostic without a trailing newline and exits, asserting the startup error includes that line even when `exit` is delivered before the stderr stream ends.

body:
## Summary

The legacy migration in `packages/web/server/lib/tunnels/managed-config.js` reads the legacy named-tunnels file whole with no size gate, no regular-file check, and no in-flight cap — inside the serialized persist lock — even though the managed store it migrates into reads through the bounded durable-store primitive.

## Evidence (main `8e6a1b73bdef`)

- `managed-config.js:176` (in `migrateManagedRemoteTunnelConfigFromLegacyFileLocked`): `const legacyRaw = await fsPromises.readFile(CLOUDFLARE_LEGACY_NAMED_TUNNELS_FILE_PATH, 'utf8');` — the whole file is buffered and `JSON.parse`d, with no stat, no cap, and no non-regular refusal.
- The migration runs under the persist lock: `migrateManagedRemoteTunnelConfigFromLegacyFile` is `enqueuePersistLock(migrateLockedOrEmpty)` (`managed-config.js:204-206`), and it is reached from the ordinary read path `readManagedRemoteTunnelConfigFromDisk` whenever the managed file is missing (`:209-216`) — i.e. on first run / after a preserve-aside, exactly when a legacy file is present.
- The legacy file holds tunnel **tokens** (sanitized at `:36-65`: id/name/hostname/token), so it is credential-bearing, and it is this server's own previous store format — not a foreign program's file. The #1656 inventory (`lib/shared/DOCUMENTATION.md`, "foreign read-only files" row) excepted it as a "one-shot legacy migration source"; the managed half of the same module was migrated to `readDurableJsonFile` (#978/#1649 discipline: handle-judged, cap enforced in flight, non-regular refused), but the legacy read was left ungated.
- Callers on hot paths: `resolveManagedRemoteTunnelToken` (`:381`) and the preset sync / upsert paths all pass through `readManagedRemoteTunnelConfigFromDisk` or the same persist lock.

## Reproduction (laptop probe vs the real `createManagedTunnelConfigRuntime`, run twice, identical)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-managed-config-legacy-20261105/probe.mjs` (laptop), using the module's own injected `fsPromises`/`constants` seam (the same seam its test suite uses).

- Control: a small legacy file migrates normally (`ids=ctl`).
- Oversized: a legacy file of 33,554,535 bytes (one tunnel whose token is a 33,554,432-char pad) was read whole, parsed whole, and migrated — the returned config carried the full 33,554,432-char token and the managed file was written at 33,554,609 bytes. No cap exists at any point.
- FIFO: with the legacy path a FIFO and the managed file missing, `readManagedRemoteTunnelConfigFromDisk()` never settled within 3 s — and a second call queued behind the persist lock never settled either (both runs; the probe process had to be killed, exit 124). One FIFO at the legacy path therefore wedges every later tunnel-config read/update that touches the lock, not just the migration.

## Why it matters

- Unbounded memory: a grown/corrupt legacy token file is buffered and parsed whole on a normal read path.
- Availability: a non-regular file at the legacy path wedges the serialized persist lock, hanging all managed tunnel config operations (token resolution for tunnel startup included) until restart.
- Inconsistent with the house contract (design #1655): every sibling store read is bound-and-judged; this one was excepted in the #1656 inventory only as a legacy source, but it sits on the live read path behind a lock.

## Acceptance criteria

- The legacy migration read is bounded: open once, judge from the handle (regular file), enforce a named byte cap in flight (cap + 1), in the style of `readBoundedFile` / the durable-store reader. A defensible cap should be stated with its derivation (the managed store's own bound is a natural reference).
- Over-cap or non-regular legacy file: migration degrades exactly as a missing/unreadable legacy file does today (empty config, warning, no write over anything, no token content in logs) — and never wedges the persist lock: a subsequent read/update settles promptly.
- Normal legacy migration behavior is unchanged (existing `managed-config.test.js` legacy tests pass).
- New tests cover: over-cap legacy file, FIFO/non-regular legacy file (settles promptly, lock usable afterwards), and the valid migration control.
- The #1656 inventory row for the legacy named-tunnels file is updated to match the new disposition.

body:
## Summary

In the web server's ripgrep content search, the child's **stdout** is decoded with a `StringDecoder` — but its **stderr** is decoded per pipe chunk and its 64 KiB cap is judged in string characters while slicing bytes. Two consequences, both verified against the real module this run:

1. A multi-byte character split across two stderr chunks is corrupted to U+FFFD replacement characters in the user-facing failure message.
2. The `STDERR_MAX_BYTES` cap (64 KiB, named in bytes) is not a byte cap: accumulated stderr reached **120,045 bytes** in the probe — ~1.8× the cap, up to ~3× for text dominated by 3-byte characters.

## Evidence (main `8e6a1b73bdef3e8123af4851f0d80546cac80897`)

- `packages/web/server/lib/fs/content-search.js:27` — `const STDERR_MAX_BYTES = 64 * 1024;`
- `packages/web/server/lib/fs/content-search.js:179` + `:255` — stdout uses `new StringDecoder('utf8')` (`stdoutDecoder.write(chunk)`), so split multi-byte sequences on stdout survive.
- `packages/web/server/lib/fs/content-search.js:268` — stderr does neither:

  ```js
  if (stderr.length < STDERR_MAX_BYTES) stderr += chunk.toString('utf8', 0, STDERR_MAX_BYTES - stderr.length);
  ```

  `stderr.length` counts UTF-16 code units; `Buffer.toString`'s `end` argument is a **byte** offset. The budget is therefore spent in chars against byte slices, and a chunk boundary inside a multi-byte sequence decodes each half independently.
- The accumulated `stderr` is user-facing: `:286` classifies via `INVALID_PATTERN_PATTERN` (`/regex parse error|error parsing|unrecognized escape/i`), and `:286-289` surface `failureMessage(stderr, …)` (`:110`) as the `invalid-pattern` / `failed` message returned to the client.

### Probe (laptop, real `createContentSearchRuntime`, injected fake spawn; run twice, identical)

- **Control** — stderr in one chunk (`rg: regex parse error: … error: unclosed group`, exit 2): `{status:"invalid-pattern", message:"unclosed group"}` ✓
- **Split €** — same stderr with the 3-byte `€` in `error: unclosed € group` split 1 byte / 2 bytes across chunks: `{status:"invalid-pattern", message:"unclosed ��� group"}` — the character is destroyed (three U+FFFD), never recovered.
- **Cap** — one stderr line of 40,000 `€` (120,000 bytes) fed in 8 KiB chunks, exit 2: result message was **40,015 chars / 120,045 bytes** against the 65,536-byte cap.

Probe: laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-content-search-stderr-20261105/probe.mjs`; outputs saved in the fleet creator evidence dir `creator-2026-11-05-2150-cst/`.

## Why it matters

- The failure message is what a user sees when a content search fails (bad pattern, unreadable tree, ripgrep error). Non-ASCII text in ripgrep's explanation — a file path, a pattern echo, a localized message — comes back mojibake exactly when the pipe happens to chunk mid-character; pipe chunking is not under the caller's control, so this is nondeterministic corruption.
- The stderr drain exists (per the comment at `:266`) so an unread pipe cannot block ripgrep forever, and its cap is the memory bound for that drain. A cap that silently admits ~2–3× its named byte size on non-ASCII output is a bound that isn't one — the same class this repo has been closing on its other readers.
- The fix pattern is already in the same function: stdout's `StringDecoder` plus byte-counted accumulation (`pendingBytes` via `Buffer.byteLength`, `:238-246`).

## Acceptance criteria

- stderr is decoded through a `StringDecoder` (flushed at close), so a multi-byte character split across any chunk boundary round-trips exactly; add a regression test splitting a multi-byte character in the error line across two stderr chunks (the existing fake-spawn harness in `content-search.test.js` supports chunked stdio) asserting the exact message.
- The stderr cap is enforced in **bytes**: accumulated stderr never exceeds `STDERR_MAX_BYTES` bytes (accounting by chunk byte length / `Buffer.byteLength`, with any truncation landing on a character boundary), verified by a test feeding >64 KiB of multi-byte stderr and asserting the surfaced message's byte length stays within the cap.
- Existing behavior is preserved: single-chunk ASCII stderr, `invalid-pattern` classification and message selection (`failureMessage`), and the drain-to-end semantics (stderr is always consumed so ripgrep cannot block) are unchanged; the existing `content-search.test.js` suite passes.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for `content-search`, `ripgrep stderr`, and `invalid-pattern`: #1283 (closed) covered the **stdout line** byte cap; the closed per-chunk decode fixes (#1336, #1553, #1567, #1577, #1590) and open #1687 cover other files/streams. No issue covers this module's stderr handler.

body:
## Summary

Found by the #1656 phase-2 inventory audit (design #1655) on main `8cc23ba52d`. `packages/web/server/lib/guests/storage.js` `runGuestStorage` (:40) judges its size gate on a **stat by path, then reads by path**: `stat.size > GUEST_STORAGE_TOTAL_BYTES` is checked, then `await fs.readFile(file, 'utf8')` buffers whatever the path names at read time — a file grown (or swapped) between the two is buffered whole, the exact pre-read-stat pattern #1605 tracks for the fs routes / VS Code bridge, in miniature for guest extension storage documents (`guest-storage/<id>.json`).

## Both halves (design #1655 rule 2)

- **Bound:** flawed, not absent — the cap value is right (the store's own write-side total-bytes clamp) but it is judged on the path stat, not on the handle / in flight, and a non-regular file is not refused before the read.
- **Disposition:** malformed or schema-invalid content throws out of the lock (never silently read as empty for the write path); missing → empty entries. No preserve-aside.

## Ask

Judge the same `GUEST_STORAGE_TOTAL_BYTES` cap from the opened handle and enforce it in flight (cap+1, non-regular refused), keeping the lock, disposition, and write-side clamps unchanged. No behaviour change for any file at or under the cap.

Filed only because no open issue covers either half for this store (#1620 covered the guest extension/auth stores, not this per-extension storage document reader) — see the inventory table on #1656.

🤖 Filed by repo-worker-openchamber, queue task 10775 (audit #1656).

## Acceptance criteria

- `runGuestStorage` judges its byte cap on the opened handle / in-flight read, not on a pre-read path stat: a file grown or swapped between stat and read cannot be buffered beyond the cap.
- Non-regular files are refused before the read.
- Tests cover the grow-between-stat-and-read case and the oversized-file case.

body:
## Problem

`packages/web/server/lib/tracked-items/persistence.js` — `createTrackedItemsPersistence(...).load()` reads the store's own state file with a plain unbounded read:

- `persistence.js:20`: `raw = await fs.readFile(filePath, 'utf8')` — no byte cap, no regular-file check, then `JSON.parse(raw)` at `:25` and the parsed records are kept whole (each record's `state` is carried through as-is at `:30`).

The file (`tracked-items.json` in the OpenChamber data dir) is wired in at `feature-routes-runtime.js:556` and loaded on the tracked-items service's restore path (`service.js`, `restored`/`ready()`): a FIFO (or any non-regular file) at that path makes `load()` never settle, so the service's `ready()` never resolves; an oversized file is buffered and parsed entire in memory before any shape check can reject it.

The legit file is small and self-bounded: the service caps its in-memory entries at `MAX_ENTRIES = 500` (`service.js:35`) and `save()` only ever writes those entries, so a real file is a few hundred small records. Nothing the writer produces needs an unbounded reader. This is the same ungated-reader class the shared bounded reader (`lib/shared/bounded-file-read.js`) exists to prevent, and the module's own header already promises the right failure semantics: "a missing, unreadable or malformed file restores nothing" — an over-cap or non-regular file should land in that same restores-nothing outcome, promptly.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe vs the real module, x2 identical)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-tracked-items-20261105/probe.mjs` on the laptop, importing the real `createTrackedItemsPersistence` from main `b1f25606a`:

1. Control: a small valid `tracked-items.json` (one Linear item, small `state`) → `load()` returned 1 item with its state intact.
2. Oversize: a schema-valid file whose record `state` carries a 33,554,432-character pad → `load()` returned the item with `state.pad` length **33,554,432** — the whole file was buffered and parsed, no rejection at any size.
3. FIFO: `tracked-items.json` replaced by a FIFO → `load()` **never settled** within 3 s (both runs), so the restore/`ready()` path hangs indefinitely.

## Why it matters

- Startup-adjacent hang: the tracked-items surface's restore promise never resolves if the file is a FIFO or is swapped for one; presence/refresh state silently never restores.
- Memory: a corrupted or externally-inflated file (disk fault, another writer, a restored backup gone wrong) is parsed whole — the reader trusts disk size completely, unlike every sibling store that has been moved to the bounded reader.
- The fix shape is house-standard: read through the shared bounded reader with a named cap sized from the writer's own bound (500 entries), and map over-cap / non-regular to the module's documented restores-nothing outcome (missing → `[]`; unreadable must not throw the restore path into its warn-and-continue with a hang).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `load()` reads `tracked-items.json` through the shared bounded reader (or an equivalent gated read) under a named byte cap justified from the writer's bound (500 entries), never buffering an over-cap file whole.
- [ ] A FIFO / non-regular file at the path is refused promptly: `load()` settles (restores nothing) instead of never settling, and the service's `ready()` resolves.
- [ ] Missing file still returns `[]`; malformed JSON still restores nothing; a valid at-cap file restores its items exactly as today.
- [ ] Regression tests: oversize valid file restores nothing (or the triage-chosen documented outcome) without parsing the pad whole; FIFO path settles promptly; control file unchanged.

body:
## Problem

`packages/web/server/lib/message-queue/runtime.js` — `enqueue()` treats the 20-item per-session cap two different ways depending on the kind of item being added:

- A **scheduled** item added to a full queue is refused: the pre-check at `runtime.js:842` throws `409 message queue is full`.
- An **ordinary** item added to a full queue is accepted — and the oldest item in the queue silently disappears. The append is `[...items, item].slice(-MAX_ITEMS_PER_SESSION)` at `runtime.js:852`, so the head item is dropped with no error to the caller, no log, and no broadcast distinction. The enqueue resolves successfully with the new `itemId`, so the UI believes the queue holds everything the user queued.

The dropped head is not always an ordinary message. If the head is a **scheduled-task item**, `setQueueItems` (`runtime.js:463-465`) sees it vanish from the list and reports it to the scheduled-task owner as `cancelled` — so a user queueing one ordinary follow-up message in a busy session silently **cancels a scheduled task** that was waiting at the head of that session's queue.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe vs the real module, x2 identical)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-mq-overflow-20261105/probe.mjs` on the laptop, importing `createMessageQueueRuntime` from main `b1f25606a`, dispatch held off (`dispatchQuietMs` large):

1. Enqueue 1 scheduled item (`proj-1`/`task-1`) + 19 ordinary items → snapshot holds 20, head is the scheduled item.
2. Control: enqueue another scheduled item → throws `409 "message queue is full"` (the scheduled path is guarded).
3. Enqueue a 21st **ordinary** item → resolves successfully; snapshot still holds 20 items, but the texts are now `msg-1..msg-19, msg-21` — the scheduled head is gone.
4. The `onScheduledTaskResult` callback fired with `{projectId: proj-1, taskId: task-1}, status: cancelled` — the scheduled task was reported cancelled as a side effect of an unrelated ordinary enqueue.

The same silent-drop applies to ordinary items themselves: the 22nd enqueue would drop `msg-1`, a prompt the user queued while the session was busy (the exact case this server-owned queue exists to never strand — see the module header: "closing the tab, locking the phone, or losing the connection no longer strands what was queued").

## Why it matters

- Silent data loss on a living surface: a queued user prompt vanishes while every surface reports success.
- Cross-kind interference: an ordinary composer action can cancel a scheduled task, and the scheduled-task system records a `cancelled` result for a task nobody cancelled.
- The asymmetry with the scheduled path (409) and with the session-count cap (documented oldest-session eviction in `DOCUMENTATION.md:227`) shows the per-session overflow was guarded for one caller and missed for the other. Docs state the limit ("20 items per session") but never a drop-oldest-on-add behavior.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Enqueueing an ordinary item into a session queue that already holds `MAX_ITEMS_PER_SESSION` items refuses with the same `409 message queue is full` the scheduled path uses (or another explicit, documented refusal the UI can surface) — it never silently drops an existing item.
- [ ] An ordinary enqueue can never remove a scheduled item or cause a `cancelled` scheduled-task result; the only paths that report `cancelled` remain explicit removal/clear/eviction of that item.
- [ ] Regression tests in `runtime.test.js`: (a) 21st ordinary enqueue into a full queue rejects and the original 20 items are intact and in order; (b) full queue whose head is a scheduled item — ordinary enqueue rejects and no scheduled-result callback fires.
- [ ] `DOCUMENTATION.md` limits section states the per-session overflow behavior explicitly, matching the implementation.

body:
## Design: bounded, and judged — one gated read for the server's own state files

**Status:** proposed — no maintainer decision needed (no user-facing surface, no changed default, no new control; it retires a scope exclusion two earlier designs wrote and consolidates behaviour the per-site fixes are already choosing one store at a time).
**Full design doc:** `files/designs/openchamber-state-file-gated-reads.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace.
**Extends, does not duplicate:** #976 (the server's own JSON state files — disposition and writes; its reader never had a bound, and only fifteen stores were migrated onto it) and #1254 (bounded reads for project/user files; its primitive's header explicitly excludes the server's own state files). The still-open per-site instances (#1490, #1608, #1609, #1610, #1613, #1614, #1621, #1622, #1624, #1627, #1628, #1631, #1632, #1635, #1636, #1638, #1641, #1643, #1644, #1645, #1651) are cited as evidence and **not adopted** — each is queue/queued with its own lifecycle; phase 1 adopts only #1649, which is the primitive-level fix.

### Problem in one paragraph

Two designs divided the server's file reads and left a seam, and the last two days' filings are that seam enumerated one store at a time: title search "no size gate" returns 49 issues in this repo, and the second wave — 27 filings in three days — is the server's own state files. Verified on current main `c11726d32e`: (1) the shared durable-store primitive is itself ungated — `lib/shared/durable-json-store.js` `readDurableJsonFile` (:90) / `readDurableJsonFileSync` (:103) buffer whole, no cap, no handle stat, no non-regular refusal, and the preserve path re-reads whole up to three times per attempt across 10 attempts (#1649, probe-verified: 33 MB store returns valid whole; a FIFO blocks all spellings) — one fix bounds its fifteen caller stores, several credential-bearing; (2) hand-rolled store readers invent both halves privately — the routing store's `readJsonFile` (:147) / `readJsonFileSync` (:171) in `lib/routing/store.js` reads whole *and* states its own disposition (ENOENT → null, empty → null, malformed → uncoded throw, no preserve), which is not #976's three-state answer; the per-site cap filings fix the bound half and leave each private disposition as invented; (3) per-site caps already diverge into a functional bug — #1647: the install copy judges SKILL.md against the 1 MiB supporting-file cap, so loadable 1–4 MiB skills can no longer install; the filings that get it right (#1608) derive the cap from the store's own write-side clamps, a rule that today exists only inside one issue body. #1649's body states the scope correction: the hazard "is about the path, not about who normally writes the file" — a state directory is user-writable, replaceable and symlinkable.

### The contract (summary — full rules in the design doc)

1. **Scope is the path, not the writer.** #1254's exclusion of server state files is retired; the `bounded-file-read.js` header is amended to say so.
2. **A state-file read owes two judgements:** the *bound* (#1254's mechanism — open once, judge from the handle, cap+1 enforced in flight, non-regular refused) and the *disposition* (#976's three-state answer — missing / valid / malformed-preserved; malformed never read as empty, never rewritten from an empty base). A store with only one half is unfinished.
3. **Composition, not a third primitive.** The durable store composes `bounded-file-read` internally. Over-cap is a fourth named state (`too-large`) — never missing or empty — and preserving an over-cap file renames rather than re-reads, so preserve never buffers what it preserves.
4. **Caps are derived, not copied** — stated at the read site, justified by the store's own write-side clamps (the #1608 derivation); a store with no write clamp gets a named generous cap and the missing clamp is a finding, not a silent 1 MiB default.
5. **Hand-rolled store readers are inventory, not architecture** — every remaining private store reader is dispositioned against both halves (migrated / conforming / excepted-with-reason). Per-site cap fixes that land meanwhile complete the bound half only; their store stays on the inventory until the disposition half is answered.

### Phases

- **Phase 1 (adopts open #1649, linked as a sub-issue, NOT re-enqueued):** the durable store composes the bounded read in all spellings including both preserve paths; the `too-large` fourth state; preserve-by-rename when over-cap; its fifteen caller stores inherit both halves with no call-site change.
- **Phase 2 (filed as a sub-issue):** the inventory — every remaining hand-rolled state-file reader in `packages/web/server/lib` dispositioned against both halves, the three VS Code readers (#1641/#1643/#1644) named as the mirror inventory, per-site follow-up issues filed for any store no open issue covers on both halves, the table recorded in `lib/shared/DOCUMENTATION.md`. No production behaviour changes. Modelled on #1530.
- **Phase 3 (NOT filed — open questions in the doc):** migration shape for the inventoried stores, the append-only-log answer (plan-notes #1638, replay #1632, route-feedback #1624 — a refuse-over-cap loses history; tail/window vs rotation vs named exception is open), the VS Code mirror (same question #1254's phase 3 left; stays open rather than filed twice), and a `check:changed` ratchet (re-asked after the phase-2 inventory exists to consume).

🤖 Filed by the repo-design-architect job, design pass 2026-11-05.

## Acceptance criteria
- The state-file read contract is decided: scope-by-path (rule 1), both judgements (rule 2), composition in the durable store with the `too-large` fourth state (rule 3), derived caps (rule 4) — with any exceptions named.
- Phase 1 lands as #1649 (adopted, linked as a sub-issue, its queue lifecycle untouched) and phase 2's inventory dispositions every remaining hand-rolled store reader in `packages/web/server/lib` against both halves, filing follow-ups for any store no open issue covers on both halves.
- Phase 3's four open questions (migration shape, append-only logs, VS Code mirror, ratchet) stay in the design doc as questions — none is silently filed or silently dropped.

body:
## Problem

The web server's npm registry config reader buffers the user's `.npmrc` whole, synchronously, with no size gate and no regular-file check:

- `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/npm-registry-config.js:20-37` — `configValues()` does `fs.readFileSync(configPath(), 'utf8')` (:23) and splits the whole buffer into lines. `configPath()` (:7-12) is the path named by `npm_config_userconfig` / `NPM_CONFIG_USERCONFIG`, or `~/.npmrc`. The only guard is a bare `catch {}` that returns an empty map.
- Callers: `resolveNpmRegistryRequest` (same file, :102) is called by `lib/opencode/routes.js:105` (the upgrade-status `latest` lookup for `@opencode/cli`) and `lib/opencode/npm-registry.js:111` (the packument lookup). Both run on the server's event loop, so the synchronous read blocks everything, not one request.

The house standard exists in the same server: `lib/shared/bounded-file-read.js:117` `readBoundedFileSync` (handle read, named cap + regular-file check), already adopted across the server's other local-file readers. Related but different prior work: #1040/#1006 capped the HTTP registry *response* bodies; nothing caps this local config *file* read. Closed #1289 was about a test hermetically reading the machine's config — not this production reader.

## Why it matters

`.npmrc` is a credential-bearing user file (registry `_authToken` / `_auth` entries are exactly what `authFor` in this module extracts) that legitimately runs to a few hundred bytes. Because the read is synchronous, a FIFO at the configured path — `npm_config_userconfig` is an environment variable any launching context can set — freezes the whole server event loop, not just the upgrade check. An oversized file is buffered and line-split whole on every registry resolution (upgrade status + every packument lookup). The failure mode for a bad file should be the reader's existing one — an empty config map, i.e. the default registry with no auth — reached through a bounded rejection, not unbounded buffering of a token file.

## Evidence (this run, laptop probe against the real module)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-npmrc-ungated-20261105/probe.mjs` on the laptop, plain `node`, importing the real `resolveNpmRegistryRequest` from the laptop primary at `c11726d32e12230ccd5353a85a0c852dfca3ad36`, with `npm_config_userconfig` pointed at a scratch file. Run twice, identical results:

- Control: a one-line `.npmrc` resolved normally (`RESOLVED_URL https://example.invalid/@opencode%2Fcli/latest`).
- Oversize: a 33,554,471-byte `.npmrc` (a 33,554,432-char `pad=` value ahead of the `registry=` line) was read whole and the registry after the pad still resolved (`RESOLVED_URL https://example.invalid/...`) — no rejection at any size.
- FIFO: with the configured path replaced by a FIFO, `resolveNpmRegistryRequest` never returned (timeout exit 124, ×2) — a synchronous block of the event loop.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `configValues()` reads the npm config file through the shared bounded reader (or an equivalent handle-based bounded read) under a named cap sized for a credential config file (house precedents for small config/auth files run 64 KiB–1 MiB; the exact value is the fix's documented choice).
- [ ] An over-cap or non-regular file lands in the reader's existing degradation exactly: an empty config map (default registry, no auth), indistinguishable from today's unreadable-file outcome.
- [ ] Regression tests in `npm-registry-config.test.js` pin the over-cap and FIFO/non-regular behaviour.
- [ ] No behaviour change for files within the cap: existing `npm-registry-config` tests pass, including scoped-registry and auth extraction cases.

## Finding

PR #1475 completed the per-kind sidebar row lines for #22 on desktop (List `listLines`, Chats `chatsLines`, Tree project `projectLines`) and recorded, in its own body, the one remaining gap: the phone sheet renders its Chats and Tree project rows with its own tree code, not the shared row model, so those two kinds do not follow `chatsLines`/`projectLines` on the phone (its List rows do follow `listLines`). Issue #22 was then closed as complete, with the closing note naming this as the "sole recorded remainder … a follow-up, not a blocker" — but no issue was ever filed for that follow-up, so the gap is tracked nowhere now that #22 is closed.

## Evidence

- Source PR: #1475 — https://github.com/developing-today-forks/openchamber/pull/1475 (merged 2026-11-03, merge commit `987e53c99dba7be3bc8d50e3a13049033e926a00`), body section "Recorded gap (also on #22)": "The phone sheet renders its Chats and Tree project rows with its own tree code, not the shared row model, so those two kinds do not yet follow `chatsLines`/`projectLines` on the phone. Its List rows follow `listLines`."
- #22 closed 2026-11-03T17:51:42Z; its closing agent note (queue task 7039) states: "Sole recorded remainder: the phone sheet's own Chats and Tree project rows do not yet follow `chatsLines`/`projectLines` (its List rows follow `listLines`) — recorded as a follow-up in the earlier note on this issue … It is a follow-up, not a blocker for this issue's criteria. body:
## Problem

The web server's quota auth-file readers buffer their files whole,
synchronously, with no size gate and no regular-file check:

- `packages/web/server/lib/quota/utils/auth.js:14-25` — the shared
  `readJsonFile` helper does `fs.existsSync` + `fs.readFileSync` whole
  (:19). Its callers read credential-bearing files:
  `providers/antigravity/auth.js:23` (the `antigravity-accounts.json`
  paths) and `providers/claude/auth.js:79-80` (the Claude Code
  `.credentials.json`).
- `packages/web/server/lib/quota/utils/auth.js:56-77` —
  `resolveConfigApiKey` resolves an OpenCode config `{file:path}`
  apiKey reference with `fs.readFileSync(target, 'utf8')` (:73) and
  returns the whole trimmed contents as the key. The target is any
  path the config names (absolute, `~/`, or config-dir-relative);
  its caller is the quota path at
  `providers/zhipuai-coding-plan.js:96`. A FIFO or grown file at that
  path is buffered whole / blocks the server event loop.
- Same-surface code-verified siblings: `providers/meta.js:84`
  `readMuseAccountToken` (`JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(~/.config/muse/auth.json))`)
  and `providers/cursor.js:74` `readFileToken` (token files named by
  `CURSOR_TOKEN_FILE` / `CURSOR_REFRESH_TOKEN_FILE`).

The house standard exists in the same server:
`lib/shared/bounded-file-read.js:117` `readBoundedFileSync` (handle
read, cap + regular-file check), already adopted by the sibling quota
credential store fixed under #1613. The VS Code package's twin
`readJsonFile` is tracked in #1643 — this is the web-server side.

## Why it matters

These readers run on quota polls, synchronously, on the server's event
loop. A FIFO at an accounts/credentials path — or at any file an
`opencode.json` `{file:}` apiKey reference points at — wedges every
request the server handles, not one quota read. An oversized but
well-formed file is buffered and parsed whole on every poll. These are
credential files: the failure mode should be a bounded, named
rejection landing in each reader's existing `null` degradation, not
unbounded buffering of credential material (for `resolveConfigApiKey`,
not an unbounded string handed onward as a bearer key).

## Evidence (this run, laptop probe against the real module)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-creator-20261105-0450/probe-web-quota-auth.mjs`
on the laptop, plain `node`, importing the real
`packages/web/server/lib/quota/utils/auth.js` from the laptop primary
at origin/main `c11726d32e12230ccd5353a85a0c852dfca3ad36`, with all
paths pointed at a scratch dir. Run twice, identical results:

- Control: a small accounts JSON read back normally
  (`CONTROL_READJSON tok-control`); a small `{file:}` key file
  resolved normally (`CONTROL_FILEKEY key-control`).
- Oversize: a 33,554,432-char padding field placed before the account
  block was parsed whole and the token after it still extracted
  (`OVERSIZE_READJSON_PAD_LEN 33554432`); a 33,554,432-char `{file:}`
  key file was returned whole as the apiKey
  (`OVERSIZE_FILEKEY_LEN 33554432`) — no rejection at any size.
- FIFO: with the accounts path replaced by a FIFO, `readJsonFile`
  never returned (timeout exit 124, ×2); with the `{file:}` target
  replaced by a FIFO, `resolveConfigApiKey` never returned
  (timeout exit 124, ×2).

The meta.js (:84) and cursor.js (:74) sites were verified by code read
(identical whole-buffer `readFileSync` pattern, existing catch → null).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `readJsonFile` (utils/auth.js) and the `resolveConfigApiKey`
      `{file:}` read go through a bounded, regular-file-checked read
      with a named byte cap per file, sized from each file's
      legitimate shape (accounts/credentials JSON holds a few short
      tokens; an apiKey file holds one short key).
- [ ] The meta.js `readMuseAccountToken` and cursor.js `readFileToken`
      reads get the same treatment, or an explicit disposition is
      recorded on this issue for each.
- [ ] Over-cap and non-regular files degrade exactly as a read failure
      does today per reader — `readJsonFile` → `null`,
      `resolveConfigApiKey` → `null`, token readers → `null` — and no
      path parses or returns a too-large file whole.
- [ ] Normal small files behave byte-for-byte as today, including
      Antigravity account selection, the Claude credentials parse,
      and `{file:}` / `{env:}` apiKey resolution.
- [ ] Regression tests pin an over-cap file for each reader and a FIFO
      at the accounts path and at a `{file:}` target returning
      promptly instead of blocking; the existing quota suites stay green.

## Summary

The skills-catalog persistence readers read their JSON files whole, synchronously, with no size gate and no non-regular-file rejection — unlike the shared bounded reader (`packages/web/server/lib/shared/bounded-file-read.js`, `readBoundedFileSync`) that the rest of the server has been adopting (see #1607, #1613–#1615, #1620–#1624):

- `packages/web/server/lib/skills-catalog/installed-sources.js:53` — lenient reader: `payload = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(installedSourcesPath(), 'utf8'))` in `readInstalledSources()`
- `packages/web/server/lib/skills-catalog/installed-sources.js:82` — strict reader for write paths: `raw = fs.readFileSync(installedSourcesPath(), 'utf8')` in `readInstalledSourcesForUpdate()`
- `packages/web/server/lib/skills-catalog/disk-cache.js:12` — `const raw = fs.readFileSync(filePath, 'utf8')` in `readJsonFile()`, behind `readDiskCache()` used by `cache.js:36` and `github-meta.js:42`

These files live in the OpenChamber data dir (`skills-installed-sources.json`, plus the catalog/github-meta disk-cache files). Their legitimate contents are small — provenance entries (name/source/subpath/scope per install) and cache objects — so a generous cap loses nothing.

## Verified evidence (this run, main f3f288763b0a0b4f958e34f29615e9b1961f23d6)

Laptop probe against the real modules extracted verbatim from `origin/main` (`~/git/fleet/probe-oc-skills-ungated-20261104/`, run twice, identical results):

- Control: a small valid `skills-installed-sources.json` reads back 1 entry.
- Oversize: a 33,554,504-byte valid file is parsed whole by `readInstalledSources()` (~69 ms, no rejection), and a 33,554,432+-byte cache object is parsed whole by `readDiskCache()` (~62 ms).
- FIFO: with `skills-installed-sources.json` replaced by a FIFO, the synchronous `readInstalledSources()` never returns — the probe was killed by a 3 s timeout on both runs. Because the read is synchronous, this blocks the whole server event loop, not just the catalog surface. Callers include the web skill routes (`lib/opencode/skill-routes.js:504`, `:641`) and the VS Code bridge (`packages/vscode/src/skillsCatalog.ts:711`).

## Why it matters

Any process or accident that leaves an oversized or non-regular file at one of these paths turns a routine catalog read / install-provenance write into unbounded memory use or a full event-loop freeze. Every sibling store that was migrated to the bounded reader rejects non-regular files from the handle (O_NONBLOCK open + fstat) and enforces the cap during the read; these three readers judge nothing at all.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `readInstalledSources`, `readInstalledSourcesForUpdate`, and the disk-cache reader go through the shared bounded reader (or an equivalent handle-judged bounded read) with a named, generous cap per file.
- [ ] Semantics preserved exactly: lenient reader still maps missing/malformed/too-large to an empty Map; strict reader still returns empty Map on missing, throws `MALFORMED` on malformed (and on too-large/non-regular, without overwriting the file), and propagates other I/O errors; `readDiskCache` still returns `null` on missing/malformed.
- [ ] Regression tests: oversized file and FIFO/non-regular file at each path are rejected in bounded time; existing `installed-sources.test.js` and cache tests still pass.
