body:
## Evidence

On current main (`072ba8c8e1c2db95897878554d4c544dd5294c7c`), `packages/ui/src/apps/useNativePushRegistration.ts:111-122` stores a token, awaits `getPushKey()`, then posts it with `registerApnsToken`. The async callback never checks whether the effect was disposed or notifications remain enabled.

Disabling notifications runs the separate effect at `:153-163`, which clears `lastTokenRef` and calls `unregisterApnsToken`. If the registration callback is waiting on the Android `PushKey.get()` call, the DELETE can finish first; the pending callback then sends its POST. The server's `packages/web/server/lib/notifications/routes.js:150-193` handles that POST as an upsert and DELETE as removal, and `apns-runtime.js:185-215` persists the registration. The device can therefore remain registered and receive remote pushes after the user disabled them. The registration UI is user-toggleable at `packages/ui/src/components/sections/openchamber/NotificationSettings.tsx:466-470`; `MobileApp.tsx:1416` mounts the hook for a connected native app.

The native push setup came from merged PR #386. Issue #389 only tracked that PR's merge cleanup and is closed; it does not cover this registration/disable race. All-state issue and PR searches for native push registration, disabling notifications, APNs registration, FCM tokens, push tokens, and PushKey found no tracker for this race.

## Reproduction

On Android, delay `PushKey.get()`. Trigger the native `registration` event, turn off notifications, wait for `unregisterApnsToken` to finish, then resolve `PushKey.get()`. The hook posts the token after the DELETE, leaving it in the server's registration store.

## Acceptance criteria

- A callback from an old or disabled registration lifecycle cannot start a registration POST after notifications are turned off.
- If a registration request is already in flight when the user disables notifications, the final server state is unregistered after the disable operation settles.
- Add deterministic coverage for delayed key lookup and the registration/unregistration ordering race.
- Keep registration-on-connect behavior when notifications remain enabled.

## Evidence Verified on fresh `origin/main` `072ba8c8e1c2db95897878554d4c544dd5294c7c`: - `packages/web/server/lib/markdown-image-grants/routes.js:155-175` removes fenced and inline code, but otherwise keeps each line unchanged. The image scanner at `:178-215` then recognizes `![...](...)` wherever that syntax appears in the retained text. - `packages/web/server/lib/markdown-image-grants/routes.js:351-365` uses the resulting reference set as the gate before inspecting a requested local path. - The chat renderer uses `Marked` in `packages/ui/src/components/chat/markdown/markdownCore.ts:727-739`; its raw-HTML renderer escapes HTML tokens for assistant output. Markdown image syntax inside a CommonMark raw HTML block is therefore not rendered as an image, while the grant scanner still sees its text. Example assistant message: ```html 
![not-rendered](/outside/private.png)
``` The grant scanner retains the image line and can accept `/outside/private.png` as a referenced source. The rendered message treats the `
` region as raw HTML content and escapes the tags, so the image syntax is visible text rather than a rendered image. This is a distinct uncovered case from OPEN #2142, which covers image syntax inside HTML comments; it is also distinct from #2150/#2151, which cover invalid fence closures and indented code blocks.

All-state issue searches for raw-HTML image grants, HTML-block image references, and Markdown image paths inside `
` found no matching tracker. All-state PR search found no matching implementation.

## Why it matters

The assistant-message reference check is intended to stop a client from requesting local image paths that the message does not actually render. Recognizing image syntax inside an escaped raw HTML block can authorize file inspection for a path mentioned only as code/text.

## Acceptance criteria

- Do not collect Markdown image references from raw HTML blocks that the chat renderer escapes rather than parsing as Markdown.
- Add an integration regression using an image path mentioned only inside `
` (and at least one other representative raw HTML block); the grant route must reject the source as unreferenced.
- Preserve authorization for the same image syntax outside raw HTML blocks, plus the existing comment, fenced-code, inline-code, and indented-code protections.

## Evidence

On `origin/main` (`072ba8c8e1c2db95897878554d4c544dd5294c7c`), `scripts/perf/seed-long-session.mjs:84-103` explicitly supports appending turns to an existing session with `--session`, but its final validation only asks for `--limit <checked> --role assistant` and checks that the result contains at least `checked` assistant messages. `packages/web/server/lib/openchamber-control/service.js:624-648` implements that query by collecting and filtering the session's assistant messages, then returning the latest `limit`; it does not scope them to prompts sent by this invocation.

Consequently, reusing a session that already has at least `checked` assistant replies can make the seeder report success even if the newly seeded prompts received fewer than `checked` replies (or none). The printed summary then claims the last turns were answered although those assistant messages predate the run. This defeats the helper's documented fixture-provider sanity check and can produce misleading performance captures.

## Suggested fix / acceptance criteria

- Capture a per-run boundary (for example, the pre-run latest message ID or the IDs of dispatched prompts) and verify assistant replies corresponding to prompts created by this invocation, not merely a count of historical assistant messages.
- Add a regression test for `--session` reuse where the session has old assistant replies but the current run's new prompts are unanswered; the seeder must fail rather than pass. Keep a successful reused-session control case.
- Preserve the fresh-session behavior and the existing JSON summary semantics, making the validation scope explicit if it changes.

## Evidence

On current `main` (`072ba8c8e1c2db95897878554d4c544dd5294c7c`), `packages/web/server/lib/scheduled-tasks/routes.js:53-59` converts a string `limit` with `Number()` and forwards it only when finite. A supplied value such as `?limit=oops` becomes `undefined`, indistinguishable from an omitted limit; `packages/web/server/lib/scheduled-tasks/run-history.js:170-173` then applies the default of 200. An empty `?limit=` converts to 0 and is clamped to 1, while repeated `limit` query parameters (parsed as a non-string) also fall back to 200.

The endpoint documents an optional limit with default 200 and maximum 1000 at `routes.js:35-37`. The neighboring time-bound validation gap is tracked separately in #2155; this issue is specifically for the `limit` parameter.

## Why it matters

A typo can silently return the default page (up to 200 rows) instead of reporting that the caller's requested bound was ignored. Empty and repeated values produce different surprising behavior, making client-side pagination errors harder to detect.

## Acceptance criteria

- Distinguish an omitted `limit` (use the documented default) from a supplied malformed, empty, or repeated `limit` (return HTTP 400).
- Preserve the documented valid-limit behavior and 1–1000 effective bound.
- Add route-level regression tests for omitted, valid, malformed, empty, and repeated limits.

## Evidence

The run-history endpoint documents `since` and `until` as epoch milliseconds or date strings in `packages/web/server/lib/scheduled-tasks/routes.js:35-37`. Its parser at lines 46-52 returns `undefined` for a supplied non-empty value that is neither numeric nor parseable by `Date.parse`, then lines 54-60 pass that value to `listRuns`. The history reader at `packages/web/server/lib/scheduled-tasks/run-history.js:170-180` skips a time bound unless it is finite.

Reproduced against the registered route handler with runs at timestamps 100, 200, and 300: `GET /api/projects/code/scheduled-tasks/run-history?since=not-a-date` returned HTTP 200 and all three runs; the malformed `since` reached `listRuns` as `undefined`. `until` uses the same parser and forwarding path.

## Why it matters

A typo or malformed timestamp silently broadens a filtered history request into an unfiltered one. Clients can show runs outside the requested interval without any indication that the filter was ignored.

## Acceptance criteria

- Treat an absent optional bound as no filter, but reject a supplied malformed `since` or `until` with HTTP 400 rather than silently omitting it.
- Add route-level regression tests for malformed `since` and malformed `until`; verify the history reader is not called for either invalid request.
- Keep valid epoch-millisecond and parseable date-string filters working, with a valid-input control test.

If message history advances past the first five entries before the notification lookup runs, the notification loses its message text (including the reply body) instead of resolving the exact assistant message that triggered it. - Preserve the no-substitution behavior from #2140; never use another assistant message when an exact ID was requested.
- Add tests where the requested message is on a later page and where it is absent after the final page; keep the page bound and existing response-size/deadline protections.

## Evidence

That window can start or end between the high and low surrogates of an emoji. The existing content-search.test.js long-line preview test checks the 200-character limit and match range, but not Unicode boundary integrity.

Reproduction of the exact slice operation with a matching line beginning needle, followed by 193 x characters and 😀tail, returns a 200-code-unit preview whose last code unit is 0xD83D (the emoji's high surrogate); UTF-8 encoding renders the trailing character as �. The content-search API returns malformed UTF-16 in user-visible snippets for valid source text. Search cards can display a replacement character or otherwise corrupt a character at either edge of the preview.

Closed #1866 fixes surrogate-pair cuts in message-search buildSnippet, a separate code path. Closed #1911 is also a different excerpt path. All-state searches for content-search preview/surrogate and content-search emoji/snippet found no direct tracker; open-PR search found no matching implementation.

## Acceptance criteria

- Adjust the preview window so neither its start nor end splits a surrogate pair, without exceeding the 200-code-unit cap.
- Keep match ranges and source columns correct after any boundary adjustment.
- Add regression tests for an emoji straddling both the leading and trailing preview boundaries; assert the returned snippet contains no lone surrogate and preserves the match range.

Reproduction input:

```md
```md

```
```

The scanner treats the four-backtick line with trailing text as a closer for the three-backtick fence, then retains `![hidden](/outside/secret.png)` as ordinary Markdown. `markdownImageSources()` therefore recognizes a path inside a code block, and the grant endpoint uses those sources as its authorization check at `routes.js:351-365`. A caller can request inspection of a path that the message does not render as an image.

The source-level reproduction using the current scanner produced the hidden image line in `collectedLines` (`imageSourceFound: true`). Existing #2134/#2135 covers retaining fence state across assistant text parts, not validating whether a candidate closing line is valid Markdown. All-state searches for markdown image-grant closing-fence/trailing-text cases and fenced-code false positives, plus an all-state PR search, found no matching item.

## Why it matters

Image grants rely on parsed message references as an authorization boundary, including for paths outside the workspace. Treating code-block text as a rendered image reference can authorize file inspection for a path the assistant did not actually include as an image.

## Acceptance criteria

- Only a matching fence run at least as long as the opener, followed only by spaces/tabs, closes a fenced block.
- Add regression coverage for both backtick and tilde fences with a too-long marker followed by trailing text; image syntax inside remains unauthorized.
- Preserve recognition of image syntax after a valid closing fence, including across assistant text parts.

```md

Since CommonMark treats the contents of an HTML comment as a comment rather than a rendered image, a client can request a grant for an image path that the message does not render. Existing `routes.test.js` covers fenced/same-line inline code and the new multiline inline-code case in #2141, but not HTML comments. The assistant-message reference check is intended to prevent a client from minting grants for paths that are not actually rendered as images. Recognizing image syntax inside comments weakens that boundary and can cause inspection of a local image path mentioned only in hidden Markdown text.

## Acceptance criteria

- Do not extract Markdown image references inside single-line or multi-line HTML comments.

## Evidence

On fresh `origin/main` `b9c8327dce20266aa77cd9e41d070b555680e4f8`, `packages/web/server/lib/markdown-image-grants/routes.js:155-175` splits each text part into lines, then at line 172 removes inline code with `/`+[^`]*`+/g` on each line. A CommonMark backtick code span may contain line breaks, so a span such as:

```md
`example
![hidden](image.png)
end`
```

is not removed by any per-line match: the image line survives extraction. I ran the current line-splitting/removal expression against that input; it returned the image line unchanged. `markdownImageSources` scans surviving lines for image references at `:178-215`. The grant route treats those extracted references as authoritative (`:351-365`): a client requesting the matching source passes the reference check and reaches image inspection.

The existing `routes.test.js:262-270` covers fenced and same-line inline code only. The recently merged #2135 / closed #2134 preserves fenced-code state across assistant text parts; this is a separate inline-code-span-over-newlines case, and current main still has the per-line inline-code removal above.

## Why it matters

The reference check is intended to prevent clients from minting image grants for paths not actually rendered as images. Treating an image example inside inline code as rendered Markdown can authorize inspection/granting of a local image path that the assistant only mentioned as code.

## Acceptance criteria

- Do not extract image references contained in a backtick code span that crosses line breaks.
- Add a regression test using a valid fixture image and a multiline inline-code example; the requested source must be rejected as unreferenced.
- Keep real image references outside inline code and current fenced-code behavior authorized/rejected as before.

body:
## Evidence

On current origin/main (7518c4fe43ee98de508bf58333e4eec2677af4ef), packages/web/server/lib/opencode/project-directory-runtime.js:73-80 handles the query value by selecting req.query.directory[0] when Express supplies repeated directory parameters. A focused Bun repro passed two valid temporary project paths and the resolver accepted the request, returning the first path rather than rejecting the ambiguous scope.

This resolver is used by project-scoped filesystem routes; for example, packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.js:326-327 delegates path resolution to it, and the upload route at :1677-1688 uses that workspace-path resolution before writing. The current resolver test suite passes 19/19 but has no repeated-query case.

Related: #2121 and #2122 reject repeated directory parameters in the separate Git-route resolver. Their issue acceptance and PR diff are scoped to packages/web/server/lib/git/routes.js; they do not cover this project-directory resolver or its filesystem/config callers.

## Why it matters

A client that accidentally serializes directory twice can silently target the first project for project-scoped filesystem or configuration operations. Rejecting ambiguous scope is safer and easier to diagnose than silently selecting one value.

## Acceptance criteria

- An array-valued req.query.directory is rejected as ambiguous instead of selecting element zero, including when a directory header is also present.
- Callers return a consistent client error for repeated values without falling back to another workspace.
- Add resolver tests for one value, repeated values, and repeated values alongside the directory header; cover a representative project-scoped filesystem route.
- Preserve single-value query and header behavior.

body:
## Evidence

On current origin/main (ef7e6352bc4fbf1e67d60b5d7c7701cfd5291861), packages/web/server/lib/scheduled-tasks/run-history.js:153-166 appends the new row, removes older rows from the in-memory array, then rewrites the history file in place with fs.writeFileSync. If compaction fails, the catch only logs and returns.

Reproduced with maxRows=1: record one row, then inject an ENOSPC failure after truncating the file during the second row compaction write. The second call returns without throwing, but the durable file has 0 bytes and a newly-created store reloads 0 rows. Thus a routine compaction write failure can erase all durable run history.

## Why it matters

Scheduled-task run history is durable evidence. An I/O failure during retention maintenance should not turn a previously valid history file into an empty one, especially when the caller is intentionally allowed to continue after history-record failures.

## Acceptance criteria

- Compaction uses a failure-atomic replacement (for example, write a sibling temporary file and rename it) so a failed rewrite preserves the previous valid history.
- In-memory rows and dedupe state remain consistent with the durable file when compaction fails.
- Add a regression test that injects a failure after the compaction target would otherwise be truncated and verifies the previous history reloads.
- Existing retention and bounded-load behavior remains covered; a run-history persistence failure remains non-fatal to the scheduled run.

Suggested fix: stage and atomically replace the compacted JSONL, and only discard aged-out in-memory rows/dedupe keys after the replacement succeeds.

body:
## Summary

A client-supplied todo ID can grow context.json past the 8 MiB read cap. The write succeeds, but the next context read treats the file as malformed, making that project's todos and context unavailable until the file is repaired manually.

## Evidence

On current origin/main (6e7afad1e5d97c3457b997defea0758a09b550f3):

- packages/web/server/lib/project-context/routes.js:20, 85-96 parses bodies up to 1 MiB and accepts an optional todo ID with z.string().optional() and no length bound. The bulk-save route also accepts any string ID (routes.js:66-80).
- runtime.js:125-143 keeps each ID as-is in sanitizeTodos; createTodo likewise keeps requestedId unchanged (runtime.js:633-644). writeJsonAtomic serializes the whole context without a write-size guard (runtime.js:327-335).
- Reads reject files above CONTEXT_FILE_READ_MAX_BYTES = 8 * 1024 * 1024 (runtime.js:34-46, 309-317); readStoredContext then throws “Stored project context is malformed” (runtime.js:462-468).

## Reproduction

Send 10 separate POST /api/project-context/<projectId>/todos requests with {"text":"x","id":"<900,000 ASCII characters>"}. Each request is below the 1 MiB parser limit and the project remains far below its 500-todo limit, but the IDs alone push the pretty-printed context past 8 MiB. A subsequent GET or mutation that reads the context fails as malformed. The runtime test suite could not be run in this worktree because the zod dependency is absent; it fails with Cannot find package 'zod' before tests start.

This is a write-side gap left by the bounded-read fix in closed #1607: the read cap is present, but todo IDs are not included in the write-side size assumptions/limits.

## Acceptance criteria

- Enforce a documented todo-ID limit on both single-create and bulk-save paths, including runtime sanitization so callers cannot bypass route validation.
- Prevent any accepted todo mutation from making context.json exceed the read cap (reject before replacing the last valid file if an aggregate bound is needed).
- Add regression coverage showing repeated individually valid requests cannot make subsequent context reads fail, and oversized/rejected writes preserve the prior readable context.

title: fix(web): do not advance durable replay state after an append failure

labels.name: kind/bug

body:
## Finding

A failed durable local-frame append is treated as committed in memory. A later successful head write can then persist a cursor past a frame that was never recorded, so after restart clients can resume beyond a missing replay event.

## Evidence

Verified against `origin/main` at `6e7afad1e5d97c3457b997defea0758a09b550f3`:

- `packages/web/server/lib/event-stream/replay-store.js:101-110` catches append errors, warns, and returns without signaling failure.
- `appendLocal()` at `:256-264` updates in-memory entries/head after `write()` returns; `appendHead()` at `:266-271` has the same behavior.
- `packages/web/server/lib/event-stream/global-hub.js:273-278` adds the local entry after `durable.appendLocal()` returns, then later fans it out (`:297-302`). The nearby comment describes persistence before fan-out.
- Reproduction with an injected one-shot `appendFileSync` failure: `appendLocal()` for position 2 did not throw; a subsequent successful `appendHead()` for position 3 persisted only `{"v":1,"t":"head","p":3,"u":"upstream:3"}`. Reload returned head position 3 with no entries. Assertions for that state passed.

The only all-state issue search hit was closed #2, the original durable-cursor feature request; it does not cover failure-path behavior. No matching open PR was found.

## Why it matters

The durable replay cursor can claim progress beyond a local event that was never persisted. After restart, replay cannot supply that event, and a client resuming from the later cursor can silently miss it.

## Acceptance criteria

- A configured-store append failure is observable and cannot be treated as a durable commit.
- The hub does not publish a local frame as committed or advance durable replay state past a failed append.
- Add a regression test for failed append → later recovery/append → store reload, asserting the persisted head cannot silently skip the failed frame.
- Preserve intentional in-memory-only behavior when no persistence path is configured.

title: fix(web): concurrent login attempts exceed the per-IP failure budget

labels.name: kind/security
labels.description: Security issue or security hardening

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Evidence

On default-branch `main` (`412eb2c5ef6500e0ee20ae79ee5639bcbda30c68`), `checkRateLimit()` reads the current counter and returns an admission decision at `packages/web/server/lib/ui-auth/ui-auth.js:107-179`. A rejected password or passkey assertion is recorded later, in a separate `recordFailedAttempt()` call (`:182-204`; password path `:969-980`, passkey path `:1049-1063`). The per-IP lock therefore does not make admission and failure accounting one atomic operation.

A local probe against the real `createUiAuth().handleSessionCreate()` implementation launched 100 simultaneous wrong-password requests with the same `req.ip`. With the default `OPENCHAMBER_RATE_LIMIT_MAX_ATTEMPTS=10`, it returned 14 responses with status 401 and 86 with 429. Repeated with 30 concurrent attempts, it admitted 14 failures again. The current tests in `ui-auth.test.js:497-553` cover shared password/passkey budgets, but send attempts in sequential loops (`:515-521`, `:530-549`), so they do not exercise concurrent admission.

## Why it matters

A client can parallelize password or passkey guesses from one source IP and exceed the configured failed-attempt budget within a single burst, weakening the login brute-force control.

## Acceptance criteria

- Admission and failure accounting (including in-flight attempts) are coordinated so concurrent failures for one client cannot exceed the configured per-IP budget.
- Add a concurrent regression test that launches more bad attempts than the limit from one IP and confirms excess attempts are throttled; preserve the existing shared password/passkey budget behavior.
- Successful authentication continues to clear the client's failure budget, and ordinary sequential window/lockout behavior remains unchanged.

A suitable fix is to atomically reserve/count an attempt under the per-IP serialization, or otherwise account for in-flight attempts before admitting more requests.

The `bun run check:changed` pre-commit gate fails on a clean main checkout at the dead code step.

Reproduced 2026-11-11 on main cd93d950b by queue lane tmp-code-h, task 14825: `bun run dead-code` (knip 5.80.0) exits 1 with 11 unused exports and 7 unused exported types, and the same run fails identically with an unrelated two-file change stashed, so the findings are pre-existing on main. None of the findings are in `packages/ui/src/stores/useUIStore.ts`, the file under change in task 14825.

Findings, from the gate output:

Unused exports: PLAN_ACTION_SEND_MODE_STORAGE_KEY (planTierDispatch.ts), FRESHNESS_WINDOW_MS (messageFreshness.ts), MAX_PENDING_FRAGMENT_KEYS (ui tunnel-codec.ts and web tunnel-codec.js), GLOBAL_SESSION_MAX_PAGES (globalSessions.ts), OPENCODE_UPSTREAM_AUTH_ORIGIN (credential-auth-error.js), MANAGED_PROCESS_ENTRY_MAX_BYTES and MANAGED_PROCESS_CLAIM_MAX_BYTES (managed-process-registry.js), MONTHLY_INCLUDED_CREDITS (command-code.js), ROTATION_DEFAULTS (pool-rotation.js), BOUNDED_OUTPUT_MAX_CHARS (bounded-output-accumulator.js).

Unused exported types: ProjectVisibilitySource, ProjectVisibilitySets, SessionProjectOwner (mobileProjectVisibility.ts), VisibleSetting (OpenChamberVisualSettings.tsx), TunnelSearchRevealMode (tunnelSearchReveal.ts), PlanActionSendMode (planTierDispatch.ts), GoalSpecDiffLine (goalSpec.ts).

Each finding needs a decision: remove the export, or keep it and record why knip should ignore it. Until this lands, every change either fails its pre-commit gate or trains its author to ignore the failure.

body:
## Problem

`CONTRIBUTING.md:140-145` tells macOS developers to run `bun run release:test:intel` and `bun run release:test:arm`. Both commands call `scripts/test-release-build.sh`. Its native path runs `bun run --cwd packages/desktop build` at line 198 and `tauri build` at line 212. This repository has `packages/electron` and no `packages/desktop`. The release workflow builds the Electron app from `packages/electron` with Electron Builder at `.github/workflows/release.yml:235-255`.

## Reproduction

On main `e895968ba30b28f5345df0661d11278265505967`:

- `bun run --cwd packages/desktop build` exits 1 with `ENOENT: No such file or directory: Could not change directory to "packages/desktop"`.
- `bun run release:test --dry-run` lists the removed `packages/desktop` and Tauri commands, exits 0, and prints `Release build test completed!` without building anything.

## Why it matters

The documented macOS pre-release checks cannot validate the current desktop release. The dry-run message can read as a successful build check even though it only prints obsolete commands.

## Suggested fix and acceptance criteria

- Update the tester and its package scripts to exercise the current Electron release path for each supported architecture, or replace those commands with a supported check and update `CONTRIBUTING.md`.
- Add a test that pins the dry-run command mapping to existing package paths and makes clear that no build ran.
- Verify the documented Intel and Apple Silicon checks on macOS, or report their exact platform prerequisites without claiming a build completed.

title: fix(scripts): updater-e2e-fixture stage silently swallows --port (and any --key typo)

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

body:
## Evidence (origin/main 101cd7f32, verified 2026-11-09 by code read)

- `packages/electron/scripts/updater-e2e-fixture.mjs:24-34` (`parseArguments`) accepts any `--key value` pair into `options` with no per-command validation.
- `main()` `stage` path (`:121-129`) stages the fixture and returns at `:129`; `options.port` is read only at `:132` in the `serve`/`run` branch. So `stage ... --port 45678` exits 0 with the fixture staged and the flag having zero effect — confirmed by the code path (a real run stages into a temp feed dir, prints `staged ...`, exit 0, nothing listening).
- Usage (`:14-17`) documents `--port` solely for `serve`/`run`, so a user debugging a port conflict who passes `--port` to `stage` gets exit 0 and chases a ghost. The lenient parser swallows typos (`--verison`) the same way.

## Why it matters

Low severity, but the exact accepted-and-ignored shape: exit 0 + no effect + no warning. E2E fixture scripts are debugged rarely and under time pressure; a swallowed flag wastes exactly the session you can least afford.

## Suggested fix shape

Reject unknown options per command in `parseArguments` (allowlist: `stage` -> arch/next/version/dir; `serve` -> dir/port; `run` -> arch/current/next/version/dir/port), throwing usage otherwise.

## Acceptance criteria

- `stage ... --port 45678` exits non-zero printing usage (instead of exit 0 + staged fixture);
- existing `updater-e2e-fixture.test.mjs` passes plus a new unknown-flag case.

title: chore(ci): scripts/test-mobile-workspace-resize.mjs runs nowhere — the mobile-fold check rots silently

labels.name: kind/ci
labels.description: CI/CD pipelines, workflows, and build automation

body:
## Evidence (origin/main 101cd7f32, verified 2026-11-09)

- `scripts/test-mobile-workspace-resize.mjs:1-70` is a real assertion-bearing check: `import assert from 'node:assert/strict'`, drives a real Chrome over CDP (`perf/cdp.mjs`), resizes through 8 viewports (keyboard-open/closed, folded phone, rotation) and asserts the unsaved draft survives in the same editor node.
- It is referenced nowhere: repo-wide grep for `test-mobile-workspace-resize` (excluding `.git`, `node_modules`) hits only its own usage comment at `:2`. No workflow, no `package.json` script, no docs entry.
- Root `test` (`package.json:46`) collects `scripts/` through `scripts/run-isolated-tests.mjs:28`, whose collector regex is `/\.(test|spec|integration)\.(js|cjs|mjs|jsx|ts|tsx)$/`. A `test-*.mjs` prefix filename never matches, so the check is silently skipped — it looks like automation but runs in no tier.

## Why it matters

This is the only automated net for unsaved-draft survival across mobile keyboard fold/unfold/rotation. It rots silently: the CDP selectors it depends on (`[aria-label=...]`, `#mobile-surface-root`) can drift with zero signal, and the first person to run it manually after months will debug the harness, not the product.

## Suggested fix shape

Either wire it (nightly/manual workflow job with Chrome + an isolated server, following the `.integration.` explicit-skip convention documented in `run-isolated-tests.mjs:24-27`) or rename to `*.manual.mjs` and document it as a manual procedure so it stops looking CI-eligible.

## Acceptance criteria

- `grep` for the filename hits a workflow or script entry that actually executes it, with its external preconditions (Chrome, isolated server URL, fold-resize.txt fixture) documented; or
- the file is renamed out of the automation-looking `test-*` shape and documented as manual.

body:
Design doc: `files/designs/openchamber-quota-provider-registry.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace. Originated by the repo design architect, 2026-11-07 pass. No Drew decision needed (no changed default, no new control; the one disposition choice — #1738's register-or-retire — was already framed as a triage pick inside #1738, and this design only supplies the rule it is picked under).

## Summary

A quota provider exists in this repo only if it exists in four places at once, and nothing states that:

1. **Web backend registry** — `packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/index.js` registers **30 providers** (:55–286).
2. **VS Code backend** — `packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.ts` (4,873 lines) hand-ports the same providers: `fetchQuotaForProvider`'s switch carries **27 cases**, and `listConfiguredQuotaProviders` re-states the set a second time in the same file.
3. **Shared UI** — `packages/ui/src/lib/quota/providers/index.ts` (`QUOTA_PROVIDERS`, **29 entries**) is the catalog every board surface iterates; `packages/ui/src/types/quota.ts` carries the `QuotaProviderId` union (**30 ids**) as a fourth list.
4. **Docs** — `packages/web/server/lib/quota/DOCUMENTATION.md`'s "Supported provider IDs (dispatcher)" table is a fifth, hand-kept list.

Disagreement table, verified on main `4e6f75b433` this run (every list read in full via the API):

| Provider id | Web registry | VS Code dispatch | UI catalog | UI type |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `mistral` | ✓ | **✗** | ✓ | ✓ |
| `command-code` | ✓ | **✗** | ✓ | ✓ |
| `opendesign` | ✓ | **✗** | ✓ | ✓ |
| `github-copilot-addon` | ✓ | ✓ | **✗** | ✓ |
| `openai` | ✗ (credential alias of `codex`; `fetchOpenaiQuota` export only) | ✗ | ✗ | ✓ |

Three recurring failure shapes:

1. **A provider lands on one surface only.** PR #475's Open Design was UI-unreachable (#480, closed); PR #1633's Mistral repeated it (#1735, closed today via PR #1805) — and #1805's landing activated the VS Code half: the shared board now requests `mistral` in VS Code, whose backend has no fetcher for it (#1757, open). Command Code + Open Design have been VS-Code-absent since they landed (#1744, open). Copilot Add-on is the mirror: both backends + type, no catalog — and its fetcher duplicates the primary Copilot fetcher exactly (#1738, open).
2. **The VS Code port lags the web fix.** A series of "the #X defect in quotaProviders.ts" filings: #492 (ex-#489), #545 (ex-#507, missed by PR #541 — the sweep porting its siblings), #911 (PR #764's credential source never ported), #912/#919 (PR #748's planLabel never mirrored), plus at least a dozen more closed port-gap filings (#506, #518–#521, #546, #560, #567, #569, #570, #573, #585, #616).
3. **Sweeps miss instances, in both directions.** The #782 sweep missed NanoGPT (#827) and Kimi (#844), each titled "the one provider the #782 sweep missed". The key-selection family — `isConfigured` judging with `||` while `fetchQuota` selects with `??` — ran Mistral (#1747, open) → eight web providers (#1751, closed) → ten VS Code fetchers (#1759, closed; landed a shared `keyOrTokenFrom` helper) → and still missed MiniMax (two ids) + Wafer in both backends (#1755, open). Verified verbatim on current main: the VS Code configured-set builder routes most providers through `keyOrTokenFrom` but still judges minimax/wafer with raw `key || token` while their fetchers select with `??`.

The 2026-11-06 design pass named this family its runner-up ("revisit if a third provider or a second registry spawns the same shape"); since then a third and fourth provider and the second-registry shape have all spawned. Dedupe: the `kind/design` list is #612/#802/#976/#1254/#1391/#1441/#1528/#1655/#1740 only — none governs the quota provider set; searches for a quota registry/manifest design return only the per-site filings above.

## The contract

1. **One logical provider set.** Exactly one set of quota provider ids; each surface's list is a view of it, stated in one checked-in **provider manifest** (id, display name, per-surface presence).
2. **Landed only when landed everywhere.** A new provider lands web fetcher + registration, VS Code fetcher + dispatch + configured entry, UI catalog + type, and the docs row in the same change. A surface that legitimately cannot serve a provider records a **named exception with a reason** in the manifest — never a silent absence (a silent absence is indistinguishable from #1744).
3. **Aliases are not providers.** A credential alias (`openai` for `codex`, per the web registry's `credentialAliases`) is recorded as an alias and appears in no surface's provider list — including the type union, where `openai` currently sits as if it were a provider.
4. **Configured and fetch select through one function.** Per provider per backend, exactly one credential-selection function (the non-empty-string fall-through pattern: `asNonEmptyString` chains in web `kimi.js`/`hyper.js`/`kilo.js`/`cline-pass.js`/`command-code.js`; `keyOrTokenFrom` in the VS Code file) serves both the configured predicate and the fetch path. Two selection expressions for one provider in one backend is the defect (#1747's family: 21 provider-instances across four filings).
5. **No distinct id for a duplicate fetcher.** A behaviour-identical fetcher's id is folded into its provider (alias / folded instance) or registered with the distinct data it adds stated. #1738's register-or-retire pick is made under this rule.

Alternatives considered (in the doc): status-quo sweeping (the sweeps are the failure mode — each re-derives the provider set from grep because no list exists to sweep against); extracting one shared quota package (the real port-lag cure, kept as a phase-4 question the manifest makes decidable); generating catalog/docs from the web registry (reaches the VS Code dispatch — the worst lagger — last); a CONTRIBUTING checklist (#480 and #1735 are both post-checklist-era landings).

## Phased breakdown

1. **Phase 1 — the manifest + conformance probe matrix (filed with this design).** One checked-in provider manifest covering every id in any of the lists, per-surface presence, known disagreements as named exceptions linked to their adopting issues; one conformance test per package (web, vscode, ui) asserting that package's lists equal the manifest minus its exceptions. Tests/docs only — no fetcher, dispatch or catalog behaviour changes.
2. **Phase 2 — the surfaces agree (ADOPTS open #1738, #1744, #1757).** Copilot Add-on's rule-5 disposition (#1738); VS Code fetchers/dispatch/configured entries for Command Code + Open Design (#1744) and Mistral (#1757). Each keeps its own queue lifecycle — linked as sub-issues, agent-noted, NOT re-enqueued.
3. **Phase 3 — one selection per provider (ADOPTS open #1747, #1755).** The key-selection origin (Mistral web) and the sweep remainder (MiniMax ×2 + Wafer, both backends) land, bringing every provider onto rule 4. Same adoption terms.
4. **Phase 4 — NOT filed.** Shared-implementation extraction (one quota package vs two conforming ports), Settings import-form parity (a possible sixth surface), Electron confirmation, and a `check:changed` ratchet beyond the conformance tests — open questions in the doc.

Non-goals: no re-filing/pre-empting the adopted filings; no change to any provider's fetch behaviour, windows or transforms; credential-file read bounds stay #1254/#1655's territory; quota *consumers* (board/routing/CLI behaviour with a result) are out of scope.

---
agent-note:v1 · Agent: repo-design-architect · state: filed · Design originated 2026-11-07; phase 1 filed as a sub-issue of this issue, phases 2–3 adopt existing open issues as sub-issues (not re-enqueued).

## Acceptance criteria

- Phase 1 lands as filed: one checked-in provider manifest covers every quota provider id in any surface list, with per-surface presence and the known disagreements recorded as named exceptions linked to their adopting issues; one conformance test per package (web, vscode, ui) asserts that package's lists equal the manifest minus its exceptions. Tests/docs only — no fetcher, dispatch, or catalog behaviour changes in phase 1.
- The manifest encodes the contract: one logical provider set; aliases (e.g. `openai` for `codex`) recorded as aliases and present in no surface's provider list, including the `QuotaProviderId` type union; a surface absence is always a named exception with a reason, never silent.
- Phases 2 and 3 proceed only through their adopted open issues (#1738, #1744, #1757; #1747, #1755), each keeping its own queue lifecycle — no re-enqueueing from this design.

body:
## Finding

The shared `settings.json` now has two different read caps depending on which reader opens it. PR #1650 capped the VS Code reader (`readOpenChamberSettings`) at 4 MiB; the web readers of the same shared file — PR #1629 (Linear auth) and PR #1666 (GitHub auth) — use 8 MiB, and #1666's own comment states the house rule: "settings.json is one shared file with one cap, matching the 8 MiB the other settings readers use". A `settings.json` between 4 MiB and 8 MiB therefore reads normally in the web server but is silently treated as `{}` in VS Code, so a configured `opencodeBinary` path stops resolving there with no error surfaced.

## Evidence

- PR #1650 (https://github.com/developing-today-forks/openchamber/pull/1650), MERGED, merge b1f25606adc2, for #1644.
- Current main 8f61a0fd3f9849606a6d976b824431f2bd82ce36 (verified twice):
  - `packages/vscode/src/opencode.ts:119` — `MAX_OPENCHAMBER_SETTINGS_BYTES = 4 * 1024 * 1024`; the read at :124 throws over-cap into the bare catch and degrades to `{}` (documented behavior in the PR).
  - `packages/web/server/lib/linear/auth.js:21` — `SETTINGS_FILE_MAX_BYTES = 8 * 1024 * 1024` for the same `settings.json` in the OpenChamber data dir.
  - `packages/web/server/lib/github/auth.js:44` — `SETTINGS_FILE_MAX_BYTES = 8 * 1024 * 1024`, with the "one shared file, one cap" comment.
  - Same file: the VS Code path is `~/.config/openchamber/settings.json` (`opencode.ts`, `path.join(os.homedir(), '.config', 'openchamber', 'settings.json')`); the web readers resolve `settings.json` in the same data dir (`OPENCHAMBER_DATA_DIR` or `~/.config/openchamber`).
- #1650's stated justification was "the same 4 MiB as … the #1641 settings cap" — i.e. it matched the VS Code *config* reader, not the shared-file cap the web readers had already standardized on in #1615/#1629/#1666.

## Why it matters

Cross-runtime settings divergence is the hardest kind to diagnose: the same file, valid and in use by the web UI, silently yields no custom OpenCode binary in VS Code once it grows past 4 MiB — and nothing logs which side refused it, because the VS Code failure degrades to `{}` by design.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] One cap for the shared `settings.json` across all readers (web + VS Code), or an explicit documented reason the VS Code reader must be stricter, stated at both cap sites.
- [ ] A regression test pins the VS Code reader's cap to the shared value (the existing `opencode-settings-cap.test.js` over-cap case should use the shared cap, not a divergent one).
- [ ] The "one shared file, one cap" comment in `github/auth.js` is accurate for every reader after the change.

body:
## Problem

In `packages/web/server/lib/git/service.js`, the new-file line counting inside `readStatus` judges its 1 MiB cap on the **pre-read stat only** and then reads the file **by path, whole**:

- `service.js:3342-3343` — `MAX_NEW_FILE_STATS = 200`, `MAX_NEW_FILE_STAT_SIZE = 1024 * 1024`
- `service.js:3370-3376` — `const stat = await fsp.stat(absolutePath); if (!stat.isFile() || stat.size > MAX_NEW_FILE_STAT_SIZE) continue;` then `const buffer = await fsp.readFile(absolutePath);`

Anything that changes the file between the stat and the read defeats the gate:

1. **Grown after stat** — the read buffers the whole file however large it now is, and counts all of its lines.
2. **Swapped for a FIFO after stat** — `fsp.readFile` on a FIFO never settles. `readStatus` runs inside the per-directory serialized refresh (`createSerialRefresh`, `service.js:3163-3166`; `getStatus` at `service.js:3168`), so one wedged read blocks **every later status read for that repository** — the status surface for that project is dead until the process restarts.

This is the residual of closed #1054, which fixed the uncapped `getFileDiff` read and cited this stats gate as the conforming example ("new-file stats gate at 1 MiB"). The gate exists, but it is stat-only — the same defect class as #1684/#1685/#1659 (cap judged on pre-read stat, read by path). The shared bounded reader is already imported in this very file (`readBoundedFile`, `service.js:15`) and used elsewhere in it.

## Evidence (laptop probe vs the real module, ×2 identical)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-git-status-stats-20261106/probe5.mjs` on the laptop, against the real exported `getStatus` from the laptop primary at main `8f61a0fd3`. The probe interposes deterministically on the shared `fs.promises` object (service.js captures `fsp = fs.promises` at `service.js:23` and looks up `.stat` at call time) so the swap lands exactly between the module's own stat and its own readFile of the same path; everything else runs the module's real code.

- Control (10-line, 20-byte untracked file): `diffStats.working["new.txt"] = { insertions: 10, deletions: 0 }`
- Grown-after-stat (stat sees the 20-byte file; the read gets a 1,200,000-byte / 600,000-line file): `diffStats.working["new.txt"] = { insertions: 600000, deletions: 0 }` — read and counted whole, past the 1 MiB cap the stat had just approved.
- FIFO-after-stat: `getStatus` never settled (>6 s race), and a **second** `getStatus` for the same directory also never settled (>4 s) — the serialized per-directory queue is wedged, not just the one call.

## Why it matters

`getStatus` backs the git status surface clients poll after every agent tool call and from PR polling. The values at these paths are working-tree files in whatever repository the user has open — files that build tools, code generators, and other processes routinely rewrite while a status read is in flight. A merely *racing* writer silently defeats the size cap; a path swapped to a non-regular file (or a writer that replaces the file with a pipe/socket during generation) takes down status for that repository for the life of the server process, with no error surfaced.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The new-file stats read is bounded: the file is opened once, regular-file judged from the handle, and the byte cap enforced in flight (stop at cap+1) — e.g. via the `readBoundedFile` helper already imported in `service.js` — instead of stat-by-path then read-by-path.
- [ ] A file grown past `MAX_NEW_FILE_STAT_SIZE` between the former stat point and the read is treated exactly as an over-cap file is today (skipped from `newFileStats`), never counted whole.
- [ ] A non-regular file (FIFO/device/socket) appearing at the path cannot wedge the read: the status call settles, and subsequent `getStatus` calls for the same directory settle.
- [ ] Behavior for ordinary files is unchanged: untracked and index-added files at or under the cap are line-counted as today, binary files (NUL byte) are still detected and excluded from line counts, and the `MAX_NEW_FILE_STATS` count bound still applies.
- [ ] Regression tests in `packages/web/server/lib/git/service.test.js` (or the nearest existing suite) cover the grown-after-stat and FIFO-swap cases plus the unchanged control.

# fix(web,vscode): skills-catalog install copy judges SKILL.md against the 1 MiB supporting-file cap, so loadable skills with a 1–4 MiB SKILL.md can no longer install

## Finding

PR #1477 (fix for #1366) added install-copy caps to `copyDirectoryNoSymlinks` in both surfaces. Its per-file check applies the **supporting-file** limit (1 MiB) to *every* file in the skill tree — including `SKILL.md` itself. But `SKILL.md` is not a supporting file: everywhere else in the codebase it has its own 4 MiB limit, and the supporting-file reader explicitly excludes it. A skill whose `SKILL.md` is between 1 MiB and 4 MiB scans and loads fine, yet its install now aborts with `Skill file is too large to install: … exceeds the 1048576 byte limit`. That is a regression introduced by #1477 for a class of previously installable skills.

## Evidence

- Source PR: #1477 — https://github.com/developing-today-forks/openchamber/pull/1477 (merged 2026-11-03, head `c50b01ce46523633222eb22cdfd71cb6ed6476ea`), filed for #1366 (CLOSED).
- Web, current main `c11726d32e12230ccd5353a85a0c852dfca3ad36`: `packages/web/server/lib/skills-catalog/install.js:112-123` — `countEntry` throws when any file's `stat.size > SKILL_SUPPORTING_FILE_MAX_BYTES` (1 MiB, imported from `opencode/shared.js`); the walk calls it for every file (`install.js:145` directories, `:152` files) with no `SKILL.md` exception.
- VS Code twin, same PR: `packages/vscode/src/skillsCatalog.ts:463-472` — identical check against its local `SKILL_SUPPORTING_FILE_MAX_BYTES = 1024 * 1024` (:29), while the same file's own SKILL.md reader uses `SKILL_MD_MAX_BYTES` = 4 MiB (:20, enforced :49-59).
- The 4 MiB SKILL.md contract: `packages/web/server/lib/skills-catalog/scan.js:15` `SKILL_MD_MAX_BYTES = 4 * 1024 * 1024`, read via `readBoundedFile(filePath, SKILL_MD_MAX_BYTES)` (:34) — a 1–4 MiB SKILL.md is a legitimate, loadable skill file.
- The supporting-file cap's own scope excludes SKILL.md: `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/shared.js:953` defines `SKILL_SUPPORTING_FILE_MAX_BYTES = 1024 * 1024`, and the walk that collects supporting files skips `entry.name === 'SKILL.md'` (shared.js, `walkDir`: `} else if (entry.name !== 'SKILL.md') {`).

## Why it matters

Install is the only path that disagrees with the rest of the system about how large a SKILL.md may be. Users with a large-but-valid SKILL.md (generated catalogs, embedded reference material) get a hard install failure with a message that names the supporting-file limit, while the same skill would scan, list and load if placed on disk by any other route. The cap added for #1366 was aimed at clone-controlled bulk (entries + total bytes + supporting-file size); conflating SKILL.md into the supporting-file limit was not part of that issue's acceptance.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] In both `copyDirectoryNoSymlinks` copies (web `install.js`, vscode `skillsCatalog.ts`), a file named `SKILL.md` is judged against the 4 MiB SKILL.md limit (`SKILL_MD_MAX_BYTES` or its local equivalent); every other file keeps the 1 MiB supporting-file limit.
- [ ] The entries cap (1,000) and total-bytes cap (8 MiB) from #1477 are unchanged and still apply to the whole tree, SKILL.md included.
- [ ] Regression tests on the web copy (and the vscode copy where its harness allows): a skill with a SKILL.md of e.g. 2 MiB installs successfully; a SKILL.md over 4 MiB aborts; a supporting file over 1 MiB still aborts (existing #1477 tests keep passing).

body:
## Problem

The VS Code extension host's shared-settings runtime reads all three of its
on-disk JSON stores whole, synchronously, with no size gate and no
regular-file check:

- `packages/vscode/src/bridge-settings-runtime.ts:195` —
  `readSettingsJsonFromDisk` does
  `fs.readFileSync(OPENCHAMBER_SHARED_SETTINGS_PATH, 'utf8')`
  (`~/.config/openchamber/settings.json`) and `JSON.parse`s whatever comes
  back.
- `packages/vscode/src/bridge-settings-runtime.ts:222` —
  `readPreferencesFromDisk` does the same for `preferences.json`
  (via `parsePreferencesDocument(fs.readFileSync(...))`).
- `packages/vscode/src/bridge-settings-runtime.ts:373` —
  `readMagicPromptFile` does the same for `magic-prompts.json`. The
  per-value `MAGIC_PROMPT_TEXT_MAX_LENGTH` (200,000) is enforced only on
  *save* and in the write path — the read-side sanitizer
  (`sanitizeMagicPromptOverrides`, :329-342) checks the id pattern and
  string type only, so an on-disk override of any length is returned whole.

These are the same shared files the web server reads; the web readers of
`settings.json`/`preferences.json` are tracked separately in #1631. This
issue is the extension-host twin: same defect class, different process,
different blast radius.

## Why it matters

The extension host is single-threaded: a synchronous `readFileSync` that
blocks blocks *everything* the extension does. Callers verified on main
`f80ffdb893`:

- `bridge-config-runtime.ts:187` and `:809` call `readSettings` from
  bridge request handlers; `:258` serves `readMagicPromptOverrides`.
- `bridge-git-special-runtime.ts:380` / `:447` call `readSettings`.
- `scmCommitMessage.ts:135` / `:141` call both readers while generating
  commit messages.

So a FIFO (or a device, or a pathologically large file) at any of the
three paths freezes the whole extension host — every bridge request, the
chat panel, SCM helpers — not just one settings read. An oversized but
well-formed file is buffered and parsed whole in the extension host's
memory on every read.

The same package already knows the bounded pattern:
`opencodeConfig.ts` reads OpenCode config files through a handle-bounded
read that rejects files over `MAX_CONFIG_FILE_BYTES` = 4 MiB with
`CONFIG_FILE_TOO_LARGE` (see `packages/vscode/src/DOCUMENTATION.md`, the
`opencodeConfig.ts` entry), and the shared project-config reader caps at
1 MiB (#1247 / #1490). These three readers are the ungated outliers.

## Evidence (this run, laptop probe against the real module)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-vscode-settings-ungated-20261105/probe.test.js`
on the laptop, `bun test`, importing the real
`bridge-settings-runtime.ts` from the laptop primary at origin/main
`f80ffdb893795fbd44fdddf85cf22b0a5c74da3b`, with `vscode` and
`os.homedir()` mocked to a scratch home exactly as the module's own
`bridge-settings-runtime.test.js` harness does. Run twice, identical
results:

- Control: small `settings.json` (`defaultModel: "probe-model-x"`) and
  small `magic-prompts.json` read back normally.
- Oversize: a `settings.json` carrying a 33,554,432-char string value was
  returned whole (`OVERSIZE_SETTINGS_LEN 33554432`); a
  `magic-prompts.json` override of 33,554,432 chars was likewise returned
  whole (`OVERSIZE_MAGIC_LEN 33554432`) — no rejection at any size.
- FIFO: with `settings.json` replaced by a FIFO, `readSettings()` never
  returned — the probe process was killed by `timeout 5` (exit 124).

The `preferences.json` reader (:222) was verified by code read (identical
`fs.readFileSync` whole-buffer pattern, no gate); the probe exercised the
settings and magic-prompts paths directly.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] All three reads (settings :195, preferences :222, magic-prompts
      :373) go through a bounded, regular-file-checked read with a named
      byte cap per file (documented, sized from the legitimate shape of
      each file — settings/preferences carry bounded profile fields;
      magic-prompts text is capped at 200,000 chars per override on save).
- [ ] Over-cap and non-regular files degrade exactly as a read failure
      does today per reader — settings → `{}` (the documented coercion at
      :190-192), preferences → the existing `unreadable` result (profile
      keys withheld, file left alone), magic-prompts → the existing
      empty-store path — and a too-large file is **never** treated as
      corrupt-and-preserved or overwritten on the next write.
- [ ] Normal small files behave byte-for-byte as today, including the
      preferences seeding path and the magic-prompts corrupt-file
      preservation flow (#891).
- [ ] Regression tests in `bridge-settings-runtime.test.js` pin: an
      over-cap file for each of the three readers, and a FIFO at the
      settings path returning promptly instead of blocking.
- [ ] `packages/vscode/src/DOCUMENTATION.md` notes the caps alongside the
      existing bounded-read entries.

(magic-prompts atomic-write/corrupt-preservation, already fixed — this is
the read-size side only).

## Summary

The spaces record reader reads each per-space record file whole, synchronously, with no size gate and no non-regular-file rejection — unlike the shared bounded reader (`packages/web/server/lib/shared/bounded-file-read.js`, `readBoundedFileSync`) the rest of the server has been adopting (see #1607, #1613–#1615, #1620–#1624, #1627):

- `packages/web/server/lib/spaces/space-records.js:170` — `text = fs.readFileSync(file, 'utf8')` in the `read(spaceId)` function of `createSpaceRecords` (records live at `<dataDir>/spaces/records/<space-id>.json`)

The record schema is tightly bounded everywhere except the read itself: grants are capped at 100 (`MAX_GRANTS`), allowlist domains at 200, setup command/output lengths are capped in `space-setup.js` — so a legitimate record is small, and a generous cap loses nothing. Notably the `name` field is an unbounded `z.string()`, so an oversized record is not even rejected after the whole file has been buffered and parsed.

## Verified evidence (this run, main f3f288763b0a0b4f958e34f29615e9b1961f23d6)

Laptop probe against the real `createSpaceRecords` extracted verbatim from `origin/main` (`~/git/fleet/probe-oc-space-records-ungated-20261104/`, run twice, identical results):

- Control: a small valid record reads back `{ status: 'ok', … }`.
- Oversize: a 33,554,620-byte record (33,554,432-char `name`) is buffered and parsed whole and returned as `status: 'ok'` with the full name (~66 ms, no rejection at any stage).
- FIFO: with the record file replaced by a FIFO, the synchronous `read()` never returns — the probe was killed by a 3 s timeout on both runs. Because the read is synchronous, this blocks the whole server event loop on the spaces host path.

## Why it matters

Any process or accident that leaves an oversized or non-regular file at a record path turns a routine space listing / record read into unbounded memory use or a full event-loop freeze. The file's own design is careful everywhere else — an unreadable record is reported, never silently replaced, precisely so a bad file cannot make the host forget a network choice — but the read itself judges nothing about size or file kind before buffering.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `read` in `space-records.js` goes through the shared bounded reader (or an equivalent handle-judged bounded read) with a named, generous cap sized to the schema's own bounds.
- [ ] Semantics preserved exactly: missing file still reads `{ status: 'missing' }`; malformed, too-large and non-regular files read `{ status: 'unreadable' }` with the existing warning, and are never overwritten by `update` (which already refuses non-`ok` reads).
- [ ] Regression tests: oversized record and FIFO/non-regular record file are refused in bounded time; existing space-records tests still pass.

# fix(web): /api/fs/read and the preview serve path judge their byte caps on the pre-read stat only — a file grown between stat and read is buffered and served whole, past the cap

## Summary

The two whole-file read paths in `packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.js` enforce their byte caps **only against the pre-read `stat`**, then buffer the file whole with an unbounded `readFile`. A file that grows between the stat and the read — a build log, a dev-server output file, any workspace file a running process is appending to while the user opens it in the Files view — is read and served whole, however large it has become. This is the stat-is-only-a-hint flaw the codebase already fixed on the guest-asset serve path; these two hotter paths were left on the pre-read judgement.

## Evidence (main `41c124c7c`)

`packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.js`:

- `:173` — `MAX_SERVE_BYTES = 100 * 1024 * 1024` (preview serve cap); `:180` — `MAX_READ_BYTES = 16 * 1024 * 1024` (`/api/fs/read` cap; the comment at `:175-179` says the handler "must refuse large files up front" because it buffers the file as a UTF-8 string plus the response copy).
- `GET /api/fs/read`: the cap is judged at `:1308` (`if (stats.size > MAX_READ_BYTES)` → 413), then `:1312` runs `content = await fsPromises.readFile(canonicalPath, 'utf8')` with no during-read bound. The empty-read retry loop (`:1318-1332`) can repeat that whole read up to three more times.
- Preview serve (`GET /api/fs/preview/:grant/*`): the cap is judged at `:1519` (`stats.size > MAX_SERVE_BYTES` → 413), then `:1525` runs `const bytes = await fsPromises.readFile(canonicalPath)` unbounded.

The established house standard, in the same server:

- `packages/web/server/lib/guests/routes.js:886-892` serves guest assets through `readBoundedFile` (`../shared/bounded-file-read.js:73`), with the comment: "the cap is enforced during the read itself, judged from the opened handle (readBoundedFile): the resolver's stat is only a hint, so a file grown or swapped after it … is refused here having buffered at most the cap + 1 byte, never read whole into the server."
- The same during-read standard closed #1582 (session-goal objective read) and #1537 (project-icon serve). `/api/fs/raw` is not affected: it streams a span from an opened handle and never buffers the file.

History: #1026 (closed) added these caps when `/api/fs/read` had **no** size gate at all; it pinned the stat-time judgement. The stat-vs-read gap is the residual this issue tracks — the existing tests (`lib/fs/routes.test.js`, "rejects a file over MAX_READ_BYTES with 413 before calling readFile") mock `stat` and `readFile` independently and never model the two disagreeing.

## Reproduction (verified this run, twice)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-fsread-stat-race-20261104/probe.mjs` against the real `registerFsRoutes` extracted from `origin/main` (`41c124c7c`), using the repo's own test-harness mocking style — `stat` reports the size at stat time, `readFile` returns the grown content, modelling a concurrent writer:

- Control, `/api/fs/read`: stat size 16 MiB + 1 → **413**, `readFile` never called. ✅
- Race, `/api/fs/read`: stat size 100 → readFile returns 17 MiB → **200, served 17,825,792 bytes** against the 16 MiB cap (16,777,216).
- Control, preview serve: stat size 100 MiB + 1 → **413**. ✅
- Race, preview serve: stat size 100 → readFile returns 101 MiB → **200, served 105,906,176 bytes** against the 100 MiB cap (104,857,600).

## Why it matters

`/api/fs/read` is the Files view's text read and the preview serve path backs every HTML preview asset; both run against live workspace files, exactly the files most likely to be growing while read (logs, generated output, recordings-in-progress saved as text). One request can pull an unbounded file into server memory (for `/api/fs/read`, twice over: the string plus the response copy, and up to four times under the empty-read retry), on the same managed server whose other read paths were capped during the read precisely to prevent this (#1282's reasoning: a deadline bounds time, not memory).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `/api/fs/read` enforces `MAX_READ_BYTES` during the read (e.g. via `readBoundedFile` from `lib/shared/bounded-file-read.js`, judged from the opened handle): a file that grows past the cap between stat and read is refused 413 having buffered at most the cap + 1 byte, and the empty-read retry preserves its current semantics within the cap.
- [ ] The preview serve path enforces `MAX_SERVE_BYTES` during the read the same way; non-HTML payloads and the preview-bridge injection for HTML keep working at and below the cap.
- [ ] Regression tests in `lib/fs/routes.test.js` model stat and read disagreeing (stat under cap, read over cap) for both routes and pin the 413; the existing stat-time tests keep passing unchanged.
- [ ] `/api/fs/raw` (streamed) is untouched.

The daily upstream-sync workflow failed: https://github.com/developing-today/openchamber/actions/runs/41828572424. The sync is dispatched to an OpenCode session via pm-dispatch, so a workflow failure means the sync could not be completed (an unresolvable merge conflict, a dispatch failure, or a failed validation after its PR). Per Drew's escalation chain (2026-10-28), the fleet queue takes over from here: reproduce the upstream merge in a laptop worktree, resolve conflicts preserving both sides' features per the workflow prompt, verify, and land the sync as a PR. This issue is maintained by the jules-daily-upstream-sync workflow: repeat failures queue a follow-up task on this same issue instead of opening a duplicate; close it once a sync run succeeds.

- The automated upstream sync workflow succeeds on current main, or its failure is diagnosed to a named root cause

- A subsequent scheduled sync run is green

body:
**Status: proposed — no maintainer decision needed** (no user-facing surface, no changed default, no new control; consolidation of behaviour the per-site fixes already chose, following the precedents of #802, #976, #1254 and #1391).

## Summary

The fleet has bounded how much OpenChamber's provider reads *fetch* (#802 response bodies, #1254 file contents, #1391 directory walks) and stopped the loops that would not stop (#1313/#1315/#1317/#1320/#1322 cursor-walk page caps). The opposite failure — a collection read that stops too early and presents the prefix as the whole — never got a contract, and the last two days produced a family of nine, one per surface:

- **#1375 (closed)** — `/pulls/context` silently truncated files, issue comments and review comments at the first 100; the response carried no truncation signal.
- **#1377 (closed)** — board pickers truncated labels and reviewer candidates at the first 100 on both providers (GitHub page-1-only; GitLab `maxPages: 1`), no signal — openchamber itself has 120 labels.
- **#1383 (closed)** — `/issues/comments` truncated at the first 100, filed as "#1375 residual, distinct route".
- **#1405 (closed)** — checks summary read only the first 100 check runs: a failing run on page 3 was dropped and the summary reported **success** (probe: 250 runs → state success, total 100).
- **#1414 (closed)** — Linear comments truncated at 50 (`first: 50`, no `pageInfo`, no signal), unlike `subIssuesMore` in the same file.
- **#1418 (closed)** — GraphQL check summaries truncated contexts at `first: 100` with no `totalCount`, so a failing context past 100 reported success — "#1405 GraphQL twin".
- **#1419 (closed)** — reference detail truncated reviews/threads/replies with no `totalCount`, unlike `commentTotal`/`commitTotal` in the same query.
- **#1420 (closed)** — annotations capped at 150 by a hand-rolled `page<=3` catch-break loop "left behind when sibling collections moved to `readTotalCountCollection`", no signal.
- **#1427 (closed)** — reference search/detail truncated labels (`first: 6`) and review requests (`first: 30`) with no `totalCount`, unlike every sibling connection in the same queries.

Two open residuals: **#1496** (queue/queued — PR-status search fallback reads one page of 20 global results with no `total_count` check and returns another owner's PR; it runs exactly when the list path reported `coverage.authoritative === false`, so the module has a completeness concept its search path ignores) and **#1500** (queue/queued — the write-side twin: APNs relay `slice(0, 100)`s the token group and drops the rest while the direct path sends to all). Both are cited as evidence, NOT adopted — their queue lifecycles are untouched.

**The correct embodiments already exist — unnamed, in two shapes** (verified on origin/main `158df18debd972f7e82a81235c12161925254620`):

- `packages/web/server/lib/github/routes.js` carries three private readers with the *error* disposition: `readPullContextCollection` (:143), `readTotalCountCollection` (:169 — paginate to a short page, probe one page past the cap, error when the probe is non-empty; `total_count` honoured both ways), `readCheckRunAnnotations` (~:203 — plain-array payload, page errors propagate instead of returning pages-so-far). Their own comment states the rule: a partial list is never summarised as complete.
- `packages/web/server/lib/github/pr-summaries.js` carries the *signal* disposition for GraphQL: `contexts(first: 100)` requested **with** `totalCount` (:35-36); `summarizeCheckContexts` (:156-157) returns `{ state: 'unknown', incomplete: true, contextsTotal }` when the total exceeds what was fetched — incomplete degrades to unknown, never success (#1430 landed the UI-side gating).

What is missing is the contract that names these: the REST readers are private to one 3,655-line file, the GraphQL shape lives in one module, `lib/gitlab/` and `lib/linear/` fixed their sites with no shared shape to adopt, and `pr-status.js`'s `coverage` is a third local spelling. Nine filings in two days — three explicitly residuals/twins of a sibling fix — say the forgetting is systematic.

Out of scope: cursor walks that loop too long (#1313/#1315/#1317/#1320/#1322 — the opposite failure), response bodies (#802), file contents (#1254), directory walks (#1391), the server's own JSON state files (#976).

## The contract

1. **A collection read is complete, or it says so.** Every provider collection read feeding a list or a verdict either exhausts under a named page cap (short page ends it; probe one page past the cap; a non-empty probe is incompleteness, never an ending) or returns its completeness with the items — the provider's total where offered (`total_count`, GraphQL `totalCount`, a `*More` flag) plus an explicit incomplete flag when the items are a proper prefix. Presenting a prefix as the whole is not a disposition.
2. **Two named dispositions, chosen by the consumer.** *Verdict* (checks, PR status — output is a state word): incompleteness is an error (the `routes.js` shape) or degrades the verdict to explicit unknown/incomplete (the `pr-summaries.js` shape); never the affirmative verdict. *Display* (pickers, detail, comments): items plus the rule-1 signal, so the UI can say "showing X of Y". The disposition is recorded at the call site.
3. **One shared implementation per transport, one result shape across providers.** The three `routes.js` readers become `github/collections.js`; GraphQL connections bounded by `first:`/`last:` request `totalCount` (the `pr-summaries.js` contexts shape is the reference). GitLab/Linear keep their transport code but state completeness in the same shape. Cap *values* stay per-collection — completeness is not unboundedness; the caps stay, hitting one is explicit.
4. **Search is a collection.** A search-backed read states its coverage (the `pr-status.js` `coverage.authoritative` precedent): scoped to resolved targets, and a result from an admitted incomplete search is labelled with that coverage — never a definitive hit or miss. (#1496 is this rule's open instance; phase 3.)
5. **Fan-out follows the same rule.** A batched send/write covers the whole set (chunking at the batch size) or reports the uncovered remainder; slice-and-drop is the write-side form of the same defect. (#1500; phase 3.)

Full design doc: `files/designs/openchamber-collection-completeness.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace (problem, evidence, alternatives, risks, open questions).

## Phased breakdown

- **Phase 1 — the shared readers + the contract (filed as a sub-issue).** Move the three private REST readers from `github/routes.js` into new `github/collections.js`, behaviour-identical (same caps, probe discipline, error messages), `routes.js` importing them; state the contract (rules 1–3, two dispositions, GraphQL `totalCount` reference shape) in `github/DOCUMENTATION.md`. No call site changes behaviour; no new adoption yet.
- **Phase 2 — the inventory audit (filed as a sub-issue).** Enumerate every fixed-size collection read across `lib/github` (REST page-1/`per_page` without a total check; GraphQL `first:`/`last:` without `totalCount`), `lib/gitlab`, `lib/linear`, and web routes reading provider collections directly; disposition each in an inventory posted on the issue — *exhausts* / *signals* / *verdict-guarded* / *justified cap* (recorded reason the prefix is the product). Undispositioned sites get a per-site issue filed (one per surface), never a fix inside the audit. The audit changes no behaviour.
- **Phase 3 — NOT filed (open questions in the design doc).** Disposition of the open residuals #1496/#1500 (queued with their own acceptance — migration vs superseded-by-adoption belongs to their queue holders), GitLab/Linear migrations onto the shared shape (scope comes from phase 2's inventory), UI language for truncated display lists, VS Code shape parity (the standing phase-3 question of #802/#976/#1254/#1391 — not filed a fifth time), and a `check:changed` ratchet (same standing question — not filed a fourth time).

<!-- filed by repo-design-architect, design pass 2026-11-03 -->

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Phase 1 lands: `lib/github/collections.js` holds the three readers with their current semantics, `routes.js` imports them, existing route tests pass unchanged in expectation, and `lib/github/DOCUMENTATION.md` states the completeness contract and its two dispositions.
- [ ] Phase 2 lands: a posted inventory dispositions every fixed-size collection read in `lib/github`, `lib/gitlab`, `lib/linear` and the direct web-route reads; every undispositioned site found has its own filed issue linked from the inventory.
- [ ] Phase 3 items (#1496, #1500, GitLab/Linear adoption, UI language, VS Code, ratchet) are each dispositioned — migrated, filed, or recorded as superseded — not silently dropped.

body:
Open questions Drew recorded on #612 (2026-10-28) as living with the design. #612 itself is closing (all three phases landed: #524 via PR #620, #525 via PR #619, #614 doc+fixture), so the questions move here.

1. **watcherReady source:** session-runtime tracks no readiness flag today — nothing records whether the event subscription feeding `sessionActivityPhases` is live. Phase 1 pins honest semantics (never a fabricated `true`), but which in-process signal should own this long-term — the event-stream connection state, or the first-event-received mark?
2. **toolInFlight tracking:** no per-session in-process tool tracking exists today, so phase 1 ships `toolInFlight: null` (explicit unknown). Is adding real tool-part tracking in scope for a later phase, or does the contract keep it null until the upstream event model changes?

Neither blocked phase 1. Answering either amends the contract doc (`packages/web/server/lib/opencode/DOCUMENTATION.md`) and the conformance fixture from #614.

Parent design: #612 (closed, all phases landed).

body:
## Problem

When several sessions run on one pool target and that target's plan runs out, OpenCode fails all of them over in the same moment. Each one lands on a model with a cold prompt cache, so they all pay the full uncached context at once. Two sessions on two targets with separate quotas lose only one cache when one quota runs out.

## What happens today

- A target goes on `quotaCooldownMs` after a quota error, or is passed over once it reaches `budgets.<target>.softLimit`. Both apply to the target as a whole.
- Sessions pinned to it stay there until the provider refuses a request, then all move together.
- OpenCode keeps each session's chosen target in memory (`sessionTarget`, `continuityOf` in `packages/core/src/model-route.ts`) and has no API to move one session. Route overrides in `route-overrides.json` have no session scope, so an `avoid` moves every session at once.

## Plan

OpenChamber moves the sessions on a target one at a time before its plan runs dry, by setting each session's model to a sibling target through OpenCode's session model API. Defaults, chosen in the 2026-10-22 session:

1. **Off by default.** One switch in Settings, Routing, Model pools, Pool health.
2. **Trigger.** The target's linked plan projects to 70 percent or more of its quota window, and two or more sessions are on it.
3. **Pace.** One session per pool every 5 minutes, adjustable from 1 to 60.
4. **Order.** Subagent sessions first, then the primary session that has been idle longest, since its cache is the coldest.
5. **Destination.** Another target in the same pool that is not linked to the same plan and is not near its own limit. With no such target, nothing moves.
6. **Skipped.** Sessions on Auto, because Auto picks the model again on every send.
7. **What the user sees.** The Pool health panel lists recent moves with the session, the old target and the new one.

A moved session leaves the pool, so it no longer fails over inside it. That's the cost of the only per-session control OpenChamber has.

## Related

- #149 is a different cache problem, where tool toggles change the cached prefix.

## Acceptance criteria

Defaults from the body's plan, as criteria:
- [ ] Off by default; one switch in Settings → Routing → Model pools → Pool health turns staggered rotation on.
- [ ] Trigger: a target's linked plan projects to ≥70% of its quota window AND two or more sessions are on the target.
- [ ] Pace: at most one session per pool every 5 minutes, adjustable from 1 to 60 minutes.
- [ ] Order: subagent sessions first (see #296), then the primary session idle longest.
- [ ] Destination: another target in the same pool not linked to the same plan and not near its own limit; with no such target, nothing moves.
- [ ] Sessions on Auto are skipped.
- [ ] The Pool health panel lists recent moves with the session, the old target and the new target.
- [ ] A moved session's new model is set through OpenCode's session model API; no route-override `avoid` is used (it would move every session at once).

body:
This comes from the second item in `TODO.md`. It is a proposal that needs the maintainer's decision before code, per `CLAUDE.md`.

## Problem

`state.json` and `draining.json` are version-1 files with ad-hoc validation. A handoff is inferred from whatever state exists at startup, and ownership of an OpenCode process is inferred from `ps`. A crash in the middle of a handoff leaves no record of which step it reached.

## Idea

One versioned store that records each OpenCode generation: pid, port, binary, args, fingerprint and a state (`starting`, `active`, `draining`, `closed`). A write-ahead handoff record names the predecessor, the successor, the busy set at the switch and the outcome.

## Needs

- A migration path from version 1.
- A reaper that reads the store and stops inferring ownership from `ps`.
- Tests that replay a crash between each handoff step.

## Relation to other work

It is the data side of the supervisor issue (upgrade without dropped sessions). They can land separately, but the supervisor needs a store it can trust.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The maintainer approves a schema.
- [ ] Every handoff step has a crash-replay test.
- [ ] A version-1 install migrates with no lost generations.
