body:
### Context & Background
In OpenChamber upstream PR #4712 / commit `2b94db8470`, upstream added `awaitAnswer` support to the `openchamber_render` tool (`render.page` action). This allows agents to render an interactive HTML page containing UI buttons/tiles in the chat. The server holds the tool request open until the user clicks an option, which calls `openchamber.submit(data, summary)` via an MCP Apps `ui/message` request, sending the structured answer back to the agent in the same turn without requiring the user to type in chat.

In our fork (`developing-today`), we introduced model routing with three standardized tiers:
- `cheap` (fast, cost-effective models like Claude 3.5 Haiku, GPT-4o-mini)
- `standard` (generalist models like GPT-4o)
- `frontier` (flagship reasoning models like Claude 3.5 Sonnet)
along with official `models.dev` token catalog pricing.

### Feature Objective
Implement an interactive Model Tier Chooser and Quota Fallback UI using `render.page({ awaitAnswer: true })` whenever:
1. Routing needs a user choice (e.g., ambiguous prompt, or explicit `/route` command without arguments).
2. A provider quota error (HTTP 429) or token window limit is reached during agent execution.

Instead of writing out long text instructions in chat, the agent renders an interactive choice card with styled option tiles and pricing info. Clicking a tile returns the selected tier/provider to the agent immediately.

---

### Specifications

#### 1. Interactive Route Chooser HTML Card
When routing decision requires user confirmation or selection:
- The agent calls `openchamber_render` with `action: 'render.page'` and parameters:
  - `title`: `"Select Execution Tier"`
  - `awaitAnswer`: `true`
  - `html`: An HTML card using OpenChamber's native CSS variables and styling classes (`font-sans`, CSS vars `--bg-base`, `--text-primary`, `--border-base`, `--accent-primary`):
    - Option 1 (Cheap): Model name, input/output cost per 1M tokens from `models.dev`, estimated latency.
    - Option 2 (Standard): Model name, pricing, general capabilities.
    - Option 3 (Frontier): Model name, pricing, deep coding benchmark tier.
    - Each tile contains a button that calls `openchamber.submit({ tier: "cheap", model: "<model_id>" }, "Selected Cheap Tier (<model_id>)")`.

#### 2. Live 429 / Quota Fallback Card
When a model API call returns a 429 rate limit or quota exceeded:
- Rather than immediately terminating the turn or failing, the agent or error handler invokes `render.page` with `awaitAnswer: true`:
  - `title`: `"Quota Limit Reached"`
  - Options presented as interactive tiles:
    1. **"Switch Provider (Frontier)"**: Fallback to alternate frontier model (e.g. Anthropic Sonnet -> OpenAI GPT-4o / O1).
    2. **"Downgrade to Standard/Cheap"**: Switch to an available model tier with active quota.
    3. **"Wait for Window Reset"**: Wait for quota window reset (with countdown timer if known).
- Clicking an option submits `{ action: "fallback", provider: "...", tier: "..." }`, allowing the agent to switch credentials or model and resume the task in the same turn.

#### 3. Agent Tool & Skill Coordination
- Provide a helper template or skill snippet in OpenCode/OpenChamber (`packages/core/src/tool/plugin/` or `packages/web/server/lib/openchamber-control/`) to generate the standardized HTML card with valid styling and click handlers.
- Ensure the result payload handled in `packages/ui/src/lib/renderPageAnswer.ts` and `packages/web/server/lib/openchamber-control/render-page.js` passes the structured tier data cleanly back into the session context.

---

### Key Files & References
- `packages/web/server/lib/openchamber-control/render-page.js`: `createPageAnswers`, `wait`, `submitAnswer`, `RENDER_PAGE_WHEN`

body:
## Problem

`PUT /api/behavior/agents-md` replaces the user's global OpenCode behavior prompt with `fs.promises.writeFile(AGENTS_MD_PATH, content, 'utf8')`. A direct `writeFile` truncates the destination before writing. If the write fails partway (for example, ENOSPC/EIO or process interruption), the old prompt is lost and the file may be empty or partial; a concurrent OpenCode reader can also observe the truncate/write window.

This is inconsistent with `/api/fs/write`, which explicitly writes to a temporary sibling and renames it so concurrent readers do not see an empty file during the `O_TRUNC` window. `AGENTS.md` is consumed as OpenCode behavior configuration, so loss or partial reads can silently change session instructions.

## Evidence

- `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/routes.js:713-762`: the PUT handler validates the optional expected-content conflict check and then directly writes the target at line 759.
- `packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.js:1690-1700`: the filesystem write route uses a temp sibling and `renameWithRetry`, with a comment explicitly citing avoidance of the `O_TRUNC` reader window.
- Existing `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/config-paths.test.js:86-230` tests final content and size/read behavior, but does not establish preservation of the old file when replacement fails or atomic visibility to readers.
- Fresh all-state searches for `agents-md`, `behavior/agents-md`, and AGENTS.md atomic writing found no matching open issue or PR. Closed #1132/#1151/#1410 cover read size gates, not write atomicity.

## Acceptance criteria

- Replace the global AGENTS.md without exposing a truncated/partial destination to readers; a failed replacement preserves the previous file.
- Clean up the temporary file on failure and retain the existing size and expected-content conflict behavior.
- Add a focused regression test for failed replacement preserving the old file (and cover atomic replacement semantics as practical).
- Explicitly consider the current direct-write symlink behavior: the bounded GET rejects non-regular files, while rename-based replacement would replace a symlink rather than follow it.

body:
## Problem

`state.windowGeometryRevisions` retains an entry for every window that has had geometry persisted. `debounceWindowStatePersist` increments and stores the revision at `packages/electron/main.mjs:923-927`; when its timer completes, it deletes only the timer at `:936-938`. The `BrowserWindow` `closed` handler at `:2746-2762` does not clear either map. Repository-wide search on current main found no other cleanup or reader of these entries. The main process therefore accumulates per-window revision state over repeated window lifetimes.

## Required fix

- Remove/invalidate the window revision and timer state when debounce completes and when the window closes.
- Ensure a stale timer callback cannot persist after close or delete state belonging to a newer revision/timer.
- Preserve main-window geometry persistence behavior.

## Tests

Add focused tests covering repeated geometry updates, debounce completion, and closing while a timer is pending. Assert closed-window IDs do not remain in either map and stale callbacks do not persist. No existing tests directly cover these symbols.

body:
## Evidence

On current `origin/main` (`a52ae96a69ca24b9117e0eed2fd1ea01fc92da8c`), `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/skill-routes.js:887-897` parses `scope` and `source` with `asNonEmptyString`. Express supplies an array for a repeated query parameter. If `scope` is repeated while `source` is absent, both values become null; the `if (scope || source)` validation is skipped, and `deleteSkill` is called without a location.

I reproduced this against the live Express route with a temporary project and an instrumented delete callback:

```text
DELETE /api/config/skills/repro-skill?scope=user&scope=project
HTTP 200
 deleteSkill(..., location) received location = undefined
```

`packages/web/server/lib/opencode/skills.js:724-770` documents and implements the no-location behavior as deleting every copy in project and user directories. Thus a malformed/repeated scope query can silently broaden a requested scoped deletion to all copies. The same fail-open shape applies to repeated `source` when `scope` is absent. When the other field is present as a valid string, the allowlist does return 400, which is why the malformed single-field case matters.

## Why it matters

A malformed query or client that repeats only one optional filter can delete same-named skills outside the intended scope/source, including the user's copy when the request intended a project copy. This is destructive and the response reports success rather than rejecting the ambiguous request.

## Acceptance criteria

- Reject repeated/non-string `scope` or `source` values with HTTP 400 before calling `deleteSkill`; never fall back to an unscoped delete when a filter was supplied but malformed.
- Preserve documented behavior when both filters are absent (delete all copies), and targeted deletion for valid single scope/source values.
- Add route regression coverage for repeated `scope` alone, repeated `source` alone, both repeated, valid targeted filters, and absent filters; assert malformed cases leave all copies untouched.

body:
## Finding

The scheduled-task run-history endpoint still silently widens a filtered request into an unfiltered one when `since` or `until` is supplied more than once. PR #2342 (for #2155) made a supplied malformed string bound a 400, but its guard only fires for string values: a repeated parameter arrives from Express as an array, `parseTime` returns `undefined` for any non-string, and `parseTimeFilter` only errors when `typeof value === 'string'`, so the array falls through as `{ value: undefined }` — "no filter" — and the handler returns the full history with HTTP 200 and no signal to the client. That is exactly the silent-widening defect #2155 set out to remove, reached through the repeated-parameter shape instead of a malformed string. The sibling fix for the same endpoint's `limit` in PR #2344 (#2156) explicitly treats a repeated limit as a 400, so this route already has the intended judgement for repeats — `since`/`until` were left out of it.

## Evidence

- Source PR: #2342 "fix(web): reject malformed scheduled-task run-history time filters" — MERGED 2026-11-17T02:15:43Z, head `49832c149a5a`, merge commit `c738c57930bfcaf126646a2f54fb0bad5f572c4e` (ancestor-verified against current main: compare behind=0).
- PR #2342's diff (`packages/web/server/lib/scheduled-tasks/routes.js`): `parseTimeFilter` returns an error only when `typeof value === 'string' && value.length > 0 && parsed === undefined`; the new tests in `run-history-routes.test.js` cover malformed `since`/`until` strings, valid epoch/date strings, and absent bounds — no repeated-parameter case.
- Verified verbatim on current main `7ca8f6c388225dcb749f77c2956bb3e2637254df`: `routes.js:49-55` `parseTime` returns `undefined` when `typeof value !== 'string'`; `routes.js:56-62` `parseTimeFilter` errors only for strings; `routes.js:63-70` forwards `since.value`/`until.value` to `listRuns`. A repeated `?since=100&since=200` (Express array) therefore reaches `listRuns` as `since: undefined`.
- That a repeated query parameter arrives as an array on this stack is the pinned premise of merged PR #2338 in the same batch ("A repeated query parameter arrives as an array and is ambiguous", `project-directory-runtime.js`) and of PR #2344's repeated-`limit` 400 for this very route.

## Why it matters

Run history is evidence for what a scheduled task did. A client (or a hand-built URL) that serializes a bound twice — the same ambiguity the repo has been systematically rejecting on sibling routes (#2121, #2123, #2291, #2292, #2312) — silently gets the unfiltered history it explicitly asked to narrow, with a 200 that looks like a correct filtered answer. The route's own two recent fixes establish the house rule for this handler: supplied-but-invalid means 400, never a silent fallback.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A repeated `since` or `until` on `GET /api/projects/:projectId/scheduled-tasks/run-history` returns HTTP 400 naming the parameter, and `listRuns` is not called (mirroring PR #2344's repeated-`limit` handling on the same route).
- [ ] Single valid epoch-millisecond and date-string bounds, and absent/empty bounds, behave exactly as today (existing `run-history-routes.test.js` cases keep passing).
- [ ] New route-level regression tests cover repeated `since` and repeated `until`.

body:
## Problem

Three local-file readers on the VS Code extension's quota surface buffer
their files whole, synchronously, with no size gate and no regular-file
check — in the single-threaded extension host:

- `packages/vscode/src/quotaCredentials.ts:29` — `readCredential` does
  `JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(target(provider), 'utf8'))` on
  `quota/<provider>.json` (the exe-dev / cursor / zenmux credential
  files, secrets at rest). It is called on quota status/fetch paths
  (`quotaProviders.ts:957-958`, `:1058`, `:2646`, `:2715`) and from
  `bridge-system-runtime.ts`.
- `packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.ts:351-356` — the shared
  `readJsonFile` helper does `fs.existsSync` + `fs.readFileSync` whole.
  Its callers read credential-bearing files: `resolveAntigravityAuth`
  (:1249, the `antigravity-accounts.json` paths at :286-287) and
  `readMuseAccountToken` (:4040, `~/.config/muse/auth.json`).
- `packages/vscode/src/quotaProviders.ts:4553` —
  `readKiloOrganizationIdFromUserConfig` does
  `JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(configPath, 'utf8'))` on
  `OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR/opencode.json` whole; it is the default
  `readOrganizationId` for `fetchKiloQuota` (:4570).

The same package already has the bounded pattern: `opencodeConfig.ts`
reads config files through a handle-bounded read capped at
`MAX_CONFIG_FILE_BYTES` = 4 MiB, and this package's quota *response*
bodies are byte-capped (`bounded-response-body.ts`, #1282/#1298). These
local-file readers are the ungated outliers. The web server's own quota
credential store is tracked separately in #1613.

## Why it matters

A synchronous `readFileSync` that blocks blocks the whole extension
host. A FIFO (or device, or pathologically grown file) at any of these
paths freezes every bridge request, the chat panel and the quota
surfaces — not one request. An oversized but well-formed file is
buffered and parsed whole in extension-host memory on every quota poll.
These are also secrets files: the failure mode should be a bounded,
named rejection, not unbounded buffering of credential material.

## Evidence (this run, laptop probe against the real modules)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-oc-vscode-quota-ungated-20261105/probe.test.js`
on the laptop, `bun test`, importing the real `quotaCredentials.ts` and
`quotaProviders.ts` from the laptop primary at origin/main
`c11726d32e12230ccd5353a85a0c852dfca3ad36`, with `vscode` mocked and
`OPENCHAMBER_DATA_DIR` / `OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR` pointed at scratch dirs.
Run twice, identical results:

- Control: a small `exe-dev.json` credential read back normally
  (`CONTROL_CRED tok-control`); a small Kilo `opencode.json` produced
  the expected `x-kilocode-organizationid` header (`org-control`).
- Oversize: a credential whose `usageToken` is 33,554,432 chars was
  returned whole (`OVERSIZE_CRED_LEN 33554432`); a 33,554,432-char
  padding field placed *before* the provider block in `opencode.json`
  was parsed whole and the organization id after it still extracted
  (`OVERSIZE_KILO true org-probe-big`) — no rejection at any size.
- FIFO: with `exe-dev.json` replaced by a FIFO, `readCredential` never
  returned — the probe was killed by `timeout` (exit 124), twice.

The `readJsonFile` call sites (:1249, :4040) were verified by code read
(identical whole-buffer `fs.readFileSync` pattern behind the shared
helper at :356); the probe exercised the credential and Kilo-config
paths directly.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] All three readers (quotaCredentials :29, quotaProviders
      `readJsonFile` :356 and the Kilo config read :4553) go through a
      bounded, regular-file-checked read with a named byte cap per
      file, sized from each file's legitimate shape (credential files
      hold a few short tokens; `opencode.json` is already capped at
      4 MiB on save/read by `opencodeConfig.ts`).
- [ ] Over-cap and non-regular files degrade exactly as a read failure
      does today per reader — credential → `null`, `readJsonFile` →
      `null`, Kilo organization id → `null` — and no path parses a
      too-large file whole.
- [ ] Normal small files behave byte-for-byte as today, including the
      Antigravity account selection and the Muse token extraction.
- [ ] Regression tests pin an over-cap file for each reader and a FIFO
      at the credential path returning promptly instead of blocking;
      the existing vscode quota suites stay green.
- [ ] `packages/vscode/src/DOCUMENTATION.md` notes the caps alongside
      the existing bounded-read entries.

Found by: new-issue-creator-openchamber run, 2026-11-05 03:50 CST.
Related: #1613 (web-server quota credential store twin), #1641 (same
package's bridge settings readers), #1282/#1298 (quota response bodies,
already capped — this is the local-file side).

body:
The scheduled `opencode-update` workflow failed on main in run 45238211230 while building `.#openchamber` after updating the OpenCode input to `00595a6537f00bf3bfc239f41532cf10e0d69045`.

title: fix(web): scope POST /api/fs/clone destinationPath to the active workspace

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

body:
## Problem

`POST /api/fs/clone` resolves its clone target with no workspace containment, so any normally-authenticated caller can materialize arbitrary remote repo content at any server-writable path. Every other mutating fs route enforces the workspace boundary; clone — the route that writes whole trees of attacker-controlled bytes — does not.

In `packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.ts:1030-1134` the legacy clone handler computes:

`resolvedDestination = path.resolve(normalizeDirectoryPath(destination))` (:1049)

and delegates it straight to `cloneRepository` (:1096-1101). It never calls `resolveWorkspacePathFromContext`, `containedPath`, or `containedMkdirPath`, and `req` is otherwise unused. The Git service side does not scope it either: `planWithDeadline` in `packages/web/server/lib/git/network-operation-plan.ts` has no workspace/contained/outside logic, and the first-party planned-clone path goes through the same unscoped destination.

Contrast, same file:
- write (:1701-1719): `resolveWorkspacePathFromContext` + `containedWritePath`, outside → 403
- delete (:1947…), rename (:2013-2047, `containedRenamePaths`), mkdir (:1000-1014, `containedMkdirPath`), upload (403 `outside-workspace` per DOCUMENTATION.md:317)

## Evidence (live route probe, since removed)

Registered the real `registerFsRoutes` (project directory `/repo`, ENOENT stat/access, stub `cloneRepository`):

- `POST /api/fs/clone` `{ destinationPath: '/outside/evil' }` → **200 `{ success: true, path: '/outside/evil' }`, delegated as `/outside/evil`** — accepted with no project check
- `POST /api/fs/write` `{ path: '/outside/evil.txt' }` (control) → **400 `Path is outside of active workspace`**

The repo's own clone tests encode the gap: `routes.test.js` `fs clone` cases clone to `/workspace/…`, `/private/work/…`, `/new/repo` while the project directory is `/repo`, asserting success — no test asserts an outside destination is refused.

## Why it matters

Clone writes attacker-controlled content (repo files, symlinks, git config) rather than caller-supplied bytes. The destination-exists guard (409) stops direct overwrites but not creation of new paths anywhere the server user can write (dotfiles, autostart entries, config dirs). The route's transport confirmation (`unverifiedConfirmed`) gates *which remote*, not *where it lands*. Reads of outside paths need explicit `allowOutsideWorkspace=true`; clone has no equivalent opt-in — it is unscoped by default.

Siblings fixed, none covering clone: #2455 (deletes), #2457 (mkdir), #2476 (write/delete/rename), #2520 (reveal), #2458 + #2564 (read/stat symlink escapes). No open/closed issue and no open PR covers the clone destination.

## Suggested fix shape

Resolve `destinationPath` through `resolveWorkspacePathFromContext` + `containedMkdirPath` (same as mkdir/write) before the inferred-name/exists logic, so symlink parents and alias bases are canonicalized the same way. Alternatively require `allowOutsideWorkspace=true` parity with the read routes. Either way:

- in-workspace destination (incl. trailing-separator and existing-directory name inference) → delegated unchanged
- outside-workspace destination → 403/400 `outside-workspace`, `cloneRepository` never called

Also consider: `deriveCloneDirectoryName` blocks `..` but permits `\`, which is a separator on win32 — worth a separator check alongside the scoping fix.

## Acceptance

- New route test: project `/repo`, `destinationPath: '/outside/evil'` → refused with an outside-workspace error and `cloneRepository` not called (mirror of the probe above)
- Existing clone inference/exists/redaction tests keep passing

title: workflow-audit: fail caller jobs that under-grant the called workflow's declared permissions
body:
## Problem

`.github/scripts/audit-workflow-caller-jobs.py` (the #1399 guard) checks reusable-workflow caller jobs for disallowed *keys*, but not for under-granting: a caller job whose `permissions:` are narrower than the permissions the called workflow's jobs declare. That is exactly the defect that killed every Canary run at startup with zero jobs in #2554 — the `build-android` / `build-ios` caller jobs granted only `contents: write` while `mobile-release.yml` jobs need `actions: read`, and the audit passed the file throughout.

## Proposed check

For each caller job of a local reusable workflow (`uses: ./.github/workflows/<file>`), compute the union of permissions declared by the called workflow (its job-level `permissions:` blocks, floored by its top-level `permissions:`), and fail the caller when its effective grant does not cover that union, naming the missing scope(s).

## Acceptance

- A fixture caller that under-grants (e.g. `contents: write` only, calling a workflow whose jobs declare `actions: read`) fails the audit, naming `actions`.
- A fixture caller whose grant covers the called workflow's union passes.
- The audit stays clean over the repo's current `.github/workflows/` (post-#2554 fix, `release.yml` and `canary.yml` both cover `mobile-release.yml`'s union of `actions: read` + `contents: write`).

Origin: prepared by Lane TV during the #2554 triage and offered there as a follow-on; filed by lane felix alongside queue task 21314's fix PR #2558 so the guard extension is its own reviewable change.

title: fix(vscode): save the global AGENTS.md, prompt, plugin and skill files atomically — the web side is fixed, the extension bridge still writes in place

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator

labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Problem

The VS Code extension bridge saves the same OpenCode-watched files the web server just learned to replace atomically, but it still writes them in place. A direct `writeFile` truncates the destination before writing bytes, so an interrupted or failed write (ENOSPC/EIO, crash, power loss) destroys the previous content and leaves an empty or partial file; a concurrent OpenCode reader can also observe the truncate window.

## Evidence (origin/main 54a18447)

- `packages/vscode/src/bridge-config-runtime.ts:255-256`: `api:behavior/agents-md:save` validates the UTF-8 byte cap, then `await fs.promises.writeFile(AGENTS_MD_PATH, content, 'utf8')` directly on the user's global `OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR/AGENTS.md` (path defined at line 99).
- `packages/vscode/src/opencodeConfig.ts:601-604` (`writePromptFile`), `:1756` (plugin-dir write) and `:3625-3631` (`writeSkillSupportingFile`): the same three writers the web side just converted to `writeFileAtomic` still `fs.writeFileSync` in place. They are reachable from the bridge: `bridge-config-runtime.ts:990` calls `writeSkillSupportingFile`, and `opencodeConfig.ts:2601,2825` call `writePromptFile` on agent/template saves.
- The extension already imports the shared helper (`opencodeConfig.ts:22,1304,2339` and `plugin-switches.ts:4,39` use `writeFileAtomic`), so the fix is a call-site change, not new plumbing.

Mechanism repro (node, scratch checkout): an 8 MiB file reduced to 10 bytes after an open(O_TRUNC) + partial write + close — the content before the crash point is unrecoverable. The handler's code path above shows the same O_TRUNC-first shape.

## Why it matters

AGENTS.md is consumed as OpenCode behavior configuration, and prompt/plugin/skill files are watched by OpenCode — a torn save silently changes session instructions. The web surface was hardened twice for exactly this failure mode; the extension bridge exposes the same loss through a different entry point.

## Dedupe

- #2441 CLOSED / fixed by #2443 (merge f79d2747c): web `PUT /api/behavior/agents-md` only — diff touches `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/routes.js` + its test, nothing under `packages/vscode/`.
- #2378 CLOSED / fixed on main (53e0f09ad): web `writePromptFile`, `writeSkillSupportingFile`, `writePluginDirFile` and the snippet writer routed through `writeFileAtomic` — web files only, vscode copies untouched.
- Open #2506 (workflow.save writes in place), #2363 (/api/fs/write drops mode), #2515 (save-image/save-markdown caps) are different files/defects.
- All-state and open-issue searches for vscode atomic writes and agents-md atomic handling found no tracker for the vscode path.

## Acceptance criteria

- Replace the global AGENTS.md via the vscode bridge without exposing a truncated/partial destination to readers; a failed replacement preserves the previous file and cleans up the temp file.
- Route the vscode `writePromptFile`, plugin-dir write and `writeSkillSupportingFile` through the shared `writeFileAtomic` helper (mode/symlink semantics as appropriate).
- Keep the existing byte-size caps and expected-content/conflict behavior.
- Add a focused regression test for failed replacement preserving the old file (same shape as the web config-paths atomic test).

title: fix(vscode): contain api:fs:mkdir targets to the workspace or chats root

labels.name: kind/security
labels.description: Security issue or security hardening

body:
## Evidence

`packages/vscode/src/bridge-fs-runtime.ts` (`api:fs:mkdir` handler) resolves its target with `deps.resolveUserPath(...)` and passes the result straight to `vscode.workspace.fs.createDirectory`. There is no workspace containment check and no symlink resolution: an absolute path is used unchanged, and a workspace-relative path can escape through a symlinked ancestor. The handler is reachable — the webview routes `/api/fs/mkdir` POSTs to it (`packages/vscode/webview/main.tsx`), and the webview files API exposes it as `createDirectory`.

The web twin already enforces the intended contract (`packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.ts`, `POST /api/fs/mkdir`): a truthy `allowOutsideWorkspace` is refused without a trusted grant, and the target must canonicalize inside the workspace or an allowed managed root (the chats root), using the nearest-existing-ancestor canonicalization in `packages/web/server/lib/fs/workspace-target.ts`. The VS Code bridge handler ignores `allowOutsideWorkspace` entirely (the webview router does not even forward it) and performs no containment at all.

Found while working #2476: that issue's write/delete/rename handlers were removed as dead surface, leaving mkdir as the only reachable bridge filesystem mutation.

## Acceptance criteria

- `api:fs:mkdir` rejects targets whose canonical path (nearest existing ancestor resolved, remaining segments appended) falls outside the active workspace and outside the OpenChamber chats root, including symlink-ancestor escapes and unchecked absolute paths.
- A truthy `allowOutsideWorkspace` payload flag is refused, matching the web route's no-grant behaviour, and the webview `/api/fs/mkdir` route forwards the flag so the refusal can trigger.
- Legitimate creation keeps working: nested in-workspace directories, and the chats-root bootstrap directory used by the empty-window flow.
- Real-filesystem regression tests cover: outside absolute target rejected and not created, symlink escape rejected and not created, in-workspace symlink to an in-workspace directory still usable, in-workspace nested creation succeeds, chats-root creation succeeds, `allowOutsideWorkspace` refused.

title: fix(web): contain file-reveal requests to the active workspace
body:
## Evidence

`packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.ts:2070-2086` resolves `/api/fs/reveal` input with `path.resolve()` and checks only that the path exists before launching the host file browser. Unlike the adjacent read/list/mutation routes, it does not require the target to be within the active workspace or an explicit managed root. The VS Code bridge has the same gap at `packages/vscode/src/bridge-fs-runtime.ts:460-470`: it accepts an arbitrary path/URI and invokes `revealFileInOS` without containment.

This is reachable from rendered assistant Markdown: `packages/ui/src/components/chat/markdown/MarkdownLink.tsx:192,229-231` recognizes local `file://` links as folders and calls `revealPath`; the web runtime's `useRevealMarkdownPath` enables that behavior outside browser/VS Code runtimes. A model-emitted or otherwise untrusted file link can therefore cause the host UI to open/reveal an arbitrary existing path outside the workspace. This is a local file-browsing/privacy boundary, even though it does not read file contents.

## Why it matters

The reveal operation is a host-side capability. It should follow the same workspace/managed-root boundary as the neighboring filesystem operations rather than trusting a path supplied through rendered content.

## Acceptance criteria

- Resolve and validate reveal targets against the active workspace (and any intentionally supported managed roots) using canonical paths so symlink escapes are rejected.
- Apply equivalent containment in the VS Code bridge, or document and test a deliberate, narrowly scoped exception if reveal is intentionally broader there.
- Preserve supported reveal behavior for valid in-workspace files and directories.
- Add regression tests showing an outside path and a symlink escape are rejected, while an in-workspace path succeeds.

body:
## What happens

`server/lib/git/service.test.js` > createWorktree > "fails with the command output and drops the branch it made when the command fails" fails on the laptop against current main (`88ca37a75`), in a plain run and with a scrubbed environment. It is **not** one of the #2495 container failures: it fails identically with all local changes stashed, outside any container or namespace.

The test expects the create command's captured output to be exactly `source checkout is dirty`, but the received message is prefixed with a terminal title sequence:

```
- Worktree create command failed: source checkout is dirty
+ Worktree create command failed: ]0;
+ Command failed: echo "source checkout is dirty" >&2; exit 3
+ source checkout is dirty
```

(The `]0;` is the tail of an OSC 0 window-title escape, ESC `]0;` BEL.)

## Why it matters

The worktree create-command path captures the command's output into the user-facing failure message. On a machine whose shell startup emits a title sequence (or whose shell is wrapped by one), that sequence leaks into the message and the message no longer starts with the command's own words. The test's exact-match assertion is the only thing standing watch over that.

## Evidence

- `bunx vitest run server/lib/git/service.test.js -t "fails with the command output and drops the branch"` on the laptop, main @ `88ca37a75`: 1 failed. Same result with `env -i` (only HOME/PATH set) and with the #2495 worktree changes stashed.
- Found during the #2495 slice (lane-gh): in the non-reaping-init namespace run of the git file, this was the only failure (544 passed), and it reproduces outside the namespace too, so it is independent of the zombie-reaping failures.

## What to check first

Where the create command's shell is spawned: whether it runs through a login/interactive shell whose startup files emit the title sequence on this machine, and whether the output sanitiser for command failures should strip terminal escape sequences before the text becomes a user-facing message.

title: fix(vscode): bound api:files/save-image base64 decode (and save-markdown write) to the attachment cap
body:
## Finding

`api:files/save-image` in `packages/vscode/src/bridge-fs-runtime.ts:386-420` decodes an unbounded `dataUrl` with `Buffer.from(base64, 'base64')` and writes it with no size gate. The sibling read/attach paths are capped (`readUriAsAttachment` refuses over 20 MiB in `bridge-fs-helpers-runtime.ts:8,118,126`; `api:fs:read` refuses over 16 MiB at `bridge-fs-runtime.ts:64,255`), but this write side has neither an up-front base64-length check nor a decoded-byte check. A large image/data URL from the webview (or a pasted screenshot/canvas payload) is buffered whole in the extension host, so one oversized save can spike memory or OOM the extension host before `showSaveDialog` even matters. `Buffer.from` also silently skips invalid base64 characters, so a corrupt payload writes a corrupt file with success reported.

The adjacent `api:files/save-markdown` (`:422-449`) has the same shape: `content` is buffered whole via `Buffer.from(content, 'utf8')` with no byte cap.

Verified on `origin/main` `88ca37a75`: traced `webview/api/vscode.ts:26-32` (`saveImage`/`saveMarkdown` with `timeoutMs: 0`) through `webview/main.tsx:710-732` (`extractJsonBody`, itself uncapped in `requestBodyTransport.ts:78-81`) into the bridge handler. No handler-side or transport-side cap exists, and no test pins one (`grep save-image|save-markdown` under `packages/vscode/src` hits only the handler). Deduped: all-state `save-image` search is empty; `save-markdown` hits are only the closed write-stranding issue #1444 (plugin/skill/md parsers, a different surface); no open PR touches these handlers.

## Why it matters

The caps on the read side exist so a hostile or accidental oversized blob is never buffered whole. The save side defeats that protection in the worst direction: the oversized blob is created BY OpenChamber through its normal export flow (export image / export session), freezing or crashing the extension host that is doing the saving.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `api:files/save-image` rejects a payload whose decoded bytes would exceed the attachment cap (20 MiB, matching `MAX_FILE_ATTACH_SIZE_BYTES`) with the existing `{ success: false, error }` shape, preferably with an up-front base64-length check so the giant buffer is never allocated; a refused save writes nothing.
- [ ] `api:files/save-markdown` refuses `content` over a stated byte cap (UTF-8 bytes, e.g. the same 20 MiB or the 16 MiB fs-read cap) with the same error shape; a refused save writes nothing.
- [ ] Regression tests: over-cap image and markdown payloads are refused and write nothing; exactly-at-cap payloads succeed (mirroring the at-cap pins the read gates carry).

body:
## Evidence
In `packages/web/server/lib/appearance/project-icon-routes.ts`, the `PUT /api/projects/:projectId/icon` handler writes the new image at lines 505-512, then calls `removeProjectIconFiles(projectId, iconPath)` at line 512 before persisting the updated `iconImage` metadata at line 520. If `persistSettings` fails, the old metadata remains but its referenced icon file has already been removed; the new file is also not rolled back. The GET handler uses the metadata to select the stored icon path, so subsequent reads can return 404.

The `/discover` handler has the same ordering at lines 648-663: it writes and removes previous candidates before `persistResolvedSettings` commits the new metadata.

## Impact
A transient settings-write failure can turn a previously valid project icon into a broken reference. The endpoint returns 500, but the destructive file cleanup has already happened.

## Acceptance criteria
- Preserve the prior icon file and metadata until the new icon metadata is durably persisted.
- On persistence failure, clean up the newly written file and leave the previous icon readable.
- Apply the same failure-safe ordering to upload and discovery paths.
- Add regression tests that inject a settings persistence failure and verify the old icon remains readable and metadata unchanged.

title: fix(web): cloudflare quick-tunnel spawn error is not wired to the startup promise — startup hangs 30s on a misleading timeout

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Finding

In the cloudflared quick-tunnel startup path, a child-process spawn `error` (ENOENT/EACCES/EPERM) is only logged and does not settle the startup promise, so startup hangs until the 30s watchdog and reports a misleading "Tunnel URL not received within 30 seconds". The ngrok provider already handles this correctly, and the managed cloudflare path has the same gap.

## Evidence

Verified against `origin/main` at `598b45582`:

- `packages/web/server/lib/cloudflare-tunnel.ts:482-485`: `child.on('error')` logs and cleans the temp dir, but does not reject the promise created at `:497`. The promise settles on URL-ready (`:506-512`), child `exit` (`:514-527`), or the 30s timeout (`:498-504`). For a spawn failure no process exists, so no `exit` fires and the caller waits the full 30s.
- Contrast `packages/web/server/lib/ngrok-tunnel.ts:457-473`, where the startup promise handles the spawn error and settles immediately with the real failure.
- Same gap in the managed path: `waitForManagedTunnelReady` (`cloudflare-tunnel.ts:325-440`) registers no `error` handler; the managed remote/local callers' outside `child.on('error')` handlers (`:601-616`, `:680-689`) log/cleanup but do not settle the wait, so a spawn error surfaces after the ~20s hard timeout as "Timed out waiting for cloudflared..." with misleading config/credentials advice.
- No spawn-error test coverage found in `cloudflare-tunnel.test.js` for either path.

## Why it matters

The two most common startup failures (missing binary, bad permissions) produce the least helpful error after the longest wait, and the temp-dir cleanup ordering runs early from the error handler. Misleading timeouts send users debugging tunnel config/credentials instead of the actual spawn problem.

## Acceptance criteria

- A spawn `error` during quick-tunnel and managed-tunnel startup rejects the startup promise promptly with the spawn error (ngrok path is the in-repo pattern to mirror).
- Regression tests inject a spawn error and assert prompt rejection with the underlying error, not the 30s/20s timeout message. All-state searches found no open issue or PR covering this; #2508 (tunnel start-route cleanup) is the adjacent route-layer issue.

title: fix(web): global hub ignores durable appendTrim/appendReset/appendHead failures and appendReset drops queued writes — follow-up to #2111

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/high
labels.description: Important and time-sensitive

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Finding

Closed #2111 fixed one durable-append failure path: `global-hub` no longer treats a failed `durable.appendLocal()` as committed (`global-hub.ts:379-388` guards on the boolean return). The three sibling appends are not guarded — their `false` returns are ignored — so in-memory stream state still advances past what the durable file recorded. Worse, `appendReset` clears the store's queued pending writes while the hub has already advanced, losing previously failed writes entirely.

## Evidence

Verified against `origin/main` at `598b45582`:

- `packages/web/server/lib/event-stream/global-hub.ts:247-250`: `trimLocalEntries` advances `droppedLocalThroughPosition` then calls `durable.appendTrim(removedThrough)` and ignores the return.
- `global-hub.ts:343-344`: resync path advances `droppedLocalThroughPosition` then calls `durable.appendReset(...)`, ignoring the return — while `commitEvent` has already cleared `replay`, `localEntries`, and advanced `position`.
- `global-hub.ts:389-391`: upstream-event path calls `durable.appendHead(...)`, ignoring the return, even though the comment block at `:325-328` promises durable-first ordering.
- `packages/web/server/lib/event-stream/replay-store.js:320-345`: `appendHead`, `appendTrim`, and `appendReset` all return `false` on failed appends (contract documented at `:307-308`: "failed durable write nothing advances"). `appendReset` sets `pendingLines = []` (`:339`) *before* attempting the write, so a failed reset drops queued earlier writes that the store had deliberately retained.
- Consequence: after a failed trim/reset/head write and a restart, `createReplayStore().load()` returns stale durable state — trimmed local frames can be resurrected, pre-resync frames/head can be resurrected, or the durable head can lag behind the in-memory committed position, causing incorrect resume/replay. `event-stream/replay-store.test.js` covers the store contract, and `global-hub.test.js`/`global-resume.test.js` have no tests for durable `appendReset`/`appendHead`/`appendTrim` returning `false`.

## Why it matters

#2111's fix is incomplete: the same divergence it closed for local frames remains for trim, reset, and head advances. On disk-full/permission/EISDIR failures, clients can resume from cursors the durable store cannot back, silently missing replay events.

## Acceptance criteria

- `global-hub` honors the boolean returns of `appendTrim`/`appendReset`/`appendHead` the way it already does for `appendLocal`: in-memory state must not claim more than the file holds.
- A failed `appendReset` does not discard the store's queued pending writes.
- Add regression tests mirroring the #2111 coverage for each of the three paths (failed append → reload asserts durable state never advances past the failure). All-state searches found only closed #2111 and closed #2/#756/#1632; no open issue or PR covers these three paths.

title: fix(web): tunnel start-route catch orphans the tunnel process and desyncs active-tunnel state

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/high
labels.description: Important and time-sensitive

labels.name: app/web
labels.description: Package: web (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Finding

The `POST /api/openchamber/tunnel/start` catch block nulls the active-tunnel controller and clears tunnel auth without stopping the provider process, and it does so unconditionally — even when the failure happened before `tunnelService.start()` touched any state.

## Evidence

Verified against `origin/main` at `598b45582`:

- `packages/web/server/lib/tunnels/routes.ts:677-695`: the catch calls `setActiveTunnelController(null)` and `tunnelAuthController.clearActiveTunnel()`, but never `tunnelService.stop()`. After a failure, `POST /api/openchamber/tunnel/stop` (`:698-716`) checks `getActiveTunnelController()` and only then calls `tunnelService.stop()`, so an orphaned process is unreachable through the API.
- `packages/web/server/lib/tunnels/index.ts:104-141`: on the success path, `tunnelService.start()` sets the controller (`:135`) after `provider.start()` spawns the process. The route then performs post-start work — `issueBootstrapToken`, `readManagedRemoteTunnelConfigFromDisk()` (`routes.ts:643-645`), response assembly — any of which throwing lands in the catch with a live process whose controller reference was just dropped.
- The same catch also fires for failures that occur *before* `tunnelService.start()` mutates state: `startTunnelWithNormalizedRequest` (`routes.ts:145-194`) throws for enterprise mode, missing UI password, or token-upsert errors, and `tunnelService.start()` itself throws `TunnelServiceError` for validation/availability failures (`index.ts:84-112`) before touching the existing controller. In that case the catch clears a previously active controller and auth state while the old tunnel process keeps running, untracked.

## Why it matters

Case A leaves a cloudflared/ngrok/tailscale process running with no stop handle and revoked/bootstrap-cleared auth artifacts; the user-visible state says "no tunnel" while a public URL may still be live. Case B turns a rejected start request (e.g. a validation error) into silent loss of the currently running tunnel's API handle.

## Acceptance criteria

- On post-start failure, the catch stops the just-started provider process (or otherwise transfers ownership back) before clearing controller/auth state.
- On pre-mutation failure (validation/enterprise/password checks, unsupported provider), the catch preserves the previously active controller and auth state.
- Add regression tests: post-start throw leaves no live process and stop reports none; pre-mutation throw preserves the prior active tunnel. No matching open issue or PR covers this (all-state searches for tunnel orphan/startup cleanup returned none).

title: Login-shell environment capture leaks OPENCODE_DB into launches the caller isolated
body:
OpenChamber copies the login shell's environment into its own process and into the managed OpenCode it launches (`server/lib/opencode/env-runtime.ts` `applyLoginShellEnvSnapshot`, and `lifecycle.ts` launch env `{ ...shellEnv, ...process.env }`). Variables the caller already set win; variables the caller did not set are filled from `$SHELL -lic env`, which runs the user's real profile even when HOME and the XDG directories point elsewhere.

What happened: a test run of the nix-built OpenChamber was started with `env -i`, a temporary HOME and temporary `XDG_DATA_HOME`/`XDG_CONFIG_HOME`/`XDG_STATE_HOME`/`XDG_CACHE_HOME`. The login shell set `OPENCODE_DB=~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db`, the capture filled it in, and the managed OpenCode (a newer version than the user's) opened the user's real database and applied 14 schema migrations to it. No data was lost this time; the run was meant to be isolated and was not.

Expected: a launch the caller isolated (HOME or XDG data/config dirs set to other paths than the shell's) does not take path-bearing OpenCode variables from the login shell (`OPENCODE_DB`, `OPENCODE_CONFIG`, `OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR`, `XDG_*`, `HOME`), or there is an explicit switch that turns the capture off, documented for test and CI runs. The launch log names the database path before OpenCode starts.

Workaround today: set `OPENCODE_DB` explicitly to a temporary path; explicitly set variables are not overwritten.

Found during the upstream sync (sync/upstream-main-20261122).

title: Restore the marked sticky-rule pin under Streamdown (Safari/iOS freeze on long messages)
body:
## What is missing

The fork pinned marked's anchored lexer rules to sticky regexes (`packages/ui/src/components/chat/markdown/markedAnchoredRules.ts`, added in 8af16f98c4, "fix(markdown): long messages froze Safari and the iOS app for up to a minute"). The upstream v2.8.0 merge replaced the fork's Markdown pipeline with Streamdown and dropped the module and its tests.

Streamdown still runs marked's `Lexer` to split a message into blocks (`parseMarkdownIntoBlocks`, which `mathBlocks.ts` calls for streaming and windowed rendering), so the freeze the fix addressed can come back there.

## Who is affected

marked's block and inline rules start with `^`. Older JavaScriptCore retries a failed `^` match at every later position, so a long message costs the square of its length. The fork measured:

- Safari and the iOS app's WKWebView with WebKit older than the one in macOS 27.0.1: the `hr` rule alone took 7.9 s on a long message in that system JavaScriptCore.
- Bun 1.3.11: 16,000 short paragraphs took about 70 s.
- Not affected: V8 (Chrome, Electron, VS Code webviews), Bun 1.4.3 and later, WebKit from macOS 27.0.1.

## Why it is not ported yet

`packages/ui` has no direct dependency on `marked`; Streamdown brings it in (resolved as `marked@18.1.1` in `bun.lock`). The fix has to reach the same `Lexer.rules` instance Streamdown uses. No path without a dependency was found:

- Streamdown exports no lexer, rule set or marked instance; `parseMarkdownIntoBlocksFn` only replaces the splitter, and ours already delegates to Streamdown's marked-based one.
- A bun patch of marked (`patchedDependencies`) also changes `bun.lock`, and patches a transitive package.

## Proposed change

Add `marked` to `packages/ui` dependencies at the version Streamdown already resolves (`18.1.1`, so the lockfile keeps one copy), restore `markedAnchoredRules.ts` with its call at module load next to the Streamdown setup, and port the fork's three tests from `markedAnchoredRules.test.ts` at fa945cfdd1:

- `replaces the anchored rules, and only once`
- `lexes the same tokens as before`
- `a rule matches from the start of each input, whatever the last match left`

Add one test that `parseMarkdownIntoBlocks` from `streamdown` sees the pinned rules (same `Lexer` instance), so a future version split fails the test instead of silently dropping the fix.

Found in the fork-test audit of the v2.8.0 merge (sync/fork-test-port-20261122).

labels.name: app/vscode
labels.description: Package: vscode (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/xs

body:
## Evidence

On fresh `origin/main` (`18e3687ee9b35c452d077b4acbf864f6dd943959`), `packages/vscode/src/bridge-fs-runtime.ts:276-284` handles the webview-reachable `api:fs:mkdir` message by resolving the caller-supplied path against the workspace and immediately passing it to `vscode.workspace.fs.createDirectory`. It does not check that the target is inside the active workspace or resolve symlink ancestors. The shared `resolveUserPath` helper at `packages/vscode/src/bridge-fs-helpers-runtime.ts:203-211` returns absolute paths unchanged and lexically resolves relative ones, so an absolute path outside the workspace or a `..` traversal can create directories outside it. The webview exposes this operation through `packages/vscode/webview/api/files.ts:65-72`.

Fresh all-state search for `api:fs:mkdir` and workspace/mkdir terms found no duplicate. OPEN #2457 covers the separate web `/api/fs/mkdir` route; OPEN #2476 covers VS Code write/delete/rename, and #2458/#2459/#2488 cover VS Code read/stat, list, and search respectively. None addresses this VS Code mkdir handler. No open PR implements it.

## Why it matters

A caller of the workspace-scoped VS Code Files API can create arbitrary directories outside the active project, including in sensitive user-controlled locations. This bypasses the boundary users expect from workspace file operations.

## Acceptance criteria

- Enforce active-workspace containment for `api:fs:mkdir`, including absolute paths and symlinked ancestors; reject out-of-workspace targets before creating anything.
- Preserve valid in-workspace directory creation.
- Add real-filesystem regression tests showing absolute-path, `..`, and symlink escapes are rejected and ordinary in-workspace creation succeeds.

title: test(web): 18 process-tree tests fail in the fleet build container on main
body:
## What happens

18 tests in 6 files fail when the web package suite runs in the fleet build container (the `fleet-run` runner, image `ghcr.io/developing-today/fleet-build:full`, command run as the `vscode` user inside `nix develop .#fleet`). The same files fail the same way on `main` (3ed7fa1) and on an unrelated feature branch, so this is the environment, not a code change.

Failing files, all of them process-tree tests whose assertions wait for spawned processes to be dead or reaped:

- `server/lib/spaces/run-command.test.js` (5)
- `server/lib/spaces/code-out.test.js` (4)
- `server/lib/spaces/code-in.test.js` (1)
- `server/lib/opencode/lifecycle-process.test.js` (6)
- `server/lib/guests/service-registry.test.js` (1)
- `server/lib/git/service.test.js` (1)

The shared shape: a test kills a process tree or waits out a host timeout, then polls for the pids to be gone, and they are still alive when the poll gives up. One example, from `lifecycle-process.test.js`: `expected [ 772708, 772811 ] to deeply equal []` after the reaper ran.

## Evidence

- Baseline run on `main`: https://github.com/developing-today/fleet/actions/runs/45038745422 (leg 1: 18 failed, 719 passed in the 6 files)
- Same failures inside a full-suite run of a feature branch: https://github.com/developing-today/fleet/actions/runs/45037670009 (21 failed there; the other 3 were the branch's own and are fixed)

## Why it matters

This repo has no running GitHub Actions (see #2274), so the fleet runner is the only full-suite signal, and 18 permanent failures train everyone to ignore it. A real regression in process reaping would hide in this list.

## What to check first

Whether the container's init (PID 1) reaps zombies and whether process-group kills reach grandchildren under `runuser`: the failures cluster on tree kills and orphan reaping, and the same tests pass on a developer machine.

title: handoff probe: successor hangs if the predecessor dies before answering hello (PR #2491 review follow-up)
body:
## Problem

Found in review of PR #2491 (#81 stages 2-4), non-blocking, recorded here for the follow-up.

In `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/handoff-probe.js` (the handoffProtocol 2 probe gate), the gate's verdict promise has no successor-side timeout and no IPC `disconnect` handling. If the predecessor dies between spawning the successor and answering the hello, the successor hangs indefinitely holding its fd 3 copy: the port is wedged, requests queue in the backlog. No session or data loss, but the successor never exits and never serves.

Outside the design's section 6 test matrix (comment 6783127941 on #81), which is why it did not block the merge.

## Suggested fix

Exit-on-disconnect guard on the successor side (process exits when the IPC channel disconnects before a verdict), plus a process-matrix test: predecessor killed after spawn, before hello — successor exits, port released.

## Drive-by

`DOCUMENTATION.md`'s new probe bullet says the probe checks `state.json` and `store.json`; the code checks `state.json` and `draining.json` (the v1 pair the design names). One-word doc fix, can ride with the guard change.

body:
## Evidence

`packages/vscode/src/bridge-fs-runtime.ts:264-273` accepts the caller-provided `directory` for the reachable `api:fs:search` bridge and passes it directly to `deps.searchDirectory`. In `packages/vscode/src/bridge-fs-helpers-runtime.ts:447-463`, `searchDirectory` resolves an absolute directory unchanged (`resolveUserPath` returns absolute paths unchanged) and uses it as `rootPath` without checking workspace containment. Both search paths consume that root: the recursive fallback starts reading it with `vscode.workspace.fs.readDirectory` (`:324-346`), and the query path passes it to `vscode.RelativePattern` (`:469-480`). The webview exposes the handler through `packages/vscode/webview/api/files.ts:37-47`.

This is distinct from OPEN #2458 (read/stat), #2459 (list), and #2476 (write/delete/rename): none validates the directory supplied to the search handler. A caller can request searches rooted at an absolute path outside the active workspace and receive matching file paths/names.

## Why it matters

The VS Code Files API presents search as a workspace-scoped operation, but the bridge currently lets its directory argument select an arbitrary filesystem root. That can disclose names and paths from outside the workspace, including through a symlinked directory if the root is inside the workspace lexically.

## Acceptance criteria

- Reject `api:fs:search` roots outside the active workspace after canonical path resolution; define whether intentional in-workspace symlinks are allowed.
- Apply the same boundary to both the VS Code `RelativePattern` search and recursive fallback paths.
- Add regression tests for an outside absolute directory and a workspace symlink pointing outside, plus an in-workspace control that still returns results.

title: Allow prompt candidate generation with project-only model configuration
body:
## Problem

A model configured only in a project's `opencode.json` can appear in the prompt-candidate model picker, but it cannot generate candidates through the current stateless API.

OpenCode's Generate handler binds its services to `global.config`. The published [V2 OpenAPI description](https://opencode.ai/v2/openapi.json) also says stateless text generation uses the server's base configuration. Passing a directory through the scoped client does not change that behavior.

The diagnostic fix in [PR #2479](https://github.com/developing-today-forks/openchamber/pull/2479) names the unavailable models and explains the server-wide configuration requirement. It merged as `8d504209e9b25d5de1f2127e733b6f9dcdd9ee0e`. Project-only generation support remains undecided, so this issue stays open.

## Evidence

Checked on 2026-11-22 against isolated OpenCode `2.0.30+b70580b`, with the OpenChamber client pinned to `@opencode/client` `2.0.32` and OpenChamber base commit `14e72f2074`.

- A fresh project configuration defines `prompt-fixture/project-only`; the project's live model catalog includes it.
- Calling `generate.text` for that model returns HTTP 400, `Model unavailable: prompt-fixture/project-only`. No request reaches its synthetic provider.
- Models configured in the isolated server's global configuration do reach the provider, including their model aliases and chosen effort.
- A mixed request keeps 4 valid candidates from 2 global models while separately reporting the project-only model and an invalid-format response.
- The integration check uses only a loopback synthetic provider, creates no generation sessions, and leaves a source artifact unchanged.

The added check is:

```sh
MULTIRUN_TEST_URL=http://127.0.0.1:4899 \
MULTIRUN_TEST_ROOT=<isolated-root> \
bun test packages/ui/src/lib/multirun/promptCandidates.integration.test.ts
```

Start that root with `bun run profile:serve`. The completed mixed-scope check passed 1 test with 15 assertions. Before the diagnostic change, the UI's scope-specific regression fails because it shows only the generic generation error.

## Options requiring a decision

1. **Retained generation sessions.** Create model-specific sessions in the requested project and use the existing transient `session.generate` operation. Preserve generated output in those sessions and retain them. This changes the visible session list and needs a product decision about how the sessions and results appear. Do not delete temporary sessions as an implicit generation consequence.
2. **Upstream project-scoped stateless generation.** Add an explicit optional project scope to Generate while preserving its current server-wide default, then use it from OpenChamber. This needs an upstream API change and corresponding client/version support.

Keep the chosen model explicit. Do not silently substitute another provider or model, modify the user's global configuration, or discard other models' successful candidates.

body:
## Evidence

`packages/vscode/src/bridge-fs-runtime.ts:368-427` implements reachable `api:fs:write`, `api:fs:delete`, and `api:fs:rename` bridge messages. Each calls `deps.resolveUserPath(...)` and passes the resulting URI directly to the VS Code filesystem API, without checking that the target remains inside the active workspace or resolving symlink ancestors. The helper at `packages/vscode/src/bridge-fs-helpers-runtime.ts:203-217` returns absolute paths unchanged and lexically resolves relative paths. The webview exposes these operations through `packages/vscode/webview/api/files.ts:87-113`; `FilesView` invokes writes, renames, and deletes (`packages/ui/src/components/views/FilesView.tsx:1633-1729,1978`).

Reproduced on fresh `origin/main` (`14e72f207402beec28df43bece51115379d121a3`): invoking the registered `api:fs:write` handler with an absolute path to a temporary file outside the workspace returned success and overwrote that file. The delete handler likewise calls recursive `vscode.workspace.fs.delete(..., { recursive: true, useTrash: false })` on the unchecked resolved target; rename accepts unchecked source and destination paths (with overwrite disabled).

Dedupe: fresh all-state issue and open-PR inventories found no issue or PR for these VS Code mutation handlers. OPEN #2458 covers VS Code read/stat canonical containment, and OPEN #2459 covers VS Code directory listing; neither covers writes, deletes, or renames. CLOSED #2455/merged PR #2456 cover the separate web delete route, and OPEN #2457 covers web mkdir; neither changes the VS Code bridge handlers.

## Why it matters

A caller of the VS Code filesystem bridge can overwrite or recursively delete files outside the active workspace, or move files across that boundary, despite using the workspace-scoped Files API. Absolute paths bypass containment entirely; a workspace-relative path can also escape through a symlinked ancestor. Recursive delete makes this especially destructive.

## Acceptance criteria

- Enforce workspace containment for `api:fs:write`, `api:fs:delete`, and both source and destination of `api:fs:rename`, including canonical checks that reject symlink-ancestor escapes.
- Define and preserve any intentional in-workspace symlink behavior; do not allow an unchecked absolute path to bypass the workspace boundary.
- Reject deletion of the workspace root itself.
- Add real-filesystem regression tests demonstrating outside absolute targets and symlink escapes are rejected for each operation, while ordinary in-workspace writes, deletes, and renames still succeed.

body:
## Evidence

`redactGitText` in `packages/web/server/lib/git/redaction.js` redacts URLs, quoted credential values, Bearer/Basic-headed assignments, and a small set of whole-line assignments. It has no generic rule for a sensitive `key=value` occurring after other text on the line. Its sibling `redactSensitiveText` in `packages/web/server/lib/source-control/url-redaction.js` does have a generic sensitive-key assignment rule.

Reproduced by importing the current `redactGitText` directly:

| Input | Current output |
| --- | --- |
| `fatal: api_key=abc123 failed` | unchanged |
| `error: client_secret=sek999 rejected` | unchanged |
| `run with x-api-key=zzz` | unchanged |
| `msg: access_token=tok1 bad` | unchanged |

The existing Git redaction tests cover quoted forms and Bearer/Basic-headed assignments but not ordinary inline assignments. `redactGitText` is used on Git route/network-operation output and filesystem clone errors/output (`packages/web/server/lib/git/routes.js`, `packages/web/server/lib/git/network-operations.js`, and `packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.js:1063,1072`), so an echoed credential in those messages can reach the client unredacted.

Dedupe: all-state searches for `redactGitText`, Git redaction and inline sensitive assignments found only closed #1920, #2074 and #2128, which cover the other redactor's missing shapes and quoted/Bearer forms; none tracks generic mid-line assignment values in the Git redactor. The fresh open-PR inventory contains no related redaction change. This is the inverse direction of #1920's convergence request, but the current missing pattern is a distinct uncovered credential shape.

## Why it matters

Git and clone errors can include command/config fragments containing tokens, passwords, API keys or client secrets. Because the secret is echoed mid-line rather than as a standalone line, it bypasses the current patterns and is returned in otherwise redacted output.

## Acceptance criteria

- Redact ordinary mid-line assignments for the sensitive key set (including `api_key`, `x-api-key`, `client_secret`, `access_token`, `password`, `secret`, and `token`) in both `:` and `=` forms.
- Preserve non-sensitive assignments and existing Bearer/Basic scheme handling.
- Add regression tests asserting a probe secret never appears for representative inline inputs, while safe text remains unchanged.
- Keep behavior aligned with `redactSensitiveText` or document why the two surfaces intentionally differ.

body:
## Evidence

`packages/vscode/src/bridge-fs-runtime.ts:227-235` handles the reachable `api:fs:list` bridge message by calling `deps.resolveUserPath(target, workspaceRoot)` and then `deps.listDirectoryEntries(resolvedPath)`. The path resolver in `packages/vscode/src/bridge-fs-helpers-runtime.ts:203-212` returns absolute input unchanged and resolves relative input against the workspace, but this handler never checks that the result is inside the workspace or resolves symlinks before listing. `api:fs:list` is documented as a reachable VS Code filesystem route in `packages/vscode/src/DOCUMENTATION.md:302-304`.

Reproduced against fresh `origin/main` (`750372c93a868b60f3650132b05ed66f55388b2f`) by invoking the registered bridge handler with workspace `/workspace` and an absolute path to a temporary directory outside it. The handler returned `success: true` and included the outside directory entry (`marker.txt`) in its response. The route also accepts relative paths whose symlink ancestors lead outside the workspace.

Dedupe: fresh all-state searches for `"api:fs:list"` and `VS Code directory listing outside workspace path traversal` found no matching issue; the open-PR search for `api:fs:list workspace containment` found none. OPEN #2458 covers canonical containment for VS Code file read/stat consumers, not this separate list handler (which uses `resolveUserPath` directly). OPEN #2457 covers the web `/api/fs/mkdir` creation boundary, not directory listing.

## Why it matters

A reachable VS Code bridge caller can enumerate directory names outside the active workspace despite the workspace-oriented filesystem surface. File names and directory structure can disclose sensitive project, account, or machine information. Symlink ancestors provide the same escape even when the request appears workspace-relative.

## Acceptance criteria

- Reject absolute and relative `api:fs:list` targets that resolve outside the selected workspace, including targets escaping through symlink ancestors; resolve/check both the workspace root and target canonically.
- Preserve legitimate in-workspace paths and symlinks whose canonical targets remain inside the workspace.
- Add real-filesystem regression tests proving outside absolute paths and outside symlink targets are rejected, while an in-workspace listing still succeeds.

## Evidence

`packages/vscode/src/bridge-fs-helpers-runtime.ts:634-652` resolves a requested file with `fs.promises.realpath`, but checks containment against the *unresolved* `resolved` path (`:648`) and returns the canonical path (`:652`). `isPathInside` is only a lexical `path.resolve`/prefix check (`:139-143`). A workspace symlink therefore passes the check while resolving to an outside file.

Reproduced on fresh `origin/main` (`750372c93a868b60f3650132b05ed66f55388b2f`) with a real filesystem fixture: `workspace/link -> outside`; request `workspace/link/secret.txt`. `realpath` returned the outside path, the exact lexical containment check returned `true`, and reading the returned canonical path yielded `outside-secret`. This helper is used by the VS Code `api:fs:read` and `api:fs:stat` bridge cases (`bridge-fs-runtime.ts:291-365`) and the local filesystem proxy (`bridge-localfs-proxy-runtime.ts:132+`).

Dedupe: fresh all-state searches for `VS Code filesystem symlink read containment`, `api:fs:stat symlink`, and `resolveFileReadPath canonicalPath` found no matching tracker. CLOSED #2304 covers traversal out of a skill directory, and OPEN #2457 covers the separate web `/api/fs/mkdir` creation boundary; neither covers the VS Code file-read/stat canonical-path check. No open PR implements this behavior.

## Why it matters

The workspace-scoped VS Code filesystem read API can disclose the contents of any file readable by the extension host when an in-workspace symlink points outside the workspace. The stat API also leaks outside-file metadata. This defeats the intended workspace containment check and is a confidentiality boundary, distinct from the directory-creation behavior in #2457.

## Acceptance criteria

- Check containment using the canonical target returned by `realpath` (and a canonical workspace root), rejecting symlinked targets outside the selected workspace/access root.
- Preserve supported symlinks whose canonical targets remain inside the access root.
- Add real-filesystem regression coverage proving an outside symlink target is rejected for read and stat, and an in-root symlink remains usable.
- Exercise the shared resolution through the VS Code bridge and local filesystem proxy, or otherwise demonstrate both consumers inherit the corrected guard.

body:
## Problem

`POST /api/fs/delete` resolves the requested path lexically beneath the active workspace, then calls `fsPromises.rm(resolved.resolved, { recursive: true, force: true })` without checking the canonical target or rejecting the workspace root.

A path such as `<workspace>/linked/victim.txt`, where `linked` is a symlink to a directory outside the workspace, passes lexical resolution and deletes the outside file. Passing the workspace directory itself also succeeds and recursively removes the workspace.

## Evidence

Verified on `origin/main` at `750372c93a868b60f3650132b05ed66f55388b2f`:

- `packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.js:1842-1865` resolves with `resolveWorkspacePathFromContext` and directly calls recursive `rm`.
- `resolveWorkspacePath` at `packages/web/server/lib/fs/routes.js:250-271` checks only lexical containment; the resolver does not canonicalize the delete target.
- Invoked the registered `/api/fs/delete` route against temporary directories: deleting a child through an intermediate symlink returned 200 and removed the outside target; deleting the workspace root returned 200 and removed the workspace directory.
- Existing route tests cover normal managed-chat lifecycle and other filesystem symlink cases, but no `/api/fs/delete` test rejects an escaping symlink or the workspace root.

A tracker search found no open issue or PR for this web filesystem-delete containment defect. #2445 is about ownership of a fixed Electron autostart file; #2452 is a race on a fixed handoff request file. Neither covers this path-containment risk.

## Acceptance criteria

- Delete targets are canonically checked so symlinks in any path component cannot cause recursive deletion outside the permitted workspace/managed root.
- Reject deletion of a workspace or managed root itself; preserve deletion of ordinary in-root files and directories.
- Add real-filesystem route regression tests for an intermediate symlink escaping the workspace and for deleting the workspace root, asserting outside/workspace contents remain intact.

## Evidence

`packages/web/server/lib/opencode/handoff-request.js:36-46` reads `handoff-request.json` and unconditionally unlinks that pathname in `finally`. The CLI writer (`packages/web/bin/lib/commands-lifecycle.js:417-424`) can atomically replace the same path from another process between the consumer's read and unlink. The consumer then returns the older request while deleting the newer one, so the handoff initiated by the newer CLI invocation is lost.

Reproduced against the production `consumeHandoffRequest` function in a temporary directory by interleaving a replacement at the unlink boundary: it returned `/old/cli.js` and `replacementStillExists` was false. This boundary represents the real cross-process race between the server and CLI writer.

## Impact

A concurrent self-handoff request can be silently discarded. The newer CLI may wait for a handoff that was never initiated, then report failure/timeout even though its request replaced the earlier one.

## Acceptance criteria

- Consuming one request cannot unlink a different request atomically published after that request was read.
- Add a deterministic regression test for replacement between read and cleanup, plus existing consume/validation tests.
- Preserve single-consumer behavior for the request that was actually read; use an ownership-safe consume pattern (for example, atomically claim/rename the observed request before reading, with collision-safe handling) rather than an unconditional pathname unlink after read.

title: fix(electron): Linux autostart reconcile rewrites and deletes openchamber.desktop without ownership — user edits revert at every launch, foreign entries get rm-ed

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: status/in-progress
labels.description: Actively being worked

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.description: Has a queued task in the Supabase agent queue

labels.name: app/electron
labels.description: Package: electron (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## What happens

On Linux, the packaged app's launch-at-login support treats any `openchamber.desktop` in the XDG autostart directory as its own, with no ownership mark and no foreign-entry check — unlike the AppImage launcher entry, which already solved this exact problem with a managed key and `findForeignEntry` (`packages/electron/linux-desktop-entry.mjs:11-13`, `:22`, `:70-89`).

Three user-impacting consequences, all in `packages/electron/linux-autostart.mjs`:

1. **Startup reconcile clobbers user edits on every launch.** At every packaged startup, when `readLinuxAutostartEnabled()` is true, `packages/electron/main.mjs:6488-6497` rewrites the entry from scratch via `setLinuxAutostartEnabled({ enabled: true, ... })`, which `fsp.writeFile`s fixed contents (`linux-autostart.mjs:90-98`, no `writeIfChanged`-style comparison and no preservation of unknown keys). A user's own customizations — `X-GNOME-Autostart-delay`, `X-GNOME-Autostart-Phase`, an `env`/wrapper `Exec`, `OnlyShowIn`, `Hidden=true` for a temporary disable — are silently reverted at each app start.
2. **The toggle deletes files it does not own.** `readLinuxAutostartEnabled` (`:64-72`) only checks existence, so a foreign or hand-written entry with the same well-known file name is reported as "enabled". Toggling launch-at-login off runs `fsp.rm(filePath, { force: true })` (`:85-88`) and deletes the user's file outright; toggling on overwrites it. A distro package, another tool, or the user's own script may legitimately own `~/.config/autostart/openchamber.desktop`.
3. **The entry is indistinguishable from a foreign one.** `buildLinuxAutostartDesktopEntry` (`:37-62`) writes no managed key (contrast `X-OpenChamber-Managed=true` in `linux-desktop-entry.mjs:46`), which is what makes (1) and (2) unsafe.

## Why it matters

Autostart is the one config file this app owns that users are most likely to customize (delay, phase, per-DE visibility), and Linux DEs honor those keys. Today every restart silently reverts them, and the off-toggle deletes any same-named file regardless of authorship — data loss in the user's config directory. The repo's own desktop-entry module documents and implements the correct ownership pattern; the autostart module just predates it.

## Evidence

- Verified on `origin/main` `f79d2747c827dd41d366af98d7f77a05e3d7fed2` (2026-11-21).
- `packages/electron/linux-autostart.mjs:37-62` — entry has no managed/ownership key.
- `packages/electron/linux-autostart.mjs:64-72` — enabled check is existence-only; cannot distinguish a foreign entry.
- `packages/electron/linux-autostart.mjs:85-98` — disable is `rm(force)` of any same-named file; enable is an unconditional `writeFile` (also a non-atomic in-place write; the sibling `linux-desktop-entry.mjs` and `#99`'s atomic-write helpers show the house pattern).
- `packages/electron/main.mjs:6488-6497` — reconcile rewrites the entry at every packaged Linux startup when it exists.
- Correct-pattern reference in the same package: `packages/electron/linux-desktop-entry.mjs:11-13`, `:22`, `:70-89` (`X-OpenChamber-Managed`, `findForeignEntry`, `writeIfChanged`).
- Existing tests (`linux-autostart.test.mjs`) cover write/read/remove only; nothing covers reconcile-clobber or foreign-entry ownership.

## Acceptance criteria

- The autostart entry carries an ownership mark (e.g. `X-OpenChamber-Managed=true`, matching `linux-desktop-entry.mjs`).
- Startup reconcile leaves a foreign (unmarked) entry alone, and does not rewrite a managed entry whose contents already match (change-detect like `writeIfChanged`) — user-added unknown keys in a managed entry are preserved, not stripped.
- Toggling off removes the file only when the entry is managed; a foreign same-named entry is left in place (report it rather than delete). Toggling on does not overwrite a foreign entry.
- Tests: managed-entry rewrite/preserve cases, foreign-entry read/leave-alone cases for enable and disable, and reconcile idempotence.

Out of scope: the macOS/Windows login-item paths (`early-startup.mjs`), which use platform APIs with no shared file.
